Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 1:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾. These are the four disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) with which this surah opens. Their names are pronounced as "alif, lam, mim, sad," just as the teacher of beginning students in the writing school (al-maktab) pronounces the letters when teaching spelling (al-hija'), because what is intended by them is the names of the letters, not their referents (musammayatuha) and shapes (ashkaluha). Just as, when you report about someone a piece of news, you mention the name of the person you are reporting about without presenting his image or his essence, so you say, for example, "I met Zayd," and do not say, "I met this image," nor "I met this essence."

So the pronouncing of the names of the letters is the necessary consequence of their occurring at the beginnings of the surahs that open with them, for the purpose of allusion (al-ta'rid) to challenge those who denied that the Qur'an was sent down from God, Exalted is He, that is, to challenge their eloquent ones (bulaga'uhum) to oppose it with something like it, as was explained earlier in Surah al-Baqarah.

Page 10
As for their being written in the codices (al-masahif) with the forms of the letters rather than their names, that is, with the referents of the letters whose names are pronounced, and not written in the way their names are read: taking into account the situation of spelling. In my estimation, had they written them with the letters that are pronounced when their names are mentioned, they would have feared that the collection of letters of the names would be confused with words such as Ya-Sin; had they been written with the names of their letters, it would have been confused with the calling of one whose name is Sin.

So they turned to writing the letters, knowing that the reader of the codex, upon finding the form of the letter, pronounces the name of that form, according to their customary spelling, to keep the writing uniform in one pattern.

Yet the orthography of the codex is a practice (sunnah) established by the scribes of the codices and it was approved. The essential basis for pronouncing the Qur'an is transmission (al-riwayah) and receiving from teachers (al-talaqqi), and the writing of the codex was made only as a reminder and an aid to the one receiving.

This was discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, and what is here contains additions to it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 2:**

﴿A Book that has been sent down to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers.﴾

We mentioned at the opening of Surah al-Baqarah that the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs are followed by a mention of the Qur'an, or the Revelation, or something similar in meaning. This indicates that the purpose of these letters is spelling out (al-tahajji), to make the challenge to the Arabs of their inability to produce the like of the Qur'an more emphatic, and to lighten the burden on the Prophet ﷺ. Thus they form an independent sentence, and here it is counted as a verse, though in some surahs it is not counted.

His saying ﴿Kitab﴾ ("a Book") is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the subject is an indefinite noun. This is permitted either because it is intended as a category rather than a single individual, so that there is no ambiguity in the judgment made about it, as in the expressions "a man came to me" (meaning not a woman) and "a date is better than a locust." The benefit of intending the category is to refute the polytheists who denied that the Qur'an is from Allah and considered it unlikely. So Allah reminded them that it is a Book of the same kind as the books sent down to the prophets. Just as the scrolls of Ibrahim and the Book of Musa were sent down, so this Qur'an was sent down. Thus the indefiniteness expresses categorization, to dispel the sense of unlikelihood. A parallel is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other"﴾ (Sad 38:22), where the indefiniteness expresses categorization.

Or it is because the indefiniteness is intended to express magnificence, as in the saying "an evil that bares a fang," meaning a great evil. And the words of 'Uwayf al-Qawafi:

*A report came to me of 'Uyayna, a grievous one,*
*over which the livers were nearly split apart.*

meaning: it is a great Book, extolling its status, so the indefiniteness takes on the sense of description.

Or it is because the indefiniteness is intended to express wonder at the status of this Book in all that surrounds it of eloquence, rhetorical excellence, inimitability and guidance, and that it was sent down upon an unlettered man.

His saying ﴿unzila ilayka﴾ ("sent down to you") may be a description of ﴿Kitab﴾, in which case it is a second justification for beginning with an indefinite noun. It may also be the predicate (khabar). If it is the predicate, the purpose of the statement may be to remind those who deny and obstinately oppose, since the Prophet ﷺ and the believers know that it was sent down from Allah and so have no need to be told this. The predicate is then used allusively, to expose the error of the polytheists and the obstinate, and of those who intend to anger the Messenger ﷺ by turning away. Or the purpose of the predicate may be to express favour and to remind of a blessing, so that the predicate is used to express favour by way of a compound metonymy (majaz mursal murakkab, a figurative usage in which a whole expression is used for a related meaning).

It is also possible to make the predicate the saying ﴿unzila ilayka﴾ together with what is joined to it of the consequential and causal clause, meaning: this is a Book that has been sent down to you, so be open-hearted about it, for it has been sent down to you so that you may warn the disbelievers with it and remind the believers. The purpose is to calm the soul of the Prophet ﷺ, to anger the disbelievers, and to console the believers; that is, it is a Book sent down for a benefit, and the benefit has been achieved, so let there be no constriction in your breast if they deny it. By these considerations, and because some of them do not contradict others, the speech is understood as intending all of them together, and this is among the wondrous features of the openings of the surahs in eloquence.

Some exegetes posited an elided subject and made ﴿Kitab﴾ its predicate, meaning: this is a Book, that is, the Qur'an present in the mind is what is indicated, or the surah is what is indicated, and it was called a Book. Others made ﴿Kitab﴾ the predicate of the expression ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:1). But all of this is far from the strength of the meaning.

The verb ﴿unzila﴾ is given in the passive form, for brevity, since the agent of the sending down is known, because the one who sends down the Books upon the Messengers is Allah, Exalted. Also, the root of "sending down" (inzal) implies that it comes by revelation to the angels of the heavenly realms.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-la yakun fi sadrika﴾ ("so let there be no ... in your breast") is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), since the clause is inserted between the verb ﴿unzila﴾ and its complement, which is ﴿li-tundhira bihi﴾. A parenthetical clause may be linked with a fa' just as it may be linked with a waw, as in His saying: ﴿This—so let them taste it: boiling water and dark pus﴾ (Sad 38:57), and His saying: ﴿If he is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them, so do not follow [your] desire﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:135), and the words of a poet, which is among the evidences:

*Know, for a man's knowledge will benefit him,*
*that whatever is decreed will surely come.*

And the words of Bashshar ibn Burd:

*Like one who says, "The donkey, drive it away*
*from the fodder, by the people of refined sesame."*

The fa' is not superfluous for the sake of parenthesis, but it returns to the sense of causation. The parenthesis arises only from placing its clause between two connected things, by the speaker's haste to convey something of importance. The original order of the speech here is: "A Book sent down to you, so that you may warn by it and as a reminder for the believers, so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it." Al-Suyuti... [Note: The commentary as given does not contain this sentence; translation stops here.]

The Mughni al-Labib mentioned the entry of the fa' into a parenthetical clause but did not mention this in its section on the meanings of the fa'. So some people mistakenly thought that the fa' does not occur within a parenthetical clause.

The meaning is that Allah sent it down to you not so that there would be constriction in your breast, but so that your breast would be expanded by it. Therefore the negation of constriction is expressed in the form of a prohibition against constriction arising in the breast of the Prophet ﷺ, so that the prohibition is a prohibition of creation (nahy takwini), in the sense of bringing about the negation, as opposed to a command of creation, which means bringing about affirmation. The bringing about of the negation of constriction from his breast is depicted as the prohibition given to a rational person who understands the address, against entering a place. The author of al-Kashshaf made the prohibition in reality directed at the Prophet ﷺ, that is, a prohibition against concern for those who deny the Qur'an and grief over their conduct; and he made the prohibition in the apparent wording directed at the constriction itself, for the sake of emphasis in the obligation, by uprooting it from its origin, following the Arabic usage "I will not see you here," meaning "do not be present so that I see you," and "I will not know you doing such-and-such," meaning "do not do it so that I know you by it," as a prohibition by way of metaphor (kinayah). Whatever the case, the consequential clause suits the meanings of the indefiniteness assumed in the word ﴿Kitab﴾. That is: "So let there be no constriction in your breast because of it" in respect of what its sending down brought of the denial of your people and their rejection of its descent; "so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it" in respect of its great importance and majesty; and "so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it," for it is the cause of the expansion of your breast with its meanings and eloquence.

The "min" in ﴿min﴾ ("because of") is initial (ibtida'iyyah, indicating origin), meaning a constriction that arises and spreads as a result of what was mentioned, that is, because of the denial of those who deny it. Since denial of it is among its aspects, and it is the cause of constriction, it is correct to make the constriction caused by the Book indirectly. The meaning, with an elided genitive (mudaf), is "constriction because of its rejection," that is, the rejection of its being sent down from Allah.

The root meaning of ḥaraj is a narrow place among dense thickets of trees, such that movement within it is difficult. It is used metaphorically for the state of the soul in grief, anger and regret, because they imagined that the angry and grieving person has a narrowness in the breast, when they find that breathing is difficult for him due to the constriction of the nerves of the passages of breath. In the sense of the verse is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you would leave some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constricted by it, because they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?" You are only a warner﴾ (Hud 11:12).

And ﴿li-tundhira﴾ ("that you may warn") is connected with ﴿unzila﴾ in the sense of a causal object (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Its being attached to the particle of purpose (lam al-ta'lil) rather than using a verbal noun in the accusative is because the subject of the governing verb differs from the subject of the warning. The warning by it is placed first in the expression of purpose, because it is the most important aim, for nullifying the falsehood the polytheists hold and the false customs they leave among the people, whose removal is laboured after their conversion.

﴿wa-dhikra﴾ ("and as a reminder") may be conjoined to ﴿li-tundhira bihi﴾ in view of its being equivalent to a verbal noun, in which case it is in the genitive position. It may also be a conjunction of a whole clause, with ﴿dhikra﴾ being a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, with the sense "and remind with the reminder of the believers," in which case it is in the accusative position and the clause is parenthetical.

He omitted the complement of ﴿tundhira﴾ and stated the complement of ﴿dhikra﴾, because the omitted complement is clear from the mention of its counterpart. The sense is "that you may warn by it the disbelievers." He stated the complement of the reminder but not the complement of ﴿tundhira﴾, to honour the believers and, by way of allusion, to belittle the disbelievers in contrast to the mention of the believers.

[Page 15]

It is an explanation of the clause "so that you may warn thereby" (li-tundhira bihi), as indicated by its concluding phrase, the Almighty's words: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾. The address is directed to the polytheists, and the Muslims are included in it all the more so. After God had praised the Book sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ), and had explained that the wisdom of its revelation is warning and reminder, He commanded people to follow what was sent down to them, each group following what is most closely tied to them. What was sent down to the polytheists is the prohibition of association (shirk) and the argument against their misguidance, while what was sent down to the Muslims is the command, the prohibition, and the obligations. So each is commanded to follow what was sent down to him. The primary intended group is the polytheists, by implication, that they have disbelieved the blessing of their Lord. Therefore the description "Lord" (rabb) is used here rather than the Name of Majesty (Allah), to remind of the obligation to follow His command, because the attribute of lordship requires obedience to His commands. He also forbade them from following their "allies" (awliya') whom they had made into gods besides Him. The ones addressed by the prohibition are the polytheists, as indicated by His words: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

Ittiba' (following), in its true sense, is walking behind a walker. Its meaning therefore requires two parties: a follower (tabi') and one who is followed (matbu'). It is said: ittaba'a and tabi'a. It is used figuratively for acting upon the command of one who commands, as in: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92–93]. This is an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), based on comparing two states. It is also used figuratively for imitating a conduct or a saying, as in: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqara: 168]. This is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara musarraha), based on comparing the perceptible with the intelligible. Like His words: ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [al-An'am: 50], and among this is His saying here: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾.

What is meant by "what has been sent down" is the Book mentioned in His words: ﴿A Book has been sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2].

His words: ﴿and do not follow, besides Him, allies﴾ are an explicit statement of what is contained in ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. This is because what was sent down to them from their Lord includes that God is one God with no partner, that He is the Protecting Friend (al-Wali), and that those who take allies besides Him should know that God is Watchful over them (hafiz 'alayhim), that is, He will requite them, and nothing of their doing is hidden from Him, along with other verses of the Qur'an. The purpose of this prohibition is to affirm the requirement of the command to follow what was sent down to them, with special attention to this aspect of what was sent down to them, and to record it against the polytheists, and to cut off their excuses, lest they say: "We followed what was sent down to us, and we see our allies only as intercessors for us with God, and we worship them only so that they may bring us near to God in closeness." For indeed they used to disguise (their position) with the like of this. Do you not see that they used to say in their talbiya (invocation): "Here I am, O God, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and he owns nothing." So the placement of His words: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you﴾ is the placement of the comprehensive distinguishing clause (al-fasl al-jami') in a definition, and the placement of "and do not follow" is the placement of the excluding distinguishing clause (al-fasl al-mani') in a definition.

The awliya' (allies) is the plural of wali, who is the one who befriends (muwali), that is, the one who is constant (mulazim) and helpful (mu'awin). The term applies to the helper, the ally, and the true friend. It is used figuratively here for the object of worship and for the deity, because worship is the strongest state of befriending. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But God, He is the Protector﴾ [al-Shura: 9]. This was mentioned under His words: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than God as a protector?﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in Surat al-An'am, and this is what is meant here.

The following (ittiba') in His words: ﴿and do not follow, besides Him, allies﴾ may be used in the same sense in which following is used in His words: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. This is on the assumption: "and do not follow what comes to you from allies besides God," because the polytheists attribute the misguided religion they hold to the false gods, or to the custodians (sadana) of the gods and their soothsayers (kuhhan), as was mentioned under His words: ﴿Likewise, their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137], and His words: ﴿They say: This is for God, by their claim, and this is for our partners﴾ [al-An'am: 136], as in Surat al-An'am. According to these considerations, the supposition applies to His word "allies" (awliya'): that is, do not submit to the allies, or to their command, or to the callers to the allies and their custodians.

It is also possible that following is used figuratively for seeking and taking, that is, do not take as allies other than Him, like the saying: "He follows the slip of so-and-so." In a hadith: "He pursues with it the peaks of mountains and the places of rain," that is, he seeks them.

The min (from) in His word "min dunihi" (besides Him) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya), and dun is a noun of place denoting a place that is beyond and separate, and it has been put in the genitive by the preposition min, which is used with adverbs of place. It is used figuratively for abandonment and turning away.

[Page 17]

The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "take" (tattakhidhu), meaning: do not follow allies while taking them besides Him. For although the polytheists acknowledged God's divinity and followed His command by their own claim in many of their acts, such as the pilgrimage and its rites, and swearing by His name, they also followed the idols by worshipping them or ascribing religion to them. So every act by which they drew near to the idols, and every act they performed in compliance with a command attributed to the idols, when they perform it they are following in a way that involves turning away from God and abandoning drawing near to Him. This is following besides God, and it falls under the prohibition. And by this prohibition the doors of polytheism and its interpretations have been closed to them, such as their saying: "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to God in closeness." So His words: ﴿and do not follow, besides Him, allies﴾ have come in the highest degree of brevity and comprehensiveness of meaning.

The whole of His words: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow, besides Him, allies﴾ conveys the meaning of a restrictive construction (qasr), as if He had said: "Do not follow except what your Lord has commanded," that is, rather than what your allies command you. But He turned away from the form of restriction so that the clause "and do not follow, besides Him, allies" would be independent and clear in its meaning, giving attention to its content, in the manner of the saying of al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi:

"Our souls flow along the edges of swords, and they do not flow except along the edges of swords."

The clause "little is it that you remember" (qalilan ma tadhakkarun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to "do not follow" (la tattabi'u). It is a causal circumstantial clause that reveals its subject, and it does not restrict the prohibition, because it is evident that those who follow allies besides God are only those who remember very little. It is also permissible to treat the clause as a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiradh tadhyili). The word "qalilan" (little) may be taken in its literal sense, because they may indeed remember and then turn away from remembering in most of their situations, so they are heedless and averse. It is also possible that "qalilan" is used figuratively for the meaning of negation and nonexistence, by way of allusion, like His words: ﴿Then little is it that they believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 88], since faith is not described as few or many.

The tadhakkur (remembrance) is the verbal noun of dhikr (with a dammah on the dhal), and it is the presence of an image in the mind.

[Page 18]

Qalil (little) is used for nonexistence in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum) toward one who neglects a beneficial matter. It is said to him: "You are very rarely doing the beneficial matter," to alert him to his error. And if there is negligence in this, it should not go beyond the limit of diminishing it, not wasting it entirely.

The ma is a verbal ma (masdariyya), and the estimate is: "little is your remembrance." It is also possible that "qalilan" is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun indicated by "tadhakkarun," and "ma" is redundant (za'ida) to emphasize the paucity, meaning a kind of weak paucity, like His words: ﴿that He should strike a parable, whatever﴾ (an yadriba mathalan ma). The discussion of its counterpart was mentioned under His words: ﴿Then little is it that they believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 88] in Surat al-Baqara. The meaning is: if you had remembered, you would not have followed besides Him allies, and you would not have needed the prohibition against following besides Him allies. This is a rebuke for their neglect of reflection and inference concerning the attributes of God and the defects of their supposed allies.

Ibn Kathir... [no]

The majority (al-Jumhur) read: ma tadhdhakkarun with a single upper ta' and a shaddah on the dhal, on the basis that its original form is tatadhakkarun with two upper ta's, the second of which was changed into a dhal because their articulation points are close, so that it could be lightened by assimilation (idgham).

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with the dhal lightened, by deleting one of the two ta's for brevity. Ibn 'Amir read: yatadhakkarun, with a lower-letter ya' (yaa) at its beginning and then an upper ta', and the pronoun returns to the polytheists in the manner of iltifat (a shift) from address to the third person. He turned away from them and directed the speech to others among the listeners: the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿How many a town have We destroyed! Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were taking their midday rest.﴾ ﴿Their cry, when Our punishment came upon them, was only that they said: "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾

Page 19

This is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the sentence "and do not follow" (wa lā tattabiʿū). This report is used as a threat to the polytheists, who were addressed by the allusion in the first verse, and to those intended by the generality. It has been made threefold here by specifying the address to them.

The destruction of towns (qurā) is singled out for mention, rather than mentioning peoples (umam), as in His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overpowering blast; and as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious, violent wind﴾. This is because those addressed by the allusion are the people of Makkah, and it is the Mother of the Towns (Umm al-Qurā), so it was fitting that the threat be to its people with what befell the towns and their people. Also, because the attachment of the verb "We destroyed" (ahlaknā) to the town rather than to its people is for the purpose of encompassing and generality. Thus it dispenses with tools of generality, and the listener knows that what is meant by the town is its people, because the lesson and admonition lie only in what happened to the people of the town. A parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾, and a parallel to both together is His saying: ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed; will they then believe?﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 6]. All of this is from brilliant concision (ījāz badīʿ), and the meaning is according to an elided modifier (muḍāf), which is an elision of meaning.

The two pronouns in His saying ﴿We destroyed it, so Our punishment came upon it﴾ are kept in the singular and feminine in deference to the wording "town" (qarya), so that there is correspondence between the wording of the antecedent and the wording of its pronoun in closely connected speech. Then the pronouns referring to the town were put in the plural form in the clause branching from the first, in His saying: ﴿or they were taking their midday rest﴾ ... ﴿Their cry, when it came upon them﴾, etc., because of the interposition between the pronoun and the wording of its antecedent by a clause containing a pronoun referring to something other than the wording "town", namely ﴿Our punishment by night﴾, because "by night" (bayātan) carries a pronoun for the punishment, i.e., making them spend the night, and it moved from that to the pronoun of the town, considering its people, so He said: ﴿or they were taking their midday rest﴾ ﴿Their cry, when it came upon them﴾. And "kam" is a noun of quantity indicating a large number, and here it is an informative statement about abundance; it was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Anʿām.

Destruction (ihlāk): annihilation and uprooting. The verb "We destroyed it" (ahlaknāhā) may be used with the meaning of intending the act, with its signified occurring, and it may be used in its apparent meaning.

Page 20

The fa' in His saying "﴿so Our punishment came upon it﴾" is coordinating the clause "so Our punishment came upon it" to the clause "We destroyed it". The basic function of the coordinating fa' is to indicate that the coordinated item occurs after the item it is coordinated to. Since the arrival of the punishment occurs together with the destruction or before it, as it is its cause, the meaning of the placement of the fa' here was difficult for a group of exegetes, to the point that al-Farrāʾ said that the fa' does not indicate sequence absolutely. He also said: when the meanings of the two verbs are one or close to one, you may place whichever you wish first, like "he insulted me so he did wrong" and "he did wrong so he insulted me". Some said the speech proceeded by way of inversion (qalb), and the original is "Our punishment came upon them so We destroyed them", but that is an inversion empty of any subtle point, so it is rejected. What the majority explained is that the verb "We destroyed it" is used in the sense of intending the act, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Naḥl: 98] and His saying ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 6], meaning: when you intend to recite, and when you intend to rise to prayer. Using the verb in the sense of intending the occurrence of its meaning is a metonymic figure (majāz mursal) according to al-Sakkākī. He said: among examples of figurative speech is His saying ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God﴾, using "you recite" in place of "you intend to recite", because the recitation is caused by the intention to recite, a figurative usage by the indication of the fa' in "seek refuge in God", and His saying ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ in place of "We intended to destroy it", by the indication of ﴿Our punishment came upon it﴾, and "ba's" is destruction.

Expressing the intention of an act by mentioning the form that indicates the act's occurrence is for conveying the agent's resolve to do the act, a resolve from which action does not lag, such that the word indicating the realization of the intended is borrowed for the intention because of their resemblance. As for bringing the particle of sequence after that, it is to indicate no delay. Thus the whole utterance indicates that He, Exalted, intends and so creates the causes of the intended act, and the act occurs; all of this occurs like closely adjacent things. This closeness has been conveyed by expressing the intention with a form that requires the occurrence of the act, and by expressing the occurrence of the cause with the particle of sequence. The purpose of this is to threaten the obstinate listeners and warn them lest the wrath of God descend upon them, so He intends their destruction, and He has narrowed the respite for them, so that they do not delay in remedying their situation and hastening to repentance. What the verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqūn) hold is that the sequence in the coordinating fa' may be sequence of mention (al-tartīb al-dhikrī), i.e., the order of reporting one thing after reporting the item it is coordinated to. So in the verse, He reported the manner of their destruction after reporting the destruction, and this order is most often detail after summary, so it is coordination of the detailed upon the summarized. The fa' in His saying ﴿فَلَنَسْألَنَّ﴾ (*fa-lanas'alanna*, "so We will surely question") is conjunctive (*'atifah*) for the sequencing of reports, because the presence of the *lam al-qasam* (the lam of oath) is a sign that it begins a new statement (*kalam unuf*), a transition from one report to another and from one narrative to another. It is a transition from the report about their worldly state to the report about their condition in the Hereafter.

The report is emphasized by the *lam al-qasam* and the *nun al-tawkid* (the emphatic nun) to remove doubt about it.

The questioning of those to whom messengers were sent is a question about the delivery of the message. It is a question of rebuke on that Gathering, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And [warn of] the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your answer to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65].

The questioning of the messengers about their conveying the message is a question meant to terrify their peoples, because when they hear the testimony of their messengers against them, they become certain that they are being driven to punishment. This has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 41], and His saying: ﴿The Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your answer?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109].

Those to whom messengers were sent are the nations of the messengers. He expressed them by the relative pronoun (*al-ladhina*) because of what the relative clause indicates as a cause: the purpose of sending is the response of the messengers, so it is no wonder that those to whom they were sent are asked about that. Since the more important intended aim of the questioning is the nations, in order to establish the proof against them regarding their deserving punishment, their mention was placed before the mention of the messengers. And because of what the relative clause of (*alladhi*) and the definite article (*al-*) indicate, the thing asked about is what relates to the matter of the message, which is the questioning of both groups about whether the delivery occurred.

When the expression "those to whom they were sent" and the expression "the messengers" indicated this meaning, there was no need to mention the answer of those questioned, since it is evident that it is the affirmation of delivery and conveyance.

The fa' in His saying ﴿فَلَنَقُصَّنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (*fa-lanaqussanna 'alayhim*, "then We will surely relate to them") is for consequence and sequence following His saying "So We will surely question," meaning: We will question them, then We will inform them of the details of what their answer summarized. That is, We will relate to them the details of their conditions. In other words, Our knowledge does not depend on their answer, but the questioning serves another purpose.

The indefinite noun *'ilm* in His saying ﴿بِعِلْمٍ﴾ (*bi-'ilmin*, "with knowledge") indicates the intent of detail, meaning great knowledge, since the *tanwin* on *'ilm* is for magnification, and the perfection of knowledge appears only in knowing many matters. This was made clearer by His saying ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا غَائِبِينَ﴾ (*wa-ma kunna ghaʼibin*, "and We were not absent"), which means that nothing escapes Our knowledge, being absent from Us, and We are not absent from it.

*Al-qass* means informing. It is said *qassa 'alayhi*, meaning *akhbarahu* (he informed him). It was discussed in His saying ﴿يَقُصُّ الْحَقَّ﴾ (*yaqussu al-haqq*, "He relates the truth") in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا غَائِبِينَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿فَلَنَقُصَّنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ بِعِلْمٍ﴾ and is in the position of a concluding addition (*tadhyil*).

[Page 27]

*Al-ghaʼib* is the opposite of *al-hadir* (the present). Here it is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for the ignorant, because absence customarily entails ignorance, that is, ignorance of the conditions of the one who is absent. Even if reports reach him, they are not complete for him as they are for the one who witnesses. So the meaning is: We were not ignorant of anything of their conditions, because We are aware of them. This negation of absence is like the affirmation of companionship in His saying ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4].

Affirming the questioning of the nations here does not contradict its negation in His saying ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾ [al-Qasas: 78], and His saying ﴿So on that Day no one will be asked about his sin, man or jinn﴾ [al-Rahman: 39]. This is because what is asked about here is the delivery of the message, whereas what is negated in the two other verses is questioning to learn the details of their sins, and that is what is intended here in His saying ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا غَائِبِينَ﴾.

﴿The weighing on that Day is the truth. As for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs.﴾

The sentence ﴿The weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the sentence "so We will surely relate (to them)," because of the knowledge of people's good deeds and their bad deeds that the preceding sentence contains. Accordingly, it indicates that the manifestation and effect of that knowledge is reward and punishment, and the gradation of the ranks and descents of the doers, a gradation in which no doer is wronged even to the weight of an atom, and nothing that he deserves is lost. The only exception is that God may show grace to someone by raising his rank, or forgiving a lapse for the sake of a sound heart, or through intercession, or something similar, which God knows about among His servants. Therefore, the sentence "so We will surely relate (to them)" is followed by the sentence ﴿The weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, as if it were said: ﴿So We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾ [Al-A'raf: 7] and We will recompense them for their deeds with a recompense in which no one is cheated.

The tanwin in His saying "on that Day" (yawmaʾidhin) is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for a genitive noun that is indicated by ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ [Al-A'raf: 6] and what is conjoined to it with waw and fa'. The implied meaning is: "On that day, We will question them, question their messengers, and relate their sins to them."

Literally, weighing (wazn) is the balancing of one body against another in order to know the heaviness of one of the two bodies, or both, through their equality or their difference in quantity. Since the equality of the two weighed bodies is rarely achieved, other bodies were made by which the amount of difference is known. Thus there must be an instrument into which things are placed, called the scale (mīzān), which has various shapes and sizes.

The bodies that are made to determine quantities are called scales (mawāzīn), the singular of which is also mīzān, and they are also called weights (awzān), the singular of which is wazn. The word wazn is also used for the knowledge of the measure of a state in terms of merit or the like. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So on the Day of Resurrection We will not assign them any weight﴾ [Al-Kahf: 105]. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: "Indeed, a great, fat man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and he will not weigh the wing of a mosquito in the sight of God." It is also used figuratively, in a metaphor of representation (istiʿāra tamthīliyya), for arranging matters, as in the saying of al-Rāʿī:

*"Umayya weighed her affair, and so she summoned for it one who was neither inexperienced nor unknown."*

So the weighing in this verse is intended to determine the measures of the reward and punishment that deeds deserve, a determination without injustice, like the determination of the scale according to what God has appointed as reward or punishment for deeds. This is among the things that God, the Exalted, knows: such as whether a righteous deed was for God or was for show, and whether jihad was to raise the word of God or was merely for the desire of booty. Thus the recompense will be according to the measure of the deed. So the weighing is a metaphor. It is also permissible that it be meant literally. It has been said that the pages on which the angels wrote the deeds will be placed in something that God created for this purpose on the Day of Resurrection; it speaks or takes a form in a certain manner, and thus indicates the measures of the deeds for their owners. This is possible. Reports have been transmitted describing this scale, but none of them is authentic.

Expressions in such a context fall short of describing the realities, because they are among the extraordinary matters beyond what is customary. Therefore expressions can do no more than bring the realities close and represent them with the utmost of what the people of the language are accustomed to. So whatever comes in the form of a verbal noun (maṣdar) not connected to a verb that requires an instrument is interpreted as the well-known metaphor, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So on the Day of Resurrection We will not assign them any weight﴾ [Al-Kahf: 105]. And whatever comes in the form of nouns (asmāʾ) is open to interpretation like this verse, in His saying: "Whose scales are heavy..." etc., and like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two words, light on the tongue, heavy in the scale." And what is connected to a verb that requires an instrument is interpreted either as a representation or as a created thing among the matters of the Hereafter, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 47].

The scale is mentioned in the Sunna in the hadith of the card (biṭāqa) on which the word of the testimony of Islam is written, in al-Tirmidhi from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, and in the hadith of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Anas ibn Malik: "Seek me at the scale," transmitted by al-Tirmidhi.

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed over whether there exists a created thing that shows the measure of the reward for the deed, called the scale, in which deeds are literally weighed. The majority affirmed it, and a group denied it, including al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and al-Aʿmash, who said: it is the straight judgment (al-qaḍāʾ al-sawiyy). The later scholars followed this disagreement: the majority of the Ashʿariyya (Ash'arites) and some of the Muʿtazila (Mu'tazilites) adopted the interpretation of the majority, while some later Ashʿariyya and the majority of the Muʿtazila adopted what Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Aʿmash held. The matter is minor, and the argument is not conclusive. The intended meaning is the meaning, not the instrument itself.

As for the predication of "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) to the weighing: if the weighing is a metaphor for determining the measures of reward, then "truth" means justice, i.e., the recompense is just and not unjust, since it is one of the kinds of judgment and wisdoms. If the weighing is a representation by the form of the scale, then "justice" means evenness: that is, the weighing on that day is equal to the deeds, neither tilted nor deficient.

On both interpretations, describing it with the verbal noun (maṣdar) is an intensification of its being true.

From its being "the truth" follows His saying: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful﴾. It is a detailed explanation of the weighing by stating its effect according to the measure of what is weighed. The place of the consequence is His saying: ﴿those are the successful﴾ and His saying: ﴿those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾, since that is subsequent to His saying: ﴿whoever's scales are heavy﴾, and "whoever's scales are light."

Heaviness of the scale, in its literal sense, is the tilting of the scale by the weighed object. Here it is a metaphor for considering righteous deeds as predominant and abundant, i.e., whoever's scales are heavy with righteous deeds. He did not mention what the scales were made heavy with because it is known from the consideration of weighing, since it is the custom of people to weigh things that are desired to be bought, that are competed for in measuring their quantities, and in which people deal with mutual gain and loss.

The heaviness, along with that metaphor, is also a supporting image (tarshīḥ) for the metaphor of the scale for recompense. Then lightness is used as a metaphor for the absence of righteous deeds, taking the extreme of lightness on the pattern opposite to heaviness. It is also a second supporting image (tarshīḥ) for the metaphor of the scale. What is intended here is intense lightness, which is the absence of righteous deeds, as indicated by His saying: ﴿because they wronged Our signs﴾.

Success (falāḥ) is the attainment of good and the reaching of what is sought.

The definite article in "the successful" (al-mufliḥūn) is either generic or anaphoric (ʿahd), and it has been discussed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [Al-Baqara: 5] in Surat al-Baqara.

The indefinite referent of "whoever" (man) is singular, in accordance with His saying "his scales" (mawāzīnuhu). Since this singular is not specific, but rather is each person in whom the content of the conditional clause is realized, it is a general term, and it is valid to consider it plural in the demonstrative and the two pronouns in His saying: ﴿those are the successful﴾.

The use of the demonstrative is to draw attention to the fact that they achieved success only because of the heaviness of their scales. The demonstrative of distance was chosen to indicate the abstract, notional distance.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is for the purpose of restriction (inḥiṣār), i.e., "they are the ones among whom the realization of the successful is restricted." That is, if you know a group known as the successful, then they are them.

Loss (khusrān), in its literal sense, is the opposite of profit: it is the merchant's failure to obtain what he expects in excess from his sale. It is used figuratively for the loss of the benefit of something from which benefit is hoped. So the meaning of "they lost their souls" is that they lost their benefits, for everyone hopes from his endowments, which are the totality of his self, that they will bring him benefit and avert harm from him: through sound judgment, and through the devising of beneficial action. The souls of the polytheists had embellished for them deeds that were the cause of the lightness of their deeds' scales, i.e., the cause of the absence of righteous deeds from them. So their souls were like the capital of a merchant who hoped from it to increase his livelihood, but squandered all of it, so he is a loser of it. Likewise, these people lost their souls, since they brought them into torment that abides. Refer to what preceded in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾ [Al-An'am: 12] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [Al-Baqara: 16] in Surat al-Baqara.

The bāʾ in His saying "because they" (bimā kānū) is the bāʾ of causality, and "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), meaning "because of their having wronged Our signs in the world." So the imperfect form in His saying "they wrong" (yaẓlimūn) narrates their state, in the renewal of wrongdoing in what has passed, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And God is He who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them﴾ [Fatir: 9].

Wrongdoing here is the opposite of justice: that is, they wrong the signs, so they do not give them their due of truthfulness. "Wrong" (yaẓlimūn) has been given the implication of "deny" (yukadhdhibūn), which is why it takes the bāʾ, as if it were said: "because they were wronging by denying Our signs," in accordance with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [Al-Naml: 14].

Their denial was made wrongdoing only because it is a denial of what the proofs have established as true, so denying it is a wrong to the proofs by refuting them and not acting upon them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "with Our signs" before its governing verb "they wrong" is for the sake of emphasizing the signs.

The verse has mentioned the state of the righteous believers and the state of the denying polytheists, since on the day this verse was revealed people were of two groups: the group of believers, all of whom did righteous deeds and multiplied them, and the group of polytheists, who were empty of righteous deeds. Between these there remained a group of believers who mixed righteous deeds with bad ones. This verse does not address that group, since it is not the purpose of the context, and other verses address it.
