Then lightness is used as a metaphor for the absence of righteous deeds, taking the extreme of lightness on the pattern opposite to heaviness. It is also a second supporting image (tarshīḥ) for the metaphor of the scale. What is intended here is intense lightness, which is the absence of righteous deeds, as indicated by His saying: ﴿because they wronged Our signs﴾.

Success (falāḥ) is the attainment of good and the reaching of what is sought.

The definite article in "the successful" (al-mufliḥūn) is either generic or anaphoric (ʿahd), and it has been discussed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [Al-Baqara: 5] in Surat al-Baqara.

The indefinite referent of "whoever" (man) is singular, in accordance with His saying "his scales" (mawāzīnuhu). Since this singular is not specific, but rather is each person in whom the content of the conditional clause is realized, it is a general term, and it is valid to consider it plural in the demonstrative and the two pronouns in His saying: ﴿those are the successful﴾.

The use of the demonstrative is to draw attention to the fact that they achieved success only because of the heaviness of their scales. The demonstrative of distance was chosen to indicate the abstract, notional distance.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is for the purpose of restriction (inḥiṣār), i.e., "they are the ones among whom the realization of the successful is restricted." That is, if you know a group known as the successful, then they are them.

Loss (khusrān), in its literal sense, is the opposite of profit: it is the merchant's failure to obtain what he expects in excess from his sale. It is used figuratively for the loss of the benefit of something from which benefit is hoped. So the meaning of "they lost their souls" is that they lost their benefits, for everyone hopes from his endowments, which are the totality of his self, that they will bring him benefit and avert harm from him: through sound judgment, and through the devising of beneficial action. The souls of the polytheists had embellished for them deeds that were the cause of the lightness of their deeds' scales, i.e., the cause of the absence of righteous deeds from them. So their souls were like the capital of a merchant who hoped from it to increase his livelihood, but squandered all of it, so he is a loser of it. Likewise, these people lost their souls, since they brought them into torment that abides. Refer to what preceded in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾ [Al-An'am: 12] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [Al-Baqara: 16] in Surat al-Baqara.

The bāʾ in His saying "because they" (bimā kānū) is the bāʾ of causality, and "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), meaning "because of their having wronged Our signs in the world." So the imperfect form in His saying "they wrong" (yaẓlimūn) narrates their state, in the renewal of wrongdoing in what has passed, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And God is He who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them﴾ [Fatir: 9].

Wrongdoing here is the opposite of justice: that is, they wrong the signs, so they do not give them their due of truthfulness. "Wrong" (yaẓlimūn) has been given the implication of "deny" (yukadhdhibūn), which is why it takes the bāʾ, as if it were said: "because they were wronging by denying Our signs," in accordance with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [Al-Naml: 14].

Their denial was made wrongdoing only because it is a denial of what the proofs have established as true, so denying it is a wrong to the proofs by refuting them and not acting upon them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "with Our signs" before its governing verb "they wrong" is for the sake of emphasizing the signs.

The verse has mentioned the state of the righteous believers and the state of the denying polytheists, since on the day this verse was revealed people were of two groups: the group of believers, all of whom did righteous deeds and multiplied them, and the group of polytheists, who were empty of righteous deeds. Between these there remained a group of believers who mixed righteous deeds with bad ones. This verse does not address that group, since it is not the purpose of the context, and other verses address it.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 7, verse 10:**

﴿Indeed, We have established you upon the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood. Little are you grateful.﴾

It is a coordination (ʿaṭf) on the clause: ﴿And do not follow, besides Him, protectors. Little do you remember.﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 3]. This is a reminder to them that Allah is the Protector of creation, because He is their Creator upon the face of the earth and the Creator of that by which they sustain life, through which their existence continues until a known term. It is also a rebuke for the scarcity of their gratitude, as indicated by the concluding clause of the verse, ﴿Little are you grateful.﴾ For souls that are not restrained by threat may be benefited by fond recollections. One of the Khawārij (Kharijites) said, when he was asked to go out to fight al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, and he had been showered by him with favors:

*Shall I fight al-Ḥajjāj for his authority, with a hand that acknowledges that it is his client?*

The emphasis of the statement by the oath-particle lām and qad, which signify certainty, is a treatment of those who are the intended addressees as if they were those who deny the content of the statement. This is because, when they worshipped other than Allah, their condition was like that of one who denies that Allah is the One who established them on the earth, or like that of one who denies that establishment occurred at all.

Tamkīn (establishment) is placing a thing in a place, and it is applied to empowering someone to act, by way of metonymy (kināya). This has been discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿We established them on the earth as We did not establish you﴾ [al-Anʿām: 6], in Surah al-Anʿām. It is used here in its metonymic sense, not its literal sense. That is, We made for you power, meaning We empowered you over the affairs of the earth and granted you disposal over its creatures. This is through what Allah placed in mankind of the strength of intellect and reflection, which qualified him for mastery of this world and for overcoming its difficulties. The meaning of tamkīn here is not the power and rule intended in His saying, ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 84], because that is not attained by all mankind except by interpretation. Nor is the meaning of tamkīn its literal sense, which is making a place within the earth, because His saying "in the earth" prevents that. For had it been so, He would have said, "We have established you the earth." And He said of ʿĀd: ﴿We had established them in that wherein We have not established you﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 26], meaning We made what We empowered them over greater than what We empowered you over, that is, in their traces upon the earth. As for the basic settling in the earth, it is a path between these two.

Maʿāyish is the plural of maʿīsha, which is what a living being sustains itself with, of food and drink. It is derived from ʿaysh, which is life. The origin of maʿīsha is a verbal noun of ʿāsha (to live). He said, ﴿Indeed, for him is a straitened living﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 124]. The thing by which life is obtained is named by it, by naming a thing after its cause in the manner of metonymy (majāz), which became so common that it became equal to the literal sense.

The yāʾ of maʿāyish is an original letter of the word, because it is the radical of the word from the verbal noun ʿaysh. So the pattern of maʿīsha is maf'ila, and maʿāyish is mafāʿil. Its correct pronunciation in the plural is therefore with yāʾ, and it should not be changed into a hamza. This is because the usage of the Arabs regarding the vowel-letter that is in the singular is that when they pluralize it with an added alif, they restore it to its origin as wāw or yāʾ after the alif of the plural, as in mafāza and mafāwiz, where the origin is wāw from fawz, and maʿība and maʿāyib, where the origin is yāʾ. When the vowel-letter in the singular is not original, they, when pluralizing it with an added alif, change the vowel-letter into a hamza, as in qilāda and qalāʾid, ʿajūz and ʿajāʾiz, and ṣaḥīfa and ṣaḥāʾif. This usage is among the subtle distinctions between the original vowel-letter and the added one. The readers (qurrāʾ) agreed on reciting it with yāʾ. Khārija ibn Muṣʿab and Ḥumayd ibn ʿUmayr reported from Nāfiʿ that he recited maʿāʾish with a hamza after the alif, but this is an anomalous transmission from him that is not to be regarded. It was also recited in the anomalous (shādh) reading, maʿāʾish, transmitted by al-Aʿraj. In the Kashshāf, the attribution of this reading to Ibn ʿĀmir is a slip by al-Zamakhsharī.

[p. 35]

His saying, ﴿Little are you grateful﴾ is like His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Little do you remember﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 3], and its parallels.

The address is specifically to the polytheists, because they are the ones whose gratitude to Allah was scant, since they took other gods alongside Him.

"Little" (qalīlan) is an adjective that is used to mean nonexistent, as was mentioned just before at the beginning of the surah. It may also be taken in its literal sense, that is, your gratitude to Allah is little, because when they recognized that He is their Lord, they had indeed thanked Him. But most of their condition was turning away from thanking Him and turning toward worshipping idols and what follows from them. It is also possible that the smallness is a metonymy for nonexistence, by way of the restrained manner of speech, to draw down their remembrance.

Qalīlan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees, and mā is a verbal (maṣdarīya) particle. The verbal phrase in the position of the subject of qalīlan, so it is a causal state (ḥāl sababīya).

In the sequencing of this verse after the verse, ﴿How many a town We destroyed﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 4], there is an indication that neglecting to be grateful for a blessing exposes its possessor to its loss, which is what His saying "We destroyed" indicates.

[Page 36]

It is coordinated with the sentence "And We had certainly established you on the earth" [al-A'raf: 10], as a reminder of the blessing of bringing the species into existence. This is a blessing of care, because existence is superior to non-existence, setting aside what may befall the existent of troubles and hardships. It is also a blessing of honouring the species over others, by commanding the angels to prostrate to their origin. Woven into this favour is an admonition and a warning about the enmity of Satan towards the human species since ancient times, so that this may serve as a preparation for warning against his whispering and misleading, and as an incitement to abandon what has drawn people into shirk and error. This is the aim of the sura, and it appears at His words, "O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden" [al-A'raf: 27], and what follows it of verses. Therefore this passage stands in the manner of an argument, inserted in the midst of the exhortation.

The address is to all people, but what is intended by it is the polytheists, because they are the focus of this sura.

The emphasis of the statement by "bi-l-lam" (the lam of emphasis) and "qad" is for the reason already mentioned in His words, "And We had certainly created you" [al-A'raf: 11]. The transitivity of the two verbs of creating and fashioning to the pronoun of the addressees, given that it refers to the creation of the species of which they are individuals, makes it necessary that the meaning be: "We created your origin, then We fashioned him," and he is Adam, as His words clarify: "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'"

Creation (al-khalq) is bringing a thing into existence and making it appear into being. This is the meaning intended when it is attributed to God Most High or when God is described by it.

Fashioning (al-taswir) is making a thing into a form (surah). The form is the shape by which a body is shaped, just as clay is shaped into the form of a kind of species.

The clause "fashioned you" is joined by the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates the delay of the rank of fashioning from the rank of creating, because fashioning is a state of perfection in creation, in that the human being is in the human form, perfected in beauty and nobility, with what it contains of faculties of perception and management. This holds whether the fashioning is concomitant with creation, as in the creation of Adam, or occurs after creation by a period, as in the fashioning of embryos from bones, flesh, sinews, veins and faculties, as in His words, "Then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh" [al-Mu'minun: 14].

[Page 37]

The transitivity of the two verbs "We created" and "We fashioned" to the pronoun of address falls within the same thread as what the pronoun referred to before it in His words, "And We had certainly established you on the earth" [al-A'raf: 10] and what follows. So the address is to all people, as a preparation for His words later: "O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden" [al-A'raf: 27]. What is specifically intended by it is the polytheists, because they are the ones whom Satan embellished to them the ingratitude for these blessings, as His words after that show: "And when they commit an indecency they say, 'We found our fathers doing it'" [al-A'raf: 28], and His words previously: "Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you remember" [al-A'raf: 3].

As for the connection of the two verbs of creating and fashioning to the pronoun of the addressees, what is meant is the first origin of their species, namely Adam, by the indication of its being followed by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'" The creation of the origin of their species is thus treated as the creation of the individuals of the species among whom are the addressees, because the purpose is to remind them of the blessing of bringing into existence, so that they may give thanks to their Creator. A parallel to this is His words: "Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship" [al-Haqqah: 11], meaning: We carried your forefathers, who were with Noah, and from them people multiplied after the flood, because the purpose is to bestow favour upon the addressees by the saving of their forefathers from whom they descended. It is also permissible to interpret the two verbs of creating and fashioning as meaning the intention of their occurrence, as in His words, related from the speech of the angels to Abraham: "So We brought out those of the believers who were in it" [al-Dhariyat: 35], meaning: We intended to bring out those who were in it, since this statement occurred before the command to Lot and those who believed in him to leave the town.

His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" indicate that what was created and fashioned is Adam. The meaning of the speech is: We created your origin and fashioned him, so he emerged existing and specified, named Adam, because naming is a means of determining the named. Then We manifested his excellence and the wondrous craftsmanship of Ours in him, so We said to the angels, "Prostrate to him." Thus there occurred a wondrous conciseness in the composition of the speech.

[Page 38]

As for "thumma" in His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" it is conjoining a clause to a clause, and it restricts the delay to be one of rank, not of time, because the content of the conjoined clause here is higher in rank than the content of the clause it is conjoined to.

As for His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" its explanation has already been given. The explanation of what preceded it: God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, after the manifestation of the excellence of what God taught him of the names, which He did not teach the angels. This is at His words, "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' they prostrated, except Iblis" [al-Baqarah: 34], in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The definite article in "al-malaikah" (the angels) is generic, so it does not follow that the command applies to all the angels. Rather, those commanded may be the angels who were in the place where Adam was created, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also possible that the sense is all-encompassing, covering all the angels. The manner of commanding them all and their all prostrating to Adam is known only to God, because the ways by which they know the will of God concerning them in the higher world cannot be measured by what is familiar in the world of the earth.

Know that God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam does not necessitate that Adam was created in the world in which the angels are. Rather this is a possibility, and it is possible that when God created Adam He gathered the angels and made them aware of this wondrous creation, since the angels move from place to place. The verse is therefore not explicit that Adam was created in the heavens, nor that he was in the Garden, which is the abode of reward and punishment, although its apparent meaning suggests that. The majority of the People of the Sunnah took this apparent meaning, and this was discussed in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The exception of Iblis from "those who prostrated" in His words "except Iblis" indicates that he was counted among the angels, because he was mixed with them. Al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah: Iblis was counted among the angels by way of predominance (taghlib).

The clause "he was not among those who prostrated" [al-A'raf: 11] is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to Iblis. It is a circumstantial clause emphasising the content of its governing element, which is what is indicated by the exception, because the exception requires the affirmation of the opposite of the judgement of the excepted from what is excepted from. This is exactly the meaning of "he was not among those who prostrated," so the circumstantial clause is an emphasis.

[Page 39]

In choosing to report the negation of his prostration by making him one of those who did not prostrate, there is an indication that the prostration was negated from him with an intense negation. This is because your saying "So-and-so was not among the guided" conveys a stronger negation than your saying "So-and-so was not guided," as in His words: "Say, 'I will not follow your desires; I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided'" [al-An'am: 56], in the sura of al-An'am.

In the verse there is therefore an indication that God Most High created in the very nature of Iblis a disposition that pushes him to disobedience whenever the command does not agree with his desire, and He made for him a desire and an opinion, so his nature was contrary to the nature of the angels. He remained among the angels only because no command had arisen that contradicted his desire. When the command to prostrate arrived, the trait of disobedience latent in him appeared. Thus His words, "he was not among those who prostrated," are an indication that it had not been decreed for him to be among the group of those who prostrate, that is, his prostration was negated by a negation that postponed its occurrence afterwards. It is known that he refused to prostrate with refusal. This prepares for the narration of the question and answer in His words, "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" [al-A'raf: 12].

The clause "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" is the beginning of the dialogue, because Iblis's abandonment of prostration to Adam stands in the position of an answer to God's words, "Prostrate to Adam." So it was apt that an inquiry about the reason for his abandoning prostration should be directed at him. The pronoun in "He said" refers to something known from the context, that is, God Most High said, as is indicated by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate.'" The apparent form would have been "We said," but the shift to the third-person pronoun is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Its purpose is to transform the setting of the speech, since the setting was one of command to the angels and those in their company, and it became a setting of rebuke directed specifically at Iblis.

"Ma" is interrogative. It is an interrogative whose apparent meaning is genuine, but mixed with rebuke. The purpose of the interrogation is to show the angels the intent of Iblis.

"Mana'aka" means "hindered you" and "restrained you" from prostrating. The apparent form would have been "What prevented you that you prostrate?" because he merely held back from prostration, not from negating prostration. God says in another verse: "What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?" [Sad: 75]. Therefore the particle "la" (not) here is contrary to the apparent form. It has been said that it is extra for emphasis and does not convey negation, because the particle added for emphasis conveys no meaning other than emphasis. "La" is among the particles with which speech is emphasised, as in His words, "I do not swear by this city" [al-Balad: 1], and His words, "So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of God" [al-Hadid: 29], meaning: so that the People of the Book may know with certain knowledge. And His words, "And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they will not return" [al-Anbiya': 95], meaning: it is certainly prohibited that they return, a prohibition that is certain. This is the interpretation of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari. But in directing the meaning of emphasis to the verb, while the prostration did not occur, the emphasis is not to be relied upon, because emphasis is confirmation of the occurrence of the emphasised act, so this interpretation should not be relied upon, since its obscurity is evident.

It has been said that "la" is negative, and its presence implies a verb understood from context, indicated by "mana'aka," because whoever is prevented from something is called to its opposite. It is as if it were said: "What prevented you from prostrating so that it called you to not prostrate?" Then either "mana'aka" is used in the sense of "called you," by way of metaphor, and "la" is the indicator of the metaphor. This is al-Sakkaki's interpretation in al-Miftah in the section on linguistic metaphor, and close to it is that of 'Abd al-Jabbar as transmitted by al-Razi, and it is the better interpretation. Or both verbs are intended, so one is mentioned and the other omitted, and the omitted one is indicated by a complement suitable for it, and this is a case of concise omission. This is al-Tabari's choice and that of those who followed him.

See what I have said at His words, "He said, 'O Harun, what prevented you when you saw them going astray, from following me?'" [Ta-Ha: 92–93], in the sura of Ta-Ha.

His words, "when I commanded you," are an adverbial phrase (zarf) governing "prostrate." Attaching its pronoun to the command requires that the command given to the angels includes him. This is either because he is a category of the angels, so God created Iblis as an origin

[Page 41]

for the jinn, so that He would make of it a kind distinct from the rest of the angels by its acceptance of disobedience. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and many jurists (fuqaha') held this view. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and so on. Or, because the jinn are another kind of the immaterial beings (al-mujarradat), and Iblis was the origin of that kind, and Allah placed him among the angels. Thus their command included him, based on the view that the angels were created from light and the jinn were created from fire.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire." This is the view of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) and some of the Ash'ariyya (al-Ash'ariyya). The "fire" may mean light mixed with matter, and the "light" may mean pure light, so that the jinn would be a kind of the genus of angels, lower in rank, just as the human being is a kind of the genus of animals, higher in rank.

﴿He said: "I am better than him"﴾ is disconnected (fasl) because it occurs in the manner of dialogue.

He explained his refusal to prostrate: he saw himself as better than Adam, so he did not obey Allah's command to him to prostrate to Adam. This is clear disobedience. His words ﴿I am better than him﴾ are given as a reason for the refusal, and for that reason the preposition "li" (for) was omitted before it.

The clause ﴿You created me from fire﴾ explains the clause ﴿I am better than him﴾, and for that reason it is disconnected, since it has the status of an explanatory apposition (‘atf al-bayan) to what it explains.

Iblis came to know that he was created from fire through information from the angels who witnessed his creation, or through information from Allah the Exalted.

That he was created from fire is established. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He created the human being from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14], ﴿and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. Iblis is of the kind of the jinn, as Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis; he was of the jinn, and he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50].

He based his claim of superiority upon the excellence of the element from which he was created over the element from which Adam was created.

[Page 42]

Fire is the intense heat that, by its extremity, produces combustion, which exists in bodies melted by their original nature, like the fire that is in the sun. When the heat reaches the point of combustion, fieriness comes to a body from a mineral, a plant or earth, like the fire that remains in ash.

Fire is superior to earth because of the strength of its effect and its dominion over the bodies it meets, because it gives light, and because it is pure, so that impurities do not cling to it. Earth does not share it in these qualities, though both share in that all living bodies are formed from them.

As for the light from which the angel was created, it is more pure than the ray that emanates from fire, free of the corporeal admixtures found in fire.

Clay (tin) is earth mixed with water, and water is another element upon which animal life depends together with fire and earth. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an throughout the verses of this story is that the nobility of fire over earth is established, and that Iblis was seized for his disobedience of Allah's command, a definitive disobedience. When Allah the Exalted commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, He knew Adam's worthiness of that, by the power that Allah deposited in him, which can reach him to the level of the angels in purity and sanctity. As for Iblis, the purity of his element deceived him, and that alone is not sufficient for preference unless his constitution from that element prepares him to attain perfections. This is because what counts is the manner of composition and the consideration of the properties of the matter composed, after composition, according to the purpose of the Creator at the time of composition. The condition of the matter in isolation is of no account. So Allah the Exalted composed Iblis from the element of fire in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in corruption, and rush towards it by nature without reflection, according to the properties of the matter of which he is composed. He composed Adam from the element of earth in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in goodness and righteousness, and rush towards increasing perfection by pure choice and reflection, according to what the properties of the composed matter permit. All of this is subject to the wisdom of the Creator of the composition. He composed the angels from the element of light in a form that makes them employ their elemental powers in pure goods, and rush

[Page 43]

towards that by nature without choice or reflection, according to the properties of their element. Therefore the attainment of the human being to angelic virtues is higher and more marvelous, and his descent to satanic vices is lower and easier. For this reason he was addressed with obligation (al-taklif).

For this very meaning, Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, the origin of the human kind, because it was a prostration of acknowledgment to Allah the Exalted of the manifestation of His great power. And He commanded Iblis to prostrate to him in the same way. The angels obeyed Allah's command without knowing His wisdom, and awaited the explanation, as He related of them in His saying: ﴿They said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. Then the explanation came in summary by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], then in detail with the account of His saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels and said: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], up to His saying ﴿and what you used to conceal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah punished him for his disobedience by removing him from the place where he had been in elevation, which is the heaven, and He settled the angels in it, and made it a sacred and excellent place above the earth. All of this is by a divine decree, through the outpouring of lights and the constant presence of the angels. So He said to him: ﴿Then descend from it; it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

The expression "descent" (al-hubut) is either literal, if the place is high, or metaphorical, for distance from the honored place, by likening distance from it to descending from a high place. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The fa' in ﴿then descend﴾ indicates that the command to descend is a consequence of his reply. It is thus the conjoining of the speech of one speaker to the speech of another speaker, because the two statements have the status of one statement in the context of dialogue, like the conjunction in His saying: ﴿He said: "I am making you an imam for the people." He said: "And of my descendants?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The fa' indicates that his command to descend is caused by his answer.

The feminine pronoun in the genitive governed by min in His saying "minha" (from it) refers to the place known between the speaker and the addressee. Its feminine form is either in observance of its meaning as a locality, or in observance of the word "heaven", because it is the place of the angels. This feminine pronoun is repeated in the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿So it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾ — the fa' is causal and consequential, giving the reason for the command to descend. It is a specific punishment: the punishment of banishment from the sacred place, because his character had become unsuited to what Allah made that place for. That character is arrogance. The place was a sacred and excellent place, not to be but purified of everything that has an attribute contrary to it. This is a principle that the wise thinkers who search for the virtuous city have sought. Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Do not introduce innovation in our city." This verse is a foundation for the right of the people of a neighbourhood to expel from their neighbourhood anyone whose conduct is feared to spread corruption among them.

His saying ﴿So it is not for you﴾ indicates that this attribute is not excused in him, because the negation in the form "mā yakūnu laka kadhā" is stronger than the negation with "laysa laka kadhā", as was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 79] in Āl ʿImrān. It implies here a prohibition, because He negated it of him while it had occurred. On this basis, the restriction of the negation of arrogance to being in heaven is because it was the cause of the specific punishment, which is the punishment of expulsion from heaven. So that restriction does not indicate that he would be permitted to be arrogant elsewhere. How could it, when it is known that arrogance is a disobedience that does not befit the people of the higher world?

His saying: "fa-akhraja" (so He expelled him) is an emphasis of the clause "fa-ihbiṭ" (descend) with a synonym. The fa' was repeated with the second clause to further emphasize that arrogance was the cause of his expulsion from the Garden.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are of the debased﴾ may be a resumptive clause of explanation (istiʾnāf bayānī), if the meaning of the statement is to inform of the existence of debasement in him, by Allah the Exalted making him debased and abject wherever he is. Its separation from the preceding clause is then for resumption. It may also be in the position of giving the reason for the expulsion, in the manner of using "inna" in such a context in the manner of using the fa' of causation. This is the case if the meaning of the statement is to make manifest the debasement and abjectness in him which he overlooked, so that his heedlessness of it led him to arrogance.

His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of the debased﴾ is stronger in establishing debasement for him than saying "innaka ṣāghir" (you are debased) or "qad ṣaghurta" (you have become debased), as was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿Then I would have gone astray, and I would not be of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying above: ﴿He was not of those who prostrated﴾. The ṣāghir is one characterized by ṣaghār, which is humiliation and abjectness. Debasement is for him before Allah because his disposition has become other than what pleases Allah. This is the debasement of misguidance, and for this reason he said after this: "Because You have led me astray" (fa-bimā aghwaytanī).

[Page 36]

It is coordinated with the sentence "And We had certainly established you on the earth" [al-A'raf: 10], as a reminder of the blessing of bringing the species into existence. This is a blessing of care, because existence is superior to non-existence, setting aside what may befall the existent of troubles and hardships. It is also a blessing of honouring the species over others, by commanding the angels to prostrate to their origin. Woven into this favour is an admonition and a warning about the enmity of Satan towards the human species since ancient times, so that this may serve as a preparation for warning against his whispering and misleading, and as an incitement to abandon what has drawn people into shirk and error. This is the aim of the sura, and it appears at His words, "O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden" [al-A'raf: 27], and what follows it of verses. Therefore this passage stands in the manner of an argument, inserted in the midst of the exhortation.

The address is to all people, but what is intended by it is the polytheists, because they are the focus of this sura.

The emphasis of the statement by "bi-l-lam" (the lam of emphasis) and "qad" is for the reason already mentioned in His words, "And We had certainly created you" [al-A'raf: 11]. The transitivity of the two verbs of creating and fashioning to the pronoun of the addressees, given that it refers to the creation of the species of which they are individuals, makes it necessary that the meaning be: "We created your origin, then We fashioned him," and he is Adam, as His words clarify: "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'"

Creation (al-khalq) is bringing a thing into existence and making it appear into being. This is the meaning intended when it is attributed to God Most High or when God is described by it.

Fashioning (al-taswir) is making a thing into a form (surah). The form is the shape by which a body is shaped, just as clay is shaped into the form of a kind of species.

The clause "fashioned you" is joined by the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates the delay of the rank of fashioning from the rank of creating, because fashioning is a state of perfection in creation, in that the human being is in the human form, perfected in beauty and nobility, with what it contains of faculties of perception and management. This holds whether the fashioning is concomitant with creation, as in the creation of Adam, or occurs after creation by a period, as in the fashioning of embryos from bones, flesh, sinews, veins and faculties, as in His words, "Then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh" [al-Mu'minun: 14].

[Page 37]

The transitivity of the two verbs "We created" and "We fashioned" to the pronoun of address falls within the same thread as what the pronoun referred to before it in His words, "And We had certainly established you on the earth" [al-A'raf: 10] and what follows. So the address is to all people, as a preparation for His words later: "O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden" [al-A'raf: 27]. What is specifically intended by it is the polytheists, because they are the ones whom Satan embellished to them the ingratitude for these blessings, as His words after that show: "And when they commit an indecency they say, 'We found our fathers doing it'" [al-A'raf: 28], and His words previously: "Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you remember" [al-A'raf: 3].

As for the connection of the two verbs of creating and fashioning to the pronoun of the addressees, what is meant is the first origin of their species, namely Adam, by the indication of its being followed by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'" The creation of the origin of their species is thus treated as the creation of the individuals of the species among whom are the addressees, because the purpose is to remind them of the blessing of bringing into existence, so that they may give thanks to their Creator. A parallel to this is His words: "Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship" [al-Haqqah: 11], meaning: We carried your forefathers, who were with Noah, and from them people multiplied after the flood, because the purpose is to bestow favour upon the addressees by the saving of their forefathers from whom they descended. It is also permissible to interpret the two verbs of creating and fashioning as meaning the intention of their occurrence, as in His words, related from the speech of the angels to Abraham: "So We brought out those of the believers who were in it" [al-Dhariyat: 35], meaning: We intended to bring out those who were in it, since this statement occurred before the command to Lot and those who believed in him to leave the town.

His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" indicate that what was created and fashioned is Adam. The meaning of the speech is: We created your origin and fashioned him, so he emerged existing and specified, named Adam, because naming is a means of determining the named. Then We manifested his excellence and the wondrous craftsmanship of Ours in him, so We said to the angels, "Prostrate to him." Thus there occurred a wondrous conciseness in the composition of the speech.

[Page 38]

As for "thumma" in His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" it is conjoining a clause to a clause, and it restricts the delay to be one of rank, not of time, because the content of the conjoined clause here is higher in rank than the content of the clause it is conjoined to.

As for His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" its explanation has already been given. The explanation of what preceded it: God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, after the manifestation of the excellence of what God taught him of the names, which He did not teach the angels. This is at His words, "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' they prostrated, except Iblis" [al-Baqarah: 34], in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The definite article in "al-malaikah" (the angels) is generic, so it does not follow that the command applies to all the angels. Rather, those commanded may be the angels who were in the place where Adam was created, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also possible that the sense is all-encompassing, covering all the angels. The manner of commanding them all and their all prostrating to Adam is known only to God, because the ways by which they know the will of God concerning them in the higher world cannot be measured by what is familiar in the world of the earth.

Know that God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam does not necessitate that Adam was created in the world in which the angels are. Rather this is a possibility, and it is possible that when God created Adam He gathered the angels and made them aware of this wondrous creation, since the angels move from place to place. The verse is therefore not explicit that Adam was created in the heavens, nor that he was in the Garden, which is the abode of reward and punishment, although its apparent meaning suggests that. The majority of the People of the Sunnah took this apparent meaning, and this was discussed in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The exception of Iblis from "those who prostrated" in His words "except Iblis" indicates that he was counted among the angels, because he was mixed with them. Al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah: Iblis was counted among the angels by way of predominance (taghlib).

The clause "he was not among those who prostrated" [al-A'raf: 11] is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to Iblis. It is a circumstantial clause emphasising the content of its governing element, which is what is indicated by the exception, because the exception requires the affirmation of the opposite of the judgement of the excepted from what is excepted from. This is exactly the meaning of "he was not among those who prostrated," so the circumstantial clause is an emphasis.

[Page 39]

In choosing to report the negation of his prostration by making him one of those who did not prostrate, there is an indication that the prostration was negated from him with an intense negation. This is because your saying "So-and-so was not among the guided" conveys a stronger negation than your saying "So-and-so was not guided," as in His words: "Say, 'I will not follow your desires; I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided'" [al-An'am: 56], in the sura of al-An'am.

In the verse there is therefore an indication that God Most High created in the very nature of Iblis a disposition that pushes him to disobedience whenever the command does not agree with his desire, and He made for him a desire and an opinion, so his nature was contrary to the nature of the angels. He remained among the angels only because no command had arisen that contradicted his desire. When the command to prostrate arrived, the trait of disobedience latent in him appeared. Thus His words, "he was not among those who prostrated," are an indication that it had not been decreed for him to be among the group of those who prostrate, that is, his prostration was negated by a negation that postponed its occurrence afterwards. It is known that he refused to prostrate with refusal. This prepares for the narration of the question and answer in His words, "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" [al-A'raf: 12].

The clause "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" is the beginning of the dialogue, because Iblis's abandonment of prostration to Adam stands in the position of an answer to God's words, "Prostrate to Adam." So it was apt that an inquiry about the reason for his abandoning prostration should be directed at him. The pronoun in "He said" refers to something known from the context, that is, God Most High said, as is indicated by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate.'" The apparent form would have been "We said," but the shift to the third-person pronoun is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Its purpose is to transform the setting of the speech, since the setting was one of command to the angels and those in their company, and it became a setting of rebuke directed specifically at Iblis.

"Ma" is interrogative. It is an interrogative whose apparent meaning is genuine, but mixed with rebuke. The purpose of the interrogation is to show the angels the intent of Iblis.

"Mana'aka" means "hindered you" and "restrained you" from prostrating. The apparent form would have been "What prevented you that you prostrate?" because he merely held back from prostration, not from negating prostration. God says in another verse: "What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?" [Sad: 75]. Therefore the particle "la" (not) here is contrary to the apparent form. It has been said that it is extra for emphasis and does not convey negation, because the particle added for emphasis conveys no meaning other than emphasis. "La" is among the particles with which speech is emphasised, as in His words, "I do not swear by this city" [al-Balad: 1], and His words, "So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of God" [al-Hadid: 29], meaning: so that the People of the Book may know with certain knowledge. And His words, "And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they will not return" [al-Anbiya': 95], meaning: it is certainly prohibited that they return, a prohibition that is certain. This is the interpretation of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari. But in directing the meaning of emphasis to the verb, while the prostration did not occur, the emphasis is not to be relied upon, because emphasis is confirmation of the occurrence of the emphasised act, so this interpretation should not be relied upon, since its obscurity is evident.

It has been said that "la" is negative, and its presence implies a verb understood from context, indicated by "mana'aka," because whoever is prevented from something is called to its opposite. It is as if it were said: "What prevented you from prostrating so that it called you to not prostrate?" Then either "mana'aka" is used in the sense of "called you," by way of metaphor, and "la" is the indicator of the metaphor. This is al-Sakkaki's interpretation in al-Miftah in the section on linguistic metaphor, and close to it is that of 'Abd al-Jabbar as transmitted by al-Razi, and it is the better interpretation. Or both verbs are intended, so one is mentioned and the other omitted, and the omitted one is indicated by a complement suitable for it, and this is a case of concise omission. This is al-Tabari's choice and that of those who followed him.

See what I have said at His words, "He said, 'O Harun, what prevented you when you saw them going astray, from following me?'" [Ta-Ha: 92–93], in the sura of Ta-Ha.

His words, "when I commanded you," are an adverbial phrase (zarf) governing "prostrate." Attaching its pronoun to the command requires that the command given to the angels includes him. This is either because he is a category of the angels, so God created Iblis as an origin

[Page 41]

for the jinn, so that He would make of it a kind distinct from the rest of the angels by its acceptance of disobedience. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and many jurists (fuqaha') held this view. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and so on. Or, because the jinn are another kind of the immaterial beings (al-mujarradat), and Iblis was the origin of that kind, and Allah placed him among the angels. Thus their command included him, based on the view that the angels were created from light and the jinn were created from fire.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire." This is the view of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) and some of the Ash'ariyya (al-Ash'ariyya). The "fire" may mean light mixed with matter, and the "light" may mean pure light, so that the jinn would be a kind of the genus of angels, lower in rank, just as the human being is a kind of the genus of animals, higher in rank.

﴿He said: "I am better than him"﴾ is disconnected (fasl) because it occurs in the manner of dialogue.

He explained his refusal to prostrate: he saw himself as better than Adam, so he did not obey Allah's command to him to prostrate to Adam. This is clear disobedience. His words ﴿I am better than him﴾ are given as a reason for the refusal, and for that reason the preposition "li" (for) was omitted before it.

The clause ﴿You created me from fire﴾ explains the clause ﴿I am better than him﴾, and for that reason it is disconnected, since it has the status of an explanatory apposition (‘atf al-bayan) to what it explains.

Iblis came to know that he was created from fire through information from the angels who witnessed his creation, or through information from Allah the Exalted.

That he was created from fire is established. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He created the human being from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14], ﴿and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. Iblis is of the kind of the jinn, as Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis; he was of the jinn, and he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50].

He based his claim of superiority upon the excellence of the element from which he was created over the element from which Adam was created.

[Page 42]

Fire is the intense heat that, by its extremity, produces combustion, which exists in bodies melted by their original nature, like the fire that is in the sun. When the heat reaches the point of combustion, fieriness comes to a body from a mineral, a plant or earth, like the fire that remains in ash.

Fire is superior to earth because of the strength of its effect and its dominion over the bodies it meets, because it gives light, and because it is pure, so that impurities do not cling to it. Earth does not share it in these qualities, though both share in that all living bodies are formed from them.

As for the light from which the angel was created, it is more pure than the ray that emanates from fire, free of the corporeal admixtures found in fire.

Clay (tin) is earth mixed with water, and water is another element upon which animal life depends together with fire and earth. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an throughout the verses of this story is that the nobility of fire over earth is established, and that Iblis was seized for his disobedience of Allah's command, a definitive disobedience. When Allah the Exalted commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, He knew Adam's worthiness of that, by the power that Allah deposited in him, which can reach him to the level of the angels in purity and sanctity. As for Iblis, the purity of his element deceived him, and that alone is not sufficient for preference unless his constitution from that element prepares him to attain perfections. This is because what counts is the manner of composition and the consideration of the properties of the matter composed, after composition, according to the purpose of the Creator at the time of composition. The condition of the matter in isolation is of no account. So Allah the Exalted composed Iblis from the element of fire in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in corruption, and rush towards it by nature without reflection, according to the properties of the matter of which he is composed. He composed Adam from the element of earth in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in goodness and righteousness, and rush towards increasing perfection by pure choice and reflection, according to what the properties of the composed matter permit. All of this is subject to the wisdom of the Creator of the composition. He composed the angels from the element of light in a form that makes them employ their elemental powers in pure goods, and rush

[Page 43]

towards that by nature without choice or reflection, according to the properties of their element. Therefore the attainment of the human being to angelic virtues is higher and more marvelous, and his descent to satanic vices is lower and easier. For this reason he was addressed with obligation (al-taklif).

For this very meaning, Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, the origin of the human kind, because it was a prostration of acknowledgment to Allah the Exalted of the manifestation of His great power. And He commanded Iblis to prostrate to him in the same way. The angels obeyed Allah's command without knowing His wisdom, and awaited the explanation, as He related of them in His saying: ﴿They said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. Then the explanation came in summary by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], then in detail with the account of His saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels and said: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], up to His saying ﴿and what you used to conceal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah punished him for his disobedience by removing him from the place where he had been in elevation, which is the heaven, and He settled the angels in it, and made it a sacred and excellent place above the earth. All of this is by a divine decree, through the outpouring of lights and the constant presence of the angels. So He said to him: ﴿Then descend from it; it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

Little do you remember" [al-A'raf: 3].

As for the connection of the two verbs of creating and fashioning to the pronoun of the addressees, what is meant is the first origin of their species, namely Adam, by the indication of its being followed by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'" The creation of the origin of their species is thus treated as the creation of the individuals of the species among whom are the addressees, because the purpose is to remind them of the blessing of bringing into existence, so that they may give thanks to their Creator. A parallel to this is His words: "Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship" [al-Haqqah: 11], meaning: We carried your forefathers, who were with Noah, and from them people multiplied after the flood, because the purpose is to bestow favour upon the addressees by the saving of their forefathers from whom they descended. It is also permissible to interpret the two verbs of creating and fashioning as meaning the intention of their occurrence, as in His words, related from the speech of the angels to Abraham: "So We brought out those of the believers who were in it" [al-Dhariyat: 35], meaning: We intended to bring out those who were in it, since this statement occurred before the command to Lot and those who believed in him to leave the town.

His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" indicate that what was created and fashioned is Adam. The meaning of the speech is: We created your origin and fashioned him, so he emerged existing and specified, named Adam, because naming is a means of determining the named. Then We manifested his excellence and the wondrous craftsmanship of Ours in him, so We said to the angels, "Prostrate to him." Thus there occurred a wondrous conciseness in the composition of the speech.

[Page 38]

As for "thumma" in His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" it is conjoining a clause to a clause, and it restricts the delay to be one of rank, not of time, because the content of the conjoined clause here is higher in rank than the content of the clause it is conjoined to.

As for His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,'" its explanation has already been given. The explanation of what preceded it: God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, after the manifestation of the excellence of what God taught him of the names, which He did not teach the angels. This is at His words, "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' they prostrated, except Iblis" [al-Baqarah: 34], in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The definite article in "al-malaikah" (the angels) is generic, so it does not follow that the command applies to all the angels. Rather, those commanded may be the angels who were in the place where Adam was created, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also possible that the sense is all-encompassing, covering all the angels. The manner of commanding them all and their all prostrating to Adam is known only to God, because the ways by which they know the will of God concerning them in the higher world cannot be measured by what is familiar in the world of the earth.

Know that God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam does not necessitate that Adam was created in the world in which the angels are. Rather this is a possibility, and it is possible that when God created Adam He gathered the angels and made them aware of this wondrous creation, since the angels move from place to place. The verse is therefore not explicit that Adam was created in the heavens, nor that he was in the Garden, which is the abode of reward and punishment, although its apparent meaning suggests that. The majority of the People of the Sunnah took this apparent meaning, and this was discussed in the sura of al-Baqarah.

The exception of Iblis from "those who prostrated" in His words "except Iblis" indicates that he was counted among the angels, because he was mixed with them. Al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah: Iblis was counted among the angels by way of predominance (taghlib).

The clause "he was not among those who prostrated" [al-A'raf: 11] is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to Iblis. It is a circumstantial clause emphasising the content of its governing element, which is what is indicated by the exception, because the exception requires the affirmation of the opposite of the judgement of the excepted from what is excepted from. This is exactly the meaning of "he was not among those who prostrated," so the circumstantial clause is an emphasis.

[Page 39]

In choosing to report the negation of his prostration by making him one of those who did not prostrate, there is an indication that the prostration was negated from him with an intense negation. This is because your saying "So-and-so was not among the guided" conveys a stronger negation than your saying "So-and-so was not guided," as in His words: "Say, 'I will not follow your desires; I would then have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided'" [al-An'am: 56], in the sura of al-An'am.

In the verse there is therefore an indication that God Most High created in the very nature of Iblis a disposition that pushes him to disobedience whenever the command does not agree with his desire, and He made for him a desire and an opinion, so his nature was contrary to the nature of the angels. He remained among the angels only because no command had arisen that contradicted his desire. When the command to prostrate arrived, the trait of disobedience latent in him appeared. Thus His words, "he was not among those who prostrated," are an indication that it had not been decreed for him to be among the group of those who prostrate, that is, his prostration was negated by a negation that postponed its occurrence afterwards. It is known that he refused to prostrate with refusal. This prepares for the narration of the question and answer in His words, "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" [al-A'raf: 12].

The clause "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?'" is the beginning of the dialogue, because Iblis's abandonment of prostration to Adam stands in the position of an answer to God's words, "Prostrate to Adam." So it was apt that an inquiry about the reason for his abandoning prostration should be directed at him. The pronoun in "He said" refers to something known from the context, that is, God Most High said, as is indicated by His words, "then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate.'" The apparent form would have been "We said," but the shift to the third-person pronoun is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Its purpose is to transform the setting of the speech, since the setting was one of command to the angels and those in their company, and it became a setting of rebuke directed specifically at Iblis.

"Ma" is interrogative. It is an interrogative whose apparent meaning is genuine, but mixed with rebuke. The purpose of the interrogation is to show the angels the intent of Iblis.

"Mana'aka" means "hindered you" and "restrained you" from prostrating. The apparent form would have been "What prevented you that you prostrate?" because he merely held back from prostration, not from negating prostration. God says in another verse: "What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?" [Sad: 75]. Therefore the particle "la" (not) here is contrary to the apparent form. It has been said that it is extra for emphasis and does not convey negation, because the particle added for emphasis conveys no meaning other than emphasis. "La" is among the particles with which speech is emphasised, as in His words, "I do not swear by this city" [al-Balad: 1], and His words, "So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of God" [al-Hadid: 29], meaning: so that the People of the Book may know with certain knowledge. And His words, "And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they will not return" [al-Anbiya': 95], meaning: it is certainly prohibited that they return, a prohibition that is certain. This is the interpretation of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari. But in directing the meaning of emphasis to the verb, while the prostration did not occur, the emphasis is not to be relied upon, because emphasis is confirmation of the occurrence of the emphasised act, so this interpretation should not be relied upon, since its obscurity is evident.

It has been said that "la" is negative, and its presence implies a verb understood from context, indicated by "mana'aka," because whoever is prevented from something is called to its opposite. It is as if it were said: "What prevented you from prostrating so that it called you to not prostrate?" Then either "mana'aka" is used in the sense of "called you," by way of metaphor, and "la" is the indicator of the metaphor. This is al-Sakkaki's interpretation in al-Miftah in the section on linguistic metaphor, and close to it is that of 'Abd al-Jabbar as transmitted by al-Razi, and it is the better interpretation. Or both verbs are intended, so one is mentioned and the other omitted, and the omitted one is indicated by a complement suitable for it, and this is a case of concise omission. This is al-Tabari's choice and that of those who followed him.

See what I have said at His words, "He said, 'O Harun, what prevented you when you saw them going astray, from following me?'" [Ta-Ha: 92–93], in the sura of Ta-Ha.

His words, "when I commanded you," are an adverbial phrase (zarf) governing "prostrate." Attaching its pronoun to the command requires that the command given to the angels includes him. This is either because he is a category of the angels, so God created Iblis as an origin

[Page 41]

for the jinn, so that He would make of it a kind distinct from the rest of the angels by its acceptance of disobedience. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and many jurists (fuqaha') held this view. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and so on. Or, because the jinn are another kind of the immaterial beings (al-mujarradat), and Iblis was the origin of that kind, and Allah placed him among the angels. Thus their command included him, based on the view that the angels were created from light and the jinn were created from fire.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire." This is the view of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) and some of the Ash'ariyya (al-Ash'ariyya). The "fire" may mean light mixed with matter, and the "light" may mean pure light, so that the jinn would be a kind of the genus of angels, lower in rank, just as the human being is a kind of the genus of animals, higher in rank.

﴿He said: "I am better than him"﴾ is disconnected (fasl) because it occurs in the manner of dialogue.

He explained his refusal to prostrate: he saw himself as better than Adam, so he did not obey Allah's command to him to prostrate to Adam. This is clear disobedience. His words ﴿I am better than him﴾ are given as a reason for the refusal, and for that reason the preposition "li" (for) was omitted before it.

The clause ﴿You created me from fire﴾ explains the clause ﴿I am better than him﴾, and for that reason it is disconnected, since it has the status of an explanatory apposition (‘atf al-bayan) to what it explains.

Iblis came to know that he was created from fire through information from the angels who witnessed his creation, or through information from Allah the Exalted.

That he was created from fire is established. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He created the human being from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14], ﴿and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. Iblis is of the kind of the jinn, as Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis; he was of the jinn, and he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50].

He based his claim of superiority upon the excellence of the element from which he was created over the element from which Adam was created.

[Page 42]

Fire is the intense heat that, by its extremity, produces combustion, which exists in bodies melted by their original nature, like the fire that is in the sun. When the heat reaches the point of combustion, fieriness comes to a body from a mineral, a plant or earth, like the fire that remains in ash.

Fire is superior to earth because of the strength of its effect and its dominion over the bodies it meets, because it gives light, and because it is pure, so that impurities do not cling to it. Earth does not share it in these qualities, though both share in that all living bodies are formed from them.

As for the light from which the angel was created, it is more pure than the ray that emanates from fire, free of the corporeal admixtures found in fire.

Clay (tin) is earth mixed with water, and water is another element upon which animal life depends together with fire and earth. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an throughout the verses of this story is that the nobility of fire over earth is established, and that Iblis was seized for his disobedience of Allah's command, a definitive disobedience. When Allah the Exalted commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, He knew Adam's worthiness of that, by the power that Allah deposited in him, which can reach him to the level of the angels in purity and sanctity. As for Iblis, the purity of his element deceived him, and that alone is not sufficient for preference unless his constitution from that element prepares him to attain perfections. This is because what counts is the manner of composition and the consideration of the properties of the matter composed, after composition, according to the purpose of the Creator at the time of composition. The condition of the matter in isolation is of no account. So Allah the Exalted composed Iblis from the element of fire in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in corruption, and rush towards it by nature without reflection, according to the properties of the matter of which he is composed. He composed Adam from the element of earth in a form that makes him employ the effects of elemental power in goodness and righteousness, and rush towards increasing perfection by pure choice and reflection, according to what the properties of the composed matter permit. All of this is subject to the wisdom of the Creator of the composition. He composed the angels from the element of light in a form that makes them employ their elemental powers in pure goods, and rush

[Page 43]

towards that by nature without choice or reflection, according to the properties of their element. Therefore the attainment of the human being to angelic virtues is higher and more marvelous, and his descent to satanic vices is lower and easier. For this reason he was addressed with obligation (al-taklif).

For this very meaning, Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, the origin of the human kind, because it was a prostration of acknowledgment to Allah the Exalted of the manifestation of His great power. And He commanded Iblis to prostrate to him in the same way. The angels obeyed Allah's command without knowing His wisdom, and awaited the explanation, as He related of them in His saying: ﴿They said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. Then the explanation came in summary by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], then in detail with the account of His saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels and said: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], up to His saying ﴿and what you used to conceal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah punished him for his disobedience by removing him from the place where he had been in elevation, which is the heaven, and He settled the angels in it, and made it a sacred and excellent place above the earth. All of this is by a divine decree, through the outpouring of lights and the constant presence of the angels. So He said to him: ﴿Then descend from it; it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

The expression "descent" (al-hubut) is either literal, if the place is high, or metaphorical, for distance from the honored place, by likening distance from it to descending from a high place. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The fa' in ﴿then descend﴾ indicates that the command to descend is a consequence of his reply. It is thus the conjoining of the speech of one speaker to the speech of another speaker, because the two statements have the status of one statement in the context of dialogue, like the conjunction in His saying: ﴿He said: "I am making you an imam for the people." He said: "And of my descendants?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The fa' indicates that his command to descend is caused by his answer.

The feminine pronoun in the genitive governed by min in His saying "minha" (from it) refers to the place known between the speaker and the addressee. Its feminine form is either in observance of its meaning as a locality, or in observance of the word "heaven", because it is the place of the angels. This feminine pronoun is repeated in the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿So it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾ — the fa' is causal and consequential, giving the reason for the command to descend. It is a specific punishment: the punishment of banishment from the sacred place, because his character had become unsuited to what Allah made that place for. That character is arrogance. The place was a sacred and excellent place, not to be but purified of everything that has an attribute contrary to it. This is a principle that the wise thinkers who search for the virtuous city have sought. Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Do not introduce innovation in our city." This verse is a foundation for the right of the people of a neighbourhood to expel from their neighbourhood anyone whose conduct is feared to spread corruption among them.

His saying ﴿So it is not for you﴾ indicates that this attribute is not excused in him, because the negation in the form "mā yakūnu laka kadhā" is stronger than the negation with "laysa laka kadhā", as was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 79] in Āl ʿImrān. It implies here a prohibition, because He negated it of him while it had occurred. On this basis, the restriction of the negation of arrogance to being in heaven is because it was the cause of the specific punishment, which is the punishment of expulsion from heaven. So that restriction does not indicate that he would be permitted to be arrogant elsewhere. How could it, when it is known that arrogance is a disobedience that does not befit the people of the higher world?

His saying: "fa-akhraja" (so He expelled him) is an emphasis of the clause "fa-ihbiṭ" (descend) with a synonym. The fa' was repeated with the second clause to further emphasize that arrogance was the cause of his expulsion from the Garden.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are of the debased﴾ may be a resumptive clause of explanation (istiʾnāf bayānī), if the meaning of the statement is to inform of the existence of debasement in him, by Allah the Exalted making him debased and abject wherever he is. Its separation from the preceding clause is then for resumption. It may also be in the position of giving the reason for the expulsion, in the manner of using "inna" in such a context in the manner of using the fa' of causation. This is the case if the meaning of the statement is to make manifest the debasement and abjectness in him which he overlooked, so that his heedlessness of it led him to arrogance.

His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of the debased﴾ is stronger in establishing debasement for him than saying "innaka ṣāghir" (you are debased) or "qad ṣaghurta" (you have become debased), as was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿Then I would have gone astray, and I would not be of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying above: ﴿He was not of those who prostrated﴾. The ṣāghir is one characterized by ṣaghār, which is humiliation and abjectness. Debasement is for him before Allah because his disposition has become other than what pleases Allah. This is the debasement of misguidance, and for this reason he said after this: "Because You have led me astray" (fa-bimā aghwaytanī).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 14–15:

﴿He said, "Give me respite until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾

When Allah placed in him (Iblis) smallness and abasement after the might and nobility of the angelic state, the objects of his aspiration turned to base things (as the saying goes: "If there are no camels, then goats will do"). So he asked for respite, a long life until the Day of Resurrection, since he had known beforehand that he was among the enduring creatures, for he is of the people of the enduring world. When he was brought down to the earthly world, he thought that he was heading toward non-existence, and therefore he asked for respite, seeking to preserve what he had enjoyed before. Since this was by the decree and knowledge of Allah the Exalted, and Iblis's request for respite had escaped from him, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾, meaning: indeed, you are among the created beings that endure.

The emphasis conveyed by "inna" (indeed) and the statement in the form "among those given respite" indicate that his being given respite is a matter that Allah had decreed and predestined before his request. That is, your being among the group who were given respite until the Day of Resurrection has been realized. Allah created a kind of creature and decreed their survival until the Day of Resurrection, so He revealed to Iblis that he is a part of the total of those given respite, before the disobedience occurred from him. Allah does not change what He has decreed for him. Therefore, Allah's answer to Iblis is a report about a matter that has already been realized, and it is not a response to Iblis's request, because it is too trivial for Allah to answer him with a request. This is the point in deviating from saying the answer as "I have given you respite" or "I have answered your request," which would indicate honoring him by granting his request. Rather, He informed him that what he asked for is an already-accomplished matter, so his asking is a request for something already obtained.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 14–15:

﴿He said, "Give me respite until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾

When Allah placed in him (Iblis) smallness and abasement after the might and nobility of the angelic state, the objects of his aspiration turned to base things (as the saying goes: "If there are no camels, then goats will do"). The emphasis conveyed by "inna" (indeed) and the statement in the form "among those given respite" indicate that his being given respite is a matter that Allah had decreed and predestined before his request.
