Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 16–17:

﴿He said, "Because You have sent me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path.﴾ ﴿Then I will surely come at them from before them and behind them, and from their right and from their left. And You will not find most of them grateful.﴾

The fa' (فَ) here indicates sequence and causation, following from His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reduced to disgrace﴾ [al-A'raf: 13], and then His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those given respite﴾ [al-A'raf: 15].

The meaning of those two statements indicates that God created in the soul of Iblis a capacity to lead people astray, through His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reduced to disgrace﴾ [al-A'raf: 13], and that He kept him remaining and acting through his evil powers until the Day of Resurrection. So Iblis perceived that he would be a caller to misguidance and disbelief, by a natural disposition to which God turned his heart, a turning that belongs to the psychic transformation (al-maskh al-nafsani). He would certainly do this, while knowing that what issues from him is misguidance and corruption. The issuing of this from him is like the issuing of a bite from a snake, or like the blinking of the eyelids when something passes over the eye, even though the owner of the eye does not intend to move them.

The bi' (بِ) in His words, ﴿So because You have sent me astray﴾, is causal (sababiyyah). It is an adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr) functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the subject of la-a'qu'anna (لَأقْعُدَنَّ), meaning: "I swear that I will surely sit in wait for them, in a state where this is from me because of Your leading me astray." The lam in la-a'qu'anna is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), intended to emphasize the realization of that act and the firmness of the resolve upon it.

He placed the prepositional phrase before its governing verb to convey the sense of causation, which is close to the conditional. For this reason, fronting is warranted, since when a prepositional phrase is fronted it may convey a meaning close to the conditional, as in the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As you are, so you will be ruled over," in a narration where taku-na (تَكُونُوا) is in the jussive, without treating its governing verb as the apodosis of a conditional with the jussive marker; thus yuwalla (يُوَلّى) is only narrated with an alif at its end, without considering the jussive. This arises from the emphasis placed on the complement, since it was the cause of the attainment of what is attached to it; so the fronting is for emphasis. Therefore this fronting does not compete with the lam of oath opening its clause, although we do not insist on this, for it has been departed from in much of Arabic speech.

Ma (مَا) is a verbal-masdar particle, and "sitting" (al-qu'ud) is a metonymy for constancy and persistence, as in the words of al-Nabigha: "Sitting by their tents, they keep them dyed; may God cast into those hands the disabling blows." That is, remaining persistently at the tents of others, while they desire to sit down, since they may be asking while standing or walking. The basis of the metonymy is that persistence in a place entails fatigue from standing there, so the one who persists sits to rest. From this usage, the term "qa'id" was applied to one who seeks protection, and from the application of qa'id to one who persists is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two receivers receive, one on the right and one on the left, seated [qa'id]﴾ [Qaf: 17], that is, persistently present, since an angel is not described as sitting or standing.

Since the verb la-a'qu'anna was given the sense of persistence, "Your path" (sirata-ka) is in the accusative as a direct object. Alternatively, it is governed by a verb implied by the meaning of la-a'qu'anna, which may be estimated as: "I will surely block Your path," or "I will surely cut off Your path from them." The lam in lahum (لَهم) denotes purpose, as in His words: ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

The annexation of "the path" (al-sirat) to the Name of Majesty (God) is on the estimate of a pronoun of address (ka), meaning the path which is Yours, that is, which You have made a way for you. The way belonging to God is the action by which what pleases God is attained through obedience to His command, namely doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds. So the statement is a depiction of the state of those resolved to do good and their determination upon it, and of Satan confronting them to prevent them from doing it, in the form of one who seeks a destination that benefits him, when a highwayman blocks him on his road and prevents him from passing through it.

The pronoun in lahum refers to humankind, whose reference is indicated by the context of the dialogue. That dialogue has been abbreviated here by an abbreviation called for by limiting the discourse to its intended purpose, which is the reminder of the blessing of creation and the warning against the plotting of the enemy of mankind. The detailed dialogue indicates that when God created Adam, He addressed the people of the exalted assembly, that He created him to populate the earth with him and his offspring, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority [khalifah]"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So the earth was already created on that day, and God created Adam to populate it with his descendants. Iblis knew this from God's report to the angels. So God related from his speech what is needed here, namely His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, and so on. The verse of Surat al-Hijr indicates that Iblis mentioned in his discourse what shows that he intends to lead astray the people of the earth, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have sent me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all, [Except among them Your chosen servants]"﴾ [al-Hijr: 39–40]. If Adam was created in the Garden in the heaven and then sent down to the earth, then Iblis's knowledge that Adam would go to the earth came from God's report that He would place him on earth as a successor, so he knew he would go to the earth after a while. If Adam was created in a garden of the gardens of the earth, the matter is evident. This was already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

This statement indicates that Iblis knew that God created humankind for goodness and benefit, that He deposited in them the knowledge of perfection, and helped them reach it by guidance. Therefore, in the reported speech of Iblis, the works of goodness were called "the straight path," and its attribution to the pronoun of Majesty is because God called to it and wanted people to follow it. For this reason also he made necessary: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will surely come at them from before them and behind them﴾.

On this basis, Iblis was an enemy to the children of Adam, because he seeks from them what they were not created for and what is contrary to the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which God created mankind. So enmity is rooted and innate between the nature of Satan and the untainted human nature (fitrah). This is what the divine decree alluded to in His words, "Some of you are enemies to others" made clear. Thereby it will become evident how enmity turned into alliance between the devils and those humans who preferred misguidance and disbelief over faith and righteousness.

The clause "﴿Then I will surely come at them﴾": the thumma (ثُمَّ) here is for rank-ordering (al-tartib al-rutbi), namely progression in reporting to a more important report, because the content of the following clause is more pertinent to the purpose of the speech than the content of the preceding clause. The first clause conveyed lying in wait for humans to lead them astray, while the following clause conveyed an assault upon them by every means.

Just as the example was struck for the state of eagerness to lead astray by sitting on the road, so too was the state of seeking to lead astray by every means depicted as the state of the seeker, eager to seize his enemy, who comes at him from every direction until he finds the direction in which he can seize him. So he comes at him from before him, from behind him, from his right and from his left, until the strength of his resistance weakens. The statement is a figure of speech, and Satan has no way into a person except through his own self and intellect, by casting whispering into his soul. The four directions mentioned in the verse are not literal, but are a figurative, illustrative metaphor drawn from what is customary in people's attempts and deceptions. For this reason the verse does not mention coming at them from above or from below, since that is not part of the manner of people in deception or assault.

"﴿Before them﴾" and "﴿behind them﴾" are connected by the preposition min (مِن), while "﴿their right﴾" and "﴿their left﴾" are connected by the preposition 'an (عَنْ), following what is common in Arabic speech in the transitivity of verbs to names of directions. The original sense of 'an in the expression 'an yamínihi wa 'an shimálihi is separation: from the side of his right, separated from him and turned away from him. Then this spread until 'an came to mean 'ala (on). Just as they say jalasa 'ala yamínihi ("he sat on his right"), they also say jalasa 'an yamínihi. Likewise min in the expression min bayni yadayhi originally denotes starting point. It is said: atáhu min bayni yadayhi, that is, from the place facing him. Then this spread until min became like a superfluous particle through which the adverb is governed, and so adverbs that are constantly adverbial, like 'inda (near), were governed by it, because the presence of min is like its absence. Al-Hariri said in the Grammatical Maqamah: "What is in the accusative as an adverb is governed by no particle but a letter," so min here is superfluous, and it is permissible to consider it an initial (ibtida'iyyah) particle.

Al-Ayman is the plural of yamin, and yamin here is a side of the human body which, when a person faces the rising sun, is on the side of the south pole. People recognize it by custom, so its knowledge is widespread, and they do not notice applying the rule we mentioned. Thus yamin is a direction by which the positions of the body's organs are identified: one says the right eye, the right hand, and the like. It is also used to identify the positions of other things, as God says: ﴿They will say, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right [‘an al-yamin]"﴾ [al-Saffat: 28]. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Upon a cloud at al-Shaym, its rightmost rain..."

For this reason the lexicographers said: the lands of Yemen were called Yaman because it is on the right side of the Ka'bah. They treated the Ka'bah as a person facing the rising sun, so its Yamani corner, which is the angle of the wall containing the Black Stone, is considered as the right hand of a human. It is not known whether the derivation of the word yamin is original, nor whether al-yaman is its root or a derivative of it. Al-Ayman is a regular plural.

Al-Shama'il is the plural of shimal, which is the side that is on the left for one facing the rising sun. It is an irregular plural.

His words, "﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾," are an addition explaining the strength of his misguiding, such that only a few people escape falling into his snares. This is known by intuitive knowledge and by the sequence of effects.

Denial of gratitude is used as a metonymy for disbelief, since there is no intermediate state between them, as God says: ﴿Remember Me, and I will remember you; and be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. The point of this metonymy, if it is reported as Iblis's own speech, is that he intended courtesy toward God, so he did not state explicitly in His presence the disbelief of his followers, which would imply that he commands them to disbelieve. If it is from God's speech, then it contains a warning that those who associate partners with God have committed a grave matter, for they did not thank Him for His abundant blessings upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 16–17:

﴿He said, "Because You have sent me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path.﴾ ﴿Then I will surely come at them from before them and behind them, and from their right and from their left. And You will not find most of them grateful.﴾

The fa' (فَ) here indicates sequence and causation, following from His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reduced to disgrace﴾ [al-A'raf: 13], and then His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those given respite﴾ [al-A'raf: 15].

The meaning of those two statements indicates that God created in the soul of Iblis a capacity to lead people astray, through His words: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reduced to disgrace﴾ [al-A'raf: 13], and that He kept him remaining and acting through his evil powers until the Day of Resurrection. So Iblis perceived that he would be a caller to misguidance and disbelief, by a natural disposition to which God turned his heart, a turning that belongs to the psychic transformation (al-maskh al-nafsani). He would certainly do this, while knowing that what issues from him is misguidance and corruption. The issuing of this from him is like the issuing of a bite from a snake, or like the blinking of the eyelids when something passes over the eye, even though the owner of the eye does not intend to move them.

The bi' (بِ) in His words, ﴿So because You have sent me astray﴾, is causal (sababiyyah). It is an adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr) functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the subject of la-a'qu'anna (لَأقْعُدَنَّ), meaning: "I swear that I will surely sit in wait for them, in a state where this is from me because of Your leading me astray." The lam in la-a'qu'anna is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), intended to emphasize the realization of that act and the firmness of the resolve upon it.

He placed the prepositional phrase before its governing verb to convey the sense of causation, which is close to the conditional. For this reason, fronting is warranted, since when a prepositional phrase is fronted it may convey a meaning close to the conditional, as in the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As you are, so you will be ruled over," in a narration where taku-na (تَكُونُوا) is in the jussive, without treating its governing verb as the apodosis of a conditional with the jussive marker; thus yuwalla (يُوَلّى) is only narrated with an alif at its end, without considering the jussive. This arises from the emphasis placed on the complement, since it was the cause of the attainment of what is attached to it; so the fronting is for emphasis. Therefore this fronting does not compete with the lam of oath opening its clause, although we do not insist on this, for it has been departed from in much of Arabic speech.

Ma (مَا) is a verbal-masdar particle, and "sitting" (al-qu'ud) is a metonymy for constancy and persistence, as in the words of al-Nabigha: "Sitting by their tents, they keep them dyed; may God cast into those hands the disabling blows." That is, remaining persistently at the tents of others, while they desire to sit down, since they may be asking while standing or walking. The basis of the metonymy is that persistence in a place entails fatigue from standing there, so the one who persists sits to rest. From this usage, the term "qa'id" was applied to one who seeks protection, and from the application of qa'id to one who persists is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the two receivers receive, one on the right and one on the left, seated [qa'id]﴾ [Qaf: 17], that is, persistently present, since an angel is not described as sitting or standing.

Since the verb la-a'qu'anna was given the sense of persistence, "Your path" (sirata-ka) is in the accusative as a direct object. Alternatively, it is governed by a verb implied by the meaning of la-a'qu'anna, which may be estimated as: "I will surely block Your path," or "I will surely cut off Your path from them." The lam in lahum (لَهم) denotes purpose, as in His words: ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

The annexation of "the path" (al-sirat) to the Name of Majesty (God) is on the estimate of a pronoun of address (ka), meaning the path which is Yours, that is, which You have made a way for you. The way belonging to God is the action by which what pleases God is attained through obedience to His command, namely doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds. So the statement is a depiction of the state of those resolved to do good and their determination upon it, and of Satan confronting them to prevent them from doing it, in the form of one who seeks a destination that benefits him, when a highwayman blocks him on his road and prevents him from passing through it.

The pronoun in lahum refers to humankind, whose reference is indicated by the context of the dialogue. That dialogue has been abbreviated here by an abbreviation called for by limiting the discourse to its intended purpose, which is the reminder of the blessing of creation and the warning against the plotting of the enemy of mankind. The detailed dialogue indicates that when God created Adam, He addressed the people of the exalted assembly, that He created him to populate the earth with him and his offspring, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority [khalifah]"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So the earth was already created on that day, and God created Adam to populate it with his descendants. Iblis knew this from God's report to the angels. So God related from his speech what is needed here, namely His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, and so on. ﴿He said, "Get out of it, disgraced and banished. Whoever among them follows you, I will surely fill Hell with all of you."﴾

Allah repeated His command to descend from the heaven, to emphasize the two earlier commands: He said, "﴿Get down from it﴾ [al-A'raf: 13]," up to His saying "fa-ukhruj" (so go out).

Madhu'um (مَذْءُومٌ) is a passive participle from dha'amahu (ذَأمَهُ), with a hamza, meaning he found fault with him and blamed him, dha'man (ذَأْمًا). The hamza of dha'ama (ذَأمَ) may be softened so that it becomes an alif, and one says dhama (ذامَ), but the hamza is not softened in its other derived forms.

Madhhur (مَدْحُورٌ) is a passive participle from daharahu (دَحَرَهُ), meaning he drove him far away and removed him. That is, "Go out in the manner of one who is blamed and expelled." The blame is for the vices he has taken on, and the expulsion is to purify the realm of holiness ('alam al-qudus) from his mixing with it.

The lam in ﴿liman tabi'aka﴾ (لَمَن تَبِعَكَ) is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatti'ah) for the oath.

Man (مَن) is conditional, and the lam in la-amla'anna (لَأمْلَأنَّ) is the lam of the answer to the oath. The answer to the oath has taken the place of the answer to the condition. The sense is: "I swear, whoever among them follows you, I will surely fill Hell with them and with you." The pronoun has been given the form of address, because the single existing individual covered by this generality is the one addressed, who is Iblis, and because he is the primary target of this threat, since it is a threat for his own act. As for the threat against those who follow him, it comes indirectly, through him. This differs from the pronoun in the verse of al-Hijr, which is His saying: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 43]. That verse came after turning away from the threat against his act, and with concern to explain the rank of the sincere servants of Allah over whom Iblis has no authority, and then with concern for the threat against the misguided.

This is like His saying in Surat al-Hijr:

[Page 52]
﴿He said, "This is a path leading straight to Me." [al-Hijr: 41] ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those of the misguided who follow you﴾ [al-Hijr: 42] ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 43].

The emphasis with "ajma'in" (أجْمَعِينَ) is to make the generality explicit, so that it is not taken as a figure of speech in which the majority stands for the whole. This is because the speech was addressed to a community under the description of being followers of one person, and the Arabs sometimes apply generality in such a case to the group rather than to every individual, as they say: "Tamim killed so-and-so," when only some of them killed him. Al-Nabigha said about the Banu Hunn, with a pointed (unpronounced) ḥā' (حُنٍّ) with a dammah:

"And they killed the Ta'i man in the open valley by force."

﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers.﴾

The "wa" (و) in His saying "and O Adam" is conjunctive (عاطفة, ʿātifah, a conjunctive particle), joining this sentence to the sentence "Get out of it, disgraced and expelled" [al-A'raf: 18]. So this "wa" belongs to the reported speech itself, not to the act of reporting. The call and the command are part of what was said. The meaning is: God said to Iblis, "Get out of it," and said to Adam, "And O Adam, dwell." This is a speaker joining one part of his speech to another part when the two parts are connected and relevant to each other, and when the two statements are not both addressed to the same person, while the setting of the speech remains one. This is like a speaker who, in one gathering with several listeners, addresses each one with words specific to him. Among examples is the Prophet's ﷺ words in the case of the man and the Ansari, whose son had been a hired laborer for the man: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, I will judge between you both by the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for the goats and the slave-girl, they are returned to you. As for your son, he shall receive a hundred lashes and a year's exile. And go, O Unays, to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, stone her." Among the styles of this verse is His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is of your guile; indeed, your guile is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28], and ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29], quoting the words of the Aziz, meaning the Aziz joined the address to his wife to his address to Joseph.

[Page 53]

The "wa" in His saying "and O Adam, dwell" is therefore not conjunctive to the verbs of saying that precede it, such that the sentence would be read as "And We said, O Adam, dwell." That reading would not yield the points we have mentioned. This all happened in one setting in which Adam, the angels, and Iblis were present.

Addressing Adam with this favour in the presence of Iblis after his expulsion adds to his humiliation. Granting blessings to the one who is pleased with God, at the very time the one who deserved punishment is being punished, increases the grief of the one punished and shows the difference between the one deserving favour and the one deserving punishment. The sentence therefore does not convey the meanings that the conjunction to the reported speech conveys, and if that were intended, the verb of saying would have been repeated. Furthermore, if Adam was created in the Garden and was dwelling there from before, then the command in His saying "dwell" is a command of confirmation: that is, remain in the Garden. If Adam was created outside the Garden, the command is one of permission, honouring him. In either case, this command, heard by Iblis, is a rebuke to Iblis. If Iblis was dwelling in the Garden before, the rebuke is clear, since God expelled him and settled the one he had arrogantly refused to prostrate to in the honoured place that had been his before his arrogance. And if Iblis had not been dwelling in the Garden before, then honouring the one he despised and exalted himself above is itself a rebuke to him. The placement of this sentence in this surah indicates a great meaning of rebuking Iblis, beyond what is in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, even though the two are identical in wording. This wonderful meaning is derived from the placement, and this is among the wonders of the inimitability of the Qur'an.

The choice of this verse with this particularity is found in the fact that this speech is directed at the polytheists who took Satan as a guardian besides God. As for what is in Surat al-Baqarah, it is for admonishing the Children of Israel, who are among those who beware of Satan and do not follow his footsteps.

The call (النداء, al-nidāʾ, the vocative) serves to draw attention to Adam and to give him prominence in that assembly. The bringing of the separate pronoun after the command, "you" (أنت, anta), is intended to increase the rebuke of Iblis, because mentioning his pronoun in a position of conjunction reminds others that he is not like him. Although the pronoun is of the category of the epithet (لقب, laqab, a designation that is not restricted), and it has no implicit contrary meaning (مفهوم مخالفة, mafhūm mukhālafah, the meaning implied by excluding the opposite), it may still convey exclusion of other than the pronoun's owner through contextual indication, by way of allusion (تعريض, taʿrīḍ, indirect implication). This consideration is not prevented by the pronoun being expressed to improve or validate the conjunction to the hidden pronoun of the nominative, because validating or improving the conjunction is achieved by any separator between the governing verb with its hidden pronoun and the conjoined word, not specifically by the pronoun. It could be said, "O Adam, dwell in the Garden, you and your wife." The separation by the separate pronoun was chosen only because of the allusion to others that it conveys. This is a point I had missed in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, so add it to it as well.

What is said about His saying, ﴿dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾, is known from what has passed in the discussion of its counterpart in Surat al-Baqarah.

Except that what occurred in Surat al-Baqarah is "and eat" with "wa," while here it is with "fa" (فـ), and conjunction with "wa" is more general. So the verse here conveys that God permitted Adam to enjoy the fruits of the Garden immediately after commanding him to dwell in it. This is an immediate favour that indicates the completion of honour. Since that was present in that setting, and since it increased the distress of Iblis, who had arrogantly considered himself superior to him, the situation required informing the listeners of it in the context in which the anger against Iblis and his expulsion are narrated. As for the verse of al-Baqarah, it only informed the listeners that God bestowed on Adam the favour of dwelling in the Garden and enjoying its fruits, because the context there is to remind the Children of Israel of Adam's merit, his sin, his repentance, and the warning against Satan's guile, the guile into which they fall in a great measure.

Moreover, the verse of al-Baqarah did not lack mention of what contains honour for him, which is His saying "abundantly" (رَغَدًا, raghadan), because it is praise of the one who grants the favour or a supplication for Adam. Thus from the combination of the two verses there result several honours for Adam, distributed according to the Qur'an's custom of distributing the aims of narratives among their places, so that the benefit is renewed, to energise the listener and to vary the styles of narration, since the most important purpose of stories in the Qur'an is lesson, admonition, and exemplarity.

His saying, ﴿but do not approach this tree﴾, is stronger in warning than forbidding eating from it, because forbidding approaching it closes the means (سد الذريعة, sadd al-dharīʿah, blocking the path to a prohibited act) to eating from it. Its counterpart has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

The prohibition of approaching a particular tree among the trees of the Garden may be a prohibition of trial. God made one tree excepted from the permission to eat from the trees of the Garden, as a preparation for the obligation to resist desire in order to comply with the prohibition. Therefore He made the prohibition of taking from it surrounded by the trees permitted, so that their minds would turn to it by leaving it. This is the apparent meaning, so that the various mental faculties in the intellect of the species would be formed by establishing them in the origin of the species, and then they would be transmitted to its offspring. This is among the divine gentleness in the formation of the species and among the manifestations of the reality of Lordship and being a servant. The faculties are all obtained gradually, so that establishing them all at once does not burden the capacity of the intellect. The verses indicate that when the thought of disobedience arose in Adam, he ate from the forbidden tree, and the eating was followed by the arising of the awareness of the deficiencies within him, which he perceived by natural disposition. So its meaning is that simplicity and innocence departed from him. It may also be that this was due to a special property in that tree, that it stirs in the soul the knowledge of good and evil, as the Torah says that God forbade him from eating the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But this, in my view, is far-fetched. God has only related to us the manner of the development of the human intellect in the creation of the origin of the human species, in parallel with His workmanship in His saying, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31].

The pointing to a tree is an observed reference, and weak narrations have been transmitted concerning the identification of its kind, which was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word "fa-takūnā" (فَتَكُونا) is in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition. The state of being among the wrongdoers is a consequence of approaching what is forbidden, not a consequence of the prohibition itself. This is the original basis for the accusative in an answer to a prohibition, as in an answer to a negation: the causation is taken as a consequence of the negated or forbidden act. This differs from the jussive (الجزم, al-jazm) in an answer to a prohibition, since in that case what is caused is jussive upon the utterance of the prohibition, not upon the forbidden act. The difference between them is that the accusative is based on considering causation, and causation arises from the act, not from report or utterance, whereas the jussive is based on considering the answer, by analogy with the conditional. Therefore, the meaning of uttering the prohibition is considered in it, making the utterance analogous to a condition.

[Page 54]

By "the wrongdoers" (الظالمين, al-ẓālimīn) is meant those who rightly deserve the description of wrongdoing, either because they wronged themselves and cast themselves into evil consequences, or because they transgressed against the right of others, since disobedience is a wrong against the right of the Lord, whose obedience is obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 20–21:

﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was concealed from them of their private parts, and said, "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the immortal."﴾ ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors."﴾

The whispering of Satan occurred close to the prohibition of Adam from eating from the tree. The closeness is expressed by the particle of sequence (ḥarf al-ta'qīb), indicating that it was a near closeness, because the sequence of each thing is according to its nature.

Al-waswasah (whispering) is hidden speech that is heard only by one who is close to the speaker. Ru'bah said, describing a hunter:
"He whispered, calling earnestly on the Lord of the daybreak, secretly, and he had already bent in the bending of the bow-string."

The casting of Satan is called waswasah because he cast to them a hidden enticement of speech that he addressed to them, or an agitation in their souls.

It is like the manner of a deceiver and a schemer who conceals speech from those present, lest they spoil his deceit by exposing its harms. So he cast to them words in the form of murmuring, so that he would give them the impression that he is a sincere advisor to them and that he speaks in a hushed manner. In the other verse, the enticement of Satan is expressed as speech: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:120). Then the usage of the Qur'an and the speech of the Messenger, peace be upon him, followed the designation of Satan's casting into the souls of people as "wasāwis" (evil promptings), bringing closer the meaning of that casting to the understanding, as in His saying: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer who withdraws﴾ (al-Nas 114:4). And this specification of Satan's casting of his scheme is unique to this verse, distinct from the verse in surah al-Baqarah, because that one is an address encompassing the polytheists, who were ignorant of that knowledge, so it was fitting to make the actions of Satan repugnant before them.

[page 57]

The lam in "li-yubdiya" is the lam of consequence (lam al-'āqibah), if Satan did not know that disobedience would lead them to the arising of the thought of evil in their souls and the appearance of their private parts. So he made the occurrence of the effect following the act resemble the occurrence of the effect after its cause, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8). They did not pick him up in order that he would become for them a comfort of the eye. The aptness of this is that the exposure of their private parts is something that pleases Satan. It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of motive (lam al-'illah al-bā'itha), if Satan knew that by inspiration or by reflection. Then Satan whispered to Adam and his spouse for the purpose of causing them to fall into disobedience from the outset, because that is his nature which he was created to act upon; then for the purpose of harming them, since he sought what would harm them, and he envied them for the pleasure of God with them; and he knew that disobedience would lead them to a bad state in general, so the manifestation of that bad state was the exposure of their private parts. Thus the detailed cause of the general cause became, for the agent, the cause itself, even if it did not occur to his mind. It is also possible that Satan knew that by a knowledge that had reached him previously. The conclusion is that he intended harm, because enmity toward humanity has become settled in his nature, as will be stated explicitly later, and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ (Fatir 35:6).

Al-ibdā' (exposure) is the opposite of al-ikhfā' (concealment). So al-ibdā' is the uncovering and manifestation of a thing. It is used metaphorically for knowing a thing after ignorance of it, as one says, "It appeared to me (badā lī) that I should do such and such."

The exposure of the private parts is ascribed to Satan because he is the one who causes it, by way of rational metaphor (al-majāz al-'aqlī). The word sawā'āt is the plural of sawʾah, which is a term for what is bad and shameful of defects. Among the Arabs' expressions of reproach is "sawʾatan laka" (shame on you), and among their expressions of lamentation is "yā sawʾatā" (alas for my shame). The private parts are referred to euphemistically by sawʾah. The meaning of wūriya 'anhumā is that it was screened and concealed from them, derived from al-muwārāh, which is covering and concealment. Al-muwārāh is also used metaphorically for diverting a person from knowledge of a thing by secrecy or deception.

The word "sawʾāt" here may be the plural of sawʾah in the sense of a blameworthy trait, as in the verse of Abu Zubayd:
"He did not respect the sanctity of the boon-companion, and the (two) wives (of) ... for my people, to the evil and bad trait."
In that case the plural form is in its literal sense, and sawʾāt is then used in its plain meaning. It is also permissible that it be the plural of sawʾah, used euphemistically for the private parts, and this interpretation has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, as in His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing that covers your private parts﴾ (al-A'raf 7:26). In this case, the plural form is used for the two (of them) for lightness, as in His saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed deviated﴾ (al-Tahrim 66:4). The clarification of the meaning of this exposure will come at His saying after this: ﴿So when they tasted of the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ (al-A'raf 7:22).

The conjoining of the clause "and said, 'Your Lord has forbidden you...'" to the clause "Then he whispered" indicates that Satan whispered to them a whispering other than his saying "Your Lord has forbidden you..." etc. Then he doubled his whispering by saying "Your Lord has forbidden you." If the clause "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree..." to its end were an explanation (bayān) of the clause "Then he whispered," the clause "and said, 'Your Lord has forbidden you'" would have come without a conjunction, because explanation is not conjoined to what it explains. In this conjunction there is an indication that Adam and his spouse hesitated in acting upon Satan's whispering, so Satan began to entice them. Do you not see that his saying in Surah Ta-Ha was not conjoined: "Then he whispered to him, Satan, saying, 'O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?'" For that is a narration of the beginning of his whispering. He began the whispering in general terms, so he did not specify for Adam the tree from which he was forbidden to eat, in order to draw him down to disobedience and to make his foot slip. Then he proceeded to interpret God's prohibition to them against eating from it, and said what is reported of him in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels﴾, etc. So he pointed to the tree after it had become known to them, as an increase in enticing them to disobedience by eating from the tree. Thus the whispering and its conclusion were distributed over the two forms, according to the Qur'an's custom of brevity in narrating stories, being content with the intended point of the story, so that the narrative would not become a primary aim of the revelation.

The indication in His saying "from this tree" refers to a specific tree that had become clear to Adam after Satan whispered to him, that it was the tree from which God had forbidden him. So Iblis intended his committing disobedience and removing his fear by making him think ill of God's intention in the prohibition.

The exception in His saying: ﴿only lest you become angels﴾ is an exception from causes (istithnā' min 'ilal). That is: "He forbade you for a cause and purpose only for the purpose that you become angels." So it is necessary to estimate a lam of causation before "an" (that), and the omission of the prepositions entering upon "an" is common in Arabic speech when there is no ambiguity.

That they become angels or immortals is the cause of the prohibition: that is, your being angels is the motive of the prohibition, except that it is a motive in terms of the negation of its occurrence, not in terms of its occurrence. That is, it is a cause in a general sense. For this reason, Sibawayh and al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as "out of dislike that you become." This is an interpretation of meaning, not an interpretation of grammatical parsing, as has preceded in surah al-An'am. It was said that "la" (not) was omitted after "an," and its omission is present; and the Kufans interpreted it accordingly, and the discussion of this has preceded. Iblis made Adam and his spouse think that they were able to become two of the angels if they ate from the tree. This was part of his deception and trickery, since he found Adam and his spouse not discerning the realities of things, nor knowing the possible extent of transformation of essences and the development of existing things. They witnessed the preference of the angels with God, their nearness, and their vast capacity, so Iblis tempted them into thinking they would become of the angels if they ate from the tree. It was also said that the intended meaning is a eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh), that is: "except that you be in nearness and proximity like the two angels." He gave them an example of what they knew of the perfection of the angels.

[page 60]

His saying: ﴿or become among the immortal﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that you become angels﴾. The basic meaning of "aw" (or) is indicating alternation between one of two things or among things, whether together with permitting the possibility of all the conjoined items, in which case it is for permissibility after a command, and for possibility after a statement, or for doubt; or with the prevention of some while permitting some, in which case it is for choice after a command, and for doubt or alternation after a statement. Alternation does not contradict the certainty that one of the two matters necessarily occurs, as is the case here. So the meaning of the speech is that whoever eats from this tree will become an angel and immortal, as He said about it in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:120). So God's prohibition to them from eating is made to amount to nothing more than the intention of one of the two matters. It is understood from the context that He may intend to deprive them of both matters together by way of implication (dalālat al-fahwā). Adam at that time did not know that eternity is unattainable, and that death, gathering, and resurrection are decreed upon people, for that is received from revelation, as in His saying to them in the other verse: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ (al-A'raf 7:24).

﴿And he swore to them﴾, that is, he swore to them by what gives the appearance of his truthfulness. The word al-muqāsamah is a reciprocal form (mufā'alah) from aqsama, meaning "he swore," with the hamzah removed when forming the reciprocal form, as it is removed in al-mukāramah. The reciprocal form here is for intensification of the act, and not for the act occurring from both sides; its parallel is 'āfāhu Allāh (God granted him well-being). Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, made it: "as if they both said to him, 'Swear by God that you are among the sincere advisors,' and he swore, so their request for the oath was made equivalent to the oath." That is, the reciprocal form would be on its proper pattern. The emphasis of his report about himself regarding advising them with three emphatic particles is evidence of the degree of Adam and his spouse's doubt in his advice to them, and of what they saw on them of signs of hesitation regarding his truthfulness. They doubted his advice only because they found what he commanded them to be contrary to what God had commanded them, whose intention of good for them they knew by innate nature (al-fiṭrah).

This is a continuation of the clause: ﴿So Satan whispered to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] and what is conjoined to it.

The meaning of ﴿fa-dallahuma﴾ (so he brought them down) is that he led them forward, and they did an act by which they hoped for a benefit, but they were disappointed in it. The root *dalla* (to lower) is a metaphor for one who seeks something from its expected source but does not find it, like one who lowers his bucket or his legs into a well to draw water and finds no water in it. It is said *dalla fulan* ("so-and-so lowered"), just as one says *adlā*.

The *bā'* (with) is for accompaniment, meaning he lowered them while accompanied by deception, that is, while deception had taken hold of them. Deception (*ghurur*) is believing a thing to be beneficial according to its outward appearance, while there is no benefit in it when it is tested. On this analogy one says *dallāhu bi-ghurur* when he causes him to fall into hope in something that has no benefit, as in this verse. It is also in the verse of Abu Jundub al-Hudhali, who is the son of Murra, and I have not found his biography. If he was an Islamic-era poet, then he took his saying from the Qur'an, as one who is lowered by deception. Otherwise, the expression was in use before:

*"I protect, and I do not grant protection; and whoever I protect, is not like one who is lowered by deception."*

On this usage, the verb *dalla* is used intransitively, and it is used transitively when someone else is made to be lowered. This is what is derived from the words of the lexicographers regarding this term, and there are other explanations of it, but there is no benefit in mentioning them.

The words ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ indicate that they did what Satan whispered to them, so they ate from the tree. Therefore His words ﴿When they tasted the tree﴾ are a consequence of ﴿he brought them down by deception﴾, and the clause has been omitted and dispensed with by the mention of the apparent noun in the conditional clause of *lamma* (when). The implied meaning is: "they ate from it," as is explicitly stated in Surat al-Baqara: "When they tasted it, their private parts became apparent to them."

*Dhawq* (tasting) is perceiving the flavour of food or drink with the tongue, and it occurs at the beginning of eating or drinking. This verse indicates that the exposure of their private parts occurred at the first perception of the taste of the tree, which shows the speed with which the forbidden matter follows at the first act of disobedience. Thus this verse adds to the verse of al-Baqara.

This was the first whisper that came from Satan, and the first misleading of man by him.

*Lamma* has indicated that the exposure of their private parts was timed to the moment of their tasting the tree, because *lamma* is a particle that indicates the existence of one thing at the existence of another. It is therefore only for timing the content of its response to the time of the existence of its condition. This is the meaning of the grammarians' saying: "a particle of existence for existence," where the *lām* in their phrase "for existence" means "at." For this reason some said it is an adverb meaning "when," referring to its origin. Since they required that it be preceded by what indicates the time and not by what is timed, it resembled the conditional particles, so they said: "a particle of existence for existence," just as they said of *law* (if): "a particle of prohibition for prohibition," and of *lawla* (if not): "a particle of prohibition for existence." However, the *lām* in the grammarians' expression explaining the meaning of *law* and *lawla* is the *lām* of causation, unlike its use in their expression regarding *lamma*, because *lamma* has no indication of a cause. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when He delivered you safely to the land, you turned away﴾ [al-Isra': 67]? Deliverance is not the cause of turning away. But since there is a concomitance between cause and effect, the meaning of causality frequently occurred in the condition and response of *lamma*, without being consistent. Therefore His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ indicates nothing more than that the exposure of the private parts occurred at the tasting of the tree. That is, God made the two matters concurrent in time. But this concurrence is because the two matters have a single cause, which is the evil thought that Satan breathed into them. It caused them to proceed to disobey the good instructions, and to feel deficiency. Adam and his wife were, in the stage of innocence of knowledge and soundness of nature, similar to the angels, not proceeding to any corruption or harm, nor turning away from the advice of an adviser whose sincerity they knew, toward the report of a informant whose truthfulness they doubted, and whose deception they anticipated. Nor did they perceive evil in actions, nor in their means and concomitants. For God created them in a angelic world, then their intellect developed to the stage of manipulating the modification of their inner sense, so the doing of what they had been forbidden came about in them. From that development arose the perception of evil for others, and evil for oneself, and the perception of things that lead to evil, that accompany evil and are bound to it.

Then, if *al-sawat* (the private parts/the evils) means what is evil among deficiencies, or means the private parts, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿that He might reveal to them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], then the exposure of that to them accompanied the tasting of the tree, which is the effect of advancing toward disobedience and rejecting advice, leading to following deception and being deluded by its division. For when the thought of evil in action arose in them, and the will to proceed with it, that state that motivated the act accompanied the emergence of perceiving bad things, namely the things by which bad acts appear, or which become a pretext for them. Just as the knowledge of the instrument of cutting arises at the resolve to kill, and from the thought of theft comes the knowledge of the place where one hides, so too arises the knowledge of things that are bound to evil and accompany it, even if they are not evil in themselves. Just as the knowledge of the night arises from the thought of theft or flight, so that its dislike arises in people's souls and it is attributed to the commission of evils. If its meaning is the private part, then it belongs to the second category, that is, the thing accompanying what is bad, because the private part accompanies a bad act of perceptible deficiencies. Then, when he grows up, thoughts of evil begin to visit him within his inner self, and he entertains them, generates them, and is affected by them, or acts in accordance with what they indicate to him.

For when they perceived their private parts in both senses, they knew some of its particulars, namely the nakedness, and there arose in their souls the perception of the ugliness of its exposure. So they began to hide it from their sights, out of disgust and aversion. Since they perceived this by natural inspiration, where there was no teacher to teach them that and no instruction to instruct them, it became established in people's souls that uncovering the private parts is ugly by nature, and that covering them is required. This is from the judgment of the estimative faculty (*al-quwwa al-wahima*), which accompanied humankind in its origin, and so it indicates that it is a rooted natural illusion. Therefore the religion of nature came with affirming the covering of the private parts, in agreement with what is established in human souls. God gave the estimative faculty authority over human souls for long ages, because following it helps refine character and remove the animal coarseness of the species, since the estimative faculty does not exist in animals. Then the laws, the counsels of the wise, and the teachings of educators began to remove the following of illusions from human minds gradually over time, and they retained from it only what was necessary to preserve virtue in custom among people. Until Islam came, which is the final law, and the attachment of rulings in the religion of Islam to illusory matters became cancelled in most rulings, as I have explained in my book *Maqasid al-Shari'a* and my book *Usul Nizam al-Ijtima' fi al-Islam*.

This is the apparent meaning here, since He did not say *yakhsifan waraq al-Janna* (they stitched the leaves of the Garden).

The *min* in His saying ﴿from the leaves of the Garden﴾ may be a noun meaning "some," in the position of the object of *yakhsifan*, meaning they stitched some of the leaves of the Garden, as in His saying: "from those who are Jews, they distort" [al-Nisa': 46]. It may also be explanatory of an omitted object implied by *yakhsifan*, and the implied meaning is: they stitched a stitching from the leaves of the Garden.

﴿And their Lord called out to them: "Did I not forbid you from that tree, and tell you that Satan is a clear enemy to you?" They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

This is coordinated with the response of *lamma*, so it is among what occurred at the tasting of the tree. The reports about the events that occurred at the tasting of the tree have been ordered according to the order of their occurrence in existence. For their private parts became apparent to them, so they began to stitch, and this was followed by God's call to them.

This is a principle in the arrangement of sentences in the craft of composition, unless the situation requires a departure from that. A parallel to this arrangement is His saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was troubled by them and felt distressed for them, and said: "This is a difficult day."﴾ [Hud: 77]. I have explained this in my book *Usul al-Insha' wa al-Khitaba*, and I do not know that I was preceded in discovering it.

The call of the Lord to them was delayed until their private parts became apparent to them, and they tried to cover their nakedness, so that the rebuke would have a firm effect on their souls, when it comes after the corruptions of their disobedience have become apparent to them, so that they would know that good lies in obedience to God, and that in disobedience to Him there is harm.

The root meaning of *nida'* (calling) is raising the voice. It is derived from *nada* (with a fatha on the nun and a short vowel), which means the carrying distance of the voice. Mídhar ibn Shayban al-Namari said:

*"I said: 'Call out, and I will call out, for the most far-carrying of voices is that of two callers calling out.'"*

It is a well-known metaphor in speech that is intended to seek someone's attention toward you, and it has well-known particles in Arabic that indicate seeking attention. The term *nida'* has become widely applied to this, to the extent that it has become a real meaning. From it branched the seeking of listening and the attention of the mind from one near to you, and this attention is metaphorical.

﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾ is used in its well-known meaning, which is seeking attention, though the attention is necessarily metaphorical, so it is like His saying: ﴿And Zachariah, when he called to his Lord﴾ [al-Anbiya': 89], and this is common in speech.

It may also be used in speech with a raised voice, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of one who calls out to what hears nothing but calling and crying out﴾ [al-Baqara: 171], and His saying: ﴿And they are called out to: "That is the Garden, which you have been given as an inheritance"﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], and the saying of Bashshar:

*"I called out: 'Indeed love has made me feel the killing, and I did not commit any sin.'"*

Raising the voice occurs for various purposes, and its interpretation here is that it is a voice of anger and rebuke.

The apparent sense of attributing the calling to God is that God called to them with speech without an intermediary angel, like the speech with which God spoke to Moses. This occurred before the descent to the earth, so it does not contradict what is reported that Moses was the first prophet God spoke to without an intermediary. It is also possible that Adam's calling was through one of the angels.

The clause ﴿Did I not forbid you﴾ is in the position of explanation for the clause ﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾, and for this reason the clause is separated from the one before it.

The interrogative in ﴿Did I not forbid you﴾ serves *taqrir* (eliciting an affirmation, i.e. a confirmatory question) and *tawbikh* (rebuke). The negative particle was placed first for added *taqrir*, because God's prohibition to them had actually occurred, so its negation is negated. When the interrogative particle is introduced and the one being questioned affirms the opposite of the negation, his affirmation is stronger in establishing accountability for its consequence, since he has been left no way to deny it. Had he been able to deny it, [it would have been different], as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], in Surat al-An'am. For this reason they acknowledged that they had wronged themselves.

The conjunction of the clause ﴿and I say to you both﴾ with the clause "did I not forbid you" serves to intensify the rebuke, because the prohibition was accompanied by a warning about Satan, who is the one who incited them to eat from the tree. Thus they had neglected two commandments. The purpose of relating this statement here is to remind the community of Satan's enmity toward the root of the human species, so that they know that this enmity exists between the two kinds, and so that they beware of everything that is attributed to Satan and counted among his whisperings. For since he was created with wickedness and disgrace, he calls to that by his very nature, and likewise his mind is not at ease as long as his enemy and the one he envies is in a good state.

*Mubin* (manifest) originally means "that which makes clear," i.e., makes the enmity evident, such that it is not hidden from one who follows the traces of his whispering and deception, and of how he treated Adam from the time of his creation until the time of his deceiving him. In all of that there is a clear demonstration of his enmity. The reason for that enmity is that his nature contradicts the natural perfection in the human being, which is supported by divine success and guidance. Thus he does not love that a human be anything other than in a state of misguidance and corruption. It is also permissible for *mubin* to be used metaphorically to mean "strong, intense," because the nature of an intense attribute is that it becomes visible to the eye.

They were thus wronging themselves, because they brought upon themselves entry into the state of the manifestation of their private parts and the hardship of taking up something to cover their nakedness. And [they acknowledged] that they had brought upon themselves the wrath of God Most High, so they are in expectation of the due consequences of punishment. They were certain that they would be among the losers if God did not forgive them, either by way of inspiration (*ilham*) or some kind of revelation, or by inference about the outcomes from their beginnings. This is a continuation of the clause: ﴿So Satan whispered to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] and what is conjoined to it.

The meaning of ﴿fa-dallahuma﴾ (so he brought them down) is that he led them forward, and they did an act by which they hoped for a benefit, but they were disappointed in it. The root *dalla* (to lower) is a metaphor for one who seeks something from its expected source but does not find it, like one who lowers his bucket or his legs into a well to draw water and finds no water in it. It is said *dalla fulan* ("so-and-so lowered"), just as one says *adlā*.

The *bā'* (with) is for accompaniment, meaning he lowered them while accompanied by deception, that is, while deception had taken hold of them. Deception (*ghurur*) is believing a thing to be beneficial according to its outward appearance, while there is no benefit in it when it is tested. On this analogy one says *dallāhu bi-ghurur* when he causes him to fall into hope in something that has no benefit, as in this verse. It is also in the verse of Abu Jundub al-Hudhali, who is the son of Murra, and I have not found his biography. If he was an Islamic-era poet, then he took his saying from the Qur'an, as one who is lowered by deception. Otherwise, the expression was in use before:

*"I protect, and I do not grant protection; and whoever I protect, is not like one who is lowered by deception."*

This was the first whisper that came from Satan, and the first misleading of man by him.
