**[Page 68]**

The Qur'an omits here the mention of Adam's repentance, because the purpose of the story in this surah is to remind people of Satan's enmity and to warn them against following his whispering, and to show the loss and corruption that follow from obeying him. The context of this admonition calls for turning away from mention of repentance, in order to confine the discussion to the causes of loss. Repentance is mentioned in the verse of al-Baqarah, whose purpose is to explain Adam's merit and his honour before his Lord, "and every context has its own discourse."

The address is to Adam, his wife, and Iblis.

The command is a cosmic (takwini) command, and by it Adam, his wife, and Iblis became inhabitants of the earth.

The clause ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject pronoun of "descend," which is governed by the cosmic command. This circumstantial clause therefore also conveys a cosmic meaning, namely that enmity between them is concomitant with their existence on earth. By this cosmic decree the pre-existing innate (jibillah, innate natural disposition) enmity was reinforced, took firm root, and increased. The "some" in the verse refers to the two parties that differ in kind: one of the two parties is Adam and his wife, and the other party is Iblis. Since this enmity was cosmic between the two origins of the two kinds, it was inherited by their offspring. The purpose is to remind the children of Adam of Satan's enmity toward them and toward their origin, so that they may suspect every whisper that comes to them from him. This enmity arose from Iblis's envy, then spread and branched out until it became complete enmity in every aspect of existence. It is therefore diffused in thought and body, and it requires complete antagonism between the two kinds.

Since the souls of the devils are by their innate nature inclined to evil, it follows that the human intellect is by its innate nature inclined toward good, but it is exposed to the whispering of the devils, so it falls into deviation from its original fitrah (primordial natural disposition). This provides the key to the meaning that people are born upon the fitrah, that Islam is the religion of the fitrah, and that the original state of people is goodness. As for whether the original state of people is uprightness ('adalah) or impugnment (jarh), this is considered with regard to the fear of falling into deviation, since the judge and the narrator do not know the circumstances of such deviation, which are obscure; therefore it is necessary to examine all circumstances carefully.

**[Page 69]**

The clause ﴿and for you on earth is a settled abode﴾ is joined (ʿuṭifat) to the clause ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾.

The word "mustaqarr" is a noun of place (masdar mimi), and "istiqrar" means staying and remaining. Its discussion has already preceded at the verse ﴿for every news there is a time of settlement﴾ [al-An'am: 67] and at the verse ﴿then a settled abode and a place of storage﴾ [al-An'am: 98] in Surat al-An'am.

What is meant by it is existence, that is, the existence of the human species and its characteristics. It does not mean burial, as some exegetes have explained, because His words "and enjoyment" preclude that, and because devils and jinn are not buried in the earth.

"Mata'" (enjoyment) and "tamattu'" mean attaining pleasures and desirable things that are not lasting. "Mata'" is also applied to what one enjoys and benefits from among things, and this was discussed in His words ﴿if you were to be heedless of your weapons and your goods﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] in Surat al-Nisa'.

"Hin" (a span of time) is a period of time, long or short. It is here indefinite and not specified, because its quantity differs according to the kinds and individuals. What is meant by it is the duration of life that enables its possessor to attain pleasures. In it the continuation of pleasures occurs, not dispersed, not vanished, and not annihilated. This time coexisting with the state of life and perception is what is named the term (ajal), that is, the period which the living being reaches by its life in the knowledge and decree of God Most High. When the term ends and life ceases, the settled abode and the enjoyment come to an end. This is an announcement from God of what He has decreed for the two kinds, and there is in it neither a bestowal of favour nor a punishment of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 25:

﴿He said: "Therein you will live, and therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."﴾

The verb "qala" (he said) is repeated in this sentence as a fresh beginning (isti'naf), not joined by a conjunction, and it is not dispensed with by a conjunctive waw, even though the speaker is one and the purpose is one. This departs from what the apparent norm (muqtada al-zahir) requires, since in such a case the norm is coordination (al-'atf). The eminent exegetes, al-Zamakhshari and others, have neglected to explain the omission of coordination. Perhaps they regarded it as one of the stylistic methods of narration (hikaya). The first I have seen attempt to explain the omission of coordination is the Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Arafa al-Tunisi, in his dictations on exegesis (Imla'at al-Tafsir) as transmitted from him, for he said, in commenting on the verse of God, the Exalted, that comes later in this surah: ﴿He said: "Shall I seek for you a god other than God?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 140], after His words: ﴿He said: "Surely you are a people who are ignorant."﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], that he took the reason for repeating the word "qala" to be the gap between the two statements. The first refers merely to the report of the falsehood of idol-worship in itself, and the second to the argument for its falsehood. Al-Khafaji has mentioned its meaning when commenting on the verse that follows this one, but he did not attribute it to Ibn 'Arafa, so perhaps it is a coincidence of thoughts (tawarud al-khawatir).

Abu al-Su'ud said: the repetition of "qala" is either to show concern for the content of what follows it, which is His words: ﴿Therein you will live﴾, or to signal an omitted statement between the two sayings, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿He said: "What is your business?"﴾ [al-Hijr: 57], after His words ﴿He said: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord?"﴾ [al-Hijr: 56]. For the Friend (Khalil, i.e. Abraham) first addressed the angels without reference to their being messengers, then addressed them by the title of their being messengers when it became clear that their coming was not merely for good tidings; therefore he said: ﴿"What is your business?"﴾ [al-Hijr: 57]. And as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿"Do you see this one whom You have honored above me?"﴾ [al-Isra': 62], after His words ﴿He said: "Shall I prostrate to one whom You have created from clay?"﴾ [al-Isra': 61], for he said his second statement after the respite that followed his request for respite, which he did not state explicitly, being content with what was mentioned in other places. This is the substance of his words in several places. The second explanation is rejected, since in reporting statements it is not necessary to be comprehensive or to be continuous.

What I hold is that this is not a stylistic device in reporting speech from which the eloquent may choose; rather it is equivalent to coordination with "thumma" (then), and to combining a conjunction with the repetition of the verb "qala", as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: "You had no superiority over us"﴾ [al-A'raf: 39], after His words ﴿And the last of them will say to the first of them: "Our Lord, these led us astray"﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. If it is not so, then the explanation of the repetition of the verb "qala" and of its being a fresh beginning is that it is an initial resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) to give attention to the report, signalling a change of address, such that there is a difference between the two addresses. The addressees of the first are Adam, his wife and Satan, and the addressees of the second are Adam, his wife and their offspring. If this address was before offspring came to them, as the apparent context indicates, then it is an address to them while signalling that they are the progenitors of a great multitude, all of whom are in this condition; this is the figure of speech of prioritizing the existent over the non-existent. If it occurred after offspring had come to them, then the reason for the separation is clearer and more fitting. The indication that Iblis is not included in the address is His words: ﴿and from it you will be brought forth﴾, because bringing forth from the earth requires previously having entered into its interior, and that is burial after death, and devils are not buried. God has granted Iblis respite with life until the Day of Resurrection, so he will then be gathered, or he will die and be resurrected; and none knows that except God, the Exalted.

It has been said that the change of style is a means of reaching the address to the children of Adam after this. The plural pronoun indicates a concise implied statement: that Adam and his wife settled on the earth, and offspring appeared for them, and that God informed them by one of the means of divine information that the earth is their dwelling-place and from it will be their resurrection. This ruling includes those of them existing on the day of the address and those who will exist afterward.

It has also been said that the reason for the change of style between the two sayings is that the earlier saying is a saying of address, while the one after it is a saying of decree and judgment, i.e. God decreed: you will live therein, die therein, and be brought forth from it.

The fronting of the three prepositional phrases before their complements is for the sake of giving attention to the earth in which their dwelling and their provision were placed, since it is the place of all their conditions.

This fronting has also been made a means of observing parallelism (muraa'at al-nazir), since the earth is made to encompass these conditions. The earth is one, and in it the very different conditions of its inhabitants have alternated.

Al-Jumhur read tukhrajuna with a damma on the taa' and a fatha on the ra', in the passive voice. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it in the active voice.

**[p. 72]**

If we follow the apparent meaning of the commentaries, His saying ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ and the rest of the verse is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i). It returns the address to all people, who were addressed at the beginning of the surah with His saying ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 3] and what follows. They are the community of the call (ummat al-da'wa), because the purpose of the surah is to nullify the polytheism of the Arab idolaters and its consequences in the pre-Islamic religious practices. His saying ﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11] was a digression (istitrad), reminding them of His favour upon them while they disbelieve in it, as was explained earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly created you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11]. This verse therefore addresses all the children of Adam with some of the matters intended in the surah. This verse thus serves as an introduction to the purpose that comes in His saying ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31]. Its occurrence in the midst of the verses warning against the snares of Satan makes it, relative to those verses, like a digression, although it is itself part of the principal purpose.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ and what resembles it, which begins with the phrase ﴿O children of Adam﴾ four times, is part of the speech related by His saying ﴿He said: therein you will live﴾ [al-A'raf: 25]. Then it would be among what God addressed to the children of Adam at the beginning of their era of settling the earth, through the tongue of their father, or by one of the means of divine information, even by inspiration (ilham), through which these realities arise in their souls. He began by informing them of His favour upon them, that He sent down for them clothing to cover their nakedness, and by which they adorn themselves, in connection with what God related to them of the nakedness of their two parents when their private parts became apparent to them. Then came the warning against the snares and temptation of Satan in His saying ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. Then He commanded them to take clothing, which is the adornment of man, at places of worship to God, exalted is He, in His saying ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31]. Then He took a covenant from them to believe the messengers and benefit from their guidance, in His saying ﴿O children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among you﴾ [al-A'raf: 35] and what follows. In between all of that He digressed with admonitions that benefit those for whom this narrative was intended, namely the idolaters who denied Muhammad (ﷺ). They are thus the intended audience of this speech,

**[p. 73]**

however its methods vary and its composition harmonises. In any case, the primary intended audience of these addresses, or of their narration, are the idolaters of the Arabs and the deniers of Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason, digressions (mustatradat) and allusions (ta'ridat) suited to what the idolaters had invented of falsehoods in overturning the matter of the natural disposition (fitra) are interspersed among these addresses.

The three clauses: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾, His saying ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], and His saying ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], are closely connected with the story of Satan's temptation of Adam and his wife, or they are connected with the speech related by His saying ﴿He said: therein you will live﴾ [al-A'raf: 25], by way of enumerating what was said, an enumeration that resembles repetition.

This address includes both believers and polytheists, but the greater share of it belongs to the polytheists. The believers' share of it is gratitude for their certainty that they are conforming in their affairs to the pleasure of their Lord, while the polytheists' share is a warning that they are disbelievers in the blessing of their Lord, exposed to His wrath and punishment.

The address begins with a vocative so that their attention falls on what follows with the innermost depths of their hearts. The choice of summoning them, when addressing them, under the title "children of Adam" twice, has a striking effect after the completion of the mention of the story of the creation of Adam and what he met with of Satan's whispering. This is because it is the nature of descendants to avenge their forefathers, to be hostile to their enemy, and to guard against falling into his snare.

Since God's inspiring Adam to cover himself with the leaves of the Garden was a favour upon him, and his offspring have inherited it, the people were addressed with the inclusion of this favour for them, under a title that indicates that it is an inherited favour. This is more effective and more compelling to gratitude. For this reason the facilitation of clothing for them and the inspiring of it to them was called "sending down" (inzal), to honour this manifestation, which is the first manifestation of civilisation, by declaring that it is sent down upon people from God. Or it is because what was given to Adam descended with him from the Garden to the earth where he is, so that the sense of "sending down" had a greater particularity,

**[p. 74]**

Moreover, mere inspiration toward its use, by divine subjection, together with what it contains of great benefit and advantage for people, makes it fitting to borrow the verb "sending down" for it, to honour its matter. Sharing in this meaning are other inspired things of great benefit, as in His saying ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is severe might and benefits for people﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], meaning: We sent down the inspiration to use it and to defend with it. Likewise His saying ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], meaning: He created them for you on the earth by His arrangement, and taught you to employ them and to benefit from what is in them. This does not apply to everything that humans have been inspired to that is less than these in benefit. That clothing with which Adam descended was the origin of the clothing that humans use.

This is an alert that clothing is part of the original human nature (fitra), and the natural disposition is the first of the foundations of Islam, and that it is among what God honoured the human species with since its appearance on the earth. In this there is an allusion against the idolaters, since they made the removal of their clothing part of their devotion, by performing the pilgrimage naked, as will come at His saying ﴿Say: who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32]. Thus they opposed the natural disposition. Nations have also celebrated their religious festivals with the finest clothing, as God related of Moses, peace be upon him, and the people of Egypt: ﴿He said: your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59].

Clothing (libas) is the name for what a person wears, that is, what he covers a part of his body with. So a shirt is clothing, a waist-wrap is clothing, a turban is clothing. It is said "he wore (labisa) the crown" and "he wore the ring", God, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And you extract ornaments that you wear﴾ [Fatir: 12]. The verbal noun of labisa is al-lubs, with a dammah on the lam.

The clause ﴿covers your nakedness﴾ is an attribute of libas. It is the kind of necessary clothing. This attribute is one of praise for clothing, meaning that it is of its nature to do so, even though much clothing is not for covering nakedness, such as the turban, the cloak, and the robe. The verse contains an indication of the obligation to cover the severe nakedness (al-awra al-mughallaza), which is the private part (sawa). As for covering what is other than that, for man or woman, the verse does not indicate it. Some of it has been established by the Sunna, and some by analogy (qiyas) and by delving into its details and causes from the matters of jurisprudence (fiqh).

**[p. 75]**

The word "rish" is clothing of adornment beyond what covers the nakedness. It is metaphorically borrowed from the feathers of birds, because they are the bird's adornment. Clothing of adornment is also called "riyash".

The conjunction of "rishan" with ﴿clothing that covers your nakedness﴾ is the conjunction of one kind with another kind. The meaning is: We facilitated for you clothing that covers you, and clothing with which you adorn yourselves.

His saying ﴿and the clothing of piety﴾ was read by Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Ja'far with the accusative (nasb), conjoined to "libasan", so it is among the clothing that was sent down, that is, inspired. Then it is necessarily literal clothing, meaning something worn. "Taqwa", according to this reading, is a verbal noun in the sense of protection (wiqaya). What is meant is the armour of war: coats of mail, breastplates, and helmets. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from heat, and garments that protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. The demonstrative pronoun, in the singular, refers to what is mentioned, namely clothing in its three kinds: a good thing God gave to the children of Adam. The clause is then either resumptive (mustanafa) or a circumstantial clause (hal) of "libasan" and what is conjoined to it.

It was read by Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamza, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Khalaf with the nominative (raf'): ﴿and the clothing of piety﴾, on the basis that the clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿We have certainly sent down to you clothing﴾. So it is possible that what is meant by "the clothing of piety" is similar to what is meant in the accusative reading. It is also possible that what is meant by piety is the piety of God and fear of Him, and clothing is applied to it, either by imagining piety as a garment that is worn, or by likening the constancy of the piety of God to the constancy of one who wears his clothing, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], together with what makes this application good, namely the parallelism (mushakala).

This meaning, with the nominative, is more fitting for it. It is then a digression (istitrad) to exhort toward piety of God, for it is better for people than the benefits of adornment. The demonstrative pronoun on this reading is for magnifying the thing pointed to.

His saying ﴿That is among the signs of God, that perhaps they will remember﴾ is a second resumptive sentence on the reading ﴿and the clothing of piety﴾ in the accusative, in that after mentioning the kinds of clothing as a favour, two resumptive sentences were begun which indicate the magnitude of the blessing: the first, that clothing is good for people; the second, that clothing is one of the signs of God indicating His knowledge and gentleness, and indicating

**[p. 76]**

His existence. In it is another sign, namely the indication of God's knowledge that a community will come in which misguidance will prevail, so that they will perform their pilgrimage naked. For this reason He emphasised the charge concerning it. The thing pointed to by the demonstrative in the second clause is the very thing pointed to by the demonstrative in the first clause. Because of the importance of both clauses, the second was made independent, not conjoined.

On the reading with the nominative of ﴿and the clothing of piety﴾, the clause ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾ is one single resumptive sentence, and the demonstrative in the second clause refers to what was mentioned before among the kinds of clothing, including the figurative kind, on the interpretation of "the clothing of piety" as figurative.

The pronoun of absence in ﴿that perhaps they will remember﴾ is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), meaning: God made that a sign so that perhaps you will remember the great power of God, exalted is He, and His singularity in creation, measuring, and gentleness. In this shift there is an allusion to those among the children of Adam who do not remember, as though they were absent from the presence of the address. Moreover, pronouns of absence in such a context in the Qur'an are often intended to refer to the idolaters of the Arabs.

[Page 77]

The address "O Children of Adam" is repeated. This call completes the verses before it. It is built on a warning against following Satan, and it extends to showing his scheming to people from the very beginning of their creation, since he schemed against their origin.

The address by the title "Children of Adam" is for the reason I mentioned in the verse before it, with added emphasis on the favour of clothing. This serves as a firm implicit rebuke of the folly of those who perform the pilgrimage naked.

They were forbidden to let Satan seduce them. The seduction (*futun*) of Satan is the occurrence of the effects of his whispering. That is, do not allow Satan to seduce you. The meaning is a prohibition against obeying him, and this is an intensified form of prohibition. Among its uses is the Arabs' saying, "Let me not find you doing such-and-such" (*la a'rifanaka taf'alu kadha*), meaning, "Do not do it, lest I come to know your deed." Another is their saying, "Let me not see you here" (*la oraynaka huna*), meaning, "Do not be present here, lest I see you." So the meaning is: do not obey Satan in his seductions, lest he seduce you. Such usage is a metonymy for forbidding an act and forbidding approaches to its causes.

The seduction that Satan directs at people is likened to his seduction of Adam and his wife, when he led them to eat from the forbidden tree, so that he removed them from a bliss they had been in. This is a reminder to mankind of the greatest temptation with which Satan tempted their kind. It encompasses every individual of the kind, since each was deprived of the bliss that would have been realised for him had his parents remained in the Garden and had their offspring multiplied there. Also in this is a reminder that the enmity of humans toward Satan is inherited, which makes it more effective in prompting them to beware of his scheming.

The "*ma*" in His words, "*kama akhraja*" ("as He removed"), is a verbal-source particle (*masdariyyah*). The prepositional phrase in the place of a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, which is an absolute object of "*layaftinannakum*" ("he will surely seduce you"). The estimated sense is: a seduction like His removal of your two parents from the Garden. Indeed, his removal of them from the Garden was a great seduction, to which the seduction of Satan is likened when it is intended to bring its meaning near to people and to frighten them of it.

"*Al-abawan*" is the dual of "*ab*" (father), and what is meant by them is the father and the mother, by the rhetorical device of precedence (*taghlib*), which is a common usage in speech. It was mentioned earlier at His words, "*wa li-abawayhi*" in Surat al-Nisa'. The word "*ab*" is here applied to the grandfather, because he is a higher father, as in the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib."

The clause "*yanzi'u 'anhuma libasahuma*" ("stripping them of their clothing") is in the place of a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (*hal muqarinah*), relating to the pronoun concealed in "*akhraja*" or to "*abawaykum*." The purpose of this circumstance is to make the manner of the removal appalling, by describing it as occurring while their private parts were exposed, since the exposure of the private parts is among the greatest atrocities and disgraces in common human custom.

The past event is expressed by the present tense to evoke the marvellous image of his being able to leave them naked.

Clothing was mentioned shortly before. Here it may be taken literally: it was a garment that God covered them with in that Garden, concealing their private parts. It is related that it was a veil of light, and it is also related that it was like the peel of fingernails, but these reports are not authentic. The more apparent view is that the stripping of clothing is a figurative depiction of the state of being the cause of the exposure of nakedness.

He repeated the emphasis on clothing to prepare for His later words: "*Take your adornment at every place of worship*" (7:31).

Attributing the removal, the stripping, and the showing to Satan is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), based on the leniency of attribution by treating the cause as if it were the agent. This holds whether the stripping is taken literally or figuratively, since the terms of a rational metaphorical attribution may be literal, figurative, or mixed, as established in the science of *ma'ani* (rhetoric of meaning).

The lam in His words "*li-yuriyahuma saw'atihima*" ("so that he might show them their private parts") is the lam of purpose in a claimed sense (*lam al-ta'lil al-idda'i*), following the rational metaphor. Since the removal, the stripping, and the showing were attributed to him by way of rational metaphor, he was made as if he were the agent of the removal, the stripping of their clothing, and the showing of their private parts. It was therefore fitting that he be given a purpose for those harmful acts. His being intent on that shamefulness and atrocity is like the way agents have hidden purposes behind their acts, in completing the scheme. In reality Satan is only the cause of their seeing their private parts. Thus the claimed attribution and the claimed purpose are coherent, and the lam of cause serves to strengthen the metaphorical attribution and to reinforce it. For this reason we do not take the lam here to mean consequence (*al-'aqibah*), as we did in His words, "*Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was hidden from them of their private parts*" (7:20), since in that place the lam was not accompanied by a metaphorical attribution.

The verse contains an indication that Satan is concerned with exposing the private parts of the children of Adam, because it pleases him to see them in a state of ugliness and atrocity.

[Page 79]

The clause "*innahu yarakum huwa wa qabiluhu*" ("indeed he and his tribe see you") stands in the position of a reason for the prohibition against being seduced by Satan's seduction, and for the warning against his scheming. This is because the way of a cautious person is to keep watch on the feared thing with his eye, so that he may guard against it when he sees its early signs. God therefore informed people that the devils see humans, while humans do not see them, to make clear the disparity between the side of their scheming and the side of people's caution against them. The side of their scheming is strong and firmly established, while the side of people's caution against them is weak, because they come upon the one being plotted against from a direction he does not perceive.

Therefore the purpose of His words "*innahu yarakum huwa wa qabiluhu min haythu la tarawnahum*" ("indeed he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them") is not to teach a fact about the hidden realities of bodies, which are beyond the senses and which are called immaterial beings (*mujarradat*) in the terminology of the philosophers, and which our scholars call the lower spirits (*al-arwah al-sufliyyah*). This is because it is not among the purposes of the Qur'an to undertake teaching of this kind, except what has an effect on spiritual purification and admonition.

The pronoun to which "*inna*" is attached refers to Satan. "*Wa qabiluhu*" ("and his tribe") is conjoined to the concealed pronoun in His words "*yarakum*" ("he sees you"). Therefore it was separated by the detached pronoun. The "*qabil*" is mentioned, and it has the meaning of "*qabilah*" (tribe), to indicate that he has helpers who support him at a time when people are heedless. In this sense is an approximation of the state of the enmity of the devils to what the Arabs know of the severity of an enemy seizing his enemy while the other is unaware, as the Arabs say: "The enemy came upon them while they were heedless" (*atahumu al-'aduwwu wa hum ghafiruna*).

The emphasis of the report with a particle of emphasis is to treat the addressees, in their turning away from caution against Satan and his seduction, as those who waver over whether Satan sees them and whether they do not see him.

"*Min haythu la tarawnahum*" ("from where you do not see them") is the beginning of an indefinite place in which the human sight is negated, meaning: from every place where you do not see them. It thus conveys: he sees you and his tribe while you do not see him, whether they are near or far. The devils were therefore veiled from human sight, and this was the usual state of both kinds. The seeing of the devils' essences is therefore certainly negated, though God may grant the sight of devils or jinn appearing in the forms of physical things as a miracle for the prophets, as is recorded in the authentic report: "Indeed an ifrit of the jinn broke loose upon me last night during my prayer, and I resolved to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque..." (the hadith). Or as a marvel for the righteous among the nations, as in the hadith of the man who came to steal from the zakat al-fitr, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, and the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Abu Hurayrah: "That was a devil," as in the two Sahihs. This can only be on the basis of a devil or jinn taking on a form other than its true form, by God's subjugation, so that human sight may perceive it. What is seen in reality is the form behind which the essence of the devil lies. This is like seeing a place of which one knows that there is a devil in it, and the way of knowing this is a true report, since without the report it would not be known.

The clause "*inna ja'alna al-shayatina awliya' li-alladhina la yu'minun*" ("indeed We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe") is a resumed statement by way of new beginning (*istinaf ibtida'i*), intended to shift to the states of the polytheists in their conspiring under the command of Satan, as a warning to believers against being included in their company, and as a repulsion from their conditions. The connection is the warning, and this sentence has no connection with the sentence "*innahu yarakum huwa wa qabiluhu*."

The emphasis of the report with the particle of emphasis is for the sake of attention to the report, with respect to the one who hears it among the believers.

"*Al-ja'l*" (making) here is creational making, as known from His words: "Some of you are enemies to others" (7:24), with the meaning: We created the devils.

"*Awliya'*" ("allies") is a circumstantial state of "*al-shayatin*," and it is a prospective state (*hal muqaddarah*), meaning: We created them with their allyship over those who do not believe as a prospect. This is because God made the kinds and species of created beings with natures they do not depart from and cannot change, such as predation in the lion and stinging in the scorpion. He created for humans reason and thought and made them able to acquire what they choose. Since it is part of the devils' nature to love what is corruption, and since it is within human capacity and acquisition that he may seek a matter that leads to corruption, when he has in it an immediate desire or when it resembles good things at a foolish first glance, a person in this state conforms to the nature of the devils and is directed by what they whisper to him. Then the acquisition of corruption and evil prevails over those who go deep into it and proceed step by step, until it becomes the master of their wills. That is the rank of the polytheists. The ranks of this allyship vary, so there necessarily arose between them and the devils an allyship and an agreement due to the closeness of their motives. Thereby the enmity that is in the nature, which His words "*Indeed Satan is an open enemy to you both*" (7:22) and "*Some of you are enemies to others*" (7:24) established, turned into allyship and affection when a son of Adam reached the lowest depths of corruption, which is polytheism and what it entails. This became a new making that abrogates (*nasikh*) the making in His words "*Some of you are enemies to others*" (7:24), as the reference to it was previously indicated there. Therefore what is in this verse restricts the absolute statement in the other verse, as an alert that it is the right of a believer not to take Satan as an ally.

What is meant by "*alladhina la yu'minun*" ("those who do not believe") is the polytheists, because they were the opponents of the believers in Mecca. A further explanation of this verse will come at His words, "O Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves" (7:35) in this surah.

[Page 82]

﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say: "We found our fathers doing it, and God commanded us to do it." Say: "God does not command indecency. Do you say about God what you do not know?"﴾

﴿And when they commit an indecency﴾ is conjoined to ﴿for those who do not believe﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. It therefore belongs to the relative clause (ṣilah), and it contains an integration (idmāj) that exposes their falsehood in their excuses and their corrupt pleas. That is, [the verse describes] those who refuse faith, who commit indecencies, and who excuse their deeds by claiming that they followed their fathers and that God commanded them to do so. This applies specifically to the condition of the polytheists who denied, as indicated by His saying ﴿Say: "God does not command indecency"﴾. The purpose of the two clauses of the relative clause is to present the horror of their religion as the commission of indecencies, and to present the horror of their reasoning for these deeds as something that does not hold up before people of sound intellect. The condition is introduced with the particle idhā (when), which by its nature conveys certainty that the condition will occur, to indicate that this is bound to happen from them.

The word fāḥisha (indecency) is, originally, an adjective for an omitted noun, meaning "a shameful act." Then the adjective took the place of a noun because of how frequently it was used, so fāḥisha became a name for a blameworthy deed. It derives from al-fuḥsh (with a dammah on the fa'), which means abundance and intensity in a blameworthy or detestable thing. Fāḥisha came to prevail for acts of extreme ugliness, those from which the sound natural disposition (fiṭrah) recoils, or those from which harm and corruption arise, such that people of sound reason reject them, people of wisdom disapprove of them, and their doer is ashamed before people and conceals them. Examples include prostitution, fornication, infanticide, and theft. Then the true laws (sharā'i') forbid them. Thus an act is described as fāḥisha even before revelation of the law, like the practices of the people of the jāhiliyyah, such as prostrating to images and stones, seeking intercession from them although they are inanimate, going naked during the Hajj, not mentioning God's name over sacrificial animals although they are among God's creations and subjected by Him, prostitution, consuming the wealth of orphans and the weak, depriving relatives of inheritance, consulting the arrow-shafts (azlām) before undertaking or abandoning an action, killing a non-killer because he belongs to the killer's tribe, and their forbidding for themselves many of the good things God made lawful while making lawful the foul things such as carrion and blood.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbās that the intended meaning of "indecency" in the verse is going naked during the Hajj. The proper understanding of his statement is that going naked during the Hajj was among the first things meant by "indecency," not that the term is restricted to it. The leaders of polytheism had prepared excuses for their followers regarding those deeds and taught them to them. The summary of these excuses is that they attributed the deeds to their ancestors, who were models for their successors, and they believed that their ancestors knew better what benefits lay within those practices, benefits which, had those who denied them known of them, they would have recognized as they denied them. Then they added that God commanded them, meaning that their ancestors did not establish these customs of their own accord, but established them by a command from God, the Exalted. From this it is understood that they excused both themselves and their ancestors. So the meaning of their saying ﴿and God commanded us to do it﴾ is not a claim that a command from God had reached them. Rather, they meant that God commanded their ancestors who established those customs and made them traditions, so God's command to their ancestors was a command to them as well, because He intended that these practices remain among their descendants. This is the meaning of their argument. The concision of the Qur'an has left it implicit, relying on the discernment of the addressees.

The verb and the saying are attributed to the pronoun of ﴿those who do not believe﴾ in His saying ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say﴾, in the sense of attribution to the pronoun of a group. The speaker may be other than the doer, and the doer other than the speaker, since some of them confirmed one another in this, so it is as though all of them committed it and all of them offered the excuse.

The conditional construction connects their committing the indecency with their saying ﴿We found our fathers doing it﴾, on the basis of a concision in the speech that the context indicates. The implied meaning is that when they committed an indecency and were rebuked for it or forbidden from it, they said: "We found our fathers doing it." The rebuke and the prohibition are not limited to the prohibition of Islam against their error, but refer to the prohibition of any forbidder and the rebuke of any censurer. Those tribes who did not agree with them about these indecencies would rebuke them, for the religion of the polytheists was scattered and divided. Those among the Arabs who abandoned polytheism, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, would rebuke them. Zayd ibn 'Amr said to them: "God created the sheep, sent down water for it from the sky, and made grass grow for it, and then you slaughter it for other than Him." Also rebuking them was one who was uncomfortable with their practices but could not avoid following them under compulsion.

Those whose deeds did not agree with their desires also rebuked them, as happened to Imru' al-Qays when he resolved to fight the Banu Asad after they killed his father Hujr. He went to Dhu al-Khalasa, the idol of Khath'am, and sought a decision from it by the arrows. The arrow that came out was for forbidding, so he broke the arrows and said:

"If you were, O Dhu al-Khalasa, avenged, like me, and your ancestor lay buried,
you would not have forbidden me from killing the enemies in vain."

Then Islam came and condemned their corrupt deeds and made them hear the thunderous verses of the Qur'an. At that point they resorted to excuses. It is known from the context that their excuse is reprehensible and their argument is corrupt.

The verse indicates the denial of anything similar to this line of reasoning, that is, every argument that leans on following the fathers in matters whose corruption and indecency are evident, and every argument that rests on something the one arguing has no means to know. Their saying ﴿and God commanded us to do it﴾ is a baseless claim, since God's command to that effect had not reached them through any messenger, for they denied prophethood. So from where would they have received the intention of God, the Exalted?

God refuted this for them by His saying to His Messenger: ﴿Say: "God does not command indecency"﴾. He turned away from refuting their saying ﴿We found our fathers doing it﴾, because if it were to be refuted as a lie, they would not be lying in their statement, since their fathers did commit those indecencies. And if it were to be refuted on the ground that it is not suitable as proof, that is evident, because the rebuke and the prohibition clearly extend to their fathers, since what is permissible for the like is permissible for the similar. So the refutation of this premise of their argument became self-evident, and the refutation of the major premise, which is the basis of their reasoning, namely their saying ﴿and God commanded us to do it﴾, was more important.

So His saying ﴿Say: "God does not command indecency"﴾ is a rejection of their claim that God commanded them to those indecencies, and it is a refutation of them, an instruction to them, and a waking of them from their delusion. For God is characterized by perfection, so He does not command what is deficient, which the intelligent have not approved and have rejected. Thus the fact that the act is an indecency suffices to show that God does not command it, since God has supreme perfection. Their excuse that God commanded it arose only from ignorance. For this reason God rebuked them with the rebuking interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾, meaning: what you do not know that God commanded. The object is omitted because what preceded it indicates it, for they did not know that God commanded them to do this, since they had no basis for it, and they only said it out of mere supposition, and because they did not know that it is unbecoming of God's majesty and perfection to command such vices.

"Taqūlūn" (you say) is construed as implying either "tukadhdhibūn" (you lie) or "tataqawwalūn" (you fabricate), which is why it takes ʿalā (about/against). Had it been a correctly attributed statement, it would have taken ʿan. Since the rebuke is directed at saying about God what they do not know, saying about God something whose non-occurrence from God is certain is more fitting.

With this refutation, their practice of those indecencies became purely a matter of error, delusion, and following the inspiration of the devils to their allies, the leaders of disbelief and the commanders of polytheism, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who instituted the worship of idols; Abu Kabsha, who established the worship of Sirius (al-Shi'rā) among the stars; Zalim ibn As'ad, who instituted the worship of al-'Uzzā; and al-Qalammas, who established the intercalation (al-nasī'). And so on with what is connected to these fabrications of the custodians of idols and the houses of polytheism.

Know that there is no basis in the verse for invalidating taqlīd (imitation) in legal matters (furū') or in the fundamentals of religion (uṣūl al-dīn). This is because the taqlīd that God condemned in the polytheists was their imitation of those who were not fit to be imitated, since they did not rise above the rank of their imitators except by being earlier in generation and being their fathers. The polytheists did not excuse themselves by saying that they found the righteous and the guides of the community practicing this, nor that it was something Abraham and his sons had practiced. Moreover, the taqlīd that God condemned was imitation in practices whose corruption is self-evident, and imitation in corruption is equal to establishing it as a precedent in blame. Yet establishing corruption as a precedent is more blameworthy than imitating it, as the authentic hadith indicates: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a portion of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to institute killing." And the hadith: whoever "establishes a bad precedent, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection."

Therefore, what those among the commentators who incline toward kalām (speculative theology) impose on this verse, in terms of speech about blaming taqlīd, looks at treating polytheism as included within the committing of indecencies.

[Page 86]

﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration and invoke Him, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. As He originated you, [to Him] you will return."﴾ ﴿A group He has guided, and a group upon whom error was justly decreed. Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think that they are guided.﴾

After he refuted, in general terms, their claim that Allah had commanded them to do the abominations they practised, through His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality."﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], he resumed with a digressive resumption (istinaf istitradi) that contains the essential elements of the true religion, which is comprehended by the meaning of qist (justice, equity), i.e., 'adl (fairness). This is to teach them the opposite of their ignorance, and to draw attention to the majesty of Allah, the Exalted, by making them aware of what it is befitting for Allah to command. Because of the importance of this purpose, and because it stands in opposition to their claim that was negated in the sentence ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality."﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], this sentence has been separated from the one before it. The verb of saying was not conjoined to the previous saying, nor the content of the speech to the previous content, because repeating the verb "say" and not conjoining it to its counterpart draws minds toward it.

Qist means 'adl, and here it is 'adl in its more general sense, namely the act that is a mean between excess and deficiency in things. It is the virtue of every act. Thus Allah has commanded the virtues and what sound intellects testify to be pure goodness and upright rectitude, like His saying: ﴿And [He is] they who, when they spend, do so not excessively or sparingly but are ever between that [extremes]﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. So tawhid is a mean between shirk and ta'til (negation of the Creator's attributes), and retaliation against the killer is a mean between letting blood go unavenged and killing a group from the killer's tribe on account of a crime committed by one of its members whom they could not reach. Allah has also commanded ihsan (excellence), which is a mean between miserliness and extravagance. So qist is an attribute of the act itself, in that it is suitable for welfare, both immediately and ultimately, that is, free from the consequences of corruption. It has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that qist is the saying "There is no god but Him," and he meant by this that tawhid is among the greatest forms of qist. This is a refutation of the abominations that they claimed Allah had commanded them to do, because none of those abominations is [page 87] qist.

Likewise with clothing: going naked is deficiency, and excess in the wearing of clothing is extravagance, while 'adl is the clothing that covers the private parts and protects against the harm of cold or heat. Likewise with food: forbidding some of it is extremism, and indulging in it without restraint is gluttony, while the middle course is moderation. So His saying ﴿My Lord has commanded justice﴾ is a comprehensive statement that refutes everything they claimed Allah had commanded them with, which does not belong to the category of qist.

Then he followed it with the command to the Prophet ﷺ to say to them, on Allah's behalf: ﴿And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration﴾. The phrase "and set your faces" is conjoined to the phrase "My Lord has commanded justice," meaning: say to those addressed, "Set your faces [toward Him]." The primary purpose of it is to refute some of what they claimed Allah had commanded them, by way of commanding them to the opposite of what they claimed, so that their being commanded to what pleases Allah is achieved explicitly. And it refutes by implication something they claimed Allah had commanded them with, because a command to something is a prohibition of its opposite. Or, if you wish, you may say: whoever intends to forbid something and does its opposite commands its opposite, so both aims are achieved through his command.

Setting the faces is a metaphor for complete devotion to the worship of Allah, the Exalted, in the places of His worship, by the condition of one who prepares to witness an important matter, when he turns his face toward it, not looking to the right or the left. That pure orientation is called iqamah (setting upright) because he has made the face upright, that is, not negligent nor slack in turning toward Him. This is in the sense of "standing" meaning "strength in performing an act," as is said: "the market stood" (qamat al-suq) and "the prayer stood" (qamat al-salah). This was already discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿and they establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. And from it is His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining [to truth]﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. So the meaning is that Allah commanded setting the faces at the masajid (places of prostration), because that is the glorification of the one worshipped and the place of worship. He did not command glorifying Him or glorifying His masajid by anything other than that, such as going naked, and associating others with Allah in worship is incompatible with it as well. This is like what has been related in the hadith: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord, so let him not spit in front of his face." So the prohibition of going naked is intended here, because the wording includes it, and because the context indicates it through the repetition of the reminder of favour and the command about clothing, from His saying ﴿to show them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] up to here.

The meaning of ﴿at every place of prostration﴾ is at every place set apart for the worship of Allah, the Exalted. The term masjid has been transferred in Islam to the specific, defined place set apart for prayer, and this was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people [for having barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram] incite you to transgression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], in Surat al-'Uqud. So the rites in which they performed the acts of Hajj are all masajid, and they had no masajid other than the rites of Hajj. Thus the mention of masajid in the verse specifies that what is meant is setting the faces when turning toward Allah in Hajj, by not associating with Him anything else among their idols in intention. This is as they had placed Hubal on the roof of the Ka'bah, so that the circumambulation of the Ka'bah would be for Allah and for Hubal, and they placed Isaf and Na'ilah on al-Safa and al-Marwah, so that the sa'y would be for Allah and for them. A group of them used to chant the talbiyah (Hajj invocation) toward Manat at al-Mushallal. So the command to set the faces at all the masajid is a command to adhere to tawhid and to perfection of state in all the rites of Hajj. This is the reason for conjoining His saying ﴿And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration﴾ after the denial that Allah would command immorality in their conduct, and the affirmation that He commanded what is contrary to it, justice.

Although this command was directed at the polytheists, since they were the ones characterised by its opposite, the believers too have a share in continuing to uphold it, just as the polytheists had a share in turning away from it and neglecting it.

The invocation in His saying ﴿and invoke Him, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ carries the meaning of worship, i.e., worship Him, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 194].

Ikhlas (sincere devotion) is the purifying of a thing from being mixed with something else.

Din, in the sense of obedience, comes from their saying "dint li-fulan," meaning "I obeyed him."

From it Allah, the Exalted, is named al-Dayyan, that is, the Subduer, the one who humbles and makes obedient all existent things. The parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. Its aim is the refutation of shirk in the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and in refuting it there is an affirmation of the meaning of qist mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice,"﴾ as we have stated there. Mukhlisin (sincerely devoted) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ud'uhu (invoke Him).

The sentence ﴿As He originated you, [to Him] you will return﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in His saying "mukhlisin," and it is a presumed circumstance (hal muqaddarah), i.e., "estimating your return to Him and that your return is like your origination." This is a warning that they will be held accountable for not being sincere in worship. So the intended part of it is His saying "you will return," meaning to Him, and the phrase "as He originated you" has been incorporated into it as a reminder of the possibility of the resurrection, which they denied. So this is a warning to them that they will return to Him and be recompensed for their associating others with Him in His worship. It is also an argument against them regarding the futility of their worship of other than Allah, and an affirmation of the resurrection which they denied, by removing the basis of their deeming it unlikely, when they say: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82], and they say ﴿Will we indeed be returned to our former state? When we have become decayed bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10], and similar things. [The argument is] that that re-creation is not more marvellous than their first creation, as He said: ﴿Were We incapable of the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15], and as He said: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], i.e., by the opposite of their assumption of the improbability of the second creation. It is also a reminder to them that Allah alone is responsible for their second creation, just as He alone is responsible for their first creation, so He alone is responsible for recompense, and their gods will avail them nothing.

So the kaf in His saying ﴿As He originated you, [to Him] you will return﴾ is for comparing the return of their creation with its beginning, and "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). The estimate is: "you will return a new return like His originating you." The complement that indicates the comparison has been placed before its verb, "you will return," for emphasis on it. Some interpretations of the verse have explained it in meanings that are far from its context and its composition.

[Page 90] "Fariqan" (a group), both the first and the second, are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses: either from the nominative pronoun in "you will return," meaning "you will return to Allah as two groups," so the detailed account of the two groups was omitted, and then the details were given which indicate the summary, by way of hastening the mention of the detail, because the context is one of encouragement and warning. The meaning of ﴿A group He has guided﴾ is that a group Allah guided in this world, and "a group upon whom error was justly decreed," i.e., in this world, as is indicated by the causal clause "Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah." Or they are from the hidden pronoun in "mukhlisin," meaning "invoke Him, being sincerely devoted, as two groups": a group Allah guided to sincerity and renouncing shirk, and a group that persisted in error and clung to shirk.

The clause "He has guided" is in the position of a descriptive clause for the first "fariqan," and the connecting object pronoun has been omitted: i.e., "Allah guided them." The clause "upon whom error was justly decreed" is a descriptive clause for the second "fariqan."

All of this is a warning against falling into error, a caution against following Satan, and an incitement to seek the guidance that comes from Allah, the Exalted, as indicated by ascribing it to the divine name in "He has guided." So the listeners know that, when they return to Him as two groups, the successful group is those whom Allah, the Exalted, has guided, as He said: ﴿Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], and that the losing group are those upon whom error has been justly decreed and who took the devils as allies instead of Allah, as He said: ﴿Those are the party of Satan. Unquestionably, the party of Satan are the losers﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 19]. The fronting of the first and second "fariqan" before their governing verbs is for emphasis on the detail.

The meaning of ﴿upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ is that error was established for them and they clung to it, and did not desist from it. That is because those addressed were all polytheists, so when they were commanded to worship Allah sincerely, they split into two groups: a group Allah guided to tawhid, and a group that clung to shirk and error. No new state arose for them. By this the fitness of the word haqqa ("was justly decreed") here becomes apparent, rather than saying "Allah misguided them," because their error was ancient and continuous, something they acquired for themselves, as He said in a parallel verse: ﴿Among them are those whom Allah guided, and among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ [al-Nahl: 36], then He said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, then indeed Allah does not guide those who lead astray﴾ [al-Nahl: 37].

So the change of style between "a group He has guided" and "a group upon whom error was justly decreed" is not a means of avoiding attributing misguidance to Allah, as the author of al-Kashshaf imagined, because He has attributed misguidance to Allah in a parallel verse, as is known, and in many verses. Rather, the difference in style is due to the difference in circumstances.

The verb haqqa is used without the feminine marker because its subject is not of real feminine gender. The feminine marker has been expressed in its parallel in His saying: ﴿Among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ [al-Nahl: 36].

His saying ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) intended to give the reason for the clause "upon whom error was justly decreed" [al-Nahl: 36]. This is the nature of inna when it occurs at the beginning of a clause following another clause: it serves for connection and causation, and it takes the place of the fa' (therefore), as has been mentioned on more than one occasion.

The meaning is that this group, upon whom misguidance has been decreed, when they heard the call to monotheism and Islam, did not seek salvation and did not reflect upon the clear misguidance of polytheism. Rather, they took their devils as their inspirers, their souls were pleased with their whisperings, they complied with their command, and they took them as protectors. Therefore it is inevitable that they persist in their misguidance, because of their taking the devils as protectors apart from Allah.

And the clause "and they reckon" (wa yahsabuna) is conjoined to the clause "they have taken," so that their misguidance becomes compound misguidance, for they have gone astray in complying with the command of the leaders of disbelief and the protectors of the devils. And when they heard the summoner to guidance, they did not reflect and neglected to examine, because they reckon that they are rightly guided, and no doubt approaches them that they are guided. Therefore it did not occur to their minds that there was any need to examine the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ).

Al-husban (reckoning) means opinion (zann), and here it is an opinion unsupported by any proof, and that is the most common meaning intended by zann and its synonyms in the Qur'an.

Page 92

The conjunction of this clause with the preceding one, and treating them as equal in reporting about the group upon whom misguidance has been decreed, is for the purpose of indicating that their misguidance is present in each of the two statements: taking the devils as protectors is misguidance, and their reckoning their misguidance to be guidance is also misguidance, whether all of that results from error or from obstinacy, since there is no excuse for the one who is astray in his misguidance by error, because Allah has set up the proofs for the truth and for distinguishing between truth and falsehood.

Setting the faces is a metaphor for complete devotion to the worship of Allah, the Exalted, in the places of His worship, by the condition of one who prepares to witness an important matter, when he turns his face toward it, not looking to the right or the left. That pure orientation is called iqamah (setting upright) because he has made the face upright, that is, not negligent nor slack in turning toward Him. This is in the sense of "standing" meaning "strength in performing an act," as is said: "the market stood" (qamat al-suq) and "the prayer stood" (qamat al-salah). This was already discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿and they establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. And from it is His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining [to truth]﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. So the meaning is that Allah commanded setting the faces at the masajid (places of prostration), because that is the glorification of the one worshipped and the place of worship. He did not command glorifying Him or glorifying His masajid by anything other than that, such as going naked, and associating others with Allah in worship is incompatible with it as well. This is like what has been related in the hadith: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord, so let him not spit in front of his face." So the prohibition of going naked is intended here, because the wording includes it, and because the context indicates it through the repetition of the reminder of favour and the command about clothing, from His saying ﴿to show them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] up to here.

The meaning of ﴿at every place of prostration﴾ is at every place set apart for the worship of Allah, the Exalted. The term masjid has been transferred in Islam to the specific, defined place set apart for prayer, and this was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people [for having barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram] incite you to transgression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], in Surat al-'Uqud. So the rites in which they performed the acts of Hajj are all masajid, and they had no masajid other than the rites of Hajj. Thus the mention of masajid in the verse specifies that what is meant is setting the faces when turning toward Allah in Hajj, by not associating with Him anything else among their idols in intention. This is as they had placed Hubal on the roof of the Ka'bah, so that the circumambulation of the Ka'bah would be for Allah and for Hubal, and they placed Isaf and Na'ilah on al-Safa and al-Marwah, so that the sa'y would be for Allah and for them. A group of them used to chant the talbiyah (Hajj invocation) toward Manat at al-Mushallal. So the command to set the faces at all the masajid is a command to adhere to tawhid and to perfection of state in all the rites of Hajj. This is the reason for conjoining His saying ﴿And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration﴾ after the denial that Allah would command immorality in their conduct, and the affirmation that He commanded what is contrary to it, justice.

Although this command was directed at the polytheists, since they were the ones characterised by its opposite, the believers too have a share in continuing to uphold it, just as the polytheists had a share in turning away from it and neglecting it.

The invocation in His saying ﴿and invoke Him, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ carries the meaning of worship, i.e., worship Him, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 194].

Ikhlas (sincere devotion) is the purifying of a thing from being mixed with something else.

Din, in the sense of obedience, comes from their saying "dint li-fulan," meaning "I obeyed him."

From it Allah, the Exalted, is named al-Dayyan, that is, the Subduer, the one who humbles and makes obedient all existent things. The parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. Its aim is the refutation of shirk in the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and in refuting it there is an affirmation of the meaning of qist mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice,"﴾ as we have stated there. Mukhlisin (sincerely devoted) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ud'uhu (invoke Him).

The sentence ﴿As He originated you, [to Him] you will return﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in His saying "mukhlisin," and it is a presumed circumstance (hal muqaddarah), i.e., "estimating your return to Him and that your return is like your origination." This is a warning that they will be held accountable for not being sincere in worship. So the intended part of it is His saying "you will return," meaning to Him, and the phrase "as He originated you" has been incorporated into it as a reminder of the possibility of the resurrection, which they denied. So this is a warning to them that they will return to Him and be recompensed for their associating others with Him in His worship. It is also an argument against them regarding the futility of their worship of other than Allah, and an affirmation of the resurrection which they denied, by removing the basis of their deeming it unlikely, when they say: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82], and they say ﴿Will we indeed be returned to our former state? When we have become decayed bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10], and similar things. [The argument is] that that re-creation is not more marvellous than their first creation, as He said: ﴿Were We incapable of the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15], and as He said: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], i.e., by the opposite of their assumption of the improbability of the second creation. It is also a reminder to them that Allah alone is responsible for their second creation, just as He alone is responsible for their first creation, so He alone is responsible for recompense, and their gods will avail them nothing.

So the kaf in His saying ﴿As He originated you, [to Him] you will return﴾ is for comparing the return of their creation with its beginning, and "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). The estimate is: "you will return a new return like His originating you." The complement that indicates the comparison has been placed before its verb, "you will return," for emphasis on it. Some interpretations of the verse have explained it in meanings that are far from its context and its composition.

[Page 90] "Fariqan" (a group), both the first and the second, are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses: either from the nominative pronoun in "you will return," meaning "you will return to Allah as two groups," so the detailed account of the two groups was omitted, and then the details were given which indicate the summary, by way of hastening the mention of the detail, because the context is one of encouragement and warning. The meaning of ﴿A group He has guided﴾ is that a group Allah guided in this world, and "a group upon whom error was justly decreed," i.e., in this world, as is indicated by the causal clause "Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah." Or they are from the hidden pronoun in "mukhlisin," meaning "invoke Him, being sincerely devoted, as two groups": a group Allah guided to sincerity and renouncing shirk, and a group that persisted in error and clung to shirk.

The clause "He has guided" is in the position of a descriptive clause for the first "fariqan," and the connecting object pronoun has been omitted: i.e., "Allah guided them." The clause "upon whom error was justly decreed" is a descriptive clause for the second "fariqan."

All of this is a warning against falling into error, a caution against following Satan, and an incitement to seek the guidance that comes from Allah, the Exalted, as indicated by ascribing it to the divine name in "He has guided." So the listeners know that, when they return to Him as two groups, the successful group is those whom Allah, the Exalted, has guided, as He said: ﴿Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], and that the losing group are those upon whom error has been justly decreed and who took the devils as allies instead of Allah, as He said: ﴿Those are the party of Satan. Unquestionably, the party of Satan are the losers﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 19]. The fronting of the first and second "fariqan" before their governing verbs is for emphasis on the detail.

The meaning of ﴿upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ is that error was established for them and they clung to it, and did not desist from it. That is because those addressed were all polytheists, so when they were commanded to worship Allah sincerely, they split into two groups: a group Allah guided to tawhid, and a group that clung to shirk and error. No new state arose for them. By this the fitness of the word haqqa ("was justly decreed") here becomes apparent, rather than saying "Allah misguided them," because their error was ancient and continuous, something they acquired for themselves, as He said in a parallel verse: ﴿Among them are those whom Allah guided, and among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ [al-Nahl: 36], then He said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, then indeed Allah does not guide those who lead astray﴾ [al-Nahl: 37].

So the change of style between "a group He has guided" and "a group upon whom error was justly decreed" is not a means of avoiding attributing misguidance to Allah, as the author of al-Kashshaf imagined, because He has attributed misguidance to Allah in a parallel verse, as is known, and in many verses. Rather, the difference in style is due to the difference in circumstances.

The verb haqqa is used without the feminine marker because its subject is not of real feminine gender. The feminine marker has been expressed in its parallel in His saying: ﴿Among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ [al-Nahl: 36].

His saying ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) intended to give the reason for the clause "upon whom error was justly decreed" [al-Nahl: 36]. This is the nature of inna when it occurs at the beginning of a clause following another clause: it serves for connection and causation, and it takes the place of the fa' (therefore), as has been mentioned on more than one occasion.

The meaning is that this group, upon whom misguidance has been decreed, when they heard the call to monotheism and Islam, did not seek salvation and did not reflect upon the clear misguidance of polytheism. Rather, they took their devils as their inspirers, their souls were pleased with their whisperings, they complied with their command, and they took them as protectors. Therefore it is inevitable that they persist in their misguidance, because of their taking the devils as protectors apart from Allah.

And the clause "and they reckon" (wa yahsabuna) is conjoined to the clause "they have taken," so that their misguidance becomes compound misguidance, for they have gone astray in complying with the command of the leaders of disbelief and the protectors of the devils. And when they heard the summoner to guidance, they did not reflect and neglected to examine, because they reckon that they are rightly guided, and no doubt approaches them that they are guided. Therefore it did not occur to their minds that there was any need to examine the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ).

Al-husban (reckoning) means opinion (zann), and here it is an opinion unsupported by any proof, and that is the most common meaning intended by zann and its synonyms in the Qur'an.

Page 92

The conjunction of this clause with the preceding one, and treating them as equal in reporting about the group upon whom misguidance has been decreed, is for the purpose of indicating that their misguidance is present in each of the two statements: taking the devils as protectors is misguidance, and their reckoning their misguidance to be guidance is also misguidance, whether all of that results from error or from obstinacy, since there is no excuse for the one who is astray in his misguidance by error, because Allah has set up the proofs for the truth and for distinguishing between truth and falsehood.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah al-A'raf, verse 31:

﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.﴾

The repetition of the address (al-nida') at the beginning of this sentence serves to draw attention, and the addressees are identified by the construction of the vocative with the attribute "Children of Adam," in continuation of the earlier address in His words, ﴿O Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

This sentence, in relation to the one that follows it, namely His words ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], stands in the position of the conclusion of an argument. It has been placed before the argument, so it becomes a purpose standing in the position of a claim, and the argument is made as proof for the claim. This is one of the methods of composition in arranging meanings and their results.

The purpose of His words ﴿take your adornment﴾ is to nullify what the polytheists claimed regarding the necessity of going naked during the Hajj in specific circumstances and at specific places of worship. Muslim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A woman would circumambulate the House while naked, saying: 'Who will lend me a cloth for circumambulation, which she would place over her private part, and she would say:

Today some of it or all of it appears,
and what appears of it, I do not make lawful."

Page 93
Muslim also reported from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, except the Hums. The Hums were Quraysh and those they had given birth to. The others would circumambulate naked unless the Hums gave them clothing, so men would give men and women would give women." Also from him: that when they reached Mina, they would cast off their clothes and come to the mosque naked. It is also reported that the Hums used to say: "We are the people of the Sanctuary, so it is not fitting for anyone of the Arabs to circumambulate except in our clothing, nor to eat when he enters our land except from our food." Whoever among the Arabs had no friend in Makkah to lend him a garment, and did not find what he could hire, was left between one of two matters: either to circumambulate the House naked, or to circumambulate in his clothes; then when he finished his circumambulation, he would cast off his garment and no one would touch it. That garment was called al-Luqa (with the lam vowelled with a fatha), and their poet said:

Enough grief is my returning to it, as if it were
a discarded garment among the circumambulators, forbidden.

In al-Kashshaf, on the authority of Tawus: "One of them would circumambulate naked and leave his clothes behind the mosque; and if he circumambulated while wearing them, he was beaten and they were taken from him, because they said: 'We do not worship Allah in clothes in which we have committed sins.'" The Prophet ﷺ nullified this when he commanded Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) in the year of his pilgrimage, the ninth year, to proclaim during the season: "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one circumambulates the House naked."

It is also reported from al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas: "The people of the Jahiliyyah had committed themselves to forbidding fat and grease during the days of the season, and would not eat any food except staples, and would not eat anything rich in fat." Al-Kashshaf attributes this to the Banu 'Amir. The Hums would say: "It is not fitting for anyone, when he enters our land, to eat except from our food." In the Tafsir of al-Tabari, on the authority of Jabir ibn Zayd: "When they performed Hajj, they forbade the sheep, its milk and its ghee." And in it, on the authority of Qatadah: "The verse intended what they forbade for themselves of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ha'mi."
