So the command in His words ﴿take your adornment﴾ is for obligation, and in His words ﴿and eat and drink﴾ it is for permission, for the children of Adam, past and present.

The purpose of directing the command, or of narrating it, is to nullify the prohibition which the people of the Jahiliyyah had established, by which they violated what is settled in the original nature (fitrah) of what Allah commanded all the children of Adam, and bestowed upon them as a favour, since He created for them everything on the earth. This resembles the command that comes after a prohibition, for its origin is the nullification of the prohibition, which is permission, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], after His saying: ﴿not violating the hunting while you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. It may also happen that what nullifies a prohibition is obligatory. It has thus become clear from the context of these verses that uncovering the 'awrah is among the indecencies, so clothing in the Hajj is necessarily obligatory: it is what covers the 'awrah, and whatever exceeds that is permissible and allowed, nullifying its prohibition. As for the command to eat and drink, it is for permission, nullifying the prohibition, and no one is obligated to eat meat and fat.

His words ﴿at every place of worship﴾ are a generalisation, meaning: do not single out some mosques for going naked, such as the Sacred Mosque and the mosque of Mina. A parallel of this has already occurred in His words: ﴿and set your faces toward every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].

The connection of the command to eat and drink to the command to take adornment has now become clear from what has passed.

Page 95
Excess (israf) was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and do not eat them excessively﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], in Surah al-Nisa'. It is going beyond the customary limit in something. That is: do not be excessive in eating, by eating too much meat and fat, for that returns harm to the body, and grievous illnesses arise from it.

It has been said that this verse gathers the principles of preserving health with regard to nourishment. The prohibition of excess is thus a prohibition of guidance, not of unlawfulness, as evidenced by the permission that follows in His words ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 32] up to His words ﴿and the good things of provision﴾ [al-A'raf: 32]. Also, the measure of excess is not fixed, so the obligation does not attach to it; rather it is left to people's own management of their interests. This returns to the meaning of justice (qist) occurring in His earlier words: ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 29], for abandoning excess is part of the meaning of justice.

His words ﴿Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive﴾ are a concluding clause (tadhyil), and the discussion of its like has preceded in Surah al-An'am.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verse 32**

﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision? Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who know.﴾

This is an interjected resumptive sentence (*istinaf mu'taridh*, a parenthetical sentence that breaks into the flow of the speech) placed between the reported speech and the direct address. Its purpose is to refute the claims of the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic Arabia) regarding what they had forbidden themselves of clothing and food. It also serves as an added emphasis on the permissibility of covering oneself (*al-tasattur*) in the mosques. The preceding discourse began by stating that clothing is a blessing from Allah, then repeated the command to take one's adornment at every mosque, and then gave a third statement, denying that there exists any prohibition on clothing.

The opening of the sentence with *qul* ("say") indicates that the speech is directed at rebuttal, denial, and debate.

The interrogative is a denial (*istifham inkari*), intended as mockery (*tahakkum*, sarcastic ridicule). It treats them as though they were people of knowledge from whom a clarification and an explanation are sought, similar to the verse ﴿Say: Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out to us?﴾ (Al-An'am 6:148), and His saying ﴿Inform me with knowledge if you are truthful﴾ (Al-An'am 6:143). The indicator of this mockery is the attribution of the adornment to the name of Allah, the description of it as something Allah brought forth for His servants, and the description of provision as "good things." All of this requires that it not be forbidden. Thus the interrogative ultimately amounts to a denial that it is forbidden.

Because the non-existence of its prohibition is clear, and because no sane person would say otherwise, and because the question is one asked by someone who already knows (not by a seeker of knowledge), the questioner is commanded to answer his own question himself. Therefore what is in the form of a question is followed by His saying ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾, following the same method as His saying ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ (Al-An'am 6:12) in Surah Al-An'am, and His saying ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ (An-Naba' 78:1–2). The question and its answer thus become two statements.

The pronoun in *hiya* ("they are") refers to the adornment and the good things, regardless of the description of the one who forbade them. That is: the adornment and the good things, in and of themselves, are permissible for those who believed. Whoever forbids them upon himself has, in fact, deprived himself.

The *lam* in ﴿for those who believed﴾ is the *lam* of exclusivity (*lam al-ikhtisas*), which indicates permissibility. The meaning is: they are not forbidden, but rather permitted for those who believed. The polytheists forbade themselves categories of these things in the life of this world, all of them, such as the *bahirah*, the *sa'ibah*, the *wasilah*, and the *ham* and what is in their bellies (these were animal-related prohibitions of the Jahiliyyah). Some of the polytheists also forbade themselves certain things at certain times of this worldly life, which they had prohibited upon themselves: clothing during circumambulation and at Mina, and eating meat, fat, ghee, and milk. Thus success belonged to the believers, for they followed Allah's command to make all of that permissible at all times of the life of this world.

As for His saying ﴿purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection﴾: Nafi' alone read *khalisatan* with a *raf'* (nominative), as a second predicate of *hiya* ("they are"). That is: they are theirs in this world, and they are theirs purely on the Day of Resurrection. The rest of the ten readers read it with a *nasb* (accusative), as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject. That is: they are theirs now, in a state where they are pure in the Hereafter. The meaning of both readings is one and the same: the adornment and the good things will be pure for the believers on the Day of Resurrection.

The more apparent view is that the concealed pronoun in *khalisah* refers to the very adornment and good things that existed in the life of this world. That is: they will be purely theirs in the Hereafter. There is no doubt that those adornments and good things have passed away in this world, so the meaning of their purity (*khalas*) is their clarity (*safa'*). As for it being "on the Day of Resurrection," it means that the Day of Resurrection is the manifestation of their clarity, i.e., their being free of the consequences attached to them. These consequences include the consequences of forbidding them, and the consequences of partaking of some of them while disbelieving in the Giver of them. The believers, when they partook of them in this world, partook of them by the permission of their Lord, unlike the polytheists, who will be questioned about them and punished for what they consumed in this world, because they disbelieved in the blessing of the Giver, associating others with Him. As Allah, the Exalted, said about them: ﴿And you make your provision [to be] that you deny [it]﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah 56:82). This meaning is what the interpretation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr points to. The matter, according to the reading with *raf'* (*khalisatun*), is that it is an informative statement about this adornment and these good things: that they will not bring their enjoyers any consequences or harms. According to the reading with *nasb*, it is an accusative of a presumed circumstantial state (*hal muqaddarah*).

It is possible that the pronoun in *khalisah* refers to the adornment and the good things with respect to their kinds, not with respect to their individual instances. Then the meaning would be: and for them there will be their equivalents on the Day of Resurrection, purely.

The meaning of *khalas* is *tamahhud* (pure, unmixed, exclusive). Here it means being purely theirs, free from the sharing of others of the people of the Day of Resurrection. The intended meaning is that the polytheists and other disbelievers will have no adornment and no good things of provision on the Day of Resurrection; in this world, these things were theirs but shared with the polytheists who also had them. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and his companions.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs﴾: the meaning is "like this detailing," which began with His saying ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:26) and onward, or with His saying ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:3). A parallel of this construction has preceded in Surah Al-An'am.

The "signs" here means the proofs that indicate the immense power of Allah, the Exalted, and His exclusive divinity; and the proofs that indicate the truthfulness of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), since he clarified the corruption of the religion of the people of the Jahiliyyah. It also taught the people of Islam a complete knowledge in which the good and the corrupt of deeds are not mixed, when He said ﴿Take your adornment﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:31), and said ﴿Eat and drink﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:31), then said ﴿but do not be excessive; indeed He does not like the excessive﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:31). It also [shows] that He punished the polytheists for their polytheism, their obstinacy, and their denial with a punishment in this world, by abandoning them until they established for themselves a law that deprived them of many good things, and disfigured them before the assembly during Hajj by being naked in the open, so they became an example of evil. Then He punished them for that in the Hereafter. And [it shows] that He granted success to the believers when they prepared themselves to accept the call of His Messenger and followed him; so He granted them enjoyment of all the good things in this world, without being deprived of anything, except for things in which there was harm that Allah knew of, so He forbade them, and He protected them from punishment for them in the Hereafter.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿for a people who know﴾ is the *lam* of cause (*lam al-'illah*), and it is connected to the verb *nufassil* ("We detail"). That is: the detailing of the signs is not understood except by a people who know. For when Allah detailed the signs, He knows that its detailing is for a people who know. It is also permissible that the prepositional phrase be a stable adverbial complement (*zarf mustaqarr*) in the position of a circumstantial state of *al-ayat* ("the signs"). That is: the signs are in a state of being proofs for a people who know, for those who do not know cannot have them as signs, since they do not comprehend them, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ (Al-An'am 6:99) in Surah Al-An'am. That is: this same detailing which I have detailed for you here, We detail [and] continually renew Our detailing of the signs, out of eagerness for the benefit of a people who know.

The meaning of "a people who know" is praise for the Muslims who understood the signs and were grateful for them. It is also an allusion to the ignorance and misguidance of the minds of the polytheists, who persisted in their obstinacy and misguidance despite the signs that were detailed to them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verse 33:**

﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecent acts, whether apparent or hidden, and sin, and transgression without right, and that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about God what you do not know.﴾

When His saying, ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has brought forth for His servants?﴾ (al-A'raf 7:32), through to its end, informed that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) were deprived of adornment and the good things of provision, and when His saying, exalted is He, before that, ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say: We found our fathers doing it, and God has commanded us to it﴾ (al-A'raf 7:28), informed that the people of the Jahiliyyah attributed their misguidance in religion to God, the result of that was that they claimed that what they had forbidden of adornment and good things was forbidden to them by God. Thus He followed their argument with a clarification of what God had truly forbidden, while they were engaged in it and devoted to its practice.

The restriction conveyed by ''innama'' (only) is a restriction relative to a particular case (qasr idafi). Its meaning is that God has forbidden indecent acts and what is mentioned with them, not what you have forbidden of adornment and good things. This refutes their belief. Furthermore, it indicates by way of allusion (ta'rid) that what God has enumerated among the prohibitions whose prohibition is established, they have indeed engaged in. For when He enumerated things, and people know that the prohibitions are not confined to them, the listener knows that what He specified is intended to specify what they were engaged in. Thus the form of restriction yields a rebuttal to them from both sides of what the particle ''innama'' contains of affirmation and negation, since it has the meaning of (ma ... illa, "not ... except"). So it conveys the permissibility of what they claimed to be forbidden and the prohibition of what they had made lawful of indecent acts and what accompanies them.

[p. 100]

''Al-fawahish'' is the plural of ''fahisha'', and the meaning of ''fahisha'' has already been discussed at His saying, ''Indeed, it was an indecency and a hateful way'' in Surah al-Nisa', and it was mentioned just before at His saying, ''And when they commit an indecency'' (al-A'raf 7:28).

''Ma zahara minha'' (what is apparent of them) refers to what people display among their companions and intimates, such as fornication and taking lovers. ''Wa ma batana'' (and what is hidden) refers to what people do not display, such as infanticide and theft. Its counterpart was discussed in His saying, ''And do not approach indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden'' (al-An'am 6:151) in Surah al-An'am. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to consider these indecent acts lawful, though they are ugly corruptions about which intelligent people, if asked, would have no doubt that God does not approve of them. It has been said that the intended meaning of ''al-fawahish'' is fornication, and that ''what is apparent of it and what is hidden'' are two states of the states of fornicators. According to this view, the use of the plural form is necessitated by consideration of the multiplicity of its acts and states, but this is far-fetched.

As for ''al-ithm'' (sin), it is every sin, so it is more general than the indecent acts. It was discussed at His saying, ''Say: In both of them is a great sin'' (al-Baqarah 2:219) in Surah al-Baqarah, and at His saying, ''Leave the outward and the inward of sin'' (al-An'am 6:120) in Surah al-An'am. Therefore the mention of the indecent acts before it is for the sake of emphasis (ihtimam) in warning against them before warning against sins in general. This is the mention of the particular before the general for the sake of emphasis, like the mention of the particular after the general. However, the emphasis obtained through specification together with precedence is stronger, because it contains emphasis from two directions.

As for ''al-baghy'' (transgression), it is aggression against the right of others by seizing their wealth or harming them, and arrogance towards people is a form of transgression. Whatever is done with a right is not called transgression, but it is harm. God, exalted is He, said, ''And as for the two who commit it among you, harm them'' (al-Nisa' 4:16). Transgression was widespread in the Jahiliyyah: the strong would devour the weak, and the mighty would raid people's livestock and kill their enemies among them. Among transgression was that they would beat whoever circumambulated the House in his clothes if he was not of the Hums (the Quraysh and their allies who regarded themselves as the people of the sanctuary). They would also compel him not to eat any food except the food of the Hums, and not to circumambulate except in their clothes.

[p. 101]

His saying, ''without right'' (bi-ghayri al-haqq), is a descriptive qualifier clarifying ''transgression'', like ''the late night prayer'' (al-'isha' al-akhirah), because transgression can only be without right.

The conjunction of ''transgression'' with ''sin'' is the conjunction of the particular with the general, for the sake of emphasis on it, because transgression was their habitual practice in the Jahiliyyah. Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrab al-Sa'di said:

''And I am always a man of wars; if I do not commit a crime, I am a shield of the criminal.''

Associating partners with God (al-shirk) is well known, and God has forbidden it through the tongues of all the prophets since He created mankind.

His saying, ﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾, is a relative clause with its complement, and ''ma'' is the object of ''tushrikū bi-Allah'' (you associate with God). ''Sultan'' means proof and argument. The prepositional phrase in His saying ''bihi'' (for which) is a qualifier of ''sultanan'' (authority), and the ''ba'' is for accompaniment, in the sense of ''ma'ahu'' (with it), meaning He has not sent down an argument accompanying it, which is the accompaniment of the argument to the claimant. This is a metaphorical accompaniment. It is also permissible that the ''ba'' carries the sense of ''ala'' (upon), for metaphorical elevation (isti'la'), as in His saying, ''Of whom if you entrust a qintar'' (Al 'Imran 3:75), meaning authority over it, that is, proof. The pronoun in ''bihi'' refers back to ''ma'', and it is the connecting pronoun of the relative clause. Thus the meaning of the negation of sending down an argument concerning the partners is the negation of an argument indicating the affirmation of the attribute of partnership with God in divinity. This is the attachment of the ruling to the essence, while the intended meaning is its attribute, like ''Forbidden to you is carrion'', meaning its eating. This relative clause indicates the rebuke of the polytheists and the negation of their excuse for associating partners, in that there is no proof that might be confused for people concerning the non-entitlement of the idols to worship. So it defines the supposed partners by way of description (rasm), in that their distinguishing feature is that there is no authority for their partnership with God in divinity. Thus every idol among their idols clearly has this distinguishing feature. The relative pronoun and its clause are among the methods of definition, and this is not like an adjective. The relative clause does not have a sense of contrary implication (mafhum mukhalafa), and relative pronouns are not counted among the forms of implication. Therefore what al-Fakhr (al-Razi) raised is not valid, namely that someone might say: this gives the impression that among associating partners there is something for which God has sent down authority, and that it needs to remove this impression. Nor is valid what the author of al-Intisaf followed up on, namely comparing the negation of authority in this verse to a line like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

''Upon a faint path whose landmarks cannot guide one.''

[p. 102]

Nor is valid what the author of al-Kashshaf pursued, namely making this relative clause run in the manner of mockery (tahakkum).

His saying, ﴿and that you say about God what you do not know﴾, its counterpart was mentioned just before at His saying in this surah: ''Say: Indeed God does not command indecency. Do you say about God what you do not know?'' (al-A'raf 7:28).

This verse has gathered the foundations of the conditions of the people of the Jahiliyyah regarding the indecent acts and sins in which they were engaged, while they claimed that they abstained from circumambulating in clothes and from eating some good things during the pilgrimage. This relates to His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin), but barring from the way of God, disbelieving in Him, and (barring from) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater in the sight of God; and fitnah (persecution) is greater than killing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:217).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 7, verse 34:**

﴿For every nation there is a term (*ajal*). When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (*iʿtiraḍ*) placed between the statement ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:31] and the statement ﴿O children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:35]. When God condemned the polytheists for their misguidance and obstinacy, after He had called them to faith and they had turned away from it, through disputation, rebuke, and exposing their faults with clear proof, and when their state was that of people who would not desist from what they were engaged in, He followed this with a warning and threat against them, to establish the proof against them and to leave them without excuse before the punishment descended upon them.

This sentence emphasizes the purpose of the statement ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:4]. It admits of two meanings:

The first: the intended addressees of this report are the polytheists, either in that God turns to address them directly, or commands His Prophet to address them, since this address is one of threat and warning.

[Page 103]

The second: the intended addressee of the report is the Prophet ﷺ, so that it is a promise to him of victory over those who deny him, and an informing him that his way is the way of the other messengers, by way of making the custom of his community like the custom of other communities.

The mention of all nations in this threat, although the intended addressees are the polytheists of the Arabs who did not believe, is only for the sake of exaggeration in warning and threatening, bringing its occurrence close, as it occurred for others among the nations. This follows the method of citing the evidence of history, reasoning from the present to the past, so that the threat becomes a report supported by evidence and proof. As God said in many verses, among them: ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents, so travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:137]. That is: you are nothing but one nation among the nations that denied, and for every nation there is a term, so you too have a term whose time will arrive.

The mention of the term here, rather than saying "for every nation there is a punishment or annihilation," serves to awaken their minds lest the respite deceive them into thinking that God will not call them to account for their denial, as they said: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:32]. It also serves to reassure the Messenger (peace be upon him) that the delay of the punishment from them is only in accordance with God's custom of granting respite to the wrongdoers, in the manner of His saying: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them﴾ [Yūsuf 12:110], and His saying: ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:196], ﴿a brief enjoyment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:197].

The meaning of "for every nation there is a term" is: for every denying nation there is a respite. The qualifier "denying" is omitted, so that the word "nation" stands alone, meaning "denying."

A limit (*nihāyah*) has been set for that period of time, which is the appointed moment for the expiry of the respite. The word *ajal* is used both for the duration of the respite and for the fixed moment at which the respite ends. Undoubtedly it was originally coined for one of these two meanings and then used for the other, by understanding it as the end of the duration or as the postponed end; both usages have become common. In the first sense one says "he fulfilled the term," meaning the duration, as God said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:28]. In the second sense one says "the term of so-and-so has drawn near." God's saying ﴿and We have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:128] is also in this sense. The expression in this verse is suitable for both usages, since the first *ajal* may mean the duration and the second the moment fixed for a particular event.

By "nation" (*ummah*) here is meant the group that shares the creed of polytheism or the denial of the messengers, as the context indicates from His saying ﴿and that you associate partners with God﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:33], and so on. It does not mean a group united by lineage or language, since it is inconceivable that such a group should be wholly extinct, and history has not recorded the extinction of any such nation. What has happened is that in some peoples most of the men perished in great calamities, such as Ṭasm, Jadīs, and ʿAdwān, so that their remnants merged into neighbouring nations. Thus one does not say of a nation that it has a term in which it will become extinct, except in the sense of a group united by the fact that a messenger was sent to it and it denied him. This is how the referent of this verse was realized. When Muḥammad ﷺ was sent to the Arabs, he began his call among them and to them. Some believed in him, and believers followed in successive groups, while the people of Makkah denied him, and those around them followed them. God, in His wisdom and by the mercy of His Prophet ﷺ, granted the Arabs respite, when he said: "Perhaps God will bring forth from their loins those who will worship Him." God was kind to them by making them mixed, believers and polytheists together. Then the believers emigrated, and Makkah remained a land of polytheism, and those whom God knew would not believe were purified (of believers). God then sent against them His believing servants, who annihilated them group after group, at the Battle of Badr and what followed of the days of Islam, until the eradication of the polytheists was complete with the killing of the remnant of those killed among them at the conquest, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khaṭal and those killed with him. When Makkah was conquered, the Arabs submitted to Islam, the polytheists became extinct, and no standard of polytheism rose again after that. God showed His care for the Arab nation, since from the beginning of the Prophet's call it was not wholly given over to polytheism, but there were Muslims from the first day of the call, and they continued to increase.

The meaning of the "term of the nation" in the verse is not the term of its individuals, that is, the lifespan of each one of them. This is because it has no connection with the context, and because attributing it to the nation indicates that it is the term of the group as a whole, not of its individuals. Had the terms of individuals been intended, he would have said "for every person" or "for every living being there is a term."

[Page 105]

"When" (*idhā*) is a temporal adverb referring to the future, and it generally implies the sense of a condition, because the senses of temporal adverbs are close to those of conditions, since they contain conditionality. Here the particle of consequence (*fāʾ*) introducing the governing verb of the adverb has dispensed with the need for a *fāʾ* in the answer to *idhā*, because the connective and conditional sense is evident from the combination of temporality and consequence. The consequent is: "their term has come." The adverb was placed before its governing verb to give it emphasis, so that this placement reinforces the sense of conditionality.

The word "came" (*jāʾa*) is a metaphor for the arrival that is supposed for it, as in the saying "winter has come."

The singular "term" in "when their term comes" is understood in the sense of a genus that covers many instances, as indicated by its being attached to a plural pronoun.

The word "term" is expressed explicitly in "when their term comes," rather than relying on its pronoun, to add emphasis to the judgment about it, and so that this clause stands on its own without depending on the hearing of anything else, since it functions like a proverb. Sending forth a speech that is fit to serve as a proverb is one of the methods of eloquence.

"They delay" (*yastākhirūna*) and "they advance" (*yastaqdimūna*) mean "they lag behind" (*yatakhhkharūna*) and "they go ahead" (*yataqaddamūna*). The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in them are for emphasis, like in *istajāba*.

The meaning is: they do not exceed it by delay, nor do they hasten it by advancing. The intended sense is that they cannot be put off from it. Thus the conjunction of "nor can they advance it" completes the explanation that what God knows and has decreed in accordance with His knowledge cannot be changed or diverted by anyone. Therefore the phrase "nor can they advance it" has no connection with the purpose of threatening. Close to this is the saying of Abū al-Shīṣ:

*Love has halted me where you are, so for me there is no one who lags behind it, nor one who goes ahead.*

All of this is based on depicting the state of one who cannot escape a threat or the like, by the image of one who is confined in a place where he cannot pass beyond it either forward or backward.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 35–36:

﴿O Children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses, then whoever is righteous and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿But those who deny Our verses and show arrogance toward them—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

What may occur in the interpretation of this sentence is what preceded in the discussion of its counterpart, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to conceal your private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

The interpretation that we preferred there appears more clearly in this fourth counterpart. The plural form in His saying "messengers" (rusul) and His saying "relating" (yaqussuna) requires the expectation of the coming of several messengers, and this is excluded after the sending of the Final Messenger, the one who gathers and comes last (al-hashir al-'aqib), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. Therefore it is confirmed that this address is to the Children of Adam present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an. It is also favoured that these four calls are a narration of a speech addressed to the first Children of Adam, whose beginning is: "He said: therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It seems that this is an address to all nations, past and present; it is firmly established for them, and it is inferred for the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ that this is the ruling of Allah in the world since He brought it into being. He intends that Allah conveyed this address to people through the tongue of every prophet, from Adam onward, and there is no prophet or messenger except that he conveyed it to his community, and commanded them that the present should convey it to the absent, until it was revealed in the Qur'an to Muhammad ﷺ, and his community knew that they were included in the generality of the Children of Adam."

If this is definite in this verse, or nearly definite, then it is required to consider the like of it in its three preceding counterparts. So hold firmly to it, and pay no heed to whoever would turn you away from it.

As for when the address in this verse is taken as directed to the polytheists at the time of revelation, by the designation of their being from the Children of Adam, then it becomes necessary to turn the meaning of the conditional toward what comes in time after the revelation of the verse, because the conditional generally implies the future. It is as if it were said: if you missed following what was sent down to you in the past, you will not miss it in what remains. It becomes necessary to interpret "ya'tiyannakum" (will come to you) as "yad'unannakum" (will call you), and it becomes necessary to make the plural "messengers" refer to one messenger, out of magnification for him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the people of Noah when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37], meaning they denied their messenger Noah, and His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. It has many parallels in the Qur'an.

This verse and the one following it are connected in meaning with the content of His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And how many a town We have destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], and so on, the connection of detail to its summary.

It emphasises their warning from the snare and seduction of Satan, and shows them through it the methods of right guidance which help to avoid his snare, by the call of the messengers to them to piety and reform, as He indicated in His saying in the preceding address: ﴿O Children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. And it informed them that Satan has threatened the human race, in what Allah related of his saying: ﴿He said: because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], and so on. Therefore Allah warned the Children of Adam against the snare of Satan, and made them aware of Satan's strength by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], perhaps they would prepare the means of deliverance from the claws of his seduction. He followed that with a warning against his party and his callers, who seduce the believers. Then He strengthened that by informing them that He had helped them to guard against Satan, by sending to them a people of the party of Allah who convey to them from Allah what contains deliverance for them from the snare of the devils, by His saying: ﴿O Children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you﴾, and so on, so He enjoined them to affirm them and to obey them.

"In" (idma) is composed of "in" the conditional particle and "ma" the superfluous particle that emphasises the conditional sense. The masters of orthography agreed on writing it as a single word, in observance of its pronunciation with the assimilation of the nun into the mim. The more apparent view is that it conveys, together with the emphasis, the generality of the condition, like its sisters "mahma" and "aynama". When it is joined to the conditional "in", the emphatic nun is attached to the verb of the condition, as in His saying: ﴿And if you see any human, say﴾ [Maryam: 26]. Because the conditional emphasis resembles an oath, and this attachment of the nun is frequent; and because, when it became an emphasis of the condition, it was placed by the conditional particle in the position of a part of the word.

His saying "from among you" (minkum) means from the Children of Adam. This is an alert to the Children of Adam that they should not expect that the messengers of Allah would come to them from among the angels, because the sent one is of the same kind as those to whom he is sent. In this there is an allusion to the ignorant among the nations who denied the messengers' mission because they were of their own kind, like the people of Noah, when they said: ﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves﴾ [Hud: 27], and like the polytheists of Mecca when they denied the mission of Muhammad ﷺ on the ground that he was human. Allah said: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said: Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra: 94] ﴿Say: If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the sky an angel as a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 95].

The meaning of ﴿relating to you My verses﴾ (yaqussuna 'alaykum ayati) is that they recite them and narrate them. It is also possible that it means "they follow one verse with another", and it is possible that it means "they make manifest". All of these are figurative meanings of "qass", because the root sense of qasas is following a trace, from tracing the footprints and following them, so that the direction of the walker may be known. On the first meaning, it is like His saying in another verse: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. Whatever the case, it is possible to take it as comprising all of them, by using the word in both its figurative senses.

The word "ayah" originally means a sign indicating something, whether speech or action. The signs of Allah are the proofs which He made indicative of His existence, or of His attributes, or of the truthfulness of His messengers, as already mentioned at His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our verses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿And they say: Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-An'am: 37] in Surat al-An'am. Among them are the verses of the Qur'an, which Allah made an indication of His purpose to people, as a rebuke to the polytheists of the Arabs who denied the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. The way the verses indicate this is either because they came in an arrangement which humans cannot match, and that is among the distinctive features of the Qur'an; or because they contain rulings and meanings for which no one other than Allah and His messenger has the capacity to comprehend the like; or because they call to a righteousness the people had not known, so that what they contain indicates that it is what Allah intends for people, like the rest of the books which the messengers brought; or because they were accompanied by matters beyond the ordinary custom, with which the messenger who was sent challenged his community by those words. This is the meaning of calling them "verses", and the meaning of their being attributed to Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that what is meant by the "verses" includes non-verbal miracles, such as the gushing of water from between the fingers of Muhammad ﷺ, the turning of Moses' staff into a serpent, peace be upon him, and the healing of the blind and leper by Jesus, peace be upon him. The meaning of denying them is obstinacy, by rejecting and repudiating them.

The clause ﴿so whoever is righteous and reforms﴾ is the answer to the condition. Between it and the clause "(﴿if there come to you﴾)" there is an omitted element, whose estimate is: "then a group of you obeyed and a group denied, so whoever is righteous, and so on." This clause is also conditional, and its answer is ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾, meaning: whoever follows My messengers, fears Me, reforms himself and his deeds, there will be no fear for them nor will they grieve. Since the coming of the messengers has as its benefit the reform of people, and not the benefit of the messengers, He turned away from making the answer "following the messengers" and made it "piety and righteousness", as an allusion to the wisdom of sending messengers, and as an incitement to follow them, by the fact that its benefit is for the nations and not for the messengers. As Shu'ayb said: ﴿I do not intend to differ from you in what I forbid you. I intend only reform, as far as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88]. That is, there is no fear for them of the punishment of Allah in this world and the Hereafter, nor will they grieve over anything

of that. The fear and grief negated are what punishment necessitates; and fear and grief may be entirely negated from them to the degree of the strength of piety and righteousness. This is among the secrets between Allah and His righteous servants. Similar is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62] ﴿those who believed and were mindful of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 63] ﴿for them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64].

Fear has been negated by the absolute negation of its kind, with the negating "la", and its subject has been put in the nominative, because the nominative is equivalent to the construction on the fatha in such a case, since fear is among the abstract kinds, in whose negation it is not supposed that the intended meaning is the negation of a single individual. Had it been put in the accusative, it would have been correct. Among this is the saying of the fourth of the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihama: neither hot nor cold, neither fear nor weariness." It has been transmitted both with the nominative and with the fatha.

The "'ala" in His saying "there will be no fear upon them" is for figurative elevation, which is accompaniment and attachment; that is, no fear will reach them.

His saying "nor will they grieve" is a clause conjoined to the clause "﴿there will be no fear upon them﴾" [al-Baqarah: 38]. He turned away from coordinating a single noun, by saying "nor grief", to a full clause, so that by it the verbal predicate could be built upon their pronoun, which indicates that grief occurs to others, namely those who disbelieved. For constructing a verbal predicate upon a subject placed before it gives the restriction of that predicate to that subject, like: "I did not say this", for it is the negation of the utterance proceeding from the speaker while the utterance is issued by another. On this is the verse from the Proofs of I'jaz, by al-Mutanabbi:

"I did not make my body ill with it, nor did I kindle a fire in the heart."

It thus indicates that those who disbelieved grieve, by way of implication, so as to serve as an introduction to the report about them afterward, that they are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide forever.

The clause ﴿but those who denied Our verses and showed arrogance toward them, those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is conjoined to the clause "(﴿so whoever is righteous and reforms﴾)", and the connecting pronoun is omitted, its estimate being: "and those among you who disbelieved and denied."

"Istikbar" is an intensification of "takabbur" (arrogance); the sin and ta' are for intensification. It is for a person to regard himself as great, that is, magnificent, while he is not so. The sin and ta' are for counting and reckoning. Both matters indicate their excess in that and that they overstepped their measure.

"Istikbar" has been given the meaning of turning away, so the pronoun of the verses is attached to it. The meaning is: "they showed arrogance and so turned away from them."

The affirmation that they are heading to the Fire is conveyed by the way of restricting the constancy of the Fire upon them in His saying: ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾, because the word "ashab" (companions) indicates constancy, and by what the nominal sentence indicates of permanence and stability in His saying: "they will abide therein forever."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 35–36:

﴿O Children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses, then whoever is righteous and reforms, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿But those who deny Our verses and show arrogance toward them—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

What may occur in the interpretation of this sentence is what preceded in the discussion of its counterpart, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to conceal your private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

The interpretation that we preferred there appears more clearly in this fourth counterpart. The plural form in His saying "messengers" (rusul) and His saying "relating" (yaqussuna) requires the expectation of the coming of several messengers, and this is excluded after the sending of the Final Messenger, the one who gathers and comes last (al-hashir al-'aqib), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. Therefore it is confirmed that this address is to the Children of Adam present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an. It is also favoured that these four calls are a narration of a speech addressed to the first Children of Adam, whose beginning is: "He said: therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It seems that this is an address to all nations, past and present; it is firmly established for them, and it is inferred for the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ that this is the ruling of Allah in the world since He brought it into being. He intends that Allah conveyed this address to people through the tongue of every prophet, from Adam onward, and there is no prophet or messenger except that he conveyed it to his community, and commanded them that the present should convey it to the absent, until it was revealed in the Qur'an to Muhammad ﷺ, and his community knew that they were included in the generality of the Children of Adam."

If this is definite in this verse, or nearly definite, then it is required to consider the like of it in its three preceding counterparts. So hold firmly to it, and pay no heed to whoever would turn you away from it.

As for when the address in this verse is taken as directed to the polytheists at the time of revelation, by the designation of their being from the Children of Adam, then it becomes necessary to turn the meaning of the conditional toward what comes in time after the revelation of the verse, because the conditional generally implies the future. It is as if it were said: if you missed following what was sent down to you in the past, you will not miss it in what remains. It becomes necessary to interpret "ya'tiyannakum" (will come to you) as "yad'unannakum" (will call you), and it becomes necessary to make the plural "messengers" refer to one messenger, out of magnification for him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the people of Noah when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37], meaning they denied their messenger Noah, and His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. It has many parallels in the Qur'an.

This verse and the one following it are connected in meaning with the content of His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And how many a town We have destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], and so on, the connection of detail to its summary.

It emphasises their warning from the snare and seduction of Satan, and shows them through it the methods of right guidance which help to avoid his snare, by the call of the messengers to them to piety and reform, as He indicated in His saying in the preceding address: ﴿O Children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. And it informed them that Satan has threatened the human race, in what Allah related of his saying: ﴿He said: because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], and so on. Therefore Allah warned the Children of Adam against the snare of Satan, and made them aware of Satan's strength by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], perhaps they would prepare the means of deliverance from the claws of his seduction. He followed that with a warning against his party and his callers, who seduce the believers. Then He strengthened that by informing them that He had helped them to guard against Satan, by sending to them a people of the party of Allah who convey to them from Allah what contains deliverance for them from the snare of the devils, by His saying: ﴿O Children of Adam, if there come to you messengers from among you﴾, and so on, so He enjoined them to affirm them and to obey them.

"In" (idma) is composed of "in" the conditional particle and "ma" the superfluous particle that emphasises the conditional sense. The masters of orthography agreed on writing it as a single word, in observance of its pronunciation with the assimilation of the nun into the mim. The more apparent view is that it conveys, together with the emphasis, the generality of the condition, like its sisters "mahma" and "aynama". When it is joined to the conditional "in", the emphatic nun is attached to the verb of the condition, as in His saying: ﴿And if you see any human, say﴾ [Maryam: 26]. Because the conditional emphasis resembles an oath, and this attachment of the nun is frequent; and because, when it became an emphasis of the condition, it was placed by the conditional particle in the position of a part of the word.

His saying "from among you" (minkum) means from the Children of Adam. This is an alert to the Children of Adam that they should not expect that the messengers of Allah would come to them from among the angels, because the sent one is of the same kind as those to whom he is sent. In this there is an allusion to the ignorant among the nations who denied the messengers' mission because they were of their own kind, like the people of Noah, when they said: ﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves﴾ [Hud: 27], and like the polytheists of Mecca when they denied the mission of Muhammad ﷺ on the ground that he was human. Allah said: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said: Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra: 94] ﴿Say: If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the sky an angel as a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 95].

The meaning of ﴿relating to you My verses﴾ (yaqussuna 'alaykum ayati) is that they recite them and narrate them. It is also possible that it means "they follow one verse with another", and it is possible that it means "they make manifest". All of these are figurative meanings of "qass", because the root sense of qasas is following a trace, from tracing the footprints and following them, so that the direction of the walker may be known. On the first meaning, it is like His saying in another verse: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. Whatever the case, it is possible to take it as comprising all of them, by using the word in both its figurative senses.

The word "ayah" originally means a sign indicating something, whether speech or action. The signs of Allah are the proofs which He made indicative of His existence, or of His attributes, or of the truthfulness of His messengers, as already mentioned at His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our verses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿And they say: Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-An'am: 37] in Surat al-An'am. Among them are the verses of the Qur'an, which Allah made an indication of His purpose to people, as a rebuke to the polytheists of the Arabs who denied the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. The way the verses indicate this is either because they came in an arrangement which humans cannot match, and that is among the distinctive features of the Qur'an; or because they contain rulings and meanings for which no one other than Allah and His messenger has the capacity to comprehend the like; or because they call to a righteousness the people had not known, so that what they contain indicates that it is what Allah intends for people, like the rest of the books which the messengers brought; or because they were accompanied by matters beyond the ordinary custom, with which the messenger who was sent challenged his community by those words. This is the meaning of calling them "verses", and the meaning of their being attributed to Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that what is meant by the "verses" includes non-verbal miracles, such as the gushing of water from between the fingers of Muhammad ﷺ, the turning of Moses' staff into a serpent, peace be upon him, and the healing of the blind and leper by Jesus, peace be upon him. The meaning of denying them is obstinacy, by rejecting and repudiating them.

The clause ﴿so whoever is righteous and reforms﴾ is the answer to the condition. Between it and the clause "(﴿if there come to you﴾)" there is an omitted element, whose estimate is: "then a group of you obeyed and a group denied, so whoever is righteous, and so on." This clause is also conditional, and its answer is ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾, meaning: whoever follows My messengers, fears Me, reforms himself and his deeds, there will be no fear for them nor will they grieve. Since the coming of the messengers has as its benefit the reform of people, and not the benefit of the messengers, He turned away from making the answer "following the messengers" and made it "piety and righteousness", as an allusion to the wisdom of sending messengers, and as an incitement to follow them, by the fact that its benefit is for the nations and not for the messengers. As Shu'ayb said: ﴿I do not intend to differ from you in what I forbid you. I intend only reform, as far as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88]. That is, there is no fear for them of the punishment of Allah in this world and the Hereafter, nor will they grieve over anything

of that. The fear and grief negated are what punishment necessitates; and fear and grief may be entirely negated from them to the degree of the strength of piety and righteousness. This is among the secrets between Allah and His righteous servants. Similar is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62] ﴿those who believed and were mindful of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 63] ﴿for them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64].

Fear has been negated by the absolute negation of its kind, with the negating "la", and its subject has been put in the nominative, because the nominative is equivalent to the construction on the fatha in such a case, since fear is among the abstract kinds, in whose negation it is not supposed that the intended meaning is the negation of a single individual. Had it been put in the accusative, it would have been correct. Among this is the saying of the fourth of the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihama: neither hot nor cold, neither fear nor weariness." It has been transmitted both with the nominative and with the fatha.

The "'ala" in His saying "there will be no fear upon them" is for figurative elevation, which is accompaniment and attachment; that is, no fear will reach them.

His saying "nor will they grieve" is a clause conjoined to the clause "﴿there will be no fear upon them﴾" [al-Baqarah: 38]. He turned away from coordinating a single noun, by saying "nor grief", to a full clause, so that by it the verbal predicate could be built upon their pronoun, which indicates that grief occurs to others, namely those who disbelieved. For constructing a verbal predicate upon a subject placed before it gives the restriction of that predicate to that subject, like: "I did not say this", for it is the negation of the utterance proceeding from the speaker while the utterance is issued by another. On this is the verse from the Proofs of I'jaz, by al-Mutanabbi:

"I did not make my body ill with it, nor did I kindle a fire in the heart."

It thus indicates that those who disbelieved grieve, by way of implication, so as to serve as an introduction to the report about them afterward, that they are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide forever.

The clause ﴿but those who denied Our verses and showed arrogance toward them, those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is conjoined to the clause "(﴿so whoever is righteous and reforms﴾)", and the connecting pronoun is omitted, its estimate being: "and those among you who disbelieved and denied."

"Istikbar" is an intensification of "takabbur" (arrogance); the sin and ta' are for intensification. It is for a person to regard himself as great, that is, magnificent, while he is not so. The sin and ta' are for counting and reckoning. Both matters indicate their excess in that and that they overstepped their measure.

"Istikbar" has been given the meaning of turning away, so the pronoun of the verses is attached to it. The meaning is: "they showed arrogance and so turned away from them."

The affirmation that they are heading to the Fire is conveyed by the way of restricting the constancy of the Fire upon them in His saying: ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾, because the word "ashab" (companions) indicates constancy, and by what the nominal sentence indicates of permanence and stability in His saying: "they will abide therein forever."

[Page 112]

The *fa'* (فَ) here marks a consequence drawn from the preceding discourse. This is like a *fadhlakah* (a summation, a concluding recapitulation) of what has come before, showing that the attributes of misguidance, whose bearers were left unnamed, apply to the polytheists who denied the mission of Muhammad (upon him be peace and blessings). Allah had mentioned the allies of the devils and some of their attributes in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. He also mentioned that Allah had covenanted with the children of Adam from earliest times to follow whatever messengers came to them from Allah with His signs, so that they would be mindful and reform themselves. He promised them, for following what came to them, the removal of fear and grief, and threatened them, for denial and arrogance, that they would be the companions of the Fire. Thus He had given them a warning and made them aware of the consequences. From this it follows that whoever lies against Allah, claiming that Allah ordered him to commit abominations, or denies the signs of Allah that His Messenger brought, has wronged himself with a great wrong, so that he is asked about who is more unjust than him.

You may also take the clause ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah...﴾ etc. as a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridah*) placed between the clause ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-A'raf: 36] and the clause ﴿Those will receive their share of the Book﴾, as will come in its place. The discussion of the construction "*man azlamu mimman*" (مَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ) has already been given at His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114] in Surah al-Baqarah, and that the interrogation is one of denial, meaning that no one is more unjust.

The discussion of *iftira'* (fabrication, افْتِرَاء) and *kadhib* (lying, كَذِب) has already been given at His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surah al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah). This verse is connected to the verse ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], in that it contains the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter and the terrifying description of its horrors.

The *man* (مَنْ) is an interrogative of denial used to magnify the wrongdoing of this group, expressed by ﴿one who fabricates against Allah a lie﴾. The second *man* (مَنِ) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), general to everyone in whom the relative clause is realized. They were the most unjust of people, and none was more unjust than them, because injustice is transgression against a right, and the greatest of rights are the rights of Allah, the Exalted. The greatest transgression against the right of Allah is to transgress against Him by belittling His Great Owner, which occurs when one denies what has come from Him, or when one lies against Him by conveying from Him what He did not command. If one combines both matters, he has nullified the purpose of Allah from two directions: the direction of invalidating what indicates His purpose, and the direction of creating the illusion among people that Allah wants from them what Allah does not want.

The group intended here are the polytheists among the Arabs, for they denied the signs of Allah that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, and fabricated lies against Allah in claiming that Allah had commanded them to commit abominations, as has already been mentioned just before, at His words: ﴿And when they commit an abomination, they say: "We found our fathers doing it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

The *aw* (أَوْ) apparently indicates division, so that the most unjust are the polytheists in two groups: a group who fabricated lies against Allah, namely the chiefs and great ones of the people of polytheism, who legislated for them in religion what Allah had not permitted, and attributed it to Allah while knowing it, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, Abu Kabshah, and those who came after them. Most of this group had died out at the time the verse was revealed. The second group are those who denied the signs but did not fabricate lies against Allah, and these are the common polytheists, of the people of Makkah and its surroundings. On this interpretation, each of the two groups is not more unjust than the other, because the other group is equal to it in wrongdoing and is not more unjust than it. As for the one who combined both matters, among those who perhaps legislated for the polytheists some matters of misguidance and also denied Muhammad (ﷺ), he is more unjust. But since they could not be free of attachment to both groups, and combined both characteristics, they did not leave the category of those who are the most unjust of people. This is like His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. There is no doubt that one who combines the three characteristics is more unjust than anyone who has only one of them, and this gives him an additional degree of being the most unjust, because every intensified attribute is capable of increase.

You may also take the *aw* (أَوْ) to mean the *waw* (وَ, "and"), so that the one described as the most unjust of people is the one who is characterized by both matters, lying and denying, and this would apply to the polytheists, because their community is not free of that.

The demonstrative noun was brought in His words ﴿Those will receive their share of the Book﴾ to indicate that those referred to are deserving of the punishment, based on what the consequence indicated by the *fa'* implies.

The clause ﴿Those will receive their share of the Book﴾ may be a resumption (*isti'naf*) of an explanatory kind (*bayani*), arising from the interrogation in His words: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie﴾ and so on, because the magnification drawn from the interrogation prompts the hearer to ask about what they will encounter from Allah, against whom they fabricated and whose signs they denied.

The clause ﴿Those will receive their share﴾ may also be an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to the clause ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-A'raf: 36], meaning that they will abide forever, which is their share of the Book.

The completion of this clause is the clause ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them to take them﴾ and so on, as will come.

The root *n-y-l* (نيل) and *n-w-l* (نوال) occurs both with a *waw* as second radical (واوية العين) and with a *ya'* as second radical (يائية العين), mixed together in the lexicographical works, without clarifying the distribution of their usages between the *waw*-type and the *ya'*-type. It appears that most of the meanings of the two roots are synonymous, and that this arose from metathesis in some conjugations or from the mixing of dialects. One says *nultu* (نُلْتُ), with a *damma* on the *nun*, from *nala yanulu* (نَالَ يَنُولُ), and one says *niltu* (نِلْتُ), with a *kasra* on the *nun*, from *nala yanilu* (نَالَ يَنِيلُ). The basic meaning of *nayl* is that a person obtains something for himself with his own hand, while *nawwalahu* means he gave him, so that he obtained it. The original usage would be to say *nala fulanun kasban* (نَالَ فُلانٌ كَسْبًا, "so-and-so obtained by earning"). Here it has come in the opposite way, because the share from the Book is an abstract matter. The apparent expectation would be that the share be something given (*munawwal*) rather than something attained (*nail*), because the share does not get attained by those who fabricated lies against Allah; rather, by contrast, those who fabricated are the ones who attain it. This occurs in many verses, such as His words: ﴿Their flesh and their blood will never reach Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 37], and His words: ﴿Anger from their Lord will befall them﴾ [al-A'raf: 152]. It is therefore determined that this is either a *majaz mursal* (a metonymy, unrestricted figurative use) in the sense of simply "reaching", or that it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) built upon a reversal of the simile (*'aks al-tashbih*), in that the share is likened to a person who seeks something and attains it. This is adopted only to draw attention to the fact that what befalls them is something they dislike, and it seeks them while they flee from it, just as an enemy seeks his enemy. Thus the share from the Book has become as if it seeks to attain the group who were decreed against and to encounter them. This is close to the figure based on the reversal of the simile in the verse of Ru'bah:

*And a desert, dusty in its expanses,*
*As if the color of its earth were its sky.*

and in the saying: "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough."

The *nasib* (نَصِيب) is the portion falling to one of those who share a divided thing. It has already been discussed at His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 202] in Surah al-Baqarah, and at His words: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 7] in Surah al-Nisa'.

The *kitab* (الكِتاب) here means what the Book contains. If the Book is used in its literal sense, it is the Qur'an, and their share of it is their share of its threat, like His words just before: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-A'raf: 36]. If the Book is a figurative usage for the matter that Allah decreed and determined, on the pattern of His words: ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38], meaning the Book that is fixed in the knowledge of Allah concerning the confirmation of the word of punishment upon them, then their share of it is what Allah has informed that He decreed for them of abiding forever in punishment, and that He will not forgive them. This includes what was previously decreed for them of respite, which is their postponement until a term He willed, followed by their annihilation after it, as He informed about this just before in His words: ﴿For every nation there is a term; when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour nor advance it﴾ [Yunus: 49; cf. al-A'raf: 34].

Many exegetes understood the share to mean what reaches them of provision and respite in this world before the punishment descends upon them. This is far from the meaning of the *fa'* in His words: ﴿So who is more unjust﴾. I do not think that those who inclined to this interpretation did so except so that the attainment of the share would occur over an extended period, and so that the coming of the angels to take them would be the end point of that share, preserving the meaning of the real limit in *hatta* (حتى). But this is not required, for the inceptive *hatta* (حَتّى الِابْتِدائِيَّة) does not convey the sense of a limit in the way that the conjunctive *hatta* does, as we shall mention.

The meaning is: either that each one of the polytheists will be struck by what Allah threatened them with, in proportion to his obstinacy in denial and turning away, so that his share is what suits his condition before Allah in the measure of his punishment; or that the whole group of polytheists will be struck by what was decreed for their like among the nations who denied the messengers and turned away from the signs, of the punishment of this world. Thus let not their postponement deceive them, for it will surely befall them when their term arrives, and their share is the description of their punishment among the descriptions of punishment with which the nations were punished.

The clause ﴿until, when Our messengers came to them﴾ is an elaboration of the content of the clause ﴿their share of the Book will reach them﴾. The time indicated by His words ﴿when Our messengers come to them to take them﴾ is the starting point of the description of their share of the Book, at the moment when the respite they enjoyed in this world ends.

The *hatta* (حَتّى) is inceptive (ابتدائية), because what follows it is a clause, and it conveys causation (سَبَبِيَّة). The meaning is: "so when Our messengers come to them" and so on. The inceptive *hatta* has the opening of the speech, so the limit it indicates is the limit of what the informant reports, and it is not the limit of what the element preceding it reaches with *hatta*. This is because that requirement applies only when *hatta* is conjunctive (عاطفة), and it conveys nothing but causation, as Ibn al-Hajib said: it conveys no more than the causing of what precedes to bring about what follows. Al-Radi said: the author said that with the nominative, causation is required, because the verbal connection disappeared by means of the resumption, so causation, which entails the meaningful connection, was stipulated as a compensation for what was lost of the verbal connection. 'Amr ibn Sha's said:

*We drive off the kings from you, and they drive us off,*
*And there is no reconciliation until you and we are satisfied (taḍba'ūn wa naḍba')*

This has been partly discussed at His words: ﴿They have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 31] in Surah al-An'am. The inceptive *hatta* indicates that the content of the speech that follows it is more important to be given attention in the speaker's delivery, because it is more effective for the purpose for which the speech is directed. The speech that comes here after *hatta* contains a terrifying description of what will befall them at the seizing of their souls, and it is more effective in threatening them, frightening them, and admonishing them than the customary threat. The Qur'an has threatened the polytheists

[Page 117]

بِشَدائِدِ المَوْتِ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي آياتٍ كَثِيرَةٍ، لِأنَّهم كانُوا يَرْهَبُونَهُ. والرُّسُلُ هُمُ المَلائِكَةُ. قالَ تَعالى: ﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفّاكُمْ مَلَكُ المَوْتِ الَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمْ﴾ [السجدة: ١١]، وقالَ: ﴿ولَوْ تَرى إذْ يَتَوَفَّى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا المَلائِكَةُ﴾ [الأنفال: ٥٠].

وجُمْلَةُ ﴿يَتَوَفَّوْنَهُمْ﴾ في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ مِن ﴿رُسُلُنا﴾، وهي حالٌ مُعَلِّلَةٌ لِعامِلِها (حالٌ تُبَيِّنُ عِلَّةَ الفِعْلِ الَّذِي تَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِ)، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ولَكِنِّي رَسُولٌ مِن رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ [الأعراف: ٦١]، ﴿أُبَلِّغُكُمْ رِسالاتِ رَبِّي وأنْصَحُ لَكُمْ﴾ [الأعراف: ٦٢]، أيْ: رَسُولٌ لِأُبَلِّغَكُمْ ولِأنْصَحَ لَكُمْ.

والتَّوَفِّي نَزْعُ الرُّوحِ مِنَ الجَسَدِ، وقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ بَيانُهُ عِنْدَ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿إذْ قالَ اللَّهُ يا عِيسى إنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ﴾ [آل عمران: ٥٥] فِي سُورَةِ آلِ عِمْرانَ، وهو المُرادُ هُنا. ولا جَدْوى فِي حَمْلِهِ عَلى غَيْرِ هَذا المَعْنى، مِمّا تَرَدَّدَ فِيهِ المُفَسِّرُونَ. إلّا أنَّ المُحافَظَةَ عَلى مَعْنى الغايَةِ لِحَرْفِ (حَتّى)، فَتَوَفِّي الرُّسُلِ يَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ المُرادُ مِنهُ وقْتَ أنْ يَتَوَفَّوْهُمْ جَمِيعًا، إنْ كانَ المُرادُ بِالنَّصِيبِ مِنَ الكِتابِ الاسْتِئْصالَ، أيْ حِينَ تُبْعَثُ طَوائِفُ المَلائِكَةِ لِإهْلاكِ جَمِيعِ أُمَّةِ الشِّرْكِ.

ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ المُرادُ حِينَ يَتَوَفَّوْنَ آحادَهُمْ في أوْقاتٍ مُتَفَرِّقَةٍ، إنْ كانَ المُرادُ بِالنَّصِيبِ مِنَ الكِتابِ وعِيدَ العَذابِ. وعَلى الوَجْهَيْنِ فالقَوْلُ مَحْكِيٌّ عَلى وجْهِ الجَمْعِ، والمُرادُ مِنهُ التَّوْزِيعُ، أيْ قالَ كُلُّ مَلَكٍ لِمَنْ وُكِّلَ بِتَوَفِّيهِ، عَلى طَرِيقَةِ: رَكِبَ القَوْمُ دَوابَّهُمْ. وقَدْ حُكِيَ كَلامُ الرُّسُلِ مَعَهُمْ وجَوابُهُمْ إيّاهُمْ بِصِيغَةِ الماضِي عَلى طَرِيقَةِ المُحاوَرَةِ، لِأنَّ وُجُودَ ظَرْفِ المُسْتَقْبَلِ قَرِينَةٌ عَلى المُرادِ.

والِاسْتِفْهامُ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿أيْنَ ما كُنْتُمْ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ مُسْتَعْمَلٌ فِي التَّهَكُّمِ والتَّأْيِيسِ.

و(ما) الواقِعَةُ بَعْدَ (أيْنَ) مَوْصُولَةٌ، يَعْنِي: أيْنَ آلِهَتُكُمُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ أنَّهُمْ يَنْفَعُونَكُمْ عِنْدَ الشَّدائِدِ ويَرُدُّونَ عَنْكُمُ العَذابَ؟ فَإنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَحْضُرُوكُمْ، وذَلِكَ حِينَ يَشْهَدُونَ العَذابَ عِنْدَ قَبْضِ أرْواحِهِمْ، فَقَدْ جاءَ

[صفحة ١١٨]

فِي حَدِيثِ المُوَطَّأِ: «أنَّ المَيِّتَ يَرى مَقْعَدَهُ بِالغَداةِ والعَشِيِّ، إنْ كانَ مِن أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ فَمِن أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ، وإنْ كانَ مِن أهْلِ النّارِ يُقالُ لَهُ: هَذا مَقْعَدُكَ حَتّى يَبْعَثَكَ اللَّهُ».

وهَذا خِطابٌ لِلْأرْواحِ الَّتِي بِها الإدْراكُ، وهو قَبْلَ فِتْنَةِ القَبْرِ.

وقَوْلُهُمْ: ﴿ضَلُّوا عَنّا﴾ أيْ: أتْلَفُوا مَواقِعَنا وأضاعُونا فَلَمْ يَحْضُرُوا. وهَذا يَقْتَضِي أنَّهم لَمّا يَعْلَمُوا أنَّهُمْ لا يُغْنُونَ عَنْهُمْ شَيْئًا مِنَ النَّفْعِ، فَظَنُّوا أنَّ الَّذِي أذْهَبَهُمْ ما أذْهَبَهُمْ، وأبْعَدَهُمْ عَنْهُمْ ما أبْعَدَهُمْ، ولَمْ يَعْلَمُوا سَبَبَهُ، لِأنَّ ذَلِكَ إنَّما يَتَبَيَّنُ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الحَشْرِ حِينَ يَرَوْنَ إهانَةَ أصْنامِهِمْ وتَعْذِيبَ كُبَرائِهِمْ. ولِذَلِكَ لَمْ يُنْكِرُوا فِي جَوابِهِمْ أنَّهُمْ كانُوا يَدْعُونَهُمْ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ، بِخِلافِ ما حُكِيَ عَنْهُمْ فِي يَوْمِ الحَشْرِ مِن قَوْلِهِمْ: ﴿واللَّهِ رَبِّنا ما كُنّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ٢٣]. ولِذَلِكَ قالَ هُنا: ﴿وشَهِدُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ أنَّهُمْ كانُوا كافِرِينَ﴾، وقالَ فِي الأُخْرى: ﴿انْظُرْ كَيْفَ كَذَبُوا عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ [الأنعام: ٢٤].

والشَّهادَةُ هُنا شَهادَةٌ ضِمْنِيَّةٌ، لِأنَّهم لَمّا لَمْ يَنْفُوا أنْ يَكُونُوا يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ، وأجابُوا بِأنَّهم ضَلُّوا عَنْهُمْ، قَدِ اعْتَرَفُوا بِأنَّهُمْ عَبَدُوهُمْ.

فَأمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ ادْخُلُوا فِي أُمَمٍ﴾ [الأعراف: ٣٨]، فَهَذا قَوْلٌ آخَرُ، لَيْسَ هُوَ مِنَ المُحاوَرَةِ السّابِقَةِ، لِأنَّهُ جاءَ بِصِيغَةِ الإفْرادِ، والأقْوالُ قَبْلَهُ مُسْنَدَةٌ إلى ضَمائِرِ الجَمْعِ. فَتَعَيَّنَ أنَّ ضَمِيرَ (قالَ) عائِدٌ إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى بِقَرِينَةِ المَقامِ، لِأنَّ مِثْلَ هَذا القَوْلِ لا يَصْدُرُ مِن أحَدٍ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ تَعالى. فَهُوَ اسْتِئْنافُ كَلامٍ (جُمْلَةٌ مُسْتَأْنَفَةٌ) نَشَأَ بِمُناسَبَةِ حِكايَةِ حالِ المُشْرِكِينَ حِينَ أوَّلِ قُدُومِهِمْ عَلى الحَياةِ الآخِرَةِ، وهِيَ حالَةُ وفاةِ الواحِدِ مِنْهُمْ. فَيَكُونُ خِطابًا صَدَرَ مِنَ اللَّهِ إلَيْهِمْ بِواسِطَةِ أحَدِ مَلائِكَتِهِ، أوْ بِكَلامٍ سَمِعُوهُ وعَلِمُوا أنَّهُ مِن قِبَلِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، بِحَيْثُ يُوقِنُونَ مِنْهُ أنَّهُمْ داخِلُونَ إلى النّارِ، فَيَكُونُ هَذا مِن أشَدِّ ما يَرَوْنَ فِيهِ مَقْعَدَهُمْ مِنَ النّارِ، عُقُوبَةً خاصَّةً بِهِمْ.

والأمْرُ مُسْتَعْمَلٌ لِلْوَعِيدِ، فَيَتَأخَّرُ تَنْجِيزُهُ إلى يَوْمِ القِيامَةِ.

ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ المَحْكِيُّ بِهِ ما يَصْدُرُ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعالى يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ مِن حُكْمٍ عَلَيْهِمْ بِدُخُولِ النّارِ مَعَ الأُمَمِ السّابِقَةِ، فَذَكَرَ عَقِبَ حِكايَةِ حالِ قَبْضِ

[صفحة ١١٩]

أرْواحِهِمْ إكْمالًا لِذِكْرِ حالِ مَصِيرِهِمْ، وتَخَلُّصًا إلى وصْفِ ما يَنْتَظِرُهُمْ مِنَ العَذابِ، ولِذِكْرِ أحْوالِ غَيْرِهِمْ. وأيًّا ما كانَ، فَالإتْيانُ بِفِعْلِ القَوْلِ بِصِيغَةِ الماضِي لِلتَّنْبِيهِ عَلى تَحْقِيقِ وُقُوعِهِ عَلى خِلافِ مُقْتَضى الظّاهِرِ.

ويَجُوزُ أنْ تَكُونَ جُمْلَةُ ﴿قالَ ادْخُلُوا فِي أُمَمٍ﴾ [الأعراف: ٣٨] فِي مَوْضِعِ عَطْفِ البَيانِ (بَدَلٌ تَفْسِيرِيٌّ يُوَضِّحُ ما قَبْلَهُ) لِجُمْلَةِ ﴿يَنالُهُمْ نَصِيبُهُمْ مِنَ الكِتابِ﴾، أيْ: قالَ اللَّهُ فِيما كَتَبَهُ لَهُمْ: ﴿ادْخُلُوا فِي أُمَمٍ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ [الأعراف: ٣٨]، أيْ أمْثالِكُمْ. والتَّعْبِيرُ بِفِعْلِ المُضِيِّ جَرى عَلى مُقْتَضى الظّاهِرِ.

والأُمَمُ جَمْعُ الأُمَّةِ بِالمَعْنى الَّذِي تَقَدَّمَ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ولِكُلِّ أُمَّةٍ أجَلٌ﴾ [الأعراف: ٣٤].

و(فِي) مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فِي أُمَمٍ﴾ لِلظَّرْفِيَّةِ المَجازِيَّةِ، وهِيَ كَوْنُهُمْ فِي حالَةٍ واحِدَةٍ وحُكْمٍ واحِدٍ، سَواءٌ دَخَلُوا النّارَ فِي وسَطِهِمْ أمْ دَخَلُوا قَبْلَهُمْ أوْ بَعْدَهُمْ. وهِيَ بِمَعْنى (مَعَ) فِي تَفْسِيرِ المَعْنى. ونُقِلَ عَنْ صاحِبِ الكَشّافِ (الزَّمَخْشَرِيِّ) أنَّهُ نَظَّرَ (فِي) الَّتِي فِي هَذِهِ الآيَةِ بِـ(فِي) الَّتِي فِي قَوْلِ عُرْوَةَ بْنِ أُذَيْنَةَ:

إنْ تَكُنْ عَنْ حُسْنِ الصَّنِيعَةِ مَأْفُو ∗∗∗ كًا فَفِي آخَرِينَ قَدْ أُفِـكُـوا

ومَعْنى ﴿قَدْ خَلَتْ﴾ قَدْ مَضَتْ وانْقَرَضَتْ قَبْلَكُمْ، كَما فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿تِلْكَ أُمَّةٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ﴾ [البقرة: ١٣٤] فِي سُورَةِ البَقَرَةِ، يَعْنِي: أنَّ حالَهُمْ كَحالِ الأُمَمِ المُكَذِّبِينَ قَبْلَهُمْ. وهَذا تَذْكِيرٌ لَهُمْ بِما حاقَ بِأُولَئِكَ الأُمَمِ مِن عَذابِ الدُّنْيا، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ كَيْفَ فَعَلْنا بِهِمْ﴾ [إبراهيم: ٤٥]، وتَعْرِيضٌ بِالوَعِيدِ بِأنْ يَحِلَّ بِهِمْ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ، وتَصْرِيحٌ بِأنَّهُمْ فِي عَذابِ النّارِ سَواءٌ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 38–39:

﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them: "Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say: "For each there is double, but you do not know."﴾ ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾

Page 120
The clause ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ is a fresh, independent resumption (al-isti'naf al-ibtida'i), describing their condition in the Fire and making it dreadful to the hearer, so that their likes may take warning and the believers may rejoice in being safe from what befell them. Thus the clause ﴿until when they have overtaken one another therein﴾ falls within the scope of this resumption.
