It is also permissible that the clause ﴿Every time a nation enters﴾ be interposed (mu'taridah) between the clause ﴿He will say: Enter among nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and humankind, into the Fire﴾ and the clause ﴿until when they have overtaken one another therein﴾, etc. In that case the clause ﴿until when they have overtaken one another﴾ is linked to a clause "Enter among nations" by an omitted estimate, its estimate being: "So they enter, until when they have overtaken one another."

The (ma) in His words ﴿kullama﴾ is a temporal, verbal-source particle (zarfiyyah masdariyyah), meaning: at every time that a nation enters, it curses its sister. The estimate is: every nation among them curses its sister at every time that a nation among them enters, so it conveys the generality of times.

The word ﴿ummah﴾ is indefinite, falling within the scope of the generality of times, so it conveys generality: every nation that enters. Likewise ﴿ukhtaha﴾ ("its sister") is indefinite, since it is annexed to an indefinite pronoun and so is not definite, and it conveys generality too: every nation that enters curses every sister of its own. By "its sister" is meant one resembling it in the religion that made it deserve entry into the Fire, as one says of two nations who share a lineage: "This nation is the sister of that nation," so one says "Bakr and its sister Taghlib." From this is the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"And like Tasm and its sister in remoteness"

He means: like Tasm and Jadis.

The context determines the aspect of sisterhood. The cause of the cursing is that each nation enters the Fire only after the reckoning has been debated and the command to put them into the Fire is given, and this happens only after it has become clear to them

Page 121
that what they were upon of religion was misguidance and falsehood. Thereby an aversion to what they were upon arises in their souls, because souls dislike misguidance and falsehood once it has become clear, and because they saw that the outcome of that was bringing punishment upon them. So they increase in aversion to their religion. When they enter the Fire and see the nations that were put into the Fire before them, they know, by some mode of knowledge, that they were put into the Fire by that same cause, so they curse them out of aversion to their religion and to those who followed it.

It has been said: the intended "its sister" is its forebears who misled it.

The particle "kullama" conveys, by its meaning of timing, that this cursing occurs at the entry of the nation into the Fire. It is therefore necessary that the estimate be: it curses its sister who preceded it in entering the Fire. Thus the nation that enters the Fire first, before the other nations, does not curse a sister, and it is known that it curses whoever enters after it, the second, and whoever after that by way of priority, or else it returns the curse upon every sister who curses it. The meaning is: every time a nation of them enters, as indicated by His words ﴿it curses its sister﴾.

The ﴿hatta﴾ in His words ﴿until when﴾ is initial (ibtida'iyyah), so it is an independent clause. It has already been mentioned in the verse before this one that the initial "hatta" conveys the sense of causation, i.e., the content of what precedes causes the content of what follows. So it may be that it is semantically consequent upon the content of His words ﴿He will say: Enter among nations that have passed away﴾ etc., and it may be that it is consequent upon the content of His words "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister."

The verb ﴿ádarakū﴾ originally is ﴿tadārakū﴾, the ta' was changed to dal so that it could be assimilated into the following dal for lightness, and it was made quiescent so that the sense of assimilation would be realized, the two being moving because of heaviness, and a hamzat al-wasl was brought in for the sake of beginning with a quiescent letter. This change is not obligatory but is preferred, and it is not like the changing of the ta' in idhdhāna, izdāda, and idhdhakara. Its meaning: some of them overtook others, so the pattern tafā'ala was formed from the root of attainment (idrak). The meaning: they caught up with one another and gathered in the Fire. His words ﴿jamī'an﴾ ("all together") is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of ﴿ádarakū﴾, to confirm the comprehensiveness of the gathering, i.e., until the nations of misguidance have all gathered.

Page 122
By ﴿akhrāhum﴾ ("the last of them") is meant the later in rank, namely the followers and the common subjects of each nation among those nations, since every nation in any age is not free of leaders and rabble. By ﴿al-ūlā﴾ ("the first") is meant the first in rank and standing, namely the leaders and those followed from each nation as well. Thus "al-ukhrā" and "al-ūlā" here are attributes applied to omitted nouns: the later of the groups for the first ones. It has been said that by "al-ukhrā" is meant the later in time, and by "al-ūlā" their forebears, because they say ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 22]. But this does not suit what comes after it.

The lam in ﴿li-ūlāhum﴾ ("to the first of them") is the lam of causation, not the lam by which the verb of saying is transitive, because the speech of the last group is directed to God, Exalted, by the explicit statement of their words ﴿Our Lord, these led us astray﴾ etc., not to the first group. It is therefore like the lam in His words, Exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11].

The min is redundant (zā'idah) to emphasize the negation of superiority, because God's statement "for each there is double" is the means of knowing that there is no advantage for the last of them over the first in being punished with a punishment less than theirs. The imperative form in their words "so taste" is used for humiliation and satisfaction.

Dhawq (tasting) is used figuratively, by an extended metonymy (majāz mursal), for sensing through the sense of touch, and its parallels have been mentioned more than once.

The ba' is causal, i.e., because of what you used to earn, which necessitated for you the doubling of punishment. He expressed it with "earning" rather than "disbelief" because it is more comprehensive of their conditions, since their leading their followers astray was by disbelief, by love of boasting and display, and by what they taught them and what they established for them. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 40–41:**

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. And thus do We recompense the criminals.﴾ ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire, and above them coverings of it. And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement) serving to confirm the eternal abiding of both groups in the Fire. This is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-A'raf: 36]. Thus Allah informed that He has deprived them of the means of salvation, closed off for them the doors of goodness and righteousness, and deprived them of entering Paradise.

He emphasized the report with *inna* (indeed), the particle of emphasis, in order to despair them of entering Paradise, and to repel the supposition that the intended meaning of the abiding mentioned earlier is a metaphor for a long duration of stay in the Fire. For it has come in many places with this very meaning.

[Page 126]

The explicit noun was used in a place where a pronoun would be expected (*al-idhhar fi maqam al-idmar*), to repel the possibility that the pronoun refers to one of the two groups conversing in the Fire. Among the forms of explicit reference, the form of definition by the relative pronoun was chosen, signifying what the relative clause (*silah*) indicates of the reason for the statement's construction. That is: this is for their denial of Allah's signs and their arrogance toward them, as was mentioned in its earlier parallel just above.

The word "heaven" (*al-sama'*) is used in the Qur'an with several meanings. Most often it is meant to denote the higher worlds other than the earthly world. So "heaven" is the totality of the higher worlds, which are levels, and in which are the worlds of the Divine holiness (*al-qudus*), namely the angels and the beneficial righteous spirits, and the source of the outpouring of spiritual and physical goods upon the earthly world, and the source of the decreed destinies. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in heaven is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22]. So "heaven" here is meant to denote the world of holiness.

The "gates of heaven" are the causes of great matters, which were called "gates" to bring their realities closer to the minds. Among them is the acceptance of deeds, the pathways by which good matters issuing from the people of the earth reach (heaven), and the ways of their acceptance. This is a metaphor for the causes of purification. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And righteous deeds raise it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. None knows their realities in detail except Allah, exalted is He, because they are veiled from us. Just as the petitioners and intercessors, when they arrive at a place, may be accepted and be pleased with, so the doors of palaces and domes are opened for them and they enter honored; and they may also be turned away and be displeased with, so the doors are shut in their faces. He illustrated the exclusion of the deniers who are arrogant, and the absence of approval of them in all conditions, by the condition of one for whom the doors of dwellings are not opened. The doors were attributed to heaven to make clear that this is an image of their deprivation from the means of the divine spiritual goods. This includes the non-answering of supplication, the non-acceptance of deeds and acts of worship, and the deprivation of their spirits, after death, from witnessing the sights of Paradise and the seats of the believers therein.

So His saying: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ is a comprehensive expression for the meaning of deprivation from purely divine goods, even though they receive some of Allah's physical bounties similar to what others receive: they are given rain, and sustenance comes to them from Allah. This is an explanation of their state of abandonment (*khudhlan*) in this world, which stands between them and the means of entering Paradise, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each is made easy for that for which he was created." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for he who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ [al-Layl: 5] ﴿and believes in the best [reward]﴾ [al-Layl: 6] ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 7] ﴿But as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Layl: 8] ﴿and denies the best [reward]﴾ [al-Layl: 9] ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 10].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read *lā tuftaḥu* (لا تُفَتَّحُ) with a *ḍamma* on the first *tā'* (ت), a *fatḥa* on the *fā'* (ف), and a shadda on the second *tā'*, which is intensification in opening (*mubalaghah fi fath*), and so it conveys the affirmation of the negation of opening for them. Or, this intensification indicates that the negated opening is a specific opening, namely the opening which is opened for the believers, and it is a strong opening. Thus that indication is an addition to their distress.

Abu 'Amr read it with a *ḍamma* on the first *tā'*, a *sukūn* on the *fā'*, and a *fatḥa* on the second *tā'*, unstressed. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read *lā yaftaḥu* (لا يَفْتَحُ) with a *yā'* (ي) at its beginning, with the second *tā'* unstressed and vowelled with a *fatḥa*, considering the verb masculine because the subject is a plural of masculine.

His saying: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise﴾ is a report about their state in the Hereafter and a confirmation of their abiding in the Fire.

After He had confirmed this by emphasizing the entire report with the particle of emphasis, He added further emphasis by the method of affirming a thing by what resembles its opposite, well known among the rhetoricians as affirming praise by what resembles blame (*ta'kid al-madh bi-ma yushbih al-dhamm*). This is by His saying: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. He made the negation of their entry into Paradise an unbroken extension, since He made its limit something impossible: that the camel should pass through the eye of the needle. That is, if the negation of their entry into Paradise had a limit, its limit would be the passing of the camel, which is the beast of burden, through the eye of the needle, and this is a matter that never occurs.

The *jamal* (جَمَل, camel) is the well-known beast of the Arabs, and it was used as an example because it is the most famous of bodies in size in the custom of the Arabs. The *khiyat* (خِياط) is the *mikhyat* (مِخْيَط, needle), meaning the instrument of sewing called the needle. The form *fi'al* (فِعال) occurs as a noun synonymous with *mif'al* (مِفْعَل) in indicating the instrument of a thing, as in their saying *hizam* and *mihzam* (belt), *izar* and *mi'zar* (waist-wrap), *lihaf* and *milhaf* (quilt), *qina'* and *miqna'* (veil).

The *samm* (سَمّ) is the hole in the needle through which the thread of the sewer is passed; it is a narrow opening. In the verse it is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn* (س) according to the dialect of Quraysh, and the *sīn* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* in the dialect of the people of al-'Aliyah, which is the region between Najd and the boundaries of the land of Makkah.

The Qur'an referred to what is known among people concerning the reality of the camel and the reality of the needle, so that it may be known that the passing of the camel through the eye of the needle is impossible and unattainable as long as they remain in their two well-known states.

The indicator in His saying "And thus" (*wa kadhalika*) points to the non-opening of the gates of heaven, which His saying "The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise" includes. That is: and the like of that negation, i.e., deprivation, do We recompense the criminals, because by their criminality, which is denial and turning away, they made themselves indifferent to the means of goodness and salvation, so they neither sought them nor pursued them. Therefore Allah requited them, for their arrogance, by turning away from them and closing off for them the doors of goods.

The clause ﴿And thus do We recompense the criminals﴾ is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) that indicates that criminality is what brought them into that recompense. They have thus entered into the generality of "the criminals," who are recompensed with the like of that recompense, and they are the primary intended group within it, because the punishment of the criminals has been likened to the punishment of these people. So it is known that they are criminals, and that they are in the first rank of the criminals, to the point that the punishment of the general category of criminals has been likened to their punishment, and they became an example for that generality.

*Ijram* (إجْرام) is the act of *jurm* (جُرْم, with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*), which is sin. The original sense of *ajrama* (أجرم) is that he became one possessing *jurm*, just as it is said *albana* (he became one possessing milk), *atmara* (he became one possessing dates), *akhsaba* (he became one possessing fertility).

The *mihad* (مِهاد, with a *kasra* on the *mīm*) is what is spread out, i.e., laid flat. *Ghawash* (غَواشٍ) is the plural of *ghashiyah* (غاشِية), which is what covers a person, i.e., envelops him, like a blanket. He likened what is beneath them of the Fire to a bed, and what is above them of it to coverings. This is a metaphor for the absence of comfort for them in Hell, for a person needs a bed and a covering when lying down for rest. So when their bed and covering are the Fire, their comfort is negated. This is a mention of their evil torment after He had mentioned their deprivation of good.

His saying "coverings" (*ghawash*) is a description of an implied noun indicated by His saying "from Hell": that is, "and above them are fires like coverings."

He concluded it with His saying: ﴿And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, to indicate that the cause of that recompense in punishment is wrongdoing (*zulm*), which is polytheism (*shirk*). Since the recompense of the wrongdoers has been likened to the recompense of those who denied the signs and were arrogant toward them, it is known that these deniers are among the wrongdoers, and they are the primary intended group of this comparison, such that they became an example for the general category of wrongdoers. By these two generalities the two clauses became concluding clauses.

In this second clause there is no placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, because the two descriptions, although both are true of the deniers whose punishment was likened to the punishment of those who possess the two descriptions, the description of "criminals" is more general in meaning than the description of "wrongdoers," because criminality includes denial of the Creator (*ta'til*) and Magianism (*majusiyyah*), unlike polytheism. The true essence of placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun is only established where the explicit noun mentioned has no meaning beyond the meaning of the pronoun.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 40–41:**

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. And thus do We recompense the criminals.﴾ ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire, and above them coverings of it. And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement) serving to confirm the eternal abiding of both groups in the Fire. This is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-A'raf: 36]. Thus Allah informed that He has deprived them of the means of salvation, closed off for them the doors of goodness and righteousness, and deprived them of entering Paradise.

He emphasized the report with *inna* (indeed), the particle of emphasis, in order to despair them of entering Paradise, and to repel the supposition that the intended meaning of the abiding mentioned earlier is a metaphor for a long duration of stay in the Fire. For it has come in many places with this very meaning.

[Page 126]

The explicit noun was used in a place where a pronoun would be expected (*al-idhhar fi maqam al-idmar*), to repel the possibility that the pronoun refers to one of the two groups conversing in the Fire. Among the forms of explicit reference, the form of definition by the relative pronoun was chosen, signifying what the relative clause (*silah*) indicates of the reason for the statement's construction. That is: this is for their denial of Allah's signs and their arrogance toward them, as was mentioned in its earlier parallel just above.

The word "heaven" (*al-sama'*) is used in the Qur'an with several meanings. Most often it is meant to denote the higher worlds other than the earthly world. So "heaven" is the totality of the higher worlds, which are levels, and in which are the worlds of the Divine holiness (*al-qudus*), namely the angels and the beneficial righteous spirits, and the source of the outpouring of spiritual and physical goods upon the earthly world, and the source of the decreed destinies. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in heaven is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22]. So "heaven" here is meant to denote the world of holiness.

The "gates of heaven" are the causes of great matters, which were called "gates" to bring their realities closer to the minds. Among them is the acceptance of deeds, the pathways by which good matters issuing from the people of the earth reach (heaven), and the ways of their acceptance. This is a metaphor for the causes of purification. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And righteous deeds raise it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. None knows their realities in detail except Allah, exalted is He, because they are veiled from us. Just as the petitioners and intercessors, when they arrive at a place, may be accepted and be pleased with, so the doors of palaces and domes are opened for them and they enter honored; and they may also be turned away and be displeased with, so the doors are shut in their faces. He illustrated the exclusion of the deniers who are arrogant, and the absence of approval of them in all conditions, by the condition of one for whom the doors of dwellings are not opened. The doors were attributed to heaven to make clear that this is an image of their deprivation from the means of the divine spiritual goods. This includes the non-answering of supplication, the non-acceptance of deeds and acts of worship, and the deprivation of their spirits, after death, from witnessing the sights of Paradise and the seats of the believers therein.

So His saying: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ is a comprehensive expression for the meaning of deprivation from purely divine goods, even though they receive some of Allah's physical bounties similar to what others receive: they are given rain, and sustenance comes to them from Allah. This is an explanation of their state of abandonment (*khudhlan*) in this world, which stands between them and the means of entering Paradise, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each is made easy for that for which he was created." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for he who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ [al-Layl: 5] ﴿and believes in the best [reward]﴾ [al-Layl: 6] ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 7] ﴿But as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Layl: 8] ﴿and denies the best [reward]﴾ [al-Layl: 9] ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 10].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read *lā tuftaḥu* (لا تُفَتَّحُ) with a *ḍamma* on the first *tā'* (ت), a *fatḥa* on the *fā'* (ف), and a shadda on the second *tā'*, which is intensification in opening (*mubalaghah fi fath*), and so it conveys the affirmation of the negation of opening for them. Or, this intensification indicates that the negated opening is a specific opening, namely the opening which is opened for the believers, and it is a strong opening. Thus that indication is an addition to their distress.

Abu 'Amr read it with a *ḍamma* on the first *tā'*, a *sukūn* on the *fā'*, and a *fatḥa* on the second *tā'*, unstressed. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read *lā yaftaḥu* (لا يَفْتَحُ) with a *yā'* (ي) at its beginning, with the second *tā'* unstressed and vowelled with a *fatḥa*, considering the verb masculine because the subject is a plural of masculine.

His saying: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise﴾ is a report about their state in the Hereafter and a confirmation of their abiding in the Fire.

After He had confirmed this by emphasizing the entire report with the particle of emphasis, He added further emphasis by the method of affirming a thing by what resembles its opposite, well known among the rhetoricians as affirming praise by what resembles blame (*ta'kid al-madh bi-ma yushbih al-dhamm*). This is by His saying: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. He made the negation of their entry into Paradise an unbroken extension, since He made its limit something impossible: that the camel should pass through the eye of the needle. That is, if the negation of their entry into Paradise had a limit, its limit would be the passing of the camel, which is the beast of burden, through the eye of the needle, and this is a matter that never occurs.

The *jamal* (جَمَل, camel) is the well-known beast of the Arabs, and it was used as an example because it is the most famous of bodies in size in the custom of the Arabs. The *khiyat* (خِياط) is the *mikhyat* (مِخْيَط, needle), meaning the instrument of sewing called the needle. The form *fi'al* (فِعال) occurs as a noun synonymous with *mif'al* (مِفْعَل) in indicating the instrument of a thing, as in their saying *hizam* and *mihzam* (belt), *izar* and *mi'zar* (waist-wrap), *lihaf* and *milhaf* (quilt), *qina'* and *miqna'* (veil).

The *samm* (سَمّ) is the hole in the needle through which the thread of the sewer is passed; it is a narrow opening. In the verse it is pronounced with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn* (س) according to the dialect of Quraysh, and the *sīn* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* in the dialect of the people of al-'Aliyah, which is the region between Najd and the boundaries of the land of Makkah.

The Qur'an referred to what is known among people concerning the reality of the camel and the reality of the needle, so that it may be known that the passing of the camel through the eye of the needle is impossible and unattainable as long as they remain in their two well-known states.

The indicator in His saying "And thus" (*wa kadhalika*) points to the non-opening of the gates of heaven, which His saying "The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise" includes. That is: and the like of that negation, i.e., deprivation, do We recompense the criminals, because by their criminality, which is denial and turning away, they made themselves indifferent to the means of goodness and salvation, so they neither sought them nor pursued them. Therefore Allah requited them, for their arrogance, by turning away from them and closing off for them the doors of goods.

The clause ﴿And thus do We recompense the criminals﴾ is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) that indicates that criminality is what brought them into that recompense. They have thus entered into the generality of "the criminals," who are recompensed with the like of that recompense, and they are the primary intended group within it, because the punishment of the criminals has been likened to the punishment of these people. So it is known that they are criminals, and that they are in the first rank of the criminals, to the point that the punishment of the general category of criminals has been likened to their punishment, and they became an example for that generality.

*Ijram* (إجْرام) is the act of *jurm* (جُرْم, with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*), which is sin. The original sense of *ajrama* (أجرم) is that he became one possessing *jurm*, just as it is said *albana* (he became one possessing milk), *atmara* (he became one possessing dates), *akhsaba* (he became one possessing fertility).

The *mihad* (مِهاد, with a *kasra* on the *mīm*) is what is spread out, i.e., laid flat. *Ghawash* (غَواشٍ) is the plural of *ghashiyah* (غاشِية), which is what covers a person, i.e., envelops him, like a blanket. This is a metaphor for the absence of comfort for them in Hell, for a person needs a bed and a covering when lying down for rest. So when their bed and covering are the Fire, their comfort is negated. This is a mention of their evil torment after He had mentioned their deprivation of good.

His saying "coverings" (*ghawash*) is a description of an implied noun indicated by His saying "from Hell": that is, "and above them are fires like coverings."

Since the recompense of the wrongdoers has been likened to the recompense of those who denied the signs and were arrogant toward them, it is known that these deniers are among the wrongdoers, and they are the primary intended group of this comparison, such that they became an example for the general category of wrongdoers. By these two generalities the two clauses became concluding clauses.

The true essence of placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun is only established where the explicit noun mentioned has no meaning beyond the meaning of the pronoun.

He followed the warning and threat addressed to the deniers with good news and promise for the believers who affirmed the truth, in keeping with the Qur'an's habit of following one purpose with the other.

It is conjoined (*'ataf*) to ﴿Those who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], meaning: "And indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds..." This is because the content of the two sentences has an intermediate relevance (*munasabah*) lying between full connection (*kamal al-ittisal*) and full disconnection (*kamal al-inqita'*). That relevance is the opposition between the description of the subjects in the two sentences, namely denying the signs and believing in them, and between the judgment on the predicates, namely punishment and bliss. This belongs to what is called the imagined comprehensive (*al-jami' al-wahmi*) mentioned in the rules of separation and connection (*ahkam al-fasl wa al-wasl*) in the science of rhetorical meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*).

No complement is mentioned for *amanu* (they believed) because faith had become like a title (*laqab*) for the specific faith brought by the religion of Islam, which is faith in God alone.

The demonstrative is the second subject (*mubtada' thani*), *Ashab al-Jannah* (the companions of the Garden) is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of "those who believed." The clause ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) between the subject and the predicate, in the manner of *idmaj* (embedding one statement within another). The benefit of this embedding is to be kind to the believers. When God gave them good news of the Garden for doing righteous deeds, He set their hearts at ease by assuring them that they would not be required to do righteous deeds beyond their capacity. Thus, if they could not reach some level, they would not despair of the Garden. Rather, they are only asked for what is within their power, and that pleases their Lord.

It is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said, regarding this verse: "*illa yusraha la 'usraha*" (except its ease, not its hardship). He meant that he said it by way of interpretation (*tafsir*), not that it is a recitation (*qira'ah*).

The word *wus'* (capacity) has been discussed earlier, in His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except according to its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying, "Those are the companions of the Garden," indicates a restriction (*qasr*) of permanent residence in the Garden to them, to the exclusion of others. Thus there is another discouragement for the polytheists, by which the explicit certainty of their deprivation of the Garden and its bliss is strengthened. The clause ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the demonstrative in His saying ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 43:

﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise is to Allah, who has guided us to this. And we would not have been guided if Allah had not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do."﴾

Page 131
The coherence of the structure requires that the clause "rivers will flow beneath them" (تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهِمُ الأنْهارُ) be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in His words "they will abide therein forever" (﴿هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾) [al-A'raf: 36]. The clause "And We will remove" (ونَزَعْنا) is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ) between the clause "Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever" (﴿أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾) [al-A'raf: 42] and the clause "And they say, 'Praise is to Allah'" (﴿وقالُوا الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾) etc., which is also a parenthetical insertion, through which the state of their souls in their dealings in Paradise is clarified, to counterbalance the insertion that was embedded in the description of the punishment of the people of the Fire, and what clarifies the state of their souls in dealing with one another is His words: "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister" (﴿كُلَّما دَخَلَتْ أُمَّةٌ لَعَنَتْ أُخْتَها﴾) [al-A'raf: 38].

The expression of the future by the past tense is to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence, i.e., "And We will remove what is in their breasts of rancor." This is a well-known expression in the Qur'an, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah's command has come﴾ (﴿أتى أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾) [al-Nahl: 1].

The literal meaning of nazʿ (removal) is pulling a thing out of its place, and it was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You take away the kingdom from whom You will﴾ (﴿وتَنْزِعُ المُلْكَ مِمَّنْ تَشاءُ﴾) [Al 'Imran: 26] in Al 'Imran. The removal of rancor from the hearts of the people of Paradise is the elimination of what was in their hearts in this world of rancor upon receiving what displeases them from others, such that Allah purifies their souls in their second life from being affected by the evil thoughts of which rancor is one. So what was in their hearts of the rancor of some toward others in this world disappears; that is, He removes what was already present of rancor and removes the dispositions of rancor that are in human souls, such that it does not occur to their souls.

Ghill (rancor) is resentment, grudge and enmity that arise in the soul upon perceiving what harms it from the deed of another. Envy (ḥasad) is not part of rancor; rather it is another inner sentiment.

Page 132
The clause "rivers will flow beneath them" (تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهِمُ الأنْهارُ) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., they are in lofty places overlooking the rivers of Paradise.

The clause "And they say, 'Praise is to Allah'" (وقالُوا الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ) is coordinated with the clause "Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever" (﴿أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾) [al-A'raf: 42].

The past tense is also intended to express the future, as in His saying "And We removed" (ونَزَعْنا). This statement may be one that they say among themselves, in private, meaning drawing near to Allah by praising Him, and it may be that they say it among themselves in their assemblies.

The demonstrative in their saying "for this" (لِهَذا) refers to everything present of bliss at the time of that praise, and guidance to it is directing to its causes, which are faith and righteous deeds, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ (﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ﴾) [al-A'raf: 42], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their Lord guides them by their faith﴾ (﴿يَهْدِيهِمْ رَبُّهم بِإيمانِهِمْ﴾) [Yunus: 9], etc. He made the guidance to the bliss itself, because indicating what leads to a thing is guidance for the sake of that thing. The discussion of the verb of guidance and its transitivity has preceded in Surah al-Fatiha.

What is meant by Allah's guiding them is His sending Muhammad (ﷺ) to them, so he awakened them from their heedlessness, and they followed him, did not obstinately oppose, and did not act arrogantly. This is indicated by their saying "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth" (﴿لَقَدْ جاءَتْ رُسُلُ رَبِّنا بِالحَقِّ﴾), along with what Allah facilitated for them of accepting the call and complying with the command, for that is part of the completeness of the favor for which He is praised. This facilitation is what was denied to the deniers and arrogant, because of their beginning with denial and arrogance, rather than reflection and consideration.

The clause "we would not have been guided" (﴿وما كُنّا لِنَهْتَدِيَ﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause referring to the object pronoun, i.e., He guided us in this state, the state of our being far from being guided, and this indicates the greatness of Allah's favor upon them and the magnification and abundance of their praise. For this reason they brought the praise in a sentence comprising the utmost of the qualities discussed earlier in Surah al-Fatiha.

Page 133
His saying "we would not have been guided" (﴿وما كُنّا لِنَهْتَدِيَ﴾) indicates the remoteness of their former state from being guided, as conveyed by the negation of the verb with the lam of denial (lām al-juḥūd), as was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book and the wisdom and prophethood﴾ (﴿ما كانَ لِبَشَرٍ أنْ يُؤْتِيَهُ اللَّهُ الكِتابَ والحُكْمَ والنُّبُوَّةَ﴾) [Al 'Imran: 79] in Surah Al 'Imran. They were immersed in ancient misguidance which had firmly taken root in their souls. As for their leaders, Satan had made it attractive to them until they believed in it and established it as a custom for those after them; and as for their common folk and descendants, they saw their exemplars upon those misguidances, and it became rooted in them. So their guidance was not easy, were it not that Allah guided them by sending the messengers, by their methodical approach in the call, and by casting into their hearts the acceptance of the call.

For this reason they followed their praise and thanks to Allah with their saying: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth" (﴿لَقَدْ جاءَتْ رُسُلُ رَبِّنا بِالحَقِّ﴾). This is a resumptive sentence (جملة مستأنفة), a fresh beginning (استئنافا ابتدائيا), since it issues from the delight and gladness of their souls at what the messengers brought them. They began recalling the causes of their guidance, taking lessons from them and rejoicing, savoring speaking of it, because recalling a beloved matter and speaking of it is something souls delight in, along with the intention of praising the messengers.

The emphasis of the verb with the oath-lam and with qad, although they did not deny the coming of the messengers, is either because it is a metaphor for admiration at the correspondence of what the messengers promised them of bliss with what they found, like His saying: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in﴾ (﴿وفِيها ما تَشْتَهِيهِ الأنْفُسُ وتَلَذُّ الأعْيُنُ﴾) [al-Zukhruf: 71], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): Allah, exalted is He, said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Or it is because by this statement they intended praise of the messengers and testimony to their truthfulness all together along with praise of Allah, so they expressed the report in the form of an emphatic testimony in which there is no doubt.

Ibn 'Amir recited (ما كُنّا لِنَهْتَدِيَ) without a waw before "مَا"; likewise it was written thus in the Imam Qur'an sent to Syria. On this reading, this sentence is separated from the one before it, on the consideration that it serves as a justification (تعليل) for the praise and as an indication that it is a great praise for a great blessing, as was explained earlier.

Page 134
The clause "And they will be called" (ونُودُوا) is coordinated with the clause "And they say" (وقالُوا), so it is also a circumstantial clause, because this call is a response to their praise, indicating the acceptance of what they praised with, and Allah's pleasure with them. The call is from Allah, and for this reason its verb is built in the passive, because the intended meaning is evident. Nida' is the proclamation of address, which is the original literal meaning in the language, and nida' is generally applied to calling someone so that he may turn toward it with his self or with his understanding to hear speech, even without raising the voice: ﴿When he called to his Lord a secret call﴾ (﴿إذْ نادى رَبَّهُ نِداءً خَفِيًّا﴾) [Maryam: 3]. For this meaning there are particular letters in Arabic that indicate it. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And their Lord called them both﴾ (﴿وناداهُما رَبُّهُما﴾) [al-A'raf: 22] in this surah.

"An" (أنْ) is an explanation of "nūdū" (نُودُوا), because nida' contains the meaning of saying. The demonstrative "tilkum" (تِلْكُمُ) for Paradise, which ought to be used for a distant referent, is used although Paradise is present before them, in order to express its exalted rank and the magnification of the favor through it.

The root meaning of irth (inheritance) is the passing of a dead person's property to his closest relatives. It is said: the deceased bequeathed his property to his relatives (أوْرَثَ المَيِّتُ أقْرِباءَهُ مالَهُ), meaning he made them inherit it from him, because when he did not divert it from them by bequeathing it to another, he left it to them. It is used figuratively for a thing passing to someone without compensation or seizure, by analogy with the inheritance of the dead. So the meaning of His saying "you have been given it as an inheritance" (أُورِثْتُمُوها) is: it has been given to you as a gift, pleasant, without toil or dispute.

The bā' in His saying "for what you used to do" (بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ) is causal, i.e., because of your deeds, namely faith and righteous action. This statement is praise of them, that Allah thanked them for their deeds, and gave them this everlasting bliss because of their deeds; and that when they performed what they performed, they intended by their deeds nothing but safety from their Lord's wrath and seeking His good pleasure, thankfully for His blessings, and they did not presume that their deeds would bring them to what they were saying. This does not contradict hoping for His reward and salvation from His punishment. This is indicated by the combination of "you have been given it as an inheritance" (أُورِثْتُمُوها) with the causal bā'.

So the inheritance indicates that it is a gift without intent of exchange or contract, and that it is pure grace from Allah, exalted is He, since the servant's faith in his Lord and obedience to Him does not necessitate, by reason or by justice,

Page 135
anything beyond his salvation from the punishment which by its nature follows disbelief and disobedience, and the attainment of his Lord's pleasure with him; nor does it necessitate reward or gift. For thanking the benefactor is obligatory, so this reward and its magnitude is merely grace from the Lord upon His servant in gratitude for his faith in Him and obedience to Him. But since the cause of this gratitude in the sight of the grateful Lord is the servant's doing what He commanded him, and Allah has graciously promised it before it occurred, it is strange that the Mu'tazila say the reward is obligatory by reason. Perhaps what led them into this was confusing the attainment of reward with safety from punishment, although the intermediate state between the two is clear to people of understanding. This is better than what our companions prolong their argument with them about.

The causal bā' necessitated that "the one who gave them the abodes of Paradise" intended by it the thanking of their deeds and their reward, without intent of exchange or equivalence, so He made it like a thing the worker deserved in exchange for his work, and so borrowed for it the causal bā'.

The clause ﴿And the companions of the Garden called out to the companions of the Fire﴾ may be coordinated with the clause ﴿And they say, "Praise be to God, who guided us to this"﴾ (Q. 7:43), as a coordination of speech upon speech, since their statement expressing their delight in the bliss they are in is related, and then what they say to the people of the Fire when they see them is related.

It may also be coordinated with the clause ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Garden you have been given as an inheritance"﴾ (Q. 7:43), as a coordination of one narrative upon another, because of the transition from mention of a call from God to mention of the people of the Hereafter calling out to one another. On both readings, the reference to them as "the companions of the Garden" rather than by a pronoun is a preparation for the mention of the call of the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf) and the call of the companions of the Fire, so that each group is expressed by its own designation. It also yields the rhetorical embellishment of antithesis (tibaq) in its contrast with the phrase ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾.

This calling out is an address from the companions of the Garden. It is expressed as a "call" as a metonymy (kinaya) for its reaching the ears of the companions of the Fire from a very great distance, since the vastness of the Garden and the vastness of the Fire require this, especially with His statement ﴿and between them is a barrier﴾ (Q. 7:46). The means by which this address reaches the companions of the Fire from the Garden is a wondrous means, not commonly known.

The knowledge of God and His power have no limit to their objects.

The ﴿an﴾ in His statement ﴿that indeed we have found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾ is explanatory (tafsiriyya) of the call.

The statement ﴿we have found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾ is used in the sense of its implication, which is the expression of their satisfaction with their condition and the vexing of their enemies by their knowledge of the comfort of their state, and the reproach directed at the enemies, who used to think that they had gone astray when they left the religion of their fathers, and that they had deprived themselves of the good things of the world by abstaining from sins. These are multiple meanings, all of them implications of the statement. Kinaya meanings do not preclude being multiple, since they follow from rational implications. In this kinaya the literal meaning is combined with the kinaya meanings, but the kinaya meanings are the intended ones, since the aim is not that the people of the Fire should know what has happened to the people of the Garden, but rather what follows from that. As for the literal meanings, they are signified primarily when there is no preventing indicator.

The interrogation in the clause ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ is used figuratively (majaz mursal) with the relation of necessary concomitance (luzum), to make the addressees recognize their error, to stir their remorse and grief over what they neglected, and to gloat over them regarding the consequences of their obstinacy. Figurative meanings whose relation is necessary concomitance may be multiple, like kinaya. The indicator of the figure is that it is evident that the companions of the Garden know that the companions of the Fire have found His promise to be true.

Finding (wujdan) means coming upon a thing and encountering it. God says ﴿and he found in it two men fighting﴾ (Q. 28:15). Its verb is transitive to one object. God says ﴿and found God with him﴾ (Q. 24:39). It is common for its object to be accompanied by a description of its state. So His statement ﴿we have found what our Lord promised us to be true﴾ means: we came upon it in the state of being true, with no failure in any part of it. Therefore His statement "we found" does not indicate a prior search or seeking for correspondence, as may be supposed. Finding may also be used figuratively for perception and for supposition, and this is a widespread figurative usage.

The relative ﴿mā﴾ (what) in His statements ﴿what our Lord promised us﴾ and ﴿what your Lord promised﴾ indicates that the relative clause is known to the addressees, though to varying degrees of generality and detail. They knew that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, promised the believers a great bliss and threatened the disbelievers with a painful punishment. Some of them heard all or some of the details of that, and some of them heard its general outline, either directly or by transmission from their brethren. Thus the relative form in His statement ﴿that indeed we have found what our Lord promised us to be true, so have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ is a wondrous conciseness (ijaz badi').

The answer "Yes" (na'am) confirms what was asked about with "hal," since a question with hal implies the questioner's inclination toward the occurrence of what is asked about. So it is the answer of one who acknowledges, grieves, and confesses. The answer came fit for both the apparent and the hidden import of the question. The intent of answering with it is to confirm what was meant by the question of meanings, whether literal or figurative, since "na'am" is not exclusive to confirming literal meanings.

The object of the second verb "wa'ada" in His statement ﴿what your Lord promised you﴾ is omitted merely for conciseness, since its counterpart indicates it in His statement ﴿what our Lord promised us﴾, because the intent of the question is to ask them about what concerns them. The estimate is: "So have you found what your Lord promised you," that is, of punishment, since promising (wa'd) is used for both good and evil.

The particle "fa" (then) in His statement ﴿Then a caller called out among them﴾ indicates that the proclamation is caused by the exchange, confirming the purpose of the people of the Garden in questioning the people of the Fire, namely to expose their error and the corruption of their belief.

Proclamation (ta'dhin) is raising the voice with speech in a manner that makes even the distant hear, as far as possible. It is derived from "udhun" (with a damma on the hamza), the organ of hearing, the well-known ear. This proclamation is an announcement of a curse (la'n), which is distancing from good, that is, an announcement that the people of the Fire are removed from the mercy of God, as an increase in their despair, or an invocation against them for an increase in their distance from mercy, by multiplying the punishment or confirming their eternal abiding. That this proclamation occurs immediately after the exchange shows that by "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin), and what follows them of attributes and actions, are meant the companions of the Fire. The purpose of those attributes is to make their state appear monstrous, and to denounce the corruption of their souls and the corruption of their belief.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Qunbul from Ibn Kathir read ﴿that the curse of God﴾ with the nun of "anna" lightened, so that it is explanatory of the verb "adhdhana" (proclaimed), and "la'nat" is read in the nominative as a subject, and the sentence is explanatory. The rest read it with the nun doubled and "la'nat" in the accusative, so that the sentence is the object of "adhdhana," because it includes the sense of speaking. The estimate is: saying that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers.

Referring to them as "the wrongdoers" is identifying them by an attribute that functions as a title by which their group is known, as one says "the believers" for the people of Islam. Therefore it does not conflict that when they were described with it they were not wrongdoers at that time, because they had come to know the falsity of polytheism with the fullest knowledge. The rule for the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is that it is literally about the present and figuratively about the future, and it is not about the past. As for the application of the relative clause to them by the two present-tense verbs in His statement ﴿who bar﴾ and His statement ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾, the rule for the present tense is indicating an event occurring at the time of the present. At the time of the proclamation they were not characterized by barring from the way of God, nor by seeking to make the way crooked. So this usage is for the purpose of what the present tense conveys of recurrence of the act in connection with the sense of renewal. The meaning is describing them as repeatedly doing that in the past time. This is what the scholars of rhetoric ('ilm al-ma'ani) call "evoking the state" (istihdar al-hala), as in His statement, reported about Noah: ﴿and he was building the ark﴾ (Q. 11:38), though the time of the building of the ark had passed. Only the evocation of the state of renewal is intended. Likewise, their description by the active participle in His statement ﴿and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾, since its rule is indicating the time of the present, but it is used here for the past: that is, they were disbelievers in the Hereafter during the past of their worldly life. All of this relies on the indicator of the state of the hearers, which prevents the literal meaning from being intended by the form of the present tense and the form of the active participle, since every hearer knew that those intended had ceased to be characterized by those events at the time of the proclamation, but rather had come to be characterized by their opposites. For at that time they had come to know the truth and witnessed it, as His statement "Yes" indicates. They were identified by those past states because human souls are known by the states they were characterized by during the first life. By death the states of a human being end, and the soul's attribute becomes fixed upon what it lived upon. In the hadith: "Every servant will be raised upon what he died upon," narrated by Muslim. It is possible that this curse was one that the angels used to pronounce upon them in the world, and so they proclaimed it openly in the Hereafter, because it became like a slogan for the disbelievers, by which they are called. This is like what came in the hadith: "The muezzins will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, shouting the adhan," although the words of the adhan contain what its meaning is not intended on that day, namely "Hasten to prayer, hasten to success." In the report of this here is an announcement to the people of these attributes in the world that they deserve the curse of God, may He be exalted.

The wrongdoers meant here are the polytheists. As for barring from the way of God, it is either the polytheists' confronting those inclined to Islam with harm and turning them away from entering the religion by various means, and the way of God is that by which one reaches His good pleasure, which is Islam, so that barring is meant transitively, with an object; or it is their turning away from hearing the call to Islam and hearing the Qur'an, so that barring is meant intransitively, which is said to have a present tense with a kasra on the sad, or its present tense ought to have a kasra on the sad. It is said that the form with a kasra on the sad has not been heard, although the analogy is a kasra on the sad for the intransitive and a damma for the transitive.

The feminine pronoun in His statement ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ refers to the way of God, since "sabil" (way) is used both masculine and feminine. God says ﴿Say: "This is my way"﴾ (Q. 12:108), and He says ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ (Q. 7:146).

Crookedness ('iwaj) is the opposite of straightness. It is with a fatha on the 'ayn for physical things and with a kasra on the 'ayn for abstract meanings. Its origin is that either vowel may be used, but usage has restricted the literal meaning to one of the two forms and the figurative meaning to the other. That is one of the excellences of usage. So the report about "the way" with "crookedness" ('iwaj) is a report by the verbal noun for emphasis, meaning: they aim and attempt to show this way as crooked, that is, they fabricate defects for it and disguise these before the people, in order to repel them from Islam, as their saying ﴿Shall we show you a man who tells you that when you are utterly torn apart, you will be in a new creation?﴾ (Q. 34:7) and ﴿Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾ (Q. 34:8). Its explanation was given earlier, at His statement ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of God those who believe, seeking to make it crooked?﴾ (Q. 3:99) in Surah Al 'Imran.

Their description with disbelief came by way of the nominal sentence in His statement ﴿and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾, to indicate the permanence of disbelief in them and its firm hold upon them, since disbelief is among the rational beliefs, to which repetition is not suited. Therefore a contrast was made between it and their description with barring from the way of God and seeking to show crookedness in it, because those two are actions that accept repetition, unlike disbelief, which is not an action but a state of being affected. A parallel to this is His statement ﴿He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ (Q. 42:19).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 46–47:

﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights (al-A'raf) are men who recognize each by his mark. And they call out to the companions of Paradise: "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, though they aspire (to).﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾

The fronting of "between them" (wa-baynahuma), which is the predicate preceding the subject, is for emphasis on the place intermediate between Paradise and the Fire and on what is mentioned of its condition. With this fronting, it is valid to begin with an indefinite noun (al-ibtida' bi-l-nakira), and the indefiniteness is for magnification (al-ta'zim).

The pronoun in "baynihima" refers to the two words "Paradise" and "Fire" occurring in His saying: ﴿And the companions of Paradise call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]. These are two nouns of place, so it is fitting to consider the notion of being intermediate between them. The barrier is made a partition between them, and the dual form of the pronoun specifies this meaning. Had the pronoun been intended to refer to the two groups, the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, he would have said "baynahum," as He said in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13], and so on.

The barrier (al-hijab) is a wall struck as a separator between the place of Paradise and the place of Hell. The Qur'an has named it a wall (sur) in His saying: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13] in Surat al-Hadid, and it was called a barrier (hijab) because its purpose is screening and prevention, just as it was called a wall (sur) with regard to its encircling.

Al-A'raf is the plural of 'urf (with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ra'), though the ra' may also be vocalized with a damma. It means the highest part of a thing, and from it is named the 'urf of a horse, the hair on the top of its neck, and the 'urf of a rooster, the feathers on the top of its head.

The "al-" in "al-A'raf" is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and these are the well-known heights that stand prominently atop walls, from which observers watch the movements of the enemy and by which they become aware when it attacks them. No mention of "the heights" has preceded here so that it would be defined by the definite article of prior reference, so it is determined that they are what people know of in walls. Or the "al-" may be a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "and upon the heights of the wall." Both are possibilities in similar instances of this definiteness, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41]. In either case, the structure of the verse refuses that the intended "heights" be a specific place by which the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire are identified, since in that case there would be no reason to define it when the discourse has not previously mentioned it.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is to validate beginning with an indefinite noun, since the context requires speaking about unknown men who will be upon the heights of this barrier, before they enter Paradise, and there they will witness the conditions of the people of Paradise and the conditions of the people of the Fire, and they will recognize men from the people of the Fire who were, in the world, of the people of might and pride, and who used to deny God's promise of Paradise to the believers. The specification of "men" by mention does not necessitate that there are no women among the people of the heights, nor that these particular men spoken of are exclusively in that place to the exclusion of other men. Rather, these are men to whom this report happens, so they are mentioned here for admonition by way of coincidence, not with the intention of dividing the people of the Hereafter and their places. Perhaps the supposition that the specification of men by mention was intended as a division has put some exegetes into perplexity in seeking the meaning, because that would require that the people of the heights had deserved that place on account of a condition in which women have no share. So some exegetes took "men" literally and sought a deed that men do and women have no share in within Islam, and there is none but jihad. Some exegetes said: "These are a people who fought in holy war and were disobedient to their fathers." Other exegetes took "men" metaphorically, in the sense of individuals from among the angels, who were called "men" because they are not female, just as the word was applied to individuals of the jinn in His saying: ﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6]. Thus a reason for specifying "men" appears, following what is in some of those hadiths we have pointed to.

As for what has been transmitted from some of the early generation (al-salaf) that the people of the heights are a people whose scales of good deeds and scales of evil deeds were equal, and that the application of "men" to them is by way of predominance (taghlib), since there must be women among them, and reports are narrated on this matter attributed with chains to the Prophet (ﷺ) which have not reached the level of the sound nor descended to the rank of the weak: some of them were narrated by Ibn Majah, some by Ibn Mardawayh, and some by al-Tabari. If they are authentic, then what is meant by them is that whoever has those conditions will be among the people of the heights spoken of in the Qur'an as those who have not entered Paradise while they aspire to it. They have not entered it, though they aspire (to).﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾

The fronting of "between them" (wa-baynahuma), which is the predicate preceding the subject, is for emphasis on the place intermediate between Paradise and the Fire and on what is mentioned of its condition. With this fronting, it is valid to begin with an indefinite noun (al-ibtida' bi-l-nakira), and the indefiniteness is for magnification (al-ta'zim).

The pronoun in "baynihima" refers to the two words "Paradise" and "Fire" occurring in His saying: ﴿And the companions of Paradise call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]. These are two nouns of place, so it is fitting to consider the notion of being intermediate between them. The barrier is made a partition between them, and the dual form of the pronoun specifies this meaning. Had the pronoun been intended to refer to the two groups, the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, he would have said "baynahum," as He said in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13], and so on.

The barrier (al-hijab) is a wall struck as a separator between the place of Paradise and the place of Hell. The Qur'an has named it a wall (sur) in His saying: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13] in Surat al-Hadid, and it was called a barrier (hijab) because its purpose is screening and prevention, just as it was called a wall (sur) with regard to its encircling.

Al-A'raf is the plural of 'urf (with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ra'), though the ra' may also be vocalized with a damma. It means the highest part of a thing, and from it is named the 'urf of a horse, the hair on the top of its neck, and the 'urf of a rooster, the feathers on the top of its head.

The "al-" in "al-A'raf" is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and these are the well-known heights that stand prominently atop walls, from which observers watch the movements of the enemy and by which they become aware when it attacks them. No mention of "the heights" has preceded here so that it would be defined by the definite article of prior reference, so it is determined that they are what people know of in walls. Or the "al-" may be a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "and upon the heights of the wall." Both are possibilities in similar instances of this definiteness, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41]. In either case, the structure of the verse refuses that the intended "heights" be a specific place by which the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire are identified, since in that case there would be no reason to define it when the discourse has not previously mentioned it.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is to validate beginning with an indefinite noun, since the context requires speaking about unknown men who will be upon the heights of this barrier, before they enter Paradise, and there they will witness the conditions of the people of Paradise and the conditions of the people of the Fire, and they will recognize men from the people of the Fire who were, in the world, of the people of might and pride, and who used to deny God's promise of Paradise to the believers. Rather, these are men to whom this report happens, so they are mentioned here for admonition by way of coincidence, not with the intention of dividing the people of the Hereafter and their places. So some exegetes took "men" literally and sought a deed that men do and women have no share in within Islam, and there is none but jihad. Some exegetes said: "These are a people who fought in holy war and were disobedient to their fathers." Other exegetes took "men" metaphorically, in the sense of individuals from among the angels, who were called "men" because they are not female, just as the word was applied to individuals of the jinn in His saying: ﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6]. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 48–49:

﴿Then the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognise by their marks, saying: "Of what use to you were your multitude and your arrogance?"﴾ ﴿"Are these the ones of whom you swore that God would never grant them His mercy?" "Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve."﴾

The definiteness in His words ﴿companions of the Heights﴾ is for prior reference (li-l-ʿahd), by the indication of its earlier mention in His words ﴿And on the Heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46], and by the indication of His words here ﴿men whom they recognise﴾. It is not sound that those men are called by all who were on the Heights, nor that all who were on the Heights recognise them by their marks, given the differences of eras and nations. So what is meant by "companions of the Heights" is the men mentioned in the previous verse with His words ﴿And on the Heights are men﴾ [al-A'raf: 46]. It is as if it were said: "Those men who were on the Heights called out to men." The expression "companions of the Heights" for them here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, where the apparent form would have been "they called out to men." However, since in the previous verse there were several things to which the pronouns could refer, the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun to remove ambiguity.

[p. 145]

Calling out (al-nidāʾ) indicates the distance of the one addressed. So it appears that the people of the Heights, when they looked with their eyes towards the Fire, recognised men, or before that, when they were passed by the people of the Fire, they recognised men who had been tyrants in the world. Here, al-sīmā (the marks) must be taken to mean the personal identifying features by which individuals are distinguished, and it is not the sīmā by which all the people of the Fire are distinguished, as in the previous verse.

So the purpose of this verse is to mention something of the matter of the Hereafter. In it is a warning and an admonition to the tyrannical polytheists among the Arabs, who used to belittle the weak among the believers, among whom were slaves and the poor. When they heard the Qur'an's good tidings to the believers of Paradise, they fell silent about those of the free Muslims and their masters, and denied that those weak ones and slaves were among the people of Paradise. This was on the basis of supposition, that is, even if they supposed the true existence of a Paradise, these people are not fit to dwell in Paradise, because they did not believe in Paradise. Their aim in this was to deny the Prophet (ﷺ) and to display what they considered foolishness in his sayings. This is like their saying: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who tells you that when you are utterly torn apart, you will be in a new creation?﴾ [Saba': 7]. They made the tearing apart and perishing of bodies a proof against the resurrection, and they remained silent about the resurrection of bodies that had not been torn apart. All of this is due to misunderstanding, weakness of comprehension, and confusing customary matters with rational ones. Ibn al-Kalbi said: The people of the Heights call out while they are on the wall: "O Walid ibn al-Mughira! O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham! O so-and-so! O so-and-so!" These are the men whom they recognise by their marks, and they were among the people of power and pride.

The meaning of ﴿your multitude﴾ (jamʿukum) may be the gathering of people, that is, your numbers in which you took pride did not avail you. It may also be that by al-jamʿ is meant the verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, that is, what you gathered of wealth and property, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28].

[p. 146]

The first ﴿mā﴾ is negative, and the meaning of ﴿mā aghnā﴾ is "what did it avail", its verbal noun being al-ghanāʾ, with a fatḥa on the ghayn and with a long vowel.

The statement is used to express gloating and to make them aware of their error.

The second ﴿mā﴾ is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), that is, "and your arrogance which passed in the world." The reason for its being formed as a verb rather than as a verbal noun, when He did not say "istikbārukum", is to make use of the verb to reach its being in the present tense, which indicates that arrogance was their habit, from which they did not cease.

The clause ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that God would never grant them His mercy?﴾ is part of the speech of the companions of the Heights. The interrogative in His words ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore﴾ is used for affirmation (taqrīr).

The indication by "these" (hāʾulāʾ) is to a group of the people of Paradise who were weak in the world and belittled by the polytheists, by the indication of His words ﴿of whom you swore that God would never grant them His mercy﴾ and His words ﴿Enter Paradise﴾. The exegetes said: these are like Salman, Bilal, Khabbab and Suhayb, among the weak believers. Then either they had by that time settled in Paradise, and God displayed them to the people of the Heights and to the men who had addressed them, or that dialogue took place before they entered Paradise. Their swearing against them was to show their firmness in their belief and that no doubt had entered their minds about it, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up one who dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38].

His words ﴿that God would never grant them His mercy﴾ are the thing sworn to. They applied the negation in their speech in observance of the negation of a statement which the Messenger (ﷺ) or the believers would say. This is because the Qur'an's good tidings to those weak ones, its promise to them of Paradise, and its praise of them descended in the position of a statement saying: "God grants them with mercy," that is, His sheltering them in the abode of His mercy, which is Paradise, was placed in the position of attaining (al-nayl), which is the obtaining of a beloved matter sought after, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Those will receive their portion of the Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 37]. So the verb "attain" (yanāl) was applied to that sheltering by way of metaphor (istiʿārah).

[p. 147]

Mercy was made to stand in the position of the instrument of attaining, as one says: "He attained the fruit with a hooked stick," so the "bi" is for instrumentality. Or mercy was made to accompany the attaining, so the "bi" is for accompaniment, and "attaining" here is a metaphor. They resorted to this supposed statement and negated it, saying: "God will not grant them with mercy."

This structure in which their oath is related indicates their mockery of the weak believers in the world. The exegetes have neglected to explain this verse according to its structure.

The clause ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ is said to be the content of an omitted saying, omitted for brevity since the context indicates it. Omitting "say" in such a case is common, especially when the content is an imperative clause. The estimate is: "God said to them, 'Enter Paradise,' and God thereby denied your oath and disappointed your expectation." All of this is from the speech of the companions of the Heights. The more apparent view is that the imperative in His words ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ is for supplication (duʿāʾ), because those referred to here as "these" are people from among the people of Paradise, since at that time the people of Paradise had settled in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, as the preceding verses require, from His words ﴿And the people of the Fire call out to the companions of Paradise: "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-A'raf: 46] to His words ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-A'raf: 47]. For this reason it is necessary to take the imperative as supplication, as in the words of al-Maʿarri:

"Remain in blessing for as long as the ages endure, with a command that executes in all matters."

Since entry had already taken place, the supplication for it is for the purpose of continuance, just as the one who calls out to someone leaving says: "Go forth, without being grieved for," and from it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿and he said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security"﴾ [Yusuf: 99].

The word "fear" (khawf) is in the nominative after "lā" because the nouns of abstract meanings which have no individual instances outside the mind share the same treatment under "lā" in both the nominative and the accusative. This was explained earlier at His words: ﴿Whoever fears God and makes amends, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

The discussion of *nādā* (called out) and of *an* (that) as explanatory is the same as the discussion of: ﴿The companions of the Garden called out to the companions of the Fire, "We have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and so on. The "companions of the Fire" here refers to those among the polytheists of the community of the call, because they are the intended audience, as has already been explained, and so that it accords with His words that follow: ﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed﴾ [al-A'raf: 52].

The literal meaning of the verb *fāḍa* (to pour forth, overflow) is the flowing of water and its forceful pouring out. It is used figuratively for abundance, as in the hadith: "Wealth will overflow until no one accepts it." From it also comes a figurative usage for generosity and abundance of giving, as in the hadith that he (ﷺ) said to Ṭalḥa: "You are *al-Fayyāḍ* (the overflowing giver)." So, if *al-fayḍ* in the verse is taken in its literal sense, the companions of the Fire are asking the companions of the Garden to pour water over them so that they may drink from it. The exegetes understood it in this sense. For this reason al-Zamakhsharī made the coordination of ﴿from what Allah has provided you﴾ a coordination with the whole clause rather than with the single noun (*mufrad*). Thus an implied verb must be supplied after the conjunction particle that suits everything other than water, and its supplied form is: "or give us." He compared it with the line of verse recited by al-Farrā', which runs:

"I fed her straw and cool water, until her eyes flowed with tears."

Its implied form is: "I fed her straw and I gave her cool water to drink." On this reading, *min* (from) is in the sense of "some of," or it is an attribute of an omitted noun whose implied form is: "some of the water," because *afīḍū* (pour forth) is transitive by itself.

In my view, it is also permissible to take *al-fayḍ* in its figurative sense, namely the abundance of giving and generosity, with respect to water and provision. For the sense of pouring is not suitable here; rather what is intended is sending and bestowing favour. In this case the coordination is the coordination of a single noun with a single noun, which is the basic form of coordination (*ʿaṭf*). Their request for food would then be similar to their request for water in its abundance. In this reading there is an implicit allusion (*taʿrīḍ*) that the companions of the Garden are people of generosity. On this reading, *min* is explicative (*bayāniyya*), clarifying the meaning of pouring forth, and the verb *afīḍū* is treated as if it were intransitive (*lāzim*), so that *min* is connected to the verb *afīḍū*.

[Page 149]

The word *rizq* (provision) is intended here to mean food, as in His words: ﴿Every time they are provided with fruit from it, they say...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

The pronoun in *qālū* (they said) refers to the companions of the Garden, and it is their answer to the companions of the Fire's request. Therefore the clause is separated (from what precedes) in the manner of a dialogue.

The word *taḥrīm* (prohibition) in His words ﴿Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers﴾ is used in its linguistic meaning, which is prevention, as in the line of ʿAntarah:

"She has become forbidden to me, would that she had not become forbidden."

and His words: ﴿And it is forbidden to a town which We have destroyed that they shall not return﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 95].

By "the disbelievers" are meant the polytheists, because they are known in the Qur'an for having taken their religion as amusement and play, and they are known for denying the meeting of the Day of Gathering.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿they took their religion as amusement and play, and the life of this world deceived them﴾ has already been given in the commentary on His words: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, and whom the life of this world has deceived﴾ [al-An'ām: 70], in Sūrat al-An'ām.
