The apparent arrangement of the discourse is that His words ﴿Those who took their religion﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] up to His words ﴿the life of this world﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] are part of the report of the speech of the people of the Garden. Thus ﴿they took their religion as amusement﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51], and what follows, is an attribute of the disbelievers.

It is also permitted that ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] be a subject (*mubtada'*) with the meaning that it is part of the speech of Allah, the Exalted. This leads to making the *fa'* (so) in His words ﴿So today We will forget them﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] enter upon the predicate of the subject, by likening the relative pronoun to conditional particles, as in His words: ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them﴾ [al-Nisā': 16]. And His words ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] up to His words ﴿and they used to deny Our signs﴾ [al-A'rāf: 51] have been made a single verse in the numbering of verses in the codices of the Qur'an, but this is not binding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 51:

﴿So today We forget them, as they forgot the meeting of this day of theirs, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾ This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) in which speech is related that is announced by Allah, exalted is He, and heard by both groups. The change in the style of speech is the indication that the speaker has changed, and this is the most fitting reading according to what we have preferred: that His saying ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾ up to the end is a report of the speech of the people of Paradise.

The fa' (ف) here marks a consequence (tafrīʿ) of the words of the people of Paradise: ﴿Indeed, Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾, and so on. This conjunction with fa' is among what is called ʿaṭf al-talqīn (the conjunction of relayed speech, in which one speaker's words are joined to another's), which is usually illustrated by a conjunction with wa'. It is the conjoining of one speaker's words to another speaker's words. The implied sentence is: "He said, 'So today We forget them'," and the verb of saying has been omitted. This is a confirmation of the people of Paradise. For those who take His saying ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾ as a new, independent statement from Allah, exalted is He, the fa' is, in their view, a consequence within a single speech.

The word nisyān (forgetting) in both places is used metaphorically to mean neglect and abandonment, because it is one of the necessary implications of forgetting. They were not forgetting the meeting of the Day of Resurrection in the world; indeed, they used to mention it and speak of it in the manner of one who does not believe that it will happen.

The placing of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) with the verb ﴿We forget them﴾ serves to show that their being deprived of mercy occurred at the time when they were most in need of it. Thus the mention of the day had an effect in arousing their regret and remorse, and that is a spiritual punishment.

The meaning of the particle of comparison (kāf al-tashbīh) in His saying ﴿as they forgot﴾ indicates that their deprivation from the mercy of Allah was equivalent to their neglect of believing in the meeting. This is the equivalence of the recompense of an action to the action, and it is a notional (iʿtibārī) equivalence. Therefore it is said that the kāf in such a construction is for causation (taʿlīl), as in His exalted saying ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. Causation is only a meaning that arises from the use of the kāf for notional comparison. This comparison is not a metaphor, but a hidden reality, because the aspect of resemblance is obscure.

His saying ﴿as they forgot﴾ is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) in the position of a qualifier of an omitted noun, indicated by "We forget them", meaning: a forgetting like their forgetting.

The mā in ﴿as they forgot﴾ and in ﴿and they used to﴾ [al-A'raf: 137] is verbal-nominal (maṣdariyyah), meaning: like their forgetting of the meeting, and like their denial of the signs of Allah. The meaning of denying the signs was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33], in the surah of al-An'am.

[p. 151]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 52:

﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ The wāw in ﴿And We had certainly brought them﴾ conjunctively links this sentence to the sentence ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], as a linking of one narrative to another narrative and one purpose to another purpose. It is therefore a resumptive statement (kalam anif) by which the discourse shifts from the topic of the report about the state of the polytheists in the Hereafter to the topic of describing their states in this world, which entitle them to what they will encounter in the Hereafter. It is not from the statement that Allah followed with the speech of the companions of the Garden in His saying ﴿So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this day of theirs﴾ [al-A'raf: 51], because His saying here ﴿Do they await only its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53] etc. requires that it is a discussion of their turning away from the Qur'an in this world. Thus the pronoun of the absent plural in His saying "We brought them" refers back to ﴿those who denied﴾ [al-A'raf: 177] in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], and so on.

The Book here means the Qur'an.

The bāʾ in His saying "bi-kitābin" is for transitivity of the verb ji'nāhum, like the bāʾ in His saying ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. Its meaning is: We made a Book come to them, i.e., We made it an arriver reaching them, which amounts to: We delivered it to them and sent it to them.

The emphasis of this verb with the oath-particle lam and qad is either in view of the attribute of "kitāb", namely the clause ﴿We have detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy﴾, in which case the emphasis follows what the apparent situation requires, because the polytheists deny that the Qur'an is described with those attributes; or it is an emphasis on the verb "We brought them a Book", namely its arrival to them, in which case the emphasis departs from what the apparent situation requires, by treating the one to whom it is delivered as one who denies that the Book has reached them, since in their turning away from reflecting and pondering upon its matter they are like one whom the Book has not reached. This consideration may fit the apparent sense of His later saying: ﴿Those who had forgotten it before said: The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 53].

The indefinite form of "kitābin", although it is definite in meaning, is intended for magnifying the Book, or is intended to express its kind, i.e., it is nothing but a book like the books sent down before, as already mentioned in His exalted saying ﴿A Book has been sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2] at the opening of this surah.

"Fassalnāhu" means: We made clear, i.e., We made clear what is in it. Detailing was already discussed under His exalted saying ﴿Thus do We detail the verses, that the way of the criminals may become evident﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in Surah al-An'am.

"ʿAlā ʿilmin" is a stationary adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "fassalnāhu", i.e., while We are with knowledge. "ʿAlā" is for figurative elevation, indicating firm possession of its object, as in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] and His saying ﴿Say: Indeed I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 57] in Surah al-An'am. The meaning of this firm possession is that Allah's knowledge is intrinsic, nothing of the knowables escaping it.

The indefiniteness of "ʿilmin" is for magnification, i.e., knowing the greatest knowledge. The greatness here refers to the perfection of the genus in its reality, and the greatest knowledge is that which admits neither error nor obscurity, i.e., knowing with an intrinsic knowledge that does not fail Us and does not vary in its essence, admitting neither error nor hesitation.

﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "kitābin", or from its pronoun in His saying "fassalnāhu". Describing the Book with the two verbal nouns "guidance and mercy" points to the strength of its guiding people and bringing mercy to them.

The clause ﴿guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾ indicates that the believers are those who reached guidance and mercy through it, and that those who do not believe have been deprived of guidance and mercy. This is like His exalted saying in Surah al-Baqarah ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verse 53:**

﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إلّا تَأْوِيلَهُ يَوْمَ يَأْتِي تَأْوِيلُهُ يَقُولُ الَّذِينَ نَسُوهُ مِن قَبْلُ قَدْ جاءَتْ رُسُلُ رَبِّنا بِالحَقِّ فَهَلْ لَنا مِن شُفَعاءَ فَيَشْفَعُوا لَنا أوْ نُرَدُّ فَنَعْمَلَ غَيْرَ الَّذِي كُنّا نَعْمَلُ قَدْ خَسِرُوا أنْفُسَهم وضَلَّ عَنْهم ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾

The clause ﴿Are they waiting for anything but its ultimate reality?﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanation (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an unspoken question). The verse before it says: ﴿And We have brought them a Book which We have explained with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾ (Al-A'raf: 52). This raises the question: what keeps them from believing in this Book, which has these qualities? Is there a greater sign than it for the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ)? So the words ﴿Are they waiting﴾ serve as an answer to this question, which stirs in the mind of the listener.

The interrogative is a denial (*istifham inkari*), and that is why an exception (*istithna'*) follows it.

The meaning of ﴿yanzurun﴾ is "they await," from *nazrah* in the sense of *intizar* (waiting). The exception is from the general category of things awaited. What is meant is the things awaited of this kind, namely signs. That is, they await no greater sign ﴿except its ultimate reality﴾, that is, except the manifestation of what it threatened them with. The use of "waiting" here is a mocking metaphor (*isti'arah tahakkumiyyah*): it likens their delay until the time when what the Qur'an has threatened them with befalls them to the state of people who are waiting, though they are not actually waiting, since they deny that it will happen. This is like His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly?﴾ (Muhammad: 18) and His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed before them?﴾ (Yunus: 102). The exception is literal, and it is not a case of affirming something by means of something resembling its opposite, because the figurative usage is only in the verb ﴿yanzurun﴾.

The restriction (*qasr*) is relative (*idafi*), that is, relative to other purposes of their forgetting and denial of the signs. The discussion of a similar construction has already passed at His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come?﴾ (Al-An'am: 158), in Surah al-An'am.

*Ta'wil* (interpretation, ultimate reality) is the clarification and explanation of what is hidden, of the intended meaning of a speech or an action, and its realization. God Almighty said: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾ (Al-Kahf: 78), and: ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾ (Yusuf: 100), and: ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (*ta'wil*)﴾ (Al-Nisa': 59). Its derivation and meaning have already been discussed in the first introduction to this commentary. The pronoun in ﴿ta'wilihi﴾ refers to "Book" in His saying: ﴿We have brought them a Book which We have explained with knowledge﴾ (Al-A'raf: 52).

Its *ta'wil* is the becoming clear of the meaning of what they considered impossible and false: the Resurrection, the Recompense, the mission of a messenger from God Almighty, the oneness of God, and punishment. That is the *ta'wil* of what the Book brought, that is, its realization and its becoming clear through direct witnessing, and after direct witnessing there is only clarity.

This is explained by the clause ﴿on the day its ultimate reality comes, they will say﴾ and so on. Therefore it is separated (without a conjunction), because it stands in relation to the preceding clause as an explanation of what is meant by its *ta'wil*: the *ta'wil* that will become manifest on the Day of Resurrection. The day here is therefore the Day of Resurrection, as shown by the connection to His saying: ﴿those who forgot it before will say﴾, for they will not know this and will not say it except on the Day of Resurrection.

The coming of its *ta'wil* is a metaphor for its manifestation and clarity, through the relation of necessity, since that manifestation accompanies the coming. The *ta'wil* here means that by which the things indicating the truthfulness of the Qur'an become manifest, in what it informed them of and what it threatened them with.

﴿Those who forgot it﴾ are the polytheists, and they are the antecedent of the pronoun in ﴿yanzurun﴾. The apparent expectation would have been to say ﴿yaqulun﴾ (they will say), but it was stated with the relative clause (*mawsuliyyah*) in order to record against them that they forgot it, turned away from it, and denied it. This recording is intended to draw attention to their error and to reproach them, for by their turning away they bring the evil outcome upon themselves.

Forgetting (*nisyan*) is used in the sense of turning away and avoidance, as has already passed in His saying: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this Day of theirs﴾ (Al-A'raf: 51).

The implied genitive after ﴿qabl﴾, indicated by its being built on a *damma* (*bina' qabl 'ala al-damm*), is either *ta'wil* or the Day, that is: "before its *ta'wil*," or "before that Day," that is, in this world. The word "say" here is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for knowledge and belief, because the basic principle in statements is that they correspond to the belief of the one who makes them. That is, the truth becomes clear to them and they declare it.

This saying is said by some of them to others, acknowledging their error in denying the Messenger (ﷺ) and what he reported about the messengers before him. For this reason the messengers are mentioned in the plural here, although the discussion is about those who denied Muhammad (ﷺ). The reason is that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck examples for them with the earlier messengers, and when they denied him, their denial emboldened them to deny the sending of messengers at all: ﴿when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human"﴾ (Al-An'am: 91). Or it is because they, on that day, are witnessing what the punishment of the earlier nations for denying their messengers is, so that saying comes from their being affected by all that they have witnessed of the threat that encompasses them and those other than them among the nations.

Their saying ﴿The messengers of our Lord have indeed come with the truth﴾ is a statement used to acknowledge their error in denying the messengers, and also an expression of regret over that, and a display of perplexity as to what they should do. For this reason they arranged on it, and linked by the particle *fa* (therefore), their saying ﴿So is there for us any intercessors﴾ through to the end.

The interrogative may be genuine, said by some of them to others, perhaps one of them will guide them to a means of rescue from that predicament. This saying is made at the beginning of seeing what threatens them, before they become certain that there are no intercessors, as reported in His saying: ﴿So we have no intercessors and no close friend﴾ (Al-Shu'ara': 100–101). It may also be that the interrogative is used to express wishing (*tamanni*). It may also be used to express negation, in the sense of regret and remorse. The *min* in ﴿min shufa'a'﴾ is an emphatic extra particle (*za'ida li-l-tawkid*) in all these interpretations, so it conveys the emphasis of generality in what is asked about, to indicate that they do not ask about those whom they imagined to be intercessors among their idols, since they have despaired of them, as He said: ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners among you﴾ (Al-An'am: 94). Rather, they ask about which intercessor could intercede for them. Had only the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace, whom they opposed with enmity in the life of this world, been... Its parallel is His saying in Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿Is there any way to exit?﴾ (Ghafir: 11).

The verb ﴿fa-yashfa'u﴾ is in the accusative (*nasb*) as an answer (*jawab*) to the interrogative, or to the wish, or to the negation.

(*Al-shufa'a'*) is the plural of *shafi'*, the one who acts as an intercessor (*shafa'ah*). They name their idols "intercessors," as God Almighty said: ﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors with God"﴾ (Yunus: 18).

The meaning of intercession (*shafa'ah*) has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿nor will intercession from it be accepted﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 48) in Surah al-Baqarah; at His saying: ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 254) in Surah al-Baqarah; and at His saying: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾ (Al-Nisa': 85) in Surah al-Nisa'.

The verb ﴿nuradd﴾ is joined by *aw* (or) to the object of the interrogative. So the interrogative concerns one of two matters, because one of them cannot coincide with the other. If intercession takes place, there is no need for return (to the world), and if return takes place, one has no need for intercession.

Since the clause ﴿for us any intercessors﴾ falls within the scope of the interrogative, what is conjoined to it also falls within the scope of the interrogative. For this reason the present verb is required to be in the nominative (*raf'*) in the well-known readings, and it is nominative by its freedom from the governing particles of the accusative and the jussive. Thus it occupies the position of a noun, as al-Zamakhshari estimated following al-Farra', so it is nominative by itself, without needing to interpret the clause before it as a verbal clause by supposing: "Will intercessors intercede for us?" as al-Zajjaj estimated, since there is no compelling reason for that. For this reason ﴿fa-na'mala﴾ is in the accusative as an answer to ﴿nuradd﴾, just as ﴿fa-yashfa'u﴾ is in the accusative as an answer to ﴿fa-hal lana min shufa'a'﴾.

What is meant by "work" in their saying ﴿fa-na'mala﴾ includes belief, which is the most important, such as belief in the oneness of God, in the Resurrection, and in the confirmation of the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace, because belief is an act of the heart, and because it has practical consequences, of sayings, deeds, and obedience. What is meant by the relative clause in His saying ﴿alladhi kunna na'malu﴾ is what they used to do of matters of religion, as indicated by the context of their saying: "The messengers of our Lord have indeed come with the truth." That is: "so we would do the opposite of what we had determined upon after the coming of the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace."

The clause ﴿They have lost their souls﴾ is a resumptive clause, a fresh beginning (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), serving as a conclusion (*tadhyil*) and summary of their story. That is: the outcome of their affair was that they lost their souls from now on, and ﴿what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾.

Loss (*khasarah*) is a metaphor for failing to benefit from what was hoped to yield benefit. This has already been explained at His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls will not believe﴾ (Al-An'am: 12) in Surah al-An'am, and at His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾ (Al-A'raf: 9) at the beginning of this surah. The meaning is that what they had thrust their souls into, of polytheism and denial, has been shown to lead them to the realization of the threat against them, on the day the *ta'wil* of what the Qur'an threatened them with comes. By this it becomes established that they have lost their souls from now on, even if they are not aware.

As for His saying ﴿and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾, "straying" (*dalal*) is used as a metaphor for non-existence, in the mode of irony (*tahakkum*). It likens the non-existence of their supposed intercessors to the straying of camels from their owners, mocking them. This irony is intended to imitate their assumption on the Day of Resurrection, reported in His earlier saying: ﴿They will say, "They have strayed from us"﴾ (Al-A'raf: 37).

The *ma* in ﴿ma kanu yaftarun﴾ is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), whose referent is the intercessors whom they used to invoke besides God. The object pronoun of the relative clause is omitted, meaning "what they used to fabricate," that is, what they used to lie about when they said: ﴿These are our intercessors﴾ (Yunus: 18), while those idols are inanimate and have no share in the affairs of rational beings to be able to intercede. So they have strayed from them from now on. For this reason the verb is in the past tense, because the straying used as a metaphor for non-existence is established from times long past.

[Page 154] [Page 155] [Page 156] [Page 157] [Page 158]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 54 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself upon the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it rapidly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

The purposes of this surah came in harmonious and cohesive order. It begins with mention of the Qur'an, the command to follow it, and the rejection of whatever turns one away from it, namely following polytheism (shirk). Then it reminds [the reader] of the nations that turned away from obedience to the messengers of Allah. Then it presents evidence for the oneness of Allah, and [recounts] the favour of creating the earth and establishing [mankind] upon it, and of creating the origin of mankind and [later] their descendants. This is interspersed with a reminder of the enmity of Satan toward the origin of mankind and toward mankind in His words, "I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path" (7:16). It then moves from this to rebuke the polytheists for following Satan's embellishment in their words, "And when they commit an immorality" (7:28), and then to remind them of the covenant which Allah took from mankind in His words, "O children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves" (7:35), and so on.

[Part of the text continues:] And [the surah reminds them] that the polytheists wronged themselves by breaking the covenant, in His words, "So who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs?" (7:37). It warns them and reminds them of the states of the people of the Hereafter. Following this, it returns to mention of the Qur'an in His words, "And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge" (7:52), and concludes it with a closing statement in His words, "They have lost themselves, and what they used to invent has strayed from them" (7:53).

Therefore the ears and hearts were prepared to receive the proof that Allah is one God, and that the gods of the polytheists are misguidance and falsehood. Then [the verse comes] to demonstrate His great power and glory; for this reason the sentence "Indeed, your Lord is Allah" and the verse [following] was introduced as a fresh, independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the reminder returns to the opening of the surah in His words, "And do not follow, besides Him, any protectors" (7:3). Thus what is at the beginning of the surah stands in the position of the logical objective (al-matlub al-mantiqi), and what follows it stands in the position of the proof (al-burhan), and His words "Indeed, your Lord is Allah" stand in the position of the conclusion (al-natijah) of the proof. The conclusion is equivalent to the objective, except that it is taken in a clearer and more detailed form.

The address is initially directed at the polytheists, and for this reason the emphatic particle inna is used, its position being to refute the polytheists' denial of Allah's exclusive lordship (rububiyyah). Since what this verse contains increases the Muslims' insight into the greatness of Allah's glory and the vastness of His dominion, and increases their remembrance of the signs of His power, the address was suitable to include the Muslims, due to the suitability of the second-person pronoun for that. The particle inna is not purposeless with regard to them, because it indicates attentiveness to the information, since it holds a share for both groups. Moreover, some of what it contains is more relevant to the believers, such as "Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret" (7:55) and His words "Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good" (7:56); and some of it is more fitting for the disbelievers, such as His words "Thus will We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember" (7:57).

The subject (al-mukhbar 'anhu) is "the Lord," and the predicate (al-khabar) is the name of majesty (ism al-jalalah), "Allah." The meaning is that the Lord known to you, He whose name signifies His essence, is Allah, and not anyone else who does not bear this name, as is the normal case. This is the definition of the predicate (ta'rif al-musnad), as in: "I am your brother." It is said to one who knows the speaker and knows that he has a brother, but does not know that the speaker is his brother. The purpose of defining the predicate is to convey what is called in logic the haml al-mu'ataah (identity predication), which is the predication of "he is he." For this reason the speaker is free to make either of the two parts the subject and the other the predicate, since both are known to the addressee; what matters is that the one that is more definite for the addressee be made the subject, so that the predication is more informative. From this type is the verse of al-Ma'arri describing a horseman in a raid:

"He wades a sea whose dust is its water, which the swimmer carries in his cloak."

Since the listener already knows that the horseman has dust during a raid, and knows that the poet has attributed to the horseman a sea, and that the sea has water, the dust and the sea have become known to the listener. So he informs him that the horseman's dust is the water of the alleged sea, because this is more fitting by way of the metaphor of the sea for the dust. Otherwise, nothing would have prevented al-Ma'arri from saying "its dust is its water"; so whoever criticises the verse has not been fair to him.

This information was emphasised with the particle of emphasis, although the polytheists affirmed Allah's lordship and the Muslims have no doubt about it, because the polytheists among the addressees are treated as those who waver over whether Allah is their Lord, due to their great turning away from Him in their worship and their orientations.

His words "who created the heavens and the earth" are a qualifier (sifah) of the name of majesty, and the relative clause indicates, by allusion, the reason for the construction of the preceding predicate, namely "Indeed, your Lord is Allah," because the creation of the heavens and the earth suffices them as proof of His singularity in divinity, as was mentioned earlier at His words, "Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord" in the surah of al-An'am.

His words "in six days, then He established Himself upon the Throne" are an instruction in His great power, and from it the polytheists gain increased awareness of their misguidance in associating another with Him in divinity. The words "in six days" do not indicate that the people of Makkah knew this; and in it there is a challenge to the People of the Book, as in His words, "Does it not suffice them as a sign that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?" (26:197). The purpose of "in six days" is not to prove the oneness [of Allah], since there is no indication of that in it.

The wisdom of Allah required that the creation of the heavens and the earth be gradual and not instantaneous, because He made the worlds generate from one another, so that the creation would be more perfectly crafted than if it had been created all at once; and so that this creation would be a manifestation of the two attributes of Allah's knowledge and power. Power is capable of creating them all at once, but knowledge and wisdom required this gradualness. That period was the shortest time in which the intended generation could occur through His great power. Perhaps the repeated mention of these "days" in many verses is to draw attention to this subtle point: that they are a manifestation of the vastness of knowledge and the vastness of power.

The apparent meaning of the verses is that the "days" are the familiar days, the plural of "day," which is a period measured from the sun's appearance in the east until its next appearance in that same place. On this interpretation, the estimate for what resembles that period is six times over, because the true meaning of "day" in this sense was not realised until after the completion of the creation of the heavens and the earth, so that the light of the sun could appear on half of the earth's sphere and darkness on that half until the sun appears again. It has also been said that "days" here is the plural of the day of Allah, which is a period of a thousand years, so that "six days" refers to six thousand years, in view of His words, "Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count" (22:47), and His words, "He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a day whose extent is a thousand years of what you count" (32:5). This was narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, and al-Naqqash preferred it, and it is not far-fetched, although it contradicts what is in the Torah. It has also been said that the meaning is "in six times," since "day" is applied to a time, as in His words, "And whoever turns his back to them on that day" (8:16), meaning "at the time when they meet them in battle." The intent of this speaker is that the heavens and the earth were created as one world after another, and not all of them shared in the times of their formation. Whichever is the case, "days" is intended as measures, not the days whose singular is "day" which runs from sunrise to sunset, since there was no sun during part of that period; and to delve deeply into this question is a digression from the purpose of the Qur'an.

"Istiwa'" in its essential meaning is "levelling/equilibrium" (al-i'tidal), and what is taken from the words of the verifying scholars of lexicography and exegetes is that it is literally "rising and elevation," as in His words concerning Gabriel, "Then he rose while he was on the highest horizon; then he approached and descended" (53:6-8).

"Istiwa'" has meanings branching from its essential sense, the most well known of which are "intention" (al-qasd) and "ascent" (al-i'tila'). This term has been consistently used in the Qur'an with the pronoun of majesty as subject when reporting heavenly matters, as in this verse. Its parallels are seven verses of the Qur'an: here, in Yunus, al-Ra'd, Ta-Ha, al-Furqan, Alif-Lam-Mim al-Sajdah, al-Hadid, and Fussilat. It has become clear to me that this verb has a particularity in the speech of the Arabs, by means of which it was most suitable to convey, in summary, the intended meaning that befits the attributes of Allah and brings close to understanding the meaning of His greatness. For this reason it was chosen in these verses rather than other verbs which the exegetes interpreted it with.

Thus "istiwa'" expresses a great aspect of the greatness of the Creator, may He be exalted. It was chosen by way of metaphor and figurative representation, because its meaning is the closest of the meanings of Arabic roots to the meaning it expresses concerning His exalted matters. When Allah wished to teach meanings from the unseen world, this could not be accomplished in language except through known examples from the visible world. There was therefore no alternative but to express the hidden meanings with expressions that bring them close to what is expressed about the visible world. For this reason, metaphorical and imaginative figures of speech abound in the Qur'an in such matters.

The earlier generations (al-salaf) used to accept such expressions without investigation or questioning, because they knew the general intended meaning and were content with the meaning in summary. They called such expressions "the ambiguous" (al-mutashabihat). Then, when the era of beginning inquiry arose, whenever they were asked about this verse they would say: "Allah established Himself upon the Throne, and we do not know a how (kayf) for that." I have explained that this kind belongs to the second category of the ambiguous at His words, "and others are ambiguous" in the surah of Al 'Imran, and so they refused to interpret it. 'Iyad in al-Madarik related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah that he said: A man asked Malik, "The Merciful established Himself upon the Throne; how did He establish Himself, O Abu 'Abd Allah?" Malik remained silent for a while until sweat appeared on him, then he recovered and said: "Istiwa' is known, the how is not conceivable, asking about this is an innovation, and belief in it is obligatory; and I think you are astray." This is famously reported from Malik in many narrations, and in some of them he said to the one who asked: "I think you are a bad man; take him out from me," and he said: "Asking about it is an innovation."

From Sufyan al-Thawri, it is related that he was asked about it, and he said: "Allah did an act concerning the Throne, which He named istiwa'." The later Ash'aris interpreted it in various ways, the best of which is what Imam al-Haramayn inclined to: that the intended meaning of istiwa' is "dominion" (istila'), by the indication of its construction with the particle 'ala'. As corroboration, they recited the verse of al-Akhtal:

"Bishr has established dominion over Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

I consider this distant, because the Throne is only one of Allah's creations, so there is no basis for reporting His dominion over it; although it is possible that al-Akhtal derived it from this verse. The lexicographers said that its meanings vary with its construction with 'ala or with ila. Al-Bukhari related, from Mujahid: "istawa" means "rose above" ('ala) upon the Throne; and from Abu al-'Aliyah: "istawa ila al-sama'" means "ascended, then made their creation even."

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary is translated below. Part 2 of 3, beginning mid-argument.

I think that its metaphorical usage (istiʿarah) varies according to the preposition with which its verb is construed. If it is construed with "ʿalā" (on), as in this verse and its counterparts, then it is borrowed from the meaning of elevation (iʿtilāʾ), used in a figurative elevation that indicates the meaning of establishment and authority (tamakkun). It is possible that what is intended is a simile (tamthīl), namely the depiction of the manner of God's disposition (taṣarruf) in governing the worlds. For this reason, we find it in this construction in the seven verses, positioned after the mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth. The meaning, then, is: He created them, then He manages their affairs as a king manages the affairs of his kingdom, sitting firmly upon his throne. Something that brings this meaning closer is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "God will grip the earth and fold the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, then He will say: I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?" For this reason too, he followed the construction, in all its positions, with something that carries the meaning of disposition, such as His saying here, "He covers the night with the day," etc., and His saying in Surah Yunus: "He manages the affair; there is no intercessor except after His permission," and His saying in Surah al-Ra'd: "And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term; He manages the affair, He details the signs," and His saying in Surah al-Sajdah: "You have not, besides Him, any protector or intercessor; will you not be mindful? He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth."

The completeness of this simile requires that each part of the depicted image be likened to a part of the image used for comparison, so it requires that there be among the parts of the depicted image something resembling the throne of the king in greatness, and that it be the source of divine disposition and governance, from which the powers of managing the worlds flow. Sound reports from the words of the Messenger (peace be upon him) have indicated the existence of this great created being called the Throne, as we shall explain.

As for when the verb of istiwāʾ is construed with the preposition "lām" (to), then it is borrowed from the meaning of intention and orientation (qaṣd wa-tawajjuh) toward the meaning of the attachment of will (taʿalluq al-irādah), as in His saying, "Then He turned (istawā) to the heaven." The author of al-Kashshaf moved somewhat in this direction, but he took it along the path of metonymy (kinayah) for sovereignty: they say "so-and-so istawā upon the throne," meaning he ruled.

The throne (ʿarsh) in its literal sense is the elevated seat upon which the king sits. God the Exalted said, "And she has a mighty throne" and "and he raised his parents upon the throne." In this verse and its counterparts, it is used as part of a compound simile (tashbīh murakkab). Among the excellence of this simile is that each part of the depicted image corresponds to a part of the image used for comparison, and this is the most complete simile in Arabic eloquence, as I have previously mentioned. Since this simile was intended to bring closer one aspect of the greatness of God's kingdom through the state of a familiar human condition, it was appropriate that it include what is the emblem of the greatest managers of affairs known among people, namely kings, and that is the emblem of the throne, around which the king's dispositions proceed. The management of God over His creatures by the command of creation proceeds through the angels. The Qur'an has explained the work of some of them, such as Jibril (peace be upon him) and the Angel of Death, and the Sunnah has explained some of them: it mentioned the angel of the mountains, the angel of the winds, and the angel who directly fashions the embryo and writes its provision, its term and its final fate. Likewise, the Qur'an has pointed out that among the higher beings there is an exalted existent named the Throne, which the Qur'an mentions in many verses. When it mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth and mentioned the Throne, it mentioned it in a way that implies that it existed before this creation. The Sunnah has made clear that the Throne is greater than the heavens and what is in them, from which is the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God was, and there was nothing before Him, and His throne was upon the water, then He created the heavens and the earth." And the hadith of Abu Hurairah from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said in a long hadith: "When you ask God, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle and highest of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." It has been said that the Throne is the Kursi, and that it is what is meant in His saying, "His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth," as the discussion of it has preceded in Surah al-Baqarah.

The particle "thumma" (then) in His saying "then He istawā upon the throne" indicates a gradation of rank (tarakhi rutbi), i.e., and greater than the creation of the heavens and the earth is His istiwāʾ upon the throne, as an alert that the creation of the heavens and the earth did not introduce any change in God's dispositions by addition or subtraction. For this reason, istiwāʾ upon the throne is mentioned right after the mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth in many verses. Perhaps the purpose of this is to refute what the Jews say: that God rested on the seventh day. It is akin to the purpose of His saying, "And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us."

The clause "He covers the night with the day" (yughshī al-layla al-nahār) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalālah). With it is mentioned some of the generality of His management and disposition, implicit in istiwāʾ upon the throne, and an alert to the purpose of istiwāʾ. For this reason it came in the form of a circumstantial clause, not in the form of a predicate, as it was mentioned in general terms in the verses of Surah Yunus and Surah al-Ra'd with His saying "He manages the affair." He singled out this disposition for mention because of what it indicates of great power, and the lesson of change it contains and the evidence of having come into being, and because its occurrence is repeated in the observation of all people. Ighshā' and taghshiyah mean making a thing a covering; ghashy and ghashayān literally mean covering and overwhelming.

So the meaning of "yughshī al-layla al-nahār" is that God makes one of them a covering for the other.

Ghashy is used metaphorically for concealment, because the day removes the trace of the night and the night removes the trace of the day. Among the marvels of conciseness and elegance of construction is making "the night" and "the day" two objects of the verb of the agent of covering; both are objects, and each is suitable to be the agent of covering. For this reason, by saying "yughshī al-layla al-nahār" he dispensed with mentioning the reverse, and did not say "wa-l-nahāra al-layla," as in the verse "yukawwir al-layla ʿala al-nahār." But the original arrangement of objects in this type is that the first be the agent in meaning, and the reverse is permissible when there is no ambiguity, and all the more so when both possibilities are equal.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "yughshī" with a dammah on the yā' and sukūn on the ghayn and a light shīn. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with a dammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ghayn, and a doubled shīn; both have the same meaning in transitivity.

The clause "yaṭlubuhu" (seeking it): if it is taken as a new sentence (isti'nāf) or as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the clause "yughshī," its matter is clear. The pronoun object in "yaṭlubuhu" may refer to the night and to the day. If it is taken as a circumstantial clause, it may be considered a circumstantial clause of either of the two objects equally, for both the night and the day are considered seeker and sought, following the consideration of one of them as first or second object.

The appearance of the darkness of night spreading across the horizon from east to west at sunset, and the disappearance of daylight's light falling across the horizon from east to west until darkness covers the horizon, is likened, by way of simile, to the night seeking the day. Likewise is understood the comparison of the extension of dawn's light across the horizon from east to west and the disappearance of the darkness of night, falling in the west until light covers the horizon, to the day seeking the night, by way of simile. There is no obstacle to considering the verb-sharing (tanāzuʿ) of the two objects in the circumstantial clause, as in His saying, "So she brought him to her people, carrying him," and His saying, "And the sun and the moon and the stars subjected by His command."

"Ḥathīth" means swift, and it is a fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, from ḥathathahu, when he hastened him and repeated his urging so that he would hurry in haste. Close to this is the saying of Salamah ibn Jandal, mentioning the end of his youth and the beginning of his age of gray hair:

"Youth has passed away, whose ends bring glory;
in it we enjoyed, and there are no pleasures for gray hair.
It has departed swiftly, and this gray hair follows it;
if it were to be overtaken, it would be by the running of the pursuers."

So the meaning is: it seeks it swiftly, earnestly in haste, because it does not linger long before its trace is effaced.

As for "al-shamsa wa-l-qamara wa-l-nujuma" in the accusative according to the reading of the majority, they are conjoined to "the heavens and the earth," i.e., and He created the sun, the moon, and the stars, which are among the greatest creatures contained in the heavens. And "musakhkharātin" (subjected) is a circumstantial clause from the things mentioned.

Ibn 'Amir read "al-shamsu" and what is conjoined to it in the nominative, and "musakhkharātun" in the nominative, so the clause becomes a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the Name of Majesty, like His saying "yughshī al-layla al-nahār."

The discussion of the night and the day has already occurred at His saying, "Indeed in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day" in Surah al-Baqarah, and it will come in Surah al-Shams.

Taskhīr (subjection) in its literal sense is the taming of one who has a difficult or preoccupying task by force and fear, or by teaching and management without compensation. From it comes the subjecting of slaves and captives, the subjecting of horses and mounts, and the subjecting of cattle for milking and sheep for shearing. It is used metaphorically for directing a thing without will toward a wondrous or great work whose use is difficult, by means of a stratagem or inspiration, in a way that makes it among its properties and affairs, such as the subjecting of ships to sail the sea by wind or by rowing, the subjecting of clouds for rain, the subjecting of the day for work and the night for rest, the subjecting of night for travel in summer and the sun for warmth in winter, the shade for coolness in summer, and the subjecting of trees for eating their fruit, where they were created free of obstacles that prevent picking them, such as thick thorns. Thus the lion is not subjected in this sense, but it is such that it can be subjected when a person wishes to benefit from its flesh or skin, by a stratagem for hunting it with a pit or the like. For this reason God the Exalted said, "And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all of it from Him," using this metaphor with varying degrees of strength of connection. So His saying "al-shamsa wa-l-qamara wa-l-nujuma musakhkharātin bi-amrihi" uses taskhīr metaphorically for making them submissive to the order by which God created them without alteration, although it is in the nature of their greatness that no other than Him, the Exalted, could set them in a limited, regulated order.

The word "amr" in His saying "bi-amrihi" is used metaphorically for disposition according to the power flowing in accordance with the will. Among it is the command of creation, expressed in the Qur'an in His saying, "His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He say to it: Be, and it is." For "kun" is a near expression of the execution of power, called the subjecting attachment (taʿalluq taskhīrī), which accompanies the attachment of will that takes effect immediately. So "amr" here is of that kind, and it is the disposition of the order of all existents.

The clause "alā lahu al-khalqu wa-l-amr" is a new sentence serving as a concluding summary (tadhyīl) of the preceding discourse from His saying "who created the heavens and the earth," to indicate the generalization of creation. The estimate is: for what has been mentioned above and for other than it. So "khalq" is the bringing into existence of beings, and "amr" is their subjection to the work for which they were created.

The clause is opened with the particle of alerting so that the hearts of the hearers may attend to this comprehensive statement.

The preposition "lām" attached to the pronoun of the Name of Majesty is the lām of possession. And the fronting of the predicate here serves to restrict it to the subject.

The definite article in "al-khalq" (creation) and "al-amr" (command) is the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), so the sentence restricts the genus of creation and the genus of command to existence within the dominion of God, the Exalted. Nothing else shares any part of this genus. This restriction is relative (qasr idafi, a restriction relative to a particular context), meaning: their gods have no share in creation or in command. As for the restriction of the genus in reality to existence within the dominion of God, the Exalted, this is determined by the contextual indicators. Creation is restricted in reality to existence within His dominion, the Exalted. As for command, it is restricted to existence within the dominion of God by a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i), because many existent beings have the management of many affairs. However, since the one who manages is a creation of God, the Exalted, his management is traced back to the management of God. This is like what has been said about the restriction of the genus of praise in His saying, ﴿All praise is due to God﴾.

The clause ﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾ is an appended concluding statement (tadhyil), placed as a parenthetical between the clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God﴾ and the clause ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. This is because the context has become ready for a reminder of God's favor upon people and of His beneficial dispositions, following what was mentioned of the information about His great power, the breadth of His knowledge, and the perfection of His craftsmanship.

The verb (tabaraka) in its derived form indicates the manifestation of the attribute upon the one who possesses it, like: tathaqala (he showed heaviness in the work), ta'allala (he showed an illness), and ta'aẓẓama (he showed greatness). It may also be used to mean that the act is manifest upon the one who possesses it in a clear manner, so that it is as if its possessor displays it. From this is ﴿Exalted is God﴾, meaning His loftiness became manifest, that is, His nobility above all existent things. From this is tabaraka, meaning His blessing became manifest.

Baraka (blessing) is intense good. Its discussion has already preceded at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakka, blessed﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His saying, ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ in Surat al-An'am. Thus the blessing of God, by which He is described, is His glory, His transcendence, and His holiness, and that comprises the attributes of perfection. Among that is that to Him belong the creation and the command.

The attachment of the Name of Majesty (God) to the attribute ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ has the sense of an explanation for His deservingness of blessing and glory, because He is the one who pours forth the good things of origination and provision, and the manager of the conditions of existent beings, by the attribute of His being the Lord of the varieties of created beings. The discussion of "the worlds" has already passed in Surat al-Fatiha.

[Page 171]

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*), inserted (*iʿtirāḍ*) between the mention of the proofs of God's oneness and the mention of His great power to create things in which no one else shares. The sentence is thus a parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ and the clause ﴿And He it is who sends the winds﴾. This kind of insertion follows the Qur'an's usual practice of seizing the opportunity when hearts are prepared for remembrance.

The address in *udʿū* (call upon) is specific to the Muslims, because it is instruction in the etiquette of calling upon God and worshipping Him. The polytheists are not prepared for this kind of address. It brings the believers near, draws them close, and points to God's good pleasure with them and His love for them. Its witness is His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good﴾.

The address is directed to the Muslims by the evidence of the context.

*Duʿāʾ* (calling, supplication) is literally "calling out." It is also used for calling out to request something important. It is used figuratively for worship, because worship includes supplication and asking, whether by speech or by the tongue of the state, as in bowing and prostration, together with the speech that accompanies them. This usage is very common in the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning here is request and turning to God, because the Muslims have already worshipped God and devoted worship to Him alone. What matters is making them aware of their nearness to the mercy of their Lord and bringing their station close to it.

The Lord is identified by means of the genitive construction (*iḍāfa*) rather than by a pronoun of the third person, even though there is a nearby antecedent in His saying ﴿Blessed is God﴾, and rather than by a pronoun of the first person. This is because the word "Lord" carries the idea of bringing the believers near through the relation of being nurtured and cared for. It also serves to honour the believers and show the Lord's care for them, by joining the Lord to the pronoun of the addressees, as in His saying ﴿Rather, God is your Protector﴾.

*Tadarruʿ* (humble supplication) means showing abasement in a particular manner. The term is also applied to supplicating aloud, because loudness is part of the manner of tadarruʿ, since it is an outwardly visible abasement. In this verse, and in His saying in Sūrat al-Anʿām ﴿calling upon Him humbly and secretly﴾, it has been interpreted as supplicating aloud. This is the interpretation we prefer, because it is more fitting when contrasted with *khufya* (secrecy). Its style thus matches the style of its counterpart in His saying ﴿and call upon Him in fear and hope﴾ (7:56). The *wāw* here is for division, functioning like *aw* (or). Some have said that *wāw* is better than *aw* in this context.

Some exegetes kept *tadarruʿ* in its literal meaning, which is abasement. In that case it is a verbal noun in the sense of a circumstantial state, meaning "abasing yourselves," or an absolute object of *udʿū*, because abasement is one of the states of supplication, so it is a kind of it. They also took His words ﴿and secretly﴾ as a command with its own object, that is, "call upon Him concealing your supplication." This led some of their statements to imply that making supplication public is forbidden or not rewarded. This is an error, for the Prophet ﷺ supplicated openly on more than one occasion, and on the pulpit in the hearing of the people he said: "O God, give us rain." He also said: "O God, (let it be) around us and not upon us." And he said: "O God, deal with Quraysh (Yourself)." The hadith continues. His supplications were transmitted only because he uttered them aloud so that the one who transmitted them could hear them. Therefore the correct view is that His words ﴿humbly﴾ are a permission to supplicate both aloud and secretly. As for what has come of prohibition against loudness, it refers only to excessive loudness that goes beyond the bounds of humility.

Qur'an readers: the majority read *wa-khufyatan* (with a *ḍamma* on the *kh*). Abu Bakr read it with a *kasra* on the *kh*. This was discussed in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ stands in the position of a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the command to supplicate. It points to the fact that this command is a command of honour for the Muslims, which contains God's good pleasure with them. However, the reason is expressed by way of establishing a matter through negating its opposite, to indicate that both matters are intended and to be concise in speech. Because the clause stands in the position of a reason, it begins with *inna* (indeed), which indicates mere emphasis, since the addressees have no doubt about this report. When *inna* comes in this way, it indicates causation and linkage, and it takes the place of *fa* (so/therefore), as the Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qāhir pointed out.

The attribution of love (*maḥabba*) to God as a description, in this verse and similar ones, is a figurative usage, meaning the necessary consequence of love, based on the view that the true reality of love is an emotional state of the soul. Regarding this, I have some reservation. Some said that what is intended is the necessary consequence of love, that is, in the one loved and in the lover. Its necessary consequence is that the beloved is characterised by what pleases the lover, so that love arises, whose root is approval, and its necessary consequence is the lover's pleasure with his beloved and the conveying of benefit to him. These two necessary consequences are mutually implicating in themselves, so the attribution of love to God as a description is a figurative usage through this compound necessary consequence.

The meaning of *al-muʿtadīn* (the transgressors) here is the polytheists, because it is synonymous with *al-ẓālimīn* (the wrongdoers).

The meaning is: call upon your Lord, because He loves you and does not love the transgressors. This is like His saying ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated﴾ (40:60). It is an allusion to the promise of answering the supplication of the believers, and that He does not answer the supplication of the disbelievers. God says: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, according to one of the two interpretations of it.

Some exegetes took *tadarruʿ* to mean submission (*khuḍūʿ*). They made the verse restricted to requesting hidden supplication, to the point that some exaggerated and made supplicating aloud forbidden. Some went further and made His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ an emphasis on the meaning of the command to conceal supplication, and made supplicating aloud a form of transgression, with those who supplicate aloud being among the transgressors whom God does not love. This is reported from Ibn Jurayj, but I suspect that this report from him is not precisely transmitted in wording, for how can that be, when the Messenger of God ﷺ supplicated aloud and his companions supplicated too?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 56:

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾. The prohibition against corruption on the earth is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, as a conjunction to the manner of parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ). For when the discourse had indicated God's care for the Muslims and His nearness to them, in that He commanded them to call upon Him and honored them with that great title in His words "your Lord" (rabbukum), and alluded to His love for them rather than for their transgressing enemies, it followed this with what would prevent them from presuming upon God by yielding without restraint to what their desires dictate to them from the agitation of the two forces, the appetitive (shahwiyya) and the irascible (ghaḍabiyya), for these two generally produce corruption. So He reminded them to abandon corruption, so that their reformation would be free from being mixed with any corruption. For if they cause corruption on the earth, they corrupt many created beings, and they corrupt themselves within that corruption. Thus it resembles the position of a precaution (iḥtiraz), and this is the manner of the Qur'an: to follow encouragement with warning, and vice versa, lest people fall into despair or into complacency.

The concern with averting corruption was, in this context, a situation demanding the hastening of this prohibition, inserted between the two clauses of the command to supplicate.

In placing this prohibition immediately after His words "Indeed, He does not love the transgressors" there is an allusion (taʿrid) that the transgressors, who are the polytheists, are corrupters on the earth, and an admonition (irbaʾ) to the Muslims against resembling them; that is, it is not fitting for you, while you are those brought near to your Lord, permitted to call upon Him, that you should be like those removed from Him and hated.

As for corruption on the earth (al-ifsad fi al-ard) and reformation (al-islah), the discussion of them has already passed at His words, exalted is He, "And when it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption on the earth,' they say, 'We are only reformers,'" in Surat al-Baqara, and we explained there the roots of corruption and the realities of reformation. And the discussion of the omission of the object of tufsidu (do not cause corruption) has already passed there, being of the same kind as what is here.

"The earth" here is the spherical body designated by the term "the world" (al-dunya).

Corruption in any part of the earth is corruption of the whole earth. Yet some corruption may lead to a greater reformation than the harm that corruption brings; so it is preferred when no necessary good can be attained except by it. Thus the Messenger of God ﷺ cut down the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir, and Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, forbade the cutting of the trees of the enemy, owing to the difference of circumstances.

The "after" in His words "after its reformation" (baʿda iṣlāḥihā) is a true (ḥaqīqiyya) posteriority, because the earth was created from the outset in a state of reformation. God, exalted is He, said: "And He placed in it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance" in an orderly system suitable to what it contains; and especially man, who is the noblest of the created beings that God placed upon the earth, and for whom He created what is in the earth. He reinforced that order with laws which God established through the tongues of the messengers, the righteous, and the wise among His servants, whom He strengthened with revelation and divine address, or with inspiration, success, and wisdom. They taught people how to use what is in the earth in an order by which benefit is obtained by the beneficial, the harm within the beneficial is removed, and the harm of the harmful is avoided. That original order and the law that reinforces it are both a reformation in the earth, because the first is the bringing into existence of a thing in a good state, and the second is making the harmful good through refinement or removal. It has already passed, at His words, exalted is He, "And when it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption on the earth,' they say, 'We are only reformers,'" in Surat al-Baqara, that reformation is a term laid down for the common notion encompassing both bringing a thing into a good state and making the corrupt good. Thus reformation here is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of a static noun (ism jamid), not in the sense of a verb, for what is meant by it is a reformation that is established and fixed in the earth, not a reformation that is about to occur. So when that order is altered, the good is corrupted and the harmful is put into use in its harmfulness, or it is retained though its removal is possible, it becomes corruption after reformation, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: "And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others. If you do not do so, there will be turmoil in the earth and great corruption."

The explicit statement of posteriority here is a registration of the enormity of corruption, in that it is corruption of what is good and beneficial; so there is no excuse for its doer, nor any justification for his act in the eyes of the people of the earth.

* * *

﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope. Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good﴾. This is a return to the command to supplicate, because what preceded of the prohibition against corruption resembled a precaution inserted between the parts of the discourse. The command to supplicate was repeated so that His words "in fear and in hope" could be built upon it, intentionally to teach the motive for supplication, after they had learned its manner. This motive encompasses the purposes and kinds of supplication, so there is no difficulty in conjoining the command to supplicate with a like command, for the two differ by the difference of their objects.

Fear was discussed at His words, exalted is He, "unless they fear that they will not keep within the limits of God" (Qur'an 2:229).

Hope was discussed at His words "Do you hope that they will believe for you?" in Surat al-Baqara.

The accusative of "in fear and in hope" here is the object of purpose (mafʿul li-ajlihi), meaning that supplication occurs for the sake of a fear of Him and a hope in Him. The object of fear and hope has been omitted, the pronoun in the accusative "call upon Him" indicating it.

The waw is for division (taqsim), stating that supplication occurs in two kinds.

Fear is of His wrath and punishment, and hope is in His good pleasure and reward. Supplication for the sake of fear is like supplicating for forgiveness, and supplication for the sake of hope is like supplicating for success and mercy. It is not meant that supplication includes fear and hope in itself, as al-Fakhr explained in his third question, for that, though valid for hope, is not valid for fear except with incongruity. In the command to supplicate in fear and in hope there is evidence that among the portions of the responsible persons in their deeds is the observance of both fear of God's punishment and hope in His reward. This is among the things that the indications of the Book and the Sunna abound with. Al-Fakhr, in his second question on the interpretation of the verse, offered a statement not consonant with what is known among the scholars of the community, and took the path of the extreme Sufis; following him at length would be lengthy, so consult him if you wish.

Fear and hope have encompassed all that the purposes of the Muslims concerning their Lord relate to, in their present and their future, so that they supplicate God that He facilitate for them the means of attaining what they hope for, and that He keep them away from the means of what they fear. This requires directing their resolve toward avoiding what is forbidden for the sake of their fear of punishment, and toward carrying out what is commanded for the sake of hope in reward. Therefore it necessarily entails the command to ihsan, which is to worship God as one who is present before him, so that he is shy to disobey Him. Thus the sense is: "Call upon Him in fear and in hope, and do ihsan," by the indication of its being followed by His words "Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good." This is an abridgment (ijaz).

The clause "Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good" stands in the position of a consequence (tafrigh) upon the clause "call upon Him." Therefore it is joined with inna, which indicates emphasis, and this emphasis is merely for the sake of giving attention to the predicate, since the addressees are not doubtful about its content. When inna comes in this manner, it serves to express causation and to link the content of its clause with the content of the preceding clause, and so it dispenses with the consequential fa'. For this reason the clause is separated from the one before it and is not conjoined, because inna dispenses with the conjunctive particle.

The mercy of God is His beneficence and His bestowal of good.

Nearness in its literal sense is the nearness and adjacency of place. It is applied figuratively to hope; one says, "This is near," meaning it is possible and hoped for. From this is His words, exalted is He, "They see it as far off, and We see it as near" (Qur'an 70:6–7), for they used to deny the Resurrection, which is with God inevitably occurring. So "near" here means "likely to be attained," not nearness of place. His words "near to the doers of good" indicate an assumed element in the discourse, meaning: "and do good, for when they call upon Him in fear and in hope, they have prepared themselves to renounce what necessitates fear and to acquire what necessitates hope, so that fear and hope are not false; for one who fears does not approach what he fears, and one who hopes does not abandon the pursuit of what he hopes for." This is realized through good conduct in action, and from good conduct there necessarily follows the abandonment of evil deeds; therefore the mercy of God is indeed near to them. He omitted the opposite of "the doers of good," out of gentleness toward the believers and as an allusion that one would not suppose they would do evil, lest mercy become distant from them.

The absence of the feminine marker on the adjective "near" (qarib), although its described noun (rahma, "mercy") is feminine in form, has been explained by the grammarians in many ways, and al-Zamakhshari alluded to these in the Kashshaf. Most of them revolve around interpreting the feminine noun as synonymous with a masculine noun, or excusing it on the ground that part of what is described is not truly feminine, as here. The best of them in my view is the statement of al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda: that "qarib" or "ba'id," when applied to nearness or distance of kinship, must take the feminine marker with the feminine noun without exception; but when applied to nearness or distance of space, it may agree with its described noun, and it may also be masculine on the interpretation of "place," which is the more common usage. God, exalted is He, said: "And it is not far from the wrongdoers" (Qur'an 11:83), and "And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near" (Qur'an 33:63). Since its application in these verses is by way of metaphor from the nearness of distance, it follows the common usage in its literal sense. This is among the subtle Arabic distinctions in the use of the homonym, removing ambiguity as far as possible.

[p. 178]

﴿It is He who sends the winds as heralds of His mercy, until when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water therewith, and bring forth with it fruits of every kind. Thus do We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾

The clause ﴿It is He who sends the winds﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "He covers the night with the day" (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهارَ), and the connection between the last of the intervening clauses and the clause it interrupts, and what it is coordinated with, has been established. This is because when He mentioned the nearness of His mercy to the good-doers, He mentioned some of His general mercy, which is rain. The mention of the sending of the winds is therefore the more important purpose, since it is evidence of the greatness of power and governance. For this reason we have made it coordinated with the clause "He covers the night with the day," or with the clause "Surely His is the creation and the command." The mention of some of the circumstances that accompany the sending of the winds brings about the blending of favour (imtinan) into the argument from evidence (istidlal). That does not imply that the winds are sent only to herald rain, nor that rain falls only immediately after the sending of the winds, since the purpose is not to teach the events of the atmosphere, and since the speech contains nothing that requires the connection to be exclusive. In it there is an allusion (taʿrid) to giving good news to the believers of abundant rain upon them, and warning to the polytheists of drought and hunger, like His saying: ﴿And that if they had remained upright upon the path, We would surely have given them abundant water﴾ (72:16), and His saying: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke﴾ (44:10).

The sending (irsal) is used for movement by way of metaphor (istiʿara). So the sending of the winds is their blowing from the place in which they blow and their arrival. What made this metaphor apt is that the wind is driven (musakhkhara) toward the place where God wills it to blow, so it is likened to a rational being dispatched toward some direction. Among the marvels of this metaphor is that the wind does not leave the sphere of air, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits mankind...﴾ (2:164), in the sūrah of al-Baqarah. Thus the turning of the winds from one direction to another resembles sending more than bringing into being.

[p. 179]

Al-riyāḥ (the winds) is the plural of rīḥ, which has been discussed in the sūrah of al-Baqarah.

The majority of reciters read al-riyāḥ in the plural form. Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read al-rīḥ in the singular form, considering the genus, so it is equivalent to the plural reading. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Whoever reads in the plural form, his reading is more fortunate, because the winds wherever they occur in the Qurʾān are associated with mercy, like His saying: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilising﴾ (15:22). The singular "rīḥ" is most often mentioned in association with punishment, like His saying: ﴿a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ (51:42), and the like. Whoever reads in the singular, his restricting it by "spreading" (nashr) removes the ambiguity, i.e., the possibility of confusion. The established view is that the plural form may be intended to indicate the multiplicity of directions, or the occurrence of intervals in the blowing, and that the singular may be intended to indicate that it is pushed in a single, strong thrust without a pause between its gusts.

As for His saying "nushur" (نُشُرًا), Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr and Abū Jaʿfar read nushuran with a ḍamma on the nūn and the shīn, as the plural of nashūr with a fatḥa on the nūn, like rasūl and rusul. Nashūr is faʿūl in the sense of fāʿil. The nashūr is the living, good wind, because it spreads the clouds, meaning it disperses them and multiplies them in the atmosphere, like a spread-out thing. It is also permissible that it be faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl, meaning spread out (manshūra), i.e., scattered (mabthūtha) in the directions, dispersed within them, because nashr is dispersal in many directions. The meaning of this is that the wind of rain is gentle, coming once from the south and once from the north, and dispersing in the directions until clouds arise through it and multiply into scattered clouds. As al-Kumayt said about the cloud:

"The south has stirred it with its breaths, and the north has loosed its lowering skirts."

For this reason it was expressed in the plural form, to indicate the multiplicity of its directions. For the same reason, it was not made plural where the multiplicity of directions is not praised, like His saying: ﴿And they sailed with them on a good wind﴾ (10:22), since the good in that is that the wind is continuous.

Ibn ʿĀmir read nushran with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn. This is a lightening of nushur, which is with two ḍammas, as one says rusl for rusul. ʿĀṣim read it with a bāʾ in place of the nūn, ḍammed, and with a sukūn on the shīn and tanwīn, which is a lightening of bushuran with both ḍammed, as the plural of bashīr, like nudhur and nadhīr, i.e., giving good news to people of the approach of rain.

From the totality of these readings it results that the winds spread out the clouds, that they come from different directions in succession, which is the reason for the clouds being filled with water; that they revive the land after its death; and that they give good news to people by their blowing, so that joy enters upon them through them.

The original meaning of the phrase "bayna yadayhi fulān" (before so-and-so) is that he is in front of him, close to him. For this reason it is contrasted with "behind" in His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ (2:255). The speaker's intent is a kināya (metonymy) for "in front," but it is not explicit, since the near front is broader than being between the two hands. Then, because of the fame of this metonymy and the predominance of its agreement with the explicit meaning, it was treated as explicit, and it was permitted to use it figuratively for near precedence and anticipation, like His saying: ﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ (34:46). And in one thing's preceding another while being near it, without being in front of it and without the preceded thing having two hands, its use in this verse is likewise: that is, He sends the winds with His mercy preceding them.

This mercy is intended to mean rain, so it is the use of the verbal noun (maṣdar) to mean the object, since God shows mercy through it. The indication of the intended meaning is the rest of the speech. Mercy is not among the names of rain in the language of the Arabs, since that has not been established. And the attribution of mercy to the Name of Majesty in this verse rejects the claim of anyone who asserted it to be one of the names of rain.

The primary purpose of His saying: [p. 181] ﴿It is He who sends the winds﴾ is to rebuke the polytheists and refute their associating partners with God. It is followed by a reminder to the believers and an arousal of their reflection. This is because the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) indicates that the attribute is known to be ascribed to the relative. The polytheists know that the winds have a director and that rain has a sender, but they forget or feign forgetting the identity of that agent. For this reason they often phrase the falling of rain in the passive voice, saying: "We were given rain by the star of al-Thurayyā (nawʾ al-Thurayyā)," and they say "ghithnā mā shi'nā" in the passive, meaning "we were given relief whatever we wished." God, Exalted, informed that the agent of those actions is God. This is by attributing this relative clause to the Name of Majesty in His saying, "It is He who sends the winds," meaning: the One whom you know sends the winds and sends down water, and He is God, Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ (2:16).
