So the predicate is set forth to specify the holder of this attribute. It is like an answer to a question whose intent is to seek specification, as in the saying: "Are you departing or staying?" For this reason, this attribution does not contain restriction (qaṣr), since he did not intend by it to refute a belief. The polytheists did not claim that anyone other than God sends the winds, but they were like one who is ignorant of it because of associating others with Him. So the situation of the polytheists was taken into account first in this attribution, and the situation of the believers is taken into account incidentally, since the context fits addressing both groups, as was mentioned in the preceding verses.

And "ḥattā" (until) is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), and it is the terminal limit for the content of His saying "nushuran bayna yadayh raḥmatih" (spreading out, preceding His mercy), which has the meaning: "preceding His mercy." That is, it precedes it for a period and spreads its clouds, until, when they carry a cloud, We send down water with it. The sending down of water is the terminal limit of the winds' preceding and going before the rain. The limit has been divided into parts, the first of which is the content of His saying "they carry" (aqallat), i.e., the winds carry the cloud; then the content of His saying "heavy" (thiqālan); then the content of "We drive it" (suqnāhu), i.e., to the land whose rain God willed; then that water descends from it. All of this is a limit for the preceding of the winds, because what is derived from a limit is itself a limit.

[The term] al-thiqāl (heavy clouds) means those slow to move because of the moisture of water in them, which is vapour, and it is the cloud from which rain is hoped. Among the finest meanings of Abū al-Ṭayyib is his saying in a fine apology:

"And among good things is the slowness of your gift toward me; the swiftest of clouds in motion is the barren one."

Some of the goal has been omitted: that the winds stir the vapours that are on the surface of the earth and supply them with moisture, driving them toward it from the moist regions through which they pass, such as seas, rivers, pools and moist lands. Some of that gathers to other parts, and this is what is expressed as "stirring" (ithāra) in His saying: ﴿So it stirs up clouds﴾ (30:48). When it reaches the limit of vaporousness, the winds raise it from the surface of the earth into the atmosphere.

The meaning of "aqallat" (carried) is "bore," derived from "qilla" (fewness), because the bearer considers what he bears to be little. So the hamza in it is for making (jaʿl).

The winds' carrying the cloud is that the winds pass over the surface of the earth, so the vapour on the surface gathers with them, and the winds raise it to the height in the atmosphere, until it reaches a cold point at the top of the atmosphere. There the vapour condenses and its parts gather, becoming clouds. Whenever one cloud joins another, a cloud is produced from them that is heavier than either was when separate, so its spread lessens until it becomes a great cloud, which grows heavy, then dissolves, then descends as rain. It has become clear that what is meant by "aqallat" is other than what is meant in the other verse: "fatuthīr saḥāban" (so it stirs up clouds).

"Saḥāb" is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) for saḥāba (a single cloud), so it is permissible to treat it as masculine, given that its wording is free of a feminine marker, and it is permissible to treat it as feminine, given that it has the meaning of a plural. For this subtlety, the clouds were described at the beginning of their being sent as "they stir up," and after the limit as "heavy." This is one of the scientific miracles of the Qurʾān (al-iʿjāz al-ʿilmī). Both considerations occur in this verse: He described the cloud with "heavy" (thiqālan), taking the plural into account, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw cows being slaughtered." And the pronoun was returned to it in the singular in "suqnāhu" (We drove it).

The real meaning of driving (sawq) is making a moving thing move, with its driver behind it urging and pressing it. Here it is used figuratively for making the clouds move by the causes God established. It may also be made a figure of speech (tamthīl) if His saying "aqallat saḥāban" is taken into account, meaning: We drove it with that wind to a land. Then it is an image for the wind's driving the cloud by the state of a driver urging an animal.

[p. 183] The lām in His saying "li-baladin" (to a land) is the lām of cause, meaning for the sake of a dead land. This lām indicates divine care for that land, which is why the verb "suqnāhu" was not construed with the preposition "ilā" (to).

Al-balad (land) is a wide expanse of the earth.

Al-mayyit (dead) is a metaphor applied to the region from which vegetation has vanished. The attribution of the figurative death to the land is also a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), since what dies is really its vegetation and fruit, as the comparison in His saying "Thus do We bring forth the dead" indicates.

The pronoun in the genitive after the bāʾ in His saying "fa-akhrajnā bihi" (and We bring forth with it) may refer to the land, so the bāʾ means "in," or it may refer to the water, so the bāʾ is instrumental (lil-ālah).

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 7, verse 57 (part 2 of 2):

The generality in "from all the fruits" is a true generality (istighraq haqiqi), because the dead land is not specific but includes every dead land upon which rain falls. Thus from all the individual parcels of dead land come all the fruits which Allah has brought forth by means of water, and each land brings forth its customary fruits in it. So when you look at that particular land alone, make the generality of "all the fruits" a customary generality (istighraq 'urfi), i.e. from all the fruits known in that land. The particle min (from) is for partitive meaning (li-l-tab'id).

The clause "Thus We bring forth the dead" (ka-dhalika nukhriju al-mawta) is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), digressing into admonition and argument for the likelihood of the resurrection (al-ba'th), which they consider far-fetched. The demonstrative "thus" (ka-dhalika) refers to the bringing forth implied by the verb "fa-akhrajna" (then We brought forth), taking into account what precedes it, namely that the land is dead, then its revival, i.e. the revival of what is in it of the traces of crops and fruit. So the point of comparison is revival after death. And there is no doubt that this revival has a manner (kayfiyyah) which Allah has determined and whose description He has left general, because human understanding falls short of conceiving it.

The clause "so that you may remember" (la'allakum tadhakkarun) is a resumptive clause (mustaf'anah), and the hope expressed arises from the preceding clauses beginning with "And He it is who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy" (wa-huwa alladhi yursilu al-riyah nushran bayna yadayy rahmatihi), because the intended meaning is comprehensive remembrance which increases the believer in lesson and faith, and which by its nature would cause the polytheist to abandon the belief in polytheism and the denier of resurrection to abandon his denial.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tadhdhakarun" with a shaddah on the dhal, through assimilation of the second ta' into the dhal after converting it into a dhal. 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "tadhakkarun" with the dhal lightened, by deleting one of the two ta's.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 58:**

﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad does not come forth except meagrely. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾ This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tarida) placed between the sentence ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾ and the sentence ﴿We certainly sent Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 59]. It contains a detailed explanation of the content of the sentence ﴿then We brought forth with it fruits of every kind﴾, since it has already shown the difference in the state of the land that receives rain from the clouds. What called for this detail is that when the bringing forth of the fruits of the earth was used as a likeness for the bringing forth of the dead from them on the Day of Resurrection, as a reminder of this for the believers and as a refutation of the idea of the Resurrection's impossibility held by the polytheists, the difference in the state of the emergence of plants from the earth was here used as a likeness for the difference in the state of living people in benefiting from the mercy of God's guidance. Thus the position of His words ﴿and the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ is like the position of His words ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾. For this reason, this is followed by His words ﴿Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾, just as what precedes it was followed by His words: ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead, that you may perhaps remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 57].

The meaning is: Thus do We bring forth the dead, and thus benefits from the mercy of guidance whoever has a pure, receptive nature for guidance, like the good land that benefits from the rain. And whoever has a corrupt nature, like the bad land that does not benefit from the rain and so produces no beneficial vegetation, is deprived of benefit from guidance. Therefore the purpose of this verse is illustration (tamthil). The aim is not merely to detail the conditions of the land after the rain has fallen, because the purpose for which the speech is directed combines two matters: the lesson (al-'ibra) in God's making, and the admonition through what resembles His dealings.

So the meaning is: just as the good land brings forth its vegetation quickly and joyfully when the rain falls, while the bad land hardly produces anything, and if it does produce, it produces a bad growth with no good in it.

The word ﴿الطَّيِّبُ﴾ (al-tayyib, "good") is a descriptive adjective on the pattern fay'il (فَيْعِل), a form that indicates the intensity of the quality in the thing described, like qayyim (قَيِّم). It denotes one who is characterized by goodness. The explanation of al-tayyib has already been given at His words ﴿Say: The good things have been made lawful for you﴾ in Surat al-Ma'ida, and at His words ﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾ in Surat al-Baqara.

"The good land" (al-balad al-tayyib) is the earth described as good. Its goodness is the purity of its soil and its suitability for bringing forth good plants, for crops and trees, and it is the pure land.

﴿Alladhi khabutha﴾ (والَّذِي خَبُثَ, "that which is bad") is the opposite of good.

His words ﴿بِإذْنِ رَبِّهِ﴾ (bi-idhni rabbihi, "by the permission of its Lord") occupy the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to "its vegetation". Idhn here means command, and what is intended by it is the command of special care for it, like His words ﴿what I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad: 75], to show the nobility of that vegetation. So it has the sense of describing it as pure and wholesome. The meaning is: the good land brings forth its vegetation good and wholesome like itself. He has indicated the goodness of its vegetation by stating that its emergence is by the permission of its Lord. Thus by this permission is meant a special permission, which is the permission of care and honour, and not the permission of decree and creation, since that is a well-known permission whose explanation is not relevant in this context.

﴿Alladhi khabutha﴾ — all the exegetes (mufassirun) have taken this to be a description of the land, meaning: the land that is bad, which is the counterpart of the good land. They explained it as the land that produces only vegetation that is of no benefit and whose growth is slow, such as salt-marshes (sibakh). They took the pronoun in "yakhruju" (يَخْرُجُ, "comes forth") to refer to the vegetation, and they considered the sense of the sentence to be: "and that which is bad, its vegetation does not come forth except meagrely", so the word "vegetation" (nabat) is elided in the construction, and the genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi), which is the pronoun of the bad land in the hidden pronoun of the verb "yakhruju", has taken its place.

What appears to me is that "alladhi" (الَّذِي, "that which") refers to the vegetation of the earth, and the meaning is: "and the vegetation that is bad does not come forth except meagrely." In the sentence there is ihtibak (احْتِباك, a rhetorical device in which something is omitted from each of two parts because the other part indicates it): the description "good" is not mentioned after the vegetation of the good land, and the bad land is not mentioned before the mention of the bad vegetation, because each of the two opposites indicates the other. The sense is: "the good land—its vegetation comes forth good by the permission of its Lord, and the vegetation that is bad comes forth meagre from the bad land." This is a subtle construction which is not neglected in eloquent speech.

All the readers recited ﴿لا يَخْرُجُ﴾ (lā yakhruju, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra') except Ibn Wardan from Abu Ja'far, who read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra' (yukhraju), contrary to what is commonly known from him. It has been said that the attribution of this reading to Ibn Wardan is an error.

"Nakid" (النَّكِدُ) is a descriptive word from "nakad" (النَّكَدِ), with a fatha on the kaf, which is the verbal noun of "nakida al-shay'" (نَكِدَ الشَّيْءُ), when the thing is unsuitable and brings evil upon the one who uses it. Abu Ja'far recited ﴿إلَّا نَكَدًا﴾ (illā nakadan), with a fatha on the kaf.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the verse, there is the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The likeness of what God has sent me with of guidance and knowledge is like abundant rain that fell upon a land. Part of it was fertile ground that absorbed the water and produced abundant grass and herbage. Part of it was hard ground that held the water, so God benefited people with it: they drank, gave drink, and cultivated. And it fell upon another portion which were flat plains that hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of one who gains understanding of the religion of God and whom what God has sent me with benefits, so he knows and teaches. And the likeness of one who does not lift his head to that and does not accept the guidance of God with which I have been sent."

The indication in His words ﴿Thus do We vary the signs﴾ refers to the varied manner of reasoning by means of the proofs that point to the immense power which requires the oneness of God, and also point to the occurrence of the Resurrection after death, and to the difference in people's readiness for guidance and their benefit from it, by clear, evident reasoning brought close in all of these matters. So that is "taṣrīf", i.e. variation and diversification of the signs,

[Page 187]

that is, of the proofs.

By "the people who give thanks" is meant the believers. This is to draw attention to the fact that they are the object of the illustration by the good land, and that others are the object of the illustration by the bad land. This is like His words: ﴿And these are the parables We set forth for mankind, but none understand them except those who have knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 59:

﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great day."﴾ This is a resumption (isti'naf) to which the purpose shifted from establishing proof and favour, which began with His saying, ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 10], and from warning the people of misguidance that they are immersed in the schemes of Satan, who is the enemy of their kind, from His saying, ﴿[Satan] said, "Because You have put me in error, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path"﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], up to His saying, ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 33]. Then it moved to threatening with a description of the punishment of the Hereafter and the states of people in it, and what was interspersed within that of parables and allusions, and then to the purpose of taking lessons and admonition from what befell the earlier nations. Thus this resumption has a further connection with His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], and the matter has been extensively discussed in most of the surah. Following this consideration are other purposes: consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), and teaching his community the history of the earlier nations to whom messengers were sent, so that those Arabs who deny may know that there is no disgrace upon Muhammad (ﷺ) or upon his message from their denial, and that this does not place him below other messengers. Moreover, it would not support their claim that if he were truthful in his message, Allah would have supported him by punishing those who denied him, when they said, by way of mockery or disputation: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. And so that the People of the Book and others may know that what Muhammad (ﷺ) encountered from his people is the disposition of the people of wretchedness in the face of the call of Allah's messengers. This report is emphasized with the lam of oath and the particle of confirmation, because the purpose of these reports is

صفحة ١٨٨
to draw an analogy between the states of the nations that denied their messengers and the state of the polytheists of the Arabs in their denial of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is common in speech for the oath's answer clause to be joined with *qad*, because the oath prepares the listener's soul to anticipate an important report, so *qad* is used, since it indicates the confirmation of an expected matter, as al-Khalil and al-Zamakhshari affirmed. The expectation may be an expectation of the information conveyed, or it may be an expectation of the report itself, as here.

Noah was introduced earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33] in the surah of Al 'Imran. The people of Noah dwelt in the Jazira and Iraq, according to the presumption of the historians. The Qur'an expressed them through the form of peoplehood attached to Noah, since they had no specific name among the names of nations by which they were known, so definition by annexation here is the shortest way.

The clause ﴿So he said, "O my people"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "We sent" with *fa* (so), to indicate that this speech issued from him immediately upon his being sent; it is thus the content of what he was sent with.

Noah addressed all of his people, because the call cannot be other than general to them. In his call he used the description "people" to remind them of the bond of kinship, so that they would be certain that he is a counsellor, wishes good for them, and is compassionate toward them. He attached "people" to his own pronoun to express affection and tenderness, to attract their guidance.

His saying to them, ﴿worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him﴾, is a nullification of the condition they were in. It may be a state of polytheism like that of the Arabs, and it may be a state of idolatry by confining themselves to worshipping idols apart from Allah, like the condition of the Sabians and the ancient Greeks. The verses of the Qur'an are suitable for both states. The transmitted account in the stories is that the people of Noah were polytheists, and this is what is implied by what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas that the deities of Noah's people were names of a group of their righteous men; when they died, their people said, "If we set up in their assemblies idols (ansab), and name them after them," so they did, and when those men perished and knowledge was lost, they were worshipped.

صفحة ١٨٩
The apparent meaning of what is in Surah Nuh is that they did not worship Allah, by His saying, ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾ [Nuh: 3]. The apparent meaning of what is in Surah Fussilat is that they acknowledged Allah, by their saying, ﴿Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14], though it is possible that this was spoken in the manner of dialectical concession. If they were polytheists, then his command to them to worship Allah is restricted by the meaning of His saying, ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, that is, single Him out for worship and do not associate with Him the idols. If they confined themselves to worshipping idols, then His saying, ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾ is a justification for turning to the worship of Allah, that is, He is the deity, not your idols.

The clause ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾ on the first view is an explanation of the worship he commanded them to perform, that is, single Him out for worship apart from anything else, since no other than Him is a deity for you.

On the second view it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for the command to abandon the worship of other than Him.

Al-Jumhur read *ghayruhu* with *raf'* (nominative) as an adjective of *ilah* according to its position, since it occupies a nominative position, being the subject; it is in the genitive only because of the entry of the superfluous preposition, and its genitive is not taken into account. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read it with *jarr* (genitive), *ghayri*, as a qualifier of the word *ilah*, considering the superfluous preposition.

The clause ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ may be in the position of causal justification, as in the Kashshaf: that is, for the content of his saying ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, as if it were said: abandon the worship of other than Allah out of fear of the punishment of a great day. The construction of the speech was built upon the speaker's fear for them, indicating his sincere counsel to them and his eagerness for their welfare, to the point that what harms them is made as though it harmed him; he fears it as they fear for themselves. This is because his saying was at the beginning of his address to them with what he was sent with. It may also be that he said it after denial had appeared among them: that is, if you do not fear a punishment, then I fear it

صفحة ١٩٠
for you; and this is from the mercy of the messengers toward their peoples.

The verb "to fear" transitively takes its object directly for the thing feared, and takes a second object with *'ala* when the fear is of harm that reaches someone other than the one fearing, as al-Ahwas said:

*So when he departs, he departs from a raging one whose outbursts are feared upon the rivals.*

It may also be a second resumed clause after ﴿worship Allah﴾, for the purpose of intimidation and warning, and the secret of building the speech upon the speaker's fear for them is the same.

The threatened punishment and its day may be in the Hereafter or in this world, and the first is more apparent, because their reply, that he is in manifest error, indicates that they rejected monotheism and rejected resurrection, as is indicated by His saying in Surah Nuh, ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth; then He will return you into it and bring you forth a [final] bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Their state is thus like that of the polytheists of the Arabs, because worship of idols confines its adherents to the aims of this world.

The commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 60:

﴿The chiefs of his people said: "Indeed, we see you in clear error."﴾ The clause "qāla" (said) is separated from what precedes it, following the manner of separation (*fasl*) in dialogue. Their reply is joined with the emphatic particle (*ḥarf al-ta'kīd*, emphatic particle) to indicate that they affirmed and confirmed their belief that Nuh was immersed in error. *Al-mala'* (the chiefs) is a hamzated word without a long vowel, meaning the group whose affair is one and whose opinion is one, because they back one another, that is, they assist him and agree with him. *Al-mala'* is also applied to the notables and leaders of a people, because it is their nature that their opinion be one through consultation. This meaning is the one appropriate in this verse, by the indicator of *min* ("from") which denotes partiality, meaning that the leaders of the people are those who took up the task of disputing with Nuh and contending on behalf of their religion, in the hearing of the people whom he addressed collectively. The verb "ra'a" (see) here is of the heart, meaning knowledge, that is: "Indeed, we are certain that you are in clear error." The chiefs are not described here as "those who disbelieved," nor as "those who were arrogant," as the chiefs are described in the story of Hud as "those who disbelieved," relying on the indication of the context that they denied and disbelieved.

The locative expression "fi ḍalāl" (in error) is figurative, expressing the firm establishment of the attribute of error in him, to the extent that it is as if it encompasses him from all sides, like the container encompassing what is contained.

*Al-ḍalāl* (error) is the verbal noun (*ism maṣdar*, verbal noun) of *ḍalla*, when one misses the route that leads to the destination. *Al-mubīn* (clear) is an active participle (*ism fā'il*, active participle) from *abāna*, synonymous with *bāna*. That is the error that reaches the utmost extent of distance from the path of truth. This is a doubt (*shubha*) on their part, for they imagined that the truth is what they were upon. So there is no wonder if they regarded whatever is far from it, at a great distance, as clear error, because it opposed them. He came with what they considered impossible, for he denied divinity to their deities, and this is an opposition; and he affirmed it for God alone, and if they were idolaters, this is another opposition; and he threatened them with punishment for that, and this is also an opposition. And if the punishment with which he threatened them was the punishment of the Hereafter, then he informed them of a matter that they deemed impossible, namely the Resurrection, and this is another opposition. Thus his error, in their view, is clear, though its manifestness may vary. And he claimed that God had sent him. In their view this was deliberate lying, foolishness of intellect, and the claim of the impossible, as is related of them in the words of the Exalted: ﴿The chiefs who disbelieved from among his people said: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed we think you are among the liars."﴾ [al-A'raf: 66], and His saying here: ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63], and the verse.

[Page 191]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 61–63:**

﴿He said, "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and advise you, and I know from God what you do not know.﴾ ﴿Or do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you so that you may fear God and perhaps receive mercy?﴾" The clause "He said" is detached (fasl) in the manner of the separation of dialogues.

The vocative "O my people" in his reply to them serves to draw attention to the news. He did not restrict his address to those who had answered him but returned the address to the whole people, because his reply, although it is a dispute with the chiefs of his people, also contains a general call, as is clear. The subtle point in calling them by the description "people" joined to his pronoun was mentioned just before, so he repeated it a second time to draw in their attention, away from what would follow the address of rebuttal and nullification of their statement: ﴿Indeed, we see you in clear error﴾ [Al-A'raf: 60].

The word ḍalāla (error) is a verbal noun like ḍalāl, so its feminine form is purely lexical. The Arabs often perceive the feminine in names of abstract qualities, such as ghawāya (misguidance) and safāha (folly). So the tā' is only for the feminine form of the word, and this tā' does not carry the meaning of singularity, because names of abstract qualities do not take account of individual instances. Thus ḍalāl is not like a collective noun for ḍalāla, contrary to what is in al-Kashshaf. It seems that he (al-Zamakhshari) sought to establish a difference between the statement of his people to him, "Indeed, we see you in error," and his statement here, "There is no error in me." Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) and Ibn al-Athir in al-Mathal al-Sa'ir followed him in this. Al-Taftazani laboured to correct it, but there is no need for that, because the variation between the words ḍalāl and ḍalāla was required by stylistic variety (tafannun), since the word ḍalāl came first, and the reason for its prior mention was the intention to describe it as "clear" (mubin). Had he expressed it there with the word ḍalāla, describing it as mubina (clear) would have been an unfamiliar usage. Since the word "ḍalāl" had preceded, it was deemed good to repeat it with a word that differs from it in the sūrah, to avoid the heaviness of repetition. Thus his statement, "There is no error in me," is a rebuttal of their statement, "Indeed, we see you in clear error" [Al-A'raf: 60], with its equal, not with something more eloquent.

The bā' in his words "bī" (in me) denotes accompaniment or attachment, and it contradicts the figurative sense of the particle of place in their words "fī ḍalāl" (in error) [Al-A'raf: 60], because they made error something in which he was firmly established, whereas he denied that there is any error with which he is attached.

The omission of the feminine tā' from laysa (is not) while its subject is feminine in wording is permitted in the omission of the feminine sign from the verb when its subject is not truly feminine, and because of the separation by the prepositional phrase.

The adversative (istidrāk) in his words "but I am" (lākinnī) is to remove what they had imagined, that he is in error because he opposed their religion. That is, he is in the state of a messenger from God, together with what messengership requires of conveying, advising, and informing them of what they do not know, and that is what they had considered error. The proper function of lākin is that its clause conveys a meaning different from the meaning of the preceding clause, which the preceding clause does not indicate. That is the true sense of the adversative for which lākin is designed. There must be a connection between the contents of the two clauses, either in the predicate, as in ﴿Had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter, but God saved [you]﴾ [Al-Anfal: 43], or in the subject, as in ﴿You did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17]. So it is not good to say: "I did not travel, but I am resident." Most of its occurrences come after a negative clause, because negation is a broad meaning, so the speaker often needs further clarification after it, and then he brings the adversative. Whoever says that the true nature of the adversative is removing what the hearer imagines to be affirmed or negated has only looked at some of the uses of the adversative, or at some of the purposes of its occurrence in eloquent speech. They did not mean that the true nature of the adversative is only fulfilled by that.

The choice of the construction of annexation (idāfa) in identifying the sender, namely "a Messenger of the Lord," is because of what it implies of exalting the one annexed and the obligation of obeying him upon all people, as an allusion against his people for their disobedience to him.

The clause "I convey to you the messages of my Lord" is either a descriptive clause of "a Messenger," or a new independent clause. Its purpose is to express continuity and that he will not stop conveying because of their denial, as a way of discouraging them from hoping that he would follow them. Were it not for this purpose, the meaning of this clause would have been already present in his words "but I am a Messenger." Therefore he used the plural "messages" (risālāt), because every conveyance includes a message by what he conveys. Then, if the clause "I convey to you" is considered a descriptive clause, the shift from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in his words "I convey to you" and "my Lord" is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), considering that the described noun is a predicate of a first-person pronoun. If it is considered an independent clause, there is no iltifāt.

Tabligh and iblagh mean making a thing reach (bālig), that is, arriving at the intended place. Here it is a metaphor for informing about a matter whose knowledge is intended, as if he were transporting it from one place to another.

The majority read "ubllighukum" with a fatḥa on the bā' and a shadda on the lām. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a sukūn on the bā' and without shadda on the lām, from iblagh. The meaning is the same.

The reason for shifting from the pronoun to the explicit noun in his words "messages of my Lord" is what the annexation of the Lord to the first-person pronoun indicates of the obligation of obeying Him, and that he cannot but convey what he was commanded to convey, even if his people dislike it.

Naṣḥ and naṣīḥa is a comprehensive word, expressing good intention and the desire for good, by word or deed. In a ḥadīth: "The religion is sincere advice," and "to be sincere to whoever God has placed in charge of your affairs." The word naṣḥ is often applied to a statement that alerts the addressee to what benefits him and removes harm from him.

Its opposite is ghishsh (deceit). The original sense of naṣaḥa is that it transitively takes its object directly, but it often takes its object with an additional lām, which indicates the meaning of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), to show that the advisor intends by his advice the good of the one advised itself, not the bringing of benefit to the advisor's own self. In that there is emphasis and an indication of the purity of the advice, and that it occurred sincerely for the one advised, with his interest alone intended. For many a piece of advice benefits the advisor too, so he intends both benefits; sometimes the advisor's benefit is preferred over the advised, which is then negligence or an infringement upon the benefit of the one advised.

The use of the present tense (mudāri') indicates the renewal of advice to them, and that he will not abandon it because of their dislike or their rudeness.

He followed this with his words "and I know from God what you do not know," gathering many meanings included in the message, and as a confirmation of his steadfastness in continuing to convey and advise them, and his disregard for their dislike and harm. For he knows what they do not know, which drives him to persist in his work. So he brought this comprehensive statement. This wonderful brevity includes a threat to them of a punishment descending upon them in this life and the next, and an alert to reflect upon what he brought them, and an opening of their insight to seek knowledge of what they did not know. All of this is by its nature to move them to believe in him and accept what came to them.

The "min" (from) is initial (ibtidā'iyya), meaning: knowledge has come to me that is sent down from God, exalted is He. These meanings included in this adversative are what every sensible person would admit are of guidance and righteousness, and these are his states. They described his state as being in clear error, so in this adversative there is a rebuke of the complete foolishness of their minds.

He moved on to exposing the error in their doubt, and so he attached to his speech the words: "Or do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you" [Al-A'raf: 63], beginning the clause with the interrogative of denial after the conjunctive wāw. This indicates that they considered it impossible for him to be a messenger, arguing that he is a human like them, as his statement is recounted in another verse: ﴿This is only a human like you, who wants to make himself superior over you﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 24].

The interrogative was chosen rather than saying "no wonder," indicating that the possibility that such a thing might occur from them is something about which the sensible person's assumption about the intelligent wavers. So his words, "Or do you wonder," function as a prevention of the premise of their statement, "Indeed, we see you in clear error" [Al-A'raf: 60], because their statement is like the premise of an argument for the falsehood of what he calls them to.

The true nature of wonder (ʿajab) is an emotional reaction that arises upon perceiving something unfamiliar. Wonder may be mixed with denial of what is wondered at and with considering it far-fetched and impossible, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather they wonder that a warner from among them has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾ [Qaf: 2] ﴿"When we die and become dust, that is a far-off return!"﴾ [Qaf: 3]. Both meanings are combined in His words: ﴿And if you wonder, then strange is their saying, "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 5] ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 5]. What is in this verse is a metonymy for denial, as in His words: ﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the command of God?"﴾ [Hud: 73], where they denied to her that she counted her giving birth to a child, while she was an old woman, as something impossible.

The indefiniteness of "reminder" (dhikr) and "a man" (rajul) is for generality (naw'iyya), since there is no particularity to one reminder over another, nor to one man over another, for people are equal, and the reminder is equal in being accepted by whomever God grants success and rejected by whomever is deprived of success. That is, this event that you have magnified and made a great outcry about is nothing but "a reminder from your Lord through a man from among you." **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 61–63:**

﴿He said, "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and advise you, and I know from God what you do not know.﴾ ﴿Or do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you so that you may fear God and perhaps receive mercy?﴾" The clause "He said" is detached (fasl) in the manner of the separation of dialogues.

The vocative "O my people" in his reply to them serves to draw attention to the news. He did not restrict his address to those who had answered him but returned the address to the whole people, because his reply, although it is a dispute with the chiefs of his people, also contains a general call, as is clear. The subtle point in calling them by the description "people" joined to his pronoun was mentioned just before, so he repeated it a second time to draw in their attention, away from what would follow the address of rebuttal and nullification of their statement: ﴿Indeed, we see you in clear error﴾ [Al-A'raf: 60].

The word ḍalāla (error) is a verbal noun like ḍalāl, so its feminine form is purely lexical. The Arabs often perceive the feminine in names of abstract qualities, such as ghawāya (misguidance) and safāha (folly). So the tā' is only for the feminine form of the word, and this tā' does not carry the meaning of singularity, because names of abstract qualities do not take account of individual instances. Thus ḍalāl is not like a collective noun for ḍalāla, contrary to what is in al-Kashshaf. It seems that he (al-Zamakhshari) sought to establish a difference between the statement of his people to him, "Indeed, we see you in error," and his statement here, "There is no error in me." Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) and Ibn al-Athir in al-Mathal al-Sa'ir followed him in this. Al-Taftazani laboured to correct it, but there is no need for that, because the variation between the words ḍalāl and ḍalāla was required by stylistic variety (tafannun), since the word ḍalāl came first, and the reason for its prior mention was the intention to describe it as "clear" (mubin). Had he expressed it there with the word ḍalāla, describing it as mubina (clear) would have been an unfamiliar usage. Since the word "ḍalāl" had preceded, it was deemed good to repeat it with a word that differs from it in the sūrah, to avoid the heaviness of repetition. Thus his statement, "There is no error in me," is a rebuttal of their statement, "Indeed, we see you in clear error" [Al-A'raf: 60], with its equal, not with something more eloquent.

The bā' in his words "bī" (in me) denotes accompaniment or attachment, and it contradicts the figurative sense of the particle of place in their words "fī ḍalāl" (in error) [Al-A'raf: 60], because they made error something in which he was firmly established, whereas he denied that there is any error with which he is attached.

The omission of the feminine tā' from laysa (is not) while its subject is feminine in wording is permitted in the omission of the feminine sign from the verb when its subject is not truly feminine, and because of the separation by the prepositional phrase.

The adversative (istidrāk) in his words "but I am" (lākinnī) is to remove what they had imagined, that he is in error because he opposed their religion. That is, he is in the state of a messenger from God, together with what messengership requires of conveying, advising, and informing them of what they do not know, and that is what they had considered error. The proper function of lākin is that its clause conveys a meaning different from the meaning of the preceding clause, which the preceding clause does not indicate. That is the true sense of the adversative for which lākin is designed. There must be a connection between the contents of the two clauses, either in the predicate, as in ﴿Had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter, but God saved [you]﴾ [Al-Anfal: 43], or in the subject, as in ﴿You did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17]. So it is not good to say: "I did not travel, but I am resident." Most of its occurrences come after a negative clause, because negation is a broad meaning, so the speaker often needs further clarification after it, and then he brings the adversative. Whoever says that the true nature of the adversative is removing what the hearer imagines to be affirmed or negated has only looked at some of the uses of the adversative, or at some of the purposes of its occurrence in eloquent speech. They did not mean that the true nature of the adversative is only fulfilled by that.

The choice of the construction of annexation (idāfa) in identifying the sender, namely "a Messenger of the Lord," is because of what it implies of exalting the one annexed and the obligation of obeying him upon all people, as an allusion against his people for their disobedience to him.

The clause "I convey to you the messages of my Lord" is either a descriptive clause of "a Messenger," or a new independent clause. Its purpose is to express continuity and that he will not stop conveying because of their denial, as a way of discouraging them from hoping that he would follow them. Were it not for this purpose, the meaning of this clause would have been already present in his words "but I am a Messenger." Therefore he used the plural "messages" (risālāt), because every conveyance includes a message by what he conveys. Then, if the clause "I convey to you" is considered a descriptive clause, the shift from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in his words "I convey to you" and "my Lord" is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), considering that the described noun is a predicate of a first-person pronoun. If it is considered an independent clause, there is no iltifāt.

Tabligh and iblagh mean making a thing reach (bālig), that is, arriving at the intended place. Here it is a metaphor for informing about a matter whose knowledge is intended, as if he were transporting it from one place to another.

The majority read "ubllighukum" with a fatḥa on the bā' and a shadda on the lām. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a sukūn on the bā' and without shadda on the lām, from iblagh. The meaning is the same.

The reason for shifting from the pronoun to the explicit noun in his words "messages of my Lord" is what the annexation of the Lord to the first-person pronoun indicates of the obligation of obeying Him, and that he cannot but convey what he was commanded to convey, even if his people dislike it.

Naṣḥ and naṣīḥa is a comprehensive word, expressing good intention and the desire for good, by word or deed. In a ḥadīth: "The religion is sincere advice," and "to be sincere to whoever God has placed in charge of your affairs." The word naṣḥ is often applied to a statement that alerts the addressee to what benefits him and removes harm from him.

Its opposite is ghishsh (deceit). The original sense of naṣaḥa is that it transitively takes its object directly, but it often takes its object with an additional lām, which indicates the meaning of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), to show that the advisor intends by his advice the good of the one advised itself, not the bringing of benefit to the advisor's own self. In that there is emphasis and an indication of the purity of the advice, and that it occurred sincerely for the one advised, with his interest alone intended. For many a piece of advice benefits the advisor too, so he intends both benefits; sometimes the advisor's benefit is preferred over the advised, which is then negligence or an infringement upon the benefit of the one advised.

The use of the present tense (mudāri') indicates the renewal of advice to them, and that he will not abandon it because of their dislike or their rudeness.

He followed this with his words "and I know from God what you do not know," gathering many meanings included in the message, and as a confirmation of his steadfastness in continuing to convey and advise them, and his disregard for their dislike and harm. The interrogative was chosen rather than saying "no wonder," indicating that the possibility that such a thing might occur from them is something about which the sensible person's assumption about the intelligent wavers. So his words, "Or do you wonder," function as a prevention of the premise of their statement, "Indeed, we see you in clear error" [Al-A'raf: 60], because their statement is like the premise of an argument for the falsehood of what he calls them to.

Wonder may be mixed with denial of what is wondered at and with considering it far-fetched and impossible, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather they wonder that a warner from among them has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾ [Qaf: 2] ﴿"When we die and become dust, that is a far-off return!"﴾ [Qaf: 3]. ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people﴾. The denial came from all of his people: from their leaders and from their common folk, except for some of his family and those who believed in him right after hearing Nuh's words. So the verb is joined to his speech by the particle فَ (fa, "then"), meaning that a statement came from them that implies denying the claim that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, who conveys the message, gives sincere counsel, and knows what they do not know. This became a denial more general than the first one. For the leaders, it amounts to the sense of persisting in denial. For the common people, it was a fresh denial, occurring after they heard the words of their leaders and after the argument between them and Nuh had ended. The verb is therefore not being used to express continuation, as in the words of Allah, ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 136], because there is no reason for that meaning here. The plural pronoun refers to the people. The فَ (fa) in His words ﴿fa-anjaynahu﴾ ("so We saved him") indicates sequence, and it is a customary sequence, because the revelation to Nuh that he would not have any believers from his people beyond those who had already believed, and that no further believer could be expected, came after the denial. He was then commanded to enter the ship and carry with him those who believed, and the rest of what Allah narrated in Surah Hud.

The report of the saving was placed before the report of the drowning, even though the context of admonition would call for mentioning the drowning of the deniers first. The saving was put first to draw attention to the saving of the believers and to bring quick joy to the believing listeners, since it is Allah's custom that when He destroys the polytheists, He saves the Messenger and the believers. This ordering conveys an allusion to warning. Otherwise, the drowning occurred before the saving, since the fulfilment of Nuh's and his companions' salvation is not evident until the punishment has befallen those who did not believe him. Thus the event that followed the denial immediately was the drowning, and the saving came after it. So that this ordering could be achieved, the verb of saving is conjoined with the particle wa (و), which indicates general joining without sequence, rather than with fa.

His words ﴿fi al-fulk﴾ ("in the ship") are connected in meaning to His words ﴿ma'ahu﴾ ("with him"), because the implied sense is: they settled with him in the ship. By this connection it is understood that Allah commanded him to carry a group in the ship, and that they were believers in him. This connection is a wonderful brevity.

Al-fulk (the ship) was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 164] in Surah al-Baqarah.

﴿Those with him﴾ are those who believed in him. We will identify them when discussing his story in Surah Hud.

The use of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿and We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, rather than saying "and We drowned the rest of them" or "the remainder of them," indicates the cause of the reported act by the relative clause, that is, "We drowned them because of their denial."

The clause ﴿Indeed, they were a blind people﴾ functions as the cause of the clause "We drowned," as indicated by the particle inna. The particle inna here is not intended to remove doubt or hesitation, since there is no doubt about it. Rather, the purpose of the particle is to show emphasis on the report. When inna comes for emphasis, it can take the place of the particle of consequence fa, indicating causation and linking the sentence to what precedes it. Therefore, separating this clause is no separation at all.

ʿAmīn (عَمِينَ) is the plural of ʿamin (عَمٍ), formed with the masculine sound plural suffix wāw and nūn. It is an adjective on the pattern فَعِلٍ, like أشِرٍ (ashir, "insolent"). It is derived from al-ʿamā (the blindness), whose original meaning is the loss of sight. It is used figuratively for the loss of sound judgment, and one says ʿamā al-qalb ("blindness of the heart"). In speech, the figurative meaning has become specialized in the form of the attributive adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha), because it indicates the stability of the attribute and its firm establishment as a disposition. This applies only to the loss of judgment, since a person is generally created with it, unlike the loss of sight. For this reason, He said here ʿamīn and did not say ʿumyan, as He said in the other verse ﴿blind, mute, and deaf﴾ [Al-Isra: 97]. A similar usage is the verse of Zuhayr:

"But I am blind (ʿamm) regarding knowledge of what lies in tomorrow."

Those who denied were blind (ʿamīn) because their leaders were callers to misguidance who supported it, and their common folk accepted that call and listened to it.

This story conveys a great meaning concerning Allah's will for the development of the human species. Allah created the human being in the best of forms, and gave him outward senses and inward senses. He benefited from using some of his sensory faculties in perceiving the first principles of knowledge. However, he used some of these faculties for what brought him harm and misguidance, by applying sensory rules to what is beyond his senses and supporting them with imaginative and fantasizing faculties. He reflected upon his Creator and His attributes, and imagined for Him rivals, helpers, a clan, sons, and partners in His dominion. This grew in humanity over the passing ages, until it led them to forget their Creator, since knowledge of Him does not fall under their outward senses. They turned to worshipping imagined deities, for which they made tangible images. So Allah willed to reform humankind and refine their perception, and He sent Nuh to them. A few of his people believed in him, while most of them disbelieved. Allah then willed to select the righteous among humankind, whose intellects accepted guidance, namely Nuh and those who believed with him, and to eradicate those in whose minds misguidance had taken root, so that He might bring forth from the righteous a righteous offspring and spare humanity the corruption of the misguided. As Nuh said: ﴿If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will beget only wicked disbelievers﴾ [Nuh: 27]. Thus the mission of Nuh and what befell it was a renewal of the good of humankind and a selection of the best.

[p. 198]

[Page 200]

It is permissible for the conjunction (ʿaṭf) to be a conjunction of sentences (ʿaṭf al-jumal), by supposing after the conjunctive wāw a verb, "We sent" (arsalnā), which is indicated by the preposition "to" (ilā) in it, together with the indication of the preceding parallel in the sentence being conjoined to. The estimated phrase is "and We sent [to] ʿAd." In this case the wāw serves merely to join the words, linking one narrative to another narrative, not linking individual words. It is also permissible for it to be a conjunction of individual words (ʿaṭf al-mufradāt): the wāw links Hud to Noah, so the wāw stands in for the governing verb, which is "We sent." The estimate would be: "Indeed We sent Noah to his people, and Hud, the brother of ʿAd, to them," and "to" (ilā) has been placed first. This is then a conjunction on two complements of one governing verb. The fronting of "to" (ilā) was required by the good arrangement of the speech with regard to the return of pronouns. The first possibility is better.

The prepositional phrase was placed before the original object in order to achieve brevity through the use of a pronoun, since the intent is to describe Hud as one of the brothers of ʿAd, of their own lineage, without needing to repeat the word ʿAd, and in order to avoid a pronoun referring to something that comes later both verbally and in rank. Thus it is said: ﴿And to ʿAd [We sent] their brother Hud﴾. "Hud" is either a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition (bayān) for "their brother."

ʿAd was a great nation of the original Arabs (al-ʿArab al-ʿāribah), who perished. They were ten tribes, and it has been said thirteen tribes, and they were the sons of ʿAd ibn ʿAwṣ. ʿAwṣ was the son of Iram ibn Sam ibn Noah. This is what the historians have agreed upon.

As for Hud, his lineage has been disputed. It has been said that he was of the descendants of ʿAd, and those who held this view said he was the son of ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabāḥ ibn al-Khulūd ibn ʿAd. It has also been said that he was of the descendants of Sam, the grandfather of ʿAd, and not of the descendants of ʿAd. Those who held this view said he was Hud ibn Shālakh ibn Arpakhshad ibn Sam ibn Noah. Al-Baghawi reported from ʿAli that the grave of Hud is in Hadramawt, in a reddish sand hill. And from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit: the grave of Hud is between the Corner (al-Rukn) and the Station (al-Maqām) and Zamzam.

"ʿAd" is intended as the tribe, and its being given nunation (ṣarf) was permissible because it is triliteral with a quiescent middle letter. The dwellings of ʿAd were in the lands of Arabia, at al-Shiḥr, with a kasra on the Arabic letter shīn with a dot and a sukūn on the unpointed letter ḥāʾ, in the land of Yemen, Hadramawt, Oman and al-Aḥqāf, which are the sand dunes that lie between Hadramawt and Oman.

[Page 201]

The word "brother" (akh) is used here in the general sense of a close kinsman, by way of the unrestricted metonymy (al-majāz al-mursal). From this comes the saying of the Arabs, "O brother of the Arabs." Hud was of the sons of ʿAd. It has been said that he was a paternal cousin of Iram. The word "brother" is also used figuratively to mean a constant companion, as when they say: "he is the brother of war." From this is the verse: ﴿Indeed the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾ (al-Isrāʾ 17:27), and His saying: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾ (al-Aʿrāf 7:202). So the meaning is that Hud was of the kinsmen of his people ʿAd, and Hud and others were described in this way. Noah was not described as a brother to his people, because at the time of Noah people had not yet divided into nations and tribes. The Arabs would say to a member of a tribe, "brother of the sons of so-and-so," intending to attribute him to his people and to identify his lineage, since people may share the same names. From this verse and its parallels it is derived that the system of tribes arose only after the Flood.

The clause ﴿He said: O my people﴾ is detached (fuṣilat) and was not joined with "then" (fāʾ), as its counterpart was joined in the earlier narrative about Noah. This is because the context required here that it be a resumptive explanatory sentence (istiʾnāf bayānī), since the narrative of Hud came directly after the narrative of Noah, in which his call to his people was mentioned. The listener is therefore eager to know what Hud said to his people when God sent him to them. That was a source of a question in the listener's mind: "What did Hud call his people to, and how did they respond?" The answer then comes: "He said, O my people, worship God," and so on. This difference also adds variety to the styles of speech. And because the verb from which the saying is derived through conjunction was omitted, the derivation was not appropriate in the form of the arrangement.

The connection between the sentences is achieved in both cases, because the conjunctive "then" (fāʾ) is a verbal link joining the conjoined to what it is conjoined to, and the answer to the question links the sentence of the answer to the sentence that raised the question, by a semantic link.

The sentence ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾ is an independent initial sentence (mustaʾnafah ibtidāʾiyyah). The call of Hud to his people resembled the call of Noah to his people in the essential part of its speech, because the messengers are sent by God, and the wisdom of sending is one, so their calls are necessarily similar. In a ḥadīth: "The prophets are sons of one father (ʿallāt)." And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus﴾ (al-Shūrā 42:13).

The sentence ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ is an interrogative of denial (istifhām inkārī), conjoined with the conjunctive "then" (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ) to the sentence ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾. By mindfulness (taqwā) is meant caution against the punishment of God for their associating others with Him in worship and in the belief in divinity. In it there is an allusion to a warning of punishment if they persist in that. He began with the denial against them in order to be severe in the call and to magnify the monstrousness of association (shirk), if he said this at the beginning of his call. It is also possible that this is a report of one of his statements in repeating the call after he had called them time after time and admonished them, just as Noah said: ﴿I have called my people night and day﴾ (Nūḥ 71:5). This is supported by some of the explanations for stripping the report of his speech of the aforementioned conjunctive "then."

The description of the chiefs (al-malaʾ) as ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ here, unlike what occurred in the story of Noah, is a descriptive qualification (waṣf kāshif), not a restriction, and it is a variation in the styles of narration. Do you not see that He described the chiefs of Noah's people with ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ in the verse of Surat Hud? The explanation in the Kashshāf (of al-Zamakhsharī) here is an oversight of what is in Surat Hud.

The seeing (al-ruʾyah) is cognitive, that is, "We know that you are in folly."

Folly (safāhah) is the feebleness of reason. This root was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿They said: Shall we believe as the foolish (al-sufahāʾ) have believed?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:13), and His saying: ﴿And who turns away from the creed of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:130), in Surat al-Baqarah. They considered His saying ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾ to be a statement that would proceed only from one of deranged reason, because in their view it was a statement of impossibility.

They used the word "to think" (ẓann) for certainty in their saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾. This is a very common usage, as in His saying: ﴿those who think (yaẓunnūn) that they will meet their Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:46), which has been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. They intended to deny him in his saying ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾, and what that statement includes of his being a messenger to them from God.

[Page 203]

The statements of the people of Hud and the statements of the people of Noah resembled each other in denying the messenger, because the error of those who deny is unified, and their doubts are unified, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Their hearts resemble one another﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:118). It is as if some of them taught others, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Did they bequeath this to one another? Nay, they are a transgressing people﴾ (al-Dhāriyāt 51:53).

[Page 200]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 67–68:

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere, trustworthy adviser to you."﴾

The clause "He said" (qāla) is detached (fuṣilat) because it follows the manner of dialogue (muḥāwara), and its discussion has already preceded, just above and in what came before.

The interpretation of this verse has already been given above in its counterpart in the story of Noah, except that in the story of Noah he said ﴿and I advise you﴾ [al-A'raf: 62], whereas here he said ﴿and I am a sincere, trustworthy adviser to you﴾. Noah's words indicate that he had not ceased giving advice, for the reason mentioned earlier, while Hud's words indicate that giving advice to them is a fixed attribute in him, firmly established, and that what they considered folly is in fact advice.

The word "sincere adviser" (nāṣiḥ) is followed by "trustworthy" (amīn), which is the one characterized by trustworthiness, in response to their saying to him ﴿indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-A'raf: 66]. For the trustworthy one is the one described by trustworthiness, and trustworthiness (amāna) is a state in a person that moves him to safeguard what he must of the right of others, and prevents him from wasting it or turning it to his own benefit. Its opposite is treachery (khiyāna).

Trustworthiness is among the most noble attributes of human beings, and it is among the character traits of the Muslims. In a hadith: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness." And in a hadith: "Trustworthiness descended into the root of men's hearts, then they learned from the Qur'an, then they learned from the Sunnah." Then he said: "A man sleeps a sleep and trustworthiness is taken from his heart..." until he said: "It is said: Indeed among the sons of so-and-so there is a trustworthy man, and it is said of a man: How intelligent he is, how witty he is, how strong he is!! and there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith." So he mentioned faith in the place of trustworthiness.

Lying is a form of treachery, and truthfulness is a form of trustworthiness, because lying is the report of a matter that has not occurred, in a form that makes the listener think it has occurred, and that is treachery toward the listener. Truthfulness is the conveying of the matter as it actually occurred, and so it is the discharge of the trust of what the informant knows. Therefore his saying in the verse "trustworthy" is an attribute that gathers the qualities which make him a place of trust among his people, and among that is the negation of his being one of the liars.

The placing of "to you" (lakum) before its governing word is to signal concern for what benefits them.
