Lying is a form of treachery, and truthfulness is a form of trustworthiness, because lying is the report of a matter that has not occurred, in a form that makes the listener think it has occurred, and that is treachery toward the listener. Truthfulness is the conveying of the matter as it actually occurred, and so it is the discharge of the trust of what the informant knows. Therefore his saying in the verse "trustworthy" is an attribute that gathers the qualities which make him a place of trust among his people, and among that is the negation of his being one of the liars.

The placing of "to you" (lakum) before its governing word is to signal concern for what benefits them.

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ This is similar to the words of Nuh (Noah) to his people, and the reason for the similarity has already been mentioned just before. The explanation of its counterpart has also been given earlier.

* * *

﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh and increased you broadly in creation. So remember the favours of God that you may prosper.﴾

It is possible that His words "and remember" are coordinated with His words "worship God," and that what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion, recounting the dialogue that took place between him and his people, in which they interrupted him right after he said to them "worship God." Then, when he had finished answering what they had interrupted him with, he returned to his call, so this is a return to the main claim. It is also possible that it is coordinated with His words "Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you" (al-A'raf 63), meaning: do not deny that a reminder from your Lord has come to you, and remember His favour upon you. In that case it serves as a completion of the argument. Whichever is the case, the outcome is the same. He moved from commanding them to monotheism (tawhid) to reminding them of God's favour upon them, which they do not deny is from God alone and not from anyone else, because creation and command belong to God and to no other. This reminder aims to bring them to single out God Almighty in worship.

He commanded them to remember (bi-l-dhikr, with a dammah on the dhal) because the soul forgets favours and so becomes ungrateful to the benefactor. When a person remembers a favour, he sees that it is incumbent upon him to thank the benefactor. For this reason, the question of gratitude to the benefactor is among the most important matters of religious obligation (taklif, the duties imposed by God on the responsible person). The theologians (mutakallimun) relied on its rational goodness (husn 'aqli), whether those who relied on rational goodness alone or those who did not rely on it alone and held that it depends on the divine legal address (al-khitab al-shar'i).

And "idh" (when) is a noun of time in the accusative as a direct object (maf'ul bihi), and not as an adverb of time (zarf), because the meaning does not hold if it is taken as an adverb. The truth is that "idh" is not necessarily an adverb, but it is a flexible adverb (zarf mutasarrif), and this is the view preferred by the author of al-Kashshaf. The meaning is: remember the time when your succession after the people of Nuh became evident, in populating the earth and dominating the nations. The 'Ad were people of strength and great prosperity, as God says: ﴿And they said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ (Fussilat 15).

So "khulafa'" (successors) is the plural of "khalifa," which is one who succeeds another in something, that is, takes over the work that the other used to do. It was explained earlier at His words ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successor﴾ (al-Baqarah 30) in Surat al-Baqarah. So the meaning is: He made you successors in populating the earth. Since He said ﴿after the people of Nuh﴾, it is known that the intended meaning is that they were successors of the people of Nuh. The 'Ad were the first nation to take up civilization after the Flood. The sons of Nuh had multiplied and spread over the earth, in Armenia, Mosul, Iraq and the lands of the Arabs, and they were many nations. Or the 'Ad were the greatest of those nations and the masters of dominion over all other nations. The intended meaning is not that they left the people of Nuh in their dwellings, because according to historians the dwellings of 'Ad were different from the dwellings of the people of Nuh. This reminder is an explicit mention of the favour and an allusion to warning and threat: the people of Nuh were uprooted and destroyed only by a punishment from God for their polytheism, so whoever follows them in their deeds, a punishment may soon befall him too.

The word "khalq" (creation) may be a pure verbal noun (masdar), and it may be used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul, that which is created). It is used in both senses.

His word "basṭatan" (basṭa, expansion) is written in the codices of the Qur'an with the letter ṣad before the ṭa', and it is synonymous with "bastatan," which has sin before the ṭa'. It occurs in other verses. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) omitted the form with ṣad. The apparent wording of al-Qurtubi suggests that in this verse it is with sin, but this is not so.

"Al-basṭa" means abundance and breadth in some matter. If "khalq" means the verbal noun, then "basṭa" is an increase in natural powers, that is, He increased them in strength of mind and body, so He created them rational and healthy. It was well known among the Arabs to attribute sound judgment to 'Ad and to attribute perfection of physical strength to them. Al-Nabigha said:

*The wisdom of 'Ad and bodies purified*
*from defect, calamity and sin.*

And Waddak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini said in al-Hamasa:

*And the wisdom of 'Ad, whose companion does not fear,*
*even if the ignorant spoke, the tongue would be eloquent.*

And Qays ibn 'Ubada said:

*And lest they say: Qays has absented himself, and these*
*are the trousers of an 'Adi that Thamud grew.*

In this sense, His words ﴿in creation﴾ are connected to "basṭa." If "khalq" means people, then the meaning is: He increased you in expansion among people, by making you superior to them in all the matters in which nations differ, so it includes the superiority of intellect, strength of body, soundness from defects and calamities, and strength of might. Coats of mail were attributed to 'Ad, so they are called "'adiyya," and likewise the swords are called "'adiyya." God Almighty has also said, relating their words: ﴿And they said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ (Fussilat 15). And He related that Hud said to them: ﴿Do you build monuments as if you would live forever? And when you seize, you seize as tyrants. So fear God and obey me, and fear Him who has provided you with what you know: He provided you with livestock and sons, gardens and springs﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 129–134). In this sense, His words ﴿in creation﴾ are an established adverbial phrase in a position of circumstance (hal) from the pronoun of those addressed.

The "fa'" in His words ﴿So remember the favours of God﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasiha), meaning: if you remember the time when God made you successors on earth and the time when He increased you in expansion, then remember His many favours in detail. The speech came in the manner of analogy (qiyas), reasoning from a particular case to establish a universal ruling. He reminded them of one clear favour, namely that they were successors, and of general favours, namely the increase in their expansion, and then He reminded them of the rest of the favours using a general word, which is the plural with a possessive suffix (al-jam' al-mudaf).

"Al-ala'" (favours) is the plural of "ila," and "ila" means a favour. This is like the plural of "inab" (grapes) as "a'nab." Its counterpart is the plural of "ina" with nun, which means a time, as "anaa'." He said: ﴿not waiting for its time﴾ (al-Ahzab 53), meaning its time, and He said: ﴿and from the hours of the night, glorify﴾ (Taha 130).

The hope that they may prosper is connected to the remembrance of God's favours, because remembering favours leads to repeated gratitude to the benefactor, so that the one who receives the favour is moved to return the favours with obedience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 70–71 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we would worship God alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said: "Wrath and punishment from your Lord have already fallen upon you. Do you dispute with me over names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority? So wait, and I am with you among those who wait."﴾

They answered Hud with a reply that revealed the loss of their argument, amid the misguidance of their minds and the obstinacy of their souls. For this reason they repeated their denial of him in the form of an incredulous question about his call to monotheism (tawhid). This reply was less harsh and rough than their first reply, when they said: ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-A'raf: 66]. It is as if they intended to bring Hud down from his position and to try to turn him back from what he called them to. Therefore they limited themselves to denial, and they reminded him that the matter he denied is the religion of all their fathers, implicitly suggesting that he had disparaged his own fathers. This purpose is what required expressing their religion through the relative form (al-mawsuliyya) in their saying ﴿what our fathers used to worship﴾, as a hint at the ground of the denial against him and that he deserves to follow the religion of his fathers. This is like what the chiefs of Quraysh said to Abu Talib when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him to say, "There is no god but God," at his death. They said to Abu Talib: "Do you turn away from the creed of 'Abd al-Muttalib?"

The use of (كان) (kana, "was") is to indicate that their worship is an ancient matter that has passed through generations.

The use of the verb and its being in the present tense in his saying يَعْبُدُ (ya'budu, "worships") is to indicate that this is repeated from their fathers and renewed, and that they do not cease from it.

The meaning of أجِئْتَنا (aji'tana, "have you come to us") is: have you intended and been concerned about us, so that we would worship God alone. The verb "to come" is therefore used metaphorically to mean concern, readiness and firmness, as in the Arab saying: "he went to do such-and-such" (dhahaba yaf'alu). In the Qur'an: ﴿O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], and God says, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿Then he turned his back, striving, and gathered and proclaimed﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22]. Pharaoh did not leave his seat of rule; rather, what is meant is that he turned away and was intent. Similar is their saying "he went to do such-and-such." Al-Nabhani said:

"If you are our lord, then you have led us; but if you are for the dismissal, then go and leave."

By what the verb "to come" indicates, they intended an increase in the denial against him and to call him a fool for his concern with a matter like what he calls them to.

Wahdahu (وَحْدَهُ, "alone") is a state (hal) of the name of God. It is the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) of awhadahu, meaning when one believes Him to be one. The regular verbal noun is al-iyhad. This noun is put in the accusative as a state in one of two ways: either from the name of God, by interpreting the verbal noun as a passive participle according to the majority of scholars, meaning "made one," that is, "ascribed unity to Him." Or Yunus said it has the meaning of the active participle, that is, "affirming His oneness," so it is a state of the pronoun in "to worship" (linabud).

The meaning of "wa-nadhara" (وَنَذَرَ, "and abandon") was explained earlier at God's saying: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ [al-An'am: 70], in Surat al-An'am.

The particle fa (ف) in His saying ﴿then bring us what you threaten us with﴾ is for the consequence of their demand to realize what he threatened them with, and as a challenge to Hud, and as an indication to him that they are certain there is no truth in the threat which he threatens them with, so they do not fear the punishment he promised them. Thus the imperative in their saying fa'ti-na (فَأْتِنا, "then bring us") is for incapacitating him (ta'jiz).

Bringing (al-ita') something in its literal sense means that it comes accompanied by it, and it is used metaphorically for presenting and establishing, as here. The meaning is: hasten for us what you threaten us with of punishment, or make true for us what you claimed of your threat. A parallel is the verb derived from "coming," as in: ﴿You did not bring us any clear proof﴾ [Hud: 53], and "now you have come with the truth."

They attributed the verb to his pronoun, as an implication that what he threatened them with is one of his own fabrications and not from God the Exalted, because they claim that God does not want them to desist from worshipping their gods, since in their claim His will is not connected with seeking misguidance.

The promise they meant is a promise of evil, which is the threat. No previous statement indicates that he had threatened them with harm. So it may be an implicit threat contained in his saying: ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], because his denial of their not being wary is evidence that there is something to be cautious about. For this reason they did not specify a threat in their speech, but left it vague with their saying "what you threaten us with." It may also be that the threat is an allusion in His saying: ﴿when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69], which indicates that God uprooted the people of Noah and replaced them with 'Ad, so He is about to uproot 'Ad and replace them with others.

They concluded their speech with a conditional clause, saying: ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾, seeking to exhaust his capacity, intending to show his inability to bring the punishment, so that he has no choice but to acknowledge that he is a liar. The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated form is: "then bring it, otherwise you are not truthful."

So he answered them by informing them that God had become angry with them, and that a defilement from God had fallen upon them.

The more apparent view is that "waqa'a" (وَقَعَ, "fell/has fallen") means "was established and confirmed," from their saying about a confirmed matter: "this has occurred," and their saying about a false matter: "this has not occurred." So the meaning is: "defilement and wrath have been decreed and determined upon you."

Ar-rijs (الرِّجْسُ) is the filthy thing. It is used here metaphorically for the corruption of the inner self, that is, the corruption of the soul, as in God's saying: ﴿so He increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawba: 125], and His saying: ﴿Thus God places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. The meaning is: God afflicted their souls with corruption because of their disbelief, so they do not accept good and do not turn toward it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained ar-rijs here as the curse. The majority explained ar-rijs here as the punishment. In this case the verb "waqa'a" is in the past tense used with the meaning of the future, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. Others explained ar-rijs as the wrath, and explained al-ghadab (الغَضَبُ, "wrath") as the punishment, on the basis that it is a metonymy (majaz mursal), because the punishment is the effect of wrath. Hud informed of this from knowledge by revelation at that time, or from the time God sent him, since He informed him that if they did not return from polytheism after he had conveyed the proof to them, their not returning would be a sign that the corruption of their hearts was firmly established and would not pass away, and no faith could be hoped for from them, just as God said to Noah: ﴿None of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36].

The wrath of God is estimated to mean removal, punishment and debasement. These are the effects of wrath in events, because the true nature of wrath is an emotion from which arises aversion toward the one who is angered, distancing him and harming him.

The delay of the wrath after the defilement is because the defilement, which is the corruption of their souls, has already indicated that God created them with corruption, such that their persistence in misguidance was an innate matter. This indicates that God became angry with them. So the falling of defilement and wrath upon them is accomplished in past time relative to the time of Hud's speech. Its combination with qad (قَدْ) is to indicate the nearness of the past time to the present, as in the expression qad qamati al-salat ("the prayer has been established").

The fronting of "upon you from your Lord" before the subject of the verb is for the sake of concern, by hastening the mention of the one who is angered and the one who angers, to awaken their insight, so that perhaps they would hasten to repentance. Also because the two prepositional phrases are connected to the verb, so it is fitting that they be placed next to it. If they had been mentioned after the subject, it would be assumed that they were attributes of it. The prepositional phrase whose object is their pronoun was placed before the one that is the attribute of their Lord, because they are the primary intended object of the verb.

When he had put forward his warning to them of God's wrath, he returned to argue against them on the corruption of their belief, and he denied them their disputing about the matter of their idols.

Al-mujadala (الْمُجَادَلَةُ, "disputation") is argumentation.

He described the idols as names, that is, they are merely names that do not have the realities that they believed in and whose names they set up for the sake of summoning them. Therefore those names that were set up were merely words, because the realities for which they set up the names do not exist. The names are set up for the intended named things, and they cared for them only because divinity is part of what the name was set up for, and it is the motive for naming. So the meanings of divinity and what follows from it are considered by the one who set up those names. Since the intended meanings of those names are absent, the names are not named things in that sense, whether those that have bodies and forms, like statues and idols, or those that have no existence. Perhaps some of the gods of 'Ad were merely a name that they mentioned with divinity, without making for it a statue or an idol, like al-'Uzza among the Arabs. It is said that they made a house for her but did not make an idol for her. God has said about this: ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The people of reports mentioned that 'Ad took three idols, and they are: Samud, with the letter sad vowelled with fatha, in the pattern of zabur.

And Sada', with the letter sad vowelled with damma, as it is vocalized in the handwriting of al-Hamadhani, commentator on the Kashshaf, in a copy of his gloss called Tawdih al-Mushkilat, copied in his own hand, and with an unpointed dal after it followed by an alif. I have not found the vocalization of the dal, whether it is doubled or single. I have seen in a manuscript copy of the Kashshaf a sign of doubling placed on the dal, but I am not completely confident in the accuracy of that copy. After the alif there is a hamza, as it is in copies of the Kashshaf and the tafsir of al-Baghawi, and likewise it is in verses fabricated about the story of the people of 'Ad in books of stories. In a copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya, and in Muruj al-Dhahab by al-Mas'udi, and in a copy of the commentary of Ibn Badrun on the poem of Ibn 'Abdun al-Andalusi, it occurs without a hamza after the alif.

Al-Haba' (الهَبَاءُ), with a long vowel at its end, is vocalized in the handwriting of al-Hamadhani in the copy of his gloss on the Kashshaf, in the printed copy of the Kashshaf, in the tafsirs of al-Baghawi and al-Khazin, and in the verses mentioned just above. In a handwritten copy of the Kashshaf it occurs with an alif without a long vowel. I have not found the vocalization of the ha', and I have not seen the mention of Sada' and al-Haba' in what I have seen of the books of lexicography.

The pronoun of the addressees was coordinated with "and your fathers" (wa-aba'ukum), because among their fathers were those who set up those names for them. So the originators set them up and named them, and the imitators named them without setting them up. Both groups shared in the fact that they mention names for which there are no named things.

Sammaytumuha (سَمَّيْتُمُوها, "you named them") means: you mentioned them with your tongues, as one says: "name God" (sammi Allah), that is, mention His name. So sammā means to mention the word of the name. All words are names for their referents, and the origin of language is names. God said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqara: 31]. Labid said:

"Until the year is over, then the name 'peace be upon you both'",

that is, its wording.

The meaning of naming in the verse is not the setting of a name for a named thing, as one says: "I named my son such-and-such," because the addressees and many of their fathers had no part in naming the idols. Rather, that is the action of some of the fathers, namely those who adopted polytheism, made it a religion, and taught it to their children and their people. For this meaning intended by naming, no second object or complement was mentioned for the verb "you named," but it was limited to one object.

As-sultan (السُّلْطَانُ, "authority") is the proof by which the opponent is convinced. It was called sultan because it dominates the opponent himself and persuades him. He denied that the proof was sent down from God, because the nature of proof in such matters is that it must be reported from God the Exalted, since the matters of the unseen are among what God has kept exclusively in His knowledge. The greatest of the unseen things is the establishment of divinity, because the effort of deeds may fall short of grasping it. So it is among its nature that it be received from the divine revelation.

The fa' (ف) in His saying "fa-ntadhiru" (فَانْتَظِرُوا, "so wait") is for the consequence of this warning and the preceding threat, because the falling of wrath and defilement upon them, and their obstinacy and their arguing for what has no proof, give rise to this threat of waiting for the punishment.

The imperative form here is used for threat, as in: "Do whatever you wish." The verb *intaẓara* (to wait) is a *iftiʿāl* form derived from *naẓara* (to look), in the sense of *taraqqub* (watching and awaiting). It is as if the addressees were ordered to watch and await, and so they waited.

The object of *intaẓirū* ("wait") is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿Uncleanness and wrath﴾. The meaning is: "So wait for punishment."

His words ﴿Indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾ form an *istiʾnāf bayānī* (an explanatory resumptive clause). His threat to them raises a question in their minds, namely: "If we are awaiting the punishment, what will your state be?" So he clarifies that he is waiting along with them. This is a situation requiring *adab* (courtesy) toward God, Exalted, like His saying, addressed as instruction to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9]. Hud feared that the punishment descending upon his people might encompass him too. This is permissible, as in the hadith that Umm Salamah said: "Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." In another hadith: "Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions."

It is also possible that the punishment descended upon them while Hud saw it but it did not afflict him. This has been related in his story. It is also possible that God removed him far away, and it has likewise been related in his story that He commanded him to leave the dwellings of his people before the punishment descended.

So it may be an implicit threat contained in his saying: ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], because his denial of their not being wary is evidence that there is something to be cautious about. For this reason they did not specify a threat in their speech, but left it vague with their saying "what you threaten us with." It may also be that the threat is an allusion in His saying: ﴿when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69], which indicates that God uprooted the people of Noah and replaced them with 'Ad, so He is about to uproot 'Ad and replace them with others.

They concluded their speech with a conditional clause, saying: ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾, seeking to exhaust his capacity, intending to show his inability to bring the punishment, so that he has no choice but to acknowledge that he is a liar. The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated form is: "then bring it, otherwise you are not truthful."

So he answered them by informing them that God had become angry with them, and that a defilement from God had fallen upon them.

The more apparent view is that "waqa'a" (وَقَعَ, "fell/has fallen") means "was established and confirmed," from their saying about a confirmed matter: "this has occurred," and their saying about a false matter: "this has not occurred." So the meaning is: "defilement and wrath have been decreed and determined upon you."

Ar-rijs (الرِّجْسُ) is the filthy thing. It is used here metaphorically for the corruption of the inner self, that is, the corruption of the soul, as in God's saying: ﴿so He increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawba: 125], and His saying: ﴿Thus God places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. The meaning is: God afflicted their souls with corruption because of their disbelief, so they do not accept good and do not turn toward it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained ar-rijs here as the curse. The majority explained ar-rijs here as the punishment. In this case the verb "waqa'a" is in the past tense used with the meaning of the future, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. Others explained ar-rijs as the wrath, and explained al-ghadab (الغَضَبُ, "wrath") as the punishment, on the basis that it is a metonymy (majaz mursal), because the punishment is the effect of wrath. Hud informed of this from knowledge by revelation at that time, or from the time God sent him, since He informed him that if they did not return from polytheism after he had conveyed the proof to them, their not returning would be a sign that the corruption of their hearts was firmly established and would not pass away, and no faith could be hoped for from them, just as God said to Noah: ﴿None of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36].

The wrath of God is estimated to mean removal, punishment and debasement. These are the effects of wrath in events, because the true nature of wrath is an emotion from which arises aversion toward the one who is angered, distancing him and harming him.

The delay of the wrath after the defilement is because the defilement, which is the corruption of their souls, has already indicated that God created them with corruption, such that their persistence in misguidance was an innate matter. This indicates that God became angry with them. So the falling of defilement and wrath upon them is accomplished in past time relative to the time of Hud's speech. Its combination with qad (قَدْ) is to indicate the nearness of the past time to the present, as in the expression qad qamati al-salat ("the prayer has been established").

The fronting of "upon you from your Lord" before the subject of the verb is for the sake of concern, by hastening the mention of the one who is angered and the one who angers, to awaken their insight, so that perhaps they would hasten to repentance. Also because the two prepositional phrases are connected to the verb, so it is fitting that they be placed next to it. If they had been mentioned after the subject, it would be assumed that they were attributes of it. The prepositional phrase whose object is their pronoun was placed before the one that is the attribute of their Lord, because they are the primary intended object of the verb.

When he had put forward his warning to them of God's wrath, he returned to argue against them on the corruption of their belief, and he denied them their disputing about the matter of their idols.

Al-mujadala (الْمُجَادَلَةُ, "disputation") is argumentation.

He described the idols as names, that is, they are merely names that do not have the realities that they believed in and whose names they set up for the sake of summoning them. Therefore those names that were set up were merely words, because the realities for which they set up the names do not exist. The names are set up for the intended named things, and they cared for them only because divinity is part of what the name was set up for, and it is the motive for naming. So the meanings of divinity and what follows from it are considered by the one who set up those names. Since the intended meanings of those names are absent, the names are not named things in that sense, whether those that have bodies and forms, like statues and idols, or those that have no existence. Perhaps some of the gods of 'Ad were merely a name that they mentioned with divinity, without making for it a statue or an idol, like al-'Uzza among the Arabs. It is said that they made a house for her but did not make an idol for her. God has said about this: ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The people of reports mentioned that 'Ad took three idols, and they are: Samud, with the letter sad vowelled with fatha, in the pattern of zabur.

And Sada', with the letter sad vowelled with damma, as it is vocalized in the handwriting of al-Hamadhani, commentator on the Kashshaf, in a copy of his gloss called Tawdih al-Mushkilat, copied in his own hand, and with an unpointed dal after it followed by an alif. I have not found the vocalization of the dal, whether it is doubled or single. I have seen in a manuscript copy of the Kashshaf a sign of doubling placed on the dal, but I am not completely confident in the accuracy of that copy. After the alif there is a hamza, as it is in copies of the Kashshaf and the tafsir of al-Baghawi, and likewise it is in verses fabricated about the story of the people of 'Ad in books of stories. In a copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya, and in Muruj al-Dhahab by al-Mas'udi, and in a copy of the commentary of Ibn Badrun on the poem of Ibn 'Abdun al-Andalusi, it occurs without a hamza after the alif.

Al-Haba' (الهَبَاءُ), with a long vowel at its end, is vocalized in the handwriting of al-Hamadhani in the copy of his gloss on the Kashshaf, in the printed copy of the Kashshaf, in the tafsirs of al-Baghawi and al-Khazin, and in the verses mentioned just above. In a handwritten copy of the Kashshaf it occurs with an alif without a long vowel. I have not found the vocalization of the ha', and I have not seen the mention of Sada' and al-Haba' in what I have seen of the books of lexicography.

The pronoun of the addressees was coordinated with "and your fathers" (wa-aba'ukum), because among their fathers were those who set up those names for them. So the originators set them up and named them, and the imitators named them without setting them up. Both groups shared in the fact that they mention names for which there are no named things.

Sammaytumuha (سَمَّيْتُمُوها, "you named them") means: you mentioned them with your tongues, as one says: "name God" (sammi Allah), that is, mention His name. So sammā means to mention the word of the name. All words are names for their referents, and the origin of language is names. God said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqara: 31]. Labid said:

"Until the year is over, then the name 'peace be upon you both'",

that is, its wording.

The meaning of naming in the verse is not the setting of a name for a named thing, as one says: "I named my son such-and-such," because the addressees and many of their fathers had no part in naming the idols. Rather, that is the action of some of the fathers, namely those who adopted polytheism, made it a religion, and taught it to their children and their people. For this meaning intended by naming, no second object or complement was mentioned for the verb "you named," but it was limited to one object.

As-sultan (السُّلْطَانُ, "authority") is the proof by which the opponent is convinced. It was called sultan because it dominates the opponent himself and persuades him. He denied that the proof was sent down from God, because the nature of proof in such matters is that it must be reported from God the Exalted, since the matters of the unseen are among what God has kept exclusively in His knowledge. The greatest of the unseen things is the establishment of divinity, because the effort of deeds may fall short of grasping it. So it is among its nature that it be received from the divine revelation.

The fa' (ف) in His saying "fa-ntadhiru" (فَانْتَظِرُوا, "so wait") is for the consequence of this warning and the preceding threat, because the falling of wrath and defilement upon them, and their obstinacy and their arguing for what has no proof, give rise to this threat of waiting for the punishment.

The imperative form here is used for threat, as in: "Do whatever you wish." The verb *intaẓara* (to wait) is a *iftiʿāl* form derived from *naẓara* (to look), in the sense of *taraqqub* (watching and awaiting). It is as if the addressees were ordered to watch and await, and so they waited.

The object of *intaẓirū* ("wait") is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿Uncleanness and wrath﴾. The meaning is: "So wait for punishment."

His words ﴿Indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾ form an *istiʾnāf bayānī* (an explanatory resumptive clause). His threat to them raises a question in their minds, namely: "If we are awaiting the punishment, what will your state be?" So he clarifies that he is waiting along with them. This is a situation requiring *adab* (courtesy) toward God, Exalted, like His saying, addressed as instruction to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9]. Hud feared that the punishment descending upon his people might encompass him too. This is permissible, as in the hadith that Umm Salamah said: "Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." In another hadith: "Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions."

It is also possible that the punishment descended upon them while Hud saw it but it did not afflict him. This has been related in his story. It is also possible that God removed him far away, and it has likewise been related in his story that He commanded him to leave the dwellings of his people before the punishment descended.

[Page 214]

The fa' here indicates sequence: that is, God hastened the uprooting of 'Ad and rescued Hud and those who were with him, meaning the believers from his people. So the thing that is sequenced after is the cutting off of the root of 'Ad. The expected arrangement by the apparent sense would have been: "So We cut off the root of those who denied..., and We rescued Hud...", but the arrangement departs from what the apparent sense requires, out of concern to hasten the report of the rescue of Hud and those who believed with him. This is in the manner I established in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So they denied him, and We rescued him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], in the story of Noah mentioned earlier. The same applies to the definiteness through the relative construction in His words ﴿and those who were with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 64]. Those who were with him are those from his people who believed. The "being with" (ma'iyyah) is companionship in religion, and it is a figurative companionship. It has been said that God, exalted is He, commanded Hud and those with him to emigrate to Mecca before the punishment descended upon 'Ad, and that he died there and was buried in al-Hijr. I do not think this is established, because Mecca was built by Ibrahim, and the apparent sense of the Qur'an in Surat Hud is that there was a long time between 'Ad and Ibrahim, since it relates that Shu'ayb said to his people: ﴿Lest there befall you the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89]. This is evident that 'Ad and Thamud were far in time from the time of Shu'ayb, and that the people of Lot were not far, and the distance intended is distance in time, since the places of all of them were close, and Lot was in the time of Ibrahim. Therefore it is better that we do not specify the manner of the rescue of Hud and those with him. The more apparent view is that it was by the command to emigrate to a place far from the punishment. It is narrated from Ali that the grave of Hud is in Hadramawt, and this is closer.

His words ﴿with a mercy from Us﴾: the ba' here is causal (sababiyyah), and the indefiniteness of "mercy" (rahmah) is for magnification. Likewise, describing it as being from God is to indicate its perfection, and min (from) is for origin. It is also permissible that the ba' is for accompaniment, meaning: We rescued him and showed him mercy, so the mercy was accompanying them, since they were in a state of gentleness and kindness wherever they settled until the end of their lifetimes. The placement of "from Us" according to this interpretation is a very graceful placement, indicating that the mercy is not cut off from them, like His words ﴿Indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48].

[Page 215]

The explanation of His words ﴿and We cut off the root of those who denied﴾ is similar to His words, exalted is He, ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45] in Surat al-An'am. He sent upon them the dabur wind, and it destroyed them all, and none of them remained. The apparent view is that those whom God rescued from them had no offspring. As for the verse, it requires only the extinction of the offspring of those who denied and upon whom the punishment descended. The definition by way of the relative construction (al-mawsuliyyah) has already occurred in His words ﴿and We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 64] in the story of Noah, just above. So it serves to point to the reason for constructing the report, which is the cutting off of their root.

His words ﴿and they were not believers﴾ are coordinated (atf) upon "denied", so it is part of the relative clause. The benefit of coordinating it is to indicate that both of the two clauses are a cause for cutting off their root: they are denial and polytheism, as an allusion to the polytheists of Quraysh, and the stories were mentioned for their admonition. What befell 'Ad of uprooting was a first purification of the Arabs from the affliction of shirk, and a cutting off of the root of misguidance from them in the earliest ages of their civilization, as a preparation for what God, exalted is He, intended of the emergence of the light of the Muhammadan call among them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 73:

﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. This is the she-camel of Allah as a sign for you, so leave her to eat within Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."﴾ The wāw in His saying ﴿And to Thamud﴾ is like it in His saying ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]. The same applies to its explanation up to His saying (other than Him).

Thamud was a great nation of the extinct Arabs. They are the descendants of Thamud ibn Jathir (with a jim and a thā' as in the Qamus) ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh; thus they are joined with 'Ad in "Iram".

Page 216

Their dwellings were at al-Hijr (with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the jim), between the Hijaz and al-Sham. It is the place now called Mada'in Salih, and in the hadith about the Battle of Tabuk it is called the Hijr of Thamud.

Salih is the son of 'Abil (with a lam at its end and a fatha on the 'ayn) ibn Asif ibn Majish or Shalikh ibn 'Abil ibn Jathir (it is said Kathir) ibn Thamud. Among these names there is disagreement in their letters in the history books and elsewhere, which I think is from distortion, and they are not vowelled, except 'Abil, for it is vowelled in its namesake who is the grandfather of a tribe, as in the Qamus.

Thamud here is not diptote, because what is meant is the tribe and not its ancestor. Names of tribes are treated as diptote on account of feminine form with proper-noun status, and this is the prevalent case in the Qur'an. It has occurred in some verses of the Qur'an as triptote, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord﴾ [Hud: 68], considering it the name of a living group, so the reason for diptotion is removed, since the name is Arabic.

His saying ﴿You have no deity other than Him﴾ indicates that Thamud were polytheists, and this is stated in the verses of Surat Hud and elsewhere. It is apparent that they worshipped the idols that 'Ad worshipped, since Thamud and 'Ad were sons of one lineage, so their beliefs are likely to be similar. The commentators have said that Thamud arose after 'Ad, grew, became great, and their civilization expanded. They were monotheists, and perhaps they took warning from what befell 'Ad. Then their period lengthened and their life was pleasant, so they became insolent, forgot the blessing of Allah, and worshipped idols. So Allah sent to them Salih as a messenger calling them to monotheism, but only a few of the weak among them followed him, while their leaders and chiefs disobeyed him. In the verse of Surat Hud it is mentioned that his people did not speak harshly to him as the people of Nuh and the people of Hud had spoken harshly to their messengers. For they said: ﴿O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us﴾ [Hud: 62]. The verses of the Qur'an, and the stories explained by them, indicate that Salih gave them a long period for reflection and made the she-camel a sign for them, and that they left her alone and did not disturb her for a long time.

Page 217

Their disputing with Salih over matters of religion indicates that reasoning in argument had begun to stir in human souls, and that their arrogance in obstinacy had begun to lessen, and that the spear of their might had begun to soften, given the clear difference between the answer of the people of Nuh and the people of Hud and the answer of the people of Salih. For this reason Allah gave them respite and extended them, so that they might look and reflect upon what their prophet called them to, and weigh their affair. And He made their refraining from touching the she-camel with harm a sign of the extension of the respite, because their refraining was a sign that their souls had not been inflamed against their messenger, so his hope for their faith remained, and giving them respite was more decisive as to their excuse and more effective as proof against them. Therefore Allah delayed the punishment from them, honouring their prophet who was eager for their faith to the extent of his capacity, as He said to Nuh: that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they have been doing.

The clause ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ etc. is part of Salih's speech at a time other than the time when he began the call, because the answer of his people and their request of him for a sign have been omitted here, as indicated by the verses of Surat Hud and Surat al-Shu'ara'. In Surat Hud: ﴿He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He produced you from the earth and settled you in it, so seek His forgiveness and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."﴾ [Hud: 61] ﴿They said: "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this..."﴾ [Hud: 62], the verse. In Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿They said, "You are but one of the bewitched. You are but a human like us, so bring a sign if you should be of the truthful."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 153-154] ﴿He said, "This is a she-camel; for her is a drinking turn"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 155], the verse.

So the clause ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ is a reason for the clause ﴿Worship Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], that is, worship Him alone, because He has made for you a sign confirming me in what I have conveyed to you, and confirming His sole disposal of the created beings.

His saying ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah﴾ requires that the she-camel was present at the time of His saying ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾, because she herself is the sign.

Page 218

The bayyinah is the proof for the truthfulness of a claim, so it is synonymous with the sign, and it has been used to express the sign in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to separate until there came to them clear evidence﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1].

This is a reference to the she-camel which Allah made a sign of Salih's truthfulness. And since the she-camel is the clear evidence, the clause ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ is, relative to the preceding clause, in the position of an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān).

His saying "āyah" (a sign) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah﴾, because the demonstrative contains the meaning of a verb, and its connection with the particle of indication strengthens its resemblance to a verb; for this reason it operates on the circumstantial accusative by agreement. It has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿That We recite to you of the signs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58] in Surat Al 'Imran, and we will mention an account on this at the explanation of His saying ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72] in Surat Hud.

The clause ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence﴾ is emphasized, and in addition to emphasis it conveys what the word "for you" required of specification and of confirming that it is a sign; that is the meaning of the lam, i.e., it is a sign convincing to you and made for your sake.

So His saying "for you" (lakum) is a stationary adverbial phrase in the place of a circumstantial qualifier relative to "āyah". Its origin was an attribute, but when it was placed before the noun it modifies it became a circumstantial; its being placed first is for the sake of emphasis that it is sufficient for them despite their obstinacy.

The annexation of "she-camel" to the name of Allah the Exalted is an honouring of her, because Allah commanded kindness toward her and not harming her, and magnified her sanctity, as one says: "The Ka'bah is the House of Allah." Or because she came into being in a manner contrary to custom, so for the absence of the causes of the existence of such things which normally would be attributed to her, she was attributed to the name of majesty, as it is said: "Jesus, peace be upon him, is the Word of Allah."

As for the annexation of "earth" to the name of Allah, what is meant is that the she-camel has a right to eat from the vegetation of the earth, because the earth belongs to Allah and that she-camel is one of His creatures, so she has the right

Page 219

to benefit from what suits her benefit.

His saying this is a preface to His saying ﴿and do not touch her with harm﴾, that is, with harm that prevents her from grazing, either by death or by wound; or because when they denied him and denied his miracle they sought to prevent the she-camel from grazing so that she would die of hunger, in the sense of compulsion arising from ignorance.

Here "the earth" is meant as the genus of earth, as the annexation requires.

Allah made the safety of that she-camel a sign of their safety from the punishment of annihilation, for the wisdom I have already mentioned, and what Allah ordained concerning her is similar to a sanctuary and similar to a royal protected pasture, because it indicates the magnification of the people's souls toward the one to whom that inviolability is ascribed. For this reason Salih said to them: ﴿so leave her to eat within Allah's earth and do not touch her with harm﴾, because if anyone touches her with harm, with the consent of the rest, they have shown that they cast off the sanctity of Allah the Exalted and became enraged against His messenger, peace be upon him.

The verb "ta'kul" is apocopated (majzum) on the understanding that its original form is the answer to the imperative with an implied condition: "if you leave her, she will eat." So the meaning is according to the raf' (nominative) but the usage is according to the jazm (apocopate), as in His saying: ﴿Tell My servants who believe to establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], i.e., they establish; and this is common in speech. It seems that the origin of apocopating such forms in Arabic speech is by analogy to the presence of an imperative verb before a verb suitable for jazm. Perhaps from this is His saying: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot﴾ [al-Hajj: 27].

The verb "fa-ya'khudhakum" is put in the accusative as the answer to the prohibition, so that the answer is treated as an answer to the thing prohibited, since the particle of prohibition has no effect of its own: that is, if you touch her with harm, a punishment will seize you.

The prohibition was tied to touching with harm because touching applies even to the slightest contact of a thing with the body, so whatever reaches her with intent to harm is forbidden; this is because an animal is only hurt by what causes pain to itself, since it does not comprehend inner meanings.

The bā' in His saying "bi-su'" (with harm) is for accompaniment, and it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of "tamassuha", meaning: with intent of harm.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 74:

Page 220
﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad and settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces in its plains and hewing out the mountains as houses. So remember the bounties of God, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief.﴾
It may be that this is a conjunction (ʿatf) with His saying: (Worship God), and it may be that it is a conjunction with His saying: "Leave her to eat in God's earth," etc. The discussion concerning it is like the discussion concerning His saying: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69].

And "wa-bawwa'akum" means He lodged you, derived from al-bawʾ (return), because a person returns to his dwelling and his residence. It has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿He settles the believers in positions for battle﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121].

As for His saying "in the land" (fi al-ard), the definite article in "al-ard" may be for a specific reference (li-l-ʿahd), meaning in this land of yours, which is the land of al-Hijr. It may also be generic (li-l-jins), because when He settled them in a specific land, He had settled them in one region of the earth.

Al-suhul is the plural of sahl, which is level ground, and its opposite is the mountain (jabal).

Al-qusur is the plural of qasr, which is a dwelling. This indicates that they used to build palaces, and their remains bear witness to that. The "min" in His saying "min suhulihā" is for location (zarfiyya), meaning: you take in its plains palaces.

Al-nahth is the shaping of stone and wood with a tool according to a specific measure.

Al-jibal is the plural of jabal, which is land raised above other land, elevated. Al-jibal is the opposite of al-suhul.

Al-buyut is the plural of bayt, which is a defined place used for dwelling, whether it is built of stone or made of tents of hair or wool. The verb "nahth" is connected to "al-jibal," because nahth relates to the stones of the mountains. "Buyutan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "al-jibal," meaning becoming houses after being carved, just as one says: "Sew this cloth into a shirt," and "Sharpen this reed into a pen," because the mountain is not in the state of houses at the time of carving, but becomes houses after carving.

Page 221
The locus of the favour is that He made their dwellings of two kinds: one kind suitable for building in, and another kind suitable for carving houses. It was said: they used to dwell in palaces in summer, and in winter in the houses carved into the mountains.

The branching of the command with the mention of God's bounties upon His saying: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ is the branching of the more general upon the more specific, because He commanded them to remember two blessings, then commanded them to remember all the blessings which they cannot count, so this served as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

The verb "udhkurū" (remember) is derived from the verbal noun "dhikr" (with a dhamma on the dhal), which is remembrance by the intellect and inner reflection. Remembering God's bounties stirs gratitude, obedience, and abandoning corruption; therefore He joined their prohibition from corruption in the land to the command to remember God's bounties.

"Wa-la ta'thaw" means "and do not cause corruption." It is said: 'athiya (like radiya), and this is the more eloquent form; therefore it came in the verse with a fatha on the thā' when attached to the plural waw. It is also said: 'atha yaʿthū (from the pattern sama), ʿathwan, and this is a dialect less than the first. Kurāʿ said: it seems to be an inversion of ʿāʿa. Al-ʿathy and al-ʿathw both mean: to corrupt with the utmost corruption.

"Mufsidīn" is an emphatic circumstantial state (hal mu'akkida) for the meaning of "ta'thaw." Although it is more general than the emphasized term, emphasis is achieved through part of the meaning of the emphasized term.

Page 222

The chiefs who were arrogant turned away from disputing with Salih (peace be upon him) to testing the steadfastness of those who believed in him in their faith, and to attempting to cast doubt into their souls. Since their address to the believers was intended to corrupt the call of Salih (peace be upon him), their address was in the position of a dialogue with Salih (peace be upon him). Therefore the sentence reporting their speech was separated (from what precedes) in the manner of separating sentences that report dialogues, as we have mentioned more than once previously and before.

The explanation of "al-mala'" (the chiefs, the notables) has already been given shortly before.

Describing them as "those who were arrogant" here serves to highlight the enormity of their arrogance and their pride over the common people of their nation, and their subjugation of them. It also serves to alert that those who believed in what Salih (peace be upon him) brought were the weak among his people.

The choice of the relative-clause construction in describing them, and in describing the others as "those who were oppressed," is due to what the relative clause indicates regarding the source of this statement from them: that is, their arrogance is what diverted them from obeying their prophet, and their contempt for the believers is what made it unbearable to them that the believers preceded them to good and guidance. This is like what is related about the people of Noah, their saying: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us, immature in judgment, and we see in you no superiority over us﴾ [Hud: 27], and like what is related about the disbelievers of Quraysh in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. It may also be from the reported speech itself: that is, there is in their speech something indicating concern with the meaning of the two relative clauses, so it came in the composition of the verse indicated by the fronting of the two complements.

Ibn 'Amir recited: (wa-qala al-mala') with the conjunction, and the wa was preserved in the Mushaf sent to Syria, contrary to the practice of its counterparts. It is a conjunction upon an implied speech indicated by His saying: They said ﴿Indeed, we believe in that with which he has been sent﴾, and the implied meaning is: so some of his people believed in him, and (﴿And the chiefs of his people said﴾) [al-Mu'minun: 33], etc. Or it is a conjunction upon: "He said, O my people, worship Allah," etc. Differing from its counterparts is a variation of style (tafannun).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 77–79:**

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel and defied the command of their Lord, and said, "O Salih, bring us what you have been threatening us with, if you are indeed one of the messengers."﴾ ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes by morning.﴾

The *fa'* (then/so) here indicates immediate sequence, relating the words of those who were arrogant: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed﴾ [Al-A'raf: 76]. That is, they said this, and then they hamstrung the camel. Sequence (*ta'qib*) takes its meaning according to what it governs. When they said that, they had openly declared their denial and become firm in it, and they were unable to argue or reason. So they resolved to proceed to hurting and enraging Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed in him. As the start of their action, they determined to attack the she-camel

[Page 225]

which Salih (peace be upon him) had made for them, and established between himself and them as a sign of truce, for as long as they did not harm her. Their intention in destroying the she-camel was to remove the sign of Salih (peace be upon him), so that the number of believers in him would not increase. This is because seeing the sign of his prophethood unharmed among them stirs in the souls of many of them reflection on his truthfulness, and a sense of comfort from the silence of their elders and their acceptance of her grazing and drinking. Also, in their assault on her there was a declaration from them of their readiness to harm Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed in him afterward, and that they would show Salih (peace be upon him) that they deserved his threat when he said to them: ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾.

The pronoun in His words "*fa-'aqarū*" (so they hamstrung) refers to "those who were arrogant." The hamstringing is attributed to them all, although its actual doer was one of them, because it was done with the collusion and approval of all the elders. This is shown by the words of God Most High in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took [the sword] and hamstrung [her]﴾ [Al-Qamar: 29]. This is like the saying of al-Nabigha regarding the Banu Hunn:

*They killed the Ta'i by force in the open plain.*

But only one of them killed him.

It is mentioned in the reports that the one who undertook the she-camel was a man of their leaders named Qudar, with a *qāf* vowel, an unpointed *dāl* lightly pronounced, and a *rā'* at the end, the son of Salif. In the Hadith of al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in his sermon the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and said: "A mighty, wicked, and fierce man rose up for her among his tribe, like Abu Zam'a."

The root meaning of *al-'aqr* is a deep wound. Imru' al-Qays said:

*She says, when the saddle leaned with us together,*
*"You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!"*

That is, he wounded it by the saddle rubbing against its back from its leaning to one side. The term *al-'aqr* is also applied to cutting off a limb of an animal. From this comes the saying "he hamstrung a wild donkey," meaning he struck it with a spear

[Page 226]

and cut off a limb from it. They used to hamstring a camel intended for slaughter by cutting off one of its limbs, so that it could not flee at the time of slaughter. Therefore, *al-'aqr* was applied to slaughtering by way of metonymy (*kināya*). Imru' al-Qays said:

*And the day I slaughtered my mount for the maidens,*
*—and this verse is not like that.*

*Al-'utuww* is exceeding the limit in arrogance, and its transitive use is because it implies the meaning of turning away.

"The command of their Lord" is what He commanded them through the tongue of Salih (peace be upon him), namely his words: ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾. The prohibition is expressed as a command, because the aim of a prohibition against something is a command to do its opposite. For this reason, the scholars of legal theory (*usūl*) say that a prohibition against something necessarily entails a command to its opposite, by which the abstention from the forbidden thing is realized.

They meant by "what you threaten us with" the punishment with which he had threatened them in a general way. The relative pronoun was used to indicate that they feared nothing of what he might intend by his general threat. So the meaning is "what you threaten us with," and the verbal noun's source was taken from the root of promise (*wa'd*) rather than threat (*wa'īd*), because it is lighter.

They presumed his being a messenger with the particle *in* (if), which indicates doubt about the realization of the condition. That is: "if you are among the messengers from God." By "the messengers" is meant those to whom this title truly applies. Because of their ignorance of the reality of God's actions and His wisdom, they supposed that God's dealings are like the dealings of creatures: when He sends a messenger and the people to whom he is sent do not believe him, God becomes angry and proceeds to send punishment upon them. They do not know that God gives respite to the wrongdoers and then seizes them whenever He wills.

The clause "*fa-akhadhathumu al-rajfa*" (so the earthquake seized them) is a parenthetical clause placed between the clause "﴿so they hamstrung the she-camel﴾" and the clause "*fa-tawallā 'anhum*" (so he turned away from them). Its purpose in being parenthetical is to hasten the report that the threat was carried out against them immediately after their arrogance. Thus the sequence is customary (*'urfī*), meaning there was no long time between the hamstringing and the earthquake. There were three days between them, as is mentioned in the verse of Surah Hud:

[Page 227]

﴿So they hamstrung her, and he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾ [Hud: 65].

The root meaning of *al-akhdh* is taking something with the hand. It is used figuratively for possessing a thing, through the relation of necessary connection. It is also used for overpowering, as in His words: ﴿So God seized them for their sins﴾, and ﴿So He seized them with a mighty seizing﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 10]. The seizing of the earthquake means its destroying them and its encompassing them like the encompassing of one who seizes.

There is no doubt that God delivered Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him, as in the verse of Surah Hud. It has been reported that he went out with one hundred and ten believers. It is said that they settled in Ramlat Filastin (the sands of Palestine). It is also said that they moved away from the dwellings of their people to a place from which they could still see them. When the earthquake seized them and they perished, Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him returned and dwelt in their homes. It is also said that they settled in Mecca, and that Salih (peace be upon him) was buried there. This is far-fetched, as we have said concerning 'Ad. Among the genealogists there are those who say that the Thaqif are remnants of Thamud, that is, descendants of those among them who were saved from the punishment. The Qur'an does not mention that the line of Thamud was cut off, so it is possible that a remnant of them survived.

*Al-rajfa* is the trembling and shaking of the earth. It may come from heavenly events such as violent winds and thunderbolts, and it may come from earthly causes such as earthquakes. So *al-rajfa* is the name of the resulting state. In the Surah of Hud, it is called "*al-ṣayḥa*" (the cry), so we know that what struck Thamud was a thunderbolt or successive thunderbolts that shook their land and destroyed them, leaving them stunned. It is possible that an earthquake accompanied it.

*Al-dār* is the place that a people occupies. It is used in both singular and plural, depending on the perspective. For this reason, the verse of Surah Hud says: ﴿So they became prostrate in their homes﴾ [Hud: 67].

*Fa-aṣbaḥū* here means "they became."

*Al-jāthim* is one who lies face-down on his chest on the ground with his legs drawn in, as a hare crouches. Since this is a state of greater stillness and cessation from the agitation of the limbs, it is used in the verse as a metonymy (*kināya*) for the stillness of the body through death. It is also possible that the intended meaning is to liken the state in which they fell on their faces when they were struck to the state of the crouching one, to depict the horror of the appearance of their death. The meaning is that

[Page 228]

they became lifeless, dead bodies in the most hideous appearance of a dead person.

The *fa'* in His words "﴿So he turned away from them﴾" is conjunctive, coordinating with the clause "﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾." *Al-tawallī* is turning away in separation and anger, and it is used figuratively for not caring about something. Here it may be taken literally, so the meaning is that he left the dwellings of his people when he knew that the punishment had descended upon them. In that case the sequence refers to "﴿they hamstrung the she-camel﴾," because the apparent sequence of his turning away from them and addressing them is that it did not occur after the earthquake seized them and they became prostrate.

It may also be taken figuratively, by the context of the address too. That is: he turned away from gazing at the town after it was struck by the thunderbolt, or he turned away from grieving over them and occupied himself with the believers, as God Most High said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾.

According to the first interpretation, his words "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord…" are used as a reproach to them and a recording of their guilt. According to the second interpretation, they are used as an expression of grief or of disassociation from them. The address is then a lament, and so it does not imply that those addressed by the name are capable of hearing the address at that time, like the phrase "O regret!" in "O regret!"

His words "﴿I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you﴾" are explained in the same way as His words in the story of Noah (peace be upon him): ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I advise you﴾ [Al-A'raf: 62]. The *lām* in *la-qad* is the *lām* of oath, and its parallel was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿We certainly sent Noah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 59].

The contrastive *istidrāk* with *lākin* (but) arises from his words "﴿I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you﴾," because it is used to disclaim any negligence in addressing their disbelief, whether he said it in a way that they could hear or whether he said it to himself. That disclaimer removes any suspicion of negligence in conveying the message and giving advice, since the benefit of conveying and advising did not become apparent. So he made the contrastive statement with His words: ﴿But you do not love those who advise﴾, that is, you dislike those who advise, so you do not obey them in their advice. This is because one who loves someone obeys him. So by this he intended a metonymy (*kināya*) for their rejection of advice.

[Page 229]

The use of the present tense in His words "*lā tuḥibbūn*" (you do not love), if it refers to the time of their hearing his words, indicates renewal and repetition, meaning that this has continued to be your practice. Thus this would be the final treatment to lead them to renounce what they are in, if any remnant of willingness to renounce remained in them. If it refers to the time after they had finished listening, then the present tense recounts a past state, like it in His words: ﴿And God is the One who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9].
