The root meaning of *al-akhdh* is taking something with the hand. It is used figuratively for possessing a thing, through the relation of necessary connection. It is also used for overpowering, as in His words: ﴿So God seized them for their sins﴾, and ﴿So He seized them with a mighty seizing﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 10]. The seizing of the earthquake means its destroying them and its encompassing them like the encompassing of one who seizes.

There is no doubt that God delivered Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him, as in the verse of Surah Hud. It has been reported that he went out with one hundred and ten believers. It is said that they settled in Ramlat Filastin (the sands of Palestine). It is also said that they moved away from the dwellings of their people to a place from which they could still see them. When the earthquake seized them and they perished, Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him returned and dwelt in their homes. It is also said that they settled in Mecca, and that Salih (peace be upon him) was buried there. This is far-fetched, as we have said concerning 'Ad. Among the genealogists there are those who say that the Thaqif are remnants of Thamud, that is, descendants of those among them who were saved from the punishment. The Qur'an does not mention that the line of Thamud was cut off, so it is possible that a remnant of them survived.

*Al-rajfa* is the trembling and shaking of the earth. It may come from heavenly events such as violent winds and thunderbolts, and it may come from earthly causes such as earthquakes. So *al-rajfa* is the name of the resulting state. In the Surah of Hud, it is called "*al-ṣayḥa*" (the cry), so we know that what struck Thamud was a thunderbolt or successive thunderbolts that shook their land and destroyed them, leaving them stunned. It is possible that an earthquake accompanied it.

*Al-dār* is the place that a people occupies. It is used in both singular and plural, depending on the perspective. For this reason, the verse of Surah Hud says: ﴿So they became prostrate in their homes﴾ [Hud: 67].

*Fa-aṣbaḥū* here means "they became."

*Al-jāthim* is one who lies face-down on his chest on the ground with his legs drawn in, as a hare crouches. Since this is a state of greater stillness and cessation from the agitation of the limbs, it is used in the verse as a metonymy (*kināya*) for the stillness of the body through death. It is also possible that the intended meaning is to liken the state in which they fell on their faces when they were struck to the state of the crouching one, to depict the horror of the appearance of their death. The meaning is that

[Page 228]

they became lifeless, dead bodies in the most hideous appearance of a dead person.

The *fa'* in His words "﴿So he turned away from them﴾" is conjunctive, coordinating with the clause "﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾." *Al-tawallī* is turning away in separation and anger, and it is used figuratively for not caring about something. Here it may be taken literally, so the meaning is that he left the dwellings of his people when he knew that the punishment had descended upon them. In that case the sequence refers to "﴿they hamstrung the she-camel﴾," because the apparent sequence of his turning away from them and addressing them is that it did not occur after the earthquake seized them and they became prostrate.

It may also be taken figuratively, by the context of the address too. That is: he turned away from gazing at the town after it was struck by the thunderbolt, or he turned away from grieving over them and occupied himself with the believers, as God Most High said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾.

According to the first interpretation, his words "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord…" are used as a reproach to them and a recording of their guilt. According to the second interpretation, they are used as an expression of grief or of disassociation from them. The address is then a lament, and so it does not imply that those addressed by the name are capable of hearing the address at that time, like the phrase "O regret!" in "O regret!"

His words "﴿I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you﴾" are explained in the same way as His words in the story of Noah (peace be upon him): ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I advise you﴾ [Al-A'raf: 62]. The *lām* in *la-qad* is the *lām* of oath, and its parallel was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿We certainly sent Noah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 59].

The contrastive *istidrāk* with *lākin* (but) arises from his words "﴿I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you﴾," because it is used to disclaim any negligence in addressing their disbelief, whether he said it in a way that they could hear or whether he said it to himself. That disclaimer removes any suspicion of negligence in conveying the message and giving advice, since the benefit of conveying and advising did not become apparent. So he made the contrastive statement with His words: ﴿But you do not love those who advise﴾, that is, you dislike those who advise, so you do not obey them in their advice. This is because one who loves someone obeys him. So by this he intended a metonymy (*kināya*) for their rejection of advice.

[Page 229]

The use of the present tense in His words "*lā tuḥibbūn*" (you do not love), if it refers to the time of their hearing his words, indicates renewal and repetition, meaning that this has continued to be your practice. Thus this would be the final treatment to lead them to renounce what they are in, if any remnant of willingness to renounce remained in them. If it refers to the time after they had finished listening, then the present tense recounts a past state, like it in His words: ﴿And God is the One who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [Fatir: 9].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 77–79:**

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel and defied the command of their Lord, and said, "O Salih, bring us what you have been threatening us with, if you are indeed one of the messengers."﴾ ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes by morning.﴾

The *fa'* (then/so) here indicates immediate sequence, relating the words of those who were arrogant: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed﴾ [Al-A'raf: 76]. That is, they said this, and then they hamstrung the camel. Sequence (*ta'qib*) takes its meaning according to what it governs. When they said that, they had openly declared their denial and become firm in it, and they were unable to argue or reason. So they resolved to proceed to hurting and enraging Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed in him. As the start of their action, they determined to attack the she-camel

[Page 225]

which Salih (peace be upon him) had made for them, and established between himself and them as a sign of truce, for as long as they did not harm her. Their intention in destroying the she-camel was to remove the sign of Salih (peace be upon him), so that the number of believers in him would not increase. This is because seeing the sign of his prophethood unharmed among them stirs in the souls of many of them reflection on his truthfulness, and a sense of comfort from the silence of their elders and their acceptance of her grazing and drinking. Also, in their assault on her there was a declaration from them of their readiness to harm Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed in him afterward, and that they would show Salih (peace be upon him) that they deserved his threat when he said to them: ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾.

The pronoun in His words "*fa-'aqarū*" (so they hamstrung) refers to "those who were arrogant." The hamstringing is attributed to them all, although its actual doer was one of them, because it was done with the collusion and approval of all the elders. This is shown by the words of God Most High in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took [the sword] and hamstrung [her]﴾ [Al-Qamar: 29]. This is like the saying of al-Nabigha regarding the Banu Hunn:

*They killed the Ta'i by force in the open plain.*

But only one of them killed him.

It is mentioned in the reports that the one who undertook the she-camel was a man of their leaders named Qudar, with a *qāf* vowel, an unpointed *dāl* lightly pronounced, and a *rā'* at the end, the son of Salif. In the Hadith of al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in his sermon the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and said: "A mighty, wicked, and fierce man rose up for her among his tribe, like Abu Zam'a."

The root meaning of *al-'aqr* is a deep wound. Imru' al-Qays said:

*She says, when the saddle leaned with us together,*
*"You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!"*

That is, he wounded it by the saddle rubbing against its back from its leaning to one side. The term *al-'aqr* is also applied to cutting off a limb of an animal. From this comes the saying "he hamstrung a wild donkey," meaning he struck it with a spear

[Page 226]

and cut off a limb from it. They used to hamstring a camel intended for slaughter by cutting off one of its limbs, so that it could not flee at the time of slaughter. Therefore, *al-'aqr* was applied to slaughtering by way of metonymy (*kināya*). Imru' al-Qays said:

*And the day I slaughtered my mount for the maidens,*
*—and this verse is not like that.*

*Al-'utuww* is exceeding the limit in arrogance, and its transitive use is because it implies the meaning of turning away.

"The command of their Lord" is what He commanded them through the tongue of Salih (peace be upon him), namely his words: ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾. The prohibition is expressed as a command, because the aim of a prohibition against something is a command to do its opposite. For this reason, the scholars of legal theory (*usūl*) say that a prohibition against something necessarily entails a command to its opposite, by which the abstention from the forbidden thing is realized.

They meant by "what you threaten us with" the punishment with which he had threatened them in a general way. The relative pronoun was used to indicate that they feared nothing of what he might intend by his general threat. So the meaning is "what you threaten us with," and the verbal noun's source was taken from the root of promise (*wa'd*) rather than threat (*wa'īd*), because it is lighter.

They presumed his being a messenger with the particle *in* (if), which indicates doubt about the realization of the condition. That is: "if you are among the messengers from God." By "the messengers" is meant those to whom this title truly applies. Because of their ignorance of the reality of God's actions and His wisdom, they supposed that God's dealings are like the dealings of creatures: when He sends a messenger and the people to whom he is sent do not believe him, God becomes angry and proceeds to send punishment upon them. They do not know that God gives respite to the wrongdoers and then seizes them whenever He wills.

The clause "*fa-akhadhathumu al-rajfa*" (so the earthquake seized them) is a parenthetical clause placed between the clause "﴿so they hamstrung the she-camel﴾" and the clause "*fa-tawallā 'anhum*" (so he turned away from them). Its purpose in being parenthetical is to hasten the report that the threat was carried out against them immediately after their arrogance. Thus the sequence is customary (*'urfī*), meaning there was no long time between the hamstringing and the earthquake. There were three days between them, as is mentioned in the verse of Surah Hud:

[Page 227]

﴿So they hamstrung her, and he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾ [Hud: 65].

[Page 230]

Wa-Lūṭan (And Lot) is coordinated with Nūḥan in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 59]. The implied construction is: "And We sent Lot." The change in style at the beginning of the story of Lot and his people, in that it begins with mention of Lot just as the story of Noah began with mention of Noah, is because the people of Lot had no name by which they were known, just as the people of Noah had no name by which they were known. The word (idh, "when") is an adverbial clause connected to the implied verb "We sent," meaning: "We sent him at the time he said to his people." The time of speaking is made the adverbial time of the sending in order to convey his promptness in calling his people to what Allah sent him with. The togetherness that the adverbial sense requires between the time of the sending and the time of his speech is a customary togetherness, meaning extreme closeness, to the greatest extent possible in hastening the delivery of the message.

The people of Lot were a mixture of the Canaanites and of those who had settled around them. For this reason he is not described as their brother, since he was not from their tribes; rather, he settled among them and made his home in their lands. Lot, peace be upon him, was the son of the brother of Abraham, peace be upon him, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am, and Lot, peace be upon him, had settled in the land of Sodom, and there was no kinship between him and them.

[Page 230 continued]

The people to whom Lot, peace be upon him, was sent were the inhabitants of the town of Sodom (Sadum) and Gomorrah ('Amura) in the land of Canaan. It may sometimes be that the name Sodom and Gomorrah is applied to their inhabitants. They were the ancestors of the Phoenicians. The two towns were on the shore of the Sedim, which is the Sea of Salt, as occurs in the Torah, and it is the Dead Sea, called the Lake of Lot, near Jerusalem. Near Sodom and those with them, they had introduced the abomination of men taking pleasure with men. When Lot, peace be upon him, came down to their town of Sodom on his journey with his uncle Abraham, peace be upon him, Allah commanded him to forbid them and to be stern with them.

The interrogative in (Do you approach) is one of denial and rebuke. The "approaching" about which the question is asked is a metaphor for engaging in and doing, meaning: "Do you commit the abomination?" The word "approaching" was used as a euphemism for this particular act, and this is a well-known euphemism.

The word (fāḥisha, abomination) means a base and blameworthy deed. Its meaning was discussed earlier, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And when they committed an abomination﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]. Here the intended meaning is a well-known abomination, so the definite article is for a previously known reference.

The clause ﴿What no one in the worlds has preceded you in﴾ is a new, independent sentence, begun afresh. After He had denied them the committing of the abomination, and had expressed it as an abomination, He rebuked them for having invented it, for it was not known among mankind. They had established an evil precedent for those who commit such abominations.

It is also permissible for the clause ﴿What no one has preceded you in﴾ to be a qualifying description of the abomination, and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "you approach," or to "the abomination."

The original meaning of (sabq) is the arrival of a walker at a desired place before others arrive. It is used metaphorically for precedence in time, meaning priority and initiation, and this is the intended meaning here. The purpose is that they preceded people in this abomination, since such a construction does not intend that they began at the same time together with others.

The preposition (bi-) is for the transitivity of the verb (sabaqa), as it is used in the sense of "began." So the bi- serves to reinforce the sense of precedence. (min, "from/of") before (aḥad, "anyone") is for emphasizing the negation, to indicate the sense of comprehensiveness in the negation. The (min) before (al-ʿālamīn, "the worlds") is partitive.

[Page 231]

The clause ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ explains the clause ("Do you approach the abomination"). The emphasis by (inna, "indeed") and the (lām) is a metonymy for rebuke, because it is based on treating them as one who denies that, since they persist in it without listening to the one who forbids it.

The word "approaching" is a metonymy for doing the abomination.

Nāfiʿ, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Abū Jaʿfar read (innakum, "indeed you") with a single kasra-pointed hamza in declarative form. Then the explanation refers back to the denied matter, with the hamza of denial in (Do you approach the abomination), and by this the explanation of the denial is known. It is also permissible to consider it a declarative statement used for rebuke, and it is permissible to posit an interrogative hamza that was dropped for lightness and because of what precedes it. The rest of the readers read (a-innakum, "is it that you") with two hamzas in the interrogative form, so the explanation is for the denial, and by this the explanation of what is denied is known. The two readings are equally valid.

Al-shahwa (desire) is the longing to obtain something desired. It is the verbal noun of shahiya, like riḍiya, and it came in the pattern fa'la, but it is not intended to mean a single instance.

(shahwatan, "out of desire") is in the accusative as an object of purpose. The purpose of this object is to make the abomination and its doers appear abhorrent, in that they desire what is truly worthy of being hated and regarded as shameful.

His saying ﴿besides women﴾ is an added intensification of the abhorrence and a cutting off of any excuse for committing this abomination. It is not a restriction of the denial. The approach to men is not less abhorrent than the approach to women together with it. Rather, the intended meaning is that the approach to men as a whole occurs in a situation where the approach to women is the right one, as He said in another verse: ﴿And you leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 166].

(bal, "rather") is for a transitional turning (iḍrāb intiqālī), to move from the purpose of denial to the purpose of blame, belittling, and alerting them to the reality of their condition.

[Page 232]

Al-isrāf (excess) is the act going beyond the measure of its like in its kind, meaning: those who exceed in falsehood and crime. Its meaning was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And do not eat them excessively﴾ [al-Nisa': 6] in Surat al-Nisa', and in His saying ﴿And do not be excessive; indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾ [al-An'am: 141] in Surat al-An'am.

He described them as excessive by way of the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence, meaning: "You are a people in whom excess in desires has become firmly established, which is why they desired a strange desire when they were weary of the familiar desires." This is the nature of persistence in desires until a person's desire is no longer satisfied by anything. A similar statement is His saying about them in another verse: ﴿Rather, you are a transgressing people﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 166].

The reason this vile act is called an abomination and excess is that it includes many corruptions. Among them: using the animal desire implanted in humans for other than what it was implanted for, since Allah created in man the animal desire for the purpose of preserving the species through the law of procreation, so that the impulse toward it is compelling and man is driven toward it by his nature. Satisfying that desire for other than the purpose for which Allah placed it is an aggression against the natural disposition (fiṭra) and against the species. It also changes the specific nature of masculinity in relation to the one acted upon, since he comes to be in a position other than the one Allah set for him by his creation. It is also a pure humiliation of the one acted upon, since he is made an instrument for satisfying the desire of another, contrary to what Allah established in the order of maleness and femaleness, namely the satisfaction of both desires together. It also leads to the cutting off or reduction of offspring. And that act brings harms to both the doer and the one acted upon, through using two organs for other than what they were created for.

This abomination occurred among the Muslims in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, regarding a man called al-Fujaʾa. Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote about him to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that he had done the deed of the people of Lot. Since no definite punishment for it had been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr gathered the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and consulted them about it. ʿAlī said: "I think he should be burned with fire." The opinion of the companions agreed on this, so Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid that he should burn him, and he burned him. Likewise, Ibn al-Zubayr ruled

[Page 233]

concerning a group who committed the abomination in his time, and Hisham ibn al-Walid, and Khalid al-Qasri in Iraq. Perhaps this was an analogy to the fact that Allah rained fire upon them, as will come later.

Malik said: the doer and the one acted upon are stoned, since the doer is obeyed and both are adults, as the adulterer who is married (muḥṣan) is stoned, whether or not they were married. He analogized their punishment to the punishment Allah inflicted on the people of Lot when He rained stones upon them. What is understood from the school of Malik is that it is permissible to analogize to what Allah the Exalted did in this world. It is narrated that in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr four men who had done the deed of the people of Lot, and who were married, were taken. He ordered them to be taken out of the sacred precinct (Ḥaram) and they were stoned with stones until they died. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas were with him and did not object to it.

Abu Hanifa said: the doer is disciplined by discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), and the discretionary punishment does not reach the level of the prescribed punishment for fornication (ḥadd al-zinā). Al-Qurtubi attributed this to him. What is found in the books of the Hanafis is that Abu Hanifa holds that it is subject to discretionary punishment, unless it is repeated by him, in which case he is put to death. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: the prescribed punishment for fornication applies to it. When someone habitually does this, the discretionary punishment is by burning, or by having a wall demolished upon him, or by being thrown down from a high place and pelted with stones, or by being imprisoned until he dies or repents. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned in al-Hawi that the more sound position from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad is discretionary punishment by flogging, that is, without distinguishing between habitual practice and other cases. The context of their statements is equality in punishment between the doer and the one acted upon.

Al-Shafiʿi said: the doer is subject to the prescribed punishment for the adulterer. If he is married, then the punishment for the married applies; if he is not married, then the punishment for the unmarried applies. Al-Qurtubi related this in this way. Ibn Hubayra al-Hanbali said, in the book Ikhtilaf al-A'imma (Differences of the Imams), that al-Shafiʿi has two opinions: one of them is this, and the other is that he is stoned in every case. He did not mention a preference for either. Al-Ghazali said, in al-Wajiz: "Sodomy (liwāṭ) requires the killing of the doer and the one acted upon according to one opinion, stoning in every case according to one opinion, discretionary punishment according to one opinion, and it is like fornication according to one opinion." This statement is not precise.

In Ibn Hubayra al-Hanbali's book Ikhtilaf al-A'imma: the more apparent of the two narrations from Ahmad is that in sodomy there is stoning in every case, meaning whether married or unmarried. In another narration from him, it is like fornication. Ibn Hazm said, in al-Muhalla, that the position of Dawud

[Page 234]

and all his followers is that the practitioner of sodomy is flogged without the prescribed punishment. It has not been explicitly stated, in what they transmitted from Abu Hanifa and his two companions, nor from Ahmad, nor from al-Shafi'i, that the doer and the one acted upon are equal in the ruling, except according to Malik. What is understood from Ibn Hazm's account in al-Muhalla is that the adherents of the various schools differing about the discretionary punishment for this abomination did not distinguish between the doer and the one acted upon, except for an isolated opinion of one of the jurists of the Shafi'is, who held that the one acted upon receives a more severe punishment than the doer.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra, and he said regarding its chain of transmission that there is some objection, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill the doer and the one acted upon." It is a strange hadith, not transmitted except from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas. You know that Abu Bakr consulted about this crime, and if there had been a sound chain for it, it would have become evident on that day.

[Page 230]

Wa-Lūṭan (And Lot) is coordinated with Nūḥan in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 59]. The implied construction is: "And We sent Lot." The change in style at the beginning of the story of Lot and his people, in that it begins with mention of Lot just as the story of Noah began with mention of Noah, is because the people of Lot had no name by which they were known, just as the people of Noah had no name by which they were known. The word (idh, "when") is an adverbial clause connected to the implied verb "We sent," meaning: "We sent him at the time he said to his people." The time of speaking is made the adverbial time of the sending in order to convey his promptness in calling his people to what Allah sent him with. The togetherness that the adverbial sense requires between the time of the sending and the time of his speech is a customary togetherness, meaning extreme closeness, to the greatest extent possible in hastening the delivery of the message.

The people of Lot were a mixture of the Canaanites and of those who had settled around them. For this reason he is not described as their brother, since he was not from their tribes; rather, he settled among them and made his home in their lands. Lot, peace be upon him, was the son of the brother of Abraham, peace be upon him, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am, and Lot, peace be upon him, had settled in the land of Sodom, and there was no kinship between him and them.

[Page 230 continued]

The people to whom Lot, peace be upon him, was sent were the inhabitants of the town of Sodom (Sadum) and Gomorrah ('Amura) in the land of Canaan. It may sometimes be that the name Sodom and Gomorrah is applied to their inhabitants. They were the ancestors of the Phoenicians. The two towns were on the shore of the Sedim, which is the Sea of Salt, as occurs in the Torah, and it is the Dead Sea, called the Lake of Lot, near Jerusalem. Near Sodom and those with them, they had introduced the abomination of men taking pleasure with men. When Lot, peace be upon him, came down to their town of Sodom on his journey with his uncle Abraham, peace be upon him, Allah commanded him to forbid them and to be stern with them.

The interrogative in (Do you approach) is one of denial and rebuke. The "approaching" about which the question is asked is a metaphor for engaging in and doing, meaning: "Do you commit the abomination?" The word "approaching" was used as a euphemism for this particular act, and this is a well-known euphemism.

The word (fāḥisha, abomination) means a base and blameworthy deed. Its meaning was discussed earlier, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿And when they committed an abomination﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]. Here the intended meaning is a well-known abomination, so the definite article is for a previously known reference.

The clause ﴿What no one in the worlds has preceded you in﴾ is a new, independent sentence, begun afresh. After He had denied them the committing of the abomination, and had expressed it as an abomination, He rebuked them for having invented it, for it was not known among mankind. They had established an evil precedent for those who commit such abominations.

It is also permissible for the clause ﴿What no one has preceded you in﴾ to be a qualifying description of the abomination, and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "you approach," or to "the abomination."

The original meaning of (sabq) is the arrival of a walker at a desired place before others arrive. It is used metaphorically for precedence in time, meaning priority and initiation, and this is the intended meaning here. The purpose is that they preceded people in this abomination, since such a construction does not intend that they began at the same time together with others.

The preposition (bi-) is for the transitivity of the verb (sabaqa), as it is used in the sense of "began." So the bi- serves to reinforce the sense of precedence. (min, "from/of") before (aḥad, "anyone") is for emphasizing the negation, to indicate the sense of comprehensiveness in the negation. The (min) before (al-ʿālamīn, "the worlds") is partitive.

[Page 231]

The clause ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ explains the clause ("Do you approach the abomination"). The emphasis by (inna, "indeed") and the (lām) is a metonymy for rebuke, because it is based on treating them as one who denies that, since they persist in it without listening to the one who forbids it.

The word "approaching" is a metonymy for doing the abomination.

Nāfiʿ, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Abū Jaʿfar read (innakum, "indeed you") with a single kasra-pointed hamza in declarative form. Then the explanation refers back to the denied matter, with the hamza of denial in (Do you approach the abomination), and by this the explanation of the denial is known. It is also permissible to consider it a declarative statement used for rebuke, and it is permissible to posit an interrogative hamza that was dropped for lightness and because of what precedes it. The rest of the readers read (a-innakum, "is it that you") with two hamzas in the interrogative form, so the explanation is for the denial, and by this the explanation of what is denied is known. The two readings are equally valid.

Al-shahwa (desire) is the longing to obtain something desired. It is the verbal noun of shahiya, like riḍiya, and it came in the pattern fa'la, but it is not intended to mean a single instance.

(shahwatan, "out of desire") is in the accusative as an object of purpose. The purpose of this object is to make the abomination and its doers appear abhorrent, in that they desire what is truly worthy of being hated and regarded as shameful.

His saying ﴿besides women﴾ is an added intensification of the abhorrence and a cutting off of any excuse for committing this abomination. It is not a restriction of the denial. The approach to men is not less abhorrent than the approach to women together with it. Rather, the intended meaning is that the approach to men as a whole occurs in a situation where the approach to women is the right one, as He said in another verse: ﴿And you leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 166].

(bal, "rather") is for a transitional turning (iḍrāb intiqālī), to move from the purpose of denial to the purpose of blame, belittling, and alerting them to the reality of their condition.

[Page 232]

Al-isrāf (excess) is the act going beyond the measure of its like in its kind, meaning: those who exceed in falsehood and crime. Its meaning was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And do not eat them excessively﴾ [al-Nisa': 6] in Surat al-Nisa', and in His saying ﴿And do not be excessive; indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾ [al-An'am: 141] in Surat al-An'am.

He described them as excessive by way of the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence, meaning: "You are a people in whom excess in desires has become firmly established, which is why they desired a strange desire when they were weary of the familiar desires." This is the nature of persistence in desires until a person's desire is no longer satisfied by anything. A similar statement is His saying about them in another verse: ﴿Rather, you are a transgressing people﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 166].

The reason this vile act is called an abomination and excess is that it includes many corruptions. Among them: using the animal desire implanted in humans for other than what it was implanted for, since Allah created in man the animal desire for the purpose of preserving the species through the law of procreation, so that the impulse toward it is compelling and man is driven toward it by his nature. Satisfying that desire for other than the purpose for which Allah placed it is an aggression against the natural disposition (fiṭra) and against the species. It also changes the specific nature of masculinity in relation to the one acted upon, since he comes to be in a position other than the one Allah set for him by his creation. It is also a pure humiliation of the one acted upon, since he is made an instrument for satisfying the desire of another, contrary to what Allah established in the order of maleness and femaleness, namely the satisfaction of both desires together. It also leads to the cutting off or reduction of offspring. And that act brings harms to both the doer and the one acted upon, through using two organs for other than what they were created for.

This abomination occurred among the Muslims in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, regarding a man called al-Fujaʾa. Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote about him to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that he had done the deed of the people of Lot. Since no definite punishment for it had been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr gathered the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and consulted them about it. ʿAlī said: "I think he should be burned with fire." The opinion of the companions agreed on this, so Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid that he should burn him, and he burned him. Likewise, Ibn al-Zubayr ruled

[Page 233]

concerning a group who committed the abomination in his time, and Hisham ibn al-Walid, and Khalid al-Qasri in Iraq. Perhaps this was an analogy to the fact that Allah rained fire upon them, as will come later.

Malik said: the doer and the one acted upon are stoned, since the doer is obeyed and both are adults, as the adulterer who is married (muḥṣan) is stoned, whether or not they were married. He analogized their punishment to the punishment Allah inflicted on the people of Lot when He rained stones upon them. What is understood from the school of Malik is that it is permissible to analogize to what Allah the Exalted did in this world. It is narrated that in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr four men who had done the deed of the people of Lot, and who were married, were taken. He ordered them to be taken out of the sacred precinct (Ḥaram) and they were stoned with stones until they died. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas were with him and did not object to it.

Abu Hanifa said: the doer is disciplined by discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), and the discretionary punishment does not reach the level of the prescribed punishment for fornication (ḥadd al-zinā). Al-Qurtubi attributed this to him. What is found in the books of the Hanafis is that Abu Hanifa holds that it is subject to discretionary punishment, unless it is repeated by him, in which case he is put to death. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: the prescribed punishment for fornication applies to it. When someone habitually does this, the discretionary punishment is by burning, or by having a wall demolished upon him, or by being thrown down from a high place and pelted with stones, or by being imprisoned until he dies or repents. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned in al-Hawi that the more sound position from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad is discretionary punishment by flogging, that is, without distinguishing between habitual practice and other cases. The context of their statements is equality in punishment between the doer and the one acted upon.

Al-Shafiʿi said: the doer is subject to the prescribed punishment for the adulterer. If he is married, then the punishment for the married applies; if he is not married, then the punishment for the unmarried applies. Al-Qurtubi related this in this way. Ibn Hubayra al-Hanbali said, in the book Ikhtilaf al-A'imma (Differences of the Imams), that al-Shafiʿi has two opinions: one of them is this, and the other is that he is stoned in every case. He did not mention a preference for either. Al-Ghazali said, in al-Wajiz: "Sodomy (liwāṭ) requires the killing of the doer and the one acted upon according to one opinion, stoning in every case according to one opinion, discretionary punishment according to one opinion, and it is like fornication according to one opinion." This statement is not precise.

In Ibn Hubayra al-Hanbali's book Ikhtilaf al-A'imma: the more apparent of the two narrations from Ahmad is that in sodomy there is stoning in every case, meaning whether married or unmarried. In another narration from him, it is like fornication. Ibn Hazm said, in al-Muhalla, that the position of Dawud

[Page 234]

and all his followers is that the practitioner of sodomy is flogged without the prescribed punishment. It has not been explicitly stated, in what they transmitted from Abu Hanifa and his two companions, nor from Ahmad, nor from al-Shafi'i, that the doer and the one acted upon are equal in the ruling, except according to Malik. What is understood from Ibn Hazm's account in al-Muhalla is that the adherents of the various schools differing about the discretionary punishment for this abomination did not distinguish between the doer and the one acted upon, except for an isolated opinion of one of the jurists of the Shafi'is, who held that the one acted upon receives a more severe punishment than the doer.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra, and he said regarding its chain of transmission that there is some objection, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill the doer and the one acted upon." It is a strange hadith, not transmitted except from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas. You know that Abu Bakr consulted about this crime, and if there had been a sound chain for it, it would have become evident on that day.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 82:

﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ The clause "And the answer of his people was" is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the clause "He said to his people." The implied construction is: "And when the answer of his people was only that they said..." etc. The meaning is that they were left unable to counter the abomination they had been reproached for, nor to argue about it; so they hastened to conspire to expel Lot, peace be upon him, and his family from the town. Lot, peace be upon him, was a stranger among them, and they wished to be relieved of his denunciation of them. This is the attitude of those who sense the corruption of their own condition, who are prevented by their desires from giving up their misdeeds, and who are determined to persist in their sins: their hearts become too constricted to bear admonition, their ears are deafened to accepting it, and it has always been the way of those immersed in desire to frown upon the arrival of one who does not share their state.

The answer (al-jawab): the speech that is met with another speech, whether as confirmation, as rebuttal, or as recompense.

The word "jawab" is in the accusative as the predicate (khabar) of "kana" placed before its subject, which follows the particle of exception in the emptied (mufarragh) construction. This is the eloquent usage in such a structure when one of the two objects of "kana" is a verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb, as was mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran and Surat al-An'am. For this reason the well-known readings agree on putting the first object in the accusative.

The object pronoun in His saying "expel them" refers to a omitted antecedent known from the context, namely Lot, peace be upon him, and his family: his wife and his two daughters.

The clause ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾ is the reason (ʿilla) for the command to expel. This is the function of "inna" when it comes in a context where there is no doubt or denial, but rather for mere emphasis; it conveys the force of the connective fa' (of consequence) and indicates linkage and causation.

Al-tatahhur means to make an effort at purity (takalluf al-taharah). Its real meaning is cleanliness, and "tahara" is used metaphorically for purifying the soul and guarding against vices, which is what is intended here. This is a quality of perfection. But when the people had rebelled against wickedness, they regarded perfection as repugnant to their natures, so they could not bear to associate with the people of perfection, and they disparaged the perfections they saw in them, calling them a burden. Therefore they described Lot's aloofness and that of his household as "purification," using the form of effort and affectation. It may also be that this is a quotation of their mockery of Lot and his family. This is a reversal of realities in order to support blameworthy customs; people of debauchery and licentiousness call one who abstains from their conduct a penitent or something similar. So their saying "Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure" was intended as a reproach.

They knew this purity from the character of Lot, peace be upon him, and his family, because they had lived among them and seen their conduct. For this reason the report is expressed as a verbal sentence in the present tense, indicating that the purity is repeated and renewed among them, and that is more effective in highlighting the clash with their natures

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 83–84:

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿And We rained upon them a rain [of stones]. So see how was the end of the criminals.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: "So We saved him" (fa-anjaynahu) is a consequence (ta'qib) of the clause "and the answer of his people was not but..." or of the clause "He said to his people." This sequence indicates that Lut, peace be upon him, was sent to his people a short time before the punishment descended upon them.

"Fa-anjaynahu" is placed before its object in a transposed order (taqdim min ta'khir). The intended sense is: "We rained upon them a rain, and We saved him and his family." The report of Lut's deliverance, peace be upon him, is placed before the report of their being rained upon with the rain of punishment, in order to show concern for the matter of Lut's deliverance, peace be upon him, and to quickly bring joy to the believing listeners, so that their hearts may be reassured regarding the good outcome of their predecessors among the believers of the past nations, and so that they may know that this is the custom of God toward His servants. The explanation of this has already preceded at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ark﴾ [al-A'raf: 64] in this surah.

The family of Lut, peace be upon him, were his wife and his two unmarried daughters. He had two married daughters, as is mentioned in the Torah, whose husbands refused to leave with Lut, peace be upon him, so both perished along with the people of the town.

As for the wife of Lut, peace be upon him, God informs here that God did not save her; so she perished with the people of Lut. In Surah Hud there is mention of what apparently indicates that she did not comply with God's command to Lut, peace be upon him, that neither he nor any of his family who went out with him should look back at the towns when the punishment strikes them; so his wife looked back and the punishment struck her. In Surah al-Tahrim it is mentioned that the wife of Lut, peace be upon him, was a disbeliever. The exegetes said: she would conceal disbelief and display faith. Perhaps this is the reason for her looking back, because she was not certain of the descent of the punishment upon the people of Lut. It is also possible that she did not go out with Lut, peace be upon him, and that His saying in Surah Hud, "except your wife," is an exception from "your family" and not from "anyone" (ahad). Perhaps the wife of Lut, peace be upon him, was from the people of Sodom, whom Lut, peace be upon him, married there after his migration, for he remained in Sodom many years after the death of the mother of his daughters and before he was sent as a messenger. She was not the mother of his two daughters, for the Torah does not mention the wife of Lut, peace be upon him, except at the end of the story.

The meaning of "among those who remained behind" (min al-ghabirin) is "among those who perished." The word al-ghabir is applied to what has passed away and also to what is yet to come, so it is among the words with opposite meanings (asma' al-adad). The more common usage is "what has passed away," and for this reason it is said "ghabara" meaning "perished." This is the intended sense here: she was among those who perished, that is, she perished along with those of the people of Sodom who perished.

The word al-imtar is derived from al-matar (rain), and al-matar is the name for water descending from the clouds. It is said "matarathum al-sama'" (without a hamza), meaning "the rain fell upon them," just as it is said "ghathathum" and "wabalathum." It is said "makan mamtur," meaning it was struck by rain, but one does not say "mumtir." It is also said "umtiru" (with a hamza), meaning there descended upon them from the air something resembling rain, which is not in fact rain; so one does not say "hum mumtirun," but one says "hum mumtarun," as God said: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74], and He said ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. Thus al-Zamakhshari said here, and in Surah al-Anfal he said: the use of "al-imtar" in the sense of punishment has become common. And on the authority of Abu 'Ubayda, the distinction between "matara" and "amtara" is that "matara" is for mercy and "amtara" is for punishment. As for His saying in Surah al-Ahqaf: ﴿They said: this is a cloud bringing rain to us﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], it runs counter to both distinctions and shows that the distinction is merely predominant.

What struck the people of Lut was stones and brimstone from the upper parts of the towns, as is in the Torah, and smoke would appear from the earth like the smoke of a furnace. Some researchers have supposed that the pits of bitumen mentioned in the Torah were in the depths of the plain, and were liable to ignite because of earthquakes or the striking of lightning upon them. In another verse of the Qur'an it is mentioned that God made the high part of those towns low, and that is the sinking of the earth, which is among the effects of earthquakes. It is quite plausible that the Dead Sea over there has overwhelmed these pits or volcanoes as a result of the earthquake.

The indefinite "mataran" is for magnification and amazement, meaning: a wondrous rain, of a kind that would destroy towns.

From this marvellous narrative follows the command to consider their end, in His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the criminals.﴾ The command is for guidance and reflection. The address may be to an unspecified person, indeed to everyone capable of drawing a lesson, as is the nature of appending a lesson-drawing conclusion after an admonition, since the intended addressees of the address are everyone who is intended by the admonition. It may also be that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, as consolation for what he meets from his people who denied him, that he should not despair of God's help, and that it is the way of messengers to await the outcomes.

"The criminals" (al-mujrimun) are the doers of crime (jarima), which is disobedience and evil. This clearly shows that God punished them with that punishment for this vile deed, and that Lut, peace be upon him, was sent to them to forbid them from it, not because they were polytheists, since nothing is mentioned about this in the Qur'an, unlike what is related about the other nations. Yet their collusion in committing the vile deed and their considering it lawful indicate that they were not believers in God. This is indicated by His saying, the Exalted, in Surah al-Tahrim: ﴿God strikes an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lut﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. Thus the sending of Lut, peace be upon him, was to denounce that vile deed at the outset, purifying their souls, and then to describe to them faith, for there is no doubt that Lut, peace be upon him, conveyed the message from God, the Exalted, and that includes that he called them to faith; however, his first concern was to abolish this vile deed, and for this reason his denunciation of them and his disputes with them were limited to matters concerning that vile deed. It is known that God struck them with punishment as a retribution for that vile deed, as He said in Surah al-Ankabut: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon the people of this town a plague from the sky because they have been defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ankabut: 34], and that if they had desisted from it, their punishment for disbelief would have been deferred to another day, or to the Last Day.

In another verse of the Qur'an it is mentioned that God made the high part of those towns low, and that is the sinking of the earth, which is among the effects of earthquakes. It is quite plausible that the Dead Sea over there has overwhelmed these pits or volcanoes as a result of the earthquake.

The indefinite "mataran" is for magnification and amazement, meaning: a wondrous rain, of a kind that would destroy towns.

From this marvellous narrative follows the command to consider their end, in His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the criminals.﴾ The command is for guidance and reflection. The address may be to an unspecified person, indeed to everyone capable of drawing a lesson, as is the nature of appending a lesson-drawing conclusion after an admonition, since the intended addressees of the address are everyone who is intended by the admonition. It may also be that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, as consolation for what he meets from his people who denied him, that he should not despair of God's help, and that it is the way of messengers to await the outcomes.

"The criminals" (al-mujrimun) are the doers of crime (jarima), which is disobedience and evil. This clearly shows that God punished them with that punishment for this vile deed, and that Lut, peace be upon him, was sent to them to forbid them from it, not because they were polytheists, since nothing is mentioned about this in the Qur'an, unlike what is related about the other nations. Yet their collusion in committing the vile deed and their considering it lawful indicate that they were not believers in God. This is indicated by His saying, the Exalted, in Surah al-Tahrim: ﴿God strikes an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lut﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. Thus the sending of Lut, peace be upon him, was to denounce that vile deed at the outset, purifying their souls, and then to describe to them faith, for there is no doubt that Lut, peace be upon him, conveyed the message from God, the Exalted, and that includes that he called them to faith; however, his first concern was to abolish this vile deed, and for this reason his denunciation of them and his disputes with them were limited to matters concerning that vile deed. It is known that God struck them with punishment as a retribution for that vile deed, as He said in Surah al-Ankabut: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon the people of this town a plague from the sky because they have been defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ankabut: 34], and that if they had desisted from it, their punishment for disbelief would have been deferred to another day, or to the Last Day.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 85–87 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord, so give full measure and weight, and do not deprive the people of their due, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation. That is better for you, if you are believers.﴾ ﴿And do not sit on every path, threatening and turning away from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He multiplied you. And observe how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent, and a group who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾

The explanation of the beginning of this verse is like the explanation of its counterpart in the story of Thamud, except that the omission of the conjunction "fa" (then) before the verb "qala ya qawmi" (he said, "O my people") here most likely indicates that this statement was not the one with which he first opened his mission, but rather something he addressed to them after he had called them many times, and after those among them who believed had believed, as will come.

Madyan is a nation named after its forefather Madyan ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil ('alayhi al-salam), from his third wife whom he married at the end of his life, a concubine whose name was Qatura. Madyan married a daughter of Lut ('alayhi al-salam), and he had sons: 'Ayfa, 'Afar, Hanuk, Abyda'a, and Ald'a. Ibrahim ('alayhi al-salam) settled them in their homeland midway between the dwelling of his son Isma'il ('alayhi al-salam) and the dwelling of his son Ishaq ('alayhi al-salam). From their descendants the clans of Madyan branched out, and they numbered about twenty-five thousand. Their dwellings were between the Hijaz and the Gulf of 'Aqaba near the coast of the Red Sea. The capital of their land was Wajj on the Red Sea, and their land extended from the north to the borders of Ma'an in the lands of Sham, and to about Tabuk in the Hijaz. Their territory is called al-Aykah. It is said that al-Aykah is Tabuk, and on this view it is among the lands of Madyan. Their lands were villages and desert settlements, and Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam) was from the village, which is al-Aykah. They had become Arabized through neighboring the Arab nations, and during the time of Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam) they were under the kings of Egypt. Through their neighboring and mingling with Arab tribes, and because they were on the route to Egypt, they acquired an Arab character, and they came to be counted among the Arabized Arabs, like the sons of Isma'il ('alayhi al-salam). A poet in the pre-Islamic era known as Abu al-Hamaysa' was one of the poets of Madyan, and he is the one who said:
"If you withhold your flow, the flow of tears
runs down the cheek like the trickle of the thethe'..."
(The verses are given in the original as they stand.)
It is also said that the Arabic script first appeared in Madyan.

Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam) was a messenger to the people of Madyan, and he was one of themselves. His name in Arabic is Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam), and his name in the Torah is "Yathrun," and he is also called "Ra'wa'il." He was the son of "Nuwayla or Nuwayb ibn Ra'wil ibn 'Ayfa ibn Madyan." When Musa ('alayhi al-salam) left Egypt, he came to the land of Madyan, and Shu'ayb married him to his daughter named Safura, and Musa ('alayhi al-salam) remained with him for ten years as a hired worker.

A great number of exegetes and historians have confused the genealogy of Madyan and the genealogy of Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam), so whatever you find that contradicts this, reject it. Al-Safadi counted Shu'ayb among the blind, but I have not found this in the reliable books. He began the call with faith because in it lies the soundness of belief and of the heart, and the removal of falsehood from the intellect.

As for Shu'ayb's "clear evidence" (bayyina) mentioned in his words, it is possible that it refers to a sign he showed his people, which they recognized, and which the Qur'an did not mention, as the exegetes said. But the more evident view to me is that the "clear evidence" means a proof he established demonstrating the falsehood of their polytheism and their evil conduct, and they were unable to refute him on it, so the proof was established against them, similar to the debate recounted in Surat Hud. Thus "bayyina" is applied to what demonstrates the truth of the claim, not only to an extraordinary sign. Or he may have meant by "clear evidence" what he pointed to in his words: "so be patient until Allah judges between us," meaning he warned them of a punishment that would befall them if they did not believe, as he said in the other verse: "So drop upon us fragments of the sky if you are among the truthful" [al-Shu'ara': 187]. In that case the past tense in his words "there has certainly come to you" is meant to denote the near future, to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence. Or he may have offered them that he would show them a sign, that is a miracle, so that they would believe, but they did not ask for it and hastened to denial. The meaning would then be like what Allah related about Musa ('alayhi al-salam): "I have certainly come to you with clear evidence from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel" [al-A'raf: 105], "He said: If you have come with a sign, then bring it" [al-A'raf: 106] and so on. The meaning of "there has certainly come to you" would then be: it has been prepared to come to you if you believe when it comes.

The "fa" in his words "So give full measure and weight" is for consequence based on the meaning contained in "clear evidence," since the evidence points to his truthfulness. When the proof of his truthfulness was established, and he had commanded them with monotheism first, because it contains the soundness of the heart, he began to command them with the legal duties of actions after faith, as his later words indicate: "if you are believers." That is a call to those among his people who believed to complete their faith by adhering to the practical laws, and an announcement to those who did not believe of what is incumbent upon them after faith in Allah alone. In Shu'ayb's call to his people to practical actions after the call to monotheism was firmly established, there is an indication that human souls in that era had developed to a degree that prepared them to accept practical laws. Shu'ayb's call was broader than the calls of the messengers before him, Hud and Salih ('alayhima al-salam), since it included the legislation of practical rulings. The era of Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam) had come close to the era of Musa ('alayhi al-salam), who brought a great law touching all aspects of life.

The word "bakhs" (depriving, diminishing): they explained it as diminishing. Al-Raghib in al-Mufradat added a qualification, saying: "diminishing something in a manner of injustice." The best explanation I have seen is the statement of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in Ahkam al-Qur'an: "Bakhs in the language of the Arabs is diminishing by making something defective or undervaluing it, or deceiving about its value, or scheming to increase the measure or reduce it." Let us build on the basis of his words and say: bakhs is diminishing something of a quality or quantity that is deserving of completeness in its kind. So it includes the meaning of injustice and trickery. Ibn Sidah in al-Mukhassas mentioned bakhs under the heading of taking away a person's right, but in mentioning it he fell into what other lexicographers fell into. Bakhs is an action characterized by an agent, not an attribute of the thing deprived in itself, except in the sense of describing it by the verbal noun, as Allah said: "and they sold him for a paltry price" [Yusuf: 20], meaning below the value of its like, that is, its sellers were lax about its price because they had obtained it without exchange or cost. Know that bakhs may relate to quantity, as when a buyer says: "this jar does not weigh more than ten ratls," while he knows that its like weighs twelve ratls, or says: "this palm does not yield more than ten qintars of dates," while he knows it yields twenty qintars. It may also relate to quality, as when one says: "this camel is skittish," while it is one of the riding beasts. The means of bakhs may be speech, as we have illustrated, or action, as when one offers a cheap price for something that ought to be sold at a high price. The purpose of bakhs is that the one who depresses the value benefits, the desirous buyer of the depressed commodity, by turning people away from desiring it, so that it remains a burden on its bringer, who is then forced to sell it at a low price. It may also be intended to plant doubt in the mind of the one who brings the commodity, that his goods are below what is common among people, so that despair enters him concerning the profits of his trade and his resolve grows lax.

What occurs in the language regarding the meanings of bakhs, that it means "base" or "contemptible," perhaps is by way of some kind of metaphor or extension. By this you know that bakhs in the sense of diminishing is the act of an agent upon an object, not the diminishment that is an attribute of the diminished thing. It is more specific than "naqs" (diminishing) in usage, and also more specific in meaning.

Then, the proper form of its verb is to take one object, as in His saying: "and let him not diminish from it anything" [al-Baqarah: 282]. When it is transitive to two objects, as in His saying here: "and do not deprive the people of their things" [al-A'raf: 85], this is in the sense of transformation for the sake of achieving the general first and then the particular. The original sentence is: "and do not deprive the things of the people," so his words "their things" (ashya'ahum) are a substitute of inclusion for "the people" (al-nas). Accordingly, if the verb bakha is put in the passive, you would say: "bukhisa fulan shay'uhu" (so-and-so had his thing deprived), with "fulan" and "shay'uhu" both in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' considered it a second object, so by his parsing, if the verb were made passive, "ashya'ahum" would remain in the accusative, while by our parsing, if the verb were made passive, "ashya'uhum" would become nominative as a substitute for "al-nas." By this you know that there is a difference between bakhs and tatfif that has escaped many people.

The summary of what Shu'ayb ('alayhi al-salam) commanded his people, after the command to monotheism, is confined to three principles: preserving the rights of financial dealings, preserving the order and interests of the community, and preserving the rights of the freedom of seeking guidance.

The first is his words: "So give full measure and weight, and do not deprive the people of their things." Giving full measure and weight returns to preserving the rights of buyers, because the one who measures or weighs is the seller, and it is the love of gain that moves him to cheat in measure or weight, so that he sells the deficient thing at the price of the full thing, as the buyer supposes.

As for the prohibition against depriving people of their things, it returns to preserving the rights of the seller, because the buyer is the one who depresses the seller's goods so as to prepare him to accept a loss in the price of his goods. Both of these matters are a trick and deception for the sake of obtaining profit from wealth.

"Kayl" (measure) is a verbal noun, and it is also applied to that by which one measures, namely the measure, as in His saying: "and we shall gain the measure of a camel" [Yusuf: 65]. This is what is intended here, because it is contrasted with "mizan" (weight), and because of His saying in the other verse: "and do not diminish the measure and the weight" [Hud: 84]. The meaning of giving full measure and weight is that the instrument of measuring and the instrument of weighing should be equal to the quantity of the things measured by them. These two kinds of trickery were specifically singled out for the command and prohibition mentioned, because they were widespread among Madyan, and because trickery in financial dealings is confined to them, since dealing among desert people was limited to exchanges of goods in kind, offering and demanding.

By this it becomes clear that the prohibition in his words, "and do not deprive the people of their things," conveys a meaning different from what the command in his words, "So give full measure and weight," conveys. That prohibition is not in the position of a cause for the command, nor a reinforcement of its content, as some exegetes explained it.

[Page 245]

...and what came in this legislation is one of the foundations for the flourishing of dealings among the community, because transactions depend on mutual trust among the people. Trust arises only when honesty is widespread among them. When that happens, people become eager to trade: the producer increases production and supply in the markets, and the buyer, whether a merchant or a consumer, comes to the markets secure, fearing neither fraud, nor deception, nor cheating. Goods become abundant in the community, and the community no longer needs to import its staples, its necessities, and its refinements. The growth of the city and of civilization then rests on a firm foundation, and people live in prosperity, mutual affection, and brotherhood. The opposite is also true: the condition of the community deteriorates in proportion to the spread of its opposite.

His words, ﴿And do not corrupt the earth after it has been set in order﴾, are the second foundation of Shu'ayb's (peace be upon him) call, namely the prohibition of everything that leads to the corruption of what is already in a state of righteousness on earth. The discussion of a parallel construction has already been presented at his words, Exalted is He, in the early part of this surah: (﴿And do not corrupt the earth after it has been set in order, and call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]).

The demonstrative "that" (﴿dhalikum﴾) refers to the whole of what his speech contained, that is, "that which has been mentioned." For this reason the demonstrative is singular. What has been mentioned is: worshipping God alone, giving full measure and weight, avoiding the defrauding of people's possessions, and avoiding corruption on earth. He informed them that it is "good for you," that is, a benefit and a righteousness by which their affairs are ordered, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And the camels We have made for you as among the rites of God; in them is good for you﴾ [al-Hajj: 36].

What has been mentioned is good because it brings about the wholesomeness of life, the stability of security, the purity of goodwill among the community, and the removal of the rancor that leads to disputes and fighting. When this is achieved, the community multiplies, becomes powerful, is feared by its enemies, its reputation becomes good, and its wealth increases, because people are drawn to trade and agriculture, owing to the security of the owner of wealth from having his property seized. And there is in it the good of the Hereafter, because if they do it in obedience to the command of God, Exalted is He, through His Messenger, it earns them God's pleasure, so they are saved from punishment and dwell in the abode of reward. Therefore the indefiniteness in His words "good" (khayr) is for magnification and perfection, since it combines the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter.

His words, (﴿if you are believers﴾), are a restrictive condition attached to His words, (﴿That is good for you﴾). "Believers" is a title for those characterized by faith in God alone, as is the established usage of the sacred law (shara'i'). To take "believers" to mean "those who affirm his words, his counsel, and his trustworthiness" is an interpretation the context rejects. Rather, the meaning is: it will be good if you are believers in God alone. This is a return to the call to monotheism, like the repetition of the latter part of a speech at its beginning (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr). Its meaning is that the attainment of good from the things referred to does not occur except with faith, because if they do them while they are polytheists, no good will come from them, since the corruptions of polytheism spoil whatever good is in the deeds. As for the Hereafter, this is obvious. As for this world, polytheism calls to the opposites of those virtues, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they added nothing but ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

[Page 246]

Or it calls to corruptions with which no benefit of those goods appears. The upshot is that the purpose of the restriction is to deny complete good to those righteous deeds if their doers are not believers in God in the true sense of faith. This is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿the freeing of a neck﴾ [al-Balad: 13], ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14], ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ [al-Balad: 15], ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 16], ﴿then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. Interpreting the verse otherwise is a deviation from the clear path.

His words, ﴿And do not sit at every path, threatening and barring from the way of God who believes in Him﴾, are the third foundation of his call, and it is the prohibition of obstructing people from faith. After he commanded them to believe in God and what that requires of righteous deeds, which is the good of their own souls, he said, in effect: set yourselves right, and do not prevent anyone who desires to set himself right. That is because they used to block the arrival of people at the city in which Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) lived, so that they would not believe in him. Thus "path" here means the roads leading to meeting Shu'ayb (peace be upon him).

"Sitting" is used figuratively (kinaya) for its consequence, which is staying and remaining. It has already been discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16] in this surah.

"Every" (kull) is for generality, and it is a customary generality, meaning every path that leads to the town or to the dwelling of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). It is also possible that the word "every" is used for multiplicity, as has already been mentioned.

The "ba'" (in "bi-kulli sirat") is for attachment, or it has the sense of "fi" (in) as in its use with names of places. As in the line of Imru' al-Qays: "At the edge of al-Liwa..." (the whole verse).

The clause "threatening" (tu'iduna) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "taq'udu." "Iyad" (threatening) means promising evil. The purpose of the threatening is blocking, so the coordination of the clause "and barring" (wa tasuddun) is the coordination of a cause over an effect. Or it is intended: "threatening those who are determined to follow faith, and barring those who are not determined," in which case it is general coordination over specific.

[Page 247]

"Who believes" (man amana) is governed by both "threatening" and "barring."

The use of the past tense in His words "who believed in Him" in place of the present is because the intended meaning of "man amana" is the one who intends faith. Expressing him in the past tense confirms the resolve of the one intending faith, so that, were it not that they were preventing him, he would already have believed.

"The way of God" is religion, because it is like the path that connects to God, that is, to nearness to His good pleasure.

The meaning of "seeking it crooked" [Al 'Imran: 99] is: you seek for the way of God something crooked, since they claimed that what Shu'ayb called to was falsehood. It is said "baghahu" meaning "sought for him," so its origin is "baghā lahu," and they dropped the preposition due to frequent use, or because "baghā" is used with the sense of "a'ṭā" (gave).

"Iwaj" (with a kasra on the ayn) means lack of straightness in meanings, and with a fatha on the ayn it means lack of straightness in the essence. The meaning is: you try to describe the straight call of Shu'ayb as falsehood and error, like one who tries to bend a straight stick. A parallel of this has occurred in this surah in the mention of the call of the people of Paradise to the people of the Fire.

He delayed the prohibition against blocking the way of God until after the clause ﴿That is good for you if you are believers﴾, and did not place it within the series of the earlier commands and prohibitions followed by "That is good for you." This is because he arranged the speech by beginning with the call to monotheism, then to righteous deeds, due to the connection that all of this is the righteousness of those addressed. So he followed them with the explanation that they are good for them if they are believers. Thus he renewed their attention to faith and to its being a condition for the soundness of deeds. And by way of mentioning faith, he returned to the prohibition against barring those who desire it. This is like the ordering in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

As if I had not ridden a horse for pleasure,
nor pursued a bashful maiden of anklets,
nor poured the red wine for the guests,
nor said to my horses, "Turn back, a return after retreat."

Al-Wahidi related in his commentary on the Diwan of al-Mutanabbi that when al-Mutanabbi recited to Sayf al-Dawla his line about him:

[Page 248]

You stood, and there is no doubt in death for the one standing,
as if you were in the sheath of destruction, and it is asleep.
The heroes pass by you wounded and grieving,
and your face is bright and your smile is cheerful.

Sayf al-Dawla objected to his matching the second halves of the two lines with their first halves, and said to him: you should have made the second hemistich of the second line the second hemistich of the first, and the reverse, and you in this are like Imru' al-Qays in his line:
"As if I had not ridden a horse for pleasure," [the two lines].

The proper way according to the scholars of poetry is that the second hemistich of the first line should go with the second line and the second hemistich of the second line should go with the first, so that riding horses goes with commanding the horses to charge, and pouring wine goes with the bashful maiden. Abu al-Tayyib said: If it is true that the one who corrected Imru' al-Qays is more knowledgeable about poetry than he, then Imru' al-Qays erred and I erred too. And my lord the Amir knows that the cloth is not known by the cloth-merchant as the weaver knows it, because the merchant only knows its whole, while the weaver knows its whole and its details. For he took it out of the erotic style into the style of cloth. Imru' al-Qays combined the pleasure of women with the pleasure of riding for hunting, and combined generosity in buying wine for guests with courage in confronting enemies. As for me, when I mentioned death at the beginning of the line, I followed it with mentioning destruction because of their affinity. And since the face of the fleeing man is either frowning or his eye is weeping, I said: "your face is bright and your smile is cheerful," so as to join opposites in meaning.

By this he means that the aspects of suitability in arranging speech vary and multiply, and some are more preponderant than others.

After this, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) reminded them of God's multiplying them after they had been few. This was a favour upon them, for they had become a community after having been a small group.

The meaning of God's multiplying them is His facilitating the means of increase for them: He strengthened in them the capacity for procreation, protected them from causes of death, and made easy for their offspring the stage of youth, so that their descendants multiplied and their deaths decreased. Thus they became a great number in a period in which the arrival of a community at such a number is not customary. Therefore, their preventing people from entering the religion of God is considered an effort to reduce the party of God, which is ingratitude for the favour of God upon them in multiplying them. This is to set against the consideration of this favour the consideration of His vengeance upon those with whom He was angry, for He uprooted them after they had been numerous. This is one of the ways things are distinguished by their opposites.

[Page 249]

Therefore he followed it with His words: ﴿And look how the end of the corrupters was﴾. In this speech there is a combination of the methods of encouragement (tarhib... targhib) and warning.

"Qalil" (few) is an adjective that remains in the singular and masculine form, like "kathir" (many), and this has already been discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him were many devoted multitudes﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146] in Surat Al 'Imran.

By "the corrupters" is meant those who corrupted themselves by the creed of polytheism and by deeds of error, corrupted the society by violating the laws, and corrupted people by supplying them with misguidance and barring them from guidance. For this reason the word "al-mufsidin" is not given a complement, because it is treated as a descriptive attribute, cut off from the resemblance of a verb; that is, "those who are known for corruption." This address primarily intends the disbelievers among his people, and in it there is a reminder to the believers among them of God's favour, since it includes them as well, and of the lesson from those who passed away, for that benefits them. In this speech there is also an allusion (ta'ridh) containing a promise to the Muslims and a consolation to them for what they encounter from the corrupters among the people of polytheism, because the situation of the two groups matches the situation of the two groups among the people of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him).

The "idh" in His words "when you were few" is a noun of time, not an adverb of time. It is therefore in the position of an object, meaning: remember the time when you were few. Then He followed it by saying that He multiplied you in a short period.

"Ta'ifa" means a group with a large number, and this was discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So let a party of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa: 102] in Surat al-Nisa.

The conditional in His words ﴿And if there is a party﴾ indicates that the occurrence of what is in the consequent (the threat to the disbelievers and the promise to the believers) is made dependent on the certain realization of the content of the protasis, not on its mere expectation, because

[Page 250]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 85–87 (part 3 of 3):

It is known to have occurred.
