As for the apostasy of Shu'ayb after prophethood, it is impossible by the Shari'ah, because of Allah's protection of the prophets. So if Allah willed to strip protection from any one of them, nothing impossible in reason would follow from it, but it is not possible by the Shari'ah. You have already learned the protection of the prophets from shirk before prophethood, so their protection from it after prophethood is all the more so. Allah said, "If you were to associate partners with Him, your deeds would surely be lost," according to one of the two interpretations.

In the words of Shu'ayb, "unless Allah, our Lord, wills," there is a restriction of not returning to disbelief to the will of Allah, and this necessarily entails restricting the continuance in faith to the will of Allah, since not returning to disbelief is equivalent to steadfastness in faith. This restriction is intended for courtesy and for committing knowledge of the future to Allah, and it is a metonymy for asking Allah for continuance in faith, like His saying, "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us."

From here it is argued in support of the view of al-Ash'ari and a group headed by Muhammad ibn 'Abdus, the eminent Maliki jurist,
Page 10
that the Muslim says, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," because he does not know what will be his final end. And the view of al-Maturidi and a group of scholars of Qayrawan, headed by Muhammad ibn Sahnun, that the Muslim does not say, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," because he is certain that he is a believer, so he does not utter a word that indicates doubt about his faith, is weak.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-A'raf, verses 88–89 (part 2 of 2)

The sparks of disagreement flew for a long time in Qayrawan between Ibn 'Abdus and his companions on one side, and Ibn Sahnun and his companions on the other. Each party attributed to the other what was unbecoming to them both. The companions of Ibn Sahnun called Ibn 'Abdus and his companions "the Shakkiyya" (the doubters), and the common people of Qayrawan seized upon this dispute without understanding it, so that they sometimes boldly and slanderously attacked Ibn 'Abdus and his companions. This is detailed by 'Iyad in al-Madarik, in the biography of Muhammad ibn Sahnun and the biography of Ibn al-Tabban.

What Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd and 'Iyad verified is that the disagreement is verbal. If the person says "in shaa' Allah" and his inner faith is like his outward profession, there is no harm in that; but if it is doubt, then it is doubt regarding faith, and that is not what Ibn 'Abdus intended. The scholars who investigated the matter have said that the disagreement between the Ash'ari and the Maturidi on this question is a verbal disagreement, as verified by Taj al-Din al-Subki in his Nuniyya poem, and his student Nur al-Din al-Shirazi followed him in his commentary on it.

It is important to point out that the disagreement on this question is only assumed regarding the validity of the believer's saying, "I am a believer, in shaa' Allah," and whether that statement indicates doubt about his faith. The disagreement is not over whether, according to those who hold this view, he is obligated to say "I am a believer, in shaa' Allah." This is evident from the fact that they often set the statement of those who speak with the qualifier of "in shaa' Allah" against the statement of others: "I am a believer with Allah." Thus the matter returns to a difference of perspective regarding the state of the heart's conviction in relation to what is in Allah's knowledge of its final outcome. In this way, it became easy to reduce the disagreement to a verbal one.

The mention of the Lord's attribute, and its attribution to the first-person plural pronoun that includes the speaker, is a manifestation of the presence of absolute generality, and an allusion that Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe.

The disagreement between us and the Mu'tazila over whether Allah's will (mashi'a) may extend to disbelief and acts of disobedience is a disagreement arising from the difference over the precise meaning of will (mashi'a) and volition (irada). Each of the two parties has a technical usage (istilah) that differs from the other's usage. The matter is slight, even though the two parties have exaggerated it. Our usage is more in harmony with the Shari'a and closer to the language, and the whole question is one of the derivative issues of the question of moral obligation (taklif) and the capacity of the one who is obligated.

His saying, "Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge," is a commitment to the knowledge of Allah, meaning: except that He wills otherwise, and He knows best His intent regarding us. The repetition of the description of Lordship is a manifestation placed in the position where a pronoun would be expected, to increase the manifestation of His attribute of Lordship and to reinforce the earlier allusion until it becomes like an explicit statement.

"'Ilman" (in knowledge) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the agent, for the purpose of generalization followed by detailing, for emphasis.

"Kulla shay'in" (all things) is in the accusative as the direct object of "wasi'a" (encompassed), meaning: the knowledge of our Lord encompassed all things.

The word "si'a" (vastness, encompassing) is used metaphorically for complete encompassing of everything, because a vast thing encompasses more.

In this argument there is an incorporation (idmaj) of teaching the attributes of Allah to His followers and others, in accordance with the custom of preachers who seize the opportunity.

Then He informed that he and those who followed him had placed their trust in Allah. Tawakkul (trust) is entrusting the direct management of one's welfare to another. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, "And when you have resolved, then put your trust in Allah" in Al 'Imran. This entrusting requires seeking good, meaning: we hope that He will not strip us of true faith, nor corrupt the constitution of our minds and hearts, so that we are not tested and do not go astray; and we hope that He will suffice us against the evil of one who harbors evil against us, which is the evil of the disbelievers toward them, namely the trial concerning their families through expulsion, and concerning their religion through compulsion to follow disbelief.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the verb "tawakkalna" (we have put our trust) serves to convey exclusivity, in keeping with the meaning of monotheism and the rejection of other than Allah. And because in His saying "In Allah we have put our trust" there is an entrusting to Him for their sufficiency regarding the affair of their enemies, they stated explicitly what increases this with His saying: "Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth." They interpreted "fath" (decision) here as judgment and ruling, and said: it is the dialect of the Azd of 'Uman from Yemen, meaning "judge between us and them." It is derived from "fath" in the sense of victory, because the Arabs used to submit to no judgment except that of the sword, and they considered victory to be the judgment of Allah in favor of the victor over the vanquished.

His saying, "And You are the best of those who decide," is like His saying, "And He is the best of judges," meaning: "And You are the best of those who give victory." "The best of judges" means the most excellent of those possessing this attribute, the one in whom the perfection of this attribute is realized in what is intended by it and in its purpose, such that truth is not confused for falsehood to him, nor are trivialities passed off upon him. Judges have many ranks, so the sense of the comparative in His saying "and He is the best of judges" becomes clear; and the same analogy applies to His saying "best of helpers" and "best of schemers." It was already mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran: "Nay, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers."

[Page 13]

The clause "And the chiefs (al-mala') who disbelieved among his people said" is conjoined (with a connective particle) but not separated, unlike the clause before it. This is because the dialogue has ended, and the narration of a dialogue calls for separating its clauses. This is a fresh (isti'naf, resumptive) statement, in which the chiefs addressed their words to the general body of their people who remained in disbelief, warning them against following Shu'ayb out of fear that the call of Shu'ayb and the sincerity of his argument would take root in their souls. When they saw that his proof was clear and that they could not prevail over him in the debate, and when they had determined upon their disbelief, they turned to address those of their people who were present, to warn them against following Shu'ayb and to threaten them with loss.

The word "al-mala'" is mentioned in a place where a pronoun might have been used, because of the distance of its referent.

The chiefs were described by a relative pronoun and its clause, rather than by the definite article alone, which would have implied that the second "al-mala'" is the same as the one mentioned before. This was done to intensify the blame of the chiefs by the attribute of disbelief, just as they were blamed earlier by the attribute of arrogance.

The attribute of disbelief is applied to the chiefs here because it suits the speech reported from them, which indicates their obstinacy in their disbelief, just as they were described in the previous verse with arrogance, to suit the situation of their debate with Shu'ayb, as has already been explained. Thus it is understood from the two verses that they were arrogant disbelievers.

The addressees in the words "If you follow Shu'ayb" are those present at the time of the address before the chiefs. So the speech of the chiefs is related as it was uttered by them, and the context explains the intended addressees: the general body of Shu'ayb's people who remained in disbelief.

The lam is an introductory particle for an oath (lam al-muwatta'ah). "Indeed you would then be losers" is the answer to the oath, and it is an indication of the answer to the omitted conditional clause, as is usual in such constructions.

Loss (al-khusran) has been discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: "Those who killed their children have certainly lost" in Surat al-An'am. It is used metaphorically for the occurrence of harm where benefit was intended. What is meant here is a warning against harms that would befall them in this world as a result of the anger of their gods against them, because it is apparent that they did not believe in resurrection. If they did believe in it, then what is meant is the more general loss; but the more important matter for them is the worldly one.

The "fa" in "So the earthquake seized them" indicates immediate sequence: the seizing by the earthquake occurred immediately after their words to their people.

The explanation of "So the earthquake seized them, and they were found prostrate in their homes" has already been given in its parallel in the story of Thamud.

The earthquake (al-rajfah) that struck the people of Madyan was thunderbolts that came out of a canopy (zullah), which is a cloud. God, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Shu'ara': "So the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them." In Surat Hud the same event was expressed as "the Cry" (al-sayhah). It is therefore determined that it was of the kind of sounds that split from something uprooting and uprooted, not from something striking and struck, which is the quake (al-zilzal). The more apparent view is that a quake and thunderbolts struck them, so that the earthquake (al-rajfah) is the quake and the Cry is the thunderbolt, as indicated by His saying, "as if they had never dwelt therein."

The clause "Those who denied Shu'ayb" is a new independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i). The definition by the relative form is to hint at the reason for the predicate, namely that their annihilation and the cutting off of their last trace was a recompense for them for their denial of Shu'ayb.

[Page 14]

The meaning of "as if they had never dwelt therein" is that the state of their extermination and the effacement of their traces is compared to the condition of those who never had life. It is said: "ghaniya bi-al-makan" (like radiya) meaning he resided there. For this reason the dwelling place of a people is called "maghan." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What I have inferred from the poetry of the Arabs is that ghaniya means he resided in a residence accompanied by the enjoyment of a comfortable life, and it may be derived from al-istighna' (independence)." That is, "as if there had been no residence." This is only meant to express the erasure of their traces, as He said: "And We made them a harvest, as if they had not flourished yesterday." This indicates that a quake struck them together with the thunderbolts, to the extent that their bodies were burned, the ground swallowed them, their dwellings were overturned into the depths of the earth, and nothing remained, or only a little remained. This is the aspect of the comparison. The aspect of comparison is not the state of their death, because that occurs for every dead person and is not specific to peoples like Madyan. This is like His saying, exalted is He: "So do you see any remnant of them?"

The fronting of the subject (al-musnad ilayh) in "Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers," when kana is considered a verb and the predicate is considered verbal, is a fronting for the purpose of a benefit that strengthens the judgment. If kana is considered like a copula (al-rabitah), which is the more apparent view, then the strengthening arises from the meaning of stability conveyed by the nominal sentence.

The repetition of "Those who denied Shu'ayb" is for enumeration and for awakening the listeners, who are the idolaters of the Arabs, so that they may beware of the fate of those similar to them in polytheism and denial, by way of allusion (ta'ridh), as the explicit statement of this was made in His saying, exalted is He: "And for the disbelievers there are similar fates."

The separating pronoun (dhamir al-fasl) in "they were the losers" indicates restriction (qasr), and it is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), meaning exclusive of those who followed Shu'ayb. This is to expose the foolishness of the chiefs' statement to the common people, "If you follow Shu'ayb, indeed you would then be losers," to make those who take lessons from them reflect on the incoherence of their sayings and the folly of their opinion, and as a warning to their likes against falling into that error.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 93:

﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely, so how could I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾

The explanation of a similar verse has already been given up to his words "and I advised you sincerely," in the story of Thamud. [Page 15] The reason for using the plural form "messages" (risalat) was also explained in its parallel in the story of the people of Nuh.

His calling out to his people is a call of regret and of disavowal of their deeds. It is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) after the Battle of Badr, when he stood over the well into which the corpses of the polytheists had been thrown. He called them by the names of their chieftains, then said: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?" He used the interrogative of denial in his words, "so how could I grieve over a disbelieving people," addressing himself in the manner of tajrid (the rhetorical device of addressing oneself as if speaking to another). A thought of sorrow over them occurred to him, and he dismissed it from himself by saying that they did not deserve to be grieved over, because they had chosen this for themselves. Moreover, he had left out none of their warning, such that had he delivered it to them they would have desisted from what they were engaged in, so nothing remained that would call for his regret and remorse. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this narration﴾ and His saying: ﴿So let not your soul go away in regret over them﴾.

So the fa' in "so how could I grieve over a disbelieving people" is for tafri' (consequential linking) upon his words "I have certainly conveyed to you" etc. He made the interrogative of denial a consequence of that, because when he had conveyed the message, advised them, and they turned away from him, they deserved the anger of one who becomes angry for God's sake, namely the Messenger, and he sees that they deserve punishment. So how would he grieve over them for the punishment that befell them?

Al-asa (al-asa): intense grief. Its verb is like rada (raḍiya). The imperfect "a-asa" begins with the hamzah of the first person, so two hamzahs came together.

It is also possible that the interrogative of denial is directed outwardly at himself, while the intended meaning is to forbid those believers who were with him from grieving over their destroyed people, since it is possible that sorrow over the destroyed members of their people would arise in their souls, even though they deserved destruction.

His words "over a disbelieving people" are an explicit noun in the place where a pronoun would be expected (izhar fi maqam al-idmar). This was so that describing them with disbelief could be made explicit, as an added means of consoling himself and of abandoning grief over them.

God saved Shu'ayb from what befell his people by his departing from the abode of punishment. It is said that he went out with those who believed in him to Mecca and settled there until they died. The more apparent view is that they dwelt in a quarter of their own in their city, from which God lifted the punishment, since the remnant of Madyan remained in their land. The Torah mentions that Shu'ayb was in the land of his people when the Children of Israel passed by their dwellings during their exodus from Egypt.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 94–95:

Page 16
﴿And We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Then We substituted for the bad condition a good one until they multiplied and said, "Adversity and ease have touched our forefathers as well," so We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.﴾

The conjunction "wa" (and) links the clause "wa-ma arsalna" (and We did not send) to the clause ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf: 85] by way of conjoining the more general to the more specific; because the narratives mentioned from the beginning, from His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent Nuh to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], all have as their purpose the lesson drawn from the past nations and an admonition to the disbelievers of the Arabs. When He recounted to them the stories of five nations, He now came with a universal ruling that encompasses all the rejecting nations, by way of qiyas al-tamthil (analogical reasoning by example) or qiyas al-istiqra' al-naqis (incomplete inductive reasoning), which is the most famous form of qiyas employed in rhetorical contexts (al-maqamat al-khitabiyya). These sentences up to His saying, ﴿Then We sent after them Musa﴾, are like an interjection between the stories, to draw attention to the place of the admonition, and that is the purpose of those stories; so it is an interjection that clarifies the purpose of the speech, and this is very common in interjections within discourse.

"Arsalna" is construed with "fi" rather than "ila" because the intended meaning of "qarya" (town) is its literal sense, and a town is not sent to; rather one is sent within it, to its people. So the implied sense is: "And We did not send in a town a prophet to its people except that We seized its people..." This is like His saying, ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother [town] a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas: 59]. The meaning that applies to His saying, ﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53], which is mentioned shortly, does not apply here, since there is no need for it here.

"Min" is redundant (zā'id), for emphasis on the generality derived from the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context. Specifying the towns for the sending of messengers, rather than the desert dwellers, is as this verse and other verses of the Qur'an indicate, and as the history of religions attests; it indicates that the purpose of God, exalted is He, in sending messengers is to spread righteousness among the people of civilization, in which disorder arises through the gathering of different types of people, while the people of the desert do not refrain from inclining to the towns and seeking shelter in them for their civic needs. As for the coming of a prophet who is not a messenger to the people of the desert, Khalid ibn Sinan came as a prophet among the Banu 'Abs. As for Handhala ibn Safwan, the prophet of the people of al-Rass, it is more evident that he was a messenger, because God mentioned the people of al-Rass among the rejecting nations. It has been said that he appeared in the town of al-Rass, which is also called "Fath" with an unpointed initial letter, or "Fakh" with a dotted letter, or "Fayj" with a yā' and jīm, or "Falj" with lām and jīm, from al-Yamama.

The exception is an emptied exception (istithna' mufarragh) from circumstances: that is, "We did not send a prophet to a town in any circumstance except in the circumstance that We seized its people with adversity." There is an elliptical omission in the speech indicated by His saying, "perhaps they might humble themselves," for it indicates that they had not humbled themselves before being seized with adversity and hardship. The implied sense is: "And We did not send to a town a prophet except that the people of the town denied him, so We warned them, perhaps they would submit to God and abandon obstinacy, etc..."

The word "akhdh" (seizing) here is used metaphorically for overtaking and striking with a hardship that cannot be repelled, which is the sense of overpowering, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And We had certainly sent to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship﴾ [al-An'am: 42] in Surat al-An'am.

As for His saying, ﴿with adversity and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves﴾, what explains it has been mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And We had certainly sent to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 42] in Surat al-An'am. Some of it is also explained in His saying, ﴿and the patient in adversity and hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The past circumstantial clause dispensed with the "wa" and "qad" with the exceptive particle, so it does not combine with "qad" except rarely. That is: "We initiated with them intimidation and calamities, so that it would blunt their fervour and turn their reflection toward seeking the causes of the calamities, and they would know that these were from God's wrath upon them, and so they would repent."

"Tabdil" means substitution (ta'wid), so its proper construction is to take a second object with the preposition "bi" conveying the sense of replacement, and that second object governed by "bi" is what is abandoned, while the first object is what is taken, as in His saying, ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying, ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [al-Nisa': 2] in Surat al-Nisa'. Therefore "al-hasanah" is accusative here, because it is what is taken for them after the bad condition; so it is the first object, and "al-sayyi'ah" is what is abandoned. He turned away from governing "al-sayyi'ah" with "bi" to a expression that performs the function of the particle of substitution, namely the word "makan" (place), used metaphorically as an adverb of place for substitution. One says, "Take this instead of that," meaning, "Take it as a successor to that," because the successor occupies the place of what it succeeds. Of this kind is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And I was given a bleeding wound after a blessing"

Here he made "ba'd" a substitute for the particle of substitution.

So His saying "makan" is in the accusative as an adverb of place metaphorically, meaning: "We substituted for them a good condition in the place of the bad condition." "Al-hasanah" is a noun treated as feminine because it is interpreted as a state or an event; likewise "al-sayyi'ah." Both are originally adjectives of an omitted qualified noun, then the omission of the qualified noun became frequent because mentioning it was of little benefit, so the two adjectives became like nouns. For this reason the good is expressed in some verses by something which hints at its adjectival meaning, such as His saying, ﴿And not equal are the good and the bad. Repel [evil] with that which is best﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning: "Repel the bad with the good." When He came in the form of the relative pronoun and the relative clause with the superlative (af'al al-tafdil), the adjectival sense was hinted at in both. Likewise His saying, ﴿Repel with that which is best the evil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96]. Similar to these is "al-musibah" (calamity), as in His saying in Surat (Bara'ah): ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a misfortune strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50], meaning: "We substituted for them a good state in place of their bad state, which is the state of adversity and hardship."

The definiteness is the definiteness of the genus, which indicates that they were given a good state whose benefit is slow and which does not reach the level of blessing.

"Hatta" is a limit (ghayah) for what is implied in "baddalna" of the continuation of that, and it is inceptive (ibtida'iyya); the sentence that follows it has no grammatical place (la mahall la-ha).

"Wa 'afaw" means they multiplied. One says: "'afa al-nabat" when plants increased and grew. "Wa" conjoins "qalu" to "'afaw," so it is part of the same limit.

"Al-sarra'" means blessing and ease of life, and it is the opposite of "al-darra'."

The meaning is that We seize them with what changes their state in which they were of ease and health, perhaps they would know that the removal of blessing from them is a sign of God's wrath upon them on account of their denial of their messenger, but they do not get guided. Then We return them to their former state as a respite and a gradual drawing-on, so that they increase in error. When they see that, they make excuses for what befell them of misery and harm, saying that this change is merely an accident of the times, and that it has struck their forefathers before them, and messengers did not come to them.

This is God's custom, exalted is He, in alerting His servants, for He loves from them that they discern things, reason with the intellect, and infer causes from effects, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice? Then they do not repent, nor do they remember﴾ [al-Tawbah: 126], because when God gave man intellect, He loved that he should use it for what brings him to perfection and protects him from error.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that this statement, uttered by their tongues, circulated among them in their disputes with their messengers, when the messengers admonished them about what had befallen them and called them to repentance and faith, so that the harm might be removed from them. It is also possible that this statement arose in their souls, so that by it they might repel what occurred to their minds of the expectation that this harm was a punishment from God, exalted is He. Since it is narrated of many nations, there were various states according to the diversity of the fields of souls and conditions.

The sum of what they used to repel the indication of harm as God's wrath is that the like of this had befallen their forefathers, who had not been called by a messenger to the Oneness of God. This is a fault of analogy and corruption of reasoning, through confining a thing with multiple causes to one single cause, and neglecting the fact that causes may substitute for one another, together with neglecting the difference in analogising their condition to the condition of their forefathers: their forefathers had not been visited by messengers from God, whereas the peoples of the messengers were warned by the messengers of wrath, adversity and hardship, so they befell them. Would this not show them that what happened to them was from God's wrath upon them? Moreover, God's wrath is not confined to being consequent upon disobedience to the messenger, but may also arise from immersion in manifest error while the proofs of guidance are clear to the intellects, for associating partners with God is error, and the proofs of Oneness are clear to the intellects. So when the indication is reinforced by the sending of warning messengers, the error becomes stronger through its continuation, and its excuses are cut off. A similar fault occurs to people through the impulse of desire and attachment to the state of error.

The "fa" in His saying "fa-akhadhnahum" indicates sequence following "'afaw wa qalu," considering that they are the limit of the substitution of the good for the bad; and there is no indication in it that their saying that was the cause of their being seized suddenly, but it indicates their persistence, that is: our seizing them occurred immediately after the improvement of their state and their insolence in blessing.

The sequence is customary, so it applies to an interval that is not considered long in custom, for such momentous events occur in that time.

"Akhdh" here means destruction, as in His saying, ﴿We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am.

"Baghtah" means suddenness, and it was mentioned at His saying, ﴿until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 31], and in His saying, ﴿until when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am, and the reason for its accusative form was explained there.

The clause "wa-hum la yash'urun" (while they did not perceive) is a circumstantial clause emphasizing the meaning of "baghtah."

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 7, verses 96–99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿If the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heavens and the earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾ ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are at play?﴾ ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God? None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people.﴾

The clause "﴿If the people of the towns had believed﴾" is conjoined to the preceding clause, "﴿We never sent a prophet to a town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship﴾" (Qur'an 7:94). That is, whenever We sent a prophet to a town and its people denied him, We only warned them, tested them gradually, and then punished them. "If the people of those destroyed towns had believed in what their messenger brought them and been mindful of their Lord, We would not have afflicted them with misfortune, and We would have given them life in blessing." That is: God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.

The condition of *law* (the particle of counterfactual conditional, *law imtina'iyya*) is realised in past time. Since its clause of condition came accompanied by *anna* (the particle that conveys emphasis and makes what follows a verbal noun), and its predicate was a past-tense verb, the sense of past time was secured in the conditional clause. The meaning is: "If their belief had occurred in the past, We would have opened blessings upon them."

*Taqwa* (God-consciousness, piety): this is the taqwa of God, by keeping within His limits, and it comes after belief.

The definite article in *al-qura* (the towns) is the definite of prior reference, so the annexation of *ahl* (people) to it conveys its generality to the extent that the noun it is annexed to is general. This is an explicit statement of what was implied by the brevity of the statement "﴿We never sent a prophet to a town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship﴾" as mentioned above. It is also an allusion, warning those of the people of Mecca who denied Muhammad (ﷺ), and an allusion, giving good news to the people of the towns who believe, like the people of Medina. Earlier, at the beginning of the commentary on this surah, it was noted that it is close to the last of what was revealed in Mecca, though it has been said that some of its verses were revealed in Medina, as mentioned earlier. By this, the placement of the allusion of warning and good news to both groups among the people of the towns becomes clear. God seized the people of Mecca after the believers had left it, afflicting them with seven years of drought. He blessed the people of Medina, enriched them, and turned away from them the fever, which was directed to al-Juhfa, and al-Juhfa at that time was a land of polytheism.

*Al-fath* (opening): removing the barrier that prevents entry into a place. One says "he opened the door" and "he opened the house." Its transitivity to the house is by way of expansion (*tawassu'*), and its original form is "opening for the house." Likewise is His saying here, ﴿We would have opened upon them blessings﴾, and His saying, ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold it﴾ (Qur'an 35:2). One also says "he opened a window" (*kuwwa*), meaning he made it an opening. The word *al-fath* here is a metaphor for empowerment, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿When they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ (Qur'an 6:44), in Surah al-An'am.

The transitivity of the verb *al-fath* to *al-barakat* (blessings) here is an implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*), by likening blessings to houses in the benefit derived from what they contain. Thus there are two metaphors here: an implicit one and a subsidiary one (*isti'ara tab'iyya*). Ibn 'Amir read *lafattahna* with a doubled *ta'*, which conveys intensification.

*Al-barakat* is the plural of *barakah* (blessing). The purpose of the plural is its multiplicity, in view of the multiplicity of kinds of blessed things. The explanation of *barakah* was given earlier, at His saying, ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ (Qur'an 6:92), in Surah al-An'am. It was also mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for people is the one at Bakka, blessed﴾ (Qur'an 3:96), in Surah Al 'Imran, and earlier still at His saying, ﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾ (Qur'an 7:54), in this surah. The essence of its meaning is the good that is wholesome and for which there is no reckoning in the Hereafter. It is the best state of favour. For this reason, in the case of those who are "the ones upon whom wrath is due," those who are drawn on gradually, He expressed it with the word *hasana* (good), in the singular, in His saying, ﴿in place of evil, good﴾ (Qur'an 7:95). But for the believers He expressed it with *barakat* in the plural.

His saying "﴿from the heavens and the earth﴾" is meant in its literal sense, because what people receive of worldly goods is either produced by the earth, which is the greater part of benefits, or comes from the heavens, such as rain-water, sunlight, moonlight, the stars, the air, and favourable winds.

His saying "﴿but they denied﴾" is an exception to the negation of the condition of *law*, since denial is non-belief. This is an exceptive syllogism (*qiyas istithna'i*).

The clause "﴿so We seized them﴾" is a consequence of the clause "﴿but they denied﴾", and it is like the conclusion of a syllogism, because it is equivalent to the negation of the consequent, since their being seized for what they earned entails the absence of the opening of blessings upon them.

The meaning of *al-akhdh* (seizing) was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾ (Qur'an 7:95). What is meant by it is seizing for annihilation (*akhdh al-isti'sal*).

The *ba'* (preposition) is causal: because of what they had earned of disbelief and disobedience.

The implied sense is: "They are a losing people, since none feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people."

It is the security that arises from denying the report of the Messenger (ﷺ), and from the delusion that the religion of polytheism is the truth. So it is security that arises from disbelief. What is secured against is the threat of the messengers to them, and what is described as God's plan.

Among the kinds of feeling secure from God's punishment are other types, different from this security and close to it, and distant from it, according to the differences in people's inner states and the degrees of their intentions. As for those that rest on a legislative proof, there is no reckoning upon their holder. Such is the security of the Muslims from the sort of punishment that afflicted earlier nations, which rests on His saying, ﴿God would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ (Qur'an 8:33), and on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when there was revealed His saying, ﴿Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾ (Qur'an 6:65). When it was revealed, "or confound you into factions," he said: "This is easier." This was explained earlier in the commentary on this verse in Surah al-An'am.

None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people.﴾

That is: God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.

The meaning is: "If their belief had occurred in the past, We would have opened blessings upon them."

This is an explicit statement of what was implied by the brevity of the statement "﴿We never sent a prophet to a town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship﴾" as mentioned above. One also says "he opened a window" (*kuwwa*), meaning he made it an opening. The word *al-fath* here is a metaphor for empowerment, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿When they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ (Qur'an 6:44), in Surah al-An'am.

The transitivity of the verb *al-fath* to *al-barakat* (blessings) here is an implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*), by likening blessings to houses in the benefit derived from what they contain. Thus there are two metaphors here: an implicit one and a subsidiary one (*isti'ara tab'iyya*). Ibn 'Amir read *lafattahna* with a doubled *ta'*, which conveys intensification.

The explanation of *barakah* was given earlier, at His saying, ﴿This is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ (Qur'an 6:92), in Surah al-An'am. It was also mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for people is the one at Bakka, blessed﴾ (Qur'an 3:96), in Surah Al 'Imran, and earlier still at His saying, ﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾ (Qur'an 7:54), in this surah. The essence of its meaning is the good that is wholesome and for which there is no reckoning in the Hereafter. It is the best state of favour. For this reason, in the case of those who are "the ones upon whom wrath is due," those who are drawn on gradually, He expressed it with the word *hasana* (good), in the singular, in His saying, ﴿in place of evil, good﴾ (Qur'an 7:95). But for the believers He expressed it with *barakat* in the plural.

His saying "﴿from the heavens and the earth﴾" is meant in its literal sense, because what people receive of worldly goods is either produced by the earth, which is the greater part of benefits, or comes from the heavens, such as rain-water, sunlight, moonlight, the stars, the air, and favourable winds.

His saying "﴿but they denied﴾" is an exception to the negation of the condition of *law*, since denial is non-belief. This is an exceptive syllogism (*qiyas istithna'i*).

The clause "﴿so We seized them﴾" is a consequence of the clause "﴿but they denied﴾", and it is like the conclusion of a syllogism, because it is equivalent to the negation of the consequent, since their being seized for what they earned entails the absence of the opening of blessings upon them.

The meaning of *al-akhdh* (seizing) was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾ (Qur'an 7:95). What is meant by it is seizing for annihilation (*akhdh al-isti'sal*).

The *ba'* (preposition) is causal: because of what they had earned of disbelief and disobedience.

The *fa'* in His saying "﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾" is conjunctive, and it conveys sequence in mention (*al-tartib al-dhikri*). When He mentioned, concerning all of them, what provokes wonder at their state, He followed it with what indicates it, joined by the *fa'* of sequence. The point of wonder is their collective delusion in this heedlessness; that is, the interrogative of wonder at their delusion and their feeling secure from the wrath of the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, follows from the narrative of their denial and their being seized.

The discussion of this same structure was given earlier at His saying, ﴿Whenever a messenger comes to you, do you...﴾ (Qur'an 2:87), in Surah al-Baqara.

The phrase "﴿that Our punishment will come upon them﴾" is in the present tense, because what is meant is narrating their sense of security, which was [in the past], regarding the coming of God's punishment in the future of that time.

[Page 22]

His saying "﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will come upon them in the forenoon while they are at play?﴾" is read by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Ja'far with a sukun on the *waw*, as a conjunction by the particle *aw* (or), which is for one of two things, conjoined to the wonder: that is, it is a wonder at one of the two states. The rest read it with a fatha on the *waw*, as a conjunction by *wa* (and), preceded by the interrogative hamza, so it is the conjunction of a second interrogative by the *wa* that conveys combination. In that case both interrogatives are governed by the *fa'* of consequence, according to the view of the majority of grammarians. As for the view of al-Zamakhshari, the *wa* must be for division, that is, dividing the interrogative into two interrogatives. The two views were mentioned earlier at His saying, "﴿Whenever a messenger comes to you﴾" (Qur'an 2:87), in Surah al-Baqara.

*Bayatan* (by night): its meaning and the reason for its accusative form were mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿How many a town We destroyed; Our punishment came upon it by night﴾ (Qur'an 7:4), at the beginning of this surah.

*Al-Duha* (forenoon), with a *damma* and a short vowel, is in origin the name of the light of the sun when it has risen and become high. The jurists explained it as the sun rising a spear's length. It is synonymous with *al-dahwa* and *al-dahw*.

*Al-Duha* may be masculine or feminine. Its use for timing was widespread among the Arabs and those before them. God said, quoting Moses: ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment, and that people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ (Qur'an 20:59).

The restriction of the wonder at their sense of security from the arrival of punishment to the two times, night and forenoon, out of all other times, and to the two states, sleep and play, out of all other states, is because these two times are most fitting for the punishment to be feared at, since they are times of ease: night is for sleep after the end of work, and forenoon is for play before taking up work. So it was the condition of those who have understanding but turn away from the call of God's messengers that they should not feel secure from His punishment, especially in these two times and states.

In this wonder there is an allusion to the polytheists who denied the Prophet (ﷺ), that there may befall them what befell the earlier nations. Thus mentioning the time of night and the time of play was more fitting to the allusive meaning, as a threat to them that the punishment would strike them in its most dreadful state, for its coming upon them would be at the hour of their ease and the hour of their idleness, as a retribution against them.

His saying "﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God?﴾" repeats "﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾", its purpose being to confirm the wonder at their heedlessness and to confirm the sense of allusion toward the polytheist listeners, with the added reminder that what befell those people of God's punishment resembles the manner of a schemer's plan against the one he schemes against. So they should not think that the respite is neglect of them, and they should beware lest it be like the act of a schemer against his enemy.

*Al-makr* (plan), in its real meaning, is an act intended to harm someone in a concealed manner or in a form that one takes to be a benefit. Here it is a metaphor for respite and favour during the period of respite. It is therefore figurative (*tamthiliyya*), likening the state of favour with respite, and its being followed by vengeance, to the state of a plan. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿They plotted, and God plotted; and God is the best of plotters﴾ (Qur'an 3:54), in Surah Al 'Imran.

His saying "﴿None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people﴾" is consequent upon and branches from the wonder in His saying "﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God?﴾", because what is meant by it is to derive the conclusion that the people of the towns mentioned are losers, since it is established that they felt secure from the plan of God. The implied sense is: "Do they feel secure from the plan of God? Then they are a losing people."

This derivation was formulated in a general form that includes both those spoken of and others, so that it would function as a proverb and become a conclusion to the speech, and so that it would include those who were addressed indirectly in this admonition, namely the polytheists who were present. The implied sense is: "They are a losing people, since none feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people."

*Al-khusran* (losing) here means the loss of what would benefit them through their bad belief. It is likened to the loss of a merchant who wastes his capital through poor conduct, because by their complacency in present safety and their turning away from reflecting on what follows it, namely seizure resembling the act of a schemer, they have lost the benefit of their intellects and have lost themselves.

His saying, ﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾ (Qur'an 6:12), was mentioned earlier in Surah al-An'am, and His saying, ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ (Qur'an 7:9), was mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

It was also mentioned that applying the term *makr* (plan) to God's seizing of those deserving punishment after giving them respite is figurative, at His saying, ﴿They plotted, and God plotted; and God is the best of plotters﴾ (Qur'an 3:54), in Surah Al 'Imran.

Know that what is meant by "feeling secure from the plan of God" in this verse is the security of the same kind as the security of the denying people of the towns, which the discourse began to speak of from His saying, ﴿We never sent a prophet to a town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship, that they might humble themselves﴾ (Qur'an 7:94), then His saying, ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will come upon them by night?﴾ and the verses that follow. It is the security that arises from denying the report of the Messenger (ﷺ), and from the delusion that the religion of polytheism is the truth. So it is security that arises from disbelief. What is secured against is the threat of the messengers to them, and what is described as God's plan.

Among the kinds of feeling secure from God's punishment are other types, different from this security and close to it, and distant from it, according to the differences in people's inner states and the degrees of their intentions. As for those that rest on a legislative proof, there is no reckoning upon their holder. Such is the security of the Muslims from the sort of punishment that afflicted earlier nations, which rests on His saying, ﴿God would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ (Qur'an 8:33), and on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when there was revealed His saying, ﴿Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾ (Qur'an 6:65). He said: "I seek refuge in the glories of Your noble Face," and when it was revealed, "or from beneath your feet," he said: "I seek refuge in the glories of Your noble Face." When it was revealed, "or confound you into factions," he said: "This is easier." This was explained earlier in the commentary on this verse in Surah al-An'am.

Also like the security of the people of Badr from punishment in the Hereafter, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What makes you think? Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, for I have forgiven you." This was in the story of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a.

Likewise is the Prophet's ﷺ informing ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam that he will continue to hold fast to the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqa), and likewise the Prophets, for they are secure from the plotting of Allah, by Allah's informing them of this; and the friends of Allah (awliyaʾ Allah) are likewise. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62] ﴿those who believed and used to be God-fearing﴾ [Yunus: 63]. Among the wondrous things is what al-Khafaji mentioned, that the Hanafiyya said: feeling secure from the plotting of Allah is disbelief, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So none feels secure from the plotting of Allah except the people who are the losers﴾.

I have not ascertained the degree of authenticity of this hadith. We have mentioned more than once that what comes in the Qur'an of threats against the people of disbelief for their deeds is also intended to warn the Muslims against what resembles those deeds, to the degree that its resemblance is close.

﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins? And We seal their hearts, so they do not hear.﴾

This is conjoined to the sentence "Do the people of the towns feel secure...?" because both sentences share the meaning of an astonished interrogative. The discourse shifts from marveling at the condition of those who passed away to marveling at the condition of the present community, namely the Arab nation, who inherited the abodes of earlier nations and settled in them. Examples include the people of Najran and the people of Yemen, and those who settled the dwellings of Thamud, such as Baliyy, Ka'b, al-Daḥājim, and Bahra'. Also included are those who settled the dwellings of Madyan, such as Juhayna and Jarm. Likewise included are those who became great tribes and attained dominance over other tribes, such as Quraysh, Tayy', Tamim, and Hudhayl. Thus the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) functions as the definite article of prior reference (al-ʿahdī). It may also be intended that "those who inherit the land" refers to every nation that succeeded a nation before it, so that it includes ʿĀd and Thamud, since their prophets said to each of them: ﴿Remember when He made you successors﴾ [al-A'raf: 69], and so on. However, the idolaters among the Arabs of that day are the primary intended referents here. Thus the relative pronoun functions as the generic article (lām al-jins).

The interrogative in His words "Has it not become clear" is used for astonishment, like the one in "Do the people of the towns feel secure...?", marveling at the intensity of their misguidance, since they lacked guidance and admonition from the condition of those before them among the nations, and forgot that God is able to annihilate them if He wills.

The definite article in "the land" is the definite article of genus (ta'rīf al-jins). That is, they inherit any land that was the dwelling of a people before them. This is a common usage in Arabic speech, as they say, "This is the land of Tayy'." In the hadith about the funeral, "from the people of the land," meaning the inhabitants residing in their land, not the Muslim conquerors. Thus "land" in this sense is a generic noun applying to many individual instances, so its definiteness is generic, and by this usage it is pluralized as "aradīn." The meaning is: "Has it not become clear to those who inherit a land after its people..."

Inheritance (al-irth) is the passing of a dead person's property to one who has more right to it. It is used metaphorically for the resemblance of a living person to a dead one in attributes he possessed, such as honor or lordship, as His words, quoted from Zechariah, were explained: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam: 5], ﴿who will inherit me﴾ [Maryam: 6], meaning he will succeed me in prophethood. It may also be used for the common element between the two meanings, which is the general notion of succeeding one who has passed away. This is applicable here in either sense. For if the discourse means the people of Makkah, then inheritance is used in its metaphorical meaning. If it means the people of Makkah and the tribes who settled the lands of the earlier nations, then it is used in the common element. This is like His words: ﴿that the land shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. In any case, the qualifier "after its people" emphasizes the meaning of "inherit," intending to remind the listeners of what the people of the inherited land had been in the abundance of life, and then of the comprehensive, swift destruction they came to, depicting the admonition in its greatest form. This is like His words: ﴿and He will make you successors in the land, then He will see how you act﴾ [al-A'raf: 129].

The meaning of "lam yahdi" is: "did not make clear or explain to them." Guidance (al-hidāya) originally means showing the path to the traveler, and it became well known for general guidance, either metaphorically or as a figure of speech, as in His words: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6]. It has been established that this verb takes two objects: the first directly, and the second sometimes directly and sometimes through a preposition, either "li" or "ila." Accordingly, its transitivity to the first object by means of "li" in this verse is either because it is implicitly bearing the sense of "yubayyin" (make clear), or to strengthen the connection of the verb's meaning to the object, as in the expression "shakartu lahu" (I thanked him), and His words: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam: 5], and like His words: ﴿Has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them, through whose dwellings they walk?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 128] in Surat Ta-Ha.

"An" is the lightened form of "anna," and its subject is the dummy pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the clause "if We willed, We would afflict them" is its predicate. Since "anna," with an open hamza, is among the particles that definitely signify the verbal-noun sense (al-maṣdariyya), because it is composed of the heavy "inna" and the open light "anna" of the verbal-noun type, for this reason it is counted among the particles that introduce clauses (al-mawṣūlāt al-ḥarfiyya). What follows it is interpreted as a verbal noun formed from the word of its predicate, if the predicate is a singular derived noun, or from "kawn" (being), if its predicate is a clause. Thus the position of "an law nashāʾu aṣabnāhum" is the position of the subject of "yahdi." The meaning is: "Has it not been made clear to those who succeed the people in the land after them that the important matter is that, if We willed, We would afflict them for their sins, just as We afflicted those before them?"

These are the ones who associated others with God and denied Muhammad (ﷺ).

Affliction (al-iṣāba) is obtaining the desired thing with firm possession of it. So the meaning is: that We seize them in a seizure from which they cannot escape. The preposition "bi" in "bi-dhunūbihim" indicates causation, and it is not used to transitively extend the verb "aṣabnāhum."

[Page 28]

The clause "an law nashāʾu aṣabnāhum bi-dhunūbihim" stands in the position of a singular noun, which is the subject of "yahdi." Thus "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," which is one of the particles of emphasis and verbal-noun function, and its subject, in the lightened case, is an implied dummy pronoun of the matter. The clause of the condition of "law" and its answer is the predicate of "an."

"Law" is a conditional particle indicating that the non-occurrence of its answer is linked to the non-occurrence of its condition, whether in the past or the future. Since the verb of the condition here is in the present tense, it has the meaning of the past, because the tenses of the two verbs of the condition and the answer may not differ. They are varied in form only for mere stylistic variety, out of dislike for repeating the same form. Thus the sense of His words "law nashāʾu aṣabnāhum" is: our seizing them in the past for the sin of their denial did not occur, because of the non-occurrence of Our will in that, due to the wisdom of granting them respite, not because they were mightier than the destroyed nations or in a better condition than them. As He said: ﴿So have they not traveled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them, who were greater than them in strength and in traces left in the land? Then God seized them for their sins﴾ [Ghafir: 21], and so on. In this there is a threat that God may afflict them for their sins in the future, since no mighty one can prevent Him from that. The meaning is: the delay of punishment, together with their denial, deceived them, so they thought themselves protected from it, and they did not realize that the non-occurrence of its descent upon them is conditioned on the non-occurrence of Our will to bring it about, for a wisdom. Between them and the punishment there is nothing except that We will to seize them.

The verbal noun conveyed by "an," when the lightened "an" has a dummy pronoun of the matter as its subject, implies a firmly established affirmation drawn from the emphasized relation contained in "an" and its predicate. This is the subject of "yahdi." So the implied meaning of the verse is: "Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people the establishment of this important predicate: if We willed, We would afflict them for their sins?"

The meaning is: "Be astonished at how they did not come to realize that the delay of punishment from them is by the sheer will of Ours, and that it becomes due upon them when We will it."

The clause "wa-naṭba'u ʿalā qulūbihim" (And We seal their hearts) is not conjoined to the clause "aṣabnāhum," so that it would have the status of the answer to "law," because that would corrupt the meaning. For those who inherited the land after its people were already sealed upon their hearts, which is why the call of Muhammad (ﷺ), since his mission until the time of the revelation of this surah, had no effect on them. If it were the answer to "law," then sealing upon their hearts would become impossible, and this is corrupt. Therefore one of two possibilities is determined: either the clause "wa-naṭba'u" is conjoined to the whole interrogative clause, and so it has the same ruling of conjunction as the reports about the earlier and present nations. The implied sense is: "And We sealed upon their hearts." But it is phrased in the present tense to indicate the continuity of this sealing and its increase moment by moment. Or the "wa" is taken for resumption (al-istiʾnāf), and the clause is a new sentence, meaning: "And We now seal upon their hearts in the future, as We sealed upon them in the past." The sealing upon them in the past is known from other reports, such as His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ [al-Baqara: 6], and so on. Thus the clause serves as a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for ending the story. But the position of the "wa" at the beginning of the clause favors the first possibility, and it seems that the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) refuses to count resumption among the meanings of "wa."

The clause "fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn" (so they do not hear) is conjoined with "fa" to "naṭba'u," as a consequence of it. Hearing here means comprehending the import of what is heard, not the stopping up of the ears, by the evidence of His words "and We seal upon their hearts." The meaning of sealing was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿Rather, God sealed it upon them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa': 155] in Surat al-Nisa'.

[Page 30]

When the mention of the towns whose people denied God's messengers recurred, both specifically and generally, they became for the listeners like a present and visible thing that could be pointed to. So the demonstrative *tilka* ("those") was used to make them more vivid in the minds of the listeners, the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), so that they would take warning from the condition of the people of the towns and see that they are alike, and thus turn back to the truth.

The phrase *tilka al-qura* ("those towns") is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that serves as a summary (*fadhlaka*) of the narratives that precede it, from His saying ﴿We sent Noah to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], then His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We did not send a prophet into any town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship, so that they might humble themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], and so on.

*Al-qura* ("the towns") may be the predicate of the demonstrative, because bringing the towns to mind has made them as if witnessed by the listener, so pointing to them is pointing to them as a lesson about their condition. This serves the purpose of informing about them by name for someone who is not ignorant of the report, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35], meaning: this which you are looking at, by which you are branded, is your treasure. They already knew that it was their treasure, and the purpose of informing them that it is their treasure is to expose the error of their action. It is also possible that *al-qura* is an appositive (*bayan*) to the demonstrative.

The clause *naqussu 'alayka min anba'iha* ("We relate to you some of their reports") is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *al-qura* according to the first interpretation. The benefit of this circumstantial clause is the favour of mentioning their narratives, and as evidence for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since God taught him knowledge of the earlier peoples which his own knowledge had not preceded. It also contains the promise of more of this, by what the word *naqussu* indicates of renewal and continuity, and an indirect reproach to those who turn away from taking admonition from their reports.

Or it is a predicate of the demonstrative according to the second interpretation of *al-qura*.

The *min* ("some of") is partitive, because the reports of these towns include others not mentioned here, some of which are mentioned in other verses, and part of them was omitted because there was no need for them in conveying the message.

*Al-anba'* means reports (*akhbar*), and it has already been discussed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34], in Surah al-An'am.

What is meant by *al-qura* and the pronoun in *anba'iha* is its people, as indicated by the pronoun in *rusuluhum* ("their messengers").

The clause ﴿and their messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause *tilka al-qura*, because of the connection between the two clauses in their aim of drawing a parallel with the condition of those who denied Muhammad (ﷺ).

The plural *al-bayyinat* ("the clear proofs") indicates the repetition of clear proofs with each messenger. *Al-bayyinat* are the evidences that point to truthfulness, and this has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], in the story of Thamud in this surah.

The *fa* ("so") in His saying ﴿so they were not going to believe﴾ is for the sequence of the report of the non-occurrence of their belief after the report of the coming of the messengers to them with what should have moved them to belief.

The form *ma kanu li-yu'minu* ("they were not going to believe") conveys emphatic negation by the *lam* of denial (*lam al-juhud*), which indicates that the occurrence of belief was incompatible with their state of obstinacy in disbelief. The manner in which the *lam* of denial indicates emphasis of negation has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for any human that God should give him the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79], in Surah Al 'Imran. The meaning is: their non-belief continued, and disbelief took firm hold of them at a time when the expected course was that they should desist from it.

*Ma kadhdhabu* is a relative clause (*mawsul*) with its complement, and the returning pronoun, which is governed by a preposition, has been omitted, according to the manner of omitting such pronouns when the relative is governed by a preposition like the one omitted. It is not required that the two prepositions have the same complement, according to the view of the verifiers, including al-Radi, as in this verse.

The referent of the relative *ma* is what *kadhdhabu* ("they denied") points to: that is, they were not going to believe in something they had denied before, of what they were called to believe in, namely monotheism and resurrection. It is the nature of the relative *ma* that it refers to something non-rational, so the referent of *ma* here is not the messengers but what the messengers brought. For this reason the verb *kadhdhabu* here has an implied complement, the word *bihi* ("with it"), as is the distinction between *kadhdhabahu* and *kadhdhaba bihi*. He, may He be exalted, said ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], and He said ﴿Your people denied it, and it is the truth﴾ [al-An'am: 66]. The complement is omitted here for brevity, because the denial of the people of the towns has already been mentioned, beginning from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We did not send into any town a prophet without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship, so that they might humble themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 94]. In this context His saying has also preceded: ﴿But they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. For this reason, the complement of the verb *kadhdhabu* is not omitted in the parallel of this verse in Surah Yunus.

The meaning is: the clear proofs did not benefit them to believe in something which they had earlier denied at the beginning of the call. So the omitted noun governed by the form *qabla* ("before"), whose construction on *damm* indicates it, is to be estimated as: "before the coming of the clear proofs."

The negation of belief is attributed to the pronoun of all the people of the towns, on the basis of the majority, which is a common usage. The believers among them are excluded by His saying ﴿and We did not find in most of them any covenant; and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾.

As for His saying ﴿so God seals the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, its meaning is: like that strange sealing, which is derived from the report of their continued disbelief, and which is indicated by the verb *yatba'u* ("He seals"). Its parallels have already been mentioned more than once, including at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The meaning of sealing (*tab'*) has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa': 155], in Surah al-Nisa'.

The explicit mention of the subject in the clause *yatba'u Allah* rather than using a pronoun is because attributing the sealing to the proper name conveys a clear warning that this is a terrible sealing which leaves no outlet of guidance into their hearts, like His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿This is the creation of God﴾ [Luqman: 11], rather than saying "this is My creation." For this reason the present tense verb was chosen, which indicates the continuity and renewal of the sealing.

*Al-qulub* means intellects, and in the language of the Arabs, *qalb* ("heart") is one of the names of the intellect. This was discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿God has sealed their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The definite article in *al-kafirin* is the definite article of genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), which conveys comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), meaning: all disbelievers, both those mentioned and others.

In His saying ﴿and their messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs﴾ to the end of the verse, there is consolation for Muhammad (ﷺ), that what he met from his people is the custom of the earlier messengers, and that this is not due to any shortcoming on his part, nor to weakness in his signs, but rather to the sealing of the hearts of many of his people.

The clause *wa ma wajadna li-aktharihim min 'ahd* ("and We did not find in most of them any covenant") is coordinated with the clause ﴿and their messengers had certainly come to them﴾ and what follows from it, His saying ﴿so they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, as an alert to the entrenchment of disbelief in their souls, to the extent that the clear proofs they witnessed did not uproot it from them, nor did what God placed in the natural disposition (*fitrah*) of humanity, namely belief in one God and acceptance of the messengers who call to Him, nor did they keep what they had pledged to the messengers at the time of the call, namely that if the messengers came to them with clear proofs, they would believe in them.

The word *wijdan* ("finding") in the two places is metaphorical for knowledge, so it became one of the verbs of the heart. Its negation in the first place is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the absence of a covenant in the intended sense, that is, its fulfilment, because if it existed, the one who should know it and search for it when fulfilment of it is demanded would know it, especially since the speaker is the One from whom nothing is hidden, like His saying ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], meaning: nothing is forbidden except what has been mentioned. So the meaning of *wa ma wajadna li-aktharihim min 'ahd* is: "most of them had no covenant."

*Al-'ahd* means commitment and an emphatically confirmed promise, bound by something that prevents its breaking: an oath, a guarantee, or fear of disgrace. It is derived from *'ahida al-shay'*, meaning "he knew the thing," because the one who makes a firm promise knows it and takes care not to forget it.

The carrying out of what the one who made the commitment undertook is called fulfilment of the covenant (*al-wafa' bi-al-'ahd*). Thus *al-'ahd* here may mean the promise which the nations fulfilled for their messengers, like their saying: ﴿So bring us a sign if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 154], for the meaning of that is: if you bring us a sign, we will believe you. It may also mean a promise which the earlier nations pledged from the time of Adam, that they would not worship anyone except God, which is what is mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾ [Ya Sin: 60], and so on, so it was binding upon their descendants. It may also mean what human souls promised their Creator in the primordial time, as recounted in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This refers to God's creating the human natural disposition believing in its Creator and His oneness, and then idolatrous tendencies and satanic misguidance distorted it.

The occurrence of the name of this genus in a negative context requires its negation in all the senses in which it truly applies.

The meaning of the negation of finding it is the negation of its fulfilment, because the essence of the promise is established and exists, but since its realization appears only in the future, which is fulfilment, the non-fulfilment of it was made equivalent to the non-occurrence of it. The meaning is by estimating a noun governed by the preceding term: "We did not find for most of them any fulfilment of a covenant."

The non-finding of fulfilment of the covenant was attributed to most of them only to indicate the exclusion of the believers of each nation from this blame. The intended meaning of "most of them" is most of each nation, not one small nation among all the nations.

His saying ﴿and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾ is information that the non-fulfilment of the covenant by most of them was deliberate and treacherous. Because this meaning adds to what is in the preceding clause, it was coordinated and not made an emphasis (*ta'kid*) or explanation (*bayan*) of it, since *fisq* is disobedience to a command, and that is because they broke their promises deliberately for the sake of disbelief.

*In* is a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and after it is an omitted subject, which is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and the clause is its predicate, giving prominence to the importance of this report so that the listeners would know it.

The *lam* that enters the predicate of *wajadna* is the *lam* of commencement (*lam al-ibtida'*), taking into account that this predicate is the predicate of a clause that is the predicate of the noun that follows *in*. The *lam* was brought to distinguish between the lightened *in* and the negative *in*. A parallel of this was discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164].

[Page 34]

The ruling of breaking the covenant is attributed to most of the people of the towns, to make clear that the pronoun in *fa-ma kanu li-yu'minu* follows the mode of predominance (*taghlib*), in which the majority is used to represent the whole. Perhaps the reason for this explicit statement about this particular ruling is that it is a ruling of blame and reproach, so it was appropriate to exempt those to whom that reproach does not attach.
