The believers among them are excluded by His saying ﴿and We did not find in most of them any covenant; and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾.

As for His saying ﴿so God seals the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, its meaning is: like that strange sealing, which is derived from the report of their continued disbelief, and which is indicated by the verb *yatba'u* ("He seals"). Its parallels have already been mentioned more than once, including at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The meaning of sealing (*tab'*) has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa': 155], in Surah al-Nisa'.

The explicit mention of the subject in the clause *yatba'u Allah* rather than using a pronoun is because attributing the sealing to the proper name conveys a clear warning that this is a terrible sealing which leaves no outlet of guidance into their hearts, like His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿This is the creation of God﴾ [Luqman: 11], rather than saying "this is My creation." For this reason the present tense verb was chosen, which indicates the continuity and renewal of the sealing.

*Al-qulub* means intellects, and in the language of the Arabs, *qalb* ("heart") is one of the names of the intellect. This was discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿God has sealed their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The definite article in *al-kafirin* is the definite article of genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), which conveys comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), meaning: all disbelievers, both those mentioned and others.

In His saying ﴿and their messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs﴾ to the end of the verse, there is consolation for Muhammad (ﷺ), that what he met from his people is the custom of the earlier messengers, and that this is not due to any shortcoming on his part, nor to weakness in his signs, but rather to the sealing of the hearts of many of his people.

The clause *wa ma wajadna li-aktharihim min 'ahd* ("and We did not find in most of them any covenant") is coordinated with the clause ﴿and their messengers had certainly come to them﴾ and what follows from it, His saying ﴿so they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, as an alert to the entrenchment of disbelief in their souls, to the extent that the clear proofs they witnessed did not uproot it from them, nor did what God placed in the natural disposition (*fitrah*) of humanity, namely belief in one God and acceptance of the messengers who call to Him, nor did they keep what they had pledged to the messengers at the time of the call, namely that if the messengers came to them with clear proofs, they would believe in them.

The word *wijdan* ("finding") in the two places is metaphorical for knowledge, so it became one of the verbs of the heart. Its negation in the first place is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the absence of a covenant in the intended sense, that is, its fulfilment, because if it existed, the one who should know it and search for it when fulfilment of it is demanded would know it, especially since the speaker is the One from whom nothing is hidden, like His saying ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], meaning: nothing is forbidden except what has been mentioned. So the meaning of *wa ma wajadna li-aktharihim min 'ahd* is: "most of them had no covenant."

*Al-'ahd* means commitment and an emphatically confirmed promise, bound by something that prevents its breaking: an oath, a guarantee, or fear of disgrace. It is derived from *'ahida al-shay'*, meaning "he knew the thing," because the one who makes a firm promise knows it and takes care not to forget it.

The carrying out of what the one who made the commitment undertook is called fulfilment of the covenant (*al-wafa' bi-al-'ahd*). Thus *al-'ahd* here may mean the promise which the nations fulfilled for their messengers, like their saying: ﴿So bring us a sign if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 154], for the meaning of that is: if you bring us a sign, we will believe you. It may also mean a promise which the earlier nations pledged from the time of Adam, that they would not worship anyone except God, which is what is mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾ [Ya Sin: 60], and so on, so it was binding upon their descendants. It may also mean what human souls promised their Creator in the primordial time, as recounted in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This refers to God's creating the human natural disposition believing in its Creator and His oneness, and then idolatrous tendencies and satanic misguidance distorted it.

The occurrence of the name of this genus in a negative context requires its negation in all the senses in which it truly applies.

The meaning of the negation of finding it is the negation of its fulfilment, because the essence of the promise is established and exists, but since its realization appears only in the future, which is fulfilment, the non-fulfilment of it was made equivalent to the non-occurrence of it. The meaning is by estimating a noun governed by the preceding term: "We did not find for most of them any fulfilment of a covenant."

The non-finding of fulfilment of the covenant was attributed to most of them only to indicate the exclusion of the believers of each nation from this blame. The intended meaning of "most of them" is most of each nation, not one small nation among all the nations.

His saying ﴿and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾ is information that the non-fulfilment of the covenant by most of them was deliberate and treacherous. Because this meaning adds to what is in the preceding clause, it was coordinated and not made an emphasis (*ta'kid*) or explanation (*bayan*) of it, since *fisq* is disobedience to a command, and that is because they broke their promises deliberately for the sake of disbelief.

*In* is a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and after it is an omitted subject, which is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and the clause is its predicate, giving prominence to the importance of this report so that the listeners would know it.

The *lam* that enters the predicate of *wajadna* is the *lam* of commencement (*lam al-ibtida'*), taking into account that this predicate is the predicate of a clause that is the predicate of the noun that follows *in*. The *lam* was brought to distinguish between the lightened *in* and the negative *in*. A parallel of this was discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164].

[Page 34]

The ruling of breaking the covenant is attributed to most of the people of the towns, to make clear that the pronoun in *fa-ma kanu li-yu'minu* follows the mode of predominance (*taghlib*), in which the majority is used to represent the whole. Perhaps the reason for this explicit statement about this particular ruling is that it is a ruling of blame and reproach, so it was appropriate to exempt those to whom that reproach does not attach.

[Page 35]

This is a transition from the accounts of the earlier messages to the account of a great mission for a community that endured until the revelation of the Qur'an. God favored that community with His bounty, but it did not render the due thanks. It received its messenger with a mixture of obedience, refusal, submission, and aversion. God did not destroy it utterly. Instead, He showed it the recompense for its varied deeds, a recompense in proportion: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

The story of Moses' sending was singled out for this emphasis because of the momentous events it contains and the valuable reports it includes. His mission came with the greatest law before the law of Islam, and its messenger was sent as a guide and lawgiver, paving the way for a law that would come to a nation greater than it, one that would follow it. Also, the situation of those to whom he was sent resembles the situation of those to whom Muhammad ﷺ was sent. They were two large groups: one part followed Moses and another part disbelieved in him. Likewise, a great multitude followed Muhammad (peace be upon him), and a large group disbelieved in him. God destroyed those who disbelieved and gave victory to those who believed.

The word *thumma* ("then") indicates an interval. Moses (peace be upon him) was sent a long time after Shu'ayb, for when he set out from Egypt, he headed toward Madyan, hoping that God would guide him, and there he found Shu'ayb. His connection with Shu'ayb and his becoming related to him by marriage was a gradual step toward his acceptance of the message from God, exalted is He. So the interval is considered with respect to the whole of the peoples mentioned earlier, some of whom were separated from Moses by centuries, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Lot. Thus the interval indicated by *thumma* varies in duration, together with the sequential, rank-based sense of succession that the conjunction *thumma* implies when it links sentences, a sense that is always attached to it when sentences are joined by it. Therefore the particle *thumma* here is used in both its literal meaning of interval and its figurative meaning.

The pronoun in His saying *min ba'dihim* ("after them") refers to the towns, with regard to their inhabitants, just as the pronouns returned to them in His saying ﴿And their messengers had certainly come to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 101], and the verses that follow.

The *ba'* in *bi-ayatina* ("with Our signs") denotes accompaniment, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to Moses, meaning: accompanied by signs from Us. The *ayat* ("signs") are the proofs of the messenger's truthfulness, namely the miracles. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ [al-A'raf: 106] ﴿So he threw his staff, and suddenly it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-A'raf: 107]

"Fir'awn" (Pharaoh) is a generic proper noun (*'alam jins*) for the king of Egypt in ancient times, that is, before the Greeks ruled it, and it is a name from the language of the Copts. It is said that its origin in Coptic is *Faraha*, and perhaps the *ha'* in it is substituted for an *'ayn*, since *Ra'* is the name of the sun. Thus the meaning of *Faraha* is "the light of the sun," because they worshipped the sun, so they made the king of Egypt equivalent to the light of the sun, since he sets people right. This name was transmitted from them in the Jewish books and passed from them into Arabic, and it is likely something that Islam brought in. This name is similar to *Kisra* for the king of the kings of ancient Persia, *Qaysar* for the king of the Romans, *Nimrud* for the king of Canaan, *al-Najashi* for the king of Abyssinia, *Tubba'* for the king of the kings of Yemen, and *Khan* for the king of the Turks.

The name of the Pharaoh to whom Moses was sent is Merneptah II, one of the kings of the nineteenth dynasty of the dynasties that ruled Egypt, according to the chronology of European historians, and that was in the year 1491 BC.

*Al-mala'* means the group of the foremost people of a community, and it was mentioned shortly before. They were Pharaoh's ministers and the leaders of the people of Egypt, from among the priests and army commanders. God specified Pharaoh and his *mala'* because they were the people who loosed and bound, who would grant permission for the Children of Israel to be released. Moses was sent by God to the Children of Israel to free them from the bondage in which they lived in Egypt, and since their departure from Egypt depended on the command of Pharaoh and his *mala'*, God sent him to them so that they would know that God had sent Moses for this purpose. Within this, a call to Pharaoh to guidance was also achieved, because every prophet proclaims monotheism and commands guidance, even if the one commanded is not among those to whom he was sent, out of eagerness for guidance, although he does not remain among them or repeat that call.

The *fa'* in His saying *fa-zalamu* ("so they wronged") indicates immediate sequence, meaning: they hastened to deny.

*Al-zulm* (wrongdoing) is transgression against the right of another. It is permissible that *fa-zalamu* here be used in its original sense, with the *ba'* being causal. The object of *zalamu* is omitted to indicate generality, and the meaning is: they wronged everyone who had a right to benefit from the signs, that is, they prevented people from believing in them, and they harmed those who believed in Moses when they saw his signs, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Pharaoh said, "You believed in him before I gave you permission"﴾ [al-A'raf: 123], up to His saying ﴿"I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides"﴾ [al-A'raf: 124], and the verse.

They also wronged themselves when they were arrogant and did not believe, so the wrongdoing was on account of the signs, that is, on account of acknowledging them.

It is also possible that *zalamu* is taken to include the meaning of *kafaru* ("they disbelieved"), so it takes the *ba'* to introduce the signs, and the implied meaning is: they wronged when they disbelieved in them, because disbelief in the signs is wrongdoing, since wrongdoing is transgression against the truth. Whoever disbelieves in the clear proofs called signs has transgressed against the right of reflection and consideration.

The *fa'* in His saying *fa-unzur* ("so look") introduces a command based on this report, meaning: do not hesitate, upon hearing the report of their disbelief, to immediately reflect on what We will relate to you of their outcome.

What is to be observed is their outcome, which is indicated by His saying ﴿so We drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾. This observing is the observation of the intellect, which is reflection that leads to knowledge, and so it is among the actions of the hearts.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is intended is him and whoever reaches him. Or the addressee is unspecified, namely everyone who is capable of observing and taking lessons when hearing these verses. The implied meaning is: "Look, O observer," and this is a common usage in every speech directed to an unspecified person.

Since the outcome of the affair of Pharaoh and his *mala'* was a remarkable state, it was expressed by *kayfa*, which is used for asking about a state. The interrogation implied by *kayfa* requires an implied element, meaning: look at the outcome of the corrupters, which is asked about by *kayfa*.

The act of looking has been suspended from its object because an interrogative came after it, so the implied meaning becomes: "look," and then he began a statement with the clause "how was the outcome of the corrupters." Its implied form in such contexts is to assume: "look at the answer to 'how was the outcome of the corrupters.'"

The *'aqibah* is the end and final outcome of a matter, and it was mentioned earlier in the commentary on His saying ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the outcome of the deniers"﴾ [al-An'am: 11] in Surat al-An'am.

What is meant by "the corrupters" is Pharaoh and his *mala'*. This is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to draw attention to the fact that they were struck with a bad outcome because of their disbelief and corruption. Disbelief is the greatest corruption, because it is corruption of the heart, from which the corruption of actions arises. In a hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."

**Page 38**

﴿Moses said, "O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿It is due of me that I say nothing about God except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he cast his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

The statement of Moses is conjoined with the particle "wa" (and) and is not separated from what precedes it, even though the content of this statement serves as an explanation of the phrase "We sent Moses after them." This is because his saying "with Our signs" had already made it understood that the intention is to compare the condition of those to whom Moses was sent with the condition of the nations whose history has already been related, in their obstinate denial despite the manifest signs of truth. Thus the resemblance between the condition of the earlier people and the condition of the present deniers of Muhammad (ﷺ) would be complete. Accordingly, the narration of the dialogue between Moses and Pharaoh and his chiefs was presented as an independent report, because the statement of Moses here is not recounted alongside the showing of the sign. Rather, the sign was mentioned earlier. This differs from what is narrated in the stories before it, where the speeches of the messengers were recounted before the mention of the sign. Also, the whole story here has been related in summary by the phrases "We sent," "they wronged," and "see," so the saying "he said" became a detailed explanation of some of what preceded. Therefore it is not separated, since separation occurs only between two sentences, not between one sentence and several other sentences.

It is apparent that Moses's address to Pharaoh, "O Pharaoh," is an address of honour, since he called him by the title that denotes kingship and authority according to the custom of his people. It is not an act of arrogance toward him, because God, exalted is He, said to him and Aaron: "Speak to him gently" (20:44). It is also apparent that this statement of Moses is the first thing he addressed to Pharaoh, as indicated by the sura of Ta-Ha (Ṭā Hā).

**Page 39**

The narration of Moses's words is phrased with the emphatic particle *inna* (indeed), because the addressee is likely to deny or to be strongly doubtful about the truth of the report.

The choice of the attribute "Lord of the worlds" in announcing the Sender is a refutation of Pharaoh's belief that he is the lord of Egypt and its people, for he said to them, "I am your supreme lord" (79:24). When Moses described his Sender as "Lord of the worlds," this included Pharaoh and the people of his realm, so Pharaoh's claim that he is the god of Egypt is nullified by implication. This also covers all the lands and servants over whom Pharaoh did not claim to be a god, such as the Persians and the Assyrians.

As for his saying "it is due of me" (*ḥaqīqun ʿalayya*), Nafi' read it with the *yāʾ* at the end of "ʿalayya," which is the first-person pronoun suffix. The preposition "ʿalā" is attached to it, and the government of *ḥaqīq* by the preposition "ʿalā" is well known. God, exalted is He, said, "So the word of our Lord was due against us" (37:31). Also, *ḥaqīq* means *wājib* (obligatory), so its construction with "ʿalā" is clear.

*Ḥaqīq* is a second predicate of *innī* (indeed I), so in Nafi's reading the first-person pronoun in "ʿalayya" involves no shift (*iltifāt*, change of grammatical person). This differs from the case where *ḥaqīq* is taken as an attribute of *rasūl* (messenger). In that case the apparent requirement would be to use a third-person pronoun, saying "ḥaqīqun ʿalayhi," so the shift to the first person would be an *iltifāt*. The subject of *ḥaqīq* is the verbal noun derived from "an lā aqūla" (that I should not say), meaning: it is due of me that I do not say about God anything other than the truth.

*Ḥaqīq* is the form *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*, derived from *ḥaqqa* meaning *wajaba* (was obligatory) and *thabata* (was established), i.e., determined and obligatory upon me is the saying of the truth about God. The first "ʿalā" is for elevation in a figurative sense, and the second "ʿalā" means "ʿan" (about). The majority of readers read "ʿalā" with an *alif* after the *lām*, and it is the prepositional "ʿalā."

Concerning the attachment of "ʿalā" and its apparent object to *ḥaqīq*, there are several interpretations. The best of them is the view of al-Farra' and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi: "ʿalā" here means *bāʾ* (with/for), and *ḥaqīq* is a *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* (passive), i.e., *maḥqūq* (entitled/bound), meaning: the saying of the truth has been made a truth incumbent upon me. Compare the words of al-A'sha:

*la-maḥqūqatun an tastajībī li-qawlihi*
(She is indeed bound to respond to his word.)

And the words of Saʿid ibn Zayd: "Had Uhud collapsed upon you for what you did to Uthman, it would have been bound (*maḥqūqan*) to collapse."

**Page 40**

Among the interpretations is what the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "The more appropriate and more fitting to the subtleties of the Qur'an is that Moses emphasizes in describing himself as truthful in that situation, so he says: 'I am bound to the saying of the truth,' i.e., it is obligatory upon me that I be the one who utters it and who carries it out." His commentators said: The meaning is that if the saying of the truth were an intelligent person, I would be the one obligated to it, that it should proceed only from me and that I should be its speaker. On this view it is a metaphor based on implication: the saying of the truth is likened to intelligent beings who choose their places of arrival and departure, and what is appropriate to it is indicated by a feature of the comparison, which is that what suits it is determined upon it.

Among them is what was said: *ḥaqīq* was made to imply the meaning of *ḥarīṣ* (eager), so it governs "ʿalā" as an indication of that implication. Better than this is that *ḥaqīq* be made to imply the meaning of *makīn* (firmly established), and "ʿalā" is a metaphor for figurative elevation.

The sentence "I have come to you with a clear proof" is resumed as an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a resumptive clause that answers an implied question), because the situation of denial naturally provokes the question of a listener who would say: this is a strange claim that needs a proof.

*Bayyina* (clear proof) means argument. It was discussed earlier in the commentary on God's words, "Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord" (6:57), in the sura of al-Anʿam. Here the proof may mean the rational proofs for the truth of what Moses brought of monotheism and guidance, or it may mean the miracle that indicates the messenger's truthfulness. On the first view, the *bāʾ* in "bi-bayyina" marks the transitivity of the verb of coming. On the second view, the *bāʾ* marks accompaniment (*mulābasa*), meaning the capacity to manifest the miracle that God showed him, as in the sura of Ta-Ha: "What is that in your right hand, O Moses?" (20:17). It may also be understood in the more general sense that includes both types, according to what the statement of Moses, as translated here, allows.

The *fāʾ* in "fa-arsil" (so send) marks the consequence: the request to release the Children of Israel follows from the certainty of the message from the Lord of the worlds and from readiness to show the proof of it. Moses built his speech on what he trusted of the truth of his call, while being ready to demonstrate that truth by proofs, or by a miracle if Pharaoh asked for one, because it is the way of messengers not to begin by displaying miracles, in order to protect the station of messengership from exposing it to denial. This is what we explained at God's words: "And they swore by God with their most earnest oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it" (6:109), in the sura of al-Anʿam.

*Irsāl* (sending) means releasing and allowing. As in the saying: "He let her go free to graze." Here it is a linguistic metaphor for permission given to the Children of Israel to leave, which is what is demanded from Pharaoh.

**Page 41**

Restricting it with "maʿī" (with me) is because the purpose of bringing them out of Egypt is that they be with the messenger, so that he may guide them and manage their affairs.

Pharaoh's saying, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful," is necessarily to be understood as meaning: "If you have come with a miracle." Most occurrences of *āya* (sign) in the Qur'an refer to a miracle, and most occurrences of *bayyina* refer to a proof. So *bayyina* in Moses's words, "I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord," means the argument for establishing divinity and for the truth of his guidance to his people. Pharaoh was not persuaded by the proof of reason, or he was incapable of reflecting on it, so he moved to asking for something beyond the ordinary course of things. The meaning is: if you have come to us with the ability to manifest miracles. This is because Pharaoh said that before Moses showed his miracle. Thus the *bāʾ* in "bi-āya" is for a hypothetical accompaniment (*maʿiyya taqdīriyya*), i.e., "having the capacity for a sign," or the *bāʾ* is for accompaniment in the broad sense of *mulābasa*, i.e., "you have the capacity to manifest a sign."

His saying "then produce it" (*fa-ʾti bihā*) uses *ityān* (bringing) in the sense of manifesting, as a metonymy of a general kind (*majāz mursal*). The *bāʾ* in "bihā" marks the transitivity of the verb of bringing. Through this the link between the condition and the response becomes clear, because bringing the sign mentioned in the response is other than coming with the sign mentioned in the condition. The meaning is: if you came having the capacity to manifest a sign, then manifest this sign.

*Ilqāʾ* (casting) means throwing onto the ground, into water, or something similar. That is, he threw his staff from his hand. *Idhā* here is for sudden occurrence (*mufājaʾa*), meaning the happening of an event without prior expectation.

*Thuʿbān* is a great serpent. *Mubīn* is an active participle from *abāna*, which is intransitive and synonymous with *bāna* (became clear), meaning: manifest, that is, evident beyond any doubt or any imagining.

*Nazaʿa* means to remove the connection of one thing from another, as in the saying "he took off his garment." Here it means that he drew his hand out of the opening of his garment after he had put it in there, as mentioned in the suras of al-Naml and al-Qasas. When he drew it out, it became white, i.e., whiteness of light.

This whiteness is indicated by his words "to the onlookers," meaning a whiteness that the onlookers see with the sight of wonder at its whiteness. So the purpose of mentioning "to the onlookers" is to complete the meaning of the whiteness.

The *lām* in "lil-nāẓirīn" (to the onlookers): the commentators did not take the trouble to explain its meaning and its position, except that the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "*lil-nāẓirīn* is connected to *bayḍāʾ* (white)," without specifying the type of connection or the meaning of the *lām*, and his commentators and al-Baydawi remained silent about it. The apparent sense of his words "is connected" is that it is an adverbial phrase of looseness (*ẓarf laghw*) connected to *bayḍāʾ*. Perhaps this is because *bayḍāʾ* contains the sense of a verb, as if it were said: "it became white for the onlookers," just as a prepositional phrase is connected to a derived noun. So the meaning of the *lām* must be what Ibn Malik called the meaning of *taʿdiya* (transitivity), and by it he meant a specific transitivity, not transitivity in general, namely making an intransitive verb transitive to something that by its original form does not take an object. This is because that is found in all prepositions, so there is no doubt that he meant a specific transitivity whose reality he did not clarify. He illustrated it in the commentary on *al-Kāfiya* with God's words: "So grant me from Yourself a guardian" (19:5), and in the commentary on *al-Tashīl* he made this example an example of the meaning of resemblance to possession. Ibn Hisham preferred to illustrate transitivity with the phrase "How excellent is Zayd to ʿAmr" (*mā aḍrabā Zaydan li-ʿAmrin*).

They did not explain this specific transitivity by the *lām*. It appears to me that it is a purely verbal function, i.e., it does not convey a partial meaning like the meanings of particles. So the result is that they were confused in establishing the meaning of transitivity. In my view, God's words "white to the onlookers" are the best example for the *lām* being a marker of transitivity, and we may explain this meaning as bringing the complement marked with the *lām* (*mutaʿallaq*, the thing to which the *lām* attaches) closer to the thing it is connected to, without making it function as a direct object.

If you wish to trace the meaning of transitivity back to a root among the well-known meanings of the *lām*, then it apparently belongs to the branches of the meaning of resemblance to possession, as Ibn Malik's choice of this example for transitivity as an example of resemblance to possession implies.

Closer to this is that the *lām* means "ʿinda" (at/with), and the implication of God's words "white to the onlookers" is that it is white with a whiteness fixed in the sight of the onlookers. The adverbial phrase is then fixed, and it is taken as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun of his hand.

﴿Moses said, "O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿It is due of me that I say nothing about God except the truth. The statement of Moses is conjoined with the particle "wa" (and) and is not separated from what precedes it, even though the content of this statement serves as an explanation of the phrase "We sent Moses after them." Rather, the sign was mentioned earlier. This differs from what is narrated in the stories before it, where the speeches of the messengers were recounted before the mention of the sign. Also, the whole story here has been related in summary by the phrases "We sent," "they wronged," and "see," so the saying "he said" became a detailed explanation of some of what preceded. Therefore it is not separated, since separation occurs only between two sentences, not between one sentence and several other sentences.

It is not an act of arrogance toward him, because God, exalted is He, said to him and Aaron: "Speak to him gently" (20:44). When Moses described his Sender as "Lord of the worlds," this included Pharaoh and the people of his realm, so Pharaoh's claim that he is the god of Egypt is nullified by implication. This also covers all the lands and servants over whom Pharaoh did not claim to be a god, such as the Persians and the Assyrians.

As for his saying "it is due of me" (*ḥaqīqun ʿalayya*), Nafi' read it with the *yāʾ* at the end of "ʿalayya," which is the first-person pronoun suffix. The preposition "ʿalā" is attached to it, and the government of *ḥaqīq* by the preposition "ʿalā" is well known. God, exalted is He, said, "So the word of our Lord was due against us" (37:31). Also, *ḥaqīq* means *wājib* (obligatory), so its construction with "ʿalā" is clear.

*Ḥaqīq* is a second predicate of *innī* (indeed I), so in Nafi's reading the first-person pronoun in "ʿalayya" involves no shift (*iltifāt*, change of grammatical person). This differs from the case where *ḥaqīq* is taken as an attribute of *rasūl* (messenger). In that case the apparent requirement would be to use a third-person pronoun, saying "ḥaqīqun ʿalayhi," so the shift to the first person would be an *iltifāt*. The subject of *ḥaqīq* is the verbal noun derived from "an lā aqūla" (that I should not say), meaning: it is due of me that I do not say about God anything other than the truth.

*Ḥaqīq* is the form *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*, derived from *ḥaqqa* meaning *wajaba* (was obligatory) and *thabata* (was established), i.e., determined and obligatory upon me is the saying of the truth about God. The first "ʿalā" is for elevation in a figurative sense, and the second "ʿalā" means "ʿan" (about). The majority of readers read "ʿalā" with an *alif* after the *lām*, and it is the prepositional "ʿalā."

The best of them is the view of al-Farra' and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi: "ʿalā" here means *bāʾ* (with/for), and *ḥaqīq* is a *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* (passive), i.e., *maḥqūq* (entitled/bound), meaning: the saying of the truth has been made a truth incumbent upon me. Compare the words of al-A'sha:

*la-maḥqūqatun an tastajībī li-qawlihi*
(She is indeed bound to respond to his word.)

And the words of Saʿid ibn Zayd: "Had Uhud collapsed upon you for what you did to Uthman, it would have been bound (*maḥqūqan*) to collapse."

His commentators said: The meaning is that if the saying of the truth were an intelligent person, I would be the one obligated to it, that it should proceed only from me and that I should be its speaker. On this view it is a metaphor based on implication: the saying of the truth is likened to intelligent beings who choose their places of arrival and departure, and what is appropriate to it is indicated by a feature of the comparison, which is that what suits it is determined upon it.

Among them is what was said: *ḥaqīq* was made to imply the meaning of *ḥarīṣ* (eager), so it governs "ʿalā" as an indication of that implication. Better than this is that *ḥaqīq* be made to imply the meaning of *makīn* (firmly established), and "ʿalā" is a metaphor for figurative elevation.

The sentence "I have come to you with a clear proof" is resumed as an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a resumptive clause that answers an implied question), because the situation of denial naturally provokes the question of a listener who would say: this is a strange claim that needs a proof.

*Bayyina* (clear proof) means argument. It was discussed earlier in the commentary on God's words, "Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord" (6:57), in the sura of al-Anʿam. Here the proof may mean the rational proofs for the truth of what Moses brought of monotheism and guidance, or it may mean the miracle that indicates the messenger's truthfulness. On the first view, the *bāʾ* in "bi-bayyina" marks the transitivity of the verb of coming. On the second view, the *bāʾ* marks accompaniment (*mulābasa*), meaning the capacity to manifest the miracle that God showed him, as in the sura of Ta-Ha: "What is that in your right hand, O Moses?" The *fāʾ* in "fa-arsil" (so send) marks the consequence: the request to release the Children of Israel follows from the certainty of the message from the Lord of the worlds and from readiness to show the proof of it. Moses built his speech on what he trusted of the truth of his call, while being ready to demonstrate that truth by proofs, or by a miracle if Pharaoh asked for one, because it is the way of messengers not to begin by displaying miracles, in order to protect the station of messengership from exposing it to denial. This is what we explained at God's words: "And they swore by God with their most earnest oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it" (6:109), in the sura of al-Anʿam.

*Irsāl* (sending) means releasing and allowing. As in the saying: "He let her go free to graze." Here it is a linguistic metaphor for permission given to the Children of Israel to leave, which is what is demanded from Pharaoh.

**Page 41**

Restricting it with "maʿī" (with me) is because the purpose of bringing them out of Egypt is that they be with the messenger, so that he may guide them and manage their affairs.

Pharaoh's saying, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful," is necessarily to be understood as meaning: "If you have come with a miracle." Most occurrences of *āya* (sign) in the Qur'an refer to a miracle, and most occurrences of *bayyina* refer to a proof. So *bayyina* in Moses's words, "I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord," means the argument for establishing divinity and for the truth of his guidance to his people. Pharaoh was not persuaded by the proof of reason, or he was incapable of reflecting on it, so he moved to asking for something beyond the ordinary course of things. The meaning is: if you have come to us with the ability to manifest miracles. This is because Pharaoh said that before Moses showed his miracle. Thus the *bāʾ* in "bi-āya" is for a hypothetical accompaniment (*maʿiyya taqdīriyya*), i.e., "having the capacity for a sign," or the *bāʾ* is for accompaniment in the broad sense of *mulābasa*, i.e., "you have the capacity to manifest a sign."

His saying "then produce it" (*fa-ʾti bihā*) uses *ityān* (bringing) in the sense of manifesting, as a metonymy of a general kind (*majāz mursal*). The *bāʾ* in "bihā" marks the transitivity of the verb of bringing. Through this the link between the condition and the response becomes clear, because bringing the sign mentioned in the response is other than coming with the sign mentioned in the condition. The meaning is: if you came having the capacity to manifest a sign, then manifest this sign.

*Ilqāʾ* (casting) means throwing onto the ground, into water, or something similar. That is, he threw his staff from his hand. *Idhā* here is for sudden occurrence (*mufājaʾa*), meaning the happening of an event without prior expectation.

*Thuʿbān* is a great serpent. *Mubīn* is an active participle from *abāna*, which is intransitive and synonymous with *bāna* (became clear), meaning: manifest, that is, evident beyond any doubt or any imagining.

*Nazaʿa* means to remove the connection of one thing from another, as in the saying "he took off his garment." Here it means that he drew his hand out of the opening of his garment after he had put it in there, as mentioned in the suras of al-Naml and al-Qasas. When he drew it out, it became white, i.e., whiteness of light.

This whiteness is indicated by his words "to the onlookers," meaning a whiteness that the onlookers see with the sight of wonder at its whiteness. So the purpose of mentioning "to the onlookers" is to complete the meaning of the whiteness.

The *lām* in "lil-nāẓirīn" (to the onlookers): the commentators did not take the trouble to explain its meaning and its position, except that the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "*lil-nāẓirīn* is connected to *bayḍāʾ* (white)," without specifying the type of connection or the meaning of the *lām*, and his commentators and al-Baydawi remained silent about it. Perhaps this is because *bayḍāʾ* contains the sense of a verb, as if it were said: "it became white for the onlookers," just as a prepositional phrase is connected to a derived noun. This is because that is found in all prepositions, so there is no doubt that he meant a specific transitivity whose reality he did not clarify. He illustrated it in the commentary on *al-Kāfiya* with God's words: "So grant me from Yourself a guardian" (19:5), and in the commentary on *al-Tashīl* he made this example an example of the meaning of resemblance to possession. Ibn Hisham preferred to illustrate transitivity with the phrase "How excellent is Zayd to ʿAmr" (*mā aḍrabā Zaydan li-ʿAmrin*).

They did not explain this specific transitivity by the *lām*. It appears to me that it is a purely verbal function, i.e., it does not convey a partial meaning like the meanings of particles. So the result is that they were confused in establishing the meaning of transitivity. In my view, God's words "white to the onlookers" are the best example for the *lām* being a marker of transitivity, and we may explain this meaning as bringing the complement marked with the *lām* (*mutaʿallaq*, the thing to which the *lām* attaches) closer to the thing it is connected to, without making it function as a direct object.

The adverbial phrase is then fixed, and it is taken as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun of his hand.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 109–112:

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer. He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Put him and his brother off, and send heralds into the cities﴾ ﴿to bring you every knowing sorcerer."﴾

The phrase "the chiefs said" (qāla al-mala'), here, follows the manner of disjunction (al-faṣl), because it occurs within the exchange (al-mujāwara) taking place between Musa and Pharaoh and his chiefs, for it is one single dialogue.

The discussion of "the chiefs" (al-mala') has already preceded in the earlier stories. The chiefs of Pharaoh's people are their nobles, and they are the people of Pharaoh's assembly and counsel. At first, Musa's call was confined to Pharaoh in his assembly, and it was not in the sight and hearing of the common people, because God, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 43], and He said in this verse: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103]. His call was only made widely known in the later instance after the gathering of the sorcerers.

They spoke these words in the form of consultation with Pharaoh, and in order to derive an excuse for themselves regarding the confrontation with Musa's proof before their faces. So they excused themselves to one another, saying that Musa is merely a sorcerer, knowing in sorcery, who displayed to them what they had no precedent for among the works of sorcerers. This statement expressed the opinion of all the people of Pharaoh's assembly. Pharaoh himself shared in this view, because the Qur'an related of Pharaoh in another surah that he said to the chiefs around him: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾. This excuse they adopted and agreed upon; they followed their king in it, or he followed them in it. So each one of the people of that assembly had prepared himself for this excuse. Accordingly, the address in their saying ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾ is an address of some of them to others, and it arises from the groups of that chiefdom, passed between them, one to another.

As for the basis of their inference that Musa wants to drive them out of their land: either they analogised this from Musa's words ﴿so send with me the Children of Israel﴾, by the principle that what is permissible for a like applies to its like, meaning that he only displayed the removal of the Children of Israel as a pretext for removing everyone who believes in him, so that he might take them as followers and establish a kingdom with them outside Egypt. They claimed that this was a scheme from Musa to undermine Pharaoh's kingdom.

Or the chiefs of Pharaoh included men from the Children of Israel who were close to Pharaoh and among the people of opinion in the realm; they are the intended ones of the address, that is: he wants to drive out your people from your land, which you have settled for four centuries and which has become your homeland just as it is for the Egyptians. Their purpose in this is to remind them of love for their homeland, to bring them close to themselves, and to make them forget what they had suffered of oppression and subjugation by the Copts, out of their awareness of the awkwardness of the situation.

Or they knew that if the evidence of Musa and the helplessness of Pharaoh and his chiefs spread among the community, that would introduce a trial among the common people, so they would believe in Musa, and he would become king over Egypt, and drive Pharaoh and his chiefs out of it.

It is also permissible that the chiefs addressed Pharaoh with this. Thus the pronouns of address in His saying ﴿to drive you out of your land﴾ came in the plural form, to glorify the king, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord, send me back"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]. If the addressee is Pharaoh, as previously mentioned, then the "command" is intended as a binding request that must be obeyed, as the chiefs of Bilqis said: ﴿So see what you command﴾.

The sāḥir (sorcerer) is the doer of sorcery; the discussion of sorcery has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they taught people sorcery﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause "They said: Put him off" is the answer of the consulted people, so it is stripped of the conjunction particle because it proceeds in the manner of dialogue; that is: some of the chiefs responded by giving Pharaoh an opinion regarding what he must undertake. It is also permissible that the clause (qālū arjihi) is a substitute for the clause "the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said", by repeating the verb of saying, which governs the substituted-from element, if Pharaoh is the one intended by their words "so what do you advise?"

The verb (arjihi) is an imperative from irjā' which means delay. Nāfi', 'Āsim, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Ja'far read: arjihi with a jīm, then hā'; its original form is "arji'hu" with a hamza after the jīm, then the hamza was eased, so it became a quiescent yā', and it was treated like a weak letter in the imperative. The rest read with the hamza, quiescent, according to the original form. For them there are various established aspects regarding the vowels of the pronominal hā' and its lengthening, which are established in the science of readings.

The meaning: postpone the dispute with Musa until the sorcerers who counter his sorcery are brought. The Qur'an mentions the brother here to indicate that his mention was omitted at the beginning of the story, and he was mentioned in other than this story as a starting point.

The verb of sending is followed by (fī) rather than (ilā) because the verb here is not intended to be transitive to the recipients; rather, what is intended is the senders themselves, and this is the first object, for the meaning is: "and send heralds into the cities, they will bring you the sorcerers," so it is known that they are sent for searching and bringing, not for conveying.

This is close to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32] in Surat al-Mu'minun. In the Kashshaf, he said there: the verb was not construed with fī as it is construed with ilā, but the community was made a place for sending, as Ru'bah said: "You sent in it a Mus'ab, possessor of intrusion." "Ba'atha" has come in this manner in His saying: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have sent in every town a warner﴾. Something close to this has already preceded just before, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not send in any town a prophet﴾.

"Al-madā'in" is the plural of "madīna," which is of the form fa'īla, derived from "madana bi-l-makān" when he resided. Perhaps "madana" is the root from which "madīna" is derived, not the reverse; whatever the case, the more evident view is that the mīm of madīna is original, and for this reason it is pluralised as madā'in with a hamza, just as they said "ṣaḥā'if," the plural of "ṣaḥīfa." Had it been mafā'ila from dānahu, they would have said in the plural "madāyin" with a yā', like "ma'āyish."

The cities of Egypt at that time were numerous, and we will mention some of them at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities heralds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53] in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

It has been said they meant the cities of Upper Egypt (al-Sa'id), which were the seat of the scholars of sorcery.

"Al-hāshirūn" are those who gather people and assemble them.

The matter is that the chiefs of Pharaoh should have been wise men of statecraft. They knew that the matter of Musa's call could hardly remain hidden, and that if Pharaoh imprisoned him or opposed him, people would become certain that Musa's proof had prevailed, and that would become a pretext for doubt in Pharaoh's religion. So they judged it best to be gentle with Musa, and they hoped that among the sorcerers of Egypt there would be someone who would counter the signs of Musa, so that the proof against him would be manifest to the people.

The jazm of (ya'tūka) is as an answer to the imperative, to indicate the strength of the causal connection between the sending and the coming. The estimate is: "If you send, they will come to you." It has been said regarding such a construction that it is jussive by a deleted imperative lām, and that the clause is a substitute for "arsala" (send) by a substitution of inclusion, meaning: "Send them, commanding them, so let them come to you with every knowing sorcerer." This usage is common in Arabic speech with the verb of saying, such as: ﴿Say to My servants who believe: let them establish prayer﴾; so likewise whatever carries the meaning of saying, as here.

Every (kull) used here carries the sense of abundance, meaning: with a great gathering of sorcerers, which is likely to be all of that kind.

Al-Jumhur read: bi-kulli sāḥirin ('ālim). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read: "bi-kulli saḥḥārin" (with the intensive form), for emphasis in the knowledge of sorcery. Thus the description ʿalīm serves as an emphasis of the sense of intensity, because the description ʿalīm, which is among the patterns of intensity, indicates the strength of knowledge of sorcery. The complement of ʿalīm is omitted, because it has come to occupy the position of verbs of disposition. The context indicates that what is intended is the strength of his knowledge of sorcery.

[p. 46]

The clause "The sorcerers came to Pharaoh" is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the clause "They said: Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every skilled sorcerer" (﴿قالوا أرجه وأخاه وأرسل في المدائن حاشرين يأتوك بكل ساحر عليم﴾). The sentence contains concision by omission (ījāz ḥadhf, brevity achieved by leaving out words). The implied sense is: "They said: Delay him and his brother, and send [gatherers]," so Pharaoh sent gatherers into the cities, they gathered [the sorcerers], and the sorcerers came from the cities and attended Pharaoh.

The definite article in "al-saḥaraẗu" (the sorcerers) is the definite of prior reference (taʿrīf al-ʿahd), meaning the sorcerers already mentioned. Their attendance before Pharaoh was on the day Moses had appointed for the contest with the sorcerers, which is mentioned in Surat Ṭāhā.

The clause "They said: Indeed for us there is surely a reward (﴿إن لنا لأجرا﴾)" is an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī, a clause answering an implied question), with the implied question: "What did the sorcerers say when they stood before Pharaoh?"

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥafṣ and Abū Jaʿfar read ﴿إن لنا لأجرا﴾ beginning with the particle inna without the interrogative hamza. The rest read it with an interrogative hamza before inna.

Under both readings the meaning is interrogative, as the answer "Yes" (naʿam) clearly shows, and the interrogative hamza is elided for lightness in the first reading. The meaning may also be declarative under the first reading, because they were so confident of obtaining the reward that they placed it within the realm of what is reported about Pharaoh, and Pharaoh's answer "Yes" would then confirm what they had reported about him.

The indefinite "ajran" (a reward) is indefinite of magnitude (tankīr taʿẓīm), indicated by the context of the king's status and the greatness of the task. The pronoun "naḥnu" (we) is a emphatic restatement of the pronoun in "kunnā" (we were). It signals their worthiness to prevail and their confidence that they are the most knowledgeable of people in magic, so they emphasised the pronoun to strengthen its meaning. It is not a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), since the intention is not restriction (qaṣr), because their statement that they are the victors already dispenses with restriction. It is clear that in their assumption the one defeated would be Moses, peace be upon him.

Pharaoh's answer "Yes" (naʿam) is a response to what they asked, or a confirmation of what they had surmised. This applies under the two possibilities mentioned in their earlier words "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." The particle naʿam confirms the content of the statement it answers. It is an affirmation after a declaration and an informing after a question, confirming the matter asked about. Both meanings are possible here under Nāfiʿ's reading and those who agree with him, but under the other readings only the second meaning is determined.

The conjunction of the clause "Indeed you are surely among those brought near" (﴿وإنكم لمن المقربين﴾) is to what the answer particle contains, since the implied sense is: "Yes, for you there is a reward, and indeed you are among those brought near." It is not an instance of prompting (ʿaṭf al-talqīn), because prompting is considered only where there are two speakers, not one speaker.

The clause "They said: O Moses" (﴿قالوا يا موسى﴾) is disconnected (fuṣilat) from what precedes because it occurs in the form of a dialogue among them, Pharaoh and Moses, since these were the speakers in that assembly.

"Immā" (either) is a particle indicating alternation between one of two things or several things. It has no governing function and is not governed, and what follows it is governed by the verb in the sentence. It functions as if it were part of a word, like the definite article "al-", as in the verse of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:

"They are two plans: either captivity and obligation, or blood, and death is more fitting for the free."

The phrases "an tulqiya" and "an nakūna naḥnu al-mulqīn" may be in the nominative position as subject of an inchoative, with the predicate omitted. That is: "Either your casting comes first, or our being the casters comes first." The context indicates the predicate, since they came to cast their magical instruments and claimed that Moses was like them.

In the Kashshāf (of al-Zamakhsharī) on Surat Ṭāhā, he made "immā an tulqiya" the predicate of an omitted subject, whose sense is: "The matter is your casting or our casting." Since what happens cannot be free of one of these two matters, the statement does not convey information, because the information is self-evident, like "The sky is above us." So the sentence must be used in a sense other than informing, namely choice: "Either you begin by casting your magical instruments, or we begin; you choose one of the two." This is why the two infinitive phrases can be placed in the accusative governed by an omitted verb of choice, as al-Farrāʾ suggested and as al-Zamakhsharī permitted in the Kashshāf on Surat Ṭāhā. That is: "Choose that you cast, or our being the casters." The sorcerers, in offering the choice of priority, showed their confidence in their power and that they were the victors, whether Moses began with the acts or they began.

The way the choice indicates this is that priority in illusions and trickery is more effective for the one who begins, because its first impression passes into the souls and settles there, so the souls are more strongly affected by it than by what follows. Perhaps also they wished to test the extent of Moses' confidence in what was apparent to him, namely whether he regarded both options as equal, or whether he eagerly wished to be the one who went first. For weakening the soul has a great effect in terrifying it and nullifying its resolve. They addressed him with words that terrify Moses and magnify their standing in his mind, since they took care to express what indicates their own selves, strengthening the indication in the hearer's soul, which is expressed in their speech by the emphatic pronoun in "and either that we be the casters."

From this you know that the context does not allow the supposition that they indicated a desire to cast their magic before Moses, because that would contradict showing that the two options were equal for them. This differs from what is in the Kashshāf and elsewhere. Likewise, Moses' answer, "Cast," is a show of contempt for them, since he permitted them to display their illusions and magic openly. For God strengthened Moses' soul through that answer, so that his victory over them after they had begun would be the most conclusive proof and the strongest refutation of excuse. From this it appears that there is nothing in Moses' command to them to go first, peace be upon him, that justifies opposing the call to truth, because the people were known for disbelief in what Moses brought, so opposing him is not a renewal of disbelief. Also, they came determined to oppose him, so his permission to them is not an endorsement. Rather, they gave him the choice to go first or to let them go first, and he chose that they go first, for a divine wisdom that makes the miracle more manifest, and because his allowing them to go first served to establish the proof against them more fully. Perhaps God placed this in his soul. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of beginning by stating the doubt to one who is confident he will refute it.

The clause "So when they cast" (﴿فلما ألقوا﴾) is conjoined to an omitted element for concision. The sense is: "So they cast." For the words "when they cast" imply this omitted element. The object of "they cast" is omitted because it is evident, that is: they cast their magical instruments.

The meaning of "they bewitched the eyes of the people" (﴿سحروا أعين الناس﴾) is: they made them affected by magic through the illusions and trickery they cast.

The transitive use of the verb "they bewitched" with "eyes" as object is a rational metonymy (majāz ʿaqlī, a figure in which the attribution is to something other than its real agent). The eyes are the instrument by which illusions reach perception, whereas they actually bewitched the minds. Therefore, if it were said "they bewitched the people," it would convey the same meaning, but the subtle point of drawing attention to the fact that magic consists of visible illusions would be lost. A similar addition is the mention of the eyes in the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"Thus do as long as you live, when they flee, and advance when the eyes of people scatter."

That is: when people scatter in fear that results from seeing various dangers.

"Istirhāb" (causing terror) means seeking fear, that is, dread. They reinforced the illusions of magic with other matters that stir the fear of onlookers, so that the illusions would take a firmer hold on their hearts. These other matters were words and acts that give the impression that something frightening is about to happen, such as telling the people: "Take your precaution, beware, and do not approach; something great will happen, and the chief of the sorcerers will appear," and similar deceptions, nonsense, shouting, and amazement.

You may also take the "s" and "t" in "wa-istarhabūhum" (and they terrified them) as intensive, meaning: they terrified them with great terror, just as one says "istakbara" (he became arrogant) and "istajāba" (he responded).

I have already explained in my commentary on God's words "teaching people magic" (﴿يعلمون الناس السحر﴾) from Surat al-Baqara that the basis of magic is imagination and intimidation.

Magic is described as "great" (ʿaẓīm) because it is among the greatest things sorcerers do, since it combined what was dispersed among the sorcerers of the kingdom, namely hidden properties whose causes are concealed from the common people through deception.

The sorcerers, in offering the choice of priority, showed their confidence in their power and that they were the victors, whether Moses began with the acts or they began.

The way the choice indicates this is that priority in illusions and trickery is more effective for the one who begins, because its first impression passes into the souls and settles there, so the souls are more strongly affected by it than by what follows. Perhaps also they wished to test the extent of Moses' confidence in what was apparent to him, namely whether he regarded both options as equal, or whether he eagerly wished to be the one who went first. For weakening the soul has a great effect in terrifying it and nullifying its resolve. They addressed him with words that terrify Moses and magnify their standing in his mind, since they took care to express what indicates their own selves, strengthening the indication in the hearer's soul, which is expressed in their speech by the emphatic pronoun in "and either that we be the casters."

From this you know that the context does not allow the supposition that they indicated a desire to cast their magic before Moses, because that would contradict showing that the two options were equal for them. This differs from what is in the Kashshāf and elsewhere. Likewise, Moses' answer, "Cast," is a show of contempt for them, since he permitted them to display their illusions and magic openly. For God strengthened Moses' soul through that answer, so that his victory over them after they had begun would be the most conclusive proof and the strongest refutation of excuse. From this it appears that there is nothing in Moses' command to them to go first, peace be upon him, that justifies opposing the call to truth, because the people were known for disbelief in what Moses brought, so opposing him is not a renewal of disbelief. Also, they came determined to oppose him, so his permission to them is not an endorsement. Rather, they gave him the choice to go first or to let them go first, and he chose that they go first, for a divine wisdom that makes the miracle more manifest, and because his allowing them to go first served to establish the proof against them more fully. Perhaps God placed this in his soul. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of beginning by stating the doubt to one who is confident he will refute it.

The meaning of "they bewitched the eyes of the people" (﴿سحروا أعين الناس﴾) is: they made them affected by magic through the illusions and trickery they cast.

Therefore, if it were said "they bewitched the people," it would convey the same meaning, but the subtle point of drawing attention to the fact that magic consists of visible illusions would be lost. "Thus do as long as you live, when they flee, and advance when the eyes of people scatter."

That is: when people scatter in fear that results from seeing various dangers.

They reinforced the illusions of magic with other matters that stir the fear of onlookers, so that the illusions would take a firmer hold on their hearts. The clause "The sorcerers came to Pharaoh" is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the clause "They said: Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every skilled sorcerer" (﴿قالوا أرجه وأخاه وأرسل في المدائن حاشرين يأتوك بكل ساحر عليم﴾). The sentence contains concision by omission (ījāz ḥadhf, brevity achieved by leaving out words). The implied sense is: "They said: Delay him and his brother, and send [gatherers]," so Pharaoh sent gatherers into the cities, they gathered [the sorcerers], and the sorcerers came from the cities and attended Pharaoh.

The definite article in "al-saḥaraẗu" (the sorcerers) is the definite of prior reference (taʿrīf al-ʿahd), meaning the sorcerers already mentioned. Their attendance before Pharaoh was on the day Moses had appointed for the contest with the sorcerers, which is mentioned in Surat Ṭāhā.

The clause "They said: Indeed for us there is surely a reward (﴿إن لنا لأجرا﴾)" is an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī, a clause answering an implied question), with the implied question: "What did the sorcerers say when they stood before Pharaoh?"

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥafṣ and Abū Jaʿfar read ﴿إن لنا لأجرا﴾ beginning with the particle inna without the interrogative hamza. The rest read it with an interrogative hamza before inna.

Under both readings the meaning is interrogative, as the answer "Yes" (naʿam) clearly shows, and the interrogative hamza is elided for lightness in the first reading. The meaning may also be declarative under the first reading, because they were so confident of obtaining the reward that they placed it within the realm of what is reported about Pharaoh, and Pharaoh's answer "Yes" would then confirm what they had reported about him.

The indefinite "ajran" (a reward) is indefinite of magnitude (tankīr taʿẓīm), indicated by the context of the king's status and the greatness of the task. The pronoun "naḥnu" (we) is a emphatic restatement of the pronoun in "kunnā" (we were). It signals their worthiness to prevail and their confidence that they are the most knowledgeable of people in magic, so they emphasised the pronoun to strengthen its meaning. It is not a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), since the intention is not restriction (qaṣr), because their statement that they are the victors already dispenses with restriction. It is clear that in their assumption the one defeated would be Moses, peace be upon him.

Pharaoh's answer "Yes" (naʿam) is a response to what they asked, or a confirmation of what they had surmised. This applies under the two possibilities mentioned in their earlier words "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." The particle naʿam confirms the content of the statement it answers. It is an affirmation after a declaration and an informing after a question, confirming the matter asked about. Both meanings are possible here under Nāfiʿ's reading and those who agree with him, but under the other readings only the second meaning is determined.

The conjunction of the clause "Indeed you are surely among those brought near" (﴿وإنكم لمن المقربين﴾) is to what the answer particle contains, since the implied sense is: "Yes, for you there is a reward, and indeed you are among those brought near." It is not an instance of prompting (ʿaṭf al-talqīn), because prompting is considered only where there are two speakers, not one speaker.

It has no governing function and is not governed, and what follows it is governed by the verb in the sentence. It functions as if it were part of a word, like the definite article "al-", as in the verse of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:

"They are two plans: either captivity and obligation, or blood, and death is more fitting for the free."

The clause ﴿wa-awḥaynā﴾ ("And We inspired") is conjoined to the preceding clause, "they bewitched the eyes of the people, and terrified them, and they produced a great magic." It therefore falls within the scope of the answer of *lammā* (when/as soon as), meaning: when they threw down, they cast their spells, and We inspired to Mūsā (Moses), "Throw down your staff for them."

The *an* (أنْ) is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*) for the verb *awḥaynā*. The *fa-* (الفاءُ) indicates immediate sequence (*ta'qīb*), signifying the swiftness with which its action surprised them: as soon as it was thrown, it began to swallow. The context implies two omitted clauses, for the sense is: so he threw it, and life entered into it and it became a serpent, and then, behold, it was swallowing. The first omitted clause is indicated by the command to throw, and the second by the swallowing, because that is the nature of a living creature. A staff, when life enters it, becomes a serpent without any change of form.

*Talaqquf* (التَّلَقُّفُ) is an intensive form of *laqf*, which means swallowing and gulping down.

*Mā* (ما) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: what they fabricate.

*Ifk* (الإفْكُ) means turning away from something. It is also applied to falsehood, and to fabricated lies, because there is in it a turning away from the truth and a concealing of reality. Thus it is not called *ifk* except for a deliberately contrived and disguised lie. Magic is called *ifk* because what appears from it contradicts reality, so it is likened to a false report.

The majority of reciters read *talaqqafa* with a doubled *qāf*, whose original form is *tatalaqqafu*, meaning that it strives and exerts itself to swallow as much as it can. Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read it with a sukūn on the *lām* and a light *qāf*, in the pattern of the unaugmented form.

The use of the present tense in *talaqqufu* and *ya'fikūna* indicates renewal and repetition, while bringing the striking image to mind. The meaning is: then, behold, its swallowing is renewed in response to the renewed and repeated fabrications of theirs. Calling their magic *ifk* is evidence that magic has no real effect, and that it is nothing but imaginings and deceptive appearances.

His saying ﴿fa-waqaʿa al-ḥaqq﴾ ("so the truth came to pass") is a consequence of *talaqqufu mā ya'fikūn* ("it swallows what they fabricate"). *Waqaʿa* (الوُقُوعُ) literally means a thing falling from a height to the ground, as in "the bird fell (*waqaʿa*)" when it descended to the ground. The word is used metaphorically for the manifestation of a matter of high standing, because its manifestation was by divine support, so it is likened to something that descended from a height. *Waqaʿa* is also used for "taking place," because what has taken place resembles what has come down to the ground. This is a common metaphor, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿wa-inna al-dīna la-wāqiʿ﴾ ["Indeed, the judgment is bound to occur"] [al-Dhāriyāt 51:6], meaning: it is established and will occur. The meaning here is: so the truth became manifest and was realised.

Perhaps the choice of the word *waqaʿa* here, rather than *nazala* ("descended"), is in consideration of the verb of throwing, because a thrown object falls to the ground. Thus the falling of the staff to the ground and the manifestation of the truth were concurrent.

*Al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) is the established matter that agrees with proof (*burhān*). Its opposite is *al-bāṭil* (falsehood). Here *al-ḥaqq* means the truthfulness of Mūsā, the soundness of his miracle, and the fact that what the staff did was the creation of God, and a effect of His power.

*Baṭala* (بَطَلَ) literally means "to vanish." The intended meaning is the vanishing of its purpose and the cessation of an alleged effect of a thing. One says *baṭala saʿyuhu* ("his effort was in vain"), meaning it brought no benefit; and *baṭala ʿamaluhu* ("his deed was lost"), meaning it was wasted and went unrewarded. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-yubṭil al-bāṭil﴾ ["and He nullifies falsehood"] [al-Anfāl 8:8], meaning: He removes its effect and what they intended from it. Falsehood is that which has no benefit, or no good in it. Hence the opposite of truth was called *bāṭil*, because it is something from which the desired effect does not come, namely acceptance by sound minds. This usage became so widespread that *bāṭil* came to function like a fixed noun whose meaning is the opposite of truth. *Bāṭil* is also used as an active participle of *baṭala*, thus matching the verbal noun in form, and the intended meaning of each is determined by context. The verb *baṭala* may therefore be derived from the verbal noun *buṭlān*, or it may be derived from the noun *bāṭil*, meaning that it was described as *bāṭil*, like *fahid* and *asad* (nouns of the pattern *fa'il*).

Here it may be interpreted in both senses. In the first case the meaning is: the effects of what they were doing were then annulled. In the second, the meaning is: what they were doing was characterised as *bāṭil*. On this second interpretation, the verb must be understood as meaning the manifestation of the matter, not its occurrence or coming into being, because their doing being false is a fixed attribute of it from before Mūsā cast his staff, but at the casting of the staff its falsehood became apparent. What weakens this reading is that using the verb to mean the manifestation of an event, rather than its existence or occurrence, departs from the basic usage, and one should not resort to it without a reason.

As for those who interpreted *baṭala* as meaning *in'adama* ("ceased to exist") and interpreted *mā kānū ya'malūn* ("what they were doing") as the ropes and staffs of the magicians, their interpretation departs from the usage and from the context.

The addition of His saying ﴿wa-baṭala mā kānū ya'malūn﴾ ("and what they had been doing was nullified") after ﴿fa-waqaʿa al-ḥaqq﴾ is a restatement of the content of ﴿fa-waqaʿa al-ḥaqq﴾, to register the condemnation of their deed and to announce their failure, as a comfort to the Muslims and a warning to the polytheists and the disbelievers like them.

The phrase ﴿mā kānū ya'malūn﴾ refers to the magic, meaning: the people's imaginings that the magicians' staffs and ropes were moving like serpents were nullified. It is not described as "magic" here, pointing to the fact that it was a marvellous magic, for which they had exerted themselves and brought their utmost skill.

The clause ﴿fa-ghulibū﴾ ("so they were overcome") is conjoined to it with *fa-*, indicating that their defeat came immediately after the staff swallowed their fabrications.

*Hunālika* (هُنالِكَ) is a demonstrative of place, meaning "in that place." So they were defeated at that place, which conveys the obviousness of their defeat and its manifestness to every present witness.

*Inqilāb* (الِانْقِلابُ) is the reflexive form of *qalaba*, and *qalb* means changing and altering a state. Most often it denotes a change from a customary state to a strange state.

*Inqilāb* is commonly used also for returning to the place from which one came out, because the one who returns has reversed the state he was in when he left.

*Inqalaba* is among the verbs that come with the meaning of *ṣāra* ("became"), and this is the intended meaning here, namely: they became abased. The choice of the word *inqalabū* rather than *rajaʿū* ("returned") or *ṣārū* ("became") is because it corresponds to the word *ghulibū* in form, and because of what the root of its derivation suggests of returning to a lower state. Thus the word *inqalabū* is more eloquent.

*Ṣaghār* (الصَّغارُ) means humiliation, and that humiliation is the humiliation of the manifestation of their impotence, and the humiliation of the disappointment of their hopes, of the reward and nearness to Pharaoh that they had anticipated.
