In the hadith: "Taking omen is polytheism." Its interpretation is that it is among the remnants of the religion of polytheism. After the act of taking omen, the preposition "bi" occurs, which is the "bi" of causation, entering upon the thing that prompts the omen. It may also be said: "He took omen from such-and-such."

The conjunction of "and those with him" (wa man ma'ahu), i.e., those who believed in him, is because the people of Pharaoh reckoned that the cause of Moses' ill omen was what he brought of religion, because it does not please their gods and their religion. Had it not been for his religion, he would not have been ill-omened, as Thamud said: ﴿You were among us a source of hope before this﴾ [Hud: 62].

"Ala" (unquestionably/indeed) is a particle of opening that indicates the great importance of the report that follows it, as an instruction to the community, and as an allusion to the polytheists of the Arabs.

"Al-ta'ir" (the bird) is a noun for the bird that is stirred up in order to take omen of good or ill. It is used here figuratively (isti'arah) for the true cause of the befalling of calamities upon them, by way of mushakalah (association by similarity of wording) with their saying "yattayyaru." Thus the true cause, which is what they deserved punishment for from God's anger, was likened to the bird.

"'Inda" (with) is used in the sense of disposal, figuratively, because the thing disposed of is like one fixed in a place. That is: the cause of their ill omen is determined by God. This is as occurs in the hadith: "There is no bird but your bird." So what God has decreed for people was expressed as "bird" by way of mushakalah with His saying "no bird." And whoever interprets "al-ta'ir" as fortune has strayed far from the context.

The restriction (qasr) derived from "innama" (only) is restrictive relative to a specific context: the bad state of their condition is a punishment from God, not from Moses and those with him. This does not contradict the fact that the believers know that the cause of the befalling of calamities upon the polytheists who opposed the messengers is their polytheism and their denial of the messengers. They know this from the reports of the messengers, or by the truthfulness of insight and sound reasoning, as Abu Sufyan said on the night of the Conquest, when God had guided him: "I know that if there were with Him another god, it would have availed me nothing." As for the polytheists and their likes among the people of misguided beliefs, they attribute the origin of harm and benefit to things that coincide with the occurrence of harm and benefit, so they imagine that coincidence to be causation. For this reason you find them seeking knowledge of the occurrence of good and evil from other than their causes. Among that is seeking lots by arrows, as has been mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ma'idah.

The clause "Indeed, their omen is only with Allah, but most of them do not know" (﴿ألا إنما طائرهم عند الله ولكن أكثرهم لا يعلمون﴾) is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and for that reason it is separated (fusilat) from what precedes it. The istidrak (corrective qualification) conveyed by "but" (lakinna) arises from what the emphasis placed on the preceding statement might suggest: its being introduced by the particle of opening (ala) and containing the form of restriction (qasr). The matter is such that intelligent people should not be ignorant of it, so it is corrected by stating that most of those people do not know.

The pronoun in His words "most of them" (akthariham) refers to those who said, "This is ours" (﴿لنا هذه﴾). The knowledge is negated from most of them only as an alert that a few of them do know the opposite, but they follow the saying of the majority.

[Page 68]

﴿They said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not be believers in you."﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood as distinct signs; but they were arrogant, and they were a criminal people.﴾

The clause (وقالوا, "they said") is coordinated with the clause ﴿And We had already seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought﴾. They met the calamities that Allah afflicted them with, so that they might take heed, by increasing in delusion. They despaired of taking heed from them and defied Musa when he challenged them with them. They said: "Whatever sign you bring us of the wondrous works of your magic, we will not be believers in you," meaning: "So do not exhaust yourself with magic."

(مَهْما, mahma, "whatever") is a noun that carries the meaning of a conditional particle. Its origin is (ما, ma), either the relative pronoun or the indefinite noun denoting generality, and (ما, ma) was compounded with it to make it conditional, just as (ما) was compounded with (أيْ, ayy), (مَتى, mata), and (أيْنَ, ayna), so that they became conditional nouns. The first alif was changed into a hāʾ, to avoid the repetition of two similar sounds and because the hāʾ is close to the alif, so it became مَهْما. Its meaning is "some thing whatsoever," and since it is indefinite, it is followed by (مِن, min) of specification, meaning: "If you bring us any of the signs, we will not be believers in you."

(مَهْما) is in the nominative position as a subject, the implied sense being: "Whatever thing you bring us with," and its predicate is the conditional clause and its response. It may also be in the accusative position as the object of a verb that is omitted and indicated by the mentioned (تَأْتِنا بِهِ, "you bring us with it"). The implied sense is: "Whatever thing you bring us, you bring it to us."

The pronoun in (بِهِ, "with it") is masculine in agreement with the wording of (مَهْما), which has the meaning of (أيِّ شَيْءٍ, "whatever thing"). The pronoun in (بِها, "with them") is feminine, in agreement with its position after the specification of (مَهْما) by the feminine noun (آيَةٍ, "sign").

(مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is a specification of the indefiniteness of (مَهْما).

The (آيَة, āyah) is the indicative sign. Its discussion has already been given in the commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire﴾ (2:39), and in His words: ﴿They say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ (6:37).

They named what Musa brought a sign by reference to the purpose for which Musa challenged them when he brought it, because Musa was bringing it to them as evidence for the truth of his message. They did not regard it as a sign, but they followed Musa in the naming, as indicated by their words ﴿to bewitch us with them﴾. In this there is mockery, as Allah related about the polytheists of Makkah: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, you are indeed a madman!"﴾ (15:6), as indicated by their saying: "Indeed you are a madman."

The clause ﴿so we will not be believers in you﴾ conveys emphasis in asserting the negation of their belief in Musa, because in their speech they used what the nominal sentence contained, which indicates the establishment and permanence of this negation, together with what the particle (بِ, bi) conveys of emphasis on the negation, and what the fronting of the complement of (مُؤْمِنِينَ, "believers") conveys of their concern with Musa, in making belief conditional upon him, with the negation applied to his name.

The (فاء, fa) in His words (فَأرْسَلْنا, "So We sent") is for the consequence, showing that the afflicting of them with these calamities follows from their obstinacy and defiance.

The (إرْسال, irsāl, "sending") in its literal sense is directing a messenger or a message, and it is construed with (إلى, ila) for the second object. It is here given the sense of sending from above, and so it is construed with (عَلى, ʿala) for the second object. Allah said: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ (105:3), and: ﴿And in ʿAd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ (51:41). The particle (عَلى) indicates that the clause ﴿We sent﴾ is consequent upon the punishment, a consequence of punishment and not a consequence of the increase of signs.

The (طُّوفان, ṭūfān) is a heavy, overwhelming flow of water that covers many areas and floods the dwellings and the fields. It has been said that it derives from (الطَّوَاف, al-ṭawāf, "circling"), because the water circles around the dwellings, meaning that its flow repeats around them. The flood did not enter the land in which the Children of Israel were, which was the land of (جاسان, Jasan, Goshen).

The (جَرَاد, jarād) is a flying insect of the family of the cricket and the beetle. It has six wings of yellow and red colours that spread out when it flies. It comes in large numbers, and a company of them is called a (رِجْل, rijl, "foot"). It destroys crops and trees, eating the leaves, the ears of grain, and the bark of trees, and so it is one of the causes of famine. It struck the land of the people of Pharaoh and did not strike the land of the Children of Israel.

The (قُمَّل, qummal), pronounced with a dammah on the qāf and a shaddah on the mīm with a fatḥah in the popular readings, is the name of a kind of large tick called (الحُمْنان, al-ḥumnān), with a dammah on the unpointed ḥāʾ, a sukūn on the mīm, and two nūns; its singular is (حَمْنانَة, ḥamnānah). It sucks human blood, and it is different from (القَمْل, al-qaml, "lice") with a fatḥah on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm, which is among the tiny insects found in the hair of the head and on the skin of the body, arising from the decay of the skin due to its dirt and grease, and often from the decay of the scalp. A large company of ticks afflicted the Copts, and it was difficult to guard against them, and perhaps they afflicted their livestock.

The (ضَفادِع, ḍafādiʿ) is the plural of (ضِفْدَع, ḍifdaʿ, "frog"), an animal that walks on four legs, drags its belly on the ground, swims in water, and lives in pools and stagnant water. Its croaking sounds like gurgling, and it is called (نَقِيق, naqīq). A large company of them afflicted them; they fell into their food, leapt into the cooking pots, fell into the mouths of the springs and the waterskins, and into the houses, spoiling whatever they fell into, and people trod on them, so the houses became filthy with them. The land of (جاسان, Jasan), the dwelling of the Children of Israel, was spared from them.

The (دَم, dam, "blood") is well known. It has been said that they were afflicted with a spreading nosebleed among them. It has also been said that the waters of the Copts became like blood in colour, as mentioned in the (التَّوْراة, al-Tawrāh, Torah). Perhaps this was due to the appearance of a red worm in the water, so the water was likened to blood. The waters of (جاسان), the village of the Children of Israel, were spared.

Allah named these (هاتِهِ, hātihi, "these") signs, because they are indications of the truth of Musa, by their being linked with the challenge, and because they are indications of the wrath of Allah upon them, by their combined force against them when they insisted on disbelief and defiance.

(آياتٍ, āyātin, "signs") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "the flood" and what is coordinated with it. (مُفَصَّلاتٍ, mufaṣṣalāt, "distinct") is a passive participle from (فَصَّلَ, faṣṣala), the doubled form which indicates intensity of separation. The literal meaning of (فَصْل, faṣl) is distinguishing between two things so that one does not mix with the other, and the word is used figuratively for removing confusion and ambiguity in meanings. In (مُفَصَّلاتٍ), as an adjective of (آياتٍ), the figurative sense of separation, namely the removal of confusion, is intended, because this is most fitting for signs and proofs. That is, they are signs about which there is no doubt that they are such, for whoever looks with the gaze of reflection.

It has been said that what is meant is that some of them are separated from others in time, that is, they did not all occur at one time, but some occurred after others. On this view, the form (تَفْعِيل, tafʿīl) indicates the lengthening of the interval between one and the next. It follows on this view that the punishment was stronger and lasted longer, as indicated by His words: ﴿And We do not show them any sign except that it is greater than its sister﴾ (43:48). It has been said that between one of them and the next was an interval of a month or of eight days, and that each one lasted for eight days or more. On this view, the more suitable reading is to make (مُفَصَّلاتٍ) a second circumstantial state of "the flood" and "the locusts," and not an adjective of (آياتٍ).

The (فاء, fa) in His words (فَاسْتَكْبَرُوا, "but they were arrogant") is for consequence and sequence, meaning: their arrogance followed from the sending of the flood and what came after it, just as their delusion followed from their being seized with years of drought, their thinking that this was due to the ill omen of Musa and those with him. Thus it is known that the nature of their thinking was corrupt in its foundation, namely the drawing of meanings from the opposites of their proofs. This is evidence of their immersion in error and abandonment, and their distance from happiness and success, so they remain entangled in the mire of wretchedness.

(اسْتِكْبار, istikbār, "arrogance") means intense pride, as indicated by the (سِين, sīn) and (تاء, tāʾ) of the form, meaning they regarded themselves as great, that is, they magnified themselves against believing in Musa and invalidating their religion, since they turned away from believing in those distinct signs.

The clause ﴿and they were a criminal people﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿they were arrogant﴾. The meaning is: they were arrogant and refused to acknowledge the indication of those signs, and they committed crime. The report of their crime was expressed in the nominal form to indicate the permanence of the attribute of criminality in them, its firm establishment in them, and its entrenchment in them before the arrogance occurred. In this there is an alert that the entrenched attribute of criminality in them was the cause of the arrogance that proceeded from them. Thus (كان, kāna, "were") indicates the continuity of the report, which is the attribute of criminality. (الإجْرام, ijrām, "criminality") is the act of committing a crime (جُرْم, jurm), and it was discussed earlier in the commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminals﴾ in this surah.

﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) befell them, they said, "O Moses, invoke your Lord for us by the covenant He has made with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, at a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾

Al-rijz is punishment (al-'adhab). The definite article in al-rijz here is for prior reference, meaning the punishment already mentioned, which is what is stated in His saying, ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ up to His saying, ﴿distinct signs﴾. Al-rijz is also one of the names of plague (al-ta'un). It was already discussed at His saying, ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment (rijzan) from the sky﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. It is therefore possible that al-rijz here means plague, that is, a plague struck them and drove them to humble supplication to Moses, peace be upon him. Its mention has been omitted for brevity, so the sense is: "We sent upon them the punishment, and when the punishment befell them..." etc. Al-rijz is mentioned among the signs in His saying, ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ etc., singling it out for mention because it has a remarkable story: it compelled them to acknowledge the signs of Moses and the existence of his Lord, the Exalted.

This plague is the pestilence described in chapter eleven of the Book of Exodus: "Thus says the LORD: About midnight I will go out into the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the millstones, and all the firstborn of the livestock." Then it says in chapter twelve: "And it came to pass at midnight that the LORD struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, and Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians; and there was a great cry in Egypt... And he called for Moses and Aaron by night and said, 'Rise up, get you forth from among my people, both you and the children of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take also your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone; and bless me also.'" And so on. It is said that seventy thousand men died that day from the Copts alone, and none of the Children of Israel was harmed by it.

Their saying, ﴿invoke your Lord for us﴾, was not an expression of faith in God and in the prophethood of Moses. Rather, they were polytheists who permitted the plurality of gods and that some nations and regions had gods specific to them. From their great observation of the signs of Moses there crept into their minds the idea that Moses had a lord who has authority and power, and that this lord had afflicted them with calamities because they had harmed his servant. So they asked Moses to ask his lord to restrain (yukuffa) the punishment from them, and in return (jaza'uhu) to permit the Children of Israel to leave Egypt to worship their Lord, as the Torah reports from Pharaoh in chapter twelve: "Then he said, 'Rise up, get you forth from among my people, both you and the children of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, your God.'" Worshippers of many lords permitted that one lord might overcome others, as happens between kings, as is shown by the myths of the Greeks (al-mithulujiyya, mythology) and the story of Homer's Iliad. So it appeared to Pharaoh that the way to be rid of the Children of Israel was for them to worship their Lord in a land other than Egypt, where there were other lords. For this reason he said "your Lord" and did not say "our Lord."

The object of the verb of supplication has been omitted because the meaning is clear, that is: "invoke your Lord for us so that He restrains (yakuffa) from us," as indicated by their later statement, ﴿If you remove the punishment from us﴾. The Torah in chapter twelve also records Pharaoh's saying to Moses and Aaron, "and bless me also."

Moses' condition had left Pharaoh confused; he did not know whether Moses was a messenger from a god other than the gods of the Copts. For this reason Moses said to him, ﴿by the covenant He has made with you﴾, that is, by what He has informed you of and deposited with you of secrets. This is the expression of one who is perplexed about the matter, whose evidences are confused for him.

The preposition (ba') in "bima 'ahida 'indaka" is for the transitivity of the verb of supplication. The particle (ma) is a relative pronoun with an unspecified reference, meaning: "invoke Him by what your Lord has taught you of the means of answering your supplication with your Lord." This implies that they permitted that Moses was sent by a lord who belonged to him, on the basis of their permitting the plurality of gods.

The clause ﴿If you remove the punishment from us﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory type (istinaf bayani), because their request that Moses supplicate for the removal of the punishment from them, given their prior disbelief in it, prompts Moses to ask: "So what is the reward for that?"

The lam is a preliminary to the oath (lam al-qasam), and the clause ﴿we will surely believe﴾ is the answer to the oath.

Their promise to believe in Moses is a promise to believe that he is truthful in being sent from the Lord of the Children of Israel to bring them out of the land of Egypt. It is not a promise to follow the religion that Moses, peace be upon him, brought, because they were denying him in that and claiming he was a magician who wanted to drive people out of their land. For this reason the verb of belief is linked to Moses and not to the name of God. This promise came in accordance with their assumption that the Lord to whom Moses called was a lord specific to him and his people, as indicated by their saying, "invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you." They made their intention clear by their saying, ﴿and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you﴾.

The clause ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them﴾ indicates that Moses called upon God to lift the plague and it was lifted. This is stated explicitly in the Torah, and it is omitted here for brevity.

His saying, ﴿at a term which they were to reach﴾, is connected to "kashafna" (We removed), given that removing the punishment means removing the death caused by the plague. So the removal of death is limited to a term which they will reach, namely the term God determined for their destruction. The end point is therefore considered with regard to the act of removal, not to its object, which is the punishment.

The clause ﴿behold, they broke their word﴾ is the answer to (lamma), and (idha) is a linking particle for the answer, because the answer of the conditional is a nominal clause. Since (idha) is a particle that conveys the sense of suddenness, it carries the meaning of a verb, as if it were said: "they suddenly broke the covenant," that is, they hastened to it and did not delay. This is a description of them with the concealment of disbelief in Moses and the concealment of breaking the oath.

Naks (breaking) in its literal sense is the undoing of twisted thread from a rope or yarn. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And be not like her who unravels her yarn after it had been strong, into separate strands﴾. Naks is borrowed for failing to fulfil a covenant, just as the rope (habl) is borrowed for a covenant in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except by a rope from God and a rope from men﴾. So in His saying "yankuthun" there is a contingent metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya).

This breaking was that after Pharaoh had permitted the Children of Israel to leave and they had departed from the land of Goshen (Jasan) at night, some of Pharaoh's close associates said to him, "What have we done, letting Israel go from our service?" Pharaoh regretted it, and he prepared an army to overtake the Children of Israel in order to bring them back to their dwellings, as is found in chapter fourteen of the Book of Exodus.

﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) befell them, they said, "O Moses, invoke your Lord for us by the covenant He has made with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, at a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾

Al-rijz is punishment (al-'adhab). The definite article in al-rijz here is for prior reference, meaning the punishment already mentioned, which is what is stated in His saying, ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ up to His saying, ﴿distinct signs﴾. Al-rijz is also one of the names of plague (al-ta'un). It was already discussed at His saying, ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment (rijzan) from the sky﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. It is therefore possible that al-rijz here means plague, that is, a plague struck them and drove them to humble supplication to Moses, peace be upon him. Its mention has been omitted for brevity, so the sense is: "We sent upon them the punishment, and when the punishment befell them..." etc. Al-rijz is mentioned among the signs in His saying, ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ etc., singling it out for mention because it has a remarkable story: it compelled them to acknowledge the signs of Moses and the existence of his Lord, the Exalted.

This plague is the pestilence described in chapter eleven of the Book of Exodus: "Thus says the LORD: About midnight I will go out into the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the millstones, and all the firstborn of the livestock." Then it says in chapter twelve: "And it came to pass at midnight that the LORD struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, and Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians; and there was a great cry in Egypt... And he called for Moses and Aaron by night and said, 'Rise up, get you forth from among my people, both you and the children of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take also your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone; and bless me also.'" And so on. It is said that seventy thousand men died that day from the Copts alone, and none of the Children of Israel was harmed by it.

Pharaoh regretted it, and he prepared an army to overtake the Children of Israel in order to bring them back to their dwellings, as is found in chapter fourteen of the Book of Exodus.

This is the point of the lesson (ʿibrah) in the story. The verse is a consequence drawn from the story, the conclusion (fadhlakah) of the narrative. After describing the obstinacy of Pharaoh and his chiefs, their denial of Moses' mission, and their demand that Moses bring a sign, they witnessed the sign of the staff turning into a serpent and the change in the color of his hand. They accused Moses of sorcery and of evil intent, and the magicians opposed Moses' miracle until Moses prevailed over them. God also afflicted the people of Pharaoh with calamities that were made into signs of the truth of Moses, yet they persisted in arrogance and obstinacy until they were forced to promise Moses that they would believe and release the Children of Israel with him, and they made a covenant to that effect. When God lifted the plague from them, they broke their word. God then informed that this resulted in the uprooting of the arrogant and obstinate, and the liberation of the believers who had been oppressed.

This is the point of the lesson. For this reason the verb is connected with the particle fa, which indicates sequence and causation. The passage follows the same mode of conclusion with which the earlier stories were concluded.

Intiqam (retribution) is an ifti'al form, and it means a severe punishment resembling naqm, which is the anger of rage at an offense of aggression against the one who takes revenge, one who rejects and hates its perpetrator.

The original function of the ifti'al form is to express the reflexive (mutawaʿah) of a transitive verb, such that the subject of the reflexive is the object of the base verb. The base verb "naqima" (to be displeased with) was not heard in the form "naqamahu fa-intaqama," meaning he angered him and he punished. So this reflexive has lost its base verb. They construed it with the one punished through min al-ibtidaʾiyyah (from), to indicate that he is the origin and cause of the punishment and that he deserves it. The discussion of the base form of this verb was already given at the words of His Exalted saying: ﴿Yet you took revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord﴾ (7:126).

[p. 75]

Their drowning was an act of retribution from God for His own sake, because they denied God's sole divinity, or they denied His divinity altogether. It was also retribution on behalf of the Children of Israel, because Pharaoh and his people wronged the Children of Israel, humiliated them, and enslaved them unjustly.

Al-ighraq (drowning) means casting into water that is deep and that overwhelms the one cast into it, leaving him no breath. It is an explanation of the retribution and a detailing of its general statement. So the fa in His saying ﴿fa-aghraqnahum﴾ indicates sequence in mention. It is the connection of a detailed statement to a general one, as in His saying: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ (2:54).

The author of al-Kashshaf interpreted the verb sought here as meaning resolve, so the meaning would be: "We intended to take retribution on them, so We drowned them." Its verification was discussed previously at His saying ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-yamm means the sea and the great river. It is said to be an Arabic word. This is the view of al-Kashshaf, which derived it from tayammum (intending), because it is intended by those who benefit from it. Some philologists said it is an arabized word from Syriac, whose original form there is "yama." Shaydalah said it is from Coptic. Ibn al-Jawzi said it is from Hebrew. Perhaps it occurs in all these languages. Perhaps its origin is Arabic, and other Semitic languages took it from Arabic.

The term here refers to the Sea of Qulzum, which is called in the Torah "the Sea of Suph," and it is the Red Sea. The word yamm has also been applied to the Nile in His saying: ﴿Put him into the chest, then cast it into the river﴾ (20:39), and His saying: ﴿If you fear for him, then cast him into the river﴾ (28:7). The definiteness in His saying (al-yammi) here is the definiteness of mental reference (al-ʿahd al-dhihni) according to the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani), which the grammarians call the definiteness of the genus (taʿrif al-jins). This is because the lesson is not concerned with a specific sea, but with one instance of this kind.

Pharaoh and his army were drowned in the Red Sea when they pursued the Children of Israel, intending to prevent them from leaving the land of Egypt. An allusion to this was made in Surat al-Baqarah, and its detailed account will come at His saying ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾ (10:90) in Surat Yunus.

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-annahum﴾ indicates causation, meaning: "We drowned them as a recompense for their denial of the signs."

Ghaflah (heedlessness) is the absence of the mind from remembering something. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And indeed We were unaware of their study﴾ (6:156) in Surat al-Anʿam. Here it is intended as deliberate neglect, namely turning away from reflection on the signs and refusing to consider their indication of Moses' truthfulness. Applying the word heedlessness to this is therefore metaphorical.

[p. 76]

This is an allusion to the polytheist Arabs in their turning away from reflecting on the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and on the proof of the miracle of the Qur'an. For this reason the causation of their turning away for their drowning is mentioned explicitly again, along with what is derived from the fa-connection in His saying ﴿So We took retribution on them and drowned them in the sea﴾, as an alert to the listeners to move from the story to the lesson.

The report about their turning away is expressed in the nominal sentence form, to indicate that this turning away is established for them and firmly rooted in them, and that it is the cause of the denial, whose predicate is expressed in the verbal sentence form, to indicate that it recurs whenever the signs recur.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 137:

﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land, which We had blessed.﴾

It is conjoined to "So We took vengeance upon them." The meaning: We seized them with the punishment they deserved, and We recompensed the Children of Israel with a great blessing.

The meaning of "awratha" (caused to inherit) was discussed earlier, at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people…﴾. Here the intended meaning is that the Children of Israel were given possession of the whole of the Holy Land after its people, from among the nations who had held it, such as the Canaanites and others. It has been said that Pharaoh held authority over the lands of al-Sham, but there is no need for this, since the verse does not specify the one from whom the inheritance was taken.

The people who were oppressed are the Children of Israel, as occurs in the other verse: ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾. The description of them was shifted from the form of idafa (possessive construction) to the form of a relative clause for two purposes. The first: to indicate the cause of the report, namely that God gave them possession of the land and made them a ruling community as a recompense for them, because they endured enslavement, out of God's jealousy for His servants.

The second: an allusion to the good tidings to the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ) that they too shall have the final outcome of authority, as the Children of Israel had, as a reward for their patience in the face of harm for the sake of God, and a warning to the polytheists that the authority of their religion will vanish.

The meaning of "yustad'afun" (were oppressed): they were enslaved and humiliated. The sin and ta' here are for reckoning (considering something to be so), like "istanjaba" (he deemed him noble), or for emphasis, as in "istajaba" (he responded).

The "mashariq" (eastern parts) and "maghareb" (western parts) are plural in view of the multiplicity of directions, since direction is a relative matter that multiplies with the multiplicity of assumed places. What is meant by them is the encompassing of places.

"Al-ard" (the land) is the land of al-Sham, which is the Holy Land. It begins from the northeastern shores of the Red Sea and ends at the shores of the Sea of Rome, that is the Mediterranean, and at the borders of Iraq, the borders of the lands of the Arabs, and the borders of the lands of the Turks.

"Allati barakna fiha" (which We had blessed) is a descriptive phrase modifying either "the land" or its "eastern and western parts," because their referents are identical. That is, We decreed blessing for it. The discussion of blessing has already passed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿We would have opened upon them blessings﴾ in this surah, meaning: We replaced for them the land of Egypt from which they had been expelled with a land better than the land of Egypt.

* * *

﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and what they had been building.﴾

This is conjoined to the clause "And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit…" etc. The purpose of this report is His saying "because of their patience," to honour the virtue of patience and its good outcome. It is on this basis that this clause was conjoined to the preceding one; otherwise the good word of God regarding the Children of Israel includes their inheritance of the land which God blessed, so that from the clause "And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit" to its end it takes the position of an appended conclusion that is not conjoined, and the conjunction would have required the phrase "because of their patience."

"Kalima" (word): it means speech. Here it may be that what is intended is the utterance God promised the Children of Israel through the tongue of Moses in His saying, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land," or through the tongue of Abraham, and it is the promise of giving them possession of the Holy Land. Then the fulfilment of the word is the realisation of its promise, the realisation being likened to a thing whose parts are completed. It may also be that it is the word of God in His knowledge and decree, which is God's will to release them from the enslavement of the Copts and His will to give them possession of the Holy Land, like His saying, "and His word which He cast to Mary."

The completion of the word in this sense is the manifestation of its effective connection in external reality, as in the words of Moses: "O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you." The discussion of this has already passed at His saying, may He be exalted, "And the word of your Lord was fulfilled in truth and justice," in Surat al-An'am.

"Al-husna" (the good): an adjective of "kalima," and it is an adjective of honour, as one says "al-asma' al-husna" (the most beautiful names). That is, the word of your Lord, exalted above breaking promise. It may also be that what is intended is its goodness for the Children of Israel, even though it was harmful for Pharaoh and his people, because justice is good even if it involves harm to the one judged against.

The address in "Rabbika" (your Lord) is to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is inserted into the mention of the story as an indication that the One who brought about the victory of Moses and his community over their enemy is your Lord, so He will grant victory to you and your community over your enemies, because He is that Lord who gave victory to the earlier believers, and that is His custom and practice. There is no shift in the address from the third person to the second, since the referents of the pronouns differ.

The verb "tamma" (was fulfilled) is transitive with "ala" to indicate that "tamma" implies the meaning of bestowing, or the meaning of "haqqat" (was realised).

The "ba'" in "bima sabaru" (because of their patience) denotes causation, and "ma" is verbal (masdariyya), meaning: because of their patience in the face of harm in the matter of God. In this is an alert to the benefit of patience and that the patient one arrives at victory and the realisation of hope.

"Al-tadmir" (destruction): severe devastation. It is the verbal noun of "dammara al-shay'" when one makes it ruined (damir), derived from "al-damar" (with a fatha on the dal), which is an intransitive noun. One says "damara al-qawm" (with a fatha on the mim), "yadmurun" (with a damma on the mim), "damaran", when they all perished, so they are "damirun". The apparent view is that applying "tadmir" to the destruction of what was made is metaphorical, its relationship being generality, since the apparent meaning of tadmir is the destruction of a person.

"Ma kana yasna'u Fir'awn" (what Pharaoh had been making): the structures he erected among the constructions. The attribution of the making to him is a rational metaphor, since he is the one who commanded the making. As for its attribution to the people of Pharaoh, it is literal rational attribution with respect to the people as a whole, not to each individual, by way of predominance.

"Ya'rishun" (they built): they produce from gardens having trellises. The "arish" is what is raised of vine trellises, and it is also applied to the many palm trees cultivated at one root. Perhaps the gardens of the Copts were like this, as some depicted images on their temples, carved and painted, bear witness. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And He it is who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am: 141] in Surat al-An'am.

Its verb "arasha" is of the patterns "daraba" and "nasara". The first is the reading of the majority; the second is read by Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim. That is because God destroyed the homes of Pharaoh and his mentioned people, and devastated their gardens, for what they had done wrong, through neglect, or through an earthquake, or at the hands of the armies of their enemies who ruled Egypt after them. It is also permissible that "ya'rishun" means "they raise," that is, they build up from construction, such as the structures of the pyramids and temples, and this is what suits the verb "dammarna," the raised building being likened to a throne. It is also permissible that "ya'rishun" is a metaphor for the strength of kingship and dominion, with "dammarna" being a complement (tarshih) to the metaphor.

The verb "kana" in both relative clauses indicates that this was their habit and constant practice, that is, what they devoted themselves to of crafts and gardens. The present form in both reports about "kana" serves to indicate renewal and repetition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 138–140 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to idols they had. They said, "O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said, "Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿Indeed, these—what they are in is destroyed, and what they have been doing is in vain.﴾ ﴿He said, "Should I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has preferred you over the worlds?"﴾

When the lesson of the story of Moses' (ﷺ) sending to Pharaoh and his chiefs was complete, and how Allah helped him against his enemy and helped his people, the Children of Israel, and destroyed their enemy, as is the way (sunnah) of Allah in granting victory of truth over falsehood, the discourse proceeded to describe the formation of the nation of the Children of Israel and the circumstances that deserve to be taken as a lesson from them during that time. In this there is reassurance for the souls of the righteous believers regarding their good deeds, and a warning to them against what leads them to the anger of Allah in the transgressions they consider trivial. This is because of the resemblance in all of that to Allah's (Exalted) management of the affairs of His servants, and His sunnah in supporting His messengers and their followers, and in awakening the souls of the community to watch over their thoughts and to take account of themselves in giving thanks for blessings and refuting ingratitude.

Al-mujawaza (crossing over) is distance from a place right after passing through it. It is said: jawaza meaning jaza (passed). Its verb is transitive to one object directly and to the second object with the particle bi-. When you say juztu bihi, its original meaning is that you crossed it while accompanying the one marked by bi- in the crossing. Then the particle bā' was borrowed for causation (ta'diyah), as one says: juztu bihi al-tarīq, when you make the path easy for him even if you did not travel with him. So it has the meaning of ajaztuhu, just as they said: dhahabta bihi meaning adhhabtahu. Thus the meaning of His saying here, ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾, is: We decreed their crossing for them and made it easy for them.

[Page 80]

The sea is the Red Sea of Qulzum, known today as the Red Sea, and it is what is meant by al-yamm (the sea) in the previous verse. The definite article here is for a previously mentioned referent (al-'ahd al-huduri), meaning "the sea mentioned," as is the case with a definite noun when it is repeated as definite. The change of wording is for variety (tafannun), to avoid repetition. The meaning is that they crossed the sea and came out onto its eastern shore.

The phrase ﴿came upon a people﴾ means "came to a people." Since "atau" (came) is used with the sense of "marrū" (passed by), it takes 'alā (upon). This is because they did not intend to settle among the people, but encountered them on their path.

The people were the Canaanites, who are called al-'Amaliqa by the Arabs, and are known to later historians as the Phoenicians.

The idols were images of cows, and the cow was worshipped among the Canaanites, that is, the Phoenicians, under the name Ba'l. Its explanation has already been given at His saying (Exalted is He), ﴿Then you took the calf after Him﴾ in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-'ukuf means staying constantly in a place with the intention of worship. It has already been mentioned at His saying (Exalted is He), ﴿and do not have relations with them while you are staying in the mosques﴾ [al-Baqara: 187] in Surat al-Baqara.
