This is so that through indefiniteness the intent of belittling the idols can be reached, and that they are unknown, because indefiniteness implies the obscurity of knowledge.

The idols were described as belonging to them, and it was not limited to saying "idols." Ibn 'Arafa al-Tunisi said: "Their habit is to answer that it is an addition for the purpose of shaming them and alerting to their ignorance and error, in that they worship what is in fact a possession of theirs, so they make their own property into their gods."

[Page 81]

The clause "they said" is detached and not joined with fa' (then). This is because it is the opening of a dialogue, and it is the nature of dialogue that its clauses be separated, so detachment became common. Had it been joined with fa', it would also have been permissible.

Their calling out to Moses while he was with them is used to request attentive listening to what they are saying, to show their eagerness for what they are about to ask. They called the idol a god because of their ignorance, for they supposed that making an idol benefits its maker, as if its god were with him. This indicates that the Children of Israel had departed, during their stay in Egypt, from the belief in monotheism and the ḥanīfiyya of Ibrahim and Ya'qub, which he enjoined in His saying: ﴿so do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqara: 132]. This is because, when they were in a state of humiliation and enslavement, their knowledge and the record of their glory were lost, and they merged into the religion of those who dominated them, so no distinction remained that set them apart except that they were servants and slaves.

The comparison in their saying "just as they have gods" was intended to urge Moses to grant their request, and out of delight in what they saw of the condition of the people who had settled among them. And it is enough of a shame for a nation that its minds are so base that they consider what is ugly to be good, that they take adorned appearances as a model for themselves, and that they abandon their own perfection in following the deficiencies of others.

The particle "mā" may be a supplementary (ṣila) and an emphatic particle that cancels the governing effect of the particle of comparison (kāffa 'amal ḥarf al-tashbīh). For this reason, the particle of comparison (kāf) came to precede a clause and not a single noun, and it is a clause consisting of a predicate and a subject. "Mā" may also be a verbal-nominal (maṣdariyya) particle that is not temporal, and the clause after it is in the sense of a verbal noun. The estimate is "like the existence of gods for them." Although the most common usage is that the verbal-nominal "mā" is only followed by a verb, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿they love that you suffer﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 118], so there must be an estimated verb to which the prepositional phrase "for them" is attached, or one may suffice with the stability implied by the predicate being a prepositional phrase, as in the verse of Nahshal ibn Jarir al-Tamimi:

"Like the sword of 'Amr, whose edges have never betrayed it."

The clause "He said, 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant'" is detached because it occurs as the answer in the dialogue. That is, Moses answered their words, and his answer was harsh and severe in his saying ﴿Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant﴾, because that is what suits their condition.

Ignorance (al-jahl) is the absence of knowledge, or perceiving a thing contrary to its reality. It has already been mentioned at His saying (Exalted is He), ﴿for those who do evil out of ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa': 17] in Surat al-Nisa'. What is meant is their ignorance of the corruptions of worshipping idols. Moses' describing them with ignorance was emphasizing what the nominal sentence indicated, namely that ignorance is a fixed and established attribute in them and rooted in their souls. Otherwise, at first glance, they would have had a deterrent from such a request. So the predicate is used in its two senses: the literal and the implicative. It is an implicit expression of amazement at the enormity of their ignorance.

In using the word "a people" (qawm), what is intended to be conveyed as information was made a description of a people. This is an alert that describing them with ignorance is like something established and known, part of the definition of their peoplehood. In ruling that ignorance applies to the whole people, there is emphasis on the wonder at the state of their ignorance and its generality among them, such that there is no one among them, despite their large number, who deviates from this attribute. And because of this strangeness, the ruling was emphasized with "inna" (indeed), since it is expected that the listener would hesitate over its confirmation.

The sentence "Indeed, these—what they are in is destroyed" is in the sense of giving a reason for the content of "indeed you are a people who are ignorant." Therefore it was detached from it, and it was emphasized and made a nominal sentence for the same purposes mentioned in its counterpart. The subject was defined by a demonstrative to distinguish them, with that condition they are in, in the most complete distinction, and to alert that they deserve what follows the demonstrative in attributes, namely that their affair is destroyed and their deed is vain. The predicate, which is "destroyed" (mutabbar), was placed before the subject, which is "what they are in," in order to convey that it is restricted to the subject. That is: they are the ones exposed to destruction, and it does not go beyond them at all, and it is an unavoidable fate for them. It is not valid to make "destroyed" the subject, since what is intended by the information is what they are in.

Al-mutabbir means the one who destroys. Al-tabār, with a fatḥa on the tā', is destruction. "And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction" [Nūḥ: 28]. It is said: tabara al-shay' (like ḍaraba, ta'iba, and qatala), and tabbarahu is an intensified form for causation, that is, he destroyed it. Al-tatbīr is used here metaphorically for the corruption of the state. So the passive participle remains in its literal sense in that it describes the one characterized by it at the time of the present.

It is also possible that tatbīr is used metaphorically for the bad outcome. Their outwardly adorned state is likened to the state of a joyful thing that is heading toward ruin and breakage, so the passive participle is a metaphor for the future, meaning

[Page 83]

heading toward evil.

"What they are in" is their state, which is the worship of idols and what it entails of misguidance and evil deeds. For this reason, the relative-pronoun form was chosen in defining it, because the relative clause encompasses their states that neither the speaker nor the addressees can encompass.

The sense of "in" (ẓarfiyya) here is metaphorical, borrowed for being connected with, likening the state of being involved to the containing of a container by what it contains.

Al-bāṭil is a name for the opposite of truth. Therefore, information about it is like information about the verbal noun, and it conveys exaggeration of its falsehood, because the context is one of rebuke and emphasis in denial. The meaning of "al-bāṭil" has already been mentioned just before, at His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿So the truth occurred and what they had been doing was nullified﴾ [al-A'raf: 118].

In placing the predicate, which is "vain" (bāṭil), before the subject, which is "what they had been doing," there is what there is in the parallel of His saying "destroyed is what they are in."

The repetition of the word "he said" as a new clause, in reporting the completion of Moses' answer, with His saying (Exalted is He): "He said, 'Should I seek for you a god other than Allah?'"—its explanation was given at His saying (Exalted is He): "He said, 'Go down from it, all of you'" up to "He said, 'In it you will live'" in this surah.

What appears is that it is repeated in reporting speeches when the saying is long, or because it is a transition from the purpose of rebuking their request to the purpose of reminding them of Allah's blessing upon them, and that giving thanks for a blessing requires restraining them from attempting to worship other than the Benefactor. This is part of the progression in reasoning by the method of dialectical concession, meaning: if those gods were not vain, then busying yourselves with their worship and turning away from the God who bestowed favor upon you would be ingratitude for the blessing, a call to folly, and a disassociation from sharing their foolishness.

The interrogative in "Should I seek for you a god other than Allah?" is for denial and amazement at their request that He make for them a god other than Allah. The thing being questioned was given the interrogative particle (hamza) to indicate that the locus of denial is taking a god other than Allah. So the second object was placed first for restriction, for the sake of emphasis in denial, meaning: the denial is restricted to seeking a god other than Allah.

The hamza in "abghīkum" is the hamza of the speaker for the present-tense verb, and it is the present tense of baghā meaning "to seek." Its verbal noun is al-bughā', with a ḍamma on the bā'. Its verb is transitive to one object, and its object is "other than Allah," because that is what Moses denies he would seek for his people.

Its transitivity to the pronoun of the addressees is by way of elision and conveyance (al-ḥadhf wa al-īṣāl). The original sentence would be: "abghī lakum." And "a god" (ilāhan) is a specifying accusative (tamyīz) for "other than" (ghayr).

The clause "while He has preferred you over the worlds" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). And since its governing element is a locus of denial in terms of its complement, the circumstantial clause also falls within the scope of denial and confirms its aspect.

The apparent form of this construction indicates that their preference over the worlds was known to them, because that is what suits the denial. It is also possible that he intended to inform them of that, and that it is a established matter.

Making the predicate a verb (fi'liyyan) is to convey that placing the subject before it restricts it to that verbal predicate, meaning: "and He has preferred you"—the idols did not prefer you. So the denial against them was a way of showing them to be fools, in that they are immersed in Allah's blessing while they seek to worship what does not bestow blessings.

The meaning of "the worlds" (al-'alamin) here is the nations of their era. Their being preferred over them is because they are descendants of a messenger and prophets, because among them are messengers and prophets, because Allah guided them to monotheism (tawhid) and to deliverance from the religion of Pharaoh (din Fir'awn) after they had been floundering in it, because He made them free after they had been slaves, because He brought them to possess a blessed land, He strengthened them with His victory and His signs, and He sent among them a messenger to establish the law (shari'a) for them. These virtues were not gathered for any other nation in that day. And among "the worlds" are these people who passed by them. This is a kinaya (metonymic expression) for denying their request to take idols like them, because it is the nature of the superior that he does not imitate the inferior, since adopting the conditions of others implies an acknowledgment that they are superior in opinion and better in state in that respect.

[Page 85]

It is part of Musa's speech, peace be upon him, as the context requires, and it is supported by Ibn 'Amir's reading "wa-idh anjakum" (وإذْ أنْجاكم). The meaning is: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, when He has favoured you over the worlds" ﴿وهو فَضَّلَكم عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾, and at a time when He rescued you from the people of Pharaoh through my intermediacy? So seeking another god than Him is ingratitude for His blessing. The pronoun of the speaker who is joined with others ("we," نا) refers to Allah and Musa, and its referent is indicated by His saying ﴿أغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أبْغِيكم إلَهًا﴾.

It is also permissible that this is a reminder of favour from Allah, inserted between the narrative and the promise to Musa, peace be upon him, moving from the report and the lesson to the blessing and grace. In that case the pronoun is a pronoun of majesty. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur, الجمهور) read "anjaynakum" (أنْجَيْناكم) with the nun of the speaker who is joined with others. Ibn 'Amir read "wa-idh anjakum" (وإذْ أنْجاكم), referring the pronoun back to Allah in His saying ﴿أغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أبْغِيكم إلَهًا﴾. It is likewise written this way in the Mushaf of Syria (Mushaf al-Sham, مصحف الشام), so it would be part of Musa's speech. Together, the two readings yield both meanings.

"Idh" (إذْ) is a noun of time (ism zaman, اسْمُ زَمانٍ), and it is an object (maf'ul bihi) of a deleted verb whose estimated form is: "wa-udhkuru" (واذْكُرُوا), meaning "and remember."

Al-Tabari and a group of scholars chose that His saying ﴿وإذْ أنْجَيْناكم﴾ is an address to the Jews who were present in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). In that case it begins a new address introduced with the word "idh." The allusive reminder to the polytheist Arabs ends at His saying ﴿وهو فَضَّلَكم عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾. Surat al-A'raf is Meccan, and there is nothing in the Meccan part of the Qur'an that is a dispute with the Jews.

As for His saying ﴿يَسُومُونَكم سُوءَ العَذابِ﴾ through to the end of the verse, its interpretation has already been explained in a similar verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 142:**

﴿We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was fulfilled as forty nights.﴾

This returns to the remaining events concerning the Children of Israel after they crossed the sea. The sentence is therefore conjoined (*'atf*) to the sentence ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 138].

The meaning of *al-mu'adah* (appointment or promise) has already been discussed in the parallel verse in Surat al-Baqarah. Abu 'Amr read *"wa-wa'adna"* (with *wa'dna* rather than *wa'adna*). The object of the promise is omitted, relying on the context in His words *thalathina laylatan* ("thirty nights") and what follows. *Thalathin* is in the accusative as a substitute for an adverb of time (*zarf*), because its specification (*tamyiz*) is a time-frame for what was promised, namely the presence to receive the Law. The verb *wa'adna* indicates this, because an appointment is for a meeting. Thus the governing verb *wa'adna* is understood in light of the implied element, meaning: a presence for a period of thirty nights.

God made the period of intimate communion (*munajah*) thirty nights, as an ease for him. When he had completed it, and his pure soul had increased in attachment and desire for communion with God and His worship, God added to him ten nights from this grace, so the period of communion became forty nights. Some exegetes mentioned a story about the reason for the addition of ten nights, but it is not authentic. He did not add more than forty nights either: either because he had reached the utmost limit his human strength could bear, so God kept him far from being affected by weariness in the worship of his Lord, something that is removed even from the pious, let alone the prophets. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take on of deeds what you are able to do, for God does not tire until you tire." Or because the increase in his absence from his people would lead to harm, as it was said: they worshipped the calf during the last ten of the forty nights.

The addition of the ten nights was called *itmam* (completion), pointing to the fact that God intended that Musa's communion be forty nights, but when He commanded him, He commanded it in separate parts, either for the wisdom of companionship (*al-istinas*), or so that those ten nights would be another act of worship, so that the reward would be repeated. What is meant is nights together with their days, and only the nights are mentioned because the appointment was for the purpose of withdrawal for worship and receiving communion. The soul at night is more detached from the material and more disposed to the perfections of the soul and the states of the angelic realm than during the day. This is because souls, by their original constitution, have become accustomed to finding companionship in the light of the sun and to being active for work by it, so that the preoccupation with this world, even through reflection and contemplation of existing things, does not leave them during the day. At night and in darkness, this declines, and the reflections of the soul turn inward. For this reason the Law has never ceased to encourage the night vigil and supplication to God at night. He—Exalted is He—said: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16], and ﴿And in the pre-dawn hours they seek forgiveness﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 18]. In the hadith: "Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven during the last third of the night, and says: Is there anyone seeking forgiveness, so that I may forgive him? Is there anyone calling upon Me, so that I may answer him?" Also, staying awake at night has always been a practice of the wise and the ascetics, because wakefulness refines the power of the animal faculty, just as fasting refines it. Hayakil al-Nur says: "The rational souls are from the realm of the dominion (*malakut*), and what has occupied them away from their world is the bodily faculties and their preoccupations. When the soul becomes strong through spiritual virtues and the authority of the bodily faculties weakens through reducing food and increasing wakefulness, it sometimes escapes to the world of holiness, connects with its Lord, and receives knowledge from it."

Moreover, in Arabic speech the prevalent way of expressing time is by nights, and they mean that they include their days, since the Arabic months begin with the nights, as they are tied to the appearance of the crescent moons.

His words ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was fulfilled as forty nights﴾ are a summation of the calculation, as in His words ﴿So a fast of three days during the Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. The *fa'* here is for consequence (*tafri'*).

The *tamam* (fulfilment) in His words *fa-tamma miqatu rabbihi* is used in the sense of growth and surpassing, so the appointed time became more complete and more excellent. This is like His words: ﴿as a completion upon the one who did good﴾ [al-An'am: 154], and His words: ﴿And I have completed My favour upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. This points to the fact that the addition of the ten nights was for a great wisdom: without it, the period of thirty would not have reached the utmost perfection; and that God had determined the communion to be forty nights, but He presented the matter to Musa in parts, as an ease for him, so that his turning toward completing the forty would be with yearning and strength.

The accusative of *arba'in* (forty) is as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), with the sense: reaching forty.

As for *al-miqat*, it is said to be synonymous with *al-waqt* (time). It is also said that it is a time fixed for a certain action. It has already been discussed in His words ﴿Say: they are times for people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Its attribution to "his Lord" is for honour, and also as an allusion to the ridicule of some of his people when Musa's absence from them in the communion was prolonged beyond thirty nights; so they claimed that Musa had died on the mountain, as Ibn Jurayj narrated. Some of this is supported by the text of the Torah in chapter thirty-two of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj).

\* \* \*

﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun: "Take my place among my people, and act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾

That is: Musa said to his brother when he resolved to ascend the mountain for communion, for he ascended alone, accompanied only by his attendant Yusha' ibn Nun.

The meaning of *ukhlufni* is: be a successor (*khalaf*) in my place, and a deputy (*khalifah*). This is one who takes charge of another's work when that other is absent, and that succession ends when the one who appointed him returns. So succession is a form of agency (*wakalah*). The verb *khalafa* derives from *al-khalf* (with a sukun on the lam), which is the opposite of *al-amam* (front), because the successor carries on the work of the one who appointed him when that one is absent, and the absent one places someone behind him in his place.

In his instruction he gathered the essence of governance in His words ﴿and act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾. The governance of a community revolves around the axis of *al-islah* (righteous action), which is making a thing good (*salih*). Therefore all the conduct and conditions of the community must be good, and that means that actions must return good and righteousness to their doer and to others. If they return righteousness to him but its opposite to others, they are not regarded as righteousness, and they soon turn into corruption for those who thought them righteous. Then, if an act is ambiguous, being good from one aspect and bad from another, its stronger state must be considered, and judgment made accordingly, if it is impossible to turn away from it to something more beneficial. If both aspects are equal, it is set aside if possible; otherwise one chooses. This is a command to Harun comprising what his work requires in governing the community.

His words ﴿and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ are a warning against corruption in the most eloquent form, because it combines a prohibition (and the prohibition against an act directs its wording at first to the corruption of what is prohibited) with linking the prohibition to following the way of the corrupters.

*Al-ittiba'* originally means walking behind someone, step by step. Here it is used figuratively for participation in the work of the corrupter, since the path is used figuratively for the work that leads to corruption. The corrupter is one whose attribute is corruption. When the prohibition was tied to taking the path of the corrupters, it became a warning against everything from which corruption may result. This is because corrupters may do an action which is not corrupt in itself, so one is prohibited from participating in the work of one known for corruption, since its issuing from one known for corruption suffices to make its leading to corruption expected. In this prohibition is the blocking of the means to corruption (*sadd al-dhara'i'*), and blocking the means to corruption is one of the foundations of Islam. Malik ibn Anas gave it particular attention, repeated it in his book, and this principle became well known in the foundations of his school.

Therefore it is no wonder that His words, ﴿and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾, comprise the prohibition against three levels of approaching corruption: the action known for its association with the corrupter; the action of the corrupter even if it is not something he is accustomed to; and approaching the corrupter and mixing with him.

God, through the tongue of His messenger Musa, or by informing him, made known that among Harun's subjects there were corrupters, and that they were about to follow the way of corruption, and that he (Harun) would be inclined to go along with them, because of the leniency that God knew to be in Harun's character in his governance, and as a precaution against the outbreak of rebellion among his people. This is as God related of him, in His words: ﴿Indeed, the people overpowered me and nearly killed me﴾ [al-A'raf: 150], and His words: ﴿I feared that you would say: "You have caused division among the Children of Israel"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94].

So the sentence ﴿and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ is not merely a confirmation of the content of the clause *wa-aslih* (and act righteously), as an emphasis on a thing by negating its opposite, like the saying "dead, not living". For if that were the intended purpose, it would have been stripped of the conjunction particle, and it would have been limited to a prohibition against corrupting, so that it would say: "act righteously, do not corrupt." Yes, what results from its meanings includes an emphasis on the content of the clause *wa-aslih*.

\[p. 89]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 143–144 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When Moses came at Our appointed time, and his Lord spoke to him, he said: "My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You." He said: "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me." But when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. When he recovered, he said: "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."﴾ ﴿He said: "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful."﴾

The coming of Moses at the appointed time has been made into a matter already settled, not requiring any report about it, since it is known that Moses would not delay or neglect that. The Lord's speaking to him during that appointed time has likewise been made into a matter already settled, not requiring any report about its occurrence, because it is evident that the appointment which includes the encounter includes speech; for meeting God in the true sense is not possible, so nothing arises from the requirements of the appointment except the speech issuing from God's will and power. For all this, the coming of Moses to the appointed time and God's speaking to him have been made the condition of the particle (lamma) because it is like something known, and the report has been made to relate to what follows it, which is an expression of God's greatness and majesty. So the speech is a kind of concision, by omitting the predicate of two clauses, being dispensed with because they have been made the condition of "lamma."

It is permissible to make the waw in His saying ﴿wa-kallamahu rabbuhu﴾ (and his Lord spoke to him) superfluous in the answer of (lamma), as most have said regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, and he headed with us toward the valley floor of Khabt, full of dunes, winding."

The answer of lamma is his saying "wa-intaha" (and he headed). They also permitted this in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-lamma aslama wa-tallahu lil-jabin﴾ (Saffat: 103) ﴿wa-nadaynahu an ya Ibrahim﴾ (Saffat: 104), the verse, that "wa-nadaynahu" is the answer of (lamma), so that the estimate becomes:

Page 90

"When Moses came at Our appointed time, his Lord spoke to him," making it concision by omitting one clause. And from the meaning of the act of speaking, the hope of seeing is not derived except from the necessary implication of the appointment.

The lam in His saying "li-miqatina" (at Our appointed time) is a kind of the lam of specification (ikhtisas), as al-Zamakhshari named it in the Kashshaf, and he illustrated it with their saying: "I came to him for ten nights passed of the month," meaning that it is a specification of a kind. Ibn Hisham made it in the sense of "'inda" (at), and counted that among the meanings of the lam, and this is more apparent. The meaning: "When Moses came, a coming specific to the appointment," that is, present at it, without delay in it, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿aqimi al-salata li-dulugi al-shams﴾ (Al-Isra: 78). And in the hadith: "The Messenger of God was asked which deeds are best, and he said: prayer at its time" — that is, at its time. From this is ﴿fa-tallaquhunna li-'iddatihinna﴾ (At-Talaq: 1).

It is also permissible to make the lam indicate purpose and cause, that is, he came for the sake of Our appointment, because of what we have already mentioned about the appointment including the meaning of encounter and intimate conversation, that is, he came for the sake of Our intimate conversation.

The coming (majii') is his movement from among his people to Mount Sinai, in which is the specific place of intimate conversation.

Speech (takhlim) in its true reality is uttering words that convey meanings according to an agreed convention, and this true reality is impossible for God, exalted is He, because it is among the accidents of created things. So it is necessary that the attribution of speech to God be figurative, used to indicate the intention of God, exalted is He, through words of the addressee's language, in a manner by which the addressee is certain that this speech is an effect of God's power in accordance with His will and knowledge. It is an immediate connection by an unusual way. So it is permissible that God create speech in a created thing which Moses heard, as it is related that God created speech in the tree that Moses was facing; that was the first speech God addressed to Moses, in the land of Midian, at the mountain of (Horeb). It is also permissible that God create speech through the clouds, and that speech occurring at Tur Sinai is what is meant here. It is what is mentioned in chapter 19 of the Book of Exodus.

Speech in this manner was what Moses heard when he was far from people in intimate conversation or the like, and it is one of the three states by which God speaks to His prophets, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for a human that God should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil﴾ in Surat al-Shura. It is undoubtedly an event, and its attribution to God is that it issues in an unusual manner that happens only by God's will, to deviate from the customary for its honour, and this is what is expressed by His saying "or from behind a veil." God, exalted is He, spoke to Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Isra', and I reckon all the Hadith Qudsi, or most of them, are of what God spoke to Muhammad (ﷺ) with. As for God's sending Gabriel with speech to one of His prophets, that is another manner, by casting the speech into the soul of the angel who conveys it to the prophet; the whole Qur'an is of this kind. The revelation to Moses through the angel also occurred in many states, and it is what is expressed in the Torah by its saying: "God said to Moses."

His saying ﴿qala rabbi arini﴾ (He said: My Lord, show me) is the answer of (lamma) according to the most apparent view. If we estimate the waw in His saying "wa-kallamahu" to be superfluous in the answer of (lamma), then his saying "qala" falls in the course of dialogue, and therefore it is separated.

Moses' request to see God, exalted is He, is an aspiration toward increased knowledge of the divine majesty, because since the appointment includes encounter, and encounter relies on seeing the Essence and hearing the discourse, and one of the two pillars of encounter, which is speech, was obtained by Moses, this led him to hope for the second pillar, which is witnessing. What indicates that speech is what made Moses hope to obtain the vision is the placing of the clause (﴿wa-kallamahu rabbuhu﴾) as the condition of the particle (lamma), because (lamma) indicates a strong connection between its condition and its answer, so it often happens that it is the cause of the occurrence of its answer, as mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-lamma dhaqa al-shajara badat lahuma sawatuhuma﴾ (Al-A'raf: 22) in this surah. This is on the view that "wa-kallamahu" is coordinated with the condition of (lamma) and is not its answer. We have no doubt that he asked for a vision befitting the Essence of God, exalted is He, and it is like the vision promised in the Hereafter. Moses thought that the like of it was possible in this world until God informed him that this does not occur in this world. A prophet may be ignorant of the details of divine matters before God teaches him them, and God said to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ (Ta-Ha: 114). For this reason the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah were correct in deriving from Moses' request to see God that it is possible, in a manner befitting the attributes of divinity whose reality we do not know, and this is the meaning of their saying "without how" (bila kayf).

The Mu'tazila were not correct in deriving from this the impossibility of it in every respect.

The disagreement between the two groups may ultimately return to wording, for the two groups agree on the impossibility of perception encompassing the Essence of God and on the impossibility of spatial location. Ahl al-Sunnah assert definitively that it is a vision that does not contradict God's attributes. As for what al-Zamakhshari boasted of in the Kashshaf, that is from the hostility of his partisanship against his opponents, as is his habit, and it was not fitting for the scholars of our path to stoop to answer his abuse with the like of what he abused them with, but he said "fa-awjaba" (and so he made it obligatory).

Know that Moses' request to see God, exalted is He, is a genuine request in its literal sense, as the context of the verse indicates, and it is not the request that the Children of Israel made, related in Surat al-Baqara in His saying: ﴿And when you said, O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God openly﴾ (Al-Baqara: 55). What al-Zamakhshari contrived, claiming that it is that same request, is an affectation for which there is no reason.

The object of "arini" is omitted, indicated by the pronoun in the preposition in His saying "ilayka" (to You).

His saying ﴿qala lan tarani﴾ (He said: You will not see Me) is separated because it falls in the course of dialogue.

"Lan" is used to emphasize negation and to stress negation in the future; the two are close in meaning. All of this relates only to this life, which is expressed by "the eternal." So "lan" negated Moses' seeing his Lord with a negation after which the questioner has no hope of insisting and returning, such that he knows that his request is unattainable. There is therefore no indication in this negation that it continues in the Hereafter.

The qualification derived from "lakin" (but) is to remove the addressee's assumption that the negation of vision is limited without justification or persuasion, or that he might suppose this prohibition is out of anger at the questioner and a fault in him. Therefore from the particle of qualification one knows that some of what he supposes will be removed. That is, He commanded him to look at the mountain on which he stands, whether it remains in its place. This indicates that some aspect of divine majesty will be directed at the mountain, and that the strength of the mountain will not remain firm under that mighty direction. So Moses knows that his fleeting powers are even less able to bear it, if some of the veils of God, exalted is He, were to be manifested to him.

The condition is attached with "in" (if), because its usual use is in situations where the occurrence of the condition is rare, or with an implication of its being impossible. Since the remaining of the mountain in its place was known by God to be non-existent, it is valid to attach to it the matter whose occurrence is intended to be impossible, setting aside the evidence of its non-existence. Therefore there is no proof in this conditional for Ahl al-Sunnah against the Mu'tazila that God's being seen is permissible for Him, exalted is He, contrary to what many of our scholars have customarily argued from it.

Page 93

His saying ﴿fa-sawfa tarani﴾ (then you will see Me) is not a promise of vision on the supposition, because the prior saying "you will not see Me" removed the questioner's hope of seeing. Rather, it is an announcement that the purpose of his looking at the mountain is that he may see with certainty the inability of human strength to see God, exalted is He, by a fortiori reasoning from the mountain's failure to remain firm. So the force of the speech becomes: the mountain does not remain in its place from the manifestation that occurs upon it; therefore you are not the one who will see Me, for you cannot bear it. Thus the status of the condition here is that of the counterfactual condition expressed by the particle "law" (if), by the indication of the context of what precedes.

"Tajalli" (manifestation) is literally appearance and removal of a veil, and here it is figurative. Perhaps what is meant by it is the removal of the customary barriers that God made as a veil between earthly beings and the powers of majesty, which God, exalted is He, alone controls, according to determined and graduated measures in orders arranged in an order known to God.

Its approximation for understanding resembles what the philosophers have agreed upon regarding the arrangement of the ten intellects. Those powers are attributed to God, exalted is He, because they are effects of His power without intermediary. When God removes the customary veil between some earthly bodies and some of those influential powers, with an effect beyond custom, the power connects with the body in a connection by which effects appropriate to the kind of that power appear to it. That removal is what the manifestation attributed to God, exalted is He, is borrowed for, to bring it closer to understanding. When a divine power connected with the mountain, resembling the connection of vision, the mountain crumbled. What brings this meaning closer is what at-Tirmidhi and others related through several chains from Anas: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-lamma tajalla rabbuhu﴾, and he placed his thumb near the tip of his little finger, diminishing the measure of the manifestation."

Moses swooned from the crumbling of the mountain, so Moses knew that if that manifestation had been directed at him, his body would have been scattered into dust.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 143–144 (part 2 of 2):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿دَكًّا﴾ (dakkan) with tanwin. Al-dakk is a verbal noun (masdar), and it and al-daqq are synonyms, meaning to crush and to scatter the parts apart, as in His words: ﴿وَتَخِرُّ الْجِبَالُ هَدًّا﴾ (and the mountains will collapse in ruin). The mountain is described as having been made dakk for emphasis (lil-mubalaghah), and what is meant is that it was madkuk, that is, crushed and demolished.

Al-Kisa'i, Hamzah and Khalaf read ﴿دَكَّاءَ﴾ (dakka'a), with a long vowel after the kaf and a shadda on the kaf. Al-dakka' is a she-camel with no hump, so this is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh): like a humpless she-camel, that is, its peak had been lost. The apparent meaning is that the part that was crushed away did not return, and perhaps the traces of that crushing are still visible in it to this day.

Page 94

Al-kharur is falling down to the ground.

As-sa'q is a descriptive term meaning one who has been struck (al-mas'uq), and its meaning is one who has fallen unconscious from a cry or the like. It is derived from the noun al-sa'iqah (the thunderbolt), which is the fiery fragment that reaches the earth from the electricity of lightning. When it strikes a body it burns it, and when it strikes a living creature from close by it kills it, or from a distance it causes it to faint from its smell. Khuwaylid ibn Nufayl was named al-Sa'iq as a proper name for him by predominance. We preferred that the descriptive term and the verbal noun are derived from the noun al-sa'iqah, rather than making al-sa'iqah derived from al-sa'q, because the leading lexicographers said: al-sa'q is fainting from a cry or the like. However, they extended the use of this description to one who has fainted because of a crash or a tremor, even if that was not from a thunderbolt.

Al-ifaqah is the return of perception after it has ceased due to fainting, sleep, intoxication, or the frenzy of madness.

﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (subhanaka) is a verbal noun that came in place of its verb, meaning: I glorify You. Here it is an expression of praise for God and of declaring Him free from what is unfitting for Him, in keeping with the context of his asking Him what it became clear to him was not fitting to ask without seeking His permission and verifying its possibility, as God the Exalted said to Noah: ﴿فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ (So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of) in Surah Hud.

His words ﴿تُبْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (I have repented to You) are an expression of repentance from returning to the like of that without permission from God. This is like the words of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ (My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of) [Hud: 47]. The past-tense form in His words "tubtu" (I have repented) is used performatively (fi al-insha'), so it is used for the present time, like the formulae of contracts in their saying "bi'tu" (I have sold) and "zawwajtu" (I have married), for emphasis on the realization of the act.

His words ﴿وَأَنَا أَوَّلُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and I am the first of the believers): "the first" (al-awwal) is applied to one who hastens to faith, and applying "the first" to one who hastens is a widespread metaphor that is equal to the literal meaning. What is meant by it here, and in its parallels, is a kinayah (allusion) to the strength of his faith, to the point that he hastens to it when others hesitate about it. So it is for emphasis, and its parallel has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ﴾ (and do not be the first to disbelieve in it) [al-Baqarah: 41] in Surah al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿وَأَنَا أَوَّلُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾ (and I am the first of the submitters) [al-An'am: 163] in Surah al-An'am.

What is meant by "the believers" (al-mu'minin) is those for whom faith is a description and a title for them, that is, faith in God and His attributes as befits Him. Thus faith is used in its titular meaning (ma'na laqabi), and for this reason the description is likened to the verbs of dispositions, so no complement is mentioned for it. Whoever among the exegetes proposes a complement for it has departed from the course of the meaning.

Page 95

The clause ﴿قَالَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (He said: O Musa) is disjoined because the speech occurs as a dialogue and an exchange, and the call serves to comfort and to remove fright.

The emphasis of the statement in His words ﴿إِنِّي اصْطَفَيْتُكَ﴾ (Indeed I have chosen you) is for attention to it, since it is not a place for denial.

Al-istifa' is an intensive form (ifti'al of mubalaghah) of al-isfa', and it is derived from al-safw, which is purity from what troubles. It was previously discussed at His words: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى آدَمَ وَنُوحًا﴾ (Indeed God chose Adam and Noah) [Al 'Imran: 33] in Surah Al 'Imran. "Istafaytuka" includes the meaning of preference and favouring, so it is followed by "ala" (over).

What is meant by "the people" (al-nas) is all people, that is, those existing in his time, so the comprehensiveness in "the people" is customary: he is preferred over the people of that day because he is a messenger, and for his preference through the distinction of speech. It may be said that Musa is the best of all people who passed away on that day. On both possibilities, he is better than his brother Harun, because Musa was sent with a great law and God spoke to him, while Harun was sent by God as a helper to Musa and God did not speak to him directly. For this reason He said: ﴿بِرِسَالَتِي وَبِكَلَامِي﴾ (with My messages and with My speech). As for what has come in the hadith prohibiting preference among the prophets, it is understood as referring to preference that is not based on clear evidence, or to making preference among the prophets an occupation for people in their gatherings without a valid reason for engaging in that.

This is a favour from God and an introduction (ta'rif).

Then He based on that His words ﴿فَخُذْ مَا آتَيْتُكَ وَكُنْ مِنَ الشَّاكِرِينَ﴾ (So take what I have given you and be among the grateful). The first is a consequence of the sending and the speech, and the second is a consequence of the favour. As for the referent of "ma ataytuka" (what I have given you), it has been said that it is the law and the message, so "al-ita'" (giving) is a metaphor applied to instruction and guidance, and "al-akhdh" (taking) is a metaphor for receiving and preserving. The more apparent view is that "ma ataytuka" refers to the giving of the tablets, by the indication of His words ﴿وَكَتَبْنَا لَهُ فِي الْأَلْوَاحِ﴾ (And We wrote for him on the tablets) [al-A'raf: 145], and it has been explained as such. So "ita'" is literal, and "akhdh" likewise, and this is more fitting to the structure of the speech together with His words ﴿فَخُذْهَا بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ (so take it with strength) [al-A'raf: 145], and by it is obtained the taking of the message and the speech and an addition.

The predication about "kun" (be) with His words ﴿مِنَ الشَّاكِرِينَ﴾ (among the grateful) is more eloquent than saying "kun shakiran" (be grateful), as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿قَدْ ضَلَلْتُ إِذًا وَمَا أَنَا مِنَ الْمُهْتَدِينَ﴾ (Then I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided) [al-An'am: 56] in Surah al-An'am.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, and Rawh from Ya'qub read ﴿بِرِسَالَتِي﴾ (with My message) in the singular form, while the rest read ﴿بِرِسَالَاتِي﴾ (with My messages) in the plural form, and this is according to its interpretation as the multiplicity of obligations and guidance with which he was sent.

But when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. When he recovered, he said: "Glory be to You! For all this, the coming of Moses to the appointed time and God's speaking to him have been made the condition of the particle (lamma) because it is like something known, and the report has been made to relate to what follows it, which is an expression of God's greatness and majesty. So the speech is a kind of concision, by omitting the predicate of two clauses, being dispensed with because they have been made the condition of "lamma."

"So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, and he headed with us toward the valley floor of Khabt, full of dunes, winding."

Al-Kisa'i, Hamzah and Khalaf read ﴿دَكَّاءَ﴾ (dakka'a), with a long vowel after the kaf and a shadda on the kaf. Al-dakka' is a she-camel with no hump, so this is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh): like a humpless she-camel, that is, its peak had been lost. The apparent meaning is that the part that was crushed away did not return, and perhaps the traces of that crushing are still visible in it to this day.

Page 94

Al-kharur is falling down to the ground.

As-sa'q is a descriptive term meaning one who has been struck (al-mas'uq), and its meaning is one who has fallen unconscious from a cry or the like. It is derived from the noun al-sa'iqah (the thunderbolt), which is the fiery fragment that reaches the earth from the electricity of lightning. When it strikes a body it burns it, and when it strikes a living creature from close by it kills it, or from a distance it causes it to faint from its smell. Khuwaylid ibn Nufayl was named al-Sa'iq as a proper name for him by predominance. We preferred that the descriptive term and the verbal noun are derived from the noun al-sa'iqah, rather than making al-sa'iqah derived from al-sa'q, because the leading lexicographers said: al-sa'q is fainting from a cry or the like. However, they extended the use of this description to one who has fainted because of a crash or a tremor, even if that was not from a thunderbolt.

Al-ifaqah is the return of perception after it has ceased due to fainting, sleep, intoxication, or the frenzy of madness.

﴿سُبْحانَكَ﴾ (subhanaka) is a verbal noun that came in place of its verb, meaning: I glorify You. Here it is an expression of praise for God and of declaring Him free from what is unfitting for Him, in keeping with the context of his asking Him what it became clear to him was not fitting to ask without seeking His permission and verifying its possibility, as God the Exalted said to Noah: ﴿فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ (So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of) in Surah Hud.

His words ﴿تُبْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (I have repented to You) are an expression of repentance from returning to the like of that without permission from God. This is like the words of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ (My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of) [Hud: 47]. The past-tense form in His words "tubtu" (I have repented) is used performatively (fi al-insha'), so it is used for the present time, like the formulae of contracts in their saying "bi'tu" (I have sold) and "zawwajtu" (I have married), for emphasis on the realization of the act.

His words ﴿وَأَنَا أَوَّلُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and I am the first of the believers): "the first" (al-awwal) is applied to one who hastens to faith, and applying "the first" to one who hastens is a widespread metaphor that is equal to the literal meaning. What is meant by it here, and in its parallels, is a kinayah (allusion) to the strength of his faith, to the point that he hastens to it when others hesitate about it. So it is for emphasis, and its parallel has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ﴾ (and do not be the first to disbelieve in it) [al-Baqarah: 41] in Surah al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿وَأَنَا أَوَّلُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾ (and I am the first of the submitters) [al-An'am: 163] in Surah al-An'am.

What is meant by "the believers" (al-mu'minin) is those for whom faith is a description and a title for them, that is, faith in God and His attributes as befits Him. Thus faith is used in its titular meaning (ma'na laqabi), and for this reason the description is likened to the verbs of dispositions, so no complement is mentioned for it. Whoever among the exegetes proposes a complement for it has departed from the course of the meaning.

Page 95

The clause ﴿قَالَ يَا مُوسَى﴾ (He said: O Musa) is disjoined because the speech occurs as a dialogue and an exchange, and the call serves to comfort and to remove fright.

The emphasis of the statement in His words ﴿إِنِّي اصْطَفَيْتُكَ﴾ (Indeed I have chosen you) is for attention to it, since it is not a place for denial.

Al-istifa' is an intensive form (ifti'al of mubalaghah) of al-isfa', and it is derived from al-safw, which is purity from what troubles. It was previously discussed at His words: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى آدَمَ وَنُوحًا﴾ (Indeed God chose Adam and Noah) [Al 'Imran: 33] in Surah Al 'Imran. "Istafaytuka" includes the meaning of preference and favouring, so it is followed by "ala" (over).

What is meant by "the people" (al-nas) is all people, that is, those existing in his time, so the comprehensiveness in "the people" is customary: he is preferred over the people of that day because he is a messenger, and for his preference through the distinction of speech. It may be said that Musa is the best of all people who passed away on that day. On both possibilities, he is better than his brother Harun, because Musa was sent with a great law and God spoke to him, while Harun was sent by God as a helper to Musa and God did not speak to him directly. For this reason He said: ﴿بِرِسَالَتِي وَبِكَلَامِي﴾ (with My messages and with My speech). As for what has come in the hadith prohibiting preference among the prophets, it is understood as referring to preference that is not based on clear evidence, or to making preference among the prophets an occupation for people in their gatherings without a valid reason for engaging in that.

This is a favour from God and an introduction (ta'rif).

Then He based on that His words ﴿فَخُذْ مَا آتَيْتُكَ وَكُنْ مِنَ الشَّاكِرِينَ﴾ (So take what I have given you and be among the grateful). The first is a consequence of the sending and the speech, and the second is a consequence of the favour. As for the referent of "ma ataytuka" (what I have given you), it has been said that it is the law and the message, so "al-ita'" (giving) is a metaphor applied to instruction and guidance, and "al-akhdh" (taking) is a metaphor for receiving and preserving. The more apparent view is that "ma ataytuka" refers to the giving of the tablets, by the indication of His words ﴿وَكَتَبْنَا لَهُ فِي الْأَلْوَاحِ﴾ (And We wrote for him on the tablets) [al-A'raf: 145], and it has been explained as such. So "ita'" is literal, and "akhdh" likewise, and this is more fitting to the structure of the speech together with His words ﴿فَخُذْهَا بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ (so take it with strength) [al-A'raf: 145], and by it is obtained the taking of the message and the speech and an addition.

The predication about "kun" (be) with His words ﴿مِنَ الشَّاكِرِينَ﴾ (among the grateful) is more eloquent than saying "kun shakiran" (be grateful), as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿قَدْ ضَلَلْتُ إِذًا وَمَا أَنَا مِنَ الْمُهْتَدِينَ﴾ (Then I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided) [al-An'am: 56] in Surah al-An'am.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, and Rawh from Ya'qub read ﴿بِرِسَالَتِي﴾ (with My message) in the singular form, while the rest read ﴿بِرِسَالَاتِي﴾ (with My messages) in the plural form, and this is according to its interpretation as the multiplicity of obligations and guidance with which he was sent.

[Page 96]

﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets, of everything, an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything. So take them with strength, and enjoin your people to take the best of them.﴾

This is conjoined to the sentence ﴿He said, "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people with My message"﴾ [al-A'raf: 144] and what follows it, because it contains ﴿so take what I have given you﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]. What was given to him was the tablets of the Law (al-shari'ah), or else the tablets are what is meant by His words ﴿what I have given you﴾ [al-A'raf: 144].

The definite article in "al-alwah" (the tablets) may be the definite of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd). If "what I have given you" refers to the tablets that were given to Moses during the private communion (al-munajah), then it is appropriate to make it definite by prior reference, as if it were said: "So take the tablets that I have given you. Then it was said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾." If "what I have given you" refers to the message and the speech, then the definite article in "al-alwah" is the definite of mental reference (ta'rif al-dhihni), meaning: ﴿And We wrote for him on tablets﴾ of a specific kind, from the genus of tablets.

"Al-alwah" is the plural of "lawh" (with a fatha on the lam), which is a rectangular piece of wood. They used to write on tablets. Or the tablets are known to the Muslims, to whom the details of the story were conveyed. (Although the recounting of the outline of the story is to threaten the polytheists that what befell those who denied Moses will befall them.)

Calling the tablets that God gave Moses "tablets" is a metaphor based on form (majaz bi'l-surah), because the tablets that were given to Moses were of stone, as in the Torah, in chapter twenty-four of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj). So they are named "tablets" because they were in the form of tablets. What is in chapter thirty-four is that the two tablets had written on them the Ten Commandments with which the law of Moses began, and they were two tablets, as in the Torah. So the use of the plural here is either a usage of the plural form for the dual, on the basis that the least plural is two, or because both were written on both of their faces, as chapter thirty-two of the Book of Exodus indicates, so they were like four tablets.

The writing is attributed to God, exalted is He, because it was written as an engraving in the stone without any human action, but purely by the power of God, exalted is He, as is understood from chapter thirty-two. Likewise, speech is attributed to God in His words (and by My word).

[Page 97]

The "min" (from) in His words "of everything" is partitive (tab'idiyyah) and is connected to "We wrote" (katabna). The object of "We wrote" is omitted, indicated by the verb "We wrote," meaning "written." It is also permissible to make "min" a noun meaning "some of," in which case it is in the accusative as the object of "We wrote," meaning: We wrote for him some of everything. This is like His words, exalted is He, in Surat al-Naml: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 16].

"Everything" ("kulli shay'") is general in a customary sense (umum 'urfi), meaning everything the community needs in its religion, in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ [al-An'am: 38], according to one of two interpretations regarding whether "the Book" means the Qur'an, and in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning its foundations.

What God wrote for Moses on the tablets are the foundational universal principles (usul kulliyyat) of the law that God revealed to Moses, peace be upon him. These are what is in chapter 20 of the Book of Exodus, and its text is: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments. Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain: for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it. Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee. Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's." End quote. They became known among the Children of Israel as the Ten Commandments (al-wasaya al-'ashr) and the Ten Words (al-kalimat al-'ashr), that is, the ten sentences.

These were detailed in chapter 20 through the end of chapter 31 of the Book of Exodus, and among them are the Ten Commandments which God spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai.

[Page 98]

In chapter 34 it occurs that the tablets had written on them only the Ten Words, which are in the seventeen paragraphs of it. His words here, "an admonition and a detailed explanation," require reliance on what is in the thirteen chapters.

"Al-maw'izah" (admonition) is the verbal noun of "al-wa'z," which is advice with guidance mixed with a warning of harm befalling in the outcome, or an encouragement to bring about a benefit that is neglected. It has been mentioned previously at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His words: ﴿Turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa'. And His words ﴿and good admonition﴾ [al-Nahl: 125] will come at the end of Surat al-Nahl.

"Al-tafsil" (detailed explanation) is the clarification of what is summarized (al-mujmalat). Perhaps the admonition is the Ten Words, and the detailed explanation is what is mentioned after them of the rulings in the chapters we have mentioned.

"Maw'izah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "kulli shay'" (everything), or as an appositive substitute (badal) of "min" when it is a noun. This applies if the beginning of the detailed explanation came directly after the writing of the tablets, with what God spoke to him in the private communion, from what the book of Exodus contains from chapter 21 through chapter 32, and what was revealed to him after that.

You may also make "maw'izah" and "tafsil" two circumstantial qualifiers of the subject pronoun in His words "and We wrote for him," meaning: admonishing and explaining in detail. Then "maw'izah" is a concomitant circumstantial qualifier (hal muqarinah), and "tafsil" is a prospective circumstantial qualifier (hal muqaddarah). As for making both of them substitutes for "of everything," this does not work with respect to His words "and detailed explanation."

As for His words "so take them" (fakhudha-ha), it is required that the "fa" indicates something of the meaning of what God addressed to Moses. Since nothing in what I have been able to examine can serve as a basis from which the command to take them with strength would branch off, it is determined that His words "so take them" are a substitute for His words "so take what I have given you," an inclusion substitution (badal ishtimal), because taking with strength includes general taking. This is required by the return to what God addressed to Moses after his swoon, to complete that address. So the content of what came before is repeated in order to connect it to the rest. It is then as though He said: "So take what I have given you with strength, and be among the thankful." The material between them is like a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh). Were it not for the repetition of "so take them," what lies between His words "among the thankful" and His words "and enjoin your people to take" would be a parenthetical insertion in its usual place. And since the context required this separation and the repetition of the command to take, the goodness of this requires that there be an added value in the repetition.

[Page 99]

So the restriction on taking, which is being "with strength," was delayed from being attached to the first command, and attached to the second command, which links back to the first command. Therefore His words "so take them" are not an emphasis. On this reading, the wording of the account of the address to Moses in this style is part of the Qur'an's wording.

It is also possible that the original quoted address already contained a repetition of what indicates the command to take, for the purpose of emphasizing this taking. Then it would be verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi), and the delay of the restriction would be an embellishment of the verbal emphasis, so that it carries an additional benefit. And the parenthetical insertion would fall between the emphasis and the thing emphasized. On this reading, the wording of the address follows the style of the speech with which God addressed Moses, which is related in the Qur'an in the style in which it was originally delivered.

The feminine pronoun in His words "so take them" refers to the tablets, given the prior mention in His words ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾. The one addressed, Moses, is the referent of the pronoun. In this pronoun there is an explanation of the generality in His words "what I have given you," and this supports the view that the referent of "what I have given you" is the tablets. Those who made the referent of "what I have given you" the message and the speech made the "fa" conjunctive to an omitted saying, connected to the clause "and We wrote," and the reading according to them is: "And We wrote, then We said: take them with strength." What we have chosen is better and more consistent with the wording.

"Akhdh" (taking) is grasping a thing, and here it is a metaphor for receiving and preserving.

The "ba'" in His words "with strength" is the ba' of accompaniment (musahabah).

"Quwwah" (strength) in its real meaning is a state in the body by which one is able to do what is difficult to do in the ordinary course. It is in the outer limbs, like the strength of the hands to do strenuous work, of the legs to walk long distances, and of the eyes to see fine visible things. It is also in the inner faculties, like the strength of the brain for thinking, which most people cannot manage, and for retaining what most people cannot retain. From this comes the saying "strength of intellect."

The use of the name "powers" (quwa) for the intellect, and in what Tha'lab recited:

"Two companions, resolute in their powers, were roused while sleep had overtaken them,
and they brought them to two Amuns, and so they both passed them."

The philosophers called the five inner senses "the inner powers" (al-quwa al-batiniyyah), namely: the retentive faculty (al-hafizah), the estimative faculty (al-wahimah), the cogitative faculty (al-mufakkirah), the imaginative faculty (al-mukhayyilah), and the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak).

One says: "a strong horse" and "a strong camel" in the real sense. One says "a strong piece of wood" if it is hard to break, and "a strong foundation" if it does not sink under the heavy wall built upon it, as a fairly close-to-literal usage. This state is predicated by gradation (tashkik), since in some of the things it characterizes it is stronger than in others. Its variation appears in the variation of what its bearer is able to do of the actions in which it inheres. And since one of the necessary consequences of strength is that its bearer's capacity to do what he wants is greater than the usual, and the actions are easier for him, the term came to be applied to the means by which a person seeks help in overcoming difficulties, such as weapons, equipment, wealth, and standing. This is a metonymic usage (idlaq kinai'). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said, "We are people of strength"﴾ [al-Naml: 33] in Surat al-Naml.

Because power necessarily entails the capacity to act, God, exalted is He, is described by the name "the Strong," meaning the one of complete power. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah is strong and severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 52] in Surat al-Anfal.

The "strength" here in His words ﴿so take them with strength﴾ is an image (tamthil) of the state of resolve to act upon what is in the tablets, with utmost diligence and eagerness, without delay, without slackness, without giving up at hardship or boredom, in the state of the strong one for whom no action he wants is out of reach. From this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿O John, take the Scripture with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12] in Surat Maryam.

This taking is the share of the Messenger and of his companions who convey the law and implement it. God is the Legislator, the Messenger is the implementer, and his companions and rulers are helpers in implementation. The command to the Messenger to take in this manner is singled out only because it is among his particular distinctions that whoever stands in his place in his presence and in his absence [does so], while in other matters they are like the rest of the community.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 145 (part 2 of 2):

So His saying ﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾ is a turn toward what is the share of the community at large from the Law, which is adherence to it. This "taking" (akhdh) is therefore a metaphor for adherence and practice, and for this reason it is followed by the preposition bi (ba'), which denotes attachment. One says akhadha bi-kadha ("he took hold of such-and-such") when he adheres to it and grasps it, as in His saying ﴿and he seized his brother by the head﴾ [al-A'raf: 150] and His saying ﴿Do not seize me by my beard nor by my head﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94]. The verb akhadha was not followed by bi in His saying ﴿fa-khudha-ha﴾ (take it), because it is used in the sense of receiving and preserving, since this is more important than taking in the sense of adherence and practice; for the former is the share of the ruler (waliyy al-amr) and the latter is the share of the entire community.
Page 101
The verb ya'khudhu ("they take") is in the jussive as a response to His saying (wa-'mur, "and enjoin"), to confirm that they will comply when he enjoins them.

And (bi-ahsanihā, "with the best of it") is an adjective stripped of comparison, intended to express intensification of goodness. Its annexation to the pronoun referring to the Tablets is in the sense of the lam (of possession), meaning: with the best that belongs to them, which is all that is in them, because it is evident that among the laws contained in them there is no gradation between "best" and "less than best"; rather, all of it is of one rank in what it has been specified for. It is also evident that they do not believe in taking some of the Law while abandoning some of it. Moreover, the Law details degrees of actions: if some actions were, in its view, more excellent than others, such as the recommended (mandub) compared with the permissible (mubah), and the dispensation (rukhsa) compared with the strict ruling ('azima), then the encouragement to act upon the more excellent would be mentioned in the Law, and that would be part of taking it. Thus the indicators that the comparative form has been stripped of comparison are clear and manifest, and there is no reason to hesitate in interpreting "al-ahsan" in this verse or to resort to parallels with artificial or rare constructions outside the speech of the eloquent. This verse is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 55] in Surat al-Zumar. The meaning: enjoin your people to take what is in them because of its goodness.
