﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾
This is an address directed to Musa (peace be upon him). It may be separate from what precedes it, in which case it is a fresh, independent resumption: it is a promise to him of their entry into the promised land. It may also be connected to what precedes it, in which case it is part of the clause ﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾, as a warning against neglecting anything of what was written for them in the Tablets. The meaning would then be: I will make clear to you the punishment of those who do not take hold of it.

The word dar ("abode") is the place in which a household dwells, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling﴾ [al-Qasas: 81] in Surat al-Qasas, and the place which a group occupies, whether a clan or a tribe, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿So they were in their abode prostrate﴾ [al-A'raf: 78], and this has already been discussed. The word dar is also used for the lasting state in which people or a person finds himself, and from this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿How excellent is the final abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. It may also mean a person's outcome and destination, since it is like the dwelling to which he returns regarding his affair. Something close to this has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So you will come to know to whom belongs the final abode﴾ [al-An'am: 135] in Surat al-An'am.

The plural pronoun is used in address either with regard to those with him from his companions, the elders of the Children of Israel, or with regard to the
Page 102
community of his people; so the address includes Musa and those with him.

The verb "to show" (al-ira'a) is from ra'a (to see) in its visual sense, since it takes two objects only.

The verb ureekum ("I will show you") was preferred over something like sa-udkhilukum ("I will make you enter"), because God prevented the majority of the people who were with Musa from entering the holy land when they refused to fight the Canaanites, as has been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said: it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26] in Surat al-Ma'idah. This is also found in the Torah, in the Book of Deuteronomy, in the first chapter: that God said to Moses, "But you shall not go in there." And in the chapter: "Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, and the LORD showed him all the land, and said to him: This is the land which I swore to Abraham, saying, To your seed I will give it; I have caused you to see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."

It may also be that "I will show you" is addressed to the people of Musa, in which case the verb ureekum is a metonymy for settling in the abode of the defiantly disobedient. Settling in the dwellings of a people occurs only through conquest and victory. So the showing is a symbol of the promise of conquering the lands of the defiantly disobedient, and by "the defiantly disobedient" are meant the polytheists. The statement is thus a promise to Musa and his people that they will conquer the abodes of the nations residing in the holy land which God promised them. These are the ones mentioned in the Torah in the thirty-third chapter of the Book of Exodus, in an address to the people: "Observe what I command you: behold, I drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest they become a snare in your midst; but you shall break down their altars, smash their pillars, and cut down their Asherim, for you shall not worship another god."

It is supported by what is narrated from Qatadah that the abode of the defiantly disobedient is the abode of the Amalekites and the giants, and it is Syria. It is therefore an error to interpret the abode of the defiantly disobedient as the land of Egypt, for they had been there and left it and did not return to it. It is also far-fetched to interpret the abode of the defiantly disobedient as their direction. In chapter 34 of the Book of Exodus: "Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest they play the harlot after their gods and sacrifice to their gods, and one of them invite you and you eat of his sacrifice, and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters play the harlot after their gods and make your sons play the harlot after their gods." The appropriateness of describing those peoples as "the defiantly disobedient" in this sense is evident.
Page 103
It has also been said that the abode of the defiantly disobedient refers to the dwellings of the former nations, such as the dwellings of Thamud and the people of Lot, whom God destroyed for their disbelief; that is, you will pass by them and see their dwellings, and thereby take admonition from the evil end of those who transgressed. But this is far-fetched, because the Children of Israel did not pass through these lands with Musa.

The shift from naming the nations by their names to describing them with the attribute of "the defiantly disobedient" is because it is more indicative of the attribute being the cause of the fate they came to, and because it is more comprehensive and concise. The choice of the description "defiantly disobedient" (al-fasiqin) rather than "polytheists" (al-mushrikin) or "wrongdoers" (al-zalimin), which is the common expression for shirk in the Qur'an, serves to alert that their evil end was caused by both polytheism and corrupt deeds together.

[Page 104]

It is possible that this verse is a continuation of what God addressed to Musa and his people. In that case, the clause *"sa-asrifu 'an ayati..."* (I will turn away from My signs...) and the clause introduced by *"bi-annahum"* (because they...) form an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause answering an unstated question). The Children of Israel feared those peoples and dreaded them, so it is as though they asked: "How will You show us their land and promise it to us? Will we not be destroyed before we enter it?" This is like what God related of them: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed in it there is a people of tyrants"﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 22], in the surah of al-'Uqud. It is also related in the fourteenth chapter of the Book of Numbers. So they were answered that God will turn those peoples away from His signs.

*Al-sarf* means repelling, that is, *"sa-asudd 'an ayati,"* I will prevent from My signs, meaning from their being nullified and voided.

The *ayat* (signs) here mean the Shari'ah, and God had promised its people that He would make them inherit the land of Syria. The meaning then is: "I will Myself undertake to repel them from you." This is like what occurs in the Torah in the thirty-fourth chapter: "Behold, I drive out before you the Amorites, etc." So turning away in this sense is a care from God for Musa and his people, by preparing for them the means of victory over those strong peoples, such as casting terror into their hearts, scattering their unity, and bringing about events that break the strength of their might.

Or the clause may be an answer to someone who says: "If we enter the land of the enemy, perhaps they will believe in our guidance and follow our religion, so we will not need to fight them." Then they are answered that God turns them away from following His signs, because they were created disposed to arrogance in the land and to turning away from the signs. In this case, *al-sarf* is a creative turning (*sarf takwini*) within the souls of those peoples.

Al-Hasan said: Among the disbelievers there are those who go to excess in their disbelief and reach a limit where, once they arrive at it, their hearts die.

In God's relating these words concerning Muhammad (ﷺ), there is an allusion (*ta'rid*) to the disbelievers of the Arabs: that God repels them from nullifying His signs, and that He prevents many of them from believing in them, for the reason we have just mentioned.

It is also possible that the clause *"sa-asrifu 'an ayati"* is part of God's address to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). al-Tabari related this from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. In this case the clause is an interjection (*mu'tarida*) in the midst of the story of the Children of Israel, prompted by His saying ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiant ones﴾ [Al-A'raf: 145]. It is an allusion that the state of the idolaters of the Arabs is like the state of those defiant ones, and an explicit statement of the cause of their persistence in obstinacy and turning away from belief. The clause is then a fresh, independent resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*). The previously mentioned meanings of turning away from the signs remain possible. The use of the future particle *sa-* (I will) with the verb *asrifu* indicates near futurity, alerting that God will hasten that turning away.

The placement of the prepositional phrase *"'an ayati"* before the object of *asrifu* is for emphasis on the signs, and because mentioning it right after the verb to which it relates is better.

The defining of those who are turned away from the signs through the relative construction (*mawsuliyya*) is to indicate, by the relative clauses, the cause of the turning away. That cause is what the mentioned relative clauses contain: for whoever has these attributes as his states, God will not support him; or, because when that becomes his condition, a seal is placed upon his heart, so his heart is turned away from grasping the indication of the signs, and he loses the capacity for that noble understanding.

The attributes that the relative clauses in the verse contain apply most completely to the idolaters of Makkah.

*Takabbur* means being characterized by pride. It takes the form that denotes affectation, and we have explained this at His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿he refused and was arrogant﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 34] and His saying ﴿you were arrogant﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87], in surah al-Baqarah. The meaning is that they admire themselves, consider themselves great, and so do not obey any commander nor accept counsel from any adviser.

The addition of the phrase *"fi al-ard"* (in the land) is to expose their arrogance and to make them infamous, indicating that their pride is contained within the land, that is, it is not hidden or confined to themselves, but is spread throughout the land, meaning its effect is spread out. Thus it is an arrogance widespread in the regions of the earth, like His saying ﴿they seek corruption in the land without right﴾ [Yunus: 23], His saying ﴿and they cause corruption in the land; those are the losers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 27], His saying ﴿and do not walk in the land exultantly﴾ [Al-Isra': 37], and the saying of Murrah ibn 'Adda al-Faq'asi:

*"Why did they not help me, the likes of me, when they lost their way,*
*while in the land there are scattered the brave and the scorpion."*

His saying *"bi-ghayri al-haqq"* (without right) is an addition to make the arrogance more reprehensible by mentioning an attribute inseparable from it, namely that it opposes the truth, that is, it is falsehood. This is a condition inseparable from arrogance, revealing its nature, since arrogance cannot be by right on the part of created beings. It is rather an attribute that belongs to God by right, because He is the Great over every existent. And God's arrogance is not intended here to be guarded against, so that the qualifier *"without right"* would be made to exclude it, as in al-Kashshaf.

Some commentators have tried to make the phrase *"bi-ghayri al-haqq"* a qualifier of arrogance, and have counted as arrogance what is right, because the one who is in the right may be arrogant toward the one who is in the wrong. From this comes the well-known saying: "Arrogance toward the arrogant is charity." But this saying, cited as evidence, is figurative or erroneous.

His saying ﴿and if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ is coordinated (*'ataf*) with His saying "they are arrogant," so it has the status of a relative clause. What is said about it is like what is said about His saying ﴿they do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96] and ﴿even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97] in surah Yunus. The word *kull* (every) is used here to mean abundance, as already explained at His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿and if you brought those given the Book every sign﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 145] in surah al-Baqarah.

*Al-sabil* (the way) is used metaphorically for the means to a thing, by the indication of its being attached to *al-rushd* (rightness) and to *al-ghayy* (error).

*Al-ru'yah* (seeing) is used metaphorically for perception.

*Al-ittikhadh* (taking) is literally the reflexive form (*mutawi'*) of *akhkhadhahu* with the doubled letter, when one makes him a taker. Then it was applied to taking a thing even if another did not give it to him. Here it is used metaphorically for constancy, that is, they do not keep to the path of rightness, but keep to the path of error.

*Al-rushd* means righteousness and the doing of what is beneficial. It has already been discussed at His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿if you perceive in them maturity of judgement﴾ [Al-Nisa': 6] in surah al-Nisa'. What is meant here is all of the righteous thing, from faith and righteous deeds.

*Al-ghayy* means corruption and misguidance, and in this sense it is the opposite of *al-rushd*, just as *al-safah* (foolishness) is the opposite of *al-rushd* in the sense of good judgement regarding wealth. The meaning is: if they perceive the righteous thing, they do not act on it, because desire has overwhelmed their hearts; and if they perceive corruption, they act upon it, because of the dominance of desire. Acting upon the righteous thing requires forcing the soul to hardship, and the souls raised on pursuing what they desire recoil from that. This is the condition of people who have not trained their souls by divine guidance, nor by wisdom and the counsel of sages and intelligent men. By contrast, error appeared in the world only as the effect of the appetites of souls and their calls, which the apparent and immediate adorns for them, and which makes them ignorant of the consequences of evil that come later, as is found in the hadith: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires."

The expression in the four relative clauses by present-tense verbs is to convey that those actions are renewed from them and that they persist in them.

Al-Jumhur read *al-rushd* with a dammah and then a sukun. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with two fathahs. Both are dialectal forms of the same word.

The clause *"dhalika bi-annahum kadhdhabu bi-ayatina"* (that is because they denied Our signs) is a resumptive explanatory clause, because characterizing them with those relative clauses raises a question.

What is referred to by *dhalika* (that) is what the preceding speech contained, treated as though it were present outside. This is the content of His saying ﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ up to the end of the verse. The demonstrative of the singular is used for it, reading the referent as the thing mentioned, like His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿and those who do not call upon another god with God, and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, and do not commit adultery—and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [Al-Furqan: 68], that is, whoever does the mentioned acts. This usage is common with the demonstrative, and the pronoun is attached to it in the same way, as already mentioned at His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿that is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 61] in surah al-Baqarah.

The *ba'* here indicates causation: their arrogance, their not believing, their following the path of error, and their turning away from the path of rightness, have as their cause their denial of the signs. So the clause explains the cause of arrogance and of what is coordinated with it of attributes, which are the cause of their being turned away from the signs. Thus that is the cause of a cause. This is better than referring the demonstrative to the turning away derived from *sa-asrifu*, because that interpretation makes denial a second cause of the turning away, whereas making it a cause of a cause is more elegant.

*Anna* (that), which indicates the verbal-noun and emphasis, is brought in to establish this causal relation and to confirm it, because it is a place of contention.

[Page 107]

The predicate is made a past verb to convey that the attribute of denial is ancient and firmly rooted in them. The firmness of that in them became the cause of God's creating the seal and the stamp upon their hearts, so that they do not perceive their defects and do not reform themselves. Thus they continue to be arrogant, turned away, and erring.

The meaning of ﴿they denied Our signs﴾ [Al-A'raf: 36] is that they began with denial, did not reflect, and did not care to contemplate the signs, so they persisted in arrogance and what goes with it. Thus God turned their hearts away from benefiting from the signs. The intention is not to inform that denial occurred from them, because that has already been known from His saying ﴿and if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾.

Heedlessness (*al-ghaflah*) is the turning of the intellect and the mind away from remembering a thing, whether intentionally or unintentionally. Its usage in the Qur'an is mostly for what occurs intentionally, through turning away and preoccupation. The blameworthy kind is what occurs intentionally, and that is the basis of obligation and accountability. As for heedlessness that is unintentional, there is no accountability for it, and this is what the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) mean by saying: it is impossible to impose obligation on the heedless.

To draw attention to the fact that their heedlessness was intentional, the report about them is expressed in the form of ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾ [Al-A'raf: 136], to indicate the persistence of their heedlessness and that it was their habit. It is only so when they have committed themselves to it. As for heedlessness that is not intentional, it may befall them and it may leave them.

This sentence may be coordinated (*ma'tufa*) with the sentence ﴿I will turn My signs away from those who act arrogantly on earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 146] through the end of the verses, on the two previous interpretations. It may also be coordinated with the sentence ﴿That is because they denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 146]. It may further be a concluding remark (*tadhyil*, a sentence that closes a statement with a general principle) interposed between the two narratives, in which case the *waw* is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyya*). In every case, its effect is to inform about them that if ﴿they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146]. That is the usual condition of the arrogant who reject the signs. Yet the group of the arrogant is never entirely free of a small number who take the way of right guidance out of forbearance and love of praise. These are some of the leaders and great men of the polytheists in every age. So the hearer may suppose that their deeds will benefit them. This assumption is removed by stating that their deeds do not benefit them while they deny the signs of God and the meeting of the Hereafter.

It is pointed out that denial is the cause of the nullification of their deeds, by describing them with the relative-pronoun construction (*al-mawsuliyya*) rather than with a pronoun. Although they were already mentioned, which by apparent logic would call for a pronoun, the expected form was departed from for this purpose.

The genitive construction ﴿the meeting﴾ (*wa liqa'*) with ﴿the Hereafter﴾ (*al-akhira*) is in the sense of "in" (*fi*), because it is an annexation to a place-adverb, like ʿuqbā al-dār (the final outcome of the abode). The meaning is ﴿the meeting of God in the Hereafter﴾, that is, the meeting with His promise and His threat.

Ḥabaṭ (nullification) is the corruption of a thing that was previously sound. It was discussed earlier under God's saying, ﴿whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5], in Surat al-Ma'ida.

The sentence ﴿Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanation (*isti'naf bayani*), answering a question that arises from the words ﴿their deeds have become void﴾. A questioner may ask: how can their good deeds be nullified? The answer is that they are recompensed according to what they used to do. Since they denied the signs of God, they had already rejected the message and the conveying of it from God. From where, then, would they have knowledge that their good deeds will have a good reward? That can only be known through information from God, the Exalted, and they had nullified the channel of information, which is the message. Moreover, reward appears only in the Hereafter, and they had denied the meeting of the Hereafter. Thus they had cut off the link between themselves and the reward. So the nullification of their good deeds was in accordance with their belief.

By ﴿what they used to do﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] is meant what they used to believe. The verb ﴿do﴾ (*ya'malūn*) was applied to the denial of the signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, because the effects of belief appear in the words and actions of the believer, and these are among his deeds.

The interrogation with ﴿hal﴾ (*hal*, "is it not the case that"?) carries the meaning of negation. Negation has been counted among the meanings of *hal*, and we explained this at God's saying, ﴿Will you be recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ [al-Naml: 90], in Surat al-Naml, so refer to it there.

The phrase ﴿what they used to do﴾ implies an elided noun, and the estimated phrase is ﴿the equivalent of what they used to do﴾. This is indicated by the verb ﴿will be recompensed﴾, since the reward is not the very thing that is rewarded. The verb *jaza* (to recompense) takes as its direct object the compensation made into a reward, and it takes the deed rewarded with the preposition *bi-*, as God says, ﴿and He will recompense them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾ [al-Insan: 12]. A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat al-An'am, ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾ [al-An'am: 139].

The verse is joined by a conjunction to the clause "And We appointed for Moses," as a narrative linked to another narrative. Earlier, the story of the private conversation (munajah) with God was mentioned, along with the signs and lessons that occurred in it. This verse mentions what the people of Moses did during his absence for the conversation, namely their association of partners with God (shirk).

Its phrase "after him" means after his absence, as is known from God's words, ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time﴾ (al-A'raf: 143), and from Moses' words to his brother Aaron, ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ (al-A'raf: 142).

Omitting the noun governed by "ba'd" (after), when it is attached to the name of the person spoken of, is common in Arabic speech, as was discussed earlier in its parallel in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "min" (from) in such a construction indicates the starting point (ibtida'), which is the basic meaning of "min." The "min" in "min hulyihim" (from their ornaments), however, is for partitive (tab'id), indicating a part.

"Al-hulyu," with a damma on the ha', a kasra on the lam and a shadda on the ya', is the plural of "halyun" (ornament), with a fatha on the ha', a sukun on the lam and no shadda on the ya'. The pattern of this plural is "fu'ul," as "thudiyy" (breasts) is pluralized. It is also pluralized as "hilyiyy," with a kasra on the ha' together with the lam, like "'isiyy" and "qisiyy," following the vowel of the 'ayn. The first form is read by the majority of the Ten Readers, and the second by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Ya'qub read "halyihim," with a fatha on the ha' and a sukun on the lam, in the singular form. The meaning is that they made it from their gold. In the Torah it is stated that they made it from gold, having taken off the gold earrings that were in the ears of their women, daughters and sons.

"Al-'ijl" is the young of the cow before it becomes a bull. In Surat Ta-Ha it is mentioned that the maker of the calf was a man called al-Samiri. In the Torah, its maker is said to be Aaron. This is part of the distortion of words from their places (tahrif al-kalim 'an mawadi'ihi), which occurred in the Torah after Moses. Aaron was not a goldsmith. The taking is attributed to all the people of Moses by way of rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), because they were the ones who commanded its making and were eager for it. This is a common metaphor in Arabic speech.

The meaning of "they took a calf" is the form of a calf. This is a metaphor of form (majaz al-suwrah), which is common in speech.

"Al-jasad" is a body without a soul, so it is specific to the body of an animal when it has no spirit. The meaning is that it was like the body of a calf in form and size, except that it was not alive. What occurs in the stories, that it was flesh and blood that ate and drank, is from the fabrications of the storytellers. How could that be, when the Qur'an says "from their ornaments" and says "it has a lowing sound"? If it had been flesh and blood, mentioning it would have been more striking for wonder.

"Al-khuwar," with the unpointed kha', is the sound of cattle. The maker of the calf made a hollow inside it of a certain narrowness, and he made a hidden blowing device. When the blowing device was moved, air was compressed inside it and came out through the narrow opening, so it had a sound like the lowing. This craft is like that of the whistle and the flute. The Canaanites made the same for their idol called Ba'l, using such a device.

"Jasadan" (a body) is an adjective of "'ijlan" (a calf), and likewise "lahu khuwar" (it has a lowing).

The clause "Did they not see that it does not speak to them" is a resumptive clause (isti'naf ibtida'i) explaining the corruption of their view in their belief.

The interrogative is for confirmation and for wonder at their state. For this reason the question is about the negation of seeing. The negation of seeing is not the actual state of affairs, but their state resembles that of people who do not see that it does not speak. So the question is asked about this, as if they might not have seen it, as an exaggeration. It is for wonder, not for denial, since one does not deny what does not exist. From this it is known that its being in this context like a negation of a negation arises only from treating those addressed as if they did not see. This has been explained earlier at God's words, ﴿Have you not seen those who left their homes?﴾ (al-Baqarah: 243) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeing is visual, because the calf's failure to speak to them is observable to them. Lack of speech is seen in the state of a thing that does not speak, by the absence of the organ of speech, which is the mouth suitable for speech, and by their repeatedly calling upon it while it does not answer.

The opinion of those who took the calf as a god has been shown to be foolish, since they witness that it does not speak to them and does not guide them to a way. The way this reasoning shows the foolishness of their opinion is that they have no excuse for taking it as a god, since its properties are the properties of dumb beasts. Its body is the body of a calf, and it belongs to a kind that is not the highest of the known kinds of existing things. Its sound is the sound of cattle, a sound that does not benefit the hearer, nor does it express any address. It is not one that guides them to a matter they follow, such that their guidance would make them independent of its speech. It is thus among the existing things inferior to them. This is like the words of Abraham, ﴿Ask them, if they can speak﴾ (al-Anbiya': 63), and ﴿What have they seen from it that would make it fit for divinity?﴾ Much less that they should be raised by it to the attributes that the true God deserves. Those who worshipped it were of higher rank than it and better guided. The purpose of this argument is not to establish divinity by speech and guidance, for otherwise divinity would have to be attributed to the wise men of humanity.

The clause "They took it" confirms the clause "the people of Moses took," so it is separated from it. The purpose of emphasis in such a context is repetition for the sake of wonder, as one says, "Yes, they took it." It also serves so that the clause "and they were wrongdoers" may be built upon it, so that it appears to be related to the taking of the calf. This is because the clause "the people of Moses took" is distant from it, due to what follows it. This is like God's words, ﴿Let a scribe write between you justly﴾ (al-Baqarah: 282), up to ﴿let him write﴾, where "let him write" is repeated so that the clause ﴿let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾ may be built upon it. This repetition, besides emphasis, conveys what follows from emphasis.

The clause "and they were wrongdoers" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative pronoun in "they took it." This is like God's words in Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿Then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 51).

[Page 112]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-A'raf (7), verse 149:

﴿When they were struck with remorse, and saw that they had gone astray, they said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾ The apparent order in narrating these events would have been for His saying ﴿When Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ [al-A'raf 7:150] to come before His saying ﴿When they were struck with remorse﴾ and the rest of the verse, since they were struck with remorse only after Moses returned, saw the extent of his anger, and heard his rebuke of his brother and of them. The usual order was departed from in order to hasten the mention of the outcome of their worship of the calf, which was regret, and because showing their error serves as an admonition to the listeners, so that they do not hasten to abandon their own way before they have understood the consequences of what they are turning to.

﴿Su'iṭa fī aydīhim﴾ (lit. "it was made to fall into their hands") is in the passive voice. It is a phrase which the Qur'an uses like a proverb, since it is composed with striking brevity and contains both metonymy (kināya) and metaphor (istiʿāra). The hand is used metaphorically for power and support, since with it one strikes with the sword and the spear. For this reason, when people curse themselves with evil, they say "May the fingers be paralysed from my hands" (shullat min yadayya al-anāmil), and the hand is the instrument of ability. God, exalted is He, said ﴿the Possessor of strength (dhā al-ayd)﴾ [Sad 38:17]. It is also said: "I have no hand (yad) in that," or "I have no two hands (yadān) in that," meaning "I am not able to do it." When a person suffers paralysis in the upper arm and cannot move it, it is apt to say "suqita fī yadihi" (he was made to fall into his hand), meaning that someone who fell upon him, i.e. some calamity came upon him.

Since mentioning the unnamed agent of the falling does not add more than the fact that the verb is derived from its own root, it is permissible to put the verb into the passive voice. The meaning of "suqita fī yadihi" is that something fell into his hand, and thereby rendered his hand motionless, because the intended sense is that the movement of his hand was halted by a cause that is not specified, except that it is something that entered his hand and made it incapable of action. This is a metonymy for the fact that something had overtaken him which caused his bewilderment regarding his affair, as one says "fatta fī sāʿidihi" (it weakened his forearm).

In this verse the expression has been used in the sense of regret and the clear recognition of error. It is therefore an image (tamthīl) of their situation with that of a person who has been made to fall into his hand at the time of action. The meaning is that their error and their bad treatment of their Lord and their Prophet became clear to them. Thus regret is the meaning of the whole construction, while the metonymy is in one part of the construction, namely "suqita fī al-yad."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I was told on the authority of Abu Marwan ibn Sirāj that he used to say: the Arabs' saying suqita fī yadihi is among the things that have perplexed me in meaning." Al-Zajjāj said: "It is a composition that was not heard before the Qur'an, and the Arabs did not know it."

I say: This is the decisive view, for I have not found it in any of their speech before the Qur'an. So the statement of Ibn Sirāj, "The Arabs say suqita fī yadihi," perhaps means the Arabs who came after the Qur'an.

The meaning is: when Moses returned to them, threatened them, and burned the calf, as is mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha [20:97]. The matter is stated briefly here, because it is known that they were not struck with remorse and did not see that they had gone astray except after their determination and obstinacy in worshipping the calf and their saying ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:91]. Thus the omission of that is a case of brevity, so that it may be built upon the understanding that their error did not remain hidden from them for long. For this reason the narration of their making the calf is linked to this, hastening to show the disclosure of their error, as a conclusion to the story of their error. It is as if it were said: "They were struck with remorse, and saw that they had gone astray." Then it was said: "When they were struck with remorse, they said..."

Their saying ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ is repentance and turning back to God. They knew that they had committed a grievous sin, and for this reason they emphasized the conditional clause with the oath, which the lam (of emphasis) prepared for. They placed mercy before forgiveness because mercy is the cause of forgiveness.

The predicate of kāna (the word "khāsirīn") comes with the partitive preposition "min" (among), because that is stronger in affirming loss than "we will surely be losers," as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Then I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided﴾ [al-An'am 6:56]. [p. 117]

And he meant by "al-a'da'" (the enemies)

[p. 118]

Those who had called to the worship of the calf, because Harun had denounced it to them and they therefore resented him for it. The wrongdoing people are those who associated partners with God by worshipping the calf. It is also possible that the meaning is: do not place me with them in punishment, since Musa had commanded the killing of those who worshipped the calf, so "ja'ala" is kept to its original sense.

The clause ﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾ is a reply to Harun's words, which is why it is separated (from what precedes it) without a conjunction. Musa began his supplication by seeking forgiveness for himself, showing courtesy toward God for the anger that had appeared in him. Then he sought forgiveness for his brother for whatever shortcoming or laxity may have appeared from him in deterring the worshippers of the calf from that.

Mention of the description "brother" there adds to the appeal, in hope that God will honour His messenger by forgiving his brother, like Nuh's saying ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45].

Entering into mercy (al-idkhal fi al-rahmah) is a metaphor for the all-encompassing reach of mercy to both of them in all their conditions, such that they are within it as one who settles in a house or something similar that contains. Thus "entering" is a primary metaphor, and the preposition "fi" (in) is a secondary metaphor, its particle of location being used in place of the particle of accompaniment (bi).

Here "ja'ala" carries the sense of "zanna" (to think, to deem), as in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. The wrongdoing people are those who associated partners with God by worshipping the calf. It is also possible that the meaning is: do not place me with them in punishment, since Musa had commanded the killing of those who worshipped the calf, so "ja'ala" is kept to its original sense.

The clause ﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾ is a reply to Harun's words, which is why it is separated (from what precedes it) without a conjunction. Musa began his supplication by seeking forgiveness for himself, showing courtesy toward God for the anger that had appeared in him. Then he sought forgiveness for his brother for whatever shortcoming or laxity may have appeared from him in deterring the worshippers of the calf from that.

Mention of the description "brother" there adds to the appeal, in hope that God will honour His messenger by forgiving his brother, like Nuh's saying ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45].

Entering into mercy (al-idkhal fi al-rahmah) is a metaphor for the all-encompassing reach of mercy to both of them in all their conditions, such that they are within it as one who settles in a house or something similar that contains. Thus "entering" is a primary metaphor, and the preposition "fi" (in) is a secondary metaphor, its particle of location being used in place of the particle of accompaniment (bi).

The clause ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), and the waw is either for the circumstantial state (hal) or parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). ﴿Arham al-Rahimin﴾ means the one most abundant in mercy above every merciful one.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 152–153:

﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [for worship] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the worldly life. Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed — indeed, your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾

It is possible that His saying ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ up to His saying ﴿in the worldly life﴾ is part of Musa's speech. So after he (Musa) prayed for forgiveness for his brother, he informed [them] that Allah had become angry with those who worshipped the calf, that the effect of His anger would appear upon them, and that humiliation would overtake them in this world. This was by a revelation he had received. The speech of Musa ends at His saying ﴿in the worldly life﴾. The clause ﴿and thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ is an address from Allah within the Qur'an, and so it is an interjection (i'tiraD), and the waw is an interjectory waw (waw i'tiradiyyah). Allah appended to the narration of Musa's speech this interjection, informing that He recompenses every fabricator with the like of what Musa reported about the fabricators of his people. And the clause ﴿But those who committed evil deeds﴾ to the end of the verse is a completion of the benefit by clarifying the state of the opposites of those spoken of and of their like.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ to its end is an address from Allah to Musa, as a response to his prayer for his brother for forgiveness, with an omitted verb of saying supposed: i.e., "We said: indeed, those who took the calf..." to its end, like what Allah the Exalted related about Ibrahim in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim said: "My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits, those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day." He said: "As for him who disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], the verse.

And (yanaluhum) means "will reach them" (yuṣību-hum).

Al-nawl and al-nayl mean "taking"; here it is a metaphor for affliction and befalling, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Those will receive their share of the Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 37] in this surah. And those who took the calf are those who worshipped it, so the second object of ittakhadhū (took) is omitted for brevity, i.e., they took it as a god.

Their identification by way of the relative clause (mawsuliyyah) is because it is the most concise way of bringing them to mind with a description by which they are known, and because it indicates the causality of what punishment befell them. What is meant by "anger" is the manifestation of its effect in the form of abandonment and withholding of care; as for anger itself, it is present at the moment.

The anger of Allah the Exalted is His willing evil for His servant and punishing him in this world and the Hereafter, or in one of them. Dhillah (humiliation) is a submission in the self and a subjugation resulting from inability to repel. So the meaning of humiliation overtaking them is that they become defeated before those who overcome them. This may be by the enemy being empowered over them, or by the courage being stripped from their souls, such that they are fearful of the enemy even if he is not empowered over them; or it is the humiliation of estrangement, since Allah deprived them of the kingdom of the holy land, so they were without a homeland throughout their lives until that entire generation had died out. This humiliation is a worldly punishment which repentance may not erase, for repentance only requires pardon for the punishment of obligation (taklif), and does not require the removal of accountability for worldly calamities; because worldly punishments are causal effects arising from their causes, it does not follow that repentance lifts them except by a special divine favour. This resembles the distinction between the address of positing (khitab al-wad') and the address of obligation (khitab al-taklif), as is understood from the hadith of the Night Journey, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought two vessels, one of milk and the other of wine, and he chose the milk. Jibril said: "Praise be to Allah who guided you to the fitrah; had you taken the wine, your community would have gone astray." Yet Allah may erase a worldly punishment when He is pleased with the offender, and Allah is possessor of great bounty.

The discussion of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿and thus﴾ has already occurred at His saying ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah, i.e., and like that great recompense We recompense the fabricators.

Al-iftira' is a lie whose speaker has no excuse in its invention, and it has passed at His saying the Exalted: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-Ma'idah.

What is meant by fabrication is inventing [doctrines] in the roots of religion by positing beliefs that are not supported by sound proof, whether from reason or from revelation. Musa, peace be upon him, had warned them against worshipping idols, as Allah related earlier in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to idols they had﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], the three verses mentioned just before. So Allah made their recompense for fabrication anger and humiliation, and that is when they do the like of it after the admonition has come to them from Allah. For this reason the polytheists of the Arabs were not humiliated; but when Muhammad (ﷺ) came and guided them, and they persisted in fabrication, Allah punished them with humiliation: He removed their awe from the hearts of the Arabs, uprooted them through killing and captivity, and seized their homes. Then, when those among them who embraced Islam did so, they became honoured through Islam.

It is taken from this verse that the liar is struck with abasement.

His saying ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented﴾ up to the verse is an interjection, meaning that if they repent and believe, Allah will forgive them, in keeping with the Qur'an's custom of following threat with encouragement. Forgiveness returns to the non-accountability for their sins in the punishment of the Hereafter, and to the lifting of Allah's anger against them in the future. What is meant by "evil deeds" includes disbelief, which is the greatest of evil deeds.

Repentance from it is faith (iman).

In His saying "min ba'dihā" in both places there is an omitted genitive before what the word ba'd (after) is attached to — and its omission is widespread — indicated by 'amilū: i.e., min ba'di 'amalihā (after the doing of them). The discussion of omitting the genitive with ba'du and qablu when they are attached to a noun that is itself attached to a pronoun has already occurred at His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then you took the calf after Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The particle thumma here indicates delay, and this is an incitement to accept repentance even after a long time filled with the doing of evil deeds.

His saying "min ba'dihā" is an emphasis on the meaning of the delay which the particle thumma conveys, and this is an allusion to the polytheists that if they believe they will be forgiven, even if the period of polytheism upon them was long.

Faith is coordinated with repentance, although repentance includes it in the sense that faith is a repentance from disbelief, either for the sake of giving it importance, because it is the foundation of the reckoning of righteous deeds before Allah the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is? It is freeing a neck﴾ [al-Balad: 12–13], up to His saying ﴿and then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]; and so that it is not supposed that shirk, because of its gravity, is not rescued from by repentance.

Or it is that by faith is meant a particular faith, namely faith with sincerity, which then includes performing the obligatory duties.

The address in His saying "Indeed, your Lord" is to Muhammad (ﷺ) in the most apparent reading, or to Musa, on the basis of making His saying ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ a statement from Allah to Musa.

In defining the predicate subject by the genitive construction there is a means to honouring the one added to, by stating that he is nurtured by Allah the Exalted; and mentioning the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) here is a preparation for the attribute of mercy.

Emphasizing the report with inna, the emphatic lam, and the intensive forms in ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173] is for greater concern with it: an encouragement to the disobedient to repent, and a dispelling of despair from their souls, even if their sins are great. So they should not suppose that repentance is limited by a boundary such that if sins exceed it in multitude or magnitude, repentance is not accepted from them.

The second pronoun in "min ba'dihā" is an exaggeration in expressing the favour of accepting their repentance after they have been filled with evil deeds.

The omission of the complement of ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173] is because it is evident from the context, and the estimate is: "Indeed, He is Forgiving and Merciful to them," or "to everyone who does an evil deed and repents from it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 154:

﴿And when the anger subsided in Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾

The composition of this statement is like the composition of His saying ﴿And when they were overcome with remorse﴾ [al-A'raf: 149] and His saying ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry﴾ [al-A'raf: 150]. That is: then the anger subsided in Moses, and when it subsided from him, he took up the tablets.

Page 122
This sentence is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the sentence "And when Moses returned to his people."

The "subsiding" (sukūt) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the departure of anger from him. The surging of anger within the soul of Moses, which generated thoughts of punishment for his brother and his people, and the casting down of the tablets until they broke, was likened to the speech of a person inciting him to that. What made this comparison apt is that the angry person has a turmoil of inner self-talk pushing him toward actions by which he extinguishes the surging of his anger. When his anger calms and his soul settles, that is in the position of the inciter falling silent; therefore the term "silence" is applied to it. This entails likening anger to a speaking inciter by way of the implicit metaphor (al-makniyyah). Thus two metaphors are combined, or it is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah makniyyah), since the likened image was not mentioned and was indicated by mention of one of its attendant features, namely the silence. In this there is also what supports that the casting down of the tablets was an effect of anger.

The definite article in "the tablets" is for previous reference (al-'ahd), that is, the tablets which he cast down. He took them only to preserve them for acting upon them, because their breaking does not destroy what is in them of writing.

The "nuskhah" (copy) is in the sense of "that which is copied," like "khutbah" (sermon) and "qubdah" (handful). Copying (naskh) is the transfer of the like of what is written onto another tablet or page. The phrase implies that a copy was made from these tablets, because "nuskhah" is annexed to the pronoun of "the tablets." This is a case of ellipsis (ijaz), since the implied sense is: he took the tablets, and a copy was made from them, and in its copy was guidance and mercy. This points to what is in the Torah, in the thirty-fourth chapter of the Book of Exodus: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Cut two tablets of stone like the first ones, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets which you broke.' ... So he cut two tablets of stone like the first; and the LORD said to Moses, 'Write these words for yourself...' ... And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments."

Thus describing the copy as containing guidance and mercy entails the original from which it was copied, because what is in the copy is the equivalent of what is in the original. The word "nuskhah" is mentioned here only to indicate that the original two tablets were replaced by a copy of them. It has been said that the fragments of the original tablets were placed in the Ark of the Covenant, to which His saying — exalted is He — refers: ﴿That there will come to you the Ark, in which is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248], in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾ — its attachment is contested by both (guidance) and (mercy). The lam in His saying "for their Lord they fear" is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah), which entered upon the object because the governing verb is weakened by being placed after its complement.

Page 123

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 155 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. And when the earthquake seized them, he said: "My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? This is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of forgivers."﴾ ﴿"And ordain for us good in this world and in the Hereafter. Indeed, we have turned back to You."﴾ [al-A'raf: 155-156]

The clause "wa-akhtara Musa" (and Musa chose) is conjoined to the clause "wa-attakhadha qawmu Musa" (and the people of Musa took [the calf]). This is conjunction of one narrative to another narrative (ʿatf al-qissa ʿala al-qissa), because this story too is among the places of admonition and lesson among the lessons drawn from the story of Musa with the Children of Israel. In it there is a lesson concerning the greatness of God, may He be exalted, and His mercy; there is Musa's supplication, which contains the totality of goods; and there is the good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the foundation of his law.

Al-ikhtiyar (choosing) is the distinguishing of what is desired from what is mixed of the desired and its opposite. It is the form ifti'al derived from al-khayr (goodness), and the verb is formed in this pattern without indicating reflexive effect (mutawa'a) of the verb khara (to choose).

The phrase "sab'ina rajulan" (seventy men) is a substitution (badal) for "qawmahu" (his people), a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). It has been said that "qawmahu" is in the accusative because the preposition has been elided, and the sense is: he chose from his people. They said: the elision of the preposition from a complement that stands in the rank of the second object is common with three verbs: ikhtara (to choose), istaghfara (to ask forgiveness) and amara (to command), and from this is the expression amartuka al-khayr (I commanded you the good). On this view, "sab'in" (seventy) is the first object. In any case, the construction of the speech by mentioning the people at the outset, rather than restricting it to seventy men, was required by the situation of brevity in narration, and this is one of the aims of the Qur'an.

This choosing took place when God commanded him to come for the intimate conversation (munajah) mentioned earlier in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], and so on. In the Torah, in chapter twenty-four of the Book of Exodus, it is recorded: "God commanded Moses to go up to Mount Sinai, he and (Aaron) and (Nadab) and (Abihu) and (Joshua) and seventy of the elders of Israel. The elders of Israel shall be at a certain place on the mountain, and Moses shall go forward until he enters the cloud to hear the speech of God. When God manifested Himself to the mountain, the mountain trembled, and Moses remained forty days." In chapter thirty-two and the one after it, after the mention of their worship of the calf and the breaking of the tablets, it is recorded that God commanded Moses to hew two tablets of stone like the first, to write upon them the Ten Words that were written on the two broken tablets, and to go up to Mount Sinai. A manner of ascent close to that in chapter twenty-four is described. God said to Moses: "Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book." Moses prostrated before God, may He be exalted, and asked forgiveness for his people for their lack of obedience, and said: "If You forgive their sin, well; but if not, blot me out of Your book." In chapter nine of the Book of Deuteronomy it is recorded that when Moses went up the mountain for the second intimate conversation, he fasted forty days and forty nights, eating no food and drinking no water, seeking forgiveness for the sin of his people and asking pardon for them.

Thus it becomes clear from what is in the Torah that God appointed two appointed times (miqat) for Moses for the intimate conversation, and that He chose seventy men for the first intimate conversation. The Torah does not mention their being chosen for the second intimate conversation. Since the second intimate conversation was like a completion of the first, it is established that Moses took the chosen seventy with him, and for this reason the earthquake occurred during it just as in the first time. The Qur'an does not mention that the earthquake seized them the first time; rather it mentions that Moses fell down in a swoon (ṣa'iqan). It is necessary that the seventy were afflicted by what afflicted Moses, because they too were on the mountain. The Qur'an mentions the earthquake in the second time, and the Torah does not mention it.

The pronoun in "akhadhathumu al-rajfa" (the earthquake seized them) refers to the seventy. The apparent meaning in this verse is that what is intended is the narration of the state at the second appointed time for intimate conversation, in which the seeking of forgiveness for his people took place. The earthquake narrated here is an earthquake that seized them like the earthquake that seized them at the first intimate conversation, because the earthquake occurs from the manifestation of a great effect of the divine attributes, as has been mentioned previously. Musa's saying "Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?" indicates that he means by it their worship of the calf, their presence at it, and their silence; and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿It is only Your trial﴾. Musa feared that this earthquake was a forerunner of punishment, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) used to fear that the wind might be the beginning of punishment.

It is also possible that this occurred at the first intimate conversation, and that his saying "for what the foolish among us did" means what came from the Children of Israel of obstinacy before the intimate conversation, such as their saying ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and their request to see God, may He be exalted. But the apparent meaning is that such a thing is not described by the word "did" (fa'ala) in his saying ﴿for what the foolish among us did﴾.

The essential point of the lesson in this story is guarding against the wrath of God, fear of His punishment, the station of the messengers in awe (khashya), and the supplication of Musa, etc.

The composition of the speech in his saying ﴿And when the earthquake seized them﴾ is formed in the same manner as his saying ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ [al-A'raf: 150], as has been mentioned.

The verb "akhadha" (to seize) is used figuratively for a severe affliction that firmly takes hold, in the way that the seizer firmly holds the seized.

The "law" (lau) in his saying "Had You willed, You could have destroyed them" may be used in the sense of wishing (tamanni), which is a figurative meaning arising from the meaning of impossibility (imtina') that is the original meaning of lau. From this is the proverb: "Lau dhat siwarin latamatni" (If the one with bracelets had slapped me), where the implied apodosis is: "If she had slapped me, it would have been easier for me." The apodosis is stated in the verse: "shi'ta ahlaktahum" (You willed, You destroyed them), that is: "Would that You had willed to destroy them," namely the seventy who were with him. So the clause "ahlaktahum" is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause "shi'ta" (You willed), on account of the sin of the people which caused their return to the intimate conversation.

On this reading of "lau", there is no elision of the lam in "ahlaktahum" which normally accompanies the apodosis of "lau". He said "ahlaktahum" and "iyyaya" (me) and did not say "ahlaktana" (destroyed us), in order to distinguish between the two destructions: the destruction of the seventy was for their silence regarding the worship of the calf, while Musa's destruction might be so that he would not witness the destruction of the people. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Hud...﴾ and similar instances are many. Musa feared that God would destroy the whole people by that earthquake, because the rest of the people were more deserving of destruction than the seventy. The Torah has pointed to this in the chapter: "Moses returned to God and said: the people have sinned a great sin, and they have made for themselves gods. If You forgive their sin, well; but if not, blot me out of Your book which You have written. God said to Moses: whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book." So the blotting from the book is the blotting of God's decree of life in wrath, and this is what is related in the verse by His saying: ﴿Had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ Musa feared that this earthquake was a sign of wrath and a forerunner of destruction as punishment for their worship of the calf. Therefore he said: "Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?" The foolish (al-sufaha') are those who worshipped the calf, and their polytheism was called folly (safah) because it is polytheism mixed with baseness of intellect, since they made an image they had fashioned with their own hands into a god for themselves.

It is also possible that the particle "lau" is used in its original meaning, of the impossibility of its apodosis because of the impossibility of its condition. Then one may ask why the lam was elided from the apodosis of "lau", and why he did not say "la-ahlaktahum", although the usual practice is that the apodosis of the past affirmative is accompanied by the lam. The elision of the lam here is for the point that the connection between the condition of "lau" and its apodosis here is strong, because it is evident that destruction is the act of God alone. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], surah al-Waqi'ah, and its explanation will come. The meaning is an acknowledgment of the favour of pardoning them in what preceded, and a preparation for an allusive request for their pardon now. This is the intended meaning of his saying: ﴿Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾, that is: You did not will their destruction when they were engaged in worshipping the calf, so do not destroy them now.

The interrogative in his saying "atuhlikuna" (would You destroy us) is used to express alarm, meaning: I fear that. The people deserved punishment, and he fears that the punishment of God may encompass those who were with the people who deserved it, even if they did not share in the cause of the punishment, as He said: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike those among you who have done wrong in particular﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. In the hadith of Umm Salama, she said: "O Messenger of God, will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes abundant." In another hadith: "Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions." Musa feared the evil suspicion for himself, for his brother, and for the innocent of his people: that the nations to whom news of them would reach would think they were criminals.

The pronoun in his saying "atuhlikuna" (would You destroy us) is in the plural because this destruction is the destruction anticipated from the continuation of the earthquake, and its expectation is one at one time. This differs from the destruction mentioned earlier, whose cause is different, so it was appropriate to distribute its object.

The clause "atuhlikuna" is a resumed sentence (mustani'afa) in the manner of breaking up the speech of the grieving, frightened questioner. Likewise the clause "in hiya illa fitnatuka" (this is only Your trial) and the clause "anta waliyyuna" (You are our Protector).

The pronoun in "in hiya" refers to "ma fa'ala al-sufaha'" (what the foolish did), because the referent (mas-daq) of "ma fa'ala al-sufaha'" is the trial. The meaning is: the trial that occurred through the worship of the calf is only a trial from You, that is, from Your decree and the creation of the causes of its occurrence, such as the weakness of the people's minds, their admiration for the idols of the Canaanites, Musa's absence, Aaron's leniency and his fear of the people, the fear of the elders of Israel of the common folk, and other things that God knows, and which Musa was certain of in a general way.

The statement in his saying ﴿This is only Your trial﴾, etc., is used to express praise (tamjid) of the breadth of knowledge and power, and an allusive request that they be preserved and guided. It is not used as an excuse to his people, by the evidence of his saying ﴿by which You lead astray whom You will﴾, which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from "fitnatika" (Your trial). So the leading astray by it is a state of its states.

Then he alluded to a request for their guidance by his saying ﴿and guide whom You will﴾. The prepositional phrase "bi-ha" (by it) in his saying is attached to the verb "tudillu" (You lead astray) alone, and the verb "tahdi" (You guide) does not compete for it, because trial is not a cause of guidance, by the evidence of its being named trial. So whoever estimates in the interpretation "and guide by it" or the like has been heedless.

The particle "ba'" (bi) may be for accompaniment (mula-basah), meaning: You lead astray whom You will while accompanied by it. Or it may be causal (sababiyya), meaning: You lead astray because of that trial. Thus from one aspect it is a trial, and from another aspect it is a cause of misguidance.

The fitna (trial) is that by which there occurs the disturbance of states, confusion, and the scattering of minds. Its explanation has already passed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they teach no one until they say: "We are only a trial"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in surah al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71] in surah al-'Uqud, and His saying ﴿Then their trial was only that they said: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23] in surah al-An'am.

The purpose of the clause ﴿You are our Protector﴾ is the acknowledgment of devotion to the worship of God, may He be exalted, as a preparation for the request for forgiveness and mercy, because it is the nature of a protector (wali) to show mercy to his client (mawla) and to support him.

The wali is the one who has authority (wilaya) over someone, and wilaya is an alliance or manumission that requires support and assistance. If it is between two parties of equal standing, then each of the two contracting parties is called mawla. If one of the two parties is stronger, the stronger is called wali and the weaker is called mawla. Since wilaya is not admissible of plurality, because a person does not take as protector anyone other than his own protectors, his saying ﴿You are our Protector﴾ implies the exclusion of seeking victory through other than God, and its explicit wording contains the form of restriction (qasr).

The continuation of the argument from *al-wilaya* in His saying ﴿Forgive us﴾ is a continuation of speech upon speech, and the intent is not that the Walī (the Protecting Friend) is obligated to grant forgiveness.

He placed forgiveness before mercy because forgiveness is a cause of many mercies. Forgiveness puts an end to the anger of God (*ghadab Allah*), which follows from sin. When anger ends, it becomes possible for it to be followed by good pleasure (*al-ridā*), and good pleasure requires beneficence (*al-iḥsān*).

[p. 128]

And ﴿the best of the forgivers﴾ means He who forgives abundantly. A similar expression appeared earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 150], in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

He joined the clause ﴿and You are the best of the forgivers﴾ by conjunction because it is a statement with the meaning of seeking great forgiveness. It is therefore conjoined to the supplication, as if it were said: "Forgive us, have mercy on us, and forgive us all our sins," because increase in forgiveness is among the effects of mercy.

(*Wa-uktub*, "and write") is used metaphorically for the meaning of a bestowal whose occurrence is assured and which is renewed time after time. This is because one who wishes to confirm a contract, a promise, or a gift, and whose fulfilment is related to renewal in the future, writes it in a document, so that it does not admit denial, diminution, or reversal. Such writing is called a covenant (*ʿahd*). Among this is what they wrote in the document of severance (*ṣaḥīfat al-qaṭīʿa*), and what they wrote of the alliance of Dhū al-Majāz. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said:

"Fearing oppression and mutual contention; and can the desires break what is in the scrolls of papers?"

If the bestowal or the contract were for a single occurrence, writing would not be needed, because taking possession or handing over is sufficient without writing, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except that it be a present commerce which you conduct among yourselves, then there is no blame on you that you do not write it﴾ [al-Baqara: 282]. The meaning is: "Give us good after good, during the days of our lives and on the Day of Resurrection." The word *uktub* indicates this meaning. Without it, it would be a sincere supplication for the granting of one good, and so it would need the help of context to achieve generality, because an indefinite noun in the context of supplication is intended to be general, as in al-Ḥarīrī's words in the fifth *maqāma*:

"O people of this abode, may you be protected from harm (*ḍurran*)."

That is: from every harm; it is not intended that they be protected from some specific harm.

The *ḥasana* (good) is the good condition, which in this world is that which is pleasing to people and to God, exalted is He, thus combining the good of this world and of religion; and in the Hereafter it is the condition of perfection. Its explanation has already been given in the *tafsīr* (exegesis) of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them is he who says: "Our Lord, give us in this world good"﴾ [al-Baqara: 201], in Sūrat al-Baqara.

The clause ﴿Indeed we have turned back to You﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 156] is placed as a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the request and the response. For this reason it is disjoined (not conjoined by a conjunction), and because the position of the emphatic particle at its beginning is one of concern, it conveys causation and connection, and it serves the function of the causal *fāʾ* (*fāʾ al-sababiyya*), as has been mentioned more than once.

(*Hudnā*) means "we have repented." It is said: *hāda yahūdu* when he returned and repented; and it is with a *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ* in this verse, by agreement of the widely transmitted readings (*al-qirāʾāt al-mutawātira*). The meaning is: we have repented of whatever sin and shortcoming we may have committed. This is information about himself and about those chosen from among his people, according to what He knows of the sincerity of their inner hearts.

[p. 129]

[p. 130] The clause "He said: My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will" and what follows is an answer to Moses' words. For this reason it is separated (from what precedes), because it occurs in the manner of dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once. Moses' speech, although it is a request, does not require an answer, yet the answer to one who makes a request is an act of attention and grace.

By "punishment" here is meant the punishment of this world, because the discourse is an answer to Moses' words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. Destruction is a punishment. God therefore made clear to him that the punishment of this world strikes whom God wills among His servants. God has summarized the cause of the will, and He knows it best, while Moses knows it in general terms. The discourse thus contains reassurance to Moses that the punishment will not reach him and the innocent of his people, because God is too exalted to treat them as criminals. The meaning is: I am able to restrict the punishment to those who disobeyed, and to save those who did not share in the disobedience. The discourse came in a concise manner, as is the speech of one who is not questioned about what He does.

His words ﴿and My mercy has encompassed all things﴾ are the counterpart of Moses' words "forgive us and have mercy upon us," and it is a promise by implication that the mercy requested for him and for those chosen with him will be granted. For since it has encompassed all things, they are the most hopeful of people for it. The disobedient are also submerged in mercy, and among it is the mercy of respite and provision. But God's mercy toward His servants has degrees that vary.

His words ﴿My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will﴾ up to His words ﴿all things﴾ are a general answer, which serves as a preparation for the detailed answer in His words ﴿So I will write it﴾.

The conjunction in His words ﴿So I will write it﴾ is a consequence drawn from the vastness of mercy: since it has encompassed all things, there is among it what is written, that is, what will be given in the future, to those upon whom these attributes have been bestowed. This includes a promise to Moses and to the righteous of his people, because these qualities are realized in them. It is a promise that looks back to Moses' words ﴿We have turned back to You﴾. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿akthubuha﴾ refers to ﴿My mercy﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 23], so it is a pronoun of the genus, equivalent to the noun defined by the definite article of genus. That is, "write a portion of this kind for the possessors of these attributes." It is not meant that He writes all of His mercy for these people, because this is not known in usage when speaking of genera. Yet it is known from the context that this type of mercy is a great type, by the evidence of the praise of its recipients through attributes that indicate their worthiness, and by the evidence of the silence about others. Thus it is understood that this recipient has a special, great mercy, and that others fall within some degrees of the general mercy known from His words ﴿and has encompassed all things﴾. This meaning has been made explicit by the restriction in His words at the end of the verse: ﴿Those are the successful﴾.

The meaning of ﴿akthubuha﴾ has been mentioned shortly before.

The meaning of ﴿and has encompassed all things﴾ has been mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-A'raf: 89] in this surah.

The meaning is: the mercy that Moses asked for himself and his people, God promised to give to those among them who are characterized as being among the God-fearing and those who pay zakat, and to those among them who believe in the signs of God. The "signs" are true: they are the evidences of the truthfulness of the messengers, and the words of God by which He legislated for people their guidance and direction, especially the Qur'an, since every passage of three verses of it is a sign, because it is inimitable and thus indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger. This is what is intended here. These are the ones who follow the unlettered Prophet when he comes to them, that is, they obey him in what he commands them. Since these things were made, by means of that mercy, to be [the cause of] some of it, it is known that obtaining some of these things brings about some of that mercy in a manner suited to it, on condition of faith. This is also known from other verses in which God addressed Moses, such as His words just before: ﴿And those who did evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 153]. So this mercy includes those among the Children of Israel who feared God, believed, and paid zakat before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), for their following of him was impossible to achieve before his mission. But they must be determined to follow him when he comes, if they knew of that, as He, exalted is He, said: "And [recall] when God took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will believe in him and support him.' He said: 'Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?' They said: 'We affirm.' He said: 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses'" [Al 'Imran: 81]. "And whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient" [Al 'Imran: 82].

The mercy also includes those who believe in the signs of God, and what is meant by them are the signs that will come in the future, because the faith in Moses' signs had already been established by that time. This necessitates the repetition of the relative pronoun in mentioning the people of this attribute, to indicate that they are another group, namely those who will exist at the time of the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him). For this reason the phrase ("﴿Those who follow the Messenger﴾") etc. is put in apposition to them. It refers to the Jews and Christians living at the time of the mission and after it, as shown by His words ﴿whom they find written with them﴾ and His words ﴿and He removes from them their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾. This indicates that they were a people of a law in which there was hardship and difficulty. By "the signs of God" is meant the Qur'an, because its words are the ones specifically called "signs," since they were made into miracles that the eloquent cannot match, and an indication that they are from God and a proof of the truthfulness of His Messenger, as was mentioned in the Eighth Introduction.

In this verse there is good news of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). It points to what is in the Torah from the tenth chapter through the fourteenth, and the eighteenth chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy. Moses, after reminding them of the sin of worshipping the calf, and mentioning his intercession with God to pray for their forgiveness, as the ninth chapter of that book contains, which we mentioned just before in the commentary on His words ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], then mentioned in the tenth chapter their command to be God-fearing, with His words: "Now, O Israel, what does the Lord require of you but that you fear your Lord, to walk in His ways and love Him." Then he mentioned in it and in the three following it commandments detailing piety. Then he mentioned zakat in the fourteenth chapter, saying: "Tithing, you shall tithe all the yield of your seed year by year. Tithe your wheat, your wine, your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and your flock. And at the end of every three years you shall bring out every tenth of your produce of that year and place it in your gates, and the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are in your gates will come and eat and be satisfied." Etc. Then he mentioned many rulings in the three chapters after it.

Then in the eighteenth chapter is his saying: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen, according to all you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb" — that is, the Mount of Sinai — "on the day of the assembly, when you said: 'Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire anymore, lest I die.' And the Lord said to me: 'I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.'" This indicates that this Prophet is not from the Children of Israel, because of his saying "from among your brothers," since the address is to the Children of Israel, and they cannot be brothers to themselves. Their brothers are the sons of their father's brother: Isma'il, the brother of Isaac, and they are the Arabs. Had the intended meaning been a prophet from the Children of Israel like Samuel, as the Jews interpret it, it would have said "from among you" or "from your midst." It is known that the Prophet is a messenger with a new law from His words "like you," since Moses was a prophet and a messenger.
