So the Qur'an gathered all of that in His words ﴿for those who fear God and pay zakat and those who believe in Our signs﴾ etc.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is the combining in this verse of the two descriptions of prophethood and messengerhood, to indicate that the Jews changed the description of the Messenger and expressed it by "Prophet," so that it would apply to the prophets of the Children of Israel, and they neglected the implication of His words "like you," and omitted the description "unlettered." This verse was the cause of the conversion to Islam of the great Andalusian rabbi Samaw'al ibn Yahya, the Jew, as he related about himself in his book which he named Ghayat al-Maqsud fi al-Radd 'ala al-Nasara wa al-Yahud (The Aim of the Intent in Refuting the Christians and Jews).

This great mercy is therefore specific to those among the Jews and Christians who believed in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it includes the messengers and prophets upon whom God took the covenant to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), so they were certain of his mission and believed in him, and they are treated as those who followed what he brought, because they prepared themselves for that. It also includes the Muslims among the Arabs and others besides the Children of Israel, because those who believed in Muhammad (peace be upon him) among the Jews proceeded in following the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet.

[p. 133] The mention of the description "Messenger" first is because it is the more specific and more important description. Also, mentioning it first records the distortion by the People of the Book, since they omitted this description so that the words of the Torah would apply to whoever came after Moses from the prophets of the Children of Israel. And because Muhammad (ﷺ) became famous with the description "the Unlettered Prophet," this combination became like a title for him, so it is not changed from its fame. Likewise, he is so wherever his mention occurs in the Qur'an.

The "unlettered" (al-ummi) is one who does not know writing and reading. It has been said that it is derived from "mother" (umm), meaning he is more like his mother than his father, because women among the Arabs did not know reading and writing, and they only learned them in Islam. So learning reading and writing became a mark of free women rather than slave women, as 'Ubayd al-Ra'i said, and this is an Islamic verse:

"They are the free women, not mistresses of tents, black-eyed, who do not read the surahs."

As for men, among them are those who read and write.

It has also been said that it is derived from "community" (umma), meaning one whose condition is the condition of the majority of the community, that is, the community known to them, which is the Arab community. In the pre-Islamic period, only a rare few of them knew reading and writing. For this reason, the People of the Book describe them as "unlettered," as God, exalted is He, related of them in His words: ﴿That is because they said: There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75].

The state of being unlettered is a description that God singled out for Muhammad (ﷺ) among His messengers, as a completion of the intellectual, knowledge-based miracle with which God supported him. God made unlettered-ness an essential attribute of him, so that through it he would complete his essential attribute, which is messengerhood, and to show that his perfection of soul is a divine, direct perfection, with no intermediary of the ordinary causes of perfections. Thus unlettered-ness was a description of perfection in him, while in others it is a description of deficiency. This is because he possessed knowledge and soundness of intellect that do not admit error in all aspects of knowing the true perfections, and he was certain of his knowledge and clear in his affair, to a greater degree than what those who learn attain. His unlettered-ness became a sign that what he had attained came from divine overflows.

The meaning of ﴿whom they find written﴾ is finding his attributes and qualities, in which no one else resembles him, so that his distinctive features are treated as his very essence. The pronoun of "the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet" is applied to these qualities metaphorically, by way of istikhdam (a figure where a pronoun refers to a meaning different from the one intended by its antecedent).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 156–157 (part 2 of 3):

What exists is its attribute and description, and the indication is His saying *maktuban* (written), for the essence itself is not written. He turned away from expressing it through description to show that they find a description that admits no confusion, namely: that he is *ummi* (unlettered), who commands what is good (*al-ma'ruf*), forbids what is evil (*al-munkar*), makes lawful the good things (*al-tayyibat*), makes unlawful the foul things (*al-khaba'ith*), lifts from them their burden (*isr*), and the severity of their law.

The Gospel is mentioned here because it was revealed to the Children of Israel, and a group of them believed in it, as did those who came after them of their descendants. Allah had informed Musa of this.

What is written in the Torah is what we mentioned just above. What is written in the Gospel contains many glad tidings (*bisharat*) of Muhammad ﷺ, and in some of them there is an explicit statement that he will be sent with a general mission. In the Gospel of Matthew, in chapter twenty-four: "Many false prophets will arise and will deceive many. But he who endures to the end (i.e., whose law will last until the end of the world), he will be saved, and this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come," meaning the end of the world. In the Gospel of John, in chapter fourteen: "But the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." The meaning of "in my name" is "in my likeness," which is his being a lawgiving Messenger, not a mere confirming prophet.

The mention of the Torah and the Gospel has already occurred at the beginning of surah Al 'Imran.

As for the phrase ﴿commanding them what is good﴾: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said it is an explanation of what is written among them. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yajiduna-hu* (they find it), because the pronoun refers to the mention and the name, and the mention and the name do not command. Thus the pronoun is determined to be figurative (*majaz*), and the one who commands what is good is the very person of the Messenger, not his attribute and mention. There is no doubt that the purpose of these attributes is to make them recognize him by them, so that they may identify the unlettered Messenger when he comes with a law whose characteristics are these.

Allah has made *al-ma'ruf*, *al-munkar*, *al-tayyibat*, *al-khaba'ith*, *al-isr* and *al-aghlal* related to the legislation of the unlettered Prophet and as signs. Therefore, their meaning must be what immediately comes to sound minds from the meanings of their words.

So *al-ma'ruf* (what is known to be good) includes everything that sound intellects and upright natural dispositions (*fitar*) accept, and *al-munkar* is its opposite. Their explanation has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Let there arise from you a community calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104], in surah Al 'Imran.

What unites them is the meaning of *fitrah* (natural disposition), which is the foundation of the Muhammadan law, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. This is the clearest sign for recognizing the rulings of the Muhammadan law.

*Al-tayyibat* is the plural of *tayyiba*. In its feminine form, the meaning of *al-akilah* (that which is eaten) or the meaning of *al-tu'mah* (food) was taken into account, as an alert that the intended *tayyibat* are the edible things, as is shown by His saying in its parallels, such as ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], in al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], in surah al-Ma'idah. The intended meaning is not good deeds, because deeds have been defined by the attribute of *al-ma'ruf* and *al-munkar*, and edible things do not enter into *al-ma'ruf* and *al-munkar*, since the intellect has no share in distinguishing between what is accepted and rejected of them. Rather, people's customs (*awa'id*) govern them in this matter. Since Islam is the religion of *fitrah*, and customs are not relied upon in it, it attached the status of edible things to *al-tayyib* (the good) and their prohibition to *al-khubth* (foulness). So *al-tayyib* is whatever has no harm in it, no unwholesomeness and no filth; and *al-khabith* is whatever is harmful, or whose consequence is bad, or whatever is loathsome and is not accepted by reasonable people, like impurity. This is the criterion of the permitted and the forbidden among foods. Thus customs enter only in the choice of their people among what is permitted, as they wish. Quraysh did not eat the lizard (*dabb*), and when it was placed on the table of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he disliked to eat from it and said: "It is not unlawful, but it was not from the food of my people, so I find myself averse to it." Therefore, the correct view is that everything without harm, corruption or filth is permitted, though it may be disliked (*makruh*) out of consideration for a slight harm. For this reason, a prohibition came concerning eating every animal with fangs of the predators (*siba'*). Its interpretation according to Malik, in the most famous of the reports from him, is that it is disliked (*karahah*), and this is what should not be doubted. And what harm is there in eating the flesh of a lion? Likewise, the permissibility of eating the *khishash* (small insects), the insects, and the land and sea reptiles, due to the differing customs of people in eating them or not. Jurm did not eat chicken, and Fa'qas ate dogs. So one people may not be restricted because of the dislike of others for what their taste or their people's custom dislikes. Something of this has already been mentioned in the verse of surah al-Ma'idah. The jurist must confine his consideration to the natures and attributes of the edible things, and what some of its attributes are unknown to us, while the law has forbidden it, like the prohibition of swine.

The lifting of the *isr* (burden) means the abolition of its legislation, that is, by abrogating (*naskh*) what contained hardship from the earlier divine laws. The literal sense of *wad'* (lifting/placing) is bringing down from a height to a lower place, and here it is a metaphor (*majaz*) for the abolition of obligations involving arduous deeds.

Its proper construction is to take a second object with the particle *fi* (in), which denotes location. When it is construed with *'an* (from), it indicates the removal of the first object from what follows *'an*. And when it is construed to the second object with *'ala* (upon), it indicates the lowering of the first object upon what follows *'ala*, with firm settling. So *yada'u 'anhum* (lifts from them) here is used metaphorically for removing the obligations that are like the *isr* and the *aghlal*. Thus the lifting includes the meaning of abrogation (*naskh*) and other things, as will come.

As for *al-isr*: the apparent statement of al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashshaf* and *al-Asas* is that it is literally a heavy load, with a kasra on the *tha'*, that is, a physical weight such that movement becomes difficult with it. No other lexicographers restrict it in this way, and this restriction is one of his verifications. This is also what the apparent statement of Ibn al-'Arabi in *al-Ahkam* follows. The intended meaning here is the arduous obligations and the hardship in religion. If it is as al-Zamakhshari restricted it, then ﴿and lifts from them their burden﴾ is figurative (*tamthiliyyah*), by comparing the state of the one relieved of what burdens him with obligations to the state of one who was loaded with a weight and then had its weight removed from his back, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31]. If it is not so, then *isr* is a implicit metaphor (*isti'arah makniyyah*) and *yada'* (lifts) is an imaginative expression (*takhyil*). And that is also a continuing metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*) for removal.

The law of the Torah included many severe rulings, such as the punishment of death for many sins, among them working on the Sabbath. It also included the prohibition of many good foods and the intensification of prohibition in matters that are minor, such as working on the Sabbath. The most severe aspect of the *isr* in the Torah's law is that repentance from sins was not prescribed in it, nor was the seeking of repentance by the criminal. The *isr* has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what You burdened those before us with﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], in surah al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Amir alone among the famous readings read *aşara-hum* (their burdens) in the plural. The plural and the singular in nouns of kind are equivalent.

*Al-aghlal* is the plural of *ghull* (with a damma on the *ghain*), which is an iron ring placed around the neck of a prisoner or a criminal, and held by a leather strap or an iron chain in the hand of the one assigned to guard the prisoner. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿when the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. The *ghull* is also used metaphorically for an obligation and a deed that causes pain and cannot be borne. If we build on al-Zamakhshari's statement, then *al-aghlal* is figurative (*tamthiliyyah*), by comparing the state of one freed from humiliation and disgrace to the state of one released from captivity. Thus, the lifting of the shackles is necessarily a metaphor for what the Jews suffered of humiliation among the nations among whom they settled after the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis and the loss of the kingdom of Judah. For Islam came to make its followers equal in their rights within the Islamic community, so that there remains no distinction between the original and the newcomer, or between the intimate and the attached, as was the case in the Jahiliyyah. The suitability of using shackles as a metaphor for humiliation is clearer, because shackles are a symbol of degradation in captivity, retaliation and the like.

These two attributes are particularly specific to the Jews, who are the subject of the address of Allah, exalted is He, to Musa. They do not apply to anyone else among those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, because the Jews had a law, and in it were arduous obligations, unlike the non-Jewish Arabs, Persians and others. Therefore Allah attributed the *isr* to their pronoun, and described the shackles with what their pronoun contains. Moreover, if you reflect on the condition of all nations before Islam, you will not find their laws, their regulations and their conditions free of burdens upon them, such as the prohibition of some good things in the Jahiliyyah, and arduous obligations among the Christians and the Magians that do not agree with natural ease. Likewise, you will not find them free from the oppression of tyrants, the humiliation by chiefs, the severity of the strong against the weak, and what used to happen among them of killing and raids, and the shedding of blood, and their consuming of one another's wealth in falsehood. So Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with a religion whose nature is to deliver mankind from those hardships, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. For this reason we have interpreted the lifting as encompassing abrogation and other things, and we have interpreted the shackles as that which is contrary to the meaning of the *isr*. This does not conflict with what exists in the religions of the Jahiliyyah, the Magian religion and others, of permissiveness (*tahallul*) in many rulings, for that is great corruption, which does not lighten the weight of the *isr* that is in them. This is the permissiveness that Abu Khirash al-Hudhali looked at in his saying, meaning the law of Islam:

*So it is not like the covenant of the abode, O mother of Malik,*
*But the chains have encircled the necks.*

The *fa'* in His saying ﴿So those who believe in him﴾ is the *fa' al-fasihah* (the eloquent *fa'*, which indicates an implied condition). The meaning is: if this Prophet is as you have known, from the testimony of the Torah and the Gospel to his prophethood, and from the characteristic of his law with the attribute you have heard, then you know that those who believed in him, supported him, honored him and followed his guidance, they are the successful.

[Page 138]

The restriction (*qasr*) derived from the definiteness of the predicate and from the pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), meaning: they are the ones who have succeeded, that is, rather than those who disbelieved in him, by the context of the situation. For the situation of Musa's supplication requires that he sought forgiveness, mercy and the writing of good in this world and the Hereafter for everyone who followed his religion. Musa did not intend this to include those who do not follow Islam after the coming of Muhammad ﷺ. But the restriction came in the sense of guarding against misunderstanding. It is also permissible for the restriction to be an assertive restriction (*qasr id'a'i*), indicating the meaning of the perfection of the attribute of success for those who follow the unlettered Prophet. Thus the success of others among the nations who came before them is no success, when compared with their success. That is, the Muhammadan community is the best of nations in general, and they are the ones upon whom the divine mercy descends, which encompasses everything of their affairs. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

The meaning of *'azzaruhu* is that they strengthened and reinforced him. This is by making manifest what their books contained of the glad tidings of his attributes and the attributes of his law, and by proclaiming that among the people. This is something additional to belief in him, as Abd Allah ibn Salam did, and as the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal: "This is the *namus* (the confidant of revelation) that was sent down to Musa." It is also different from *nasara* (supported), because *nasr* is assistance in war with weapons. For this reason, *wa-nasaruhu* (and they supported him) is joined after it by conjunction.

The following is the wording of the commentary, the words of the verse being quoted (here, the Qur'anic phrases within ﴿ ﴾) and the honorifics rendered as stated.

The following of the light is a metaphor for emulating what the Qur'an has brought: the state of one who takes the Qur'an's guidance as his guide is likened to the state of a traveller at night who, when he sees a light shining before him, follows it, knowing that he will find with it safety from dangers and harms of the journey. The parts of this metaphor are themselves metaphors. Thus "following" (ittiba') is suitable as a metaphor for "emulation" (iqtida'), and it is a widespread figurative usage for it; and "the light" (al-nur) is suitable as a metaphor for the Qur'an, because that which teaches the truth and right guidance is likened to light. The best of metaphors is that which is fit for the individual similes to be considered within its parts.

The indication in His saying ﴿Those are the successful ones﴾ serves to honour their station, and to show that those referred to by these attributes have become worthy of what is reported about them after the demonstrative, as in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

Page 139

In this verse there is an honouring of the great virtue of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, and there is joined to them whoever supports his religion after them.

[p. 130] The clause "He said: My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will" and what follows is an answer to Moses' words. For this reason it is separated (from what precedes), because it occurs in the manner of dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once. Moses' speech, although it is a request, does not require an answer, yet the answer to one who makes a request is an act of attention and grace.

By "punishment" here is meant the punishment of this world, because the discourse is an answer to Moses' words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. Destruction is a punishment. God therefore made clear to him that the punishment of this world strikes whom God wills among His servants. God has summarized the cause of the will, and He knows it best, while Moses knows it in general terms. The discourse thus contains reassurance to Moses that the punishment will not reach him and the innocent of his people, because God is too exalted to treat them as criminals. The meaning is: I am able to restrict the punishment to those who disobeyed, and to save those who did not share in the disobedience. The discourse came in a concise manner, as is the speech of one who is not questioned about what He does.

His words ﴿and My mercy has encompassed all things﴾ are the counterpart of Moses' words "forgive us and have mercy upon us," and it is a promise by implication that the mercy requested for him and for those chosen with him will be granted. For since it has encompassed all things, they are the most hopeful of people for it. The disobedient are also submerged in mercy, and among it is the mercy of respite and provision. But God's mercy toward His servants has degrees that vary.

His words ﴿My punishment, I afflict with it whom I will﴾ up to His words ﴿all things﴾ are a general answer, which serves as a preparation for the detailed answer in His words ﴿So I will write it﴾.

The conjunction in His words ﴿So I will write it﴾ is a consequence drawn from the vastness of mercy: since it has encompassed all things, there is among it what is written, that is, what will be given in the future, to those upon whom these attributes have been bestowed. This includes a promise to Moses and to the righteous of his people, because these qualities are realized in them. It is a promise that looks back to Moses' words ﴿We have turned back to You﴾. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿akthubuha﴾ refers to ﴿My mercy﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 23], so it is a pronoun of the genus, equivalent to the noun defined by the definite article of genus. That is, "write a portion of this kind for the possessors of these attributes." It is not meant that He writes all of His mercy for these people, because this is not known in usage when speaking of genera. Yet it is known from the context that this type of mercy is a great type, by the evidence of the praise of its recipients through attributes that indicate their worthiness, and by the evidence of the silence about others. Thus it is understood that this recipient has a special, great mercy, and that others fall within some degrees of the general mercy known from His words ﴿and has encompassed all things﴾. This meaning has been made explicit by the restriction in His words at the end of the verse: ﴿Those are the successful﴾.

The meaning of ﴿akthubuha﴾ has been mentioned shortly before.

The meaning of ﴿and has encompassed all things﴾ has been mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-A'raf: 89] in this surah.

The meaning is: the mercy that Moses asked for himself and his people, God promised to give to those among them who are characterized as being among the God-fearing and those who pay zakat, and to those among them who believe in the signs of God. The "signs" are true: they are the evidences of the truthfulness of the messengers, and the words of God by which He legislated for people their guidance and direction, especially the Qur'an, since every passage of three verses of it is a sign, because it is inimitable and thus indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger. This is what is intended here. These are the ones who follow the unlettered Prophet when he comes to them, that is, they obey him in what he commands them. Since these things were made, by means of that mercy, to be [the cause of] some of it, it is known that obtaining some of these things brings about some of that mercy in a manner suited to it, on condition of faith. This is also known from other verses in which God addressed Moses, such as His words just before: ﴿And those who did evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 153]. So this mercy includes those among the Children of Israel who feared God, believed, and paid zakat before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), for their following of him was impossible to achieve before his mission. But they must be determined to follow him when he comes, if they knew of that, as He, exalted is He, said: "And [recall] when God took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will believe in him and support him.' He said: 'Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?' They said: 'We affirm.' He said: 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses'" [Al 'Imran: 81]. "And whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient" [Al 'Imran: 82].

The mercy also includes those who believe in the signs of God, and what is meant by them are the signs that will come in the future, because the faith in Moses' signs had already been established by that time. This necessitates the repetition of the relative pronoun in mentioning the people of this attribute, to indicate that they are another group, namely those who will exist at the time of the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him). For this reason the phrase ("﴿Those who follow the Messenger﴾") etc. is put in apposition to them. It refers to the Jews and Christians living at the time of the mission and after it, as shown by His words ﴿whom they find written with them﴾ and His words ﴿and He removes from them their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾. This indicates that they were a people of a law in which there was hardship and difficulty. By "the signs of God" is meant the Qur'an, because its words are the ones specifically called "signs," since they were made into miracles that the eloquent cannot match, and an indication that they are from God and a proof of the truthfulness of His Messenger, as was mentioned in the Eighth Introduction.

In this verse there is good news of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). It points to what is in the Torah from the tenth chapter through the fourteenth, and the eighteenth chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy. Moses, after reminding them of the sin of worshipping the calf, and mentioning his intercession with God to pray for their forgiveness, as the ninth chapter of that book contains, which we mentioned just before in the commentary on His words ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], then mentioned in the tenth chapter their command to be God-fearing, with His words: "Now, O Israel, what does the Lord require of you but that you fear your Lord, to walk in His ways and love Him." Then he mentioned in it and in the three following it commandments detailing piety. Then he mentioned zakat in the fourteenth chapter, saying: "Tithing, you shall tithe all the yield of your seed year by year. Tithe your wheat, your wine, your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and your flock. And at the end of every three years you shall bring out every tenth of your produce of that year and place it in your gates, and the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are in your gates will come and eat and be satisfied." Etc. Then he mentioned many rulings in the three chapters after it.

Then in the eighteenth chapter is his saying: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen, according to all you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb" — that is, the Mount of Sinai — "on the day of the assembly, when you said: 'Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire anymore, lest I die.' And the Lord said to me: 'I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.'" This indicates that this Prophet is not from the Children of Israel, because of his saying "from among your brothers," since the address is to the Children of Israel, and they cannot be brothers to themselves. Their brothers are the sons of their father's brother: Isma'il, the brother of Isaac, and they are the Arabs. Had the intended meaning been a prophet from the Children of Israel like Samuel, as the Jews interpret it, it would have said "from among you" or "from your midst." It is known that the Prophet is a messenger with a new law from His words "like you," since Moses was a prophet and a messenger. So the Qur'an gathered all of that in His words ﴿for those who fear God and pay zakat and those who believe in Our signs﴾ etc.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is the combining in this verse of the two descriptions of prophethood and messengerhood, to indicate that the Jews changed the description of the Messenger and expressed it by "Prophet," so that it would apply to the prophets of the Children of Israel, and they neglected the implication of His words "like you," and omitted the description "unlettered." This verse was the cause of the conversion to Islam of the great Andalusian rabbi Samaw'al ibn Yahya, the Jew, as he related about himself in his book which he named Ghayat al-Maqsud fi al-Radd 'ala al-Nasara wa al-Yahud (The Aim of the Intent in Refuting the Christians and Jews).

This great mercy is therefore specific to those among the Jews and Christians who believed in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it includes the messengers and prophets upon whom God took the covenant to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), so they were certain of his mission and believed in him, and they are treated as those who followed what he brought, because they prepared themselves for that. It also includes the Muslims among the Arabs and others besides the Children of Israel, because those who believed in Muhammad (peace be upon him) among the Jews proceeded in following the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet.

[p. 133] The mention of the description "Messenger" first is because it is the more specific and more important description. Also, mentioning it first records the distortion by the People of the Book, since they omitted this description so that the words of the Torah would apply to whoever came after Moses from the prophets of the Children of Israel. And because Muhammad (ﷺ) became famous with the description "the Unlettered Prophet," this combination became like a title for him, so it is not changed from its fame. Likewise, he is so wherever his mention occurs in the Qur'an.

The "unlettered" (al-ummi) is one who does not know writing and reading. It has been said that it is derived from "mother" (umm), meaning he is more like his mother than his father, because women among the Arabs did not know reading and writing, and they only learned them in Islam. So learning reading and writing became a mark of free women rather than slave women, as 'Ubayd al-Ra'i said, and this is an Islamic verse:

"They are the free women, not mistresses of tents, black-eyed, who do not read the surahs."

As for men, among them are those who read and write.

It has also been said that it is derived from "community" (umma), meaning one whose condition is the condition of the majority of the community, that is, the community known to them, which is the Arab community. In the pre-Islamic period, only a rare few of them knew reading and writing. For this reason, the People of the Book describe them as "unlettered," as God, exalted is He, related of them in His words: ﴿That is because they said: There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75].

The state of being unlettered is a description that God singled out for Muhammad (ﷺ) among His messengers, as a completion of the intellectual, knowledge-based miracle with which God supported him. God made unlettered-ness an essential attribute of him, so that through it he would complete his essential attribute, which is messengerhood, and to show that his perfection of soul is a divine, direct perfection, with no intermediary of the ordinary causes of perfections. Thus unlettered-ness was a description of perfection in him, while in others it is a description of deficiency. This is because he possessed knowledge and soundness of intellect that do not admit error in all aspects of knowing the true perfections, and he was certain of his knowledge and clear in his affair, to a greater degree than what those who learn attain. His unlettered-ness became a sign that what he had attained came from divine overflows.

The meaning of ﴿whom they find written﴾ is finding his attributes and qualities, in which no one else resembles him, so that his distinctive features are treated as his very essence. The pronoun of "the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet" is applied to these qualities metaphorically, by way of istikhdam (a figure where a pronoun refers to a meaning different from the one intended by its antecedent).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 156–157 (part 2 of 3):

What exists is its attribute and description, and the indication is His saying *maktuban* (written), for the essence itself is not written. He turned away from expressing it through description to show that they find a description that admits no confusion, namely: that he is *ummi* (unlettered), who commands what is good (*al-ma'ruf*), forbids what is evil (*al-munkar*), makes lawful the good things (*al-tayyibat*), makes unlawful the foul things (*al-khaba'ith*), lifts from them their burden (*isr*), and the severity of their law.

The Gospel is mentioned here because it was revealed to the Children of Israel, and a group of them believed in it, as did those who came after them of their descendants. Allah had informed Musa of this.

What is written in the Torah is what we mentioned just above. What is written in the Gospel contains many glad tidings (*bisharat*) of Muhammad ﷺ, and in some of them there is an explicit statement that he will be sent with a general mission. In the Gospel of Matthew, in chapter twenty-four: "Many false prophets will arise and will deceive many. But he who endures to the end (i.e., whose law will last until the end of the world), he will be saved, and this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come," meaning the end of the world. In the Gospel of John, in chapter fourteen: "But the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." The meaning of "in my name" is "in my likeness," which is his being a lawgiving Messenger, not a mere confirming prophet.

The mention of the Torah and the Gospel has already occurred at the beginning of surah Al 'Imran.

As for the phrase ﴿commanding them what is good﴾: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said it is an explanation of what is written among them. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yajiduna-hu* (they find it), because the pronoun refers to the mention and the name, and the mention and the name do not command. Thus the pronoun is determined to be figurative (*majaz*), and the one who commands what is good is the very person of the Messenger, not his attribute and mention. There is no doubt that the purpose of these attributes is to make them recognize him by them, so that they may identify the unlettered Messenger when he comes with a law whose characteristics are these.

Allah has made *al-ma'ruf*, *al-munkar*, *al-tayyibat*, *al-khaba'ith*, *al-isr* and *al-aghlal* related to the legislation of the unlettered Prophet and as signs. Therefore, their meaning must be what immediately comes to sound minds from the meanings of their words.

So *al-ma'ruf* (what is known to be good) includes everything that sound intellects and upright natural dispositions (*fitar*) accept, and *al-munkar* is its opposite. Their explanation has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Let there arise from you a community calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104], in surah Al 'Imran.

What unites them is the meaning of *fitrah* (natural disposition), which is the foundation of the Muhammadan law, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. This is the clearest sign for recognizing the rulings of the Muhammadan law.

*Al-tayyibat* is the plural of *tayyiba*. In its feminine form, the meaning of *al-akilah* (that which is eaten) or the meaning of *al-tu'mah* (food) was taken into account, as an alert that the intended *tayyibat* are the edible things, as is shown by His saying in its parallels, such as ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], in al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], in surah al-Ma'idah. The intended meaning is not good deeds, because deeds have been defined by the attribute of *al-ma'ruf* and *al-munkar*, and edible things do not enter into *al-ma'ruf* and *al-munkar*, since the intellect has no share in distinguishing between what is accepted and rejected of them. Rather, people's customs (*awa'id*) govern them in this matter. Since Islam is the religion of *fitrah*, and customs are not relied upon in it, it attached the status of edible things to *al-tayyib* (the good) and their prohibition to *al-khubth* (foulness). So *al-tayyib* is whatever has no harm in it, no unwholesomeness and no filth; and *al-khabith* is whatever is harmful, or whose consequence is bad, or whatever is loathsome and is not accepted by reasonable people, like impurity. This is the criterion of the permitted and the forbidden among foods. Thus customs enter only in the choice of their people among what is permitted, as they wish. Quraysh did not eat the lizard (*dabb*), and when it was placed on the table of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he disliked to eat from it and said: "It is not unlawful, but it was not from the food of my people, so I find myself averse to it." Therefore, the correct view is that everything without harm, corruption or filth is permitted, though it may be disliked (*makruh*) out of consideration for a slight harm. For this reason, a prohibition came concerning eating every animal with fangs of the predators (*siba'*). Its interpretation according to Malik, in the most famous of the reports from him, is that it is disliked (*karahah*), and this is what should not be doubted. And what harm is there in eating the flesh of a lion? Likewise, the permissibility of eating the *khishash* (small insects), the insects, and the land and sea reptiles, due to the differing customs of people in eating them or not. Jurm did not eat chicken, and Fa'qas ate dogs. So one people may not be restricted because of the dislike of others for what their taste or their people's custom dislikes. Something of this has already been mentioned in the verse of surah al-Ma'idah. The jurist must confine his consideration to the natures and attributes of the edible things, and what some of its attributes are unknown to us, while the law has forbidden it, like the prohibition of swine.

The lifting of the *isr* (burden) means the abolition of its legislation, that is, by abrogating (*naskh*) what contained hardship from the earlier divine laws. The literal sense of *wad'* (lifting/placing) is bringing down from a height to a lower place, and here it is a metaphor (*majaz*) for the abolition of obligations involving arduous deeds.

Its proper construction is to take a second object with the particle *fi* (in), which denotes location. When it is construed with *'an* (from), it indicates the removal of the first object from what follows *'an*. And when it is construed to the second object with *'ala* (upon), it indicates the lowering of the first object upon what follows *'ala*, with firm settling. So *yada'u 'anhum* (lifts from them) here is used metaphorically for removing the obligations that are like the *isr* and the *aghlal*. Thus the lifting includes the meaning of abrogation (*naskh*) and other things, as will come.

As for *al-isr*: the apparent statement of al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashshaf* and *al-Asas* is that it is literally a heavy load, with a kasra on the *tha'*, that is, a physical weight such that movement becomes difficult with it. No other lexicographers restrict it in this way, and this restriction is one of his verifications. This is also what the apparent statement of Ibn al-'Arabi in *al-Ahkam* follows. The intended meaning here is the arduous obligations and the hardship in religion. If it is as al-Zamakhshari restricted it, then ﴿and lifts from them their burden﴾ is figurative (*tamthiliyyah*), by comparing the state of the one relieved of what burdens him with obligations to the state of one who was loaded with a weight and then had its weight removed from his back, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31]. If it is not so, then *isr* is a implicit metaphor (*isti'arah makniyyah*) and *yada'* (lifts) is an imaginative expression (*takhyil*). And that is also a continuing metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*) for removal.

The law of the Torah included many severe rulings, such as the punishment of death for many sins, among them working on the Sabbath. It also included the prohibition of many good foods and the intensification of prohibition in matters that are minor, such as working on the Sabbath. The most severe aspect of the *isr* in the Torah's law is that repentance from sins was not prescribed in it, nor was the seeking of repentance by the criminal. The *isr* has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what You burdened those before us with﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], in surah al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Amir alone among the famous readings read *aşara-hum* (their burdens) in the plural. The plural and the singular in nouns of kind are equivalent.

*Al-aghlal* is the plural of *ghull* (with a damma on the *ghain*), which is an iron ring placed around the neck of a prisoner or a criminal, and held by a leather strap or an iron chain in the hand of the one assigned to guard the prisoner. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿when the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. The *ghull* is also used metaphorically for an obligation and a deed that causes pain and cannot be borne. If we build on al-Zamakhshari's statement, then *al-aghlal* is figurative (*tamthiliyyah*), by comparing the state of one freed from humiliation and disgrace to the state of one released from captivity. Thus, the lifting of the shackles is necessarily a metaphor for what the Jews suffered of humiliation among the nations among whom they settled after the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis and the loss of the kingdom of Judah. For Islam came to make its followers equal in their rights within the Islamic community, so that there remains no distinction between the original and the newcomer, or between the intimate and the attached, as was the case in the Jahiliyyah. The suitability of using shackles as a metaphor for humiliation is clearer, because shackles are a symbol of degradation in captivity, retaliation and the like.

These two attributes are particularly specific to the Jews, who are the subject of the address of Allah, exalted is He, to Musa. They do not apply to anyone else among those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, because the Jews had a law, and in it were arduous obligations, unlike the non-Jewish Arabs, Persians and others. Therefore Allah attributed the *isr* to their pronoun, and described the shackles with what their pronoun contains. Moreover, if you reflect on the condition of all nations before Islam, you will not find their laws, their regulations and their conditions free of burdens upon them, such as the prohibition of some good things in the Jahiliyyah, and arduous obligations among the Christians and the Magians that do not agree with natural ease. Likewise, you will not find them free from the oppression of tyrants, the humiliation by chiefs, the severity of the strong against the weak, and what used to happen among them of killing and raids, and the shedding of blood, and their consuming of one another's wealth in falsehood. So Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with a religion whose nature is to deliver mankind from those hardships, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. For this reason we have interpreted the lifting as encompassing abrogation and other things, and we have interpreted the shackles as that which is contrary to the meaning of the *isr*. This does not conflict with what exists in the religions of the Jahiliyyah, the Magian religion and others, of permissiveness (*tahallul*) in many rulings, for that is great corruption, which does not lighten the weight of the *isr* that is in them. This is the permissiveness that Abu Khirash al-Hudhali looked at in his saying, meaning the law of Islam:

*So it is not like the covenant of the abode, O mother of Malik,*
*But the chains have encircled the necks.*

The *fa'* in His saying ﴿So those who believe in him﴾ is the *fa' al-fasihah* (the eloquent *fa'*, which indicates an implied condition). The meaning is: if this Prophet is as you have known, from the testimony of the Torah and the Gospel to his prophethood, and from the characteristic of his law with the attribute you have heard, then you know that those who believed in him, supported him, honored him and followed his guidance, they are the successful.

[Page 138]

The restriction (*qasr*) derived from the definiteness of the predicate and from the pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), meaning: they are the ones who have succeeded, that is, rather than those who disbelieved in him, by the context of the situation. For the situation of Musa's supplication requires that he sought forgiveness, mercy and the writing of good in this world and the Hereafter for everyone who followed his religion. Musa did not intend this to include those who do not follow Islam after the coming of Muhammad ﷺ. But the restriction came in the sense of guarding against misunderstanding. It is also permissible for the restriction to be an assertive restriction (*qasr id'a'i*), indicating the meaning of the perfection of the attribute of success for those who follow the unlettered Prophet. Thus the success of others among the nations who came before them is no success, when compared with their success. That is, the Muhammadan community is the best of nations in general, and they are the ones upon whom the divine mercy descends, which encompasses everything of their affairs. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

The meaning of *'azzaruhu* is that they strengthened and reinforced him. This is by making manifest what their books contained of the glad tidings of his attributes and the attributes of his law, and by proclaiming that among the people. This is something additional to belief in him, as Abd Allah ibn Salam did, and as the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal: "This is the *namus* (the confidant of revelation) that was sent down to Musa." It is also different from *nasara* (supported), because *nasr* is assistance in war with weapons. For this reason, *wa-nasaruhu* (and they supported him) is joined after it by conjunction.

The following is the wording of the commentary, the words of the verse being quoted (here, the Qur'anic phrases within ﴿ ﴾) and the honorifics rendered as stated.

The following of the light is a metaphor for emulating what the Qur'an has brought: the state of one who takes the Qur'an's guidance as his guide is likened to the state of a traveller at night who, when he sees a light shining before him, follows it, knowing that he will find with it safety from dangers and harms of the journey. The parts of this metaphor are themselves metaphors. Thus "following" (ittiba') is suitable as a metaphor for "emulation" (iqtida'), and it is a widespread figurative usage for it; and "the light" (al-nur) is suitable as a metaphor for the Qur'an, because that which teaches the truth and right guidance is likened to light. The best of metaphors is that which is fit for the individual similes to be considered within its parts.

The indication in His saying ﴿Those are the successful ones﴾ serves to honour their station, and to show that those referred to by these attributes have become worthy of what is reported about them after the demonstrative, as in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

Page 139

In this verse there is an honouring of the great virtue of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them, and there is joined to them whoever supports his religion after them.

Page 140

This sentence is an interposed clause (*i'tiraḍ*, a parenthetical insertion) placed between the narratives about the Children of Israel. It came as a digression prompted by the mention of the Unlettered Prophet, serving as a reminder to the Children of Israel of what God promised to Moses (peace be upon him), and as an awakening of their understanding to the fact that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the fulfillment of the attributes that God taught to Moses.

The address ﴿O people﴾ is addressed to all of humanity, and the first-person pronoun refers to the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ).

The emphasis of the statement with (*inna*, "indeed") is because among those addressed there are deniers and wavering people, so the call is pursued with thoroughness.

The emphasis on the pronoun of the addressees by the word ﴿all of you﴾ (*jamī'an*), which explicitly denotes generality, is to remove the possibility that his mission is restricted to the Children of Israel. For among the Jews there was a group who claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ) was a prophet, but claimed that he was the prophet of the Arabs only. Therefore, when the Messenger of God said to Ibn Sayyad, who was a Jew, "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?", Ibn Sayyad replied, "I testify that you are the Messenger of the Unlettered (*Ummiyyin*)." It is also established among the Jewish doctrines the doctrine of a group of Jews of Isfahan called the 'Isawiyya, who are the followers of Abu 'Isa al-Isfahani, the Jew, who held that Muhammad is the Messenger of God to the Arabs only, not to the Children of Israel. This is because the Jews are of two groups: one group claims that the law of Moses cannot be abrogated by any other law; and another group claims that it cannot be abrogated for the Children of Israel, and that it is permissible for a messenger to be sent to others than the Children of Israel.

The word ﴿all of you﴾ (*jamī'an*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*, a circumstantial accusative) of the pronoun in the genitive after ﴿to﴾ (*ilā*). It is a *fa'īl* in the sense of a *maf'ūl*, meaning "gathered together." For this reason it remains singular, since it does not agree with the word it describes.

Page 140 continued
﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an epithet of the Name of Majesty (Allah), indicating praise.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction (*qaṣr*, exclusivity), meaning: dominion belongs to Him and to no other, such as what the polytheists worship. It is a relative restriction (*qaṣr iḍāfī*), directed against the polytheists.

The clause ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the Name of Majesty, and in effect means "uniquely singled out in divinity." This is a real restriction (*qaṣr ḥaqīqī*) to establish the attribute of oneness, not intended as a rebuttal of the polytheists.

The clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a circumstantial clause.

The purpose of mentioning these three attributes is to remind and admonish the Jews, since they denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), claimed that there is no messenger after Moses, and considered the call of Muhammad to be too great. They held that no messenger could resemble Moses. So they were reminded that God is the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and He is the Giver of excellences, so it is not extraordinary that He should send one messenger and then send another; for dominion is in His hand. And that God is the One who has no like in His divinity, so there cannot be two gods for creation. As for the rank of messengership, it is capable of multiplicity. And that God gives life and causes death, so likewise He causes one law to die and gives life to another law. The giving of life to a law is its bringing into existence after it did not exist, because the essential meaning of "giving life" is the bringing of life into a thing that exists. From these attributes there results the nullification of the polytheists' belief in a plurality of gods and their denial of the Gathering (*ḥashr*, resurrection).

Upon these three attributes there has rightly been based the definite command to believe in this Messenger, in His saying ﴿So believe in God and His Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet﴾. The intended meaning is a command to believe in the Unlettered Prophet, since he is the one for whose sake the speech was brought. But since the command was addressed to all of humanity, among whom were those who do not believe in God, and others who believe in God but do not believe in the Unlettered Prophet, belief in God and belief in the Unlettered Prophet were combined in a single command, so that this command is directed to all groups together, so that they may combine in their faith belief in God and in the Unlettered Prophet. At the same time, the duty of courtesy toward God is observed by placing belief in Him before the command to believe in the Messenger (ﷺ), to indicate that belief in the Messenger is only for the sake of belief in God. This is in the manner indicated by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and they want to make a distinction between God and His messengers﴾. This construction is similar to His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the Messenger of God and His word, which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa: 171], and ﴿So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say "Three"﴾ [al-Nisa: 171].

Page 141
For they believed in God and His messengers, but the intended meaning is an added prohibition against believing in the Trinity, and this is the purpose of the context of the speech.

Belief in God is belief in His greatest attribute, which is divinity, contained in the Essential Name; and belief in the Messenger is belief in his most specific attribute, which is messengership. This is known from the attaching of belief to the description of the Messenger rather than to his proper name.

In His saying ﴿and His Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet﴾ there is an *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person) from the first person (speaker) to the third person (absent), in order to proclaim the realization of the attribute promised in the Torah in the person of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The description of the Unlettered Prophet by ﴿who believes in God and His words﴾ is by way of the relative construction (*mawṣūliyya*), to indicate the reason for the command to believe in the Messenger, and that there is no excuse for anyone among the People of the Book who does not believe in him. For this Messenger believes in God and in the words of God, so the belief in all the true divine religions is included in belief in him. This is similar to His saying, may He be exalted, in praise of the Muslims, ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]. The meaning of "Unlettered" (*ummī*) has been stated shortly before.

"Words" (*kalimāt*) is the plural of *kalima*, meaning speech, like His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿No! It is only a word he speaks﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], that is, His saying ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99] ﴿that I may act righteously in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. So the words of God include His books and His revelations to the messengers. Here the expression "His words" was preferred over "His books," because the intended purpose is to indicate that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) believes that Jesus is the word of God, that is, the effect of His word, which is the command of creation (*amr al-takwīn*). For Jesus' coming into being was not through the usual cause of generation, but his coming into being was by the word of God "Be!", as He, may He be exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to God is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. This implies that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) believes in Jesus, that is, in his being a messenger from God, and this removes the excuse of the Christians for hesitating to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). It also implies that the Messenger believes that Jesus is the word of God, and not the son of God. In this is an explanation of the true faith, a refutation of the Jews in what they attributed to him, and a refutation of the Christians in what they exaggerated concerning him.

The discussion of the meaning of "following" (*ittibā'*) has preceded, and likewise the discussion of such phrases as ﴿so that you may be guided﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 159:

﴿And among the people of Musa there is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice.﴾

﴿And among the people of Musa﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him, from their ornaments a calf﴾ [al-A'raf: 148]

صفحة ١٤٢
the verse. This is a specification of the apparent generality in His saying ﴿And the people of Musa took﴾ [al-A'raf: 148], intended as a safeguard lest it be supposed that the people of Musa, all of them, did that. And to draw attention to the removal of this supposition, ﴿And among the people of Musa﴾ was placed before its complement.

The people of Musa are the followers of his religion from before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). Whoever remains holding fast to the religion of Musa after the call of Islam has reached him is not one of the people of Musa, but it is said that he is of the Children of Israel or of the Jews, because the idafah (annexation) in ﴿the people of Musa﴾ indicates that they are the followers of his religion, one of whose fundamentals is awaiting the coming of the unlettered Messenger (ﷺ).

And (ummah): a large group agreed upon a work that unites them. This has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a single community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213] in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning is that there were among them, in every age before Islam, such [a community].

And ﴿they guide by the truth﴾, that is, they guide people, from the Children of Israel or from others, by spreading the virtues of the divine religion, which is what God named "the truth". And (ya'dilun), that is, they judge with a judgement free of injustice.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿and by it do justice﴾ is for emphasis on it and for the sake of the rhyme (fasilah), since there is no requirement for restriction, as evidenced by His saying ﴿they guide by the truth﴾, where the prepositional phrase was not fronted. The meaning is: they judge with justice on the basis of insight and knowledge, not merely by coincidentally hitting the truth out of ignorance. For a judge who is ignorant and rules without knowledge is one of the two judges who are in the Fire, even if he happens to hit the truth, because by his ignorance he has treated the rights of people lightly, and the coincidence of hitting the truth does not benefit him, since he has no action in that coincidence.

And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.

This is connected to His saying ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community﴾ [al-A'raf: 159] etc., since that division took place among the community who guide by the truth.

Al-taqṭī' (dividing into parts) is an intensified form of qaṭ', which means separation, and what is meant by it is division into groups. The purpose of this report is not blame, and the division is not meant as punishment, because that division was a favour from God and is one of the excellent features of the political organisation of the Mosaic Law, and one of the preliminaries of the order of the community, as the Fourth Book explains, which is the Book of Numbers, concerning the counting and division of the Children of Israel. This is similar to what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab did in recording the dīwān (the official register). They were attributed to the asbāṭ (sing. sibṭ, the tribes descended from the sons of Isaac), but they were not divided into clans while they were in Egypt, and when they crossed the sea. So the division came after their crossing of the Red Sea and before the gushing forth of the springs. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in surat al-Baqarah and in this surah, due to His saying in both, ﴿Every people had already known their drinking place﴾. Mentioning the watering here right after the division into twelve communities necessarily means that it was before the watering, because if the watering had happened before the division, the crowding for water would have led to harm for the people. The apparent meaning of the Torah is that when they passed Ḥūrīb, and Shu'ayb came to meet Moses, Shu'ayb advised Moses to appoint for them leaders of thousands, leaders of hundreds, leaders of fifties, and leaders of tens, according to chapter 18 of Exodus. That requires that the community had already been organised into tribes beforehand, so that it would be easy to set leaders over the numbers. In the second year after their departure, God commanded Moses to count all the Children of Israel, and Moses and Aaron gathered all the Children of Israel, and they were registered according to their clans and their fathers' households, as in the first chapter of the Book of Numbers. The mention of the asbāṭ has already passed at His saying, ﴿Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136] in surat al-Baqarah.

The numeral was used in the feminine form in His saying ﴿twelve﴾ because the word sibṭ was here applied to the community, so the noun specified by the numeral was omitted, as the word "umamā" indicates it.

"Asbāṭan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in "waqaṭṭa'nāhum" and it cannot be a tamyīz (specification), because the specification of "twelve" and similar numbers is only singular.

His saying "umaman" is a badal (substitute) for "asbāṭan" or for "twelve." One of the two ḥāls was avoided being made a tamyīz in the speech for brevity, and to draw attention to the intention of the favour, in that they were communities from brothers who were fathers, and that each of those tribes had become a community. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ [al-A'raf: 86], along with what is mentioned by the word asbāṭ of their being preferred, because the asbāṭ are the descendants of Isaac the son of Abraham, peace be upon him.

* * *

﴿And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked him for water: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people had already known their drinking place.﴾

This is one of the manifestations of the wisdom of dividing them into twelve tribes. This report is not joined with fa' (then), in order to indicate that it is an independent favour.

The explanation of this verse has already passed in its parallel at His saying ﴿And when Moses asked water for his people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60] in surat al-Baqarah.

"Inbajasat" is the reflexive of bajasa, when it split. The sequence indicated by fa' is a figurative sequence, likening the shortness of the interval to sequence. Its parallels are numerous in the Qur'an, and among them is what occurred in the report of the drink for Umm Zar', her saying: "He met a woman with him, two sons like two leopards playing beneath her waist with two pomegranates; so he divorced me and married her," since the implied meaning is: she pleased him, so he divorced me and married her.

﴿And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails. "Eat of the good things We have provided for you." They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

The pronouns of the third person refer to the people of Moses. This verse is a parallel of what is in surat al-Baqarah, except for a difference in the pronouns of the third person here and the pronouns of the second person there, because what is there was intended as rebuke.

The verb "qīla" in His saying ﴿And when it was said to them: Dwell in this town﴾ [al-A'raf: 161] is attributed to the passive, whereas in surat al-Baqarah it is attributed to the divine name and "wa-idh qulnā" (and when We said), because it is evident that this speech could only come from God, exalted is He.
