Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 161–162:

﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, 'Hittah (remission),' and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins. We will increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿So those who wronged among them changed the word to other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a plague from the sky for their wrongdoing.﴾ This verse is also similar to what is in Surat al-Baqarah, except that in this verse He expressed it with His saying "uskunu" (dwell), and in Surat al-Baqarah with His saying "udkhulu" (enter), because both statements were said to them; that is, it was said to them: "Enter and dwell in it," so this was divided between the two narratives, according to the Qur'an's habit of varying the style of the stories to renew the listener's attention.

And likewise the variation of expression in His saying here "wa-kulu" (and eat) and His saying in Surat al-Baqarah "fa-kulu" (so eat). For it was said to them with what is equivalent to the particle of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), as came in Surat al-Baqarah, because sequence (al-ta'qib) is a meaning added to the mere conjunction that the waw of coordination conveys. Here it is limited to reporting that it was said to them, whereas the verse of al-Baqarah was more fitting for reporting what the fa' of sequence indicates, because the verse of al-Baqarah was brought in the manner of rebuke, so what more clearly indicates the favour was suitable for it, namely hastening the benefit of the good things of the town. The verses of al-A'raf were brought merely for the lesson of the story of the Children of Israel.

Because of this difference, the verse of al-Baqarah was distinguished by repeating the relative pronoun and its clause in His saying ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a plague﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], and here it is replaced by the pronoun of "those who wronged," because the purpose in the verse of al-Baqarah is to explain the cause of sending the punishment upon them twice, the first of which is pointed to by what the relative pronoun implies of the cause of the ruling, and the second by the particle of causation. Here only the second is mentioned.

In Surat al-Baqarah the word "fa-anzalna" occurs, and here the word "fa-arsalna" occurs. Since both are restricted by His saying "from the sky," their meaning is one, so the difference is merely for variety between the two narratives.

Here it is expressed as ﴿for what they used to wrong﴾, and in al-Baqarah as ﴿for what they used to defiantly disobey﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. Because the situation in both narratives required emphasizing their description with wrongdoing, and this was conveyed in al-Baqarah by His saying ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], repeating the word "wrongdoing" a third time there was deemed burdensome, so it was turned away to what conveys its meaning, which is "fisq" (defiant disobedience), and this is also more general, so it is more suitable as a concluding clause for rebuke. Here the word "yazlimun" (they wrong) was used so that recording wrongdoing against them would not be lost for a third time. Thus the concluding clause of the verse of al-Baqarah was more suited to the intensification in censuring them, because the situation of rebuke requires it.

In this verse occurs ﴿So those who wronged among them changed﴾, and the word "minhum" (among them) does not occur in Surat al-Baqarah. The purpose of its addition here is to make explicit that the change of the statement did not proceed from all of them. This was left general in Surat al-Baqarah because, since the verse of al-Baqarah was brought in the manner of rebuke, it was fitting to frighten them with what suggests that those who did this were the whole people, since the consequences of some of a tribe are borne by its whole group.

In Surat al-Baqarah His saying (﴿and enter the gate prostrating﴾) was placed before His saying (﴿and say, Hittah﴾), and here it is reversed. This is a difference in the reporting merely for variety, since both statements occurred, whether placed first or last.

In al-Baqarah is mentioned ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish, abundantly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and the description "raghadan" (abundantly) is not mentioned here, but was reported in Surat al-Baqarah, because the addition of favour is more effective in strengthening the rebuke.

The clause (﴿We will increase the doers of good﴾) is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because His saying "you will be forgiven" stands in a context of bestowing favour with many blessings, which raises the question of a questioner who says: "Is forgiveness the utmost of their reward?" So it is answered that after it is an increase of reward over excellence, that is, over compliance.

In the parallel of this verse in Surat al-Baqarah, the clause (﴿and We will increase the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58]) is mentioned conjoined by the waw, on the presumption: "We said that to them, and We said to them: We will increase the doers of good." So the waw there is for reporting the statements, and it belongs to the reporting, not to what is reported; that is, "We said, and We said: We will increase."

It has preceded that the intended town is (Ariha'a).

Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read "tughfaru" with a taa' above, in the passive voice, and "khati'atukum" in the form of the sound plural of the feminine. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "naghfir" with a nun, in the active voice, and "khati'atikum" also in the sound feminine plural form. Abu 'Amr read "naghfir" with a nun and "khataya-kum" in the broken plural form, like the verse of al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Amir read "tughfar" with a taa' above and "khati'atukum" in the singular.

The difference between it and the verse of al-Baqarah in the reading of Nafi' and those who agree with him is a variety in narrating the story.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verses 161–162:

﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, 'Hittah (remission),' and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins. We will increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿So those who wronged among them changed the word to other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a plague from the sky for their wrongdoing.﴾ This verse is also similar to what is in Surat al-Baqarah, except that in this verse He expressed it with His saying "uskunu" (dwell), and in Surat al-Baqarah with His saying "udkhulu" (enter), because both statements were said to them; that is, it was said to them: "Enter and dwell in it," so this was divided between the two narratives, according to the Qur'an's habit of varying the style of the stories to renew the listener's attention.

And likewise the variation of expression in His saying here "wa-kulu" (and eat) and His saying in Surat al-Baqarah "fa-kulu" (so eat). For it was said to them with what is equivalent to the particle of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), as came in Surat al-Baqarah, because sequence (al-ta'qib) is a meaning added to the mere conjunction that the waw of coordination conveys. Here it is limited to reporting that it was said to them, whereas the verse of al-Baqarah was more fitting for reporting what the fa' of sequence indicates, because the verse of al-Baqarah was brought in the manner of rebuke, so what more clearly indicates the favour was suitable for it, namely hastening the benefit of the good things of the town. The verses of al-A'raf were brought merely for the lesson of the story of the Children of Israel.

Because of this difference, the verse of al-Baqarah was distinguished by repeating the relative pronoun and its clause in His saying ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a plague﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], and here it is replaced by the pronoun of "those who wronged," because the purpose in the verse of al-Baqarah is to explain the cause of sending the punishment upon them twice, the first of which is pointed to by what the relative pronoun implies of the cause of the ruling, and the second by the particle of causation. Here only the second is mentioned.

In Surat al-Baqarah the word "fa-anzalna" occurs, and here the word "fa-arsalna" occurs. Since both are restricted by His saying "from the sky," their meaning is one, so the difference is merely for variety between the two narratives.

Here it is expressed as ﴿for what they used to wrong﴾, and in al-Baqarah as ﴿for what they used to defiantly disobey﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. Because the situation in both narratives required emphasizing their description with wrongdoing, and this was conveyed in al-Baqarah by His saying ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], repeating the word "wrongdoing" a third time there was deemed burdensome, so it was turned away to what conveys its meaning, which is "fisq" (defiant disobedience), and this is also more general, so it is more suitable as a concluding clause for rebuke. Here the word "yazlimun" (they wrong) was used so that recording wrongdoing against them would not be lost for a third time. Thus the concluding clause of the verse of al-Baqarah was more suited to the intensification in censuring them, because the situation of rebuke requires it.

In this verse occurs ﴿So those who wronged among them changed﴾, and the word "minhum" (among them) does not occur in Surat al-Baqarah. The purpose of its addition here is to make explicit that the change of the statement did not proceed from all of them. This was left general in Surat al-Baqarah because, since the verse of al-Baqarah was brought in the manner of rebuke, it was fitting to frighten them with what suggests that those who did this were the whole people, since the consequences of some of a tribe are borne by its whole group.

In Surat al-Baqarah His saying (﴿and enter the gate prostrating﴾) was placed before His saying (﴿and say, Hittah﴾), and here it is reversed. This is a difference in the reporting merely for variety, since both statements occurred, whether placed first or last.

In al-Baqarah is mentioned ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish, abundantly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and the description "raghadan" (abundantly) is not mentioned here, but was reported in Surat al-Baqarah, because the addition of favour is more effective in strengthening the rebuke.

The clause (﴿We will increase the doers of good﴾) is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because His saying "you will be forgiven" stands in a context of bestowing favour with many blessings, which raises the question of a questioner who says: "Is forgiveness the utmost of their reward?" So it is answered that after it is an increase of reward over excellence, that is, over compliance.

In the parallel of this verse in Surat al-Baqarah, the clause (﴿and We will increase the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58]) is mentioned conjoined by the waw, on the presumption: "We said that to them, and We said to them: We will increase the doers of good." So the waw there is for reporting the statements, and it belongs to the reporting, not to what is reported; that is, "We said, and We said: We will increase."

It has preceded that the intended town is (Ariha'a).

Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read "tughfaru" with a taa' above, in the passive voice, and "khati'atukum" in the form of the sound plural of the feminine. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "naghfir" with a nun, in the active voice, and "khati'atikum" also in the sound feminine plural form. Abu 'Amr read "naghfir" with a nun and "khataya-kum" in the broken plural form, like the verse of al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Amir read "tughfar" with a taa' above and "khati'atukum" in the singular.

The difference between it and the verse of al-Baqarah in the reading of Nafi' and those who agree with him is a variety in narrating the story.

**[p. 147]**

The mode of address concerning the Children of Israel changes here. The mention of this story begins with a command that a questioner ask the Children of Israel who are present about it. From this we understand that these following narratives have a status different from the status of the past narratives. I think this is only because this story is not among what was written in the Torah of the Jews or in the books of their prophets, but rather it is among what was transmitted from their rabbis. For this reason it opens with the command to ask them about it, to make the Jews of the Prophetic era aware that God informed His Prophet, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, about it, while they had been concealing it. This is because the events that serve as admonitions to a community, for the transgressions and disobediences it committed, leave after the admonition a trace by which the community may be reproached. Yet that reproach is not regarded in comparison with the benefit the community gains from the admonition. A community's leaders and advisers are concerned, in their own affairs, only with setting the condition right, even if mentioning some of those conditions causes them discomfort and resentment. When the general judgment of history among the nations comes, the nations discuss the conditions of that community, judging it favorably or unfavorably. Thus the incidents of its lapses remain a blemish upon it and a disgrace by which it is reproached. This was the situation of the Jews when they lost their kingdom and homeland, lived as neighbors of other nations, and began to conceal from those neighbors the shameful aspects of their history. Then God sent Muhammad ﷺ, and taught him of their conditions what would be a miracle for their forebears and a disgrace that remains for their descendants. This was a challenge to them and a rebuke for their evil reception of the Muhammadan call, with deceit and envy.

So the question here carries the sense of affirmation, for the purpose of rebuking and reproaching the Children of Israel and enumerating their past disobediences. That is, their disobedience toward you is no novelty, for that is an ancient habit among them. It is not a question seeking information, because the Messenger ﷺ had already been informed of it by his Lord, may He be exalted. This is analogous to the interrogative hamza of affirmation: the pattern of ﴿واسْألْهم عَنِ القَرْيَةِ﴾ is like saying: "Did you transgress on the Sabbath?" For the question in the speech of the Arabs is of two kinds. The more well-known is that the questioner asks about what he does not know, in order to learn it. The other is that he asks in the manner of affirmation, when the questioner knows that the matter asked about has occurred, and the one asked knows that the questioner is knowledgeable and that he asked only to make him acknowledge it.

The clause ﴿واسْألْهم﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿وإذْ قِيلَ لَهُمُ اسْكُنُوا هَذِهِ القَرْيَةَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 161], and it is an interposed clause between the narratives of favor and the narratives of retribution that come in His saying ﴿وقَطَّعْناهم﴾. The reason for the transition to this story is that both stories contain an account concerning the people of a town among the towns of the Children of Israel.

The mention of the town has already occurred at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿ولَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا مِنكم في السَّبْتِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65], the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

This town is said to be (Aylah), which is today called (al-'Aqabah). It is a city on the coast of the Red Sea near the peninsula of Mount Sinai, and it is the beginning of the land of Syria from the direction of Egypt. It was among the kingdom of Israel in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him. It is described as "the town of the sea" in the sense of being connected to the sea and near it, because presence implies nearness. Aylah was connected to a gulf of the Red Sea, which is al-Qulzum.

It is also said that it is (Tiberias). Tiberias was called the Lake of Tiberias. The exegetes have said that this story alluded to in this verse occurred during the period of Dawud.

The word "town" is used for its people, by the indication of His saying ﴿إذْ يَعْدُونَ﴾, that is, its people.

The intended meaning is the question about their transgression on the Sabbath, by the indication of His saying ﴿إذْ يَعْدُونَ في السَّبْتِ﴾ etc. So His saying ﴿إذْ يَعْدُونَ في السَّبْتِ﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the town," and it is what is intended by the ruling. Thus the sense of the speech is: "Ask them about the time when the people of the town transgressed on the Sabbath." The ﴿إذْ﴾ here is a noun of time for the past, and it is not an adverb.

Transgression (al-'udwan) is injustice and opposition to the truth. It is derived from al-'add with a sukun on the dal, which is overstepping.

Al-Sabt is a proper name for the day that follows Friday, and it was mentioned at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿وقُلْنا لَهم لا تَعْدُوا في السَّبْتِ﴾ [al-Nisa': 154] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The choice of the imperfect form indicates that this occurred from them repeatedly.

The complementation of the verb ya'dun by fi (in) al-sabt indicates that the transgression was for the sake of the day of Sabbath, considering what the imperfect form indicates of repetition, which requires that their transgression recurred every Sabbath; and considering that mention of the time of the transgression is not something the eloquent speaker's purpose depends on unless that time has a special connection to the act. Thus it is known that the transgression was bound to a specific right of the day of Sabbath, and that right is the right of not working on it. For there is no right to the day of Sabbath in the law of Moses other than that work on it is forbidden. And this work is hunting, as the remainder of the story indicates.

The meaning of (fi) here is the sense of location, because the transgression occurred concerning the violation of the sanctity of the Sabbath.

His saying ﴿إذْ تَأْتِيهِمْ حِيتانُهُمْ﴾ is an adverbial clause for ya'dun, meaning: they transgress at the time when their fish come to them.

Al-hitan is the plural of hut, which is a fish. The word hut is also used as a collective, so it is among what is used identically for singular and plural, like fulk. Most often hut is used for the singular, and its plural is hitan.

His saying shurra'an is the plural of shari', and it is an attribute of the hut, which is the singular. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, visible upon the water, meaning that they were near the surface of the sea, safe from being hunted. That is, God inspired them to do this so that it would be a sign to the Children of Israel that respecting the Sabbath, by refraining from work on it, is from the command of God. Al-Dahhak said: shurra'an means successive, lined up in rows. So it is a metaphor for the abundance of what comes of them on the day of Sabbath.

I think this is a description derived from shara'at al-ibil toward the water, meaning the camels entered to drink. When the herders drove them, they rushed toward the water, crowding together and piling up, and sometimes entering it. Thus the state of the fish in their abundance in the water was likened to the cattle rushing toward the water, and the presence of water in both states makes this comparison fitting. This is the better interpretation.

The meaning is: they transgress on the Sabbath and did not comply with God's command to abstain from work on it, nor did they take heed of the sign of the fish being inspired to be safe on it.

His saying ﴿يَوْمَ سَبْتِهِمْ﴾ may mean that the word sabt is the verbal noun of sabata, when work is ceased, by the indication of the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ لا يَسْبِتُونَ﴾, for it is the imperfect of sabata, so the affirmative and the negative correspond. The meaning then is: if they preserved the sanctity of the Sabbath, refraining from hunting on the day of Sabbath, the fish came that day, shurra'an, safe. But if greed for abundant hunting drove them, and they prepared its tools and resolved to hunt, the fish did not come to them.

It is also possible that the phrase yawm sabtihim means the proper name of the day known by this name among the days of the week, and its attribution to the pronoun "them" indicates that it is specific to them, since they are Jews, as an implicit reproach for their making lawful the sanctity of the Sabbath. For a proper name may be attributed for this purpose, as in the saying of one of the Tayy poets:

"Our Zayd rose above on the day of the sandhill, above your Zayd, with a white, sharp-edged sword from Yemen."

And the saying of Rabi'a ibn Thabit al-Asadi:

"How far apart are the two Yazids in generosity: Yazid of Sulaym, and al-Aghharr son of Hatim."

On both interpretations, His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ لا يَسْبِتُونَ﴾ may mean: and the days on which working is not forbidden, that is, the days of the week, the fish do not come in them; or it may mean: and the days of the Sabbaths that they made lawful, so that they did not refrain from hunting in them, in which the coming of the fish ceases. It is not hidden that this mode of expression regarding the Sabbath has a rhetorical distinction, aiming at the intention of both meanings.

**[p. 148]**

So the purpose of the verse is admonition and lesson, not a favor upon them. Its indicator is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَبْلُوهم بِما كانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ﴾. That is, We test their obedience by exposing them to the call to disobedience, which is the presence of the forbidden desire.

The clause ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَبْلُوهُمْ﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) of explanatory type (isti'naf bayani), answering the question of one who says: what is the benefit of this verse, given that God knows they do not refrain from violating the sanctity of the Sabbath?

The reference to the trial indicated by nablihim is: We test them with a trial as great as this. The discussion of its counterpart has already occurred at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The original meaning of al-bala' is testing. When al-bala' is attributed to God, may He be exalted, it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), meaning that He tests people's adherence to the laws of their religion.

The ba' is causal, and ma is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning: because of their wickedness. That is, their immersion in disobedience increased them in it. So when its occasion presents itself to them, they hasten toward it and do not heed the command of God, may He be exalted.

The clause ﴿وإذْ قالَتْ أُمَّةٌ مِنهم﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿إذْ يَعْدُونَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. The implied sense is: "And ask the Children of Israel ﴿when a community among them said﴾." Here ﴿إذْ﴾ is a noun of time referring to the past, not an adverb of place, and it has the same ruling as its sister ﴿إذْ﴾ to which it is coordinated. The sense is therefore: "Ask them about the time when a community said," that is, about the time of the saying of a community among them. The pronoun governed by ﴿مِن﴾ refers back to the same referent as the pronoun in ﴿اسْألْهم﴾, not to the town, because the aim is to rebuke the Children of Israel as a whole. If this saying took place in that town, as the commentators have mentioned, then it is not considered in terms of its occurrence in that town, but rather as another manifestation of their disobedience and obstinacy and of the scant benefit of admonition among them. This is a known matter among their scholars and righteous people. For this reason, when this story was coordinated, the expression of time was repeated with it, so it was said ﴿وإذْ قالَتْ أُمَّةٌ﴾ and not "وقالَتْ أُمَّةٌ".

The ﴿أُمَّةٌ﴾ is a group of people who share in this saying. The commentators said: a community among the Children of Israel was constantly engaged in admonition and in forbidding what is evil, another community had been doing so but then despaired of the admonished taking heed and became certain that the word of punishment had come due against those admonished who had stopped their ears, and a third community was heedlessly persisting in its excess, not turning back from its misguidance and not fearing God in its deeds.

The verse has summarized what the speaking community did, in concise speech, relying on context. Their words ﴿الله مُهْلِكُهم﴾ indicate that they were objecting to those admonished, and that they knew God would destroy them only after they had tried their affair and tested their depth and seen that admonitions no longer benefited them. This would not happen except after advising them repeatedly. The context is also shown by His saying afterwards: ﴿أنْجَيْنا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وأخَذْنا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا بِعَذابٍ بَيِسٍ﴾, since He made the people into two groups. Thus we know that the speakers were from the saved group, because they were not wrongdoers, and we know that they forbade evil.

The mention of admonition has already occurred at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿فأعْرِضْ عَنْهم وعِظْهُمْ﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying just before, ﴿مَوْعِظَةً وتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in this surah.

The lam in ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ﴾ is for causation, so what is questioned concerns the kind of reasons (ʿilal). The interrogation is a denial in meaning, indicating the absence of all reasons that would call for admonition in order to achieve it. That leads to despair of their taking heed, and the addressees of ﴿تَعِظُونَ﴾ are another community.

The description of the people as those whom God will destroy is based on their having the condition which God has stated means that whoever has it will be destroyed or punished. The speakers were certain that this condition had been fulfilled in them, and those addressed were also certain of it, so that the speakers could describe them to the addressees with this revealing description, which shows that they are characterized by arriving at one of the two threats.

The two active participles in His saying ﴿مُهْلِكُهم أوْ مُعَذِّبُهم﴾ are used in the sense of the future, by the context and by the uncertainty between destruction and punishment. This indicates that which of the two matters will happen is not specified, since it is future, but their situation will not be free of one of them.

The clause ﴿قالُوا﴾ is separated (from what precedes) because it occurs in the context of dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once. That is, the addressees of ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ etc. said.

The word ﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the dhal is a noun of place/mim-form derived from the verb ʿadhara (اعْتَذَرَ) irregularly. The meaning of iʿtadhara is "to show an excuse." The ʿudhr (العُذْر), with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the dhal, is the reason by which blame for a sin or shortcoming is removed. It is like the argument that the accused presents to show that he is innocent of what is attributed to him, or that he has a valid interpretation of it. One says ʿadharahu when he accepts his excuse and confirms his innocence. The verb iʿtadhara is followed by ﴿إلى﴾ because it contains the sense of conveying and informing.

﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by the statement of the two questioners, ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ﴾. The implied sense is: "Our admonition is an excuse from us to God."

The majority read it in the nominative, while Hafs from ʿAsim read it in the accusative as an object of purpose (مفعول لأجله), meaning: "We admonished them for the sake of an excuse."

His saying ﴿ولَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾ is a second reason for continuing in admonition, meaning: for the effect of admonition on them through its repetition.

So the meaning is: the righteous of the people were two groups. One group among them despaired of the success of admonition and was certain that the threat would fall upon the people because of their deep immersion in sins. Another group did not cut off hope of the admonition having an effect through repeating it. The first group objected to the second group's continuing to bear the burden of admonition, and the second group gave as their excuse their words ﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ إلى رَبِّكم ولَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾. The first group took the dominant side, which produces assumption, while the second group took the less likely side while combining it with the dominant one, for the purpose of caution, so that they would have an excuse before God if He asked them, "Why did you stop admonishing?" and also for what might result of God-consciousness among those admonished from increasing the admonition. The use of the particle of hope in its place is because hope is predicated of its kind by gradation, so some of it is strong and some of it is weak.

The pronoun in ﴿نَسُوا﴾ refers back to ﴿قَوْمًا﴾, and forgetting (النِّسْيان) is used in the sense of turning away that leads to forgetting, as has been mentioned at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿فَلَمّا نَسُوا ما ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am.

[Page 153]

﴿الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ﴾ are the two groups mentioned in His saying just before, ﴿وإذْ قالَتْ أُمَّةٌ مِنهم لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ up to His saying ﴿ولَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾. And ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ are the people mentioned in His saying ﴿قَوْمًا اللَّهُ مُهْلِكُهُمْ﴾ etc.

Here ﴿الظُّلْم﴾ means disobedience, namely wronging oneself and wronging the right of God, may He be exalted, by not complying with His command.

﴿بَيِسٍ﴾ was read by Nafi' and Abu Ja'far with a kasra on the ba' and a lengthened vowel with a silent ya' after it, and with tanwin on the sin, on the basis that its origin is (بِئْسَ) with the hamza silent, so the hamza was softened into a ya', like their saying dhib for dhi'b.

Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿بِئْسٍ﴾ with a silent hamza and retention of the tanwin, on the basis that its origin is (بَئِيسٍ).

The majority read (بَئِيسٍ) with a fatha on the ba', a kasra on the hamza after it, a silent ya' after that, and tanwin on the sin, as an intensive pattern from the verb (بَؤُسَ) with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the hamza, when misery (البُؤْس) befalls him, which is severity of harm. Or it is a verbal noun like ʿadhir and nakir.

Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿بَيْئَسٍ﴾ on the pattern of ṣayqal, as a name for one characterized by the act of misery. The meaning, according to all the readings, is: a punishment severely harmful.

His saying ﴿بِما كانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ﴾ has had its parallel discussed shortly before.

This punishment has been stated in general terms here. It is said that it is a punishment other than the transformation mentioned after it, a punishment which befell those who forgot what they had been reminded of. Then the transformation would be a second punishment which befell a group who witnessed the punishment that had struck their brethren, and it is a more severe one, occurring after the harsh punishment. That is, God gave them warning, then He began with the punishment of severity, and when they did not desist and persisted in excess, He imposed on them the punishment of transformation.

It is also said that the harsh punishment is the transformation, so His saying ﴿فَلَمّا عَتَوْا عَنْ ما نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾ is an explanation of the general statement of the harsh punishment. His saying ﴿فَلَمّا عَتَوْا﴾ then stands in the position of an emphasis on His saying ﴿فَلَمّا نَسُوا﴾. It was phrased in this style to magnify forgetting and transgression. The meaning is: forgetting, which is turning away, occurred concurrently with transgression.

﴿ما ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ and ﴿ما نُهُوا عَنْهُ﴾ refer to one and the same thing. So the apparent form would have required: "When they forgot and transgressed in what they were forbidden and reminded of, We said to them..." So they contended over a long shadow, whose shade flutters like the smoke of a fire whose flame is kindled,
A mixed (wine) that was blended with a growing ʿarfaj, like the smoke of a fire whose sparks rise high.

His saying ﴿قُلْنا لَهم كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خاسِئِينَ﴾ has had its parallel discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿ولَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا مِنكم في السَّبْتِ فَقُلْنا لَهم كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خاسِئِينَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65] in Surat al-Baqarah. Because of the similarity between the two verses, and the mention of transgression on the Sabbath in both, and its mention here in reporting about the town, the commentators firmly stated that those who forgot what they had been reminded of and transgressed against what they had been forbidden are the people of this town, and that the community that said ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ is a community from this town. So they firmly held that the story is one. Although the context does not reject this, and it does not prevent the similarity of two groups in the punishment, I have explained that this does not contradict treating the story, in terms of consideration, as having the meaning of two stories.

The sense is therefore: "Ask them about the time when a community said," that is, about the time of the saying of a community among them. This is a known matter among their scholars and righteous people. For this reason, when this story was coordinated, the expression of time was repeated with it, so it was said ﴿وإذْ قالَتْ أُمَّةٌ﴾ and not "وقالَتْ أُمَّةٌ".

The ﴿أُمَّةٌ﴾ is a group of people who share in this saying. The commentators said: a community among the Children of Israel was constantly engaged in admonition and in forbidding what is evil, another community had been doing so but then despaired of the admonished taking heed and became certain that the word of punishment had come due against those admonished who had stopped their ears, and a third community was heedlessly persisting in its excess, not turning back from its misguidance and not fearing God in its deeds.

The verse has summarized what the speaking community did, in concise speech, relying on context. Their words ﴿الله مُهْلِكُهم﴾ indicate that they were objecting to those admonished, and that they knew God would destroy them only after they had tried their affair and tested their depth and seen that admonitions no longer benefited them. This would not happen except after advising them repeatedly. The context is also shown by His saying afterwards: ﴿أنْجَيْنا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وأخَذْنا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا بِعَذابٍ بَيِسٍ﴾, since He made the people into two groups. Thus we know that the speakers were from the saved group, because they were not wrongdoers, and we know that they forbade evil.

The mention of admonition has already occurred at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿فأعْرِضْ عَنْهم وعِظْهُمْ﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying just before, ﴿مَوْعِظَةً وتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in this surah.

The lam in ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ﴾ is for causation, so what is questioned concerns the kind of reasons (ʿilal). The interrogation is a denial in meaning, indicating the absence of all reasons that would call for admonition in order to achieve it. That leads to despair of their taking heed, and the addressees of ﴿تَعِظُونَ﴾ are another community.

The description of the people as those whom God will destroy is based on their having the condition which God has stated means that whoever has it will be destroyed or punished. The speakers were certain that this condition had been fulfilled in them, and those addressed were also certain of it, so that the speakers could describe them to the addressees with this revealing description, which shows that they are characterized by arriving at one of the two threats.

The two active participles in His saying ﴿مُهْلِكُهم أوْ مُعَذِّبُهم﴾ are used in the sense of the future, by the context and by the uncertainty between destruction and punishment. This indicates that which of the two matters will happen is not specified, since it is future, but their situation will not be free of one of them.

The clause ﴿قالُوا﴾ is separated (from what precedes) because it occurs in the context of dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once. That is, the addressees of ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ etc. said.

The word ﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the dhal is a noun of place/mim-form derived from the verb ʿadhara (اعْتَذَرَ) irregularly. The meaning of iʿtadhara is "to show an excuse." The ʿudhr (العُذْر), with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the dhal, is the reason by which blame for a sin or shortcoming is removed. It is like the argument that the accused presents to show that he is innocent of what is attributed to him, or that he has a valid interpretation of it. One says ʿadharahu when he accepts his excuse and confirms his innocence. The verb iʿtadhara is followed by ﴿إلى﴾ because it contains the sense of conveying and informing.

﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by the statement of the two questioners, ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ﴾. The implied sense is: "Our admonition is an excuse from us to God."

The majority read it in the nominative, while Hafs from ʿAsim read it in the accusative as an object of purpose (مفعول لأجله), meaning: "We admonished them for the sake of an excuse."

His saying ﴿ولَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾ is a second reason for continuing in admonition, meaning: for the effect of admonition on them through its repetition.

So the meaning is: the righteous of the people were two groups. One group among them despaired of the success of admonition and was certain that the threat would fall upon the people because of their deep immersion in sins. Another group did not cut off hope of the admonition having an effect through repeating it. The first group objected to the second group's continuing to bear the burden of admonition, and the second group gave as their excuse their words ﴿مَعْذِرَةٌ إلى رَبِّكم ولَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ﴾. The use of the particle of hope in its place is because hope is predicated of its kind by gradation, so some of it is strong and some of it is weak.

The pronoun in ﴿نَسُوا﴾ refers back to ﴿قَوْمًا﴾, and forgetting (النِّسْيان) is used in the sense of turning away that leads to forgetting, as has been mentioned at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿فَلَمّا نَسُوا ما ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am.

Or it is a verbal noun like ʿadhir and nakir.
