Because of the similarity between the two verses, and the mention of transgression on the Sabbath in both, and its mention here in reporting about the town, the commentators firmly stated that those who forgot what they had been reminded of and transgressed against what they had been forbidden are the people of this town, and that the community that said ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ is a community from this town. So they firmly held that the story is one. Although the context does not reject this, and it does not prevent the similarity of two groups in the punishment, I have explained that this does not contradict treating the story, in terms of consideration, as having the meaning of two stories.

And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict on them the worst of torment. Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful.

This is connected by 'atf (coordination) to the phrase "wa-as'alhum" (and ask them), with "udhkur" (remember) understood. The pronoun in "alayhim" (against them) refers to the Jews, who were mentioned earlier through the pronoun in "as'alhum." Their identity is clear from context, as explained fully at the verse "wa-as'alhum 'ani al-qaryah" (and ask them about the town). Those spoken of in this verse therefore have no connection to the people of the town who transgressed on the Sabbath.

"Ta'adhdhana" (declared), in its various usages, and in this instance, is derived from "al-idhn" (hearing/knowledge). It is said: "adhina," meaning "he knew." Its original sense is knowledge of a report, because the root of this verb and its derivations comes from "al-udhun" (the ear), the organ of hearing. These derivations are formed from a non-derived noun, like "istahjara al-tin" (the clay became stone) and "istansara al-bughath" (the common buzzard became an eagle). So "ta'adhdhana" is in the form "tafa'ala," which indicates the muṭāwaʿa (the sense of receiving the effect) of "fa'ala," and muṭāwaʿa is used to express the intensity of the occurrence of the act. It is said that here it has the meaning of "af'ala" (to cause to know), just as one says "tawa''ada" with the meaning of "awʿada" (to threaten). Thus the meaning of "ta'adhdhana rabbuka" is "your Lord informed and announced," and "layabʿathannahum" (He will surely send) is the statement of that announcement. The verb "a'lama" (informed) is then suspended from acting on its object by the oath particle "lam," and al-Tabari inclined to this view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is problematic from the standpoint of morphology, since attributing 'ta'adhdhana' to the agent is not the same as attributing 'a'lama,' as can be seen from transitivity and other considerations."

From Mujahid: "ta'adhdhana" means "ta'alla" (swore). Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: its meaning is "'azama rabbuka" (your Lord resolved), because one who resolves upon a matter speaks to himself about it. He meant that the implication of the sense of an oath arises from a metaphor: the verb "ta'adhdhun" was used for "'azm" (resolve), because one who resolves upon a matter speaks of it to himself; he informs his soul of his act, so his soul resolves. Then it was treated as the verb of an oath, like "'alima Allah" (God knows) and "shahida Allah" (God bears witness). For this reason the answer is given in the form used for an oath. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The inclusion of the lam in the answer led them to this view, but the word itself is far from this meaning."

From Ibn 'Abbas: "ta'adhdhana rabbuka," he said, "rabbuka" (your Lord), meaning that God made this known through His messengers.

The essential meaning is that God informed them of this, and threatened them with it. This is like His statement, exalted is He: "And when your Lord announced: If you give thanks, I will surely increase you" (Ibrahim 14:7), in the Surah of Ibrahim.

The meaning of "ba'th" is sending. Here it is a metaphor for imposing and inspiring, and it indicates that this occurs at different times, not continuously day after day. For this reason the verb "layabʿathannahum" was chosen instead of something like "layulzimannahum" (He will surely impose on them). It is given the sense of "taslit" (empowerment), so it takes "'ala," as in His statement: "We sent against you servants of Ours" and His statement: "So We sent against them the flood."

"Ila yawm al-qiyamah" (until the Day of Resurrection) is the limit of what is implied by the future sense in the oath. It is a limit intended to make the whole span of the future a container for the sending, excluding what lies beyond the limit. This comprehensiveness applies to the times of the sending, meaning that God empowers this against them throughout the whole future. The sending is absolute, not general.

"Yasumuhum" means "yafrudu 'alayhim" (imposes on them). The real meaning of "al-sawm" is determining the price that is exchanged for a thing, and it is used metaphorically for a binding dealing, by likening it to the fixed price of a thing. It was mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: "And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst of torment" (al-Baqarah 2:49), and its counterpart occurs in this Surah. So the meaning is that the worst of torment is made as their price, which is their portion.

"Su' al-'adhab" (the worst of torment) is its most severe form, because all torment is a kind of evil, so its worst is the most severe within it.

The verse points to God's threat against them, that He will empower their enemy over them whenever they break the covenant of God. This threat has recurred from the time of Moses, peace be upon him, until now, as in the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter twenty-eight, which says: "If you do not take care to observe all the words of this law... the Lord will scatter you among all peoples, and among those nations you shall find no ease, and there shall be no rest for the sole of your foot; you shall live in terror night and day, and have no assurance of your life." In the Book of Joshua, chapter twenty-three: "Be very careful to observe all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses... But if you turn back and cling to the rest of these nations... know for certain that the Lord your God will no longer drive these nations out before you; but they shall become a snare and a trap for you, a scourge on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land which the Lord your God has given you, when you transgress the covenant of the Lord your God."

The greatest of these commandments is the covenant to follow the Messenger who would be sent to them, as mentioned earlier. For this reason His statement, "He will surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection those who will inflict on them the worst of torment," means: for as long as they remain in their aversion, their obstinacy, and their being followers of the Jewish creed while not fulfilling it. But if they embrace Islam and believe in the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, they have departed from the consequence of that declaration and entered what God promised to the Muslims.

For this reason it is concluded with His statement: "Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment," meaning against them. Swiftness implies certainty, meaning that His punishment is certain and not delayed, because delay reduces certainty, since delay is the continuation of non-existence for a period.

The first to be empowered against them was "Bukhtanassar" (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon. Then calamities followed one another against them, the greatest of which was the destruction of "Urshalim" (Jerusalem) in the time of "Adriyanus" (Hadrian), emperor of Rome. Calamities continued to afflict them, and they were given respite at known periods in history.

As for His statement, "And indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful," it is a promise of deliverance from that if they repent and follow Islam, meaning He is Forgiving to whoever repents and returns to the truth. This also implies that God may grant them respite for periods of time, because God's mercy precedes His anger. The meaning of this verse is touched upon by His statement, exalted is He: "And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Scripture that you would surely cause corruption in the land twice and would surely become exceedingly arrogant" (al-Isra 17:4). "So when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the homes; and it was a promise fulfilled" (al-Isra 17:5). "Then We gave back to you the return of victory over them, and We aided you with wealth and sons, and made you more numerous in manpower" (al-Isra 17:6). "If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, they were to disfigure your faces and to enter the Temple as they had entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction" (al-Isra 17:7). "It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return, We will return" (al-Isra 17:8).

And We divided them throughout the earth into nations: some of them are righteous, and some are otherwise. We tested them with good things and bad things, so that perhaps they would return.

This is a continuation of one narrative after another, a return to the accounts that report their conditions. The passage may refer to their dispersal after they had been united. Taqti' means "division" or "separation." It can be praiseworthy, as in ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes﴾, or blameworthy. Which is meant depends on the context, not on the word taqti' itself.

Here "the earth" refers to the whole category, meaning the various regions of the earth.

Umam is the plural of umma, meaning "community" or "group." It may here mean a blameworthy division, that is, a scattering after their community had been united. This would refer to the capture of the Israelites when Shalmaneser, king of Babylon, conquered the kingdom of Israel and deported them to the mountains of Anshur and the land of Babylon, in 721 BC. Later, Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar) captured the kingdom of Judah and became its king in 578 BC, and deported the Jews from Urshalim (Jerusalem), leaving only the poor and the infirm. Then they returned to Jerusalem in 530 and rebuilt the Holy House, until Titus the Roman expelled them, and the House of the Holy Place (Bayt al-Maqdis) was destroyed early in the second century after Christ. Their community was never reunited after that, and they were scattered like the hands of Saba' (a common idiom for complete dispersal).

Describing the nations as including righteous ones indicates that the division affected both the wrongdoers and others, and that God granted the righteous a position of honour among the nations among whom they settled, as indicated by His words ﴿and We tested them with good things and bad﴾.

Page 158

His words ﴿and among them are others less than that﴾ include everyone who was not righteous, across the varying degrees of their lack of righteousness.

The righteous (al-salihun) are those who held fast to the law of Moses, who affirmed the prophets sent after him, and who believed in Jesus after his mission. After Jesus' mission the Children of Israel were not righteous, except for a few of them who believed in him. After the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), their refusal to believe in him drove them further from righteousness, except for a small group such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq.

The phrase "others less than that" (duna dhalika) is in the accusative of place, functioning as an adjective for an omitted noun indicated by the word "among them." That is, "and among them is a group below that." It is also possible that "min" (among) is used in the sense of "some," as a noun, according to those who permit this. In that case it is the subject, and "duna" is its predicate.

It is also possible that the verse refers to their dispersal throughout the earth during the period of the kings of Babylon, and that during their residence in Babylon there were among them righteous people such as Daniel and others, and others who were not. This is because the division with "among them" indicates that both groups were numerous.

His words ﴿and We tested them with good things and bad﴾ mean that We manifested the various conditions of the Children of Israel in patience and gratitude, or in impatience and disbelief, through good things and bad things. "Hasanat" and "sayyi'at" are plurals of hasana and sayyi'a, meaning "that which is good" and "that which is bad," as mentioned earlier in His words ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours," and if evil afflicted them, they blamed it on Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. On this reading, the good and bad things are a detailing of the trial, and they come from God, the Exalted: the things that are good for the righteous group and the things that are bad for the other group, distributing the state of the pronoun in His words "We tested them."

The clause ﴿perhaps they would return﴾ is an explanatory resumption, meaning in hope that they would repent, either when they recall the periods of good and bad things, or when they see the good condition of the righteous and the bad condition of those below them, according to the two interpretations mentioned above.

Return (ruju') here means turning back from breaking the covenant and from disobedience, which is the meaning of repentance (tawba). All of this follows the interpretation of the commentators (mufassirun, Qur'an exegetes) of the verse regarding the meaning of "We divided them."

In my view, it is also permissible that His words "And We divided them throughout the earth into nations" return to the accounts of the favours bestowed upon them. It would then be built upon His words ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes as nations﴾ [al-A'raf: 160], Page 159 and the division would be praiseworthy. The earth here means the Holy Land promised to them, meaning that We multiplied them and they populated all of it. The mention of "the earth" here, rather than in the verse ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes as nations﴾ [al-A'raf: 160], indicates that they populated all of it. His words ﴿among them are the righteous﴾ would then be an act of fairness toward them after mentioning the transgressions of their groups and their deafness to admonition. His words ﴿and We tested them﴾ indicate that God dealt with them at one time with mercy and at another with retribution for the deeds of their common people.

[Page 160]

The phrase "fa-khalafa min ba'dihim khalf" (﴿فَخَلَفَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ﴾) is a consequence (tafri') of His saying "wa qatta'nahum" (﴿وقَطَّعْناهم﴾), if the intended meaning is their dispersal in the lands of their enemies and their expulsion from their kingdom. In that case the verse points to the return of the Children of Israel to their lands in the time of the king Cyrus (Kurash), king of the Persians, around 530 BCE. When he conquered the land of Ashur (Assyria), he permitted the Jews whom Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) had taken captive to return to their lands. They returned and rebuilt Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) after its destruction, at the hands of Nahmiya (Nehemiah) and 'Izra (Ezra), as the Book of Nehemiah and the Book of Ezra contain. Among what they revived was that they brought the Book of the Law of Moses, which Ezra had written, and read it to the people in Urshalim (Jerusalem). Accordingly, "al-khalf" refers to the first of those Children of Israel who returned from the captivity of the Assyrians. The "inheritance of the Book" means their resuming the study of the Torah, which Ezra, known to the people of Islam as 'Uzayr, brought out to them. Their taking "the goods of this lower life" refers to the taking of some of the later generation, not all of them, because the early part of that generation were penitent, and among them were prophets and righteous people.

If, however, the intended meaning of their dispersal in the land as nations is their multiplication and the favour bestowed upon them, then His saying "fa-khalafa min ba'dihim khalf" is a consequence (tafri') of all the preceding narratives, which are the narratives of their forefathers. In that case "al-khalf" refers to those who arose from the descendants of those Jews after the dissolution of the nation and its scattering, among them those who were present at the rise of Islam, namely the Jews who were in Medina. The exegetes inclined to this meaning of "khalf."

"Al-khalf" (with a sukun on the lam) is one who comes after another who preceded him, in a place, a work or a lineage, as determined by the context or an indication. It is not restricted to one who succeeds in a bad matter. This was stated by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, contrary to many lexicographers who said: the more common usage of "khalf" (with a sukun on the lam) is for one who succeeds in evil, and with a fatha on the lam for one who succeeds in good. The Basrans said that both the vowelled and the unvowelled forms are permitted for the bad, while al-Hasan read it only with the vowelled form.

It is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the active participle, i.e. (khalif, "one who succeeds"). "Khalf" is derived from "al-khalf," the opposite of "al-qudam" (front), because whoever comes after a people is as if he came from behind them. There is no limit to the end of the succession; its extent is determined by indications, so it is not confined to one generation or one century, and the succession may extend over a long period. He—exalted is He—said after mentioning the prophets: ﴿فَخَلَفَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ أضاعُوا الصَّلاةَ واتَّبَعُوا الشَّهَواتِ﴾ (Maryam: 59), "Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed their appetites." This therefore includes those who succeeded them among their descendants, from the Arabs, the Jews and others, since He mentioned among their forefathers Idris, who was the grandfather of Nuh.

"Warithu" (ورِثُوا, "they inherited") is used figuratively (majaz) in the sense of standing in the place of another, as was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿ونُودُوا أنْ تِلْكُمُ الجَنَّةُ أُورِثْتُمُوها﴾ (al-A'raf: 43), "And they were called out: 'This is the Garden which you have been made to inherit,'" in this surah; and in His saying in it: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَهْدِ لِلَّذِينَ يَرِثُونَ الأرْضَ مِن بَعْدِ أهْلِها﴾ (al-A'raf: 100), "Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people…?" So it means succession. The meaning is: "Then there succeeded them a succession in the inheritance of the Book." This applies on both views concerning the specification of "khalf," because it is an explanation of the verb, not of the noun "khalf."

The clause ﴿يَأْخُذُونَ عَرَضَ هَذا الأدْنى﴾ ("taking the goods of this lower life") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "warithu." The purpose is to censure the successors, in that they take the goods of this lower life and say: ﴿سَيُغْفَرُ لَنا﴾ ("We shall be forgiven"). This is prepared for by stating that they inherited the Book, to show that they do this knowingly, not in ignorance, and that is the most severe blame, as He—exalted is He—said: ﴿وأضَلَّهُ اللَّهُ عَلى عِلْمٍ﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 23), "And Allah has sent him astray knowingly."

The sense of "akhdh" (taking) here is association and engagement (mulabasah), so it is figurative (majaz), i.e. they are engaged in it. It is permissible for it to be literal, as will come later.

"Al-'arad" (العَرَضُ, with a fatha on both the 'ayn and the ra') is that which passes away and does not last. It is used to mean wealth, and it is also used to mean what presents itself to a person of desires and benefits.

"Al-adna" means the nearer in place. Here it means the worldly life (al-dunya). In the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) there is an indication of belittling this goods which they desired, like the demonstrative in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"When this death comes, it will not find a need of my soul
except that I have already fulfilled its fulfilment."

It has been said that "taking the goods of the worldly life" means engagement in sins (mulabasat al-dhunub). This was the explanation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Tabari, so it includes every sin. The taking here is used figuratively, meaning engagement, so it applies to grasping with the hand and to other things; it is a case of general figurative usage. It has also been said that "the goods of the worldly life" is bribery (al-rishwa), and this was the explanation of al-Suddi and most of the exegetes. So the taking is used in its literal sense, which is grasping. This explanation may be preferred in light of His saying "wa-in ya'tihim 'arad," as will come.

The word "yaqulun" (﴿ويَقُولُونَ﴾, "and they say") refers to spoken speech. They say it to whoever denies them their engagement in sins and grasping of desires, because what follows "yaqulun" fits spoken speech. It is permissible that it means inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsani), since it is a branch of it: that is, their saying within themselves, by which they justify themselves when the restraint of prohibition stirs within them. It is then like His saying: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ في أنْفُسِهِمْ لَوْلا يُعَذِّبُنا اللَّهُ بِما نَقُولُ﴾ (al-Mujadilah: 8), "And they say to themselves: 'Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?'" This arises from their delusion in religion.

The verb "yughfaru" (يُغْفَرُ, "will be forgiven") is in the passive form because the agent is known, namely Allah, since this act can only proceed from Him. It also serves to show that they say this in a general way, not specifically regarding the sin that was denied to them or the one they were engaged in at the time of speaking. The deputy subject is omitted because it is known from the context. The estimate is: "It will be forgiven us that," or "our sins," because they reckon that all their sins are forgiven: ﴿وقالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلّا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾ (al-Baqarah: 80), "And they said: 'The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days,'" as was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. That is, "We will be forgiven without a cause of forgiveness, which is repentance," as is understood from the context, and this is their certainty about it immediately after mentioning the sin, without mention of expiation or the like.

His saying "lana" ("for us") cannot serve as the deputy of the subject, because it does not have the sense of an object, since the verb "maghfirah" (forgiveness) takes one object only. As for the noun governed after it by the preposition "li-" (lam), it has the sense of an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). One says "ghafara Allahu laka dhanbaka" (Allah forgave you your sin), as He—exalted is He—said: ﴿ألَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ (al-Sharh: 1), "Did We not expand for you your breast?" So if "sharaha" were built in the passive, it would not be valid to make "laka" a deputy of the subject.

The clause ﴿ويَقُولُونَ سَيُغْفَرُ لَنا﴾ ("and they say, 'We shall be forgiven'") is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause "yaʾkhudhuna" (they take), because both statements call for blame, and their combination is more severe in this respect.

The clause ﴿وإنْ يَأْتِهِمْ عَرَضٌ مِثْلُهُ يَأْخُذُوهُ﴾ ("and if there comes to them a similar good, they will take it") is conjoined to the one before it. The coming of the goods is used figuratively for offering it to them, if "al-'arad" means wealth. It may also mean the arising of the desire for it in their souls, if "al-'arad" means all the desires and forbidden pleasures. The use of "coming" (ityan) with essences is more fitting than its use with the arising of accidents and abstract matters, because the resemblance is closer in the first case than in the second.

The meaning is: they disobey, and they claim that their evil deeds are forgiven, and they do not desist from sins.

The clause ﴿ألَمْ يُؤْخَذْ عَلَيْهِمْ مِيثاقُ الكِتابِ﴾ ("Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them…?") is an answer to their saying "We shall be forgiven," refuting its content, because their saying "We shall be forgiven" implies that they claim that Allah promised them forgiveness on that basis. The clause is interposed in the midst of the report about the righteous and others. The purpose of this clause is to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he may argue against them with it; they are the intended addressees of the speech, as the reading ﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ with the second person (ta' of address) confirms.

The interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), whose aim is rebuke. This affirmation leaves them no option but to acknowledge it, because it is the plain text of their own Book, in the fourth chapter of the fifth book: "You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD." They do not find in the Book that they will be forgiven, but they find in it repentance, as in the chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy, and as in the first Book of Kings in the prayer of Sulayman (Solomon) when he built the Temple, in the eighth chapter. So their saying "We shall be forgiven" is a fabrication against Allah with what He did not say.

"Al-mithaq" means the covenant, which is the charge of Musa (Moses) that he conveyed to them from Allah—exalted is He—in many places. The idiomatic attribution of the covenant to the Book is in the sense of "in" (fi) or in the sense of the lam, i.e. the covenant known by it. The Book is the Torah of Musa. As for "an la yaqulu" ("that they should not say") being the content of the covenant of the Book, it is governed by the omission of the preposition before the particle "an"; the meaning is: "that they should not say," i.e. by the absence of their saying about Allah other than the truth. It is also permissible for it to be an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "mithaq," so no preposition is estimated, and the estimate is: "the covenant of the Book is the absence of their saying about Allah…" etc.

The verb "darasu" (دَرَسُوا, "they studied") is conjoined to "yu'khadh," because "yu'khadh" has the sense of the past, owing to the entry of "lam" upon it. The estimate is: "Was it not taken … and they studied?" because the purpose is to affirm that they studied the Book, not to inform about them with it, like His saying: ﴿ألَمْ نَجْعَلِ الأرْضَ مِهادًا والجِبالَ أوْتادًا وخَلَقْناكم أزْواجًا وجَعَلْنا نَوْمَكم سُباتًا﴾ (al-Naba': 6), "Have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as pegs, and created you in pairs, and made your sleep a rest?" up to His saying: ﴿وأنْزَلْنا مِنَ المُعْصِراتِ ماءً ثَجّاجًا﴾ (al-Naba': 14), "And sent down from the pressing clouds pouring water." The estimate is: "and We created you in pairs and made your sleep a rest," to the end of the verse.

The meaning is: the covenant was taken from them that they should not say about Allah except the truth, and they knew of that covenant, because they studied what is in the Book. By the combination of the two matters, the proof was established against them.

The clause ﴿والدّارُ الآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("and the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yaʾkhudhuna," i.e.: they take that, and they lie against Allah, and they persist in sin, and they cast aside the covenant of the Book knowingly, while the Last Abode is better than what they have hastened to. Placing the clause in the position of a circumstantial clause implies that they also know this, so they have deliberately preferred the goods of the world over it. This was not a heedlessness that befell them and so deprived them of the good of the Hereafter; rather they have deprived themselves. The indication of this is His saying ﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("Will you not then use your reason?"), which follows from His saying ﴿والدّارُ الآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ﴾. They have been treated, in their preference of the goods of the world, as though they had no intellects, so they are addressed with "Will you not then use your reason?" as a rebuke. It is read with the ta' of address, by way of the shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second, so that the reproach is more forceful in confronting them directly. This is the reading of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Dhakwan, Hafs from 'Asim, Ya'qub and Abu Ja'far. The rest read it with the ya' of the third person, so the rebuke is then indirect.

In His saying ﴿والدّارُ الآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ there is a metonymy (kinayah) for their having lost the good of the Hereafter by their taking the goods of this world in that manner, because the Last Abode being better than what they took implies that what they took has caused them to lose the good of the Hereafter.

In making the Hereafter a good for the God-fearing there is a metonymy for those who took the goods of the world in that manner not being among the God-fearing, because the metonymy for their losing the good of the Hereafter, together with the affirmation that the good of the Hereafter belongs to the God-fearing, implies that those who wasted the good of the Hereafter are not among the God-fearing. These many meanings are gathered in His saying: ﴿والدّارُ الآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then use your reason?"), and this is one of the wondrous aspects of its inimitability.

The clause "those who hold fast to the Book" and what follows it came directly after the preceding clause, because its content stands in contrast to the ruling of the one before it. What was understood from the preceding clause is that these later generations who took the lowly goods of this world have neglected the covenant of the Book and were not among the God-fearing. Thus it is followed by good tidings for those whose deeds are the opposite of theirs, namely those who hold fast to the covenant of the Book and act upon its good tidings concerning the Messengers, and who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). Those people will receive their reward in full, because they are reformers (muslihun).

Prayer (salah) is used here as a metonymy for belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), because prayer is the emblem (shi'ar) of the religion of Islam, to the extent that the people of Islam came to be called "the people of the qibla." Accordingly, by "these people" is meant those Jews who believed in Jesus in general, even if they did not follow Christianity, because they found it altered and distorted, so they remained awaiting the liberating Messenger of whom the Torah and the Gospel gave good tidings, and then they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) when he was sent, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

It is also possible that what is meant by "those who hold fast to the Book" is the Muslims. This is praise for them, that they are the ones who will triumph in the Hereafter, and a glad tiding for them that they do not follow the path of the Jews with their Book.

The clause ﴿Indeed We do not waste the reward of the reformers﴾ is a predicate concerning "those who hold fast," and "the reformers" are them. The implied sense is: "Indeed We do not waste their reward, because they are reformers." Their mention was omitted, being content with the description encompassing them and as praise for them, in the manner of an elegant conciseness (ijaz badi').

[Page 160]

The phrase "fa-khalafa min ba'dihim khalf" (﴿فَخَلَفَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ﴾) is a consequence (tafri') of His saying "wa qatta'nahum" (﴿وقَطَّعْناهم﴾), if the intended meaning is their dispersal in the lands of their enemies and their expulsion from their kingdom. In that case the verse points to the return of the Children of Israel to their lands in the time of the king Cyrus (Kurash), king of the Persians, around 530 BCE. When he conquered the land of Ashur (Assyria), he permitted the Jews whom Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) had taken captive to return to their lands. They returned and rebuilt Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) after its destruction, at the hands of Nahmiya (Nehemiah) and 'Izra (Ezra), as the Book of Nehemiah and the Book of Ezra contain. Among what they revived was that they brought the Book of the Law of Moses, which Ezra had written, and read it to the people in Urshalim (Jerusalem). Accordingly, "al-khalf" refers to the first of those Children of Israel who returned from the captivity of the Assyrians. The "inheritance of the Book" means their resuming the study of the Torah, which Ezra, known to the people of Islam as 'Uzayr, brought out to them. Their taking "the goods of this lower life" refers to the taking of some of the later generation, not all of them, because the early part of that generation were penitent, and among them were prophets and righteous people.

If, however, the intended meaning of their dispersal in the land as nations is their multiplication and the favour bestowed upon them, then His saying "fa-khalafa min ba'dihim khalf" is a consequence (tafri') of all the preceding narratives, which are the narratives of their forefathers. In that case "al-khalf" refers to those who arose from the descendants of those Jews after the dissolution of the nation and its scattering, among them those who were present at the rise of Islam, namely the Jews who were in Medina. The exegetes inclined to this meaning of "khalf."

"Al-khalf" (with a sukun on the lam) is one who comes after another who preceded him, in a place, a work or a lineage, as determined by the context or an indication. It is not restricted to one who succeeds in a bad matter. This was stated by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, contrary to many lexicographers who said: the more common usage of "khalf" (with a sukun on the lam) is for one who succeeds in evil, and with a fatha on the lam for one who succeeds in good. The Basrans said that both the vowelled and the unvowelled forms are permitted for the bad, while al-Hasan read it only with the vowelled form.

It is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the active participle, i.e. (khalif, "one who succeeds"). "Khalf" is derived from "al-khalf," the opposite of "al-qudam" (front), because whoever comes after a people is as if he came from behind them. There is no limit to the end of the succession; its extent is determined by indications, so it is not confined to one generation or one century, and the succession may extend over a long period. He—exalted is He—said after mentioning the prophets: ﴿فَخَلَفَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ أضاعُوا الصَّلاةَ واتَّبَعُوا الشَّهَواتِ﴾ (Maryam: 59), "Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed their appetites." This therefore includes those who succeeded them among their descendants, from the Arabs, the Jews and others, since He mentioned among their forefathers Idris, who was the grandfather of Nuh.

"Warithu" (ورِثُوا, "they inherited") is used figuratively (majaz) in the sense of standing in the place of another, as was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿ونُودُوا أنْ تِلْكُمُ الجَنَّةُ أُورِثْتُمُوها﴾ (al-A'raf: 43), "And they were called out: 'This is the Garden which you have been made to inherit,'" in this surah; and in His saying in it: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَهْدِ لِلَّذِينَ يَرِثُونَ الأرْضَ مِن بَعْدِ أهْلِها﴾ (al-A'raf: 100), "Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people…?" So it means succession. The meaning is: "Then there succeeded them a succession in the inheritance of the Book." This applies on both views concerning the specification of "khalf," because it is an explanation of the verb, not of the noun "khalf."

The clause ﴿يَأْخُذُونَ عَرَضَ هَذا الأدْنى﴾ ("taking the goods of this lower life") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "warithu." The purpose is to censure the successors, in that they take the goods of this lower life and say: ﴿سَيُغْفَرُ لَنا﴾ ("We shall be forgiven"). This is prepared for by stating that they inherited the Book, to show that they do this knowingly, not in ignorance, and that is the most severe blame, as He—exalted is He—said: ﴿وأضَلَّهُ اللَّهُ عَلى عِلْمٍ﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 23), "And Allah has sent him astray knowingly."

The sense of "akhdh" (taking) here is association and engagement (mulabasah), so it is figurative (majaz), i.e. they are engaged in it. It is permissible for it to be literal, as will come later.

"Al-'arad" (العَرَضُ, with a fatha on both the 'ayn and the ra') is that which passes away and does not last. It is used to mean wealth, and it is also used to mean what presents itself to a person of desires and benefits.

"Al-adna" means the nearer in place. Here it means the worldly life (al-dunya). In the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) there is an indication of belittling this goods which they desired, like the demonstrative in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"When this death comes, it will not find a need of my soul
except that I have already fulfilled its fulfilment."

It has been said that "taking the goods of the worldly life" means engagement in sins (mulabasat al-dhunub). This was the explanation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Tabari, so it includes every sin. The taking here is used figuratively, meaning engagement, so it applies to grasping with the hand and to other things; it is a case of general figurative usage. It has also been said that "the goods of the worldly life" is bribery (al-rishwa), and this was the explanation of al-Suddi and most of the exegetes. So the taking is used in its literal sense, which is grasping. This explanation may be preferred in light of His saying "wa-in ya'tihim 'arad," as will come.

The word "yaqulun" (﴿ويَقُولُونَ﴾, "and they say") refers to spoken speech. They say it to whoever denies them their engagement in sins and grasping of desires, because what follows "yaqulun" fits spoken speech. It is permissible that it means inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsani), since it is a branch of it: that is, their saying within themselves, by which they justify themselves when the restraint of prohibition stirs within them. It is then like His saying: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ في أنْفُسِهِمْ لَوْلا يُعَذِّبُنا اللَّهُ بِما نَقُولُ﴾ (al-Mujadilah: 8), "And they say to themselves: 'Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?'" This arises from their delusion in religion.

The verb "yughfaru" (يُغْفَرُ, "will be forgiven") is in the passive form because the agent is known, namely Allah, since this act can only proceed from Him. It also serves to show that they say this in a general way, not specifically regarding the sin that was denied to them or the one they were engaged in at the time of speaking. The deputy subject is omitted because it is known from the context. The estimate is: "It will be forgiven us that," or "our sins," because they reckon that all their sins are forgiven: ﴿وقالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلّا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾ (al-Baqarah: 80), "And they said: 'The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days,'" as was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. That is, "We will be forgiven without a cause of forgiveness, which is repentance," as is understood from the context, and this is their certainty about it immediately after mentioning the sin, without mention of expiation or the like.

His saying "lana" ("for us") cannot serve as the deputy of the subject, because it does not have the sense of an object, since the verb "maghfirah" (forgiveness) takes one object only. As for the noun governed after it by the preposition "li-" (lam), it has the sense of an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). One says "ghafara Allahu laka dhanbaka" (Allah forgave you your sin), as He—exalted is He—said: ﴿ألَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ (al-Sharh: 1), "Did We not expand for you your breast?" So if "sharaha" were built in the passive, it would not be valid to make "laka" a deputy of the subject.

The clause ﴿ويَقُولُونَ سَيُغْفَرُ لَنا﴾ ("and they say, 'We shall be forgiven'") is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause "yaʾkhudhuna" (they take), because both statements call for blame, and their combination is more severe in this respect.

The clause ﴿وإنْ يَأْتِهِمْ عَرَضٌ مِثْلُهُ يَأْخُذُوهُ﴾ ("and if there comes to them a similar good, they will take it") is conjoined to the one before it. The coming of the goods is used figuratively for offering it to them, if "al-'arad" means wealth. It may also mean the arising of the desire for it in their souls, if "al-'arad" means all the desires and forbidden pleasures. The use of "coming" (ityan) with essences is more fitting than its use with the arising of accidents and abstract matters, because the resemblance is closer in the first case than in the second.

The meaning is: they disobey, and they claim that their evil deeds are forgiven, and they do not desist from sins.

The clause ﴿ألَمْ يُؤْخَذْ عَلَيْهِمْ مِيثاقُ الكِتابِ﴾ ("Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them…?") is an answer to their saying "We shall be forgiven," refuting its content, because their saying "We shall be forgiven" implies that they claim that Allah promised them forgiveness on that basis. The clause is interposed in the midst of the report about the righteous and others. The purpose of this clause is to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he may argue against them with it; they are the intended addressees of the speech, as the reading ﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ with the second person (ta' of address) confirms.

The interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), whose aim is rebuke. This affirmation leaves them no option but to acknowledge it, because it is the plain text of their own Book, in the fourth chapter of the fifth book: "You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD." They do not find in the Book that they will be forgiven, but they find in it repentance, as in the chapter of the Book of Deuteronomy, and as in the first Book of Kings in the prayer of Sulayman (Solomon) when he built the Temple, in the eighth chapter. So their saying "We shall be forgiven" is a fabrication against Allah with what He did not say.

"Al-mithaq" means the covenant, which is the charge of Musa (Moses) that he conveyed to them from Allah—exalted is He—in many places. The idiomatic attribution of the covenant to the Book is in the sense of "in" (fi) or in the sense of the lam, i.e. the covenant known by it. The Book is the Torah of Musa. As for "an la yaqulu" ("that they should not say") being the content of the covenant of the Book, it is governed by the omission of the preposition before the particle "an"; the meaning is: "that they should not say," i.e. by the absence of their saying about Allah other than the truth. It is also permissible for it to be an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "mithaq," so no preposition is estimated, and the estimate is: "the covenant of the Book is the absence of their saying about Allah…" etc.

The verb "darasu" (دَرَسُوا, "they studied") is conjoined to "yu'khadh," because "yu'khadh" has the sense of the past, owing to the entry of "lam" upon it. The estimate is: "Was it not taken … and they studied?" because the purpose is to affirm that they studied the Book, not to inform about them with it, like His saying: ﴿ألَمْ نَجْعَلِ الأرْضَ مِهادًا والجِبالَ أوْتادًا وخَلَقْناكم أزْواجًا وجَعَلْنا نَوْمَكم سُباتًا﴾ (al-Naba': 6), "Have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as pegs, and created you in pairs, and made your sleep a rest?" up to His saying: ﴿وأنْزَلْنا مِنَ المُعْصِراتِ ماءً ثَجّاجًا﴾ (al-Naba': 14), "And sent down from the pressing clouds pouring water." The estimate is: "and We created you in pairs and made your sleep a rest," to the end of the verse.

The meaning is: the covenant was taken from them that they should not say about Allah except the truth, and they knew of that covenant, because they studied what is in the Book. By the combination of the two matters, the proof was established against them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 171:

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it was about to fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾

The discourse has returned to the lesson drawn from the stories of the Children of Israel with Musa (peace be upon him), because the account of the lifting of the Mount over them is one of the mother-narratives of their history, and it is not like the story of the town whose people transgressed concerning the Sabbath, nor like the report of their being warned that there would be those who would inflict on them the worst torment. Thus all the plural pronouns here refer to the Children of Israel who were with Musa, as indicated by the context.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentences before it.

The word (idh) is connected to an implied verb whose estimated form is: "And remember ﴿when We raised the mountain over them﴾."

Al-naql (natq) means separating and uprooting. Al-jabal here is al-Tur (the Mount).

This was a sign that God manifested to them as a means of frightening them, so that it would serve as a reminder to them. This is followed by the taking of the covenant from them, with the firm resolve to act upon the Tawrah (Torah). The lifting of the Tur was thus a miracle for Musa (peace be upon him), confirming him in what he would convey to them from God concerning the taking of the rulings of the Torah with firm resolve and constancy. The story has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah at the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63].

Al-zulla is the cloud. The sentence ﴿Take what We have given you﴾ is a quoted speech following an implied verb of saying, which the structure of the discourse indicates. Omitting the verb of saying in such contexts is common and frequent, and a parallel of it has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb (waqi') is made transitive with the preposition bi- to indicate that they were settled on the mountain; so when it rose, it fell upon them, enveloping them and crushing them. They saw its summit above them while they were at its base. This is the way to reconcile His words "above them" with the preposition bi- of contact. Some exegetes made the bi- mean "upon" (ʿala).

The sentence ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63] is a quoted speech following an implied verb of saying, and the explanation of its parallel has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 166]

This is a speech directed at other than the Children of Israel, for they were not polytheists, and God says: ﴿Or [lest] you say: "Only our fathers associated partners [with God] before, and we were offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ Thus this is a shift in the discourse to arguing against the polytheists among the Arabs, which is the purpose of the surah from beginning to end. This shift was like returning the end to the beginning (*radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr*, a rhetorical device of echoing the close back to the opening). The shift came in connection with the mention of the covenant that God took from the Children of Israel in the charge given to Moses, which is the covenant of the Book, and on the day the mountain was lifted over them. That covenant was made through a creative address (*al-khiṭāb al-takwīnī*), meaning by placing its meaning in the innate constitution of every soul and its natural disposition (*fiṭra*). Therefore the sentence is coordinated with the preceding sentences as a narrative coordinated with a narrative. Its primary intended audience is the polytheists. The change in the style of the narrative is clear, since this narrative includes an address in His words ﴿that you say on the Day of Resurrection﴾ to the end of the verse, and the pronoun of absence (in ﴿from the children of Adam﴾) is explicitly mentioned as its referent. So the generality of the admonition follows the generality of the lesson. Thus this is a beginning of rebuking the polytheists for associating partners with God, and what is mentioned after it to the end of the surah is appropriate to the circumstances of the polytheists.

The word ﴿إذ﴾ (*idh*) is a noun denoting past time, and here it is free of the sense of a time-adverb, so it is an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) of an elided verb "remember" (*udhkur*).

The verb ﴿أخذ﴾ (*akhadha*, "took") is connected to ﴿من بني آدم﴾ (*min banī ādam*, "from the children of Adam"), and it is transitive to ﴿ذرياتهم﴾ (*dhurriyyātihim*, "their offspring"). Therefore the meaning is determined to be: your Lord took from every individual of the offspring, from every individual of the children of Adam. From this it follows that every individual of the children of Adam acknowledged for himself the lordship of God, may He be exalted.

The ﴿مِن﴾ (*min*) in ﴿من بني آدم﴾ and in ﴿من ظهورهم﴾ (*min ẓuhūrihim*, "from their backs") is the *min* of origin in both.

The word ﴿الذريات﴾ (*al-dhurriyyāt*) is the plural of ﴿ذرية﴾ (*dhurriyya*), and *dhurriyya* is a collective noun for what is produced from a human being. Its plural is used here to express explicitly the generality.

The taking of the covenant from the offspring who were brought out of the backs of the children of Adam necessarily entails the taking of the covenant from the offspring who were in the back of Adam, by way of the implication (*dalālat al-faḥwā*, an understanding drawn from the broader sense of the speech). Otherwise, the sons of Adam nearest to him would not be bound by the covenant, though they are more deserving of being bound by it in the back of Adam.

Among the things that confirm this implication are many reports narrated from the Prophet ﷺ and from a group of his Companions. They vary in strength, and not one of them is free from some critique, but their multiplicity supports one another. The clearest of them is what Mālik narrated in the *Muwaṭṭa'*, in the chapter on the prohibition of speaking about *qadar* (divine decree and predestination), with its chain going back to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ being asked about this verse: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam from their backs their offspring﴾. He said: 'God, may He be exalted, created Adam, then wiped his back with His right hand, and brought forth from it offspring, and said: "I created these for Paradise, and they will do the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He wiped his back with His right hand and brought forth from it offspring, and said: "I created these for the Fire, and they will do the deeds of the people of the Fire."'" He related the hadith with more than is needed for our purpose. The meaning of this hadith is that it is an explicit statement of the implied meaning mentioned, and not an explanation of the literal wording of the verse. By it, the verse became indicative of two matters: one explicit, which is what its wording conveys, and a second implicit, which is the implication of the address. In the verse, it is stated that God took from the offspring a covenant of acknowledging the lordship of God, and this is not addressed in the hadith. The hadith mentions that He distinguished among them the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. Perhaps the hadith is limited to explaining what the questioner asked about, so the explanation of the verse is a completion of what was not mentioned in it; or there was an abridgment in the hadith by one of its narrators, who reported only some of what he heard.

The word ﴿الأخذ﴾ (*al-akhdh*, "taking") is used metaphorically for bringing out and extracting. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if God took away your hearing and your sight..."﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:46], and so on.

His words ﴿من ظهورهم﴾ are a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿من بني آدم﴾, a substitute of part for whole (*badal baʿḍ min kull*). The preposition has been repeated with the substitute for emphasis, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿and from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:99] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The phrase "to make them witness against themselves" (*al-ishhād ʿalā al-anfus*) is used for what is equivalent to acknowledgment or compelling it, and here it means compelling acknowledgment. It is borrowed for a hidden state that includes this acknowledgment, which God knows, in order that the meaning of this recognition is established in their innate disposition. The pronoun in ﴿أشهدهم﴾ (*ashhadahum*, "He made them witness") refers to the offspring, according to its meaning, since it is a noun denoting a collective.

The saying in ﴿قالوا بلى﴾ (*qālū balā*, "they said: 'Yes'") is also used metaphorically, because their state indicates their acknowledgment of the lordship of God, may He be exalted.

The clause ﴿ألست بربكم﴾ (*alastu bi-rabbikum*, "Am I not your Lord?") is a quotation of an elided saying, and it explains the clause "He made them witness against themselves," that is, He established them by this saying, and this is from the matter of creative command (*amr al-takwīn*). The meaning is one, because the *dhurriyya*, when it is attributed to the pronoun of the children of Adam, carries the sense of distribution.

The interrogative in ﴿ألست بربكم﴾ is a confirmatory question (*istifhām taqrīrī*), and the same is said about confirming someone who is suspected of denial or who is treated as if he were denying. Therefore he is confirmed in negation, to draw him on, so that when he has set his heart upon negation, he thinks that the one confirming seeks it from him, and so he proceeds to answer in the negative. But when he has not set his heart upon it, he answers by overturning the negation, and thus it becomes established that he is free of denying it. On this principle is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire, [it will be said]: "Is this not the truth?"﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 46:34], treating them as if they regarded it as not true, because they used to deny it in the world. This was previously mentioned at His words ﴿O company of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:130] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The speech is an illustrative representation (*tamthīl*) of a state among the states of the unseen, of the descent of the divine creative command upon the essences of existing things and their accidents at the time of their bringing into being. Souls cannot reach a conception of them in their reality, because they lie beyond what is customary and familiar, so this illustration is intended to bring them near. The sum of the meaning is that God placed in man, from the time of his creation, the perception of the proofs of divine unity, and placed in the natural disposition and the movement of human thought the reaching toward perceiving that and attaining its perception when he strips his soul of the accidents that enter upon his disposition and corrupt it.

The sentence ﴿قالوا بلى﴾ is an answer to the confirmatory question, and it is separated (from what precedes) because it came in the manner of dialogue, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:30] in Surat al-Baqara.

The saying is used either literally, and then it is a speech that breaks customary patterns, or metaphorically, indicating through their state that they are created and governed by God, may He be exalted, just as the saying is used for something similar in His words: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:11], meaning that the traces of the command of creation appeared in them. Abū al-Najm said:

*The bird said to him: "Go forward, rightly guided, for you will not return except praising."*

This is from the metaphor that is abundant in the speech of the Arabs.

The word ﴿بلى﴾ (*balā*) is a particle of answer to a statement that contains the sense of negation, so it requires overturning the negation and affirming what was negated. For this reason, answering with it after a negation is clearer than answering with the particle ﴿نعم﴾ (*naʿam*), because *naʿam* may confirm the negation or confirm what was negated. This is the meaning of what was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding this verse, that he said:

*Had they said "naʿam," they would have disbelieved,* meaning that their answer would have admitted of disbelief. And since the situation was one of acknowledgment, the admission of such a possibility would have been an evasion from acknowledgment.

Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb read ﴿ذرياتهم﴾ with the plural, while the rest read ﴿ذريتهم﴾ in the singular.

Their saying ﴿شهدنا﴾ (*shahidnā*, "we bear witness") is an emphasis of the content of ﴿بلى﴾, and the witnessing here is also in the sense of acknowledgment.

The phrase ﴿أن تقولوا﴾ (*an taqūlū*, "that you say") occurs in the position of a causal clause for the verbs "taking" and "making witness." It is therefore understood with an implied causal *lām* (*lām al-taʿlīl*, "in order that"), and its elision along with ﴿أن﴾ is in accordance with the common, well-known usage. The intended causation is by negating that they would say, "We were indeed heedless of this," not by bringing about the saying; so the particle of negation has been elided, following the common elision of it with the verb "say." Or it is a causal clause by way of their saying that, if their witnessing against themselves had not occurred, as was previously mentioned at His words ﴿that you say: "The Book was only sent down..."﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:156] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The majority read ﴿أن تقولوا﴾ with the *tāʾ* of address. The style has been shifted from the third person to the second person, and then from addressing the Messenger to addressing his people, making explicit that the intended purpose of the narrative of the taking of the covenant is to remind the polytheists of what God deposited in the natural disposition of monotheism. This style is a shift of address from one addressee to another, not an inversion (*iltifāt*) on account of the difference of addressees. Abū ʿAmr alone read it with the *yāʾ* of the third person, and the pronoun refers to the offspring of the children of Adam.

The demonstrative ﴿هذا﴾ (*hādhā*, "this") refers to the content of the question and its answer, which is the acknowledgment of the lordship of God, may He be exalted, supposing it to be the one mentioned.

The meaning is that, since this was placed in the natural disposition at the time of creation, human minds were inclined toward it, so none of them is heedless of it, and so on the Day of Resurrection, when they are asked about associating partners, none of them can offer the excuse of heedlessness. Therefore this is a refutation of the excuse of heedlessness, and for this reason there was an implied negative particle, meaning "that you should not say," and so on.

Coordinated with it is the excuse of ignorance rather than heedlessness, namely that they would say: "We followed our fathers and did not think that association was anything but truth." Since the knowledge of the unity of God is in the原 basic disposition, the excuse of ignorance of Him is nullified, and association is either deliberate or due to negligence, and neither of these can stand as an excuse. All of this is suitable only for addressing the polytheists, not the Children of Israel.

The meaning of ﴿وكنا ذرية من بعدهم﴾ (*wa-kunnā dhurriyya min baʿdihim*, "and we were offspring after them") is: we were upon their religion following them, because we are their offspring, and it is the nature of offspring to follow their fathers and maintain their customs. So there is an abridgment in the speech, and the cause is placed in the position of what is caused.

The phrase ﴿من بعدهم﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿ذرية﴾, because *dhurriyya* implies succession and standing in their place. The interrogative in ﴿أفتهلكنا﴾ (*a-fatuhlikunā*, "Will You destroy us") is denunciatory (*istifhām inkārī*), and destruction here is used metaphorically for punishment. The ﴿المبطلون﴾ (*al-mubṭilūn*, "the falsifiers") are those who take up falsehood, and in this context it is association.

In this verse there is evidence that belief in the one God is established in the natural disposition of reason, if it is left to itself and stripped of the doubts that arise in it from negligence in reflection, or that are cast upon it by people of error in whom error is established, whether intentionally or unintentionally. Therefore al-Māturīdī and the Muʿtazila said: belief in the one God is obligatory by reason. This is attributed to Abū Ḥanīfa, to al-Māwardī, and to some Shāfiʿīs of Iraq. On this basis the punishment of the people of the *fatra* (the interval between prophets) for associating partners is established. But al-Ashʿarī said: knowledge of God is obligatory by revelation, not by reason, holding to His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:15]. Perhaps he traced the punishment of the people of the *fatra* for polytheism back to the widespread transmission (*tawātur*) of the coming of messengers with monotheism.

The sentence ﴿وكذلك نفصل الآيات﴾ (*wa-kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt*, "And thus We detail the signs") is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*) between the two narratives, and the *wāw* is parenthetical, which is called the *wāw* of resumption (*wāw al-istiʾnāf*). That is: such detailing, We detail the signs, meaning the signs of the Qur'an. A similar expression was previously mentioned at His words ﴿And thus We detail the signs, so that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:55] in Surat al-Anʿām. Its detailing is its explanation and its clearing of ambiguity.

The clause "{وَلَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ}" ("so that perhaps they may return") is coordinated with the clause "{وَكَذَلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ الْآيَاتِ}" ("Thus do We detail the signs"). It therefore stands in the position of a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). This is a performative expression of hope (inshā' tarajjī) that the polytheists will return to monotheism (tawhīd). The meaning of hope when it is attributed to God, the Exalted, was discussed earlier, at His words, exalted is He, "{يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ}" ("O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous") [al-Baqarah: 21], in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 171]

The word "return" (rujūʿ) is used metaphorically (isti' āra) for abandoning polytheism (shirk, associating partners with God). The abandoning of the state in which they are involved is likened to the departure of one who has settled in a place other than his home, returning to his proper abode. This comparison implies that the state of associating partners with God is likened to a place of estrangement, because shirk is not part of the demands of the innate nature (fiṭra), so being engaged in it is a departure from the original created disposition, like the departure of a traveller from his homeland. It also implies that the state of monotheism is likened to a person's dwelling and tribe to which he returns. The use of "return" for the polytheists' abandonment of shirk occurs repeatedly in the Qur'an, such as His words: "{وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ إِنَّنِي بَرَاءٌ مِمَّا تَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي فَإِنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ * وَجَعَلَهَا كَلِمَةً بَاقِيَةً فِي عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ}" ("And when Abraham said to his father and his people, 'Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me, for He will surely guide me.' And he made it a word remaining among his descendants that they might return") [al-Zukhruf: 26–28], meaning that they might return from shirk. This is an indirect address (taʿrīḍ) to the Arabs, since they are the polytheists among the descendants of Abraham. The context is confirmed by His words: "{بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ هَؤُلَاءِ وَآبَاءَهُمْ حَتَّى جَاءَهُمُ الْحَقُّ وَرَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ}" ("Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger") [al-Zukhruf: 29]. I have inductively determined from the Qur'anic usage that it uses "these" (hā'ulā') to refer to the Arabs.

Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ Thus this is a shift in the discourse to arguing against the polytheists among the Arabs, which is the purpose of the surah from beginning to end. This shift was like returning the end to the beginning (*radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr*, a rhetorical device of echoing the close back to the opening). The shift came in connection with the mention of the covenant that God took from the Children of Israel in the charge given to Moses, which is the covenant of the Book, and on the day the mountain was lifted over them. That covenant was made through a creative address (*al-khiṭāb al-takwīnī*), meaning by placing its meaning in the innate constitution of every soul and its natural disposition (*fiṭra*). Therefore the sentence is coordinated with the preceding sentences as a narrative coordinated with a narrative. Its primary intended audience is the polytheists. The change in the style of the narrative is clear, since this narrative includes an address in His words ﴿that you say on the Day of Resurrection﴾ to the end of the verse, and the pronoun of absence (in ﴿from the children of Adam﴾) is explicitly mentioned as its referent. So the generality of the admonition follows the generality of the lesson. Thus this is a beginning of rebuking the polytheists for associating partners with God, and what is mentioned after it to the end of the surah is appropriate to the circumstances of the polytheists.

The word ﴿إذ﴾ (*idh*) is a noun denoting past time, and here it is free of the sense of a time-adverb, so it is an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) of an elided verb "remember" (*udhkur*).

The verb ﴿أخذ﴾ (*akhadha*, "took") is connected to ﴿من بني آدم﴾ (*min banī ādam*, "from the children of Adam"), and it is transitive to ﴿ذرياتهم﴾ (*dhurriyyātihim*, "their offspring"). Therefore the meaning is determined to be: your Lord took from every individual of the offspring, from every individual of the children of Adam. From this it follows that every individual of the children of Adam acknowledged for himself the lordship of God, may He be exalted.

The ﴿مِن﴾ (*min*) in ﴿من بني آدم﴾ and in ﴿من ظهورهم﴾ (*min ẓuhūrihim*, "from their backs") is the *min* of origin in both.

The word ﴿الذريات﴾ (*al-dhurriyyāt*) is the plural of ﴿ذرية﴾ (*dhurriyya*), and *dhurriyya* is a collective noun for what is produced from a human being. Its plural is used here to express explicitly the generality.
