The interrogative in ﴿أفتهلكنا﴾ (*a-fatuhlikunā*, "Will You destroy us") is denunciatory (*istifhām inkārī*), and destruction here is used metaphorically for punishment. The ﴿المبطلون﴾ (*al-mubṭilūn*, "the falsifiers") are those who take up falsehood, and in this context it is association.

In this verse there is evidence that belief in the one God is established in the natural disposition of reason, if it is left to itself and stripped of the doubts that arise in it from negligence in reflection, or that are cast upon it by people of error in whom error is established, whether intentionally or unintentionally. Therefore al-Māturīdī and the Muʿtazila said: belief in the one God is obligatory by reason. This is attributed to Abū Ḥanīfa, to al-Māwardī, and to some Shāfiʿīs of Iraq. On this basis the punishment of the people of the *fatra* (the interval between prophets) for associating partners is established. But al-Ashʿarī said: knowledge of God is obligatory by revelation, not by reason, holding to His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:15]. Perhaps he traced the punishment of the people of the *fatra* for polytheism back to the widespread transmission (*tawātur*) of the coming of messengers with monotheism.

The sentence ﴿وكذلك نفصل الآيات﴾ (*wa-kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt*, "And thus We detail the signs") is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*) between the two narratives, and the *wāw* is parenthetical, which is called the *wāw* of resumption (*wāw al-istiʾnāf*). That is: such detailing, We detail the signs, meaning the signs of the Qur'an. A similar expression was previously mentioned at His words ﴿And thus We detail the signs, so that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:55] in Surat al-Anʿām. Its detailing is its explanation and its clearing of ambiguity.

The clause "{وَلَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ}" ("so that perhaps they may return") is coordinated with the clause "{وَكَذَلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ الْآيَاتِ}" ("Thus do We detail the signs"). It therefore stands in the position of a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). This is a performative expression of hope (inshā' tarajjī) that the polytheists will return to monotheism (tawhīd). The meaning of hope when it is attributed to God, the Exalted, was discussed earlier, at His words, exalted is He, "{يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ}" ("O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous") [al-Baqarah: 21], in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 171]

The word "return" (rujūʿ) is used metaphorically (isti' āra) for abandoning polytheism (shirk, associating partners with God). The abandoning of the state in which they are involved is likened to the departure of one who has settled in a place other than his home, returning to his proper abode. This comparison implies that the state of associating partners with God is likened to a place of estrangement, because shirk is not part of the demands of the innate nature (fiṭra), so being engaged in it is a departure from the original created disposition, like the departure of a traveller from his homeland. It also implies that the state of monotheism is likened to a person's dwelling and tribe to which he returns. The use of "return" for the polytheists' abandonment of shirk occurs repeatedly in the Qur'an, such as His words: "{وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ إِنَّنِي بَرَاءٌ مِمَّا تَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي فَإِنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ * وَجَعَلَهَا كَلِمَةً بَاقِيَةً فِي عَقِبِهِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ}" ("And when Abraham said to his father and his people, 'Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me, for He will surely guide me.' And he made it a word remaining among his descendants that they might return") [al-Zukhruf: 26–28], meaning that they might return from shirk. This is an indirect address (taʿrīḍ) to the Arabs, since they are the polytheists among the descendants of Abraham. The context is confirmed by His words: "{بَلْ مَتَّعْتُ هَؤُلَاءِ وَآبَاءَهُمْ حَتَّى جَاءَهُمُ الْحَقُّ وَرَسُولٌ مُبِينٌ}" ("Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger") [al-Zukhruf: 29]. I have inductively determined from the Qur'anic usage that it uses "these" (hā'ulā') to refer to the Arabs.

[Page 166]

This is a speech directed at other than the Children of Israel, for they were not polytheists, and God says: ﴿Or [lest] you say: "Only our fathers associated partners [with God] before, and we were offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ Thus this is a shift in the discourse to arguing against the polytheists among the Arabs, which is the purpose of the surah from beginning to end. This shift was like returning the end to the beginning (*radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr*, a rhetorical device of echoing the close back to the opening). The shift came in connection with the mention of the covenant that God took from the Children of Israel in the charge given to Moses, which is the covenant of the Book, and on the day the mountain was lifted over them. That covenant was made through a creative address (*al-khiṭāb al-takwīnī*), meaning by placing its meaning in the innate constitution of every soul and its natural disposition (*fiṭra*). Therefore the sentence is coordinated with the preceding sentences as a narrative coordinated with a narrative. Its primary intended audience is the polytheists. The change in the style of the narrative is clear, since this narrative includes an address in His words ﴿that you say on the Day of Resurrection﴾ to the end of the verse, and the pronoun of absence (in ﴿from the children of Adam﴾) is explicitly mentioned as its referent. So the generality of the admonition follows the generality of the lesson. Thus this is a beginning of rebuking the polytheists for associating partners with God, and what is mentioned after it to the end of the surah is appropriate to the circumstances of the polytheists.

The word ﴿إذ﴾ (*idh*) is a noun denoting past time, and here it is free of the sense of a time-adverb, so it is an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) of an elided verb "remember" (*udhkur*).

The verb ﴿أخذ﴾ (*akhadha*, "took") is connected to ﴿من بني آدم﴾ (*min banī ādam*, "from the children of Adam"), and it is transitive to ﴿ذرياتهم﴾ (*dhurriyyātihim*, "their offspring"). Therefore the meaning is determined to be: your Lord took from every individual of the offspring, from every individual of the children of Adam. From this it follows that every individual of the children of Adam acknowledged for himself the lordship of God, may He be exalted.

The ﴿مِن﴾ (*min*) in ﴿من بني آدم﴾ and in ﴿من ظهورهم﴾ (*min ẓuhūrihim*, "from their backs") is the *min* of origin in both.

The word ﴿الذريات﴾ (*al-dhurriyyāt*) is the plural of ﴿ذرية﴾ (*dhurriyya*), and *dhurriyya* is a collective noun for what is produced from a human being. Its plural is used here to express explicitly the generality.

The taking of the covenant from the offspring who were brought out of the backs of the children of Adam necessarily entails the taking of the covenant from the offspring who were in the back of Adam, by way of the implication (*dalālat al-faḥwā*, an understanding drawn from the broader sense of the speech). Otherwise, the sons of Adam nearest to him would not be bound by the covenant, though they are more deserving of being bound by it in the back of Adam.

Among the things that confirm this implication are many reports narrated from the Prophet ﷺ and from a group of his Companions. They vary in strength, and not one of them is free from some critique, but their multiplicity supports one another. The clearest of them is what Mālik narrated in the *Muwaṭṭa'*, in the chapter on the prohibition of speaking about *qadar* (divine decree and predestination), with its chain going back to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ being asked about this verse: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam from their backs their offspring﴾. He said: 'God, may He be exalted, created Adam, then wiped his back with His right hand, and brought forth from it offspring, and said: "I created these for Paradise, and they will do the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He wiped his back with His right hand and brought forth from it offspring, and said: "I created these for the Fire, and they will do the deeds of the people of the Fire."'" He related the hadith with more than is needed for our purpose. The meaning of this hadith is that it is an explicit statement of the implied meaning mentioned, and not an explanation of the literal wording of the verse. By it, the verse became indicative of two matters: one explicit, which is what its wording conveys, and a second implicit, which is the implication of the address. In the verse, it is stated that God took from the offspring a covenant of acknowledging the lordship of God, and this is not addressed in the hadith. The hadith mentions that He distinguished among them the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. Perhaps the hadith is limited to explaining what the questioner asked about, so the explanation of the verse is a completion of what was not mentioned in it; or there was an abridgment in the hadith by one of its narrators, who reported only some of what he heard.

The word ﴿الأخذ﴾ (*al-akhdh*, "taking") is used metaphorically for bringing out and extracting. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if God took away your hearing and your sight..."﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:46], and so on.

His words ﴿من ظهورهم﴾ are a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿من بني آدم﴾, a substitute of part for whole (*badal baʿḍ min kull*). The preposition has been repeated with the substitute for emphasis, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿and from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:99] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The phrase "to make them witness against themselves" (*al-ishhād ʿalā al-anfus*) is used for what is equivalent to acknowledgment or compelling it, and here it means compelling acknowledgment. It is borrowed for a hidden state that includes this acknowledgment, which God knows, in order that the meaning of this recognition is established in their innate disposition. The pronoun in ﴿أشهدهم﴾ (*ashhadahum*, "He made them witness") refers to the offspring, according to its meaning, since it is a noun denoting a collective.

The saying in ﴿قالوا بلى﴾ (*qālū balā*, "they said: 'Yes'") is also used metaphorically, because their state indicates their acknowledgment of the lordship of God, may He be exalted.

The clause ﴿ألست بربكم﴾ (*alastu bi-rabbikum*, "Am I not your Lord?") is a quotation of an elided saying, and it explains the clause "He made them witness against themselves," that is, He established them by this saying, and this is from the matter of creative command (*amr al-takwīn*). The meaning is one, because the *dhurriyya*, when it is attributed to the pronoun of the children of Adam, carries the sense of distribution.

The interrogative in ﴿ألست بربكم﴾ is a confirmatory question (*istifhām taqrīrī*), and the same is said about confirming someone who is suspected of denial or who is treated as if he were denying. Therefore he is confirmed in negation, to draw him on, so that when he has set his heart upon negation, he thinks that the one confirming seeks it from him, and so he proceeds to answer in the negative. But when he has not set his heart upon it, he answers by overturning the negation, and thus it becomes established that he is free of denying it. On this principle is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire, [it will be said]: "Is this not the truth?"﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 46:34], treating them as if they regarded it as not true, because they used to deny it in the world. This was previously mentioned at His words ﴿O company of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:130] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The speech is an illustrative representation (*tamthīl*) of a state among the states of the unseen, of the descent of the divine creative command upon the essences of existing things and their accidents at the time of their bringing into being. Souls cannot reach a conception of them in their reality, because they lie beyond what is customary and familiar, so this illustration is intended to bring them near. The sum of the meaning is that God placed in man, from the time of his creation, the perception of the proofs of divine unity, and placed in the natural disposition and the movement of human thought the reaching toward perceiving that and attaining its perception when he strips his soul of the accidents that enter upon his disposition and corrupt it.

The sentence ﴿قالوا بلى﴾ is an answer to the confirmatory question, and it is separated (from what precedes) because it came in the manner of dialogue, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?"﴾ [al-Baqara 2:30] in Surat al-Baqara.

The saying is used either literally, and then it is a speech that breaks customary patterns, or metaphorically, indicating through their state that they are created and governed by God, may He be exalted, just as the saying is used for something similar in His words: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:11], meaning that the traces of the command of creation appeared in them. Abū al-Najm said:

*The bird said to him: "Go forward, rightly guided, for you will not return except praising."*

This is from the metaphor that is abundant in the speech of the Arabs.

The word ﴿بلى﴾ (*balā*) is a particle of answer to a statement that contains the sense of negation, so it requires overturning the negation and affirming what was negated. For this reason, answering with it after a negation is clearer than answering with the particle ﴿نعم﴾ (*naʿam*), because *naʿam* may confirm the negation or confirm what was negated. This is the meaning of what was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding this verse, that he said:

*Had they said "naʿam," they would have disbelieved,* meaning that their answer would have admitted of disbelief. And since the situation was one of acknowledgment, the admission of such a possibility would have been an evasion from acknowledgment.

Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb read ﴿ذرياتهم﴾ with the plural, while the rest read ﴿ذريتهم﴾ in the singular.

Their saying ﴿شهدنا﴾ (*shahidnā*, "we bear witness") is an emphasis of the content of ﴿بلى﴾, and the witnessing here is also in the sense of acknowledgment.

The phrase ﴿أن تقولوا﴾ (*an taqūlū*, "that you say") occurs in the position of a causal clause for the verbs "taking" and "making witness." It is therefore understood with an implied causal *lām* (*lām al-taʿlīl*, "in order that"), and its elision along with ﴿أن﴾ is in accordance with the common, well-known usage. The intended causation is by negating that they would say, "We were indeed heedless of this," not by bringing about the saying; so the particle of negation has been elided, following the common elision of it with the verb "say." Or it is a causal clause by way of their saying that, if their witnessing against themselves had not occurred, as was previously mentioned at His words ﴿that you say: "The Book was only sent down..."﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:156] in Surat al-Anʿām.

The majority read ﴿أن تقولوا﴾ with the *tāʾ* of address. The style has been shifted from the third person to the second person, and then from addressing the Messenger to addressing his people, making explicit that the intended purpose of the narrative of the taking of the covenant is to remind the polytheists of what God deposited in the natural disposition of monotheism. This style is a shift of address from one addressee to another, not an inversion (*iltifāt*) on account of the difference of addressees. Abū ʿAmr alone read it with the *yāʾ* of the third person, and the pronoun refers to the offspring of the children of Adam.

The demonstrative ﴿هذا﴾ (*hādhā*, "this") refers to the content of the question and its answer, which is the acknowledgment of the lordship of God, may He be exalted, supposing it to be the one mentioned.

The meaning is that, since this was placed in the natural disposition at the time of creation, human minds were inclined toward it, so none of them is heedless of it, and so on the Day of Resurrection, when they are asked about associating partners, none of them can offer the excuse of heedlessness. Therefore this is a refutation of the excuse of heedlessness, and for this reason there was an implied negative particle, meaning "that you should not say," and so on.

Coordinated with it is the excuse of ignorance rather than heedlessness, namely that they would say: "We followed our fathers and did not think that association was anything but truth." Since the knowledge of the unity of God is in the原 basic disposition, the excuse of ignorance of Him is nullified, and association is either deliberate or due to negligence, and neither of these can stand as an excuse. All of this is suitable only for addressing the polytheists, not the Children of Israel.

The meaning of ﴿وكنا ذرية من بعدهم﴾ (*wa-kunnā dhurriyya min baʿdihim*, "and we were offspring after them") is: we were upon their religion following them, because we are their offspring, and it is the nature of offspring to follow their fathers and maintain their customs. So there is an abridgment in the speech, and the cause is placed in the position of what is caused.

The phrase ﴿من بعدهم﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿ذرية﴾, because *dhurriyya* implies succession and standing in their place. On this basis the punishment of the people of the *fatra* (the interval between prophets) for associating partners is established. But al-Ashʿarī said: knowledge of God is obligatory by revelation, not by reason, holding to His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:15]. Perhaps he traced the punishment of the people of the *fatra* for polytheism back to the widespread transmission (*tawātur*) of the coming of messengers with monotheism.

The sentence ﴿وكذلك نفصل الآيات﴾ (*wa-kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt*, "And thus We detail the signs") is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*) between the two narratives, and the *wāw* is parenthetical, which is called the *wāw* of resumption (*wāw al-istiʾnāf*). That is: such detailing, We detail the signs, meaning the signs of the Qur'an. A similar expression was previously mentioned at His words ﴿And thus We detail the signs, so that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:55] in Surat al-Anʿām. Its detailing is its explanation and its clearing of ambiguity.

The clause "{وَلَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ}" ("so that perhaps they may return") is coordinated with the clause "{وَكَذَلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ الْآيَاتِ}" ("Thus do We detail the signs"). It therefore stands in the position of a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). This is a performative expression of hope (inshā' tarajjī) that the polytheists will return to monotheism (tawhīd). [Page 171]

The abandoning of the state in which they are involved is likened to the departure of one who has settled in a place other than his home, returning to his proper abode. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 175 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 172]
[Page 173]
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surah al-A'raf.

﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our verses, but he withdrew from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became of those who go astray.﴾ ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire. So his likeness is that of a dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants.﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]

It follows a passage that indicates that monotheism is placed in the natural disposition (fitrah), by mentioning the state of some people who were guided to rejecting polytheism at the beginning of their affair, and then the whisperings of Satan approach them, adorning polytheism for them.

Its connection to the preceding verses is that it is a lesson drawn from the condition of one of those whom Allah took a covenant from regarding monotheism and obedience to Allah's command. Allah granted him knowledge to help him fulfill what he pledged to Allah in the fitrah. Then all of that did not benefit him, when Allah did not decree for him continuing guidance.

The stories that open with the words ﴿And recite to them﴾ are intended to admonish the polytheists with the one concerned in the story, as indicated by His saying ﴿That is the likeness of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], etc. From this there also results an instruction like His saying ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah﴾ [Yunus: 71], ﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 69], ﴿We recite to you from the news of Moses and Pharaoh with truth﴾ [al-Qasas: 3], and their like. So the pronoun in ﴿them﴾ refers to the polytheists to whom the lessons and admonitions have been addressed from the beginning of this surah, and [the stories] relate to them
[Page 174]
the stories of nations with their messengers. Moreover, directing third-person plural pronouns to them is a style that is followed in many places in the Qur'an, as we have mentioned more than once. So this is of the kind of "the last returning to the first" (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr).

The appropriateness of the act of recitation to them is that they were a people dominated by illiteracy, so Allah wished to convey to them of the teaching what makes them equal to the state of the People of the Book in recitation. The pronoun governed by ʿalā refers to something known from the context, namely the polytheists. The third-person plural pronoun often comes in the Qur'an meaning the polytheists, as in His saying ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾.

Al-naba' is the transmitted report.

The apparent meaning of the singular relative pronoun is that the one referred to by the relative clause is a specific individual, and that the content of the relative clause is one of the states by which he was known. The closest view is that the subject of this report is among those whom the Arabs have some general acquaintance with his account.

It has been said that the one meant is Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi. This was narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, through many chains of transmission in al-Tabari, and from Zayd ibn Aslam. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: it is the most famous, and it is the view of most. That is because Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi was among those who sought to follow a religion other than polytheism, seeking the religion of truth. He examined the Torah and the Gospel and did not find salvation in Judaism or Christianity. He practiced asceticism and aimed for the hanifiyyah, the religion of Abraham. He was informed that Allah would send a prophet among the Arabs, so he hoped to be that one. He rejected the worship of idols and forbade wine. He mentioned in his poetry reports from the stories of the Torah. It is related that he had inspirations and unveilings, and he used to say: "Every religion on the Day of Resurrection before Allah is false except the religion of the hanifiyyah."
He had much poetry on matters of divinity. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, he grieved that he had not been the messenger sent among the Arabs. It happened that he went to Bahrain before the mission and stayed there eight years, then returned to Mecca and found the mission, and hesitated about Islam. Then he went to Syria and returned after the Battle of Badr, and did not believe in the Prophet (ﷺ) out of envy. He lamented those of the polytheists who were killed on the day of Badr, and went out to al-Ta'if, the land of his people, and died as a disbeliever. He used to mention in his poetry reward and punishment, the name of Allah, and the names of the prophets. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about him:
[Page 175]
"Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt nearly embraced Islam." It is narrated from Umayyah that when he fell ill with his final illness, he said: "I know that the hanifiyyah is true, but doubt creeps into me regarding Muhammad."

So the meaning of ﴿We gave him Our verses﴾ is that Allah inspired Umayyah with aversion to polytheism, cast into his soul the seeking of truth, facilitated for him the reading of the books of the prophets, and made the hanifiyyah beloved to him. Then, when the door of guidance opened for him and the light of the Muhammadan call shone, he was arrogant, envied, and turned away from Islam. Therefore, it is inevitable that his condition became that he withdrew from all that had been made easy for him, and did not benefit from it at the time when benefit was possible. So Satan was the one who diverted him from guidance, and he became of those who go astray, since he died in disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it was revealed concerning Abu 'Amir ibn Sayfi al-Rahib, whose name was al-Nu'man al-Khazraji. He was called "the monk" in the Jahiliyyah because he had become a Christian in the Jahiliyyah, wore woolen garments, and claimed that he was upon the hanifiyyah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, he entered upon the Prophet and said: "O Muhammad, what is it that you have brought?" He said: "I have brought the hanifiyyah, the religion of Abraham." He said: "Then I am upon it." The Prophet said: "You are not upon it, because you have introduced into it what is not from it." He disbelieved, and went out to Mecca inciting the polytheists to fight the Prophet (ﷺ), and went out with them until he fought at Hunayn after the conquest of Mecca. When Hawazin was defeated, he despaired and went out to Syria, and died there.

Many of the exegetes held that it was revealed concerning a man from the Canaanites, who was in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), called Balam ibn Ba'ura. They mentioned his story but mixed it up, altered it, and differed about it. The verified view is that this Balam was among the righteous people of Madyan and their soothsayers at the time of the passage of the Children of Israel through the land of Moab, but he did not deviate from the state of righteousness. That is mentioned in the Book of Numbers of the Torah, in chapters 22, 23, and 24. So it is not appropriate to turn to this view because of its confusion and mixing.

The word ītā' here is used metaphorically for enlightenment and facilitation of knowledge, like His saying ﴿and Allah gave him knowledge and wisdom﴾.

And "the verses" (al-ayat) are the proofs of God's oneness which made polytheism hateful to him and moved him to seek the hanifiyyah, with respect to Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, or the proofs in the Gospel concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ),
[Page 176]
with respect to the monk Abu 'Amir ibn Sayfi.

Al-insilakh (withdrawal) in its literal sense is the emergence of an animal's body from its skin when the skin is stripped from it, and al-salkh is the removal of the skin of a dead animal from its body. It is used metaphorically in the verse for spiritual detachment, which is abandoning being clothed in a thing or not acting upon it. The meaning of "withdrew from the verses" is ceasing to act upon what they require, because the verses had informed him of the corruption of the religion of the Jahiliyyah.

And atba'ahu, with a hamzat qat' and a sukun on the taʾ, means he overtook him without escape, like His saying ﴿So a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10] and ﴿So Pharaoh pursued them with his armies﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78]. This is more specific than ittaba'ahu with a shaddah on the taʾ and a hamzat wasl.

By al-ghawin is meant those characterized by ghayy, which is misguidance. ﴿and became of those who go astray﴾ is more intensive in attributing misguidance than saying "he strayed" or "he was a misguided one," as was mentioned previously at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I would then have strayed, and I would not be of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surah al-An'am.

The verbs of withdrawal, following, and being among the misguided are ordered by the fa' of conjunction according to the order of their occurrence, for when he was obstinate and did not act upon what Allah had guided him to, a satanic darkness arose in his soul which enabled Satan to use him and to perpetuate his misguidance. So withdrawal from the verses is an effect of Satan's whispering, and when a person obeys the whispering, Satan gains control over his reins, subjugates him, and perpetuates his misleading. This is what is expressed by atba'ahu, and he thereby joins the company of the deviators who are firmly established in misguidance.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] indicates that those verses by their nature were to be a means of guidance and purification, had Allah willed for him success and protected him from Satan's plot and temptation, so that he would not have withdrawn from them. This is a lesson for those who are granted success, that they may know the grace of Allah upon them in their success. The meaning is: had We willed, he would have increased in acting upon the verses We gave him, and Allah would have raised him by his action.

Raising (al-rif'ah) is used metaphorically for the perfection of the soul and its purity, because praiseworthy attributes make their possessor appear elevated above those beneath him. That is, had We willed, he would have acquired through his action with the verses excellence, purity, and distinction by virtue, so the meaning of ﴿We would have raised him﴾ is: We would have made easy for him the action through them by which he would be honored.

A contrast has come upon the content of His saying ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾, by mentioning what contradicts
[Page 177]
that impossible will, namely the contrast that his state was reversed, so he clung to the earth, meaning he inclined and leaned toward the earth. The statement is an image of the state of one who is characterized by defects and disbelief after faith and piety, by the likeness of one who was elevated above the earth and then descended from height to below. By mentioning the earth it is known that clinging here means leaning toward what is low, that is, being engaged in defects and corruptions.

Following desire is preferring what is pleasing to the self among blameworthy vices over what truth and right guidance call to. So "following" is used metaphorically for choosing and inclining, and "desire" has become common for blameworthy love whose outcome is ruinous.

This state is followed by the image of him as a panting dog, because his being characterized by the condition that made him similar to the state of the panting dog follows from his clinging to the earth and following his desire. So the statement amounts to saying: "But he clung to the earth, so he became in misery and obstinacy like the likeness of the dog," etc.

The Qur'an's use of the word "mathal" after the kaf of comparison is familiar, in that it is intended to compare a state with a state. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] has already come in Surah al-Baqarah. Therefore it is determined that the comparison here does not depart from what is customary in compound comparison. This astray man undertook the burden of following the upright religion and began seeking it at a time when he was not obligated to do so, in the period of fatrah (interval between prophets), and so he encountered weariness and hardship from it. When the time came to follow the truth with the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ), he bore the hardship of obstinacy and turning away from it at a time when he was deserving of resting from his toil, since his aim had been attained. So his state was like the state of the dog characterized by panting, for it pants while the causes of panting exist, such as chasing, intimidation, and hardship, which is the state of being attacked; and in the state of the absence of that cause, which is the state of being left in ease and peace. What points to this meaning is His saying "or if you leave it."

No animal has a state, in both conditions, to which a comparison can be made other than the state of the panting dog, because it pants when it is tired and when it is at rest. Panting is part of its natural constitution.

This comparison is one of the Qur'an's originalities, for panting is a state that indicates the dog's distress due to its difficulty in breathing, reflecting the agitation of its inner being, even if there is no cause for its inner agitation coming from elsewhere.
[Page 178]
So the meaning of ﴿If you attack it﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] is: if you pursue it and assault it. It derives from haml, which is an assault upon someone to fight him. It is said: "So-and-so charged against the people with a fierce charge" or "a reprehensible charge." The commentators have neglected to clarify this, and al-Raghib in his Mufradat al-Qur'an neglected this meaning of this verb.

This is a compound representative analogy (tashbih tamthil), in which the state being compared and the state it is compared to are both drawn from multiple elements. Since the phrase ﴿If you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] mentions the dog's panting in both cases, the panting must have a counterpart in the state being compared. The parts of this analogy correspond as follows: the misguided person is compared to the dog, and his misery and the turmoil of his affairs during his search for religion are compared to the dog's panting when it is left in peace. This is the comparison of an intelligible matter to a sensible one (tashbih al-ma'qul bi-al-mahsus). Likewise, his misery in turning away from the true religion when it comes to him is compared to the dog's panting when it is driven off and beaten, which is again the comparison of an intelligible matter to a sensible one.

Those who interpreted this verse neglected this point. They established the analogy as a comparison of a simple state to a simple state, merely for disfigurement or baseness. This amounts to saying that the purpose of comparing him to the dog is to show the baseness of the one compared, as is the approach adopted in al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary). Had this been the intended meaning, the phrase ﴿If you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾ would have had no great benefit. Rather, it would be limited to disfiguring the state used as the comparison, so that the state being compared acquires disfigurement. That is a shortcoming in the understanding of the analogy.

The dog is a four-legged animal with fangs and claws. It barks much at night and sleeps little during it, but sleeps much during the day. It grows attached to whoever keeps company with it, guards its place against strangers whom it does not know, and guards the livestock it keeps company with. It attacks wolves and accepts training because it is intelligent.

It pants when it is exhausted or when the heat becomes intense on it, and it also pants without these causes, because in its physical make-up there is a narrowness in the passages of breath, and it finds relief in panting.

The clause ﴿If you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the dog. The address in ﴿you attack﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] and "leave" is to an unspecified addressee, and the meaning is: if an attacker attacks it, or a leaver leaves it.

Al-lahath (panting) is rapid breathing together with the extension of the tongue due to shortness of breath. Its verb may be pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the ha', but its present tense is with a fatha only. The verbal noun is al-lahath, with a fatha on the lam and the ha'. It is also said al-luhath with a damma on the lam, because it is a kind of ailment. It is not a sound.

[Page 179]

This is a clause explaining the clause ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], and the two verses that follow it. The word *mithal* (example) here means *hal* (state or condition): that similitude is an example for the polytheists who denied the Qur'an. It is an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), because the state of the dog described is similar to the state of those who denied, but is not identical to it.

The demonstrative *dhalika* (that) refers to ﴿the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], who is the subject of the story, and he is the example of the polytheists, because they resembled him in that they were given the Qur'an and then denied it. So their state was like the state of that denier. It is more evident, however, that the demonstrative refers to the example in His words ﴿like the example of the dog﴾, meaning: the state of the dog that is mentioned is like the state of the polytheists who denied, in that they used to wish to know the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), and to desire to be equal to the People of the Book in knowledge and merit. Thus they were in toil and bewilderment during the *Jahiliyya* (the period of ignorance). Then, when a messenger from among them came to them with a clear Book, they moved on to the toil of opposing him, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Or you might say, "If the Book had been revealed to us, we would have been better guided than they."﴾ [al-An'am: 157]. This is the interpretation of what is narrated from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, that the verse ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175] to its end was revealed concerning Quraysh.

He then branched off from that by His command, ﴿So relate the stories, that perhaps they may reflect﴾, meaning: relate this story and others. This is a *tadhyil* (concluding generalization) for the story exemplified by it, which encompasses it and other stories in the Qur'an. For in stories there is reflection and admonition, so it is hoped that they will reflect and be admonished. This is because examples and the recalling of parallels have a great effect in guiding souls by them and in bringing hidden states close to heedless or inattentive souls, since by comparing with a particular story there is a recollection of witnessing the state through the senses, unlike a bare reminder that is not compared with a tangible thing.

[p. 180]

This is a resumed sentence, since it is made into an expression of censure against them, meaning that they were in a repugnant state and that they wronged themselves.

The word *zulm* (wronging) here is in its literal sense, for they wronged themselves by bringing upon themselves disbelief (*kufr*), which made them blameworthy in this world and punished in the Hereafter.

The fronting of the object (*taqdim al-maf'ul*) serves exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), meaning: they wronged none but themselves. It is the nature of a sensible person not to harm himself. It also serves to remove their boasting that they did not follow Muhammad (ﷺ), supposing that this would anger him and the Muslims, when in fact they were only harming themselves.

The clause ﴿and they used to wrong themselves﴾ may be coordinated with the relative clause (*silah*), since they were known to the Prophet and the Muslims for the content of this clause. It may also be coordinated with the clause ﴿Evil is the example of the people﴾, in which case it serves as a concluding generalization (*tadhyil*) to the preceding clause, informing about them that in their denial and their failure to reflect upon the stories, they wronged none but themselves.

His saying ﴿they used to wrong themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 162] is stronger in conveying their description with wrongdoing than saying "and they wronged themselves", as has preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75] in Surat al-An'am.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 178:

﴿Whoever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whoever He leads astray, those are the losers.﴾

This sentence is a concluding summation (tadhyil) of the story and the parable, and of what was appended to them concerning the description of the state of the polytheists. This sentence gathers all of that and functions as a proverb (majra al-mathal), and that is the highest kind of tadhyil. It also contains an honouring of the rightly guided and an instruction to the Muslims to turn to Allah, exalted is He, seeking guidance from Him and protection from the slippery paths of misguidance. That is, those who did not become guided to the truth after it had come to them, their state indicates that Allah became angry with them and deprived them of success (tawfiq).

Guidance (hidaya) in its reality is the making clear of the path (ibanat al-tariq), and it is applied to general direction towards what is beneficial, whether or not the one directed follows what he has been directed to. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or be he ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3], and He says: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

Then it is known that the verb when attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is intended to refer to the most perfect and most enduring types of that reality, unless there is an indicator (qarina) to the contrary. So His saying ﴿Whom Allah guides﴾ means whom Allah decrees the guidance of, and the meaning is not "whom Allah guides by means of proofs or through the intermediary of the messengers."

This is derived from the story appended to it, for He said in it ﴿We gave him Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. The giving of signs is a form of guidance in its original sense. Then He said in it ﴿so he withdrew from them﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], and He said ﴿but he clung to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], and He said ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. So we know that Allah guided him (in the sense of giving signs) but did not decree guidance for him. The state he was in before he clung to the earth was not a state of guidance, but a state of wavering and testing, just as the state of the hypocrite is when present with the Muslims, when he is outwardly clothed in the excellences of Islam but does not inwardly adopt them, as we previously mentioned at His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqara: 17] in Surat al-Baqara. Thus it is determined that the meaning here is: whomever Allah decrees for him to be guided, he is the one guided.

The restriction (qasr) derived from the definiteness of the two parts of the sentence, ﴿he is the one guided﴾, is a real restriction (qasr haqiqi idda'i) with respect to perfection and the continuance of guidance until the death of its possessor, and this is the question of "muwafat" (ending in faith) according to the Ash'ariyya. That is, as for others, even if they appear guided, they are not truly "the guided," so that this applies to the state of the one who was given the signs, then withdrew from them, when the matter was that he should have been raised by them.

From this you know that His saying ﴿Whom Allah guides, he is the one guided﴾ is not of the type of Abu al-Najm's saying "My poetry is my poetry" nor of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger," because those contain nothing in the second part beyond what the first part conveyed, unlike what is in the verse, for in it is the restriction.

The same applies to ﴿Whom He leads astray, those are the losers﴾. The separation by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) was added on the side of the losers to increase attention to distinguishing them by the title of loss, as a warning against it. So the restriction in it is emphatic.

The predicate in the second part was put in the plural out of consideration of the meaning of the conditional "man," and the meaning of the second "man" was observed rather than the first for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fasila) and to make clear that the intended meaning of the first "man" is not singular.

It is known from the contrast of guidance with misguidance and the contrast of the guided with the loser that the guided one is a winner and gainer, so the mention of his gain is omitted for brevity (ijaz).

Loss (khusran) is used metaphorically for achieving the opposite of the intended aim of an action, just as gain (ribh) is used for obtaining good from an action, as was previously explained at His saying ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 9] in this surah, and at His saying ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqara: 16] in Surat al-Baqara.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 179:**

﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause ﴿And recite to them the report of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 175]. The connection is that the subject of the story to which it is conjoined moved from the state of guidance to the state of misguidance, because when Allah created him, He created him to be among the people of Hell. This also has a fitting relation to the concluding statement (tadhyil) with which the story ends, namely His saying ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 178], and what follows it.

The report is emphasized with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and with qad, in order to affirm it, because its strangeness places the listener, who has no prior knowledge of it, in the position of one who doubts its interpretation. Also, those about whom the report is given are described with ﴿they have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ up to His saying ﴿rather, they are further astray﴾. Those meant are the polytheists, who deny that they are in error and assume that they are doing good. They used to think that they were people of intellect and understanding, and for this reason, in mockery, they said to the Messenger (ﷺ) ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

Dhaʾ (to create) means to create, and it has been discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And they assigned to Allah a portion of what He had created of the crops and livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136], in the surah of al-Anʿam.

The lam in ﴿li-Jahannam﴾ is the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil): that is, We created many for the sake of Hell.

Jahannam (Hell) is used here metaphorically for the actions that necessitate it, by way of the relation of causation (ʿalaqat al-musabbabiyyah), because they were created for deeds of misguidance that lead to residing in Hell. They were not created for the sake of Hell itself, because creating a creature in order to populate Hell is not something intended. The lam is not the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), because its true meaning does not apply to it. In al-Kashshaf: "He made them for their complete immersion in disbelief, and that nothing comes from them except the deeds of the people of the Fire; they were created for the Fire, as an indication of their being firmly established in what qualifies them to enter the Fire." This requires that the figurative usage (istiʿarah, metaphor) be in dhaʾ-naha, and it is a forced interpretation, by which he observed the principles of the Muʿtazilah concerning the creation of the actions of servants and the attribution of that to Allah, exalted is He.

The placing of the prepositional phrase before the object in ﴿li-Jahannam kathiran﴾ (for Hell, many) is so that its connection to dhaʾ-naha becomes clear.

The meaning of creating many for the actions of evil that lead to the Fire is that Allah created many and placed in their souls powers whose nature is to corrupt what He had deposited in people of the uprightness of the natural disposition (fitrah), which is alluded to in His saying ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 172]. These powers are the powers of desire and anger. Their creation is stronger in dominating their souls than the innate power called wisdom (hikmah). So the desire and anger, which are called passion (hawa), overcome the power of the fitrah, which is wisdom and right guidance. Thus their souls prefer the calls of desire and anger, follow them, and turn away from the fitrah. The proofs of truth are established within their souls, but they turn away from them because passion has overcome them. Thus, according to the constitution of their souls, not possessing resolve to resist desires, they are treated as if they were created for Hell, and as if the calls to truth had not been created within them in the fitrah.

Al-jinn is a creation not visible to us. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that they are rational beings, and that they are inclined toward what they were created for, of benefit or harm, good or evil. Among them are the devils (shayatin). The detailed structure of this creation is beyond our capacity, as are the modes of their receiving Allah's intention from it, exalted is He.

His saying ﴿They have hearts﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a descriptive clause (sifah) specifying mankind, since they are the ones who have hearts, intellects, eyes and ears. Nothing similar is known of the jinn. He mentioned the jinn before mankind in the mention so that it becomes definite that the attributes that follow are attributes of mankind, and by the indication of His saying ﴿Those are like livestock﴾.

Al-qulub (hearts) is, in the Arabic language, the name for the seat of the intellects, and it has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

Al-fiqh (understanding) was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿so that they may understand﴾ [al-Anʿam: 65], in the surah of al-Anʿam.

The meaning of negating understanding, seeing and hearing from their instruments that exist within them is that they rendered their functions idle by not using them in the most important matter they are suited for: knowing what brings everlasting good and repels everlasting harm. Because the instruments of perception and knowledge were created by Allah for attaining benefits and repelling harms, when they did not use them to obtain the greatest benefits and repel the greatest harms, their functioning was negated for them in general terms, for emphasis. The verb within the scope of negation generalizes, like an indefinite noun. This generality is intended to be particular, for emphasis, since what they know apart from this is not taken into account. Thus the negation is a metaphor (istiʿarah), by comparing a part of what exists to the whole of what does not exist.

The placing of the eyes before the ears is not a violation of the Qur'anic usage, which places hearing before sight, in honour of hearing, since it receives what Allah commanded, as was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts and over their hearing, and over their sight is a veil﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. Because the order in this verse of al-Aʿraf follows the path of ascent (taraqqi), from the hearts, which are the seat of perceptions, to the instruments of perception: the eyes, then the ears. So the ears have the first rank in the ascent.

The sentence ﴿Those are like livestock﴾ is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafah) beginning a new discourse, to express the horror of their condition. It was made a new beginning so that it would be more compelling to the listeners. They are identified by the demonstrative to add to their distinction by those attributes, and to alert that because of them they deserve what will be mentioned of being equated with livestock, or being made more astray than livestock. The comparison with livestock is in their not benefiting from what rational beings benefit from. Thus their hearts, eyes and ears are as the hearts, eyes and ears of livestock, in that they do not measure things against their likes, and do not benefit from some rational proofs, so they do not recognize much of what leads them to a bad end.

The "bal" (rather) in ﴿rather, they are further astray﴾ is for transition and ascent in the comparison regarding misguidance and not benefiting from what can be benefited from. Since the aspect of similarity derived from "like livestock" returns to the meaning of misguidance, the ascent in the comparison took the form of the superlative (ism al-tafdil) in misguidance.

The aspect of their being more astray than livestock is that the misguidance of livestock does not reach the point of casting them into the abysses of everlasting wretchedness, because they have an inspiration by which they escape destruction, such as stepping back from cliffs and falling into pits. This is if the superlative in misguidance is taken as superiority in its genus, which is the more apparent. If it is taken as superiority in the manner of misguidance and its accompanying circumstances, then its aspect is that the perception of livestock was created limited, not exceeding what it was created for. Thus the deficiency in their benefit from their senses is not due to any fault on their part, so they are not subject to blame. As for the people of misguidance, they have blocked themselves from their perceptions, through their own fault and turning away from reflection and inference. Therefore they are more astray in path than livestock.

[Page 185]

The sentence ﴿Those are the heedless﴾ gives the reason for their being more astray than livestock, which is their reaching the limit of extreme heedlessness. Their reaching this limit is expressed by a form of restriction (qasr) of claim ( idiʿai), since it is claimed that the attribute of heedlessness is confined to them, such that there is no heedless person other than them, because the heedlessness of others is not taken into account. Every heedlessness beside their heedlessness is as no heedlessness, because the heedlessness of these people is directed toward the most fitting thing not to be heedless of, namely that which heedlessness leads the heedless to everlasting wretchedness. So it is a heedlessness with no remedy, and a stumble for which there is no recovery.

Heedlessness (ghaflah) is the absence of awareness of what should be aware of. The term heedlessness was applied to their misguidance on the basis of likening faith to a clear and evident matter, the absence of awareness of which is considered heedlessness. Thus in His saying ﴿they are the heedless﴾ there is an implicit covert metaphor (istiʿarah makniyyah ḍimniyyah), heedlessness being one of the attributes belonging to the comparison's referent (mushabbah bihi). In the description "the heedless" there is an explicit metaphor (istiʿarah musarrahah), that they are ignorant or deniers.

The gradation in describing them with these attributes has occurred: from the negation of their benefit from their faculties, then their likening to livestock, then the ascent to their being more astray than livestock, then the restriction of heedlessness to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 180 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾

This is an address to the Muslims. It was placed in the midst of the censure of the polytheists because of the fact that the most dreadful of the states of those destined for Hell is the state of their associating others with Allah. This is because in that there is a nullification of the most distinctive of the attributes that pertain to divinity: the attribute of oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) and what is similar in meaning to it among the attributes, such as al-Fard (the Singular) and al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge). Falling under polytheism is also the negation of many attributes, such as al-Ba'ith (the Resurrector), al-Hasib (the Reckoner), and al-Mu'id (the Restorer). And from the obstinacy of the people of polytheism arose the denial of the attribute al-Rahman (the Most Gracious).

So the verses that described the misguidance of their polytheism were followed by an admonition to the Muslims to turn toward calling upon Allah by His names, which indicate the greatness of the attributes of divinity, and to persevere in that, and to turn away from the clamour and disputation of the polytheists concerning the names of Allah, exalted is He.

Among the things by which the polytheists used to vex the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims was that they denied His name al-Rahman, exalted is He. This was a denial that their ignorance did not drive them to, that Allah is described by what the form al-Rahman indicates of intense mercy; rather, what drove them to it was what drives every obstinate person: the seeking of severity and the labelling of the opponent as wrong, even concerning what he knows to be true. Ibn 'Atiyyah and others mention that it was "related concerning the occasion of revelation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾, that Abu Jahl heard some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ reciting, and in their recitation they mentioned Allah, and at another time they recited and mentioned al-Rahman. Abu Jahl said: 'Muhammad claims that the God is one, and yet he worships many gods.'" So this verse was revealed.

Thus the connection of this verse to the one before it is the connection of reports about the states and misguidance of the polytheists, and its purpose is His saying, ﴿and leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase over the predicate before the subject (lillah) is for the mere purpose of emphasis, which conveys the affirmation of His deserving them, derived from the lam (of possession). The meaning is that His being characterised by them is a established matter. This serves as a preparation for His saying, ﴿so call upon Him by them and leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾. A similar fronting has been adopted in all the verses that serve this purpose, such as His saying in Surat al-Isra': ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra: 110], Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [Ta-Ha: 8], and in Surat al-Hashr: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Hashr: 24]. All of this is an emphasis for the refutation of the polytheists who would have some of the names found in the Qur'an or in the words of the Prophet ﷺ be names of Allah, exalted is He, by imagining that multiplicity of the name is multiplicity of the named, as a deception upon the masses.

The "asma'" (names) are the words designated as proper names for the essence, either by specification or by predominance. So the name of majesty, which is (Allah), is a proper name for the essence of the true God by specification, as is the nature of proper names. Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are two names of Allah by predominance. Likewise every single word that indicates an attribute of Allah, and is used in the manner of a proper name, such as al-Rabb (the Lord), al-Khaliq (the Creator), al-'Aziz (the Mighty), al-Hakim (the Wise), al-Ghafur (the Forgiving). Not included in this is what is compound by annexation, such as Dhu al-Jalal (Possessor of Majesty) and Rabb al-'Arsh (Lord of the Throne), for that is more akin to descriptions, even if it indicates a meaning that befits none but Allah, such as "Malik Yawm al-Din" (Master of the Day of Judgement) [al-Fatihah: 4].

Al-Husna is the feminine of al-Ahsan, which is the one characterised by complete beauty in its essence, acceptable to sound minds free from desire. The intended meaning of beauty is not suitability to all people, because suitability is a relative, relational attribute: something may suit Zayd but not 'Amr. Therefore beauty is an essential attribute of the beautiful thing.

The describing of the names as "the most beautiful" is because they indicate the establishment of attributes of true perfection. As for some of them, it is because their complete meanings are not established except for Allah, such as al-Hayy (the Living), al-'Aziz, al-Hakim, and al-Ghani (the Self-Sufficient). As for the other part, it is because their meanings, absolutely, are not fitting to be attributed except in the case of Allah, such as al-Mutakabbir (the Supremely Great) and al-Jabbar (the Compeller), because the meanings of these attributes and their like were a deficiency in the created being, inasmuch as the one characterised by them was not deserving of them due to his weakness or his need. Unlike God, who is absolutely Self-Sufficient. So the created being's characterisation by them is a source of corruption on earth, while the Creator's characterisation by them is a source of goodness, because they are the source of justice and equitable recompense.

The branching (al-tafri') in His saying, ﴿so call upon Him by them﴾, is a branching from their being His names and from their being "most beautiful". That is, there is no harm in calling upon Him by them, because they are multiple names for one named, not as the polytheists claim, and because they are most beautiful, there is no harm in calling upon Allah, exalted is He, by them. This points to the fact that Allah may be called upon by everything that indicates His attributes and His acts.

The verse indicates that everything that indicates an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, or one of His affairs, in a manner that brings it closer to understanding according to what is customary, may properly be used as a name for Allah, exalted is He, so long as its occurrence is not in the manner of metaphor, such as ﴿Allah mocks at them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15], or it does not imply a meaning of deficiency in common usage, such as al-Makir (the Deceiver) from His saying, ﴿And Allah is the best of deceivers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54].

The most beautiful names of Allah are not restricted to the ninety-nine mentioned in the authentic hadith related from al-A'raj, from Abu Rafi', and from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, whoever enumerates them enters Paradise." Because the authentic hadith contains nothing that requires restricting the names to that number, but those particular names with that number have that distinction. It is established that the Prophet ﷺ supplicated saying: "O Hannan, O Mannan," and these two names do not occur among those reported of the ninety-nine. And in the hadith related with well-known sound chains there is no specification of the ninety-nine names. It occurs in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamzah, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, after his saying "entered Paradise": "He is Allah, besides whom there is no god, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," until its end, thus specifying ninety-nine attributes of Allah, exalted is He, which are the well-known ones among those who undertook to explain them. al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith, related to us by more than one through Safwan ibn Salih, and he is trustworthy according to the people of hadith, and we do not know of any chain of authentic transmission among the narrations for it that mentions the names except in this hadith."

Specifying these names does not require more than that their distinction is that whoever enumerates and memorises them enters Paradise, so it does not prevent that other names of Allah be counted. Ibn Burjan al-Ishbili in his book on the most beautiful names of Allah counted one hundred and thirty-two names extracted from the Qur'an and accepted hadiths. al-Qurtubi mentions that he (Ibn Burjan) had a book he named "al-Asna fi Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna," in which he mentioned names exceeding two hundred. He also mentions that Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi mentioned a number of His names, exalted is He, such as: (﴿Mutimmu nurihi﴾ [al-Saff: 8]), and (﴿Khayr al-Warithin﴾ [al-Anbiya': 89]), and (﴿Khayr al-Makirin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]), and Rabi' thalathah (the fourth of three), and Sadis khamsah (the sixth of five), and al-Tayyib, and al-Mu'allim, etc.

The crudeness of counting things like "fourth of three" and "sixth of five" is not hidden, for they occur in the Qur'an in a context of clear metaphor. There is no escape from the judgement of sound taste, and it is not merely a matter of stopping at an apparent form of the wording. Ibn Kathir mentions in his tafsir, from the book 'Aridat al-Ahwadhi in the explanation of al-Tirmidhi (perhaps he means 'Aridat al-Ahwadhi), that "some people collected from the Book and the Sunnah a thousand names of Allah, exalted is He." I did not find this in the copies of 'Aridat al-Ahwadhi of Ibn al-'Arabi, nor did al-Qurtubi mention it, and he was among the most specialised students of Ibn al-'Arabi. What is found in Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam al-Qur'an is that there came to him from them one hundred and forty-six names, and he cited them in the Ahkam book, and one of them fell out in the printed edition. He mentions that he set them out most fully in his book al-Amad (i.e. "al-Amad al-Aqsa") in the explanation of the names, reaching one hundred and seventy-six names. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "There has been disagreement concerning a name that entails pure praise, not connected with any doubt or sharing, but which has not been reported explicitly, whether it may be applied and used to name Allah with it. al-Baqillani explicitly permitted that, and Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari explicitly forbade it, and the jurists and the majority forbade it. The correct position is that Allah, exalted is He, should not be named except by a name the Shari'ah has applied, and that it be pure praise with no doubt and no sharing; a matter that only the few among the people of knowledge do well. Once that is permitted, whoever imagines himself to be good will climb over it and introduce into the names of Allah what is impermissible by consensus."

There has been disagreement concerning the verbs in the Qur'an, such as ﴿Allah mocks at them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] and ﴿And Allah schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], and similar, whether the active participle may be derived from them. One group said: it is not applied in any way. Another group permitted that it be said, restricted by its cause, such as: Allah is the deceiver of those who deceive in religion. As for applying it without restriction, it is forbidden by consensus.

The meaning of leaving those who deviate concerning His names is refraining from continuing in debate with them, since it is evident that they are not seeking to know the truth, or leaving off listening to their speech, lest they tempt the common believers with their doubts. That is: leave them, and do not exhaust yourselves in disputing with them, for I shall recompense them. The meaning of "dhar" has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

Ilhad is inclining away from the middle of a thing toward its side, and all its derivatives return to this meaning. Since the middle of a thing is likened to truth and rightness, the deviation from truth to falsehood was likened to ilhad, so ilhad was applied to disbelief and corruption. It is then construed with fi, treating the noun governed by it as a place for the ilhad. Most often this happens deliberately, for the purpose of corruption. It is said: lahada and alhada, and the more common is alhada.

Those other than Hamzah read yulhidun, with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha', from alhada (the hamzated form). Hamzah alone read it with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', from the unaugmented lahada.

The annexation of the names to Allah indicates that the intended names are those for which the Shari'ah has provided what requires that He be named by them.

The meaning of ilhad concerning the names of Allah is making them a manifestation of the manifestations of disbelief, by denying that He is named by names that indicate established attributes of His, when He is most deserving of the full perfection of their meanings. They denied al-Rahman, as has been mentioned, and made His being named by it in the Qur'an a means of ridicule and of insulting the Prophet, peace be upon him, by claiming that he multiplied gods. There is no greater slander and injustice in disputation than this, so it is fitting to call it ilhad, because it is a deviation from truth with the intent of obstinacy and envy.

This suits that the particle fi in His saying "fi asma'ihi" be used in the sense of causation, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat," the hadith, and the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

"And I disobeyed my relatives for your sake, so the cords of my ties with them were cut off."

The exegetes have permitted other possibilities for the meaning of ilhad concerning His names. Among them are three that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned, and I do not see them as fitting the annexation of the names to His pronoun, as is not hidden from one who considers them.

The clause ﴿they will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ takes the place of a causal explanation for the command to leave the deviators, which is why it is separated. That is: do not concern yourselves with their ilhad and do not grieve over it, for Allah will recompense them for their evil conduct. Their ilhad was called an action because it is one of the actions of their hearts and tongues.

The relative "ma" is general, meaning they will be recompensed for everything they do of disbelief, and among that is their ilhad concerning His names.

The sin (السين) is for the future, and it conveys emphasis.
It has also been said that the phrase ﴿what they used to do﴾ (ما كانوا يعملون), rather than "what they did" (ما عملوا) or "what they do" (ما يعملون), serves to indicate that this conduct is a established practice for them and something that continually recurs from them.

The verses are a continuation of ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], and the purpose is to praise the Muslims for their guidance and their being rightly guided, in contrast to the state of the polytheists in their misguidance. That is, turn away from the polytheists, for God has made you independent of them through the Muslims. Thus the referent of "a community" (ummah) is the Muslims, by the indication of the context, as in the verse of Labid:

*"Abandoner of dwellings when I am not pleased with them, or when its death seizes some of the souls."*

He means himself, since he is one of the souls. Al-Tabari narrated from Qatadah, who said: "We have been informed that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say when he recited the verse, 'This is for you, and the people before you have been given its like.'"

And His saying ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and act justly by it﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. The rest of the words of the verse have had their interpretation known from the earlier discussions of this surah.

Those who denied Our signs are the polytheists who denied the Qur'an. The reason for the verb of denial (takdhib) being followed by the preposition bi- has already been explained, to indicate the meaning of rejection, at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it﴾ [al-An'am: 57], in Surah al-An'am.

Istidraj (gradual progression towards ruin, lit. "drawing up by degrees") is derived from daraja (with two fathahs), which is a level of a building raised above the ground by the height a foot is raised to climb from it to what is above it, to ease ascent in the like of a height, a minaret or a tower. It is also one of the rungs arranged in a ladder by which one climbs to the one above it, and this rung is called mirqah. The sin and ta' in the verb istidraj indicate seeking, that is, seeking that he gradually proceed, upward or downward. The expression is a figurative representation (tamthil) of the state of one who intends to change the condition of someone into another without his awareness, by the state of one who asks another to descend from one level to another until he reaches a place he cannot reach without that. It is a wonderful figure that contains many comparisons, for it is founded on comparing a good condition to a high place and its opposite to a low place, and the context determines the intended meaning, whether a transition to a better or a worse state.

What indicates attention to this figure in the verse is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from where they do not know﴾. Since istidraj includes the sense of bringing one to the intended goal, a prepositional phrase with min al-ibtida'iyyah (the "from" of starting point) is attached to its verb: that is, starting their istidraj from a place they do not know leads them to the harmful outcome. So ḥaythu here is for place in its original sense: from a place whose outcome they do not know. The object of "they know" is omitted because istidraj indicates it, and the implied sense is "they do not know its gradual progression." This signals that it is a great istidraj, which the one it is done to would not suspect or perceive.

Imla' is on the pattern of if'al, meaning respite (imhal). The hamzah of this verbal noun replaces an original waw. It is derived from milawah, with the mim having three vowels, which means the duration of life. It is said amlahu and mallahu when one grants him respite and delays him, both with an alif and without hamzah, so it is close in meaning to 'ammarahu (granted him a long life). For this reason in supplication for life one says mallaka Allah (may God grant you long life).

The lam in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ is the lam called lam al-tabyin (the lam of specification), which has many uses, obscure in many cases. Its basis is that it is intended to specify the connection of what it governs with its operator, because there is obscurity in that connection. The derivation of amla from al-milw is not firmly established, since the derived root has no sense of an action, so no simple verb came from it, and the lam was needed to specify the connection of the object to its verb.

As for their saying amla li-l-ba'ir (he let the camel graze long) in the sense of lengthening its grazing in pasture, it came from this meaning in a manner of metaphor or figurative extension (isti'arah).

So the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ stands in the position of the cause for the two clauses before it, for istidraj and imla' are a kind of plotting (kayd), and the plot of God is firm, that is, strong, with no escape from it for the one plotted against.

The position of inna here is that of consequence and causation (tafri' wa-ta'lil), as 'Abd al-Qahir said: in this position it does the work of the fa' (then/therefore). This was explained earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96], in Surah Al 'Imran. That is: that istidraj and imla' will achieve what We intend for them, because My plot is strong.

Since "I grant them respite" (umli) is coordinated with "We will gradually lead them" (sanastadriju-hum), it shares with it the inclusion under the rule of the future, that is: and I will grant them respite.

The difference between the two verbs nastadriju and umli, in that the second has the hamzah of the first person singular while the first has the nun of majesty (plural of majesty), is a difference that eloquence requires, both because of the heaviness of the hamzah between two letters alike in pronunciation in sanastadriju-hum, and for variety, and for sufficiency in the achievement of the meaning of majesty from the first.

The meaning of kayd has not been precisely fixed in the dictionaries of the language. Its apparent sense is that it is synonymous with makr (cunning) and ḥilah (stratagem). Al-Raghib said: it is a kind of scheming, and it may be blameworthy or praiseworthy, although it is used more for the blameworthy. This implies that kayd is more specific than scheming (ihtiyal), and this is only because its use became predominant for scheming to obtain something which, if the one targeted knew of it, he would guard against; so it is scheming in which there is harm to the object. Thus al-Raghib's meaning of "blameworthy" is blameworthy in the view of the one targeted, not in the reality of the matter. Ibn Kamal Pasha said: kayd is seizing (someone) by concealment, and it does not require that the schemer show the opposite of what he conceals.

From these refinements it results that kayd is more specific than scheming and than istidraj.

The fact that the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ stands in the position of cause requires that their istidraj and their being granted respite be a plot, and so it indicates that it is a gradual drawing toward what they dislike, and a postponement for them until what they dislike befalls them, because on this reading the content of the second clause includes the content of the preceding clause together with the added description "firm." Whereas if kayd were taken in the sense of seizing by concealment, without considering the showing of the opposite of what is concealed, the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ would only indicate the reason for istidraj and imla' being from the action of one who seizes by concealment, without disguising his seizing with what deceives the one seized. So it is as if He said: ﴿We will gradually lead them from where they do not know﴾, plotting against them; indeed My plot is firm.

Its application here follows the manner of figurative representation (tamthiliyyah), by likening the condition in which God gradually leads the deniers, with the postponement of punishment from them until a term they will reach, to the state of one who prepares to seize his enemy while displaying kindness and good treatment so as to increase his enemy's delusion; and so that the arrival of the harm of the seizing will be more severe and further from the readiness to receive it.

Al-matin means strong. Its literal sense is "strong of the spine" (matn), that is the back, because the strength of its spine enables it to perform difficult tasks. The matn of anything is its central support and that by which it holds together.
