The fact that the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ stands in the position of cause requires that their istidraj and their being granted respite be a plot, and so it indicates that it is a gradual drawing toward what they dislike, and a postponement for them until what they dislike befalls them, because on this reading the content of the second clause includes the content of the preceding clause together with the added description "firm." Whereas if kayd were taken in the sense of seizing by concealment, without considering the showing of the opposite of what is concealed, the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ would only indicate the reason for istidraj and imla' being from the action of one who seizes by concealment, without disguising his seizing with what deceives the one seized. So it is as if He said: ﴿We will gradually lead them from where they do not know﴾, plotting against them; indeed My plot is firm.

Its application here follows the manner of figurative representation (tamthiliyyah), by likening the condition in which God gradually leads the deniers, with the postponement of punishment from them until a term they will reach, to the state of one who prepares to seize his enemy while displaying kindness and good treatment so as to increase his enemy's delusion; and so that the arrival of the harm of the seizing will be more severe and further from the readiness to receive it.

Al-matin means strong. Its literal sense is "strong of the spine" (matn), that is the back, because the strength of its spine enables it to perform difficult tasks. The matn of anything is its central support and that by which it holds together.

The verses are a continuation of ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], and the purpose is to praise the Muslims for their guidance and their being rightly guided, in contrast to the state of the polytheists in their misguidance. That is, turn away from the polytheists, for God has made you independent of them through the Muslims. Thus the referent of "a community" (ummah) is the Muslims, by the indication of the context, as in the verse of Labid:

*"Abandoner of dwellings when I am not pleased with them, or when its death seizes some of the souls."*

He means himself, since he is one of the souls. Al-Tabari narrated from Qatadah, who said: "We have been informed that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say when he recited the verse, 'This is for you, and the people before you have been given its like.'"

And His saying ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and act justly by it﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. The rest of the words of the verse have had their interpretation known from the earlier discussions of this surah.

Those who denied Our signs are the polytheists who denied the Qur'an. The reason for the verb of denial (takdhib) being followed by the preposition bi- has already been explained, to indicate the meaning of rejection, at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and you have denied it﴾ [al-An'am: 57], in Surah al-An'am.

Istidraj (gradual progression towards ruin, lit. "drawing up by degrees") is derived from daraja (with two fathahs), which is a level of a building raised above the ground by the height a foot is raised to climb from it to what is above it, to ease ascent in the like of a height, a minaret or a tower. It is also one of the rungs arranged in a ladder by which one climbs to the one above it, and this rung is called mirqah. The sin and ta' in the verb istidraj indicate seeking, that is, seeking that he gradually proceed, upward or downward. The expression is a figurative representation (tamthil) of the state of one who intends to change the condition of someone into another without his awareness, by the state of one who asks another to descend from one level to another until he reaches a place he cannot reach without that. It is a wonderful figure that contains many comparisons, for it is founded on comparing a good condition to a high place and its opposite to a low place, and the context determines the intended meaning, whether a transition to a better or a worse state.

What indicates attention to this figure in the verse is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from where they do not know﴾. Since istidraj includes the sense of bringing one to the intended goal, a prepositional phrase with min al-ibtida'iyyah (the "from" of starting point) is attached to its verb: that is, starting their istidraj from a place they do not know leads them to the harmful outcome. So ḥaythu here is for place in its original sense: from a place whose outcome they do not know. The object of "they know" is omitted because istidraj indicates it, and the implied sense is "they do not know its gradual progression." This signals that it is a great istidraj, which the one it is done to would not suspect or perceive.

Imla' is on the pattern of if'al, meaning respite (imhal). The hamzah of this verbal noun replaces an original waw. It is derived from milawah, with the mim having three vowels, which means the duration of life. It is said amlahu and mallahu when one grants him respite and delays him, both with an alif and without hamzah, so it is close in meaning to 'ammarahu (granted him a long life). For this reason in supplication for life one says mallaka Allah (may God grant you long life).

The lam in His saying ﴿lahum﴾ is the lam called lam al-tabyin (the lam of specification), which has many uses, obscure in many cases. Its basis is that it is intended to specify the connection of what it governs with its operator, because there is obscurity in that connection. The derivation of amla from al-milw is not firmly established, since the derived root has no sense of an action, so no simple verb came from it, and the lam was needed to specify the connection of the object to its verb.

As for their saying amla li-l-ba'ir (he let the camel graze long) in the sense of lengthening its grazing in pasture, it came from this meaning in a manner of metaphor or figurative extension (isti'arah).

So the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ stands in the position of the cause for the two clauses before it, for istidraj and imla' are a kind of plotting (kayd), and the plot of God is firm, that is, strong, with no escape from it for the one plotted against.

The position of inna here is that of consequence and causation (tafri' wa-ta'lil), as 'Abd al-Qahir said: in this position it does the work of the fa' (then/therefore). This was explained earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96], in Surah Al 'Imran. That is: that istidraj and imla' will achieve what We intend for them, because My plot is strong.

Since "I grant them respite" (umli) is coordinated with "We will gradually lead them" (sanastadriju-hum), it shares with it the inclusion under the rule of the future, that is: and I will grant them respite.

The difference between the two verbs nastadriju and umli, in that the second has the hamzah of the first person singular while the first has the nun of majesty (plural of majesty), is a difference that eloquence requires, both because of the heaviness of the hamzah between two letters alike in pronunciation in sanastadriju-hum, and for variety, and for sufficiency in the achievement of the meaning of majesty from the first.

The meaning of kayd has not been precisely fixed in the dictionaries of the language. Its apparent sense is that it is synonymous with makr (cunning) and ḥilah (stratagem). Al-Raghib said: it is a kind of scheming, and it may be blameworthy or praiseworthy, although it is used more for the blameworthy. This implies that kayd is more specific than scheming (ihtiyal), and this is only because its use became predominant for scheming to obtain something which, if the one targeted knew of it, he would guard against; so it is scheming in which there is harm to the object. Thus al-Raghib's meaning of "blameworthy" is blameworthy in the view of the one targeted, not in the reality of the matter. Ibn Kamal Pasha said: kayd is seizing (someone) by concealment, and it does not require that the schemer show the opposite of what he conceals.

From these refinements it results that kayd is more specific than scheming and than istidraj.

The fact that the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ stands in the position of cause requires that their istidraj and their being granted respite be a plot, and so it indicates that it is a gradual drawing toward what they dislike, and a postponement for them until what they dislike befalls them, because on this reading the content of the second clause includes the content of the preceding clause together with the added description "firm." Whereas if kayd were taken in the sense of seizing by concealment, without considering the showing of the opposite of what is concealed, the clause ﴿Indeed My plot is firm﴾ would only indicate the reason for istidraj and imla' being from the action of one who seizes by concealment, without disguising his seizing with what deceives the one seized. So it is as if He said: ﴿We will gradually lead them from where they do not know﴾, plotting against them; indeed My plot is firm.

Its application here follows the manner of figurative representation (tamthiliyyah), by likening the condition in which God gradually leads the deniers, with the postponement of punishment from them until a term they will reach, to the state of one who prepares to seize his enemy while displaying kindness and good treatment so as to increase his enemy's delusion; and so that the arrival of the harm of the seizing will be more severe and further from the readiness to receive it.

Al-matin means strong. Its literal sense is "strong of the spine" (matn), that is the back, because the strength of its spine enables it to perform difficult tasks. The matn of anything is its central support and that by which it holds together.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 184:

﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion; he is only a plain warner.﴾

When their denial of the signs stemmed from their denial of the one who brought them, and arose from the assumption that the signs of God are not brought by a human being, and that whoever claims to be a messenger from God is a madman, [the Qur'an] followed the report about the deniers and their threat with a call to them to consider the condition of the Messenger, and [to consider] that he is not a madman as they claim.

The Arabs' use of the interrogative hamza together with conjunctions that share the same ruling is a remarkable usage, whose explanation has already been given at His - exalted is He - saying ﴿Whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, did you not become arrogant?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence is independent (mustaʾnafah), being the beginning of a speech on their argumentation and an alert to them after the report that they are being led on gradually and given respite.

The interrogation serves to express wonder at their condition and to rebuke them. The "ma" in His saying ﴿ma bi-sahibihim min jinnah﴾ is negating, as indicated by the entry of "min" on the negated object of "ma", for the emphasis of comprehensiveness.

The verb "yatafakkaru" is treated as intransitive, so no object is to be supposed for it, being sufficient by what the negation in His saying ﴿ma bi-sahibihim min jinnah﴾ indicates, i.e., "Did they not become among those who reflect, people of consideration?" The verb suspended from operating does not have an object or complement supposed for it.

The purpose of suspending the verb is the transition from the knowledge of one who conjectures to the affirmation of the conjectured report and making it an independent proposition, so the speech becomes like two reports: one from the side of the one who conjectures or the like, and another from the side of the speaker, which has entered the category of established facts. Thus His saying - exalted is He - ﴿Indeed you know that these do not speak﴾ [al-Anbiya': 65] is in effect like saying: "You know: they do not speak; these, they speak," i.e., that is your knowledge and this is my knowledge. His saying here ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ is in effect: "Have they not reflected: their companion is not mad; there is no madness [jannah] in their companion." So the suspension of verbs of the heart is a kind of concision, and I think this is the purpose of the suspension construction, which the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani) did not point out, and the peculiarities of Arabic are not limited.

The word "sahib" (companion) in its literal sense is one who accompanies another in a state of travel or the like, from which His saying - exalted is He - ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. The wife is called "sahibah." It is used figuratively for one who has a great event or report with another, treating the constancy of mention as the constancy of the essence. From this is the saying of Abu Ma'bad al-Khuza'i to his wife, Umm Ma'bad, when she told him of the entry of the Prophet (ﷺ) into her tent on the road of the Hijrah and described to him his guidance and blessing: "This is the companion of Quraysh." And the saying of al-Hajjaj in some of his sermons to the people of Iraq: "Were you not my companions at al-Ahwaz when you intended treachery and concealed disbelief?" He means that they were the ones who fought him at al-Ahwaz; so the meaning of their being his companions is that he was much occupied with them. And the saying of al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas al-Lahbi:

Each has an intention to hate his companion; by God's blessing we shall let you go and you will let us go.

So the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) as the companion of those who denied the signs means: the one with whom they were occupied, and whose affair they persisted in discussing. This recurs in the Qur'an, such as His saying - exalted is He - ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22].

"Jinnah" with a kasra on the jim is a noun for madness, which is the derangement that afflicts a person from the effect of the jinn touching him, according to the custom of people. For this reason "jinnah" is linked, through the implied verb of being, to the preposition "bi", which indicates association.

He rebuked them and marvelled at their turning away from reflecting on the affair of the Messenger (peace be upon him), that he is not mad, in reply to their description of him as mad, when they said ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] and ﴿They say: a taught, mad one﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14]. This is like His saying - exalted is He - ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22].

The sentence ﴿He is only a plain warner﴾ is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), answering a questioner among them who says: "What then is his condition?" Or it is an affirmation of the ruling of the sentence ﴿There is no madness in their companion﴾, and so it is separated (fussilat) because of the complete connection between them, which dispenses with a conjunction.

The "nadhir" is one who warns against a harm; its origin is one who informs a people of the coming of their enemy. From it is the proverb "I am the naked warner" (ana al-nadhir al-ʿuryan). One says "anzara inadhatan" with a kasra on the nun, like "bishara," so he is "mundhir" and "nadhir."

This is among the cases in which the form fa'il occurs in place of af'il, like "hakim" in the sense of "muhkim," and the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Yakrib:

"Has Rayhanah, the caller, the hearing one [gone]?" — i.e., the one who makes hear.

"Mubin" is an active participle from "abana," meaning to make clear. The occurrence of this description after the report of "nadhir" indicates that it is a description of the report. So the meaning is that he is the clear warner, clear in his warning, such that no doubt is left concerning his truthfulness nor concerning the depiction of the condition against which he warns. Thus the purpose of following "nadhir" with the description "mubin" is an allusion to those who did not heed his warning and did not take precaution against the evil he warned them of, and this cuts off their excuse.

It is permissible to make "mubin" a second predicate of the pronoun of "sahibihim," the meaning being that he is a warner and that he is clear in what he conveys of warning and other things.

The restriction derived from the negation and exception is a restriction qualified by an attribute, and it requires that the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) be confined to warning and clarification. That is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), namely a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb): i.e., he is a clear warner, not mad as they claim. In this there is a charge of stupidity or foolishness against them, since his condition cannot be confused with the condition of the madman, given the clear difference between the condition of plain warning and the condition of a madman's raving. Their claim of his madness is either stupidity on their part, to the point that distinct realities became confused for them, or obstinacy, denial and slander against the Messenger.

Ascent in the denunciation and wonder at their condition, from their turning away from considering the state of their Messenger to a denunciation of and wonder at their turning away from considering what is clearer and more general than that: the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, and whatever things Allah has created, which are among the signs of Allah's oneness (tawhid), to which the Messenger ﷺ called them to believe. The connection between the two statements is that the Messenger's call to monotheism and the abolition of polytheism was among the greatest reasons for their denial of him: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!﴾ (38:5).

The verb "to consider" (al-nazar) is followed by its object with the particle of place (ḥarf al-ẓarfiyyah, the particle of location), because what is meant is reflection with contemplation (tadabbur), which is thinking (tafakkur), as in His saying: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ (51:21). You say "I considered my affair," and the particle of location indicates that this reflection is deep and penetrating into the kinds of existing things. This locative usage is figurative.

Malakut means great sovereignty. It has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (6:75), in Surat al-An'am.

Its annexation to "the heavens and the earth" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: the sovereignty which is the heavens and the earth, i.e. Allah's sovereignty over them both. The intended meaning is the heavens in their totality and the earth in its totality, which indicate the magnitude of Allah's dominion, may He be exalted.

The phrase ﴿and whatever things Allah has created﴾ is coordinated with "dominion," so the consideration is divided into consideration of the greatness of Allah's dominion, and consideration of His creatures and the subtleties of their conditions, which indicate the greatness of Allah's power, may He be exalted. Contemplation of the greatness of the heavens and the earth is a proof of the magnitude of Allah's dominion, so He alone is worthy of divinity to the exclusion of any other. Contemplation of created things is a proof of the magnitude of His power, and that He alone is the sole Maker, so He alone is worthy of divinity. Thus, if they had considered these things with the consideration of reflection (i'tibar), they would have known that the Maker of all of that is none other than one God, and their denial of the call of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to abolish polytheism would have ceased.

His saying ﴿and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and whatever things Allah has created﴾.

This "anna" (that) is the one with an open hamza and a doubled nun, which has been lightened. Therefore its subject is an implied pronoun of matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the affair or situation), and the clause "perhaps it will be that..." (ʿasā an yakūna ilakh) is the predicate of the pronoun of matter.

The "an" that follows ʿasā is the verbal-infinitive "an" (maṣdariyyah), which in usage is frequently added after ʿasā.

The subject of "yakūna" is also an implied pronoun of matter, because what follows "yakūna" cannot be considered a subject of kāna. The meaning is: have they not considered, in anticipation of the nearness of their term?

The discourse in this structure is formulated to convey the awfulness of the matter upon them and to frighten them, by making the object of the consideration have the sense of news, to indicate that it is a matter that should occur to souls and that people should speak of, and that it has become a talk and a report, so it is as if it were an established, settled matter.

This is the place of the pronoun of matter wherever it occurs; for this reason it is called the pronoun of the story (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah), in consideration of the fact that the clause of its predicate has become a settled thing, and something that people relate and speak of.

The meaning of consideration in anticipation of the nearness of the term is fear of that.

The term (ajal) annexed to the pronoun of the deniers is the term of the community, not the term of individuals, because the discourse is a threat with an unfamiliar term. He alerted them to reflect on the anticipation of the onset of annihilation and destruction upon them, as the deniers before them were destroyed. For if they reflected that their companion is not mad, they would come to know that he is among the sensible; a sensible person would not bring about a great calamity such as this upon his people and bring upon himself such hardship as this hardship for no great matter that he has brought, nor would he abandon lying to people and lie against Allah. And if they considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever things Allah has created, they would know that Allah is the greatest King and the Creator of creatures, and they would be certain that He is the one God. This would lead to the confirmation of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and the abolition of their belief in a plurality of gods, or at least would lead to doubt about that. Therefore it is inevitable that it would lead them to consider the anticipated outcome for them, like what befell the deniers before them.

It is also permissible that the term means the coming of the Hour and the extinction of this world. Then it is their term and the term of other people, and it would be a warning of the Day of Recompense.

Among the wondrous arrangements of these verses: when contemplation and reflection were intended regarding the establishment of realities and relations in the reality of the matter, the verbs of the heart were accompanied by the form of a proposition and a report, in His saying ﴿Have they not reflected that there is no madness in their companion?﴾ (7:184), and His saying ﴿and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾. When contemplation and reflection were intended regarding the attributes of essences, the verb of the heart was made to govern the names of essences in His saying ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever things Allah has created?﴾

Then, on the basis of the threat and warning, he followed with their rebuke and denunciation through the form of the astonished interrogation which implies disapproval, in His saying ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾. It is thus an expression of wonder mixed with disapproval of belief in what Allah has conveyed to them through the tongue of His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and what He has set before them of signs in the kinds of created things. For all of that has reached the furthest limit of clarity in speech and indication, such that there is no hope that anything else could be more indicative than it.

Here "ayy" is a noun that has taken on the meaning of interrogation. Its origin is an indefinite noun explained by what it is annexed to. It is the name of a specific portion distinguished from what shares it in a type of genus or attribute. When "ayy" takes on the meaning of interrogation, it is for asking about the identification of a counterpart sharing the description indicated by what it is annexed to, i.e. a request for its identification. So the one asked about by it is equal to a similar known counterpart. Thus His saying ﴿So in what statement﴾ is a question about the unknown statement similar to the known statement between the questioner and the one questioned. The discussion of "ayy" will come at His saying ﴿So you will see and they will see which of you is the afflicted﴾ (68:5–6) in Surat al-Qalam.

The interrogation here is used for denunciation, i.e. they will not believe in any statement after this statement.

The true meaning of ḥadīth is report and an event narrated: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ (51:24). It is also used figuratively for a matter whose nature is that it becomes a topic of talk, and this is broader than the literal meaning.

Here, if "ḥadīth" is taken in its literal sense, it may mean the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it﴾ (52:34). In that case the pronoun in His saying "after it" refers to "after the Qur'an," i.e. after its revelation. It may also mean the claim of Muhammad ﷺ to be a Messenger from Allah. Both possibilities suit His saying ﴿Have they not reflected that there is no madness in their companion?﴾ (7:184).

[Page 199]
The "bi" in His saying ﴿So in what statement﴾ on this interpretation is the transitive bā' (bā' al-ta'diyah), transitivizing the verb "they believe." If it is taken figuratively, it includes the Qur'an and other proofs of created things, in consideration of the fact that people speak of them, as in His saying ﴿So in what statement after Allah and His signs will they believe?﴾ (45:6). The pronoun in His saying "after it" then refers to the meaning of what was mentioned, i.e. what was mentioned of ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever things Allah has created, and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾. The pronoun is singular by way of interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give the women their dowries graciously; but if they give you willingly a part of it﴾ (4:4) in Surat al-Nisa'. The meaning is: then by what thing will they be guided, other than what was mentioned, after they have not benefited from the indication of what was mentioned and did not believe in it? So there is no hope of belief from them after that.

On this aspect, the "bi" is causal (sababiyyah), attached to "they believe." Here "ba'd" (after) is used metaphorically in the sense of "other than," because the adverbs indicating distance and separation are used in the manner of what is different. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾ (45:23). Taking "ba'd" in its literal sense here requires an interpretation and takes the discourse away from the straight path.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 186:

﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him. And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

This sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the disapproval expressed in His saying ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185], to convey that their misguidance is a matter whose continuation Allah has decreed, so no one should hope to guide them. Since this ruling applies directly to those who are characterized by denial, by failing to reflect on the state of the Messenger ﷺ, by failing to consider the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what Allah has created, and by anticipating the approach of their destruction, the people upon whom the judgment of non-guidance falls are a group that is not known to people. Allah alone knows them, and He informs His Messenger ﷺ of them, and some of this becomes evident at the death of some of them upon shirk. This is the issue termed al-muwafah (the issue of the end-state of one's life) among the scholars of kalam (theology).

The conjunction of the clause ﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ to the clause ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him﴾ serves to indicate the continuation of their misguidance and the negation of their guidance in the future, just as it occurred in the past.

The explanation of nadharuhum (﴿nadharuhum﴾, "We leave them") has preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and play﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am. The explanation of tughyan (transgression) and ya'mahun (wandering blindly) has preceded at His saying ﴿in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿nadharuhum﴾ with the nun and in the nominative (raf'), on the basis that it is a conjunction of one clause to another clause ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, following the device of iltifat (shift) from the third-person absent form to the first-person speaking form.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with the yā' (third-person prefix) and in the jussive (jazm), on the basis that it is a conjunction upon the place (mahall) of ﴿there is none to guide him﴾, which is the response (jawab) of the conditional.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ya'qub read it with the yā' and in the nominative (raf'), and the reasoning is evident.

[p. 201]

This is a fresh (ibtida'i) resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which mentions some of their misguidance and their attempt to put the Prophet ﷺ to the test by asking him to specify the time of the Hour.

The occasion for this resumption is the allusion to the expectation that their term is drawing near, in His words: ﴿And perhaps their term has drawn near﴾ [al-A'raf: 185]. Whether the term is understood as the term of the removal of the polytheists of the Arabs from the world, which is annihilation (al-isti'sal), or as their term and the term of the rest of humanity, which is the establishment of the Hour, the discourse about the Hour is relevant to both terms.

It is known from the habit (shinshana) of the polytheists that they denied resurrection and mocked the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, because of his report about resurrection: ﴿And those who disbelieved said: "Shall we show you a man who will inform you, when you are torn to pieces, that you will be in a new creation? Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?"﴾ [Saba': 7]. They began to ask the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour and its time, seeking to make him fail, because they imagined that since he had informed them of its matter, he claimed knowledge of its time: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" Say: "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you cannot delay an hour, nor can you advance it."﴾ [Saba': 29]

[p. 202]

So the questioners are the polytheists. This is related from Qatada, and the pronoun refers to those who denied Our signs. Similar questions are reported from them in several places of the Qur'an, such as His saying, Exalted is He, in Surah al-Nazi'at: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾, and His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news, about which they are in disagreement﴾ [al-Naba': 1–3], meaning resurrection and the Hour. Among the exegetes there is one who said: the ones meant by the questioners are the Jews, who wanted to test the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so they asked him about the Hour. But this cannot be the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse, because this surah is Meccan, it is said entirely, and it is said that two of its verses were revealed in Medina. They did not count this verse among those whose place of revelation was disputed. The surahs in which a similar question is reported are also Meccan, revealed before this surah.

"Al-sa'ah" (the Hour) is definite by the article and is a proper name by predominance in the terminology of the Qur'an, referring to the time of the end of this worldly world and the entry into the otherworldly world. It is also called the Day of Resurrection (yawm al-ba'th) and the Day of Rising (yawm al-qiyamah).

"Ayyan" is a noun denoting a question about time. It is invariable and not inflected. It is composed of "ayy" (interrogative "which") and "an," which means time. Then "ayy" was lightened, and the hamza of "an" was changed to a ya' so that idgham (assimilation) could take place. Thus "ayyan" came to mean "which time." The time asked about is specified by what follows "ayyan." For this reason it must be a noun of meaning (ism ma'na), not a noun of essence (ism dhat), since time is not predicated of an essence. As for its use as a conditional noun for the generality of times, that is by transfer from the interrogative to the conditional, just as "mata" was transferred from the interrogative to the conditional. These are extensions in the language that become renewed meanings. They (the scholars) mentioned possibilities for the derivation of "ayyan," returning it to the meanings of verbs, and all of them are unsatisfactory; what we have judged here is better than them.

So His saying "ayyan" is a predicate placed first because of the initial position of the interrogative. "Murṣahā" is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and it was originally a genitive complement of "an," since the original form is: "Which time is the time of the Hour's establishment?"

The clause ﴿ayyana mursaha﴾ is in a position of accusative (manṣub) governed by a verb of saying omitted, indicated by the verb ﴿yas'alunaka﴾. The estimate is: "They say, 'Which time is its establishment?'" This is a report of their saying in meaning. For this reason the clause has the sense of an apposition (badal) for the clause ﴿they ask you about the Hour﴾.

"Mursa" is a mimi noun (noun of place/time) from "irsa'," which means fixing, establishing. One says "rasa al-jabal" (the mountain became firm, stable) and "arsahu" (he fixed it and established it). "Irsa'" is settling after movement, as al-Akhtal said:

"And their scout said: 'Anchor, let us grapple with it.'"

"Mursa al-safinah" is the ship's settling after its sailing. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring﴾ [Hud: 41]. The word "irsa'" is used here metaphorically for occurrence, by likening the occurrence of a matter that was awaited or uncertain to the arrival of a traveler by land or sea at the place he intends.

Allah commanded His Messenger to answer them with a serious answer, and to overlook the bad intent of their question, which was mockery, in order to clear the defect from the description of prophethood by reason of not knowing the time of the Hour, and to teach those who await that from the Messenger's answer to the polytheists' question there would be knowledge for all of the specification of the time of the Hour. Now the matter of the Hour is one toward which souls strive to seek. It is recorded in the Sahih that "a man among the Muslims asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?' The Messenger of Allah said: 'What have you prepared for it?' He said: 'I have not prepared for it great deeds, except that I love Allah and His Messenger.' He said: 'You are with whom you love.'"

The knowledge of the Hour is the knowledge of determining its time, as the question indicates, and His saying ﴿None but He can reveal it at its time﴾. The annexation of "knowledge" to the pronoun of the Hour is according to an estimated noun between them, i.e., the knowledge of its time, and the annexation is from annexing a verbal noun to its object. The adverbial sense of "'inda" (with/at) is figurative, used to establish the connection of Allah's knowledge with its time.

The restriction is real (haqiqi), because it is the original meaning, and because of what its emphasis indicates afterwards in His saying ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. A real restriction includes the meaning of a relative restriction (idafi) and more, because knowledge of the Hour in precise determination is restricted to Allah, Exalted is He.

The definition by the description of the Lord and its annexation to the pronoun of the speaker is an allusion to the argument for Allah's exclusive possession of the knowledge of the time of the Hour, not the Messenger who was asked. So in it there is an allusion to their error and to the basis of their error.

"Al-tajliyah" means disclosure, and what is meant by it includes disclosure by informing and specifying, and disclosure by bringing about. Both are negated of attribution to other than Allah, Exalted is He. He is the one who knows its time, and He is the one who manifests it when He wills. When He manifests it, He has made it clear.

The "li-" in His saying ﴿li-waqtiha﴾ is for specifying time, like that in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. The meaning of specifying time is close to the meaning of "'inda," and the verified view is that its meaning arises from the meaning of the "li-" of specification (li al-ikhtisas).

[p. 203]

The meaning of "li-" fits one of the two meanings of "ijla'," which is manifestation, because it is the one which, when it occurs, the disclosure of its matter is complete, and people realize that the One capable of disclosing it had knowledge of the time of its arrival.

The clause ﴿None but He can reveal it at its time﴾ is disjoined (fusilat) because it descends from the preceding one in the position of emphasis and confirmation.

The prepositional phrase ﴿li-waqtiha﴾ was placed before the agent of "yujalliha," which occurs as an exceptive restrictive construction (istithna' mufarragh), for the purpose of giving importance to it, as a warning that the manifestation of its matter occurs at the time of its arrival, because it comes suddenly.

The clause ﴿Its weight is heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, for the purpose of conveying the dreadfulness of it, and an allusion to the wisdom of concealing it.

The verb "thaqulat" may be for the mere report of the intensity of its matter, as in His saying ﴿And they leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [al-Insan: 27].

It may also be an expression of wonder in the form "fa'ula" (with a ḍammah on the 'ayn), so the ḍammah is taken as the ḍammah of transforming the verb into an expression of wonder, although the ḍammah is originally a primary vowel in the verb. This is of the type of His saying ﴿How grave a word it is that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5].

"Thiql" (weight) is used metaphorically for hardship, as "'izam" (greatness) and "kibar" (magnitude) are used metaphorically, because the intensity of a thing's impact on souls and its hardship upon them makes the one afflicted by it imagine that he is carrying something heavy. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We shall cast upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5], meaning severe to receive, and it is the Qur'an. Describing the Hour as heavy is in terms of what is contained in its time of events, so describing it with that is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the indication is clear, which is that "thiql" in the sense of intensity cannot be a description of time, but it is a description of events. So when it is attributed to time, its attribution to it is only in terms of its being a container for the events, as in His saying: ﴿And he said, "This is a distressful day"﴾ [Hud: 77].

The heaviness of the Hour, i.e., its intensity, is the magnitude of the terrifying events that occur in it in the heavens and the earth: the collision of stars, the disruption of their orbits, earthquakes, the overflowing of volcanoes, seas, the drying up of waters, and the like, of what arises from the disruption of the order upon which the course of the world was. All of that produces a great intensity upon every being of perception among the existents.

[p. 204]

Among the wonders of concision is the transitivity of the verb "thaqulat" by the particle of location that indicates the place where the verb occurs, and the omission of what should be transitive to it, namely the particle "ila" (to), which indicates what the verb falls upon, so that it may encompass everything that the heavens and the earth contain of what the heaviness, in the sense of intensity, falls upon.

The clause ﴿It will not come to you except suddenly﴾ is a new resumptive clause, which came to complete the report about the time of the Hour's arrival, because arrival suddenly confirms the content of the report about its time, that it is not known except to Allah, and that Allah does not manifest it to anyone. So His saying ﴿It will not come to you except suddenly﴾ indicates that the negation of manifesting its time is a negation that goes deep into its kind, such that no one gains knowledge of its arrival either in its actuality or in general. As for what has been mentioned of its signs in the hadith of Gabriel's question about its signs, it does not contradict its coming suddenly, because those signs extend over long periods of time, so that no preparation for knowledge of its arrival is achieved along with them.

"Al-baghtah" is a verbal noun on the pattern of the single instance of "al-baght," which is surprise, i.e., occurrence without preparation for it. Its discussion has already passed at His saying ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 31] in Surah al-An'am.

The clause ﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾ emphasizes the clause ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ and explains the manner of their asking, so the two were separated.

The object of the question was omitted because it is known from the first clause.

"Hafiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il/fa'iyl), so it may mean the agent of "hafiya bihi" (one who is solicitous about something), from "hafiya bihi," like "ghaniyy" (rich). So one is "ghaniyy" when he asks much about the state of someone with gentleness. The meaning would be: "as if you had asked much about its time until you came to know it," so the description "hafiyy" is a metonymy (kinayah) for one who knows a thing, because much asking requires the acquisition of knowledge of the thing asked about. In this sense it was interpreted in the Kashshaf, so it is a metonymy for the request for knowledge by means of asking, since asking is a cause of knowledge, as in the verse of al-Samaw'al or 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi or others:

"Ask, if you are ignorant of people about us and about them, for the knowing and the ignorant are not equal."

And the saying of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"You are divorced if you do not ask which knight your husband was, when he met Sada' and Khath'am."

And the saying of Unayf ibn Zabban al-Nabhani:

"When we met, the sword made a separation between us, for the one asking about us, its question is thorough (hafiyy)."

It may also be derived from "ahfa" if he insisted upon him in an action, so it is "fa'il" in the sense of "muf'il," like "hakim" (wise), i.e., as if you were insistent in asking about it, that is, insistent upon God in asking the specification of the time of the Hour, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If He should ask you for it and press you, you would be stingy﴾ [Muhammad: 37].

His saying "ka-annaka hafiyy" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the addressee in His saying "yas'alunaka," an intervening clause between "yas'alunaka" and its complement.

The phrase "'anha" (about it) is connected, on both possibilities, to each of "yas'alunaka" and "hafiyy," by way of the kind of tanazu' (competition) in governance.

The word ﴿حَفِيٌّ﴾ may also be derived from ḥafiya bihi, like raḍiya, meaning he went to great lengths in showing honour. It would then be used in its plain sense, and the implied meaning is "as if you were ḥafiyy towards them," that is, honouring and gently attentive to them. This would be sarcasm toward the polytheists: they show you this attitude so that you will be drawn into discussing with them the fixing of the time of the Hour. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "as if you were a friend to them." Qatada said: the Quraysh said to Muhammad, "There is kinship between us, so tell us privately when the Hour will come." Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you as though you were keen to know of it.﴾ On this reading, ʿanha (about it) is connected to ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ﴾ (they ask you), and the object of ﴿حَفِيٌّ﴾ is omitted because it is clear.

From this you know that the placing of ʿanha (about it) later in the sentence is for the sake of completing the rhetorical balance (al-īfāʾ) according to these considerations.

The verse also indicates that the Messenger (ﷺ) did not set his aspiration on fixing the time of the Hour, since there is no benefit for him in that. Moreover, if he had been concerned with it, his concern would have amounted to seeking to nullify the wisdom behind its concealment. This also indicates that his lack of knowledge of its time does not contradict his noble standing with God, exalted is He, since God gave him a perfection of soul that turns him away from seeking that. Had he sought it, God would have informed him of it. This is like how Musa (peace be upon him) was turned away from continuing to dislike death when his term came, so that he would not have his soul taken while he was averse to it. These are lofty secrets between God and the righteous among His servants.

The first answer sentence is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with God.﴾ This reinforces its meaning, so that it is known that this answer should not be expected to be anything other than this, and that the restriction (ḥaṣr, exclusive limitation) contained in His saying ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ is a true restriction (ḥaṣr ḥaqīqī). Then a corrective addition (istidrāk, a statement that qualifies or corrects what precedes) is joined to the answer sentence, going back to the restriction in His saying ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with God﴾, to affirm that it is a true restriction, and to refute the assumption of those who think that it is the nature of the messengers to know every unknown thing. Among these unknowns is the time of the Hour, relative to their own times, which they could inform the people about. They then infer from the lack of knowledge of the Hour that the claimant to prophethood is not truthful. This belief is an error that clings to dull minds, for they imagine realities other than they are, and become certain of what their imagination presents to them, and make it a foundation on which they build their knowledge and dealings, and make it a judgment in affairs, both affirmatively and negatively. This is an extreme error, and it is indeed "a bundle of reeds upon a bundle" (ḍighth ʿalā ibbāla, a mixture of unhelpful things piled on a burden), with the letter bāʾ pronounced both doubled and single.

Ancient history has recorded a witness to what we have said. It is what came in the Book of Daniel (Sifr Daniyal) among the books of the prophets appended to the Torah: that Bukhtunassar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babil (Babylon), saw a dream that disturbed him, and he sought its interpretation. So he gathered the diviners, the astrologers and the magicians, and ordered them to tell him the form of what he had seen in his dream without him recounting it to them. When they answered him that this was beyond the capacity of any human being, and that none knows what is in the king's mind except the gods, he became angry and enraged, and ordered them killed. He then summoned Daniel the prophet, who was among the captives of the Children of Israel in Babil, and threatened him with death if he did not inform him of the form of his dream and then its interpretation. Daniel asked the king for a delay, and he turned to God in supplication, he and his companions Azariah, Mishael and Hananiah, asking God to save Daniel from being killed. God revealed to Daniel the form of what the king had seen, so Daniel informed the king of it, then interpreted it for him, and so he gained favour with him. See the second chapter of the Book of Daniel.

[p. 207]

This is an elevation in disavowing knowledge of the unseen and in disavowing control over the world. It is also an added teaching for the community about the reality of the messengership and prophethood, and a distinction between what belongs to their specific attributes and what does not.

[p. 207]

The sentence is a fresh, independent (ibtida'iyyah) resumptive sentence (*istinafiyyah*). Its resumption is intended to draw attention to its content, so that hearts turn to it. For this reason the command "Say" is repeated, although it has already occurred twice in His words ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] and ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. This is to emphasise that the speech is standing on its own, and that it is not subsumed under the reported speech preceding it. This statement is specifically about the condition of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding knowledge of the unseen. It is meant to remove from the minds of the polytheists the assumption that knowledge of the unseen is necessarily tied to the attribute of prophethood. It is a public declaration to the polytheists that he is committed to not knowing the unseen, and that this does not discredit his prophethood, so that they will despair of challenging him on this basis. It is also an instruction to the Muslims to distinguish between what prophethood necessitates and what it does not. For this reason he negated from himself knowledge of his own hidden conditions, let alone knowledge of the hidden matters of others' conditions, except what Allah wills.

In the *Tafsir al-Baghawi*, from Ibn 'Abbas: the people of Makkah said, "O Muhammad, will your Lord not inform you of cheap prices before they rise, so that you may buy and profit when prices are high, and of land that is about to become barren, so that you may move from it to land that has become fertile?" Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed ﴿Say: I possess no power over benefit or harm for myself, except what Allah wills﴾. Thus this would be among the things they used as a pretext, like their question about the Hour. The refutation of both claims has been combined in one verse (*qirn*).

The meaning of "possession" (*al-mulk*) here is capability and ability (*al-istita'ah wa al-tamakkun*). Its explanation has already preceded at His words ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surah al-Ma'idah. What is intended here includes knowledge of benefit and harm, because the context is the negation of knowledge of the unseen, and because knowledge of a thing is what directs the soul toward acting upon it.

He placed benefit before harm here, because benefit is more beloved to a person. In the verse of al-Ma'idah he reversed the order, because the aim there is to belittle the status of their deities and to show that their anger is not to be feared.

As for the conjunction of ﴿nor harm﴾ although a person does not seek to harm himself, the purpose is to generalise the conditions, since a person's conditions are nothing but beneficial or harmful. Thus the mention of these two opposites is like the mention of evening and morning, night and day, evil and good. Further explanation of this will come at His words ﴿They possess neither harm nor benefit for themselves﴾ [al-Furqan: 3] in Surah al-Furqan.

He made the negation of his possessing benefit or harm for himself a premise for the negation of knowledge of the unseen. This is because the ultimate aim of people in seeking knowledge of the unseen is to hasten toward future goods by preparing their causes and bringing them near, and to avoid the places of harm. Therefore the negation that he possesses for himself neither benefit nor harm encompasses all types of possession and all types of benefit and harm, and among the scope of this generality is what will happen in the future, which is part of the unseen.

The exception (*al-istithna'*) is from the whole of benefit and harm. It is preferable to take it as a connected exception (*muttasil*), meaning: except what Allah wills to grant me the power over, by teaching me it and enabling me to do it. If He does not will that, He does not inform me of its places. The creation of obstacles is among the causes of obtaining benefit and of averting harm. Taking it as connected corresponds to the affirmation of a capacity for the servant by the decree of Allah, exalted is He, which is called *kasb* (acquisition). Thus, when Allah wills to direct the soul of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, toward knowledge of a hidden matter, He informs him of it for the benefit of the community or to honour the community through him, as in His words ﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few﴾ [al-Anfal: 43] up to His words ﴿that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ [al-Anfal: 44]. And His words ﴿Had I known the unseen…﴾ etc. are a completion of the disavowal of knowledge of the unseen, whether that concerns his own self or matters of others.

From the whole of the two sentences it results that he possesses for himself neither benefit nor harm, in the world of the witnessed and in the world of the unseen, and that he knows nothing of the unseen that concerns his benefit and harm, or anything beyond that.

The inference of the absence of his knowledge of the unseen from the absence of abundance of good and avoidance of evil is an inference from the most specific thing which, if a person knew the unseen, he would know first: namely the unseen that concerns his own self. Moreover, if Allah willed to inform him of the unseen, the purpose would be to honour the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, so his being informed of what brings him comfort would be the first thing that should be disclosed to him. When that is negated, the negation of other things is more fitting.

The proof of the consequent (*dalil al-tali*) in this conditional proposition is the observation of the loss of worldly goods, for which he was not prepared to obtain, and the occurrence of worldly evils. Within it is an implicit rebuke for them, since they used to target him with evil.

The clause ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ is part of the speech commanded to be said, and it is a resumptive sentence of explanation (*istinaf bayani*), arising from the disavowal of his possessing benefit or harm for himself. This is because the listeners would suppose that what he negated from himself is the most distinctive attribute of a prophet. So it would be natural for them to wonder at his negation of that for himself while he says he is the messenger of Allah to them, and to ask about his function after he has negated what he negated. Thus he clarified to them that the messengership is confined to warning against corruptions and their consequences, and to bringing good tidings of the consequences of abandoning them and of acquiring good.

He placed the description of "warner" before "bringer of good tidings" here, because the context is addressing the deniers, the polytheists, and warning is more closely connected to them than good tidings.

The discussion of "warner" and "bringer of good tidings" has already preceded at His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119] in Surah al-Baqarah.

His words ﴿for a people who believe﴾ may be connected to each of "warner" and "bringer of good tidings" (*yatanaza'u ta'alluquhu kull min nadhir wa bashir*), because benefit from both matters is specific to those who are prepared for faith, by reflecting on the signs, refraining from their own desires, and speaking the truth against their fathers. It is not specific to those who have made denial, aversion, and obstinacy their habit. The present tense is intended to denote the present and the future, as is its usual function, so as to include those who are prepared for faith both now and in the outcome. As for its inclusion of those who believed in the past, it is by the implication of the address's meaning (*dalalat fahwa al-khitab*), since they are more deserving. This is in the manner of His words ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45].

In the arrangement of the speech with this style of *tanazu'*, and in placing the description of "bringer of good tidings" next to "a people who believe", there is an implication that good tidings are specific to the believers, and that the object of the warning, which is omitted from the wording, is the opposite of the believers, namely the polytheists. This meaning is intended, in the manner of His words ﴿to warn those who have wronged, and as good tidings for the doers of good﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 12].

These implied meanings are intended by the Qur'an, and they are among the aspects of its inimitability (*i'jaz*), because they convey abundant meanings from concise words.

[p. 210]

This is a new sentence, begun independently. Through it the discourse returns to establishing the proof of monotheism (tawhid) and refuting polytheism (shirk), taking up the covenant mentioned earlier in His words ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and so on. It is not part of the speech commanded in His words ﴿Say: I possess no power to benefit or harm myself﴾ [al-A'raf: 188], because that speech was intended to negate the necessary link between the attribute of prophethood and the Messenger's knowledge of the unseen, and that purpose has been accomplished. Therefore it is fitting that the other purpose be a statement directed by God, exalted is He, to the polytheists, to establish the proof against them by exposing the corruption of their reasoning in associating partners with God and in their fathers' associating partners with Him.

The reason for the transition is the mention of God's name in His words ﴿except what God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 128]. The pronoun of address in "khalaqakum" (He created you) refers to the Arab polytheists, because they are the intended audience of these proofs and reminders, although the ruling of this speech includes all of mankind. He opened this with a reminder of the blessing of creating the species, beginning with the creation of its origin, Adam, and his wife Hawwa' (Eve), as a preparation for the intended purpose.

The attaching of a verb to a collective noun, in such a usage, occurs in two ways. The first is that what is meant is the collective whole, that is, the totality of what the pronoun applies to: He created all of mankind from a single soul, so that the soul is the soul of Adam, from whom all of mankind descended.

The second is that what is meant is the distributive whole, that is, He created each one of you from a single soul, so that the soul is the father, i.e., the father of each of the addressees, in the manner of His words ﴿O mankind, We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13] and His words ﴿and He made of it the two pairs, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39].

The phrase "a single soul" alone bears both meanings, since in both creations there is a favour, and in both there is a lesson and an admonition.

Many of the exegetes have taken the single soul to be Adam. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) among them have taken the father to be of every individual. This is what is transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatadah, and al-Fakhr, al-Baydawi, [p. 211] Ibn Kathir, al-Asamm, Ibn al-Munir and al-Jubba'i followed it.

The soul is described as "single" by way of embedding (idmaj) between the lesson and the admonition, because its being single is more conducive to consideration, since many offspring issue from a single one, to the point that a single soul may become a tribe or a nation. In this description there is a reminder of this wondrous state, which indicates the greatness of power and the breadth of knowledge, in that He scattered from a single soul many men and women. This matter was discussed earlier at the opening of Surat al-Nisa'.

What appears to me is that there is an istikhdam (a usage in which one term carries two referents) in the pronouns of "taghashshaha" (he covered her) and what follows it, up to His words "in what He gave them." By this, the interpretation of the verse combines both opinions.

The "min" in His words "min nafsin wahidah" (from a single soul) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah).

He expressed on the female side by the verb "ja'ala" (made), because the intended meaning is making the female a spouse for the male, not reporting that God created her, since that is already known from His words ﴿He it is who created you from a single soul﴾.

The "min" in His words "wa ja'ala minha" (and made from it) is partitive (tab'id), and what is meant is: from its kind. His words "minha" (from it) are an attribute of "zawjaha" (its spouse), placed before the modified noun for emphasis on the favour, namely that He made the spouse, who is the female, of the same kind as its male. This wisdom is consistent in every pair of animals.

His words "li-yaskuna ilayha" (that he might find rest in her) are a causal clause explaining what the partitive "min" conveys.

"Sukun" (rest) is metaphorical for tranquillity and familiarity, meaning: He made from the same kind as the man his spouse so that he would become familiar with her and not shun her nearness. In this is the favour of companionship with her and the frequency of intimacy with her, so that he is drawn to approaching her. Had God made procreation occur without the impulse of desire, the man's soul would not have been eager to increase its offspring. And had He made it occur through a state of pain, the man's soul would have been reluctant about it, so that it would not turn to it except out of necessity after reflection and hesitation, as one turns to taking medicine or the like, whose benefits follow. He then linked to this, by the particle "fa" of consequence, what arises from part of the spouse's rest in his wife, which is intercourse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 191–192:**

﴿Do they associate with Allah those who create nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ ﴿And they cannot give them help, nor can they help themselves.﴾

These three verses are a parenthetical statement placed between the two passages that are directed at rebuking the polytheists and establishing the proof against them. They address the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Muslims, to express wonder at the minds of the polytheists. There is also an implicit element of refutation in them, since they reach the ears of the polytheists.

The interrogative is used for the purposes of wonder and denunciation.

The imperfect form in "yushrikun" (they associate) indicates the renewal of this association on their part. The negation of the imperfect in His words "mā lā yakhluqu" (those who create nothing) serves to indicate the continual renewal of the denial of creative power from them.

The basic meaning of renewal, which the verbal predicate indicates, is the occurrence of the meaning of the predicate in relation to the subject, and it is not merely established fact and settled reality. From it we understand that they will not create in the future, and that they have not created anything in the past, because if creation were a fixed attribute of theirs, it would be established in the past, the present and the future.

The pronoun of the third person in "wa-hum yukhlaqūn" (while they themselves are created) may, in my view, refer back to what the pronoun in "yushrikūn" refers to, meaning: "while the polytheists are created." The sense of the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) is to intensify the wonder at their condition, in that they associate with Allah things that create nothing, while the polytheists are created day by day, that is, their creation is continually renewed. The polytheists see the idols sitting motionless in their houses and places, not making anything. Thus the imperfect form indicates continuity by the context of the situation.

The indication of the imperfect for continuity and repetition arises from the meaning of renewal inherent in the basic verbal predicate. It is an implication of the structure, determined by the contextual indicators that specify it, and it is not described as either literal or figurative on that account. As for the meaning of the renewal of their createdness, it is that the pronoun applies to a nation and a group, and createdness does not leave them, because it is renewed moment by moment through the increase of births and the change of conditions of their states, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Creation after creation﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Thus the clause "wa-hum yukhlaqūn" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "a-yushrikūn" (do they associate).

The exegetes have referred the pronoun in "hum yukhlaqūn" back to "mā lā yakhluqu," that is, the idols, but they did not explain the meaning of the idols being created, since they are images carved by people, and their forms are not created by Allah. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant is that their material is created, which is stone.

They have made the use of the pronouns of rational beings in His words "wa-hum" (and they) and His words "yukhlaqūn" and what follows them apply to the idols, which are inanimate objects, because they were treated as though they were rational beings, based on the belief of those who were being argued against concerning them. On this interpretation, the reason for the use of the imperfect form of "yukhlaqūn" does not become apparent, because this creation is not renewed.

The pronoun in the genitive governed by the preposition lām in "lahum naṣran" (to help them) refers to the polytheists, because the object governed by lām after the verb of ability and the like is the one for whose sake the act occurs, as in "﴿they do not possess for you any provision﴾" [al-'Ankabut: 17].

The clause "wa-lā yastaṭī'ūna lahum naṣran" (nor can they give them help) is conjoined to the clause "mā lā yakhluqu shay'an" (those who create nothing), so it is a second relative complement (ṣilah).

What is said about the two verbs in "lā yastaṭī'ūn" and "﴿wa-lā anfusahum yanṣurūn﴾" (nor can they help themselves) is the same as what is said about "mā lā yakhluqu shay'an."

The fronting of the object in "﴿wa-lā anfusahum yanṣurūn﴾" is for the purpose of emphasis on negating this help from them, because it is more indicative of the powerlessness of those gods, since whoever is unable to help others would be even less able to help himself, were he able.

The meaning is: the idols do not help those who worship them when they need their help, nor do they help themselves if someone intends to attack them.

It is apparent that the singling out of help from among the actions which they imagine the idols might perform is intended to alert the polytheists to the idols' lack of capacity to benefit them, since help was the most desired thing for them. The Arabs were people of raids, fighting and blood-vengeance, so victory was among the most important matters to them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be helped﴾ [Yasin: 74], ﴿They are not able to help them﴾ [Yasin: 75]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81], ﴿No! They will reject their worship﴾ [Maryam: 82]. Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalted is Hubal" (A'lu Hubal), and he also said: "For us is al-'Uzza, and there is no al-'Uzza for you." Allah informed the Muslims of this, as an allusion to the good news that the polytheists would be defeated. He said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12]. And that they will be annihilated, and the idols will be unable to be defended by anyone.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 7, verses 191–192:**

﴿Do they associate with Allah those who create nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ ﴿And they cannot give them help, nor can they help themselves.﴾

These three verses are a parenthetical statement placed between the two passages that are directed at rebuking the polytheists and establishing the proof against them. They address the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Muslims, to express wonder at the minds of the polytheists. There is also an implicit element of refutation in them, since they reach the ears of the polytheists.

The interrogative is used for the purposes of wonder and denunciation.

The imperfect form in "yushrikun" (they associate) indicates the renewal of this association on their part. The negation of the imperfect in His words "mā lā yakhluqu" (those who create nothing) serves to indicate the continual renewal of the denial of creative power from them.

The basic meaning of renewal, which the verbal predicate indicates, is the occurrence of the meaning of the predicate in relation to the subject, and it is not merely established fact and settled reality. From it we understand that they will not create in the future, and that they have not created anything in the past, because if creation were a fixed attribute of theirs, it would be established in the past, the present and the future.

The pronoun of the third person in "wa-hum yukhlaqūn" (while they themselves are created) may, in my view, refer back to what the pronoun in "yushrikūn" refers to, meaning: "while the polytheists are created." The sense of the circumstantial clause (ḥāl) is to intensify the wonder at their condition, in that they associate with Allah things that create nothing, while the polytheists are created day by day, that is, their creation is continually renewed. The polytheists see the idols sitting motionless in their houses and places, not making anything. Thus the imperfect form indicates continuity by the context of the situation.

The indication of the imperfect for continuity and repetition arises from the meaning of renewal inherent in the basic verbal predicate. It is an implication of the structure, determined by the contextual indicators that specify it, and it is not described as either literal or figurative on that account. As for the meaning of the renewal of their createdness, it is that the pronoun applies to a nation and a group, and createdness does not leave them, because it is renewed moment by moment through the increase of births and the change of conditions of their states, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Creation after creation﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Thus the clause "wa-hum yukhlaqūn" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "a-yushrikūn" (do they associate).
