Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 193:

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent.﴾

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿatf) to the clause "﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾", as an increase in wonder at the state of the polytheists, by mentioning their insistence upon polytheism despite its foolishness of intellects and weakness of proof, after mentioning what is sufficient to refute it.

The second-person pronoun in the nominative in "And if you call them" is directed to the Muslims together with the Messenger ﷺ, and the third-person plural pronoun in the accusative refers to the polytheists, just as the pronoun of "Do they associate" referred back [to them]. So, after Allah had made the Muslims wonder at the state of the people of polytheism, He informed them that they do not accept the call to guidance.

The meaning of this is that it is with regard to the majority of them. Otherwise, some of them did believe after a while, and they followed one another into faith, except those who died in polytheism.

This interpretation is the most fitting for His saying, may He be exalted, after this: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:198], so that the one spoken of in this verse is not the one spoken of in the verse that follows, due to the clear difference in position between "they will not follow you" and "they do not hear."

It is also permissible that the clause "﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾" and so on be conjoined (maʿtufah) to the relative clause (jumlat al-silah) in His saying "﴿what creates nothing, while they themselves are created﴾" [Al-A'raf 7:191]. Then the second-person pronoun in "tadʿūhum" would be addressed to the polytheists, whose discussion had been in third-person pronouns from His saying "﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾" [Al-A'raf 7:190] up to here. The apparent requirement would then be to say: "And if he calls them to guidance, they do not follow them." So the shift from the third person to the second person would be an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) from the absent to the address, turning towards them with direct address, because direct address is more effective in crushing (damgh) them with the proof.

"Guidance" in this interpretation is what one is guided to, and the purpose of mentioning it is that they do not respond when you call them to what is good for them. Thus it is known that if they were called to other than that, their not following the call would be even more certain.

The clause "﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾" is a reinforcement (muʾakkidah) of the clause "﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you﴾", and therefore it was separated (fuṣilat) from it.

"Sawāʾ" is a name for a thing that equals another, meaning that it is not preferable to it in the sense for which the speech is intended. The hamza that comes after "sawāʾ" is called hamzat al-taswiyah (the hamza of equalization), and its origin is the interrogative hamza, used for equalization, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:6]) in Surat al-Baqarah. That is: it is the same for you whether you call them or your silence from calling.

The "ʿalā" in it is for metaphorical elevation (al-istiʿlāʾ al-majāzī), and it has the meaning of "ʿindiyyah" (with/in the judgment of), i.e., "it is the same with them." The two matters were made equal for the addressees and were not made equal for those being called. So He did not say "﴿sawāʾun ʿalayhim﴾" [Al-Baqarah 2:6], although that too would be equal for them, because the purpose of the speech is to make the addressees despair of the called ones responding to what they call them to, not to give information. Although the two meanings are mutually implicated, just as they are in His saying "﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾" [Al-Baqarah 2:6], where the warning and its absence are equal for the polytheists and the believers, the aim there is to explain the absence of their benefiting from guidance.

This is the rule for distinguishing between what may have the verb of equalization ascribed to both sides, and what must be ascribed to one side when the equalization concerns only one side. As in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Burn in it; so be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you﴾ [Al-Tur 52:16], where it is necessary that the equalization be with regard to the addressees, and it is not good to say "sawāʾun ʿalaynā." And like His saying ﴿It is the same for us whether we rage or we are patient; there is for us no place of escape﴾ [Ibrahim 14:21], where it is necessary that the equalization be with regard to the speakers.

The phrase "﴿or you remain silent﴾" came as the counterpart (muʿādil) of "﴿did you call them﴾", with a difference in the style between the two clauses, the verbal and the nominal. So it did not say "am ṣamaztum" (or you were silent). In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, on the authority of Thaʿlab: that is because it is the end of a verse (raʾs ayah), i.e., merely for the sake of observing the rhyme (al-fāṣilah). He said: "ṣāmitūna" and "ṣamaztum" are one and the same according to Sibawayh (meaning the verb and the derived descriptive noun are equivalent), i.e., there is no difference between them in the basic meaning, because what follows the hamzat al-taswiyah, since it has the force of a verbal noun (maṣdar), has no trace of a difference between the verb and the noun, as the estimation is: "It is the same for you, your calling them and your silence about them." So the shift to the nominal clause has no requirement from rhetoric; rather, the two are equal for an eloquent speaker. But the shift to the nominal is required by eloquence, because the fawāṣil (verse-endings) and the asjāʿ (rhymed prose) are among the refinements of eloquence, and in them the excellence of speech appears, since in them there is the fulfilment of the rights of the verse-ending together with freedom from artificiality, just as the skill of the poet appears in fulfilling the right of the rhyme (qāfiyah) when, together with that, he is free from artificiality. Al-Marzuqi said in the preface of his commentary on the Hamasa: "The rhyme must be like the promised thing awaited, longed for by the meaning in its right and by the wording in its share; otherwise it is restless in its place, brought in for something that could do without it."

The verification is that the nominal clause indicates the establishment (thubūt) of the attribute it contains, without restriction to time and without indicating renewal, unlike the verbal clause. This is the explicit statement of the Shaykh (ʿAbd al-Qahir al-Jurjani) in Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz, and of al-Sakkaki in al-Miftah. However, the words of al-Zamakhshari on this verse call out that the clause "﴿or you remain silent﴾" indicates the continuation (istimrār) of their silence. Likewise is the statement of al-Sakkaki in showing the difference between the two clauses in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:8], and in His saying ﴿They said, "We believe"﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:121], together with His saying after it ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are with you"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:14]. The apparent meaning of al-Shirazi's statement in his commentary on al-Miftah is that establishment necessitates continuation. Al-Taftazani, the commentator, said in his commentary on al-Miftah: "The truth is that the nominal clause, when it is a shift from the verbal, indicates permanence (dawām), which is like establishment." And in his commentary on the Talkhis al-Miftah he explained establishment as the accompaniment of permanence. As for al-Sayyid (al-Sharif al-Jurjani) in his commentary on al-Miftah and in his gloss on al-Mutawwal, he made the nominal clause one that may intend permanence, affirmatively and negatively, according to the contexts. In my view, the nominal clause does not indicate more than establishment, which is the opposite of renewal (tajaddud). As for continuity and permanence, it is an implicit meaning (maʿnā kināʾī) of it, requiring a specifying indicator to derive it, and that indicator is absent here. So the meaning is: "It is the same for you whether you call them with a renewed call or you persist in silence," and the meaning is not that of permanence. The author of al-Kashshaf needed to clarify this by the method of precision, by introducing a question and answer, according to his custom. Whatever the case, the shift away from the verbal clause in the counterpart of the equalization was required by the rhetorical situation, contrary to Thaʿlab.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 194:

﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾

This sentence, on the first reading of who is being addressed (in his words, ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you﴾ [al-A'raf: 193], the verse before), is a fresh, independent resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) that moves from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims to addressing the polytheists. For this reason it is introduced with the emphatic particle (inna), because the polytheists deny that the idols are equal to them in servitude. There is also a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

By "those you invoke besides Allah" is meant the idols. Defining them with the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) serves to alert the addressees to the error of their opinion in calling upon them besides Allah, when they are not worthy of that. This relative clause is like the relative clause in the words of 'Abda ibn al-Tabib:

Indeed, those you see as your brothers, whose hearts' rage is soothed by your being thrown down.

On the second reading of the preceding address, this sentence is an explanation (bayan) and a justification (ta'lil) of the clause ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you﴾ [al-A'raf: 193], i.e., because they are servants, that is, created beings.

Al-'abd (servant) originally means the owned slave, the opposite of the free person, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. It has been used in language for a created being, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. For this reason 'ibad (servants) is applied to people. It is well known that it is applied only to created humans, so the application of "servants" to the idols is like the application of the plural pronoun for rational beings to them, based on the common usage of the Arabs of that time. The author of al-Kashshaf took it as an expression of mockery and derision directed at the polytheists, meaning that the best they can attain is to be living and rational; even if they reached that state, they would be nothing but created beings like you. He said: For this reason, He nullified their being servants by His saying after it, ﴿Do they have feet to walk with?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195], to its end.

In my view, the better reading is that the application of "servants" to them is a metaphor by the relation of the unrestricted to the restricted (ʿalaqat al-itlaq 'an al-taqyid). Its beauty is observed through the potential correspondence (al-mushakala al-taqdiriyya), because when He made them equal to the addressees in createdness, and the addressees were servants of Allah, He applied "servants" to their equals by way of correspondence.

He based the command of challenge (al-taʿjiz) on this equality, with His saying ﴿So call upon them﴾, for it is used in the sense of challenge, in view of what follows from it, His saying ﴿and let them respond to you﴾, which includes the idols' responding to them. This is because calling itself is possible, but their being answered by them is not possible. So when they call upon them and they do not respond, the powerlessness of the gods to respond to them becomes evident, and the powerlessness of the polytheists to obtain that response, despite their eagerness to obtain it to bolster their argument. Thus the manifestation of the idols' inability to respond to their worshippers results in establishing the polytheists' inability to sustain their argument, because the two powerlessnesses are mutually implicated. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ [Fatir: 14].

The more evident view is that the calling commanded here is the calling for help and aid, as al-Mazini said: when they are asked for help, they do not ask the one who calls them for what war or in what place.

By this it becomes clear that the command of challenge is a metonymy (kinaya) for the established inability of the idols to respond to them, and the inability of the polytheists to produce a call to the idols that is followed by a response.

The command with the lam in His saying ﴿let them respond﴾ is a command of challenge addressed to the idols, and it is a command in the third person, since the way to command the absent is through the command itself.

The meaning of directing a command in the third person to the hearing addressee is that he is commanded to convey the order to the absent party. This too is a metonymy for the idols' inability to respond, because of their inability to receive the conveyance from their worshippers.

The object of "sadiqin" (truthful) is omitted because the context makes it clear, i.e., truthful in attributing divinity to the idols.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 195:

﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾

This is an emphasis on what the preceding sentence contained of the matter of challenging them to act and the establishment of their incapacity. For when the means of responding are removed from the idols, their inability to answer is confirmed, and the meaning of the challenge, which is an allusion to the incapacity of the idols and the incapacity of their worshippers, is reinforced. The interrogation is denunciatory (inkari), and the placing of the predicate before the subject is for the sake of emphasis on the negation of the possession indicated by the lam (in "lahum"), like the placing in the verse of Hassan:

"For him are aspirations, with no end to their greatness."

The description of the feet with "yamshuna" (they walk), of the hands with "yabtishuna" (they strike), of the eyes with "yubsirna" (they see), and of the ears with "yasma'una" (they hear) is either to add to the recording of their incapacity in what the helper needs, or because some of those idols were made in the forms of human beings, such as Hubal, Dhu al-Kaffayn and Ku'ayb in the shapes of men, and Suwa' was in the form of a woman. So when such idols have the forms of feet, hands, eyes and ears, they are devoid of the action which the limbs are specialized in, so no one who hopes for their help will covet it. He singled out the feet, hands, eyes and ears because they are the instruments of knowledge, of striving and of repelling for the sake of victory. For this reason the tongues were not mentioned, as you know, since the response is intended to mean rescue and support, and they did not ask about the cause of seeking help, but rather they hasten to join the one who seeks help.

Al-mashy (walking) is the movement of the two feet from one place to another in succession.

Al-batsh (striking) is seizing with the hand with force, and harming with the hand with force. Its present tense has come with kasra and damma according to the usual usage. The reading of the majority is with kasra, and Abu Ja'far read it with damma on the ta', and both are dialectal forms.

"Am" (أم) is a particle with the meaning of "aw" (or), specialized in coordinating an interrogative. It can be like "aw" for one of two things or several things, for distinguishing between things, or for permission, meaning combining them. When it falls after the interrogative hamza which seeks specification, it is like the "aw" of choice, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [Yunus: 59], meaning: specify one of them. If it falls after a non-genuine interrogative, it has the meaning of the "aw" of permission, and it is then called disconnected (munqati'a). For this reason they say it means "bal" (rather), the transitional one. In every case it is bound to the meaning of interrogation, so whenever it occurs in speech, an interrogative is presumed after it. The estimate here is: "Rather, do they have hands with which they strike? Rather, do they have eyes with which they see? Rather, do they have ears with which they hear?"

The arrangement of these four limbs in the order of the verse takes into account their importance relative to the purpose, which is victory and support. The two feet hasten to the cry for help before reflection, the two hands perform the work of support, which is stabbing and striking, and as for the eyes and ears, they are means to all of that, so they were delayed. The mention of the eyes is placed before the ears here contrary to the usual Qur'anic practice of placing hearing before sight, as has preceded at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, because the order here is by way of ascent (taraqqi).

* * *

﴿Say: Call your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾

This is a permission from Allah to His Messenger to challenge them, that if they are able, they should call upon their idols for help, so that they may gather together to plot against the Messenger, peace be upon him. The meaning is: call your partners to help you against me, so that you may be relieved of me.

Al-kayd (plotting) is harm that occurs in the form of non-harm, as has preceded at His saying, exalted is He, just before: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf: 183].

The command and prohibition in His saying ﴿plot against me, and give me no respite﴾ are for incapacitation (ta'jiz).

His saying ﴿and give me no respite﴾ is a consequence of the command to plot, meaning: when you are able to harm me, then hasten and do not delay me.

In this challenge there is an implication that he will overcome them, prevail over them, and uproot their gods. He has challenged them with the most complete circumstances of victory, which is seeking help from the most powerful beings in their belief, and that the harm to him be hidden, and that he not be given time or be waited for. If they are unable to do so, then its absence is more indicative of their incapacity and the incapacity of their gods.

The yā' of the first person is omitted from "kīdūnī" in both pause and continuation, in the reading of the majority other than Abu 'Amr. As for "tunzirūnī," all read it with the yā' omitted except Ya'qub, who affirmed it both in continuation and pause. Omitting the yā' of the first person after the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah) is very eloquent.

[p. 224]

﴿Indeed, my protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He takes care of the righteous.﴾ ﴿Those you invoke besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ This is from what was commanded by His saying, and this sentence is separated from the sentence ﴿Call upon your partners﴾ (al-A'raf: 195) because it stands in the position of a reason for the content of the challenge in His saying ﴿Call upon your partners﴾ (al-A'raf: 195), up to the end of the verse, which is the certainty of their incapacity to plot against him. So this is a justification for not being concerned about their conspiring against him and their seeking help from their partners, and for his confidence that he will be victorious over them, by what is indicated by the two imperatives of challenge (al-amr wa al-nahy al-ta'jiziyyan). The emphasis is to refute denial.

Al-waliyy means the helper and the sufficient one. It has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ (al-An'am: 14).

The attribute applied to the name of Allah in the form of a relative clause (al-mawsuliyya) indicates the relations of guardianship that the relative clause implies, for the revelation of the Book to him, while he was unlettered, is evidence of his being chosen and taken into His care.

The definite article in "al-Kitab" is for prior reference (al-ahd), meaning the Book that you know, that you have heard, and whose like you were unable to produce, which is the Qur'an, that is, the portion of it that had been revealed up to the time of the revelation of this verse.

The sentence ﴿and He takes care of the righteous﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridha), and the waw is parenthetical (waw i'tiradiyya).

The predicate being a present-tense verb (fi'l mudari') is intended to indicate the continuity and recurrence of this guardianship, and that it is a divine custom (sunnah ilahiyya): just as He took care of the Prophet, so too He takes care of the believers. This is good news to the Muslims who are upright upon the path of their Prophet (ﷺ), that Allah will help them just as He helped His Prophet and his allies.

The righteous (al-salihun) are those whose souls have been made upright through faith and righteous deeds.

The sentence ﴿Those you invoke besides Him﴾ is coordinated (atf) with the sentence ﴿Indeed, my protector is Allah﴾. The use of the relative construction in referring to the idols serves to draw attention to the error of the addressees in invoking them besides Allah, even though it is evident that they do not deserve worship, given their incapacity to help their followers or to help themselves. The discussion of ﴿cannot help you, nor can they help themselves﴾ is like the discussion of its counterpart mentioned just before.

It is repeated because here it is an address to the polytheists, whereas there it is a report about them addressed to the Prophet and the Muslims, and in order to make clear the contrast between the status of the protector of the believers and the condition of the protectors of the polytheists, and so that the proof may stand independently in both places, along with what the repetition yields of emphasis on its content.

[p. 224]

﴿Indeed, my protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He takes care of the righteous.﴾ ﴿Those you invoke besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ This is from what was commanded by His saying, and this sentence is separated from the sentence ﴿Call upon your partners﴾ (al-A'raf: 195) because it stands in the position of a reason for the content of the challenge in His saying ﴿Call upon your partners﴾ (al-A'raf: 195), up to the end of the verse, which is the certainty of their incapacity to plot against him. So this is a justification for not being concerned about their conspiring against him and their seeking help from their partners, and for his confidence that he will be victorious over them, by what is indicated by the two imperatives of challenge (al-amr wa al-nahy al-ta'jiziyyan). The emphasis is to refute denial.

Al-waliyy means the helper and the sufficient one. It has already been discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ (al-An'am: 14).
