[Page 225]

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not hear. And you see them looking at you, but they do not see.﴾

This is an attachment (ʿaṭf, coordination of clauses) to the clause ﴿Those whom you invoke besides Him are unable to help you﴾ [al-A'raf: 197], etc., meaning: Say to the polytheists: If you call those you invoke besides Allah to guidance, they will not hear.

The pronoun of the subject refers to the polytheists, and the object pronoun refers to those you invoke besides Him, i.e., the idols.

Guidance in this context is that which contains right direction and benefit for the one who is called. The mention of "to guidance" serves to establish that the idols do not hear and do not perceive, because the failure to hear a call to what benefits can only be due to a lack of perception.

For this reason, the wording here, "they will not hear," differs from his saying in the preceding verse, "they will not follow you," because following cannot come from idols, since neither literal walking (al-mashy al-haqiqi) nor figurative walking, meaning compliance (al-imtithal), can proceed from them.

The address in "and you see them" is to whoever is fit to be addressed, so it is a generic address (khitab ghayr al-muʿayyan). The meaning of "they look at you" is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh): you see them as if they were looking at you. This is because the images of many idols were in the forms of humans, and they carved for them the likes of seeing eyeballs that look at whoever stands before them. Al-Kashshaf says: "Because they fashioned their idols in the form of one who turns his eyeball toward a thing to look at it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 199:

﴿Take what is easy and forgiving, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾

This surah has fully treated the varied forms of warning and admonition directed at the polytheists, and the establishment of proof against them. It has urged them to reflect and consider the evidences of God's oneness, the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ), the guidance of His religion and His Book, and the exposure of the polytheists' misguidance and the corruption of their beliefs, along with the disparaging of their associates. All of this is interwoven to record their obstinacy and to express wonder at how they ride upon their own heads, how they turn away from their sides, how they deafen their ears and close their eyes to what they were called to hear and to consider. Their conditions have also been compared with those of the nations who denied before them, and who disbelieved God's blessing, so that there befell them what befell them of kinds of punishment. It has warned these people that the same will befall them as befell those. Then it declared their despair of ever returning to reason, and the waiting for the punishment that will strike them at the hands of the believers. It has also given firmness to the Messenger and the believers, brought them good tidings, and praised them for the guidance they possess. Thus in all of this there is a lesson for those who discern, a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and an honouring of their merit. Since this would naturally stir in the souls of the Muslims aversion towards the people of polytheism, and move them to take revenge upon them, to keep away from them, and to turn away from calling them to good, a new purpose was taken up, which serves as a conclusion to this wondrous discourse. This purpose is the command to the Messenger and the believers to pay little heed to the harshness and obstinacy of the polytheists, and to bear with them through forgiveness, and to persevere in striving to guide them and in conveying the message to them, by His saying: ﴿Take what is easy and forgiving, enjoin what is customary﴾, and so on, to the end of the verses.

The true meaning of "akhdh" (taking) is to seize something for the purpose of benefiting from it or harming it, as one says: "I seized the enemy by his collar." Hence the captive is called "akhidh," and when a people are taken prisoner it is said: "they were taken" (ukhidhu). Here it is used figuratively: it is borrowed for adopting a quality or an action from among other actions which one could have adopted. This adopting and choosing over another adoption is likened to taking one thing from among several things. Thus the meaning of "Take what is forgiving" is: act by it, make it your quality, and do not adopt its opposite. I consider that the metaphorical use of "taking" for "forgiveness" is one of the original usages of the Qur'an. For this reason I give preference to the view that the well-known line: "Take forgiveness from me, so that you may keep my affection, and do not speak in my anger when I am angry" belongs to Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, and that he followed the Qur'anic usage, and that its attribution to Asma' ibn Kharija al-Fazari or to Hatim al-Ta'i is not correct.

"Al-'Afw" is pardoning the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer and not holding him to account for his wrong. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what they should spend; say: the surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], and His saying: ﴿So pardon and overlook until God brings His command﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109], in Surat al-Baqarah. What is intended here is that which encompasses pardoning the polytheists and not holding them to account for their harshness and for their offence against the Messenger and the believers.

The verse has comprised all forms of forgiveness, because the definite article in "al-'afw" is the definite article of the genus, and so it conveys totality when no other meaning of reality or previous reference is suitable. Thus the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to pardon and overlook, which means not holding them to account for their harshness and bad conduct, so that he does not punish them nor repay them in kind, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them; had you been harsh and hard of heart, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. Nor does anything go outside this generality of the kinds, times and circumstances of forgiveness except what the legal evidences have excluded, such as pardoning the murderer who kills by treachery, and pardoning the violation of God's sacred prohibitions. The Messenger knows best the extent of what is particularized from this generality, and the Book and the Sunnah may clarify it. Whatever is analogous to that which has been clarified is attached to it. And in His saying ﴿and enjoin what is customary﴾ there is a great principle for the extent of restricting the command to forgiveness.

Then, the forgiveness of the polytheists intended here is the most readily apprehended of the individual instances of this generality, compared with the rest of them. The early scholars (al-salaf) understood nothing from the verse except the generality. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: 'Uyayna ibn Hisn came to Madinah and stayed with his nephew al-Hurr ibn Qays, and al-Hurr ibn Qays was among those whom 'Umar would bring close, and the reciters were the companions of 'Umar's gatherings and his consultations. 'Uyayna said to his nephew: "You have standing with this Commander, so ask permission for me to see him." Al-Hurr asked permission for 'Uyayna, and 'Umar granted him leave. When he entered upon him, he said: "Well, son of al-Khattab, you do not give us the abundance, nor do you judge between us with justice." 'Umar became angry until he was about to strike him. Al-Hurr said to him: "O Commander of the Believers, God said to His Prophet: Take what is forgiving, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant, and this man is of the ignorant." By God, 'Umar did not go beyond it once he had recited it to him, and he was one who stopped at the Book of God. And in it, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, he said: "God did not reveal that except concerning the character of people." As for the one who says that this verse was abrogated by the verses of fighting, he has erred, because forgiveness is a separate matter, and fighting has its own causes. Perhaps he intended by abrogation what includes the meaning of clarification or particularization in the terminology of the principles of jurisprudence.

"Al-'Urf" is a term synonymous with "al-ma'ruf" among deeds, and it is the act which souls recognise, meaning they do not reject it when left to themselves without having a motive for its opposite. Its synonymy with "al-ma'ruf" is shown by the saying of al-Nabigha: "Neither the rejected is known, nor is the recognised lost," so he contrasted "al-nukr" (the rejected) with "al-'urf" (the recognised). Its explanation has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Enjoining includes forbidding the opposite, for forbidding what is wrong is an enjoining of what is right, and enjoining what is right is a forbidding of what is wrong, because enjoining a thing is a forbidding of its opposite. Thus relying on enjoining the customary instead of forbidding the wrong is a form of conciseness. The reason why enjoining the customary alone is mentioned here is that it is the most important in calling the polytheists, because it calls them to the foundations of what is right one after another, as is recorded in the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, when the Prophet sent him to the people of Yemen: he commanded him to call them to the testimony that there is no god but God. Then he said: "If they obey you in that, inform them that God has enjoined upon them five prayers." Had the calling of the polytheists begun with forbidding the wrong, they would have fled, and the caller would have grown weary, because the wrongs are dominant among them and surround them. Included in enjoining the customary is being characterised by it and taking on its character, because it is the condition of one who enjoins something to be characterised by its like; otherwise he exposes himself to contempt. Moreover, the one who enjoins begins with himself, and so commands it, as Abu al-Aswad said:

O you who teaches others,
Why did you not teach yourself?

Furthermore, the Qur'anic address to people to command something counts as a command to the one addressed to do that thing; this is the question treated in the principles of jurisprudence, that commanding someone to command a thing is a command to that thing itself.

The definite article in "al-'urf," like that in "al-'afw," conveys totality.

The object of the command is omitted to convey the generality of those commanded. God calls to the Abode of Peace. He commanded His Messenger to command all people with every good and righteousness. Thus the polytheists enter this generality in the first place, because they are the cause of the command to this generality; that is, let not their turning away prevent you from repeatedly guiding them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾.

"Al-i'rad" (turning away) is turning the face away from looking at a thing, derived from "al-'arid," which is the cheek, for one who turns does not look at the thing. It has been explained in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He turned away and withdrew his side﴾ [al-Isra: 83]. Here it is used figuratively for not holding anyone to account for what displeases. It likens not holding someone to account for his action to not turning towards it, in that no consequence of knowing about it follows, since the nature of knowing it is that accountability should follow from it.

"Al-jahl" (ignorance) here is the opposite of forbearance and right judgment, and it is the most well-known use of "jahl" in the speech of the Arabs before Islam. So "al-jahilin" means all the foolish, because the definite article there conveys totality. The greatest ignorance is associating partners with God, for taking a stone as a god is a folly to which no other folly is equal. Then it includes every person of foolish opinion. Likewise, al-Hurr ibn Qays understood it in this sense in the report mentioned just above, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab confirmed him in that understanding.

This verse has gathered the noble qualities of character, because the excellent virtues of character are nothing other than pardoning an offence, which enters under "Take what is forgiving"; or overlooking what is displeasing, which enters under "turn away from the ignorant"; or doing good and being characterised by a virtue, which enters under "enjoin what is customary," as previously mentioned regarding the command to command a thing being a command to that thing. This is the meaning of the saying of Ja'far ibn Muhammad: "In this verse God commanded His Prophet with the noble qualities of character, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities of character than it. It is suitable that some of it explains the rest. For the command to take forgiveness is qualified by the obligation to enjoin the customary, and that applies to all rights that do not admit pardon and leniency; likewise, enjoining the customary is qualified by taking forgiveness, namely by calling people to good with gentleness and kindness."

[p. 230]

This command is primarily addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it includes his community (ummah) as well.

"Immā" here is "in" (the conditional particle) joined to the extra "mā" (which is added to some non-conditional words and turns them into conditional particles), as in "mahmā" (whatever), whose original form is "mā mā", and like "idhmā", "aynamā", "ayyānamā", "ḥaythumā", and "kayfamā". Since "mā" combined with a word that already indicates the condition gives it added conditional force, "immā" is written here as it is pronounced, and the "nūn" is not written separately from the "mā".

Al-nazgh (a prick or a jab; the term denotes pricking and piercing). This is how al-Zamakhsharī (in al-Kashshāf) explained it, and it is the correct view. Al-Rāghib and Ibn ʿAṭiyya, however, defined it as the entry of one thing into another with the aim of corrupting it. I say: close to this meaning is "al-faskh" with the letter sīn, which is piercing with a needle or similar tool for tattooing. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is rarely used except for the act of Satan," as in the verse ﴿After Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers﴾ [Yūsuf: 100].

The use of "al-nazgh" here for Satan's whispering is a metaphor: the occurrence of a satanic whisper in the soul is likened to the pricking of a needle or the like in the body, by the common feature of a hidden effect. This metaphor became widespread after the revelation of the Qur'an, until it became like a literal usage.

The meaning is: if Satan casts into you something that contradicts this command, by beautifying for you the taking of punishment, or by beautifying for you the abandonment of enjoining good upon them out of anger at them or despair of their guidance, then seek refuge in Allah from it, so that He may remove its distress from you and expand your breast to love acting upon what you have been commanded.

Al-isti'ādhah (seeking refuge) is the verbal noun of seeking al-ʿawdh, so the sīn and tāʾ in it indicate seeking. Al-ʿawdh is resorting to something that repels a harm from the one who resorts to it. It is said: "ʿādha bi-fulān" (he sought refuge with so-and-so), "ʿādha bi-l-ḥaram" (he sought refuge in the sanctuary), and "aʿādhahu" (he protected him) when he prevented him from the harm from which he sought refuge.

Allah therefore commanded the repelling of Satan's whispering by seeking refuge in Allah. Seeking refuge in Allah is resorting to Him through supplication for protection, or calling to mind what Allah has specified for him of the bounds of the Sharīʿah. This is a command to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to resort to Allah in what is difficult for him, for that is thankfulness for the blessing of prophethood and protection. Protection from sins was already his, but he thanks Allah by showing his need for Him, so that this protection may continue for him. This is like the seeking of forgiveness by the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, in his saying in the authentic hadith of Muslim: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, so I seek forgiveness from Allah more than seventy times a day." Satan does not despair of casting whispers to the prophets, because such whispering springs from his nature. He only watches for them at points where his intent is hidden, hoping for a slip from one of them, even though he knows that he cannot lead them astray. Yet he never gives up the hope of driving them to fall short in their ranks. When he does intend to whisper, they perceive it and repel it. Therefore Allah taught His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, to seek help in repelling it from Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated: "The Prophet ﷺ said: 'There is none among you but that a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him, and a companion from the angels.' They said: 'And you, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'And I, but Allah helped me against him, so he submitted (fa-aslama).'" The word "fa-aslama" has been narrated with a fatḥah on the mīm in the past tense form, with the hamzah being original: the devil accompanying him became a Muslim. This is a distinctive feature of the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been narrated with a ḍammah on the mīm in the present tense form, with the hamzah for the first person, meaning: "so I am safe from his whispering." I think the reason for the difference in the narration is that the Prophet ﷺ uttered it as a statement attributed to himself (mawqūf).

This command is general, encompassing the believers, and the believers' share of it is greater, because Satan's pricking of them is more frequent. The Prophet ﷺ is supported by infallibility, so Satan has no path over him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is in the position of the cause (ʿillah) for the command to seek refuge in Allah from Satan. This is the case with the particle "inna" when it comes in a context other than removing doubt or denial, since the Messenger ﷺ does not deny this and has no doubt about it. The intended meaning is causation through a necessary implication of this statement, namely his seeking refuge from what he has been commanded to seek refuge from. That is: We have commanded you to do this because it protects you from his whispering, since Allah is Hearing and Knowing.

"Al-Samīʿ" (the Hearing) means the one who knows what is heard. Here it is intended in its figurative sense, namely: He is Knowing of your supplication, responsive, and ready to answer the call, like the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb:

"The heart called me to her, and I am to its command *samīʿ* (obedient);
so I do not know whether her pursuit is right guidance."

That is, "obedient" (mumtathil). Thus the description "Samīʿ" is a metonymy for a promise of response.

Following it with the description "ʿAlīm" (Knowing) is an addition in the information about the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, regarding all states, because the description "Samīʿ" indicates that He knows the Messenger's, upon him be blessings and peace, seeking of refuge; then He followed it with what indicates the comprehensiveness of knowledge. It also points to the fact that the Messenger ﷺ is in the place of Allah's special care, exalted is He, so He knows what Satan intends against His servant. This is a metonymy for Allah's defense of His Messenger, like His saying ﴿for indeed you are within Our sight﴾. And His command to him to seek refuge is a pause at courtesy, thankfulness, and the manifestation of need for Allah, exalted is He.

[Page 232 marker: صفحة ٢٣٢]

This is an affirmation and confirmation of the command to seek refuge in Allah from Satan. The clause "Indeed, those who have feared Allah" (taqwa) and what follows function as a reason (ta'lil) for the command to seek refuge from Satan when one senses the prodding of Satan. For this reason it begins with *inna* (indeed), which here serves merely to express emphasis, not to remove doubt or denial, just as the preceding clause, "Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing," begins with it. The command to seek refuge is thus given two reasons. The first is that seeking refuge in Allah is a means of deliverance for the Messenger (ﷺ) from the prodding of Satan. The second is that seeking refuge in Allah from Satan involves remembering the duty to struggle against Satan and to be vigilant against his scheming, and that such vigilance is the practice of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). The Messenger (ﷺ) is therefore commanded to struggle against Satan, because he is among the God-fearing, and because he delights in following the conduct of his righteous predecessors, as Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90].

Here the reason is more general than the thing it explains, because remembrance is more general than seeking refuge.

Perhaps Allah reserved the distinctive feature of seeking refuge for this community. Thus the command to seek refuge from Satan is frequent in the Qur'an, and this practice is frequent in the sayings of the Prophet (ﷺ), whereas for those before them the command was to remember. Likewise, He reserved for us the Day of Friday.

The word "taqwa" (God-consciousness, fear of Allah) was explained earlier, at Allah's words ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah. Those intended by it are the messengers and the righteous among their communities, because the intention is to make them an example and a good model.

The word "mass" (al-massu) literally means placing the hand upon a body, and it is used figuratively for affliction or for the slightest affliction.

The "ta'if" is one who walks around a place awaiting permission to enter it; he is the one who arrives at a place before entering it. Here it is applied to the passing thought that comes to the soul and prompts it to do something Allah has forbidden. This thought, at the beginning of its circling in the soul, is likened to the visitation of the ta'if before it settles.

It was the custom of the Arabs that one who came to the people of a house, seeking the protection of the lord of the house and expecting hospitality, would seek companionship: he would circle the house and ask permission, as recorded in the story of al-Nabigha with al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir when he recited his verses, the first of which is: "Is the lord of the dome deaf, that he does not hear?"

This was already mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Fatihah. From the same practice comes the circumambulation (tawaf) of those arriving at Makkah around the Ka'bah, in imitation of those who come to kings. For this reason, tawaf was placed before all the rites, and the rites were also concluded with tawaf. Perhaps the word *ta'if* is used in the sense of a hidden, sudden visitation. Al-A'sha said: "She wakes after the fatigue of travel, as if a visitation of the jinn, a madman, had struck her." And Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Then a visitation from your Lord swept over it while they were asleep﴾ [al-Qalam: 19].

The reading of the majority is *ta'if*, with an alif after the ta' and a hamzah after the alif. The reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub is *taif*, without an alif after the ta' and with a silent yā' after the ta'. *Al-tayf* is the phantom that appears to you in sleep, and it is a common subject in poetry.

In the word *idha* (when/at once) in Allah's words ﴿when an impulse from Satan touches them﴾, together with the expression "touched them" (massahum), which indicates a contact that does not settle, there is an indication that turning to Allah for refuge from Satan should happen at the beginning, when the satanic thoughts first occur to the soul. For if those thoughts are left unchecked, they quickly become resolve, and then action.

The definite article in "Satan" (al-shaytan) may be a definite article of the category, meaning "from among the devils." It may also be a definite article of reference, meaning Iblis, on the basis that what his soldiers and followers whisper is issued by his command and authority.

Remembrance (tadhakkur) is calling to mind what is already known. The intended meaning is: they remember the commands and injunctions of Allah, as in His words ﴿and who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 135]. Remembrance also includes remembering the seeking of refuge for those among the earlier nations who were commanded to do it, if it was prescribed for them, and for this community. Thus following those who have feared Allah encompasses every state of remembering what is commanded.

The *fa* (then) indicates that seeing clearly follows from remembrance. The sense of immediate succession is emphasized by *idha* (at once) of suddenness, which indicates that what its clause describes occurs all at once, without delay. That is, they remembered with the resolve of people of determination, and their souls did not hesitate before the truth became clear to them, restraining them from acting on the satanic thoughts. So they turned away from those thoughts, held fast to the truth, and acted on what they had remembered. Thus, "then they are" steadfast upon their guidance and their God-consciousness.

Seeing (ibsar) is used figuratively for being guided, just as its opposite, blindness ('ama), is used for misguidance. The meaning is: then they are guided, saved from Satan's misleading, because Satan wanted to lead them astray, but they were spared from that. The Qur'an describes them with the active participle (ism al-fa'il, "those who see") rather than with a verb, to indicate that seeing is already established for them and is not something newly renewed. For this reason it reports about them with a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), which indicates permanence and stability.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 202:

﴿And their brothers keep them supplied in error; then they do not hold back.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, they remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 201], by way of coordinating an opposite with its opposite (ʿaṭf al-ḍidd ʿalā ḍiddihi). Opposition (al-ḍiddiyya) is a relation that makes it fitting to conjoin the state of one opposite to the other. So when He mentioned the condition of the God-conscious in repelling the phantoms of the devils, He mentioned the condition of their opposites among the people of polytheism and misguidance, just as the clause ﴿As for those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6] came after ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] and ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Zajjaj took it as a conjunction with the clause ﴿and they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 192], meaning: "and they keep them supplied in error." He intends that their associates do not benefit them, but rather harm them by increasing their error.

Al-ikhwan is the plural of akh (brother), on the pattern fiʿlān, like the plural of kharab (a male bustard), which is kharabān.

The literal meaning of akh is a partner in having the same mother and father, or in having one of them in common. The word akh is used figuratively for a loving friend, such as the Prophet's ﷺ pairing of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and Abu Bakr's words to the Prophet ﷺ when the Prophet proposed to Aisha: "I am only your brother." The Prophet ﷺ replied to him: "You are my brother, and she is lawful for me." The word akh is also used for a companion, as in their saying "akhu al-harb" (the brother of war), and for a constant follower, as in the words of ʿAbd Banī al-Hasḥās:

"Your brother, your client, your ally, and one who has lived among you and kept your company for an age."

He meant that he was their slave. It is also used for kinship and closeness, as in their saying "akhu al-ʿarab" (the brother of the Arabs) and "akhu Banī Fulān" (the brother of the Banu So-and-so).

So the pronoun in ﴿and their brothers﴾ refers to something not mentioned explicitly in the speech, since it cannot refer to the nearest preceding mention, which is "those who are mindful" (alladhina ittaqaw). The predicate ﴿keep them supplied in error﴾ cannot be connected to a pronoun referring to the God-conscious. Therefore the listener must seek a referent for the pronoun in ﴿and their brothers﴾ other than what is mentioned nearby. It is possible that the pronoun refers to something known from the context, namely the group spoken of in these verses, i.e., the polytheists referred to in His words ﴿Exalted is God above what they associate﴾ [al-A'raf: 190], ﴿Do they associate what creates nothing?﴾ [al-A'raf: 191], up to His words ﴿nor can they help them﴾ [al-A'raf: 192]. The listener then returns the pronoun to what the context indicates, by the evidence of a similar reference earlier in the discourse. For this reason al-Zajjaj said: "This verse is connected in meaning to His words ﴿nor can they help them, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 192]," meaning: "and the brothers of the polytheists," that is, their relatives and those of their tribe and religious community, as in His words ﴿and they said to their brothers when they went forth in the land﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]. The meaning is that the polytheists keep one another supplied in error and cooperate in it, so there is no deliverance for them from error.

It is also permissible that both pronouns refer to Satan mentioned just before, by considering the generic sense or the followers, as previously explained. The meaning then is "and the brothers of the devils," that is, their followers, as in His words ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra': 27]. As for the two pronouns in the nominative in His words ﴿they keep them supplied﴾ and ﴿they do not hold back﴾, they refer to what the pronoun of "their brothers" refers to, namely the devils. Most exegetes incline to this view. The meaning is: "and the brothers of the devils, the devils keep them supplied in error." So the clause ﴿keep them supplied﴾ is a predicate about "their brothers," and the predicate has been applied to someone other than its own subject, without the pronoun of the subject appearing in it, since no confusion is feared. This is like the verse of Yazid ibn Munqidh:

"They, when the horses wheel in their charges, are the cavalry horsemen, neither slight nor short."

Here the clause "wheel" (jalū) is a predicate about "the horses," and the pronoun of "wheel" refers to what the pronoun of "they" (hum) refers to, not to "the horses." And "cavalry horsemen" (fawāris) is the predicate of the plural pronoun.

It is also permissible that "the brothers" means allies, and that both pronouns refer to the polytheists too. The meaning is: "and the allies of the polytheists and their friends." Then "the brothers" would include the devils, as Qatadah explained, because if the polytheists are brothers of the devils, as is known, then the devils are brothers of the polytheists, since the relation of brotherhood requires two sides. It would also include the great leaders of the polytheists. The predicate then applies to its proper subject, and these meanings were all gathered in these verses by means of this wondrous arrangement.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read ﴿yumiddunahum﴾ with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the mīm, from al-imdād, which is strengthening something with a supply and reinforcement, as in His words ﴿He has supplied you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 133]. The rest of the readers read ﴿yamuddūnahum﴾ with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the mīm, from madda al-ḥabl yamudduhu, meaning he lengthened the rope. It is said madda lahu when he let out the rope for him, as in the saying "God extended your life" (madda Allah fī ʿumrik). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said in Kitab al-Hujja: "Most of what comes in the Revelation of the kind that is praised is with amdadtu on the pattern af'altu, as in His words ﴿that what We supply them with of wealth and sons﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55], ﴿and We supplied them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22], and ﴿Do you supply me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml: 36]; and what is contrary to this comes on the pattern madadtu. He, the Exalted, said ﴿and He lets them continue in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]." This indicates that the preferred form is the fatḥah on the yā', as the majority of readers held. As for the reading of whoever read ﴿yumiddunahum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā', it is like ﴿so give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34]: it is an ironic metaphor, and the indicator is His words ﴿in error﴾, just as the indicator in the other verse is His words "with a punishment."

You know that one of the two verbs occurring more often in one of the two senses does not require restricting its use to what is most commonly used with it among the eloquent. The reading of the majority, ﴿yamuddūnahum﴾ with a fatḥah on the letter of the present tense, requires that the verb "yamuddūnahum" be transitive to its object by means of the preposition lām, as one says madda lahu, but its transitivity without the preposition has become common by dropping the particle, as in His words ﴿and He lets them continue in their transgression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15], which has been treated in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ghayy is misguidance, which has been discussed above.

The "fī" in ﴿they keep them supplied in error﴾, according to the reading of Nafi' and Abu Ja'far, is a subordinate metaphor, by likening error to a place of fighting. As for the reading of the majority, the meaning is: "and their brothers extend the rope for them in error," from madd for a camel in length.

That is, they lengthen the tether for them in error, likening the state of those who go astray and increase in it to the state of livestock whose tether is lengthened in pasture. Error is that pasture. This is an image suitable for considering the dispersal of the comparison across the parts of a composite picture, which is the highest level of imagery. Close to this image is the verse of Tarafa:

"By your life, death has not missed the youth, like a long rope let out, with its coil in the hand."

On this pattern runs their saying: "God extended the life of so-and-so," or "his term," or "his lifetime."

Al-iqsar is refraining from an action while the one refraining is able to increase it.

"Thumma" (then) indicates sequence in rank: that is, and greater than the supplying of them in error is that they spare no effort in increasing them in seduction. Therefore you find their brothers the greatest of the misguided.

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not chosen one?" Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾

It is coordinated with the sentence ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. The connection is that this statement of theirs comes from their ignorance. The "sign" (ayah) may be understood as an extraordinary feat that breaks habitual custom, meaning that they are not content with the miracle of the Qur'an and so ask for signs of their own choosing, like their words: ﴿Cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾. This is the meaning I explained at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it﴾ [al-An'am: 109], in Surat al-An'am. This meaning is also reported from Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi.

It may also be that "sign" means a verse of the Qur'an, in which they propose praise for themselves and for their idols, as God said of them: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us said, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it"﴾ [Yunus: 15]. It is reported from Jabir ibn Zayd and Qatadah: when the revelation was delayed, the polytheists would say to the Prophet, "Why do you not bring a Qur'an from yourself?" They meant it as mockery.

"Law" (lawla) here is a particle of exhortation (tahdid), like "halla" (why not).

The word "ijtiba'" means choosing. The meaning is: "Why do you not choose a sign and ask your Lord to give it to you?" That is, "Why do you not bring us what we asked for, other than the sign of the Qur'an, so that God would answer you with what you chose?" Their aim in this is to set up proof that he is not what he claims to them, that he is the Messenger of God. This is part of the error that afflicts people of feeble minds in understanding things contrary to their realities, according to what they imagine for them and assume about them.

The answer the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to give is His saying, ﴿Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾ It is suitable for both meanings. "Following" (ittiba') is used in the sense of restricting oneself and stopping at the limit, that is, "I do not seek any sign other than what God has revealed to me." This is supported by the authentic hadith that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the prophets there was none to whom was given of signs what a human being could believe in because of it, but what I was given is a revelation that God revealed to me, so I hope that I will have the most followers on the Day of Resurrection."

The meaning may also be: "I only await what is revealed to me, and I do not hasten the descent of the Qur'an when its descent is delayed." In that case, "following" is related to time.

* * *

﴿This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾

This is a resumptive (isti'naf) sentence, beginning a statement that highlights the status of the Qur'an. It is detached from the quoted speech, to move from one topic to another, and serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) for the aims of the surah as a whole. The address is to the Muslims.

It may also be part of the speech that he was commanded to answer them with, in which case the address is to the polytheists. Then a transition (takhallus) occurs to mention the believers with His saying, ﴿and guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾.

The demonstrative "this" (hadha) refers to the Qur'an. It may also refer to what preceded in the surah, or to the last argument in it. The singular form of the demonstrative is used because the referent is interpreted as "the mentioned thing."

[Page 238]

"Basa'ir" is the plural of "basirah," which is that by which the truth becomes clear. This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There has certainly come to you insights from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104], in Surat al-An'am. This is a statement highlighting the status of the Qur'an and that it is better than the signs they ask for, because it combines the proof of the Messenger's truthfulness through the evidence of its inimitability (i'jaz), and its coming from an unlettered man, with guidance, teaching, direction, and endurance across the ages.

The plural "basa'ir" is used because the Qur'an contains kinds of guidance according to the aspects toward which it guides: illuminating the intellect in correcting belief, directing understanding of the religion, establishing laws for dealings and social relations among people, pointing to the paths of success and salvation in this world, and warning against the abysses of loss.

"Guidance" and "mercy" are used in the singular because they are general genera that include all kinds of insights. Guidance accompanies the insights, and mercy is the goal of the insights. Mercy here includes the mercy of this world, which is the stability of the affairs of the community and the orderliness of civic life, and the mercy of the Hereafter, which is attaining everlasting bliss, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

His saying "from your Lord" is both an encouragement for the believers and a warning for the disbelievers.

"For a people who believe" is connected to "insights," "guidance," and "mercy," because only believers benefit from it. The meaning is: "This is insights for you and for the believers, and guidance and mercy specifically for a people who believe," since they are the ones who have been guided. This is an indirect implication that those who do not believe are not fit to benefit from it, and that they have turned away from its guidance by seeking extraordinary feats of habitual custom.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 7, verse 204:

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it attentively and remain silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾

The conjunction (al-'atf) indicates that the address in the command "listen attentively" (fastami'u), and in ﴿remain silent﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], and in the phrase "that you may" (la'allakum), follows the address in ﴿This is insights from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 203], and so on. Thus the statement ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited﴾ is part of what the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to say to them. This is a renewed reminder to the polytheists, explicitly or allusively, not to turn away from listening to the Qur'an, and to reflect upon it so that they may know that it is a great sign, and that it is insights, guidance and mercy for whoever believes in it and does not obstinately oppose it. It is already known from the circumstances of the polytheists that they used to forbid one another from listening silently to the Qur'an: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome."﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

[p. 239]

The mention of the name "the Qur'an" is an explicit noun in the place where a pronoun would be expected (idhar fi maqam al-idmar), because the Qur'an had already been mentioned through the demonstrative pronoun. The purpose of this explicit mention is to draw attention to this matter, and to make its sentence independent in its indication, not dependent on anything else. This is among the aspects of giving importance to speech, and among the reasons for using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, which I have inferred from the speech of the eloquent.

Listening (al-istima') is attentive hearing. The form of the verb with the infix (sigha al-ifti'al) indicates intensification of the action. Listening silently (al-insat) is listening together with abstaining from speech. Thus this is an emphasis of "do not listen" with an added meaning, and it is the counterpart of their saying: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it." It is also possible that "listening" is used in its figurative meaning, which is acting upon what is in it, as previously mentioned in His words ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear﴾ [al-A'raf: 198]. In that case, "remaining silent" comprises both attentive listening and the abandonment of idle talk.

This address includes the disbelievers in the sense of conveying the message, and the Muslims in the sense of guidance, because they are more hopeful of benefiting from its guidance. This is because before it is His words ﴿guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾ [al-A'raf: 203].

There is no doubt that this verse was revealed together with the verses preceding it and in accordance with their context, whether the pronoun of address in it is understood to refer to the polytheists and Muslims together, or to the Muslims explicitly and the polytheists allusively, or to the polytheists for the purpose of guidance and the Muslims with greater priority because of their increased receptivity.

Thus the listening and silent attention commanded are what lead the hearer to reflection and inference, and to being guided by what the Qur'an contains of evidence for the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), which leads to belief in him, and by what he brought of the reform of souls. Therefore the command to listen is intended for conveying the message, and for calling for reflection and acting upon what is in it. Listening and silent attention are thus degrees, according to the degrees of the listeners.

This verse is general in its meaning regarding listening and silent attention, and regarding what the command ﴿listen to it attentively and remain silent﴾ requires. The context of the speech and the interpretation in light of its occasion of revelation, from His words, exalted is He, ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it"﴾ [Fussilat: 26], clarify part of its generality, and its clarification beyond that is referred to other evidences. The scholars of the Community have agreed that the apparent meaning of the verse, taken by itself, is in many cases to be interpreted, so none of them says that

[p. 240]

every Muslim who hears someone reciting the Qur'an must occupy himself with listening and remain silent. This is because the reciter may be reciting in the presence of a craftsman at his work; if listening were obligatory, he would be commanded to abandon his work. However, they differed regarding the scope of its interpretation. Some of them restricted it to a specific occasion which they considered to be its occasion of revelation, so they related from Abu Hurayrah that it was revealed concerning the recitation of the imam in audible prayer. Some of them narrated that a man from the Ansar prayed behind the Prophet (ﷺ) in an audible prayer, and he was reciting during the prayer while the Prophet (ﷺ) was reciting, so this verse was revealed, concerning the command to people to listen to the recitation of the imam. These scholars restricted the command to listen to a specific recitation indicated by the occasion of revelation as they understood it, in a manner close to specifying the general by the particular cause, according to those who hold such specification. This is a weak interpretation, because the revelation of the verse for this cause is not authentically established, nor does the composition of the verses surrounding it support it. What they stated on this is only an explanation and interpretation, and there is nothing transmitted on it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Others kept the command to listen in its absolute sense, close to generality, but they interpreted it as a command of recommendation (nadb). This is what is understood from the statements of the Maliki jurists. Yet if they had said that by "is recited" is meant a specific recitation, namely that the Messenger, peace be upon him, recites it to the people so that they may know what is in it and act upon it, whether disbeliever or Muslim, that would have been a better interpretation.

In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "The polytheists used to come to the Messenger of Allah when he prayed, and some of them would say to others: 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed in answer to them: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it attentively and remain silent.﴾"

Yet what has preceded of the reports concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is not sound, because the verse is Meccan, while those events occurred in Medina. As for the argument of the followers of Abu Hanifah for abandoning the recitation by the follower (ma'mum) when the imam recites silently, the verse has no bearing on it, since in that abandonment the meaning of silent attention is not realized.

It must be noted that there is no formula of general expression (sigha min siyagh al-'umum) in the verse, because what it contains are two verbs, "is recited" and "listen," and a verb has no generality in affirmation.

The conditional meaning derived from "idha" (when) necessitates the generality of circumstances or times, but not of recitations. The generality of times or circumstances does not entail the generality of persons, though the reverse holds, as is clear.

Address to the Prophet ﷺ concerning matters specific to him, after he was commanded to convey the preceding verses. The connection in this transition is that commanding people to listen to the Qur'an entails commanding the Messenger, peace be upon him, to recite the Qur'an to them audibly so that they hear it. When the discourse finished with the share of the people in the Messenger's recitation, it turned to the discourse on the Messenger's own share of the Qur'an and other matters, namely the remembrance specific to him. He was commanded to remember God as much as he is able, in whatever manner is possible for him, and at the different times of the day. Thus the clause ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ is conjoined to the preceding clauses from His saying ﴿Indeed, my guardian is God﴾ [al-A'raf: 196] up to here.

"Nafs" (self, soul) is a noun for the power by which life exists, so it is synonymous with "rūḥ" (spirit). It is also applied to the whole being composed of body and spirit. Because the seat of the nafs is in the inner part of a person, it is applied to the inner matters of a person, such as perception and intellect, as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting Jesus: ﴿You know what is in my nafs﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], which has passed in Surat al-Ma'idah. From this it extends to its application to a person's innermost self. From this is the saying in the sacred hadith (ḥadīth qudsī) in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: "And if he remembers Me in his nafs, I remember him in My nafs, and if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than them." So He contrasted His saying "in his nafs" with His saying "in an assembly."

The meaning: remember your Lord while you are in your solitude just as you remember Him in the gatherings of people.

Remembrance (dhikr) is literally the remembrance of the tongue, and this is what is intended here. It is reinforced by His saying ﴿and below the loudness of speech﴾. That includes the recitation of the Qur'an and other speech in which there is glorification of God, thanksgiving to Him, and the like, such as the word of tawḥīd (monotheism), ḥawqala (saying "there is no power and no strength except in God"), tasbīḥ (glorifying God), takbīr (proclaiming God's greatness), supplication, and the like.

"Taḍarru'" is humbling oneself. Since humbling oneself entails addressing with a raised voice according to the custom of the Arabs, he used taḍarru' as a metonym (kināya) for raising the voice, intending both its original meaning and its figurative meaning.

[Page 242]
For this reason it was contrasted with secrecy (khufya) in His saying ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ [al-A'raf: 55] at the beginning of this surah, which has passed.

Here taḍarru' is contrasted with khīfa, which is the verbal noun of fear (khawf). It is one of the nouns that came in the pattern of a state (hay'a), but the intended meaning is not the state, as in "shidda" (intensity). Since fear (khīfa) is an emotional response that a person finds within his own self, it entails speaking in a low voice for fear that someone he fears might notice him. Therefore it is used here as a metonym for speaking quietly out of fear of God. Its contrast with taḍarru' is an antithesis (ṭibāq) in the explicit meanings of the two words and their metonymic meanings. It is as if it were said: "humbly and openly, and in fear and in secrecy."

His saying ﴿and below the loudness of speech﴾ is the counterpart of each of taḍarru' and khīfa. It is the remembrance that lies between loudness and secrecy. The purpose of this is to encompass all states of remembrance by the tongue, because the soul may be more inclined to some of them than to others.

"Al-ghudw" is a noun for the time of morning, which is the first half of the day.

"Al-āṣāl" is the plural of "aṣīl," which is the afternoon, the second half of the day up to sunset.

The intention is to encompass the parts of the day according to what is customary. As for the night, it is the time of sleep, and the periods in which one is awake were singled out with a specific command, such as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]. Yet these are included in the generality of His saying ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾.

His saying ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾ indicates a warning against heedlessness regarding the remembrance of God, and there is no limit to heedlessness. It is delimited by the state of the Messenger ﷺ, and he knows himself best, for he has times in which he receives revelation and times for natural matters such as eating.

This command is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Whatever is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, of obligation, it is recommended for his community to follow him in it, except what they were forbidden from, such as continuous fasting (wiṣāl) in fasting.

It has been mentioned before that a phrase like ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾ is stronger in negation and in prohibition than a phrase like "do not be heedless," because it presupposes a group to whom the description of "the heedless" truly applies, so he is warned against being in their company. This is clearer for the state that is being forbidden.

[p. 243]

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.﴾

This serves as the reason (ʿillah) for the command to remember God. For this reason it is introduced by *inna* (indeed), which here is used merely to emphasise the report and not to dispel doubt or denial, since the addressee is too exalted to doubt God's report. In such a context the emphatic particle functions as the *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafrī'*) and conveys causation, as has been explained more than once before. The meaning is an exhortation to repeat the remembrance of God in all circumstances, because the Muslims are commanded to emulate the people of perfection among the exalted angels. There is also an implicit reproach to the polytheists who disdain the worship of God, that they are lowly compared to those ranks.

By ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾ is meant the angels. The reason for making the state of the angels the cause of the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to remember God is that the station of prophethood raises its bearer, from among humans, to the rank of the angels. Thus this causal clause is as if one were to say: "Remember your Lord, for remembrance is the practice of your kind," like the saying of Ibn Dārah, Sālim ibn Musāfiʿ:

*"If you fear evil, then [others] like you have feared it; and if you do good, then [others] like you have done it."*

This causal clause does not imply that the angels are superior to the messengers, as the Muʿtazilah (a rationalist theological school) imagine. The resemblance to the angels is in respect of their having preceded in this quality, since it is innate in them; thus they are exemplars in it. There is no doubt that a group who were not created with what the angels were created with, but who adopt the character of the angels, their elevation to that rank is more remarkable, and their deserving thanks and grace from Him is more fitting.

The reason for shifting from the word "angels" to the relative construction is what the relative clause indicates of the exalted rank of those beings, so that this serves as a means to stir rivalry in acquiring their qualities.

*ʿInda* ("with") is used figuratively for elevation of rank and divine favour.

His saying ﴿they do not disdain His worship﴾ is not intended to extol the status of the angels, for extolling them would be by something better than that. Rather, it is intended as an implicit reproach to the polytheists, and that they are the opposite of the states of the angels brought near, so it is fitting for them to be far from the stations of exaltation.

[p. 244]

The intended point is His saying "and they glorify Him," that is, they declare Him free of deficiency in word and belief. This clause is the one truly intended by the causal statement for the command to remember God.

The choice of the present tense form is because it indicates renewal and continuity, or because it is what is intended. The fronting of the complement in His saying ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾ serves to indicate exclusivity, meaning: they do not prostrate to anyone else. This too is an implicit reproach to the polytheists who prostrate to others. The present tense also indicates continuity.

Here is a place of prostration among the prostrations of the Qur'an, and it is the first of them in the order of the codices. There is agreement among the scholars of the Community that prostration is due here. What the prostration here implies is that the verse came to urge adopting the character of the angels in remembrance. When it reported a state of theirs in exalting God, namely prostration to God, the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) wished to hasten to resemble them, realising the purpose for which this report was given.

Also, before this there had been mention of the polytheists' demand that the Prophet (ﷺ) bring them a sign as they proposed. God said to him: ﴿Say: I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 203], and that he should command them to listen to the Qur'an. Since it mentioned that the angels prostrate to God, God legislated a prostration at this verse, so that the faith of the believers in the Qur'an would be manifest, and the denial of the unbelievers would be manifest, when the believers prostrate and the polytheists who attend the gatherings where the Qur'an is revealed refrain.

The survey of the positions of the Qur'an's prostrations shows that they serve no other purpose than to enrage the polytheists, or to follow the prophets and messengers. As Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding the prostration in ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, and fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Ṣād: 24], that God, Exalted, said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-Anʿām: 90]. David is among those whom Muhammad (ﷺ) was commanded to follow.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Sūrat al-Anfāl

It has been known by this name since the time of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Al-Wāḥidī narrated in *Asbāb al-Nuzūl* (Occasions of Revelation), on the authority of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who said: "When the day of Badr came, my brother ʿUmayr was killed, and I killed Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣī, and I took his sword and brought it to the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: 'Go away, to the *qabaḍ*' (with two fatḥahs, the place where the spoils are gathered). So I returned, with what none knows but God: my brother was killed and my spoils were taken. I had not gone far when the sūrah of al-Anfāl was revealed."

Al-Bukhārī also reported, on the authority of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: "I said to Ibn ʿAbbās: 'Sūrat al-Anfāl?' He said: 'It was revealed concerning Badr.'" By the name al-Anfāl it became known among the Muslims, and by it its title was written in the codex when the titles of the sūrahs were written in the time of al-Ḥajjāj. No hadith has been established concerning its naming. Its being called Sūrat al-Anfāl is either because it opens with a verse containing the word *al-anfāl*, or because the ruling on *al-anfāl* (the bonus spoils) is mentioned in it, as will come.

It is also called "the Sūrah of Badr." In *al-Itqān* (by al-Suyūṭī), Abū al-Shaykh reported on the authority of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: "I said to Ibn ʿAbbās: 'Sūrat al-Anfāl?' He said: 'That is the Sūrah of Badr.'"

All the transmitters of reports agree that it was revealed concerning the battle of Badr. Ibn Isḥāq said: "The sūrah of al-Anfāl in its entirety was revealed concerning the affair of Badr." The battle of Badr took place in Ramaḍān of the second year after the Hijrah, after a year and a half from the day of the Hijrah, and that was two months after the change of the qiblah. The beginning of its revelation was before the departure from Badr, for the first verse of it was revealed while the Muslims were at Badr, before the division of its spoils, as the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ indicates. The apparent view is that its revelation continued until after the departure from Badr.

In the statements of the authorities on the occasions of revelation there is something indicating that the verse ﴿Now God has lightened your burden and knows that among you is weakness, so if there are a hundred steadfast ones...﴾ was revealed a long time after the revelation of the sūrah, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. Its verification will come there.

[p. 246]

A group of exegetes said: the verses from ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfāl: 64] to ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾ [al-Anfāl: 65] were revealed in al-Bayḍāʾ during the battle of Badr, before the start of fighting. Thus that verse would have been revealed before the beginning of the sūrah.

This sūrah was revealed after the sūrah of al-Baqarah. It was then said that it is the second in revelation in Medina. It was also said that al-Baqarah was revealed, then Āl ʿImrān, then al-Anfāl. The more correct view is that it is the second of the sūrahs in Medina in revelation, after al-Baqarah.

I have explained in the *Muqaddimāt* (introductions) that the revelation of one sūrah after another does not imply that the following one was revealed after the completion of the revelation of the one before it. Rather, the revelation of a sūrah may begin before the completion of a sūrah whose revelation began earlier. Perhaps the sūrah of al-Anfāl was completed before the completion of the revelation of the sūrah of al-Baqarah, because the rulings contained in al-Anfāl are of one kind, namely the rulings on spoils and fighting, whereas the rulings of al-Baqarah are of many varied kinds, including rulings on social transactions. It is possible that al-Baqarah was revealed shortly after Āl ʿImrān, and shortly after the revelation of Āl ʿImrān al-Anfāl was revealed. So the beginning of the revelation of al-Anfāl came before the completion of the revelation of al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān.

In the *Tafsīr* of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfāl: 33] from this sūrah, a group said: this whole verse was revealed in Mecca. Ibn Abzá said: His saying ﴿God would not punish them﴾ [al-Anfāl: 33] was revealed in Mecca following their saying ﴿or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfāl: 32]. And His saying ﴿God would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ [al-Anfāl: 33] was revealed when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) left for Medina, while there remained believers in Mecca who were seeking forgiveness. And His saying ﴿What is it with them that God should not punish them?﴾ [al-Anfāl: 34] was revealed after Badr.

This sūrah was counted as the eighty-ninth in the enumeration of the revelation of the sūiras of the Qur'an, in the narration of Jābir ibn Zayd from Ibn ʿAbbās, and that it was revealed after the sūrah of Āl ʿImrān and before the sūrah of al-Aḥzāb.

The number of its verses, according to the counting of the people of Medina, the people of Mecca, and the people of Basra, is seventy-six. According to the counting of the people of Syria, it is seventy-seven, and according to the counting of the people of Kufa, it is seventy-five.

Its revelation was occasioned by the dispute among the people of Badr over the spoils of the day of Badr and its bonus portions. It was also said that it was occasioned by some of the fighters asking the Prophet (ﷺ) to give them from the *anfāl*, as will come at the explanation of its first verse.

* * *

[p. 247]

The aims of this sūrah:

It opens by clarifying the rulings on *al-anfāl*, which are the spoils, their division, and their allocations.

And the command to fear God in this and other matters.

And the command to obey God and His Messenger, in the matter of the spoils and other things.

And the command to the Muslims to set right their mutual relations, and that this is among the constituents of the meaning of complete faith.

And the mention of the going out to the battle of Badr, and their fear of the great number of their enemy, and what they encountered in it of victory and support from God and His kindness towards them.

And God's favour upon them in making them strong.

And the promise to them of victory and guidance if they fear God, by standing firm against the enemy and by patience.

And the command to prepare for war against the enemies.

And the command to unity of word and the prohibition of disputing.

And the command that the intention in seeking victory be for the religion, set before their eyes.

And the description of the cause that brought the Muslims out to Badr.

And the mention of the positions of the two armies, and the descriptions of what took place in the fighting.

And the reminder to the Prophet (ﷺ) of God's favour upon him, when He saved him from the plotting of the polytheists against him in Mecca and delivered him from their obstinacy, and that his residence in Mecca had been a security for its people; so when he left them, the punishment of this world became due to them for what they had committed of barring from the Sacred Mosque.

And the call to the polytheists to cease opposing Islam, and their being notified of war.

And the warning against the hypocrites.

And the setting forth of examples from past nations who opposed the messengers of God and did not give thanks for God's favour.

And the rulings on the covenant between the Muslims and the unbelievers, and what follows from their breaking the covenant, and when peace is good.

And the rulings on prisoners.

And the rulings on the Muslims who stayed behind in Mecca after the Hijrah, their guardianship, and what follows from that guardianship.
